title: ExplicitIR: Explicit Spatial Policy Fields for All-in-One Image Restoration
abstract: All-in-one image restoration aims to recover clean images blindly from inputs with various degradation types and levels using a single model. However, the adaptation policy in most existing methods remains implicitly encoded in feature representations, leaving the restoration decision neither explicitly represented nor independently controllable. Since real-world degradations vary spatially, applying uniform updates across the entire image leads to over-smoothing of clean areas and under-correction of localized degradations. To address these limitations, we present ExplicitIR, which represents the restoration policy as two explicit per-pixel fields: Budget, which determines where and how strongly to update, and Style, which selects between narrow and wide context windows. Specifically, ExplicitIR incorporates a Spatial Policy Estimator (SPE) to predict these fields, explicitly representing the restoration policy and capturing spatially-varying degradations, which are then applied by Policy-Adaptive Decoder Blocks (PADB) through adaptive fusion of narrow- and wide-window responses, enabling independent control and precise local modulation. This design enables spatially-adaptive restoration in a single forward pass, without requiring task labels, prompts, or test-time degradation estimators. Extensive experiments on three-task and five-task benchmarks demonstrate that ExplicitIR achieves performance competitive with the strongest all-in-one baselines.

title: Safely Mitigating Grid Imbalance: A Hybrid Distributional Wide-Margin Recourse Approach
abstract: This paper proposes the Multi-Agent Distributional Wide-Margin Policy Gradient (MADWMPG) framework: a dual-policy hybrid imitation and safe reinforcement learning (IL-SRL) method designed for safely mitigating grid imbalance in multiphase active distribution networks with distributed soft open points (SOPs). The framework comprises a wide-margin constraint barrier recourse (WCBR) module that seeks the maximal separation of constraint-compliant and unsafe actions and learns to proactively suppress exploratory violations. The framework addresses operational volatility using a novel adaptation of noncrossing quantile regression (NQR) distributional critics that track the complete distribution of policy returns. The set of behavior and recourse policies integrates an instantaneous physics-based and differentiable action projection mechanism that generates SOP constraint-compliant actions without relying on active learning. Policy safety is made responsive using an enhancement of conventional experience replay, and the safety performance of the framework is supported by probabilistic bounds derived in the paper. The proposed framework was trained and tested on a modified multiphase IEEE 123-bus test feeder. Results demonstrate its superiority to conventional reinforcement learning and SRL methods and show that it is highly competitive against the nonlinear AC optimal power flow.

title: Fine-Grained Japanese Clinical Named Entity Recognition: A Controlled Comparison of BERT and Open-Weight Large Language Models
abstract: Background: Generative large language models (LLMs) offer an alternative to encoder-based clinical named entity recognition (NER), but their performance on fine-grained Japanese extraction tasks and sensitivity to generation settings remain uncertain. Methods: We compared two fine-tuned BERT-CRF baselines with nine open-weight LLMs on iCorpus, which defines 113 entity categories. The evaluation used 433 sentences from 36 test documents; 1,672 sentences were used for training. LLMs were evaluated using zero-shot prompting with and without JSON Schema constraints and three-seed QLoRA fine-tuning. Fine-tuned models were assessed under different output-token limits, including 900 and larger model-specific limits of 2,600 or 4,096 tokens. Performance was measured using sentence-level label-surface matching with relaxed and exact-surface F1. Results: The highest zero-shot relaxed F1 was 0.337, compared with 0.836-0.841 for the BERT baselines. At the larger output limits, all eight fine-tuned LLMs with at least 13B total parameters exceeded both BERT baselines (relaxed F1, 0.882-0.914; exact-surface F1, 0.840-0.880). Across three-seed means, increasing the output limit improved relaxed F1 by 0.052-0.085, alongside higher recall and fewer length-limited outputs. JSON Schema constraints changed relaxed F1 by -0.014 to +0.008 among seven models outside the two reasoning-oriented configurations, while medical-general model pairs showed no consistent advantage for medical specialization. Conclusions: On this historical Japanese case-report benchmark, task-specific fine-tuning combined with adequate generation capacity was associated with stronger LLM extraction performance. Output-token limits materially affected comparisons with BERT, whereas enforcing output structure alone did not overcome low zero-shot accuracy.
authors: Feng Han;Ayako Yagahara;Kenji Hirata;Atsushi Yoshida;Kohsuke Kudo
comment: 33 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables; includes appendices with supplementary tables and one supplementary figure

title: Learning Optimal Transport Plans Via Autoregressive Token Regression
abstract: Optimal Transport (OT) provides a principled framework for finding the minimum cost coupling between probability distributions. Classical solvers remain the gold standard for this task. At the same time, OT is an ideal testbed for studying whether learning-based amortized models can internalize the structure of OT type problems. Here, ground-truth solutions are available and marginal constraints are explicitly defined. Also, exact discrete solutions have well-characterized sparsity. We describe ToR-OT, a transformer-based model that learns to predict discrete OT plans through autoregressive token regression. We reframe OT into a structured sequence generation task. ToR-OT decodes sparse transport plans as sequences instead of solving an optimization task at test time. We focus on three properties: (a) Zero-shot generalization: pretraining on a large synthetic corpus of OT instances allows a single model to generalize to unseen distribution pairs and heterogeneous cost metrics without retraining, (b) Sparse primal decoding: by exploiting the inherent sparsity in exact discrete OT solutions, the decoder predicts only nonzero entries (avoids dense coupling outputs), (c) Amortized inference: on low-dimensional discrete problems, ToR-OT gives accurate approximate plans and compares favorably with per-instance neural OT baselines. Overall, ToR-OT is not yet a replacement for classical solvers, but a step toward understanding how autoregressive transformers can learn structure of constrained optimization problems like OT.
authors: Ivan Jaen Marquez;Sotirios Panagiotis Chytas;Vikas Singh

title: Communicate the Change: Efficient Expert Parallelism via Activation Compression
abstract: Scaling has driven the success of large language models (LLM), with sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures enabling greater parameter capacity without a proportional increase in computation. At large scales, MoE models rely on expert parallelism to distribute experts across devices. Each MoE layer requires two synchronous collective communication steps during inference: dispatching hidden states to the activated experts and combining the resulting expert outputs. As compute throughput has outpaced interconnect bandwidth, these synchronous collectives have become a major bottleneck to MoE scaling and efficiency. We address this challenge with EchoMoE, a lightweight architecture modification that retrofits existing MoE models, requiring approximately 8,500x fewer training tokens than full pretraining. Motivated by the observation that transformer blocks update the residual stream incrementally, we use a hidden state from an earlier layer as a reference and communicate only the compressed difference between it and the current state, rather than communicating each hidden state in full. EchoMoE periodically refreshes these reference states and transmits only the compressed differences synchronously, reducing the traffic on latency-critical paths without significant computational overhead. EchoMoE reduces inter-node communication volume by 58% and improves throughput by 22.6%, while preserving average performance within 3.8 percentage points across 18 benchmarks. EchoMoE further improves inference throughput by up to 2.38x over bandwidth-constrained Ethernet, paving the way for wide-area distributed inference. EchoMoE also tolerates quantization of the communicated representations without measurable quality loss. We release an efficient implementation for applying EchoMoE to pretrained MoE models, together with an inference integration for vLLM.

title: Joint-ID: Transformer-based Joint Image Enhancement and Depth Estimation for Underwater Environments
abstract: Underwater imaging is a challenging task due to factors such as scattering, absorption, and turbulence, which degrade image quality and limit visibility. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for enhancing underwater images that leverages the benefits of joint learning for simultaneous image enhancement and depth estimation. We introduce Joint-ID, a transformer-based neural network that can obtain high-perceptual image quality and depth information from raw underwater images. Our approach formulates a multi-modal objective function that addresses invalid depth, lack of sharpness, and image degradation based on color and local texture. We design an end-to-end training pipeline that enables joint restoration and depth estimation in a shared hierarchical feature space. Additionally, we propose a synthetic dataset with various distortions and scene depths for multi-task learning. We evaluate Joint-ID on synthetic and standard datasets, as well as real underwater images with diverse spectra and harsh turbidity, demonstrating its effectiveness for underwater image enhancement and depth estimation. Furthermore, we demonstrate the ability of Joint-ID to perform feature matching and saliency detection for visually guided underwater robots. Our proposed method has the potential to improve the visual perception of underwater environments and benefit applications such as oceanography and underwater robotics. title: Emergence and Persistence of Maximal Atom-Field Entanglement in the Jaynes-Cummings model
abstract: We investigate the emergence and persistence of maximal entanglement between a two-level atom and a single-mode quantized electromagnetic field inside a cavity, whose dynamics are governed by the Jaynes-Cummings Hamiltonian. Using the von Neumann entropy as a measure of entanglement, we establish a direct connection between entanglement, atomic coherence, and atomic population inversion. This establishment shows that maximal atom-field entanglement is achieved when both the atomic population inversion and the $l_1$-norm of atomic coherence simultaneously vanish. By considering the atom initially in its excited state, we further demonstrate that the persistence of maximal atom-field entanglement strongly depends on the initial state of the field. For field states whose photon-number distributions have no two consecutive occupied photon-number levels, the local atomic coherence remains zero throughout the evolution. Consequently, complete collapse of the atomic population inversion for an extended period leads to persistent maximal atom-field entanglement. In contrast, for other field states, the interaction generates local atomic coherence, resulting in transient maximal entanglement. Our results demonstrate how the choice of the initial field state controls the temporal characteristics of entanglement in the Jaynes-Cummings system. The generation and persistence of maximal atom-field entanglement in such systems could be valuable for applications in quantum information processing.
authors: Siva Prasanna Karri;Mounika Sri Gudipati;Nilakantha Meher

title: Sample-efficient Personalization of Large Language Model Alignment with Multidimensional User Preference Data
abstract: Preference alignment has become a central tool to align large language models (LLMs) with human values and desired behavior, and its online variant can further advance their capabilities beyond what static data alone offer by repeatedly generating and labeling new responses with human feedback. But costly, time-consuming annotations limit its scalability, making sample efficiency essential, and existing methods typically seek to improve it by expanding coverage of the response space or selecting pairs with the highest uncertainty for comparison. Although they are effective, these methods quantify uncertainty from the perspective of the LLM, which may differ from the uncertainty perceived by the user: a pair can appear highly uncertain to the LLM even when past comparisons from the user already imply a clear ordering. In this paper, we propose multidimensional preference-guided online direct preference optimization (MPG-DPO), which leverages low-cost multidimensional evaluations from automated verifiers on the user historical comparisons to construct a personalized preference cone guiding response selection for online preference alignment. Specifically, it first discards responses that are confidently dominated under the estimated user preference, then selects two responses that are competitive under the retained preference cone yet exhibit the strongest unresolved disagreement. Theoretical analysis shows that, with high probability, the fraction of queries spent on cone-dominated responses vanishes as learning progresses. Experiments across multiple LLM families show that MPG-DPO outperforms strong contenders under matched query budgets.
authors: Zhen-Yu Zhang;Jerry Huang;Gang Niu;Takashi Ishida;Masashi Sugiyama

title: A Study of the PDE Model for the Anisotropic Consensus-Based Optimization
abstract: We investigate the nonlinear Fokker--Planck equation associated with anisotropic consensus-based optimization. Under suitable assumptions on the objective function, we establish global existence and uniqueness of density valued weak solutions for bounded initial probability densities with finite fourth moment. The main analytical challenge arises from the component-wise degeneracy of the diffusion, which vanishes along moving coordinate hyperplanes determined by the weighted consensus point. To overcome this difficulty, we develop spatial translation estimates based on weighted gradient bounds and uniform density estimates. Combined with temporal translation and moment estimates, these yield strong compactness in $L^2((0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^d)$ through the Fréchet--Kolmogorov compactness criterion, enabling passage to the limit in the regularized equations. Uniqueness is established through the associated McKean--Vlasov stochastic differential equation and Wasserstein stability of the weighted consensus point. Furthermore, we prove the propagation of $H^2$-regularity for sufficiently regular initial data.

title: ARG-Avatar: Animation-Rendering Guidance for Efficient Feedforward Avatar Reconstruction
abstract: Reconstructing animatable 3D human avatars from images is important for applications such as gaming and augmented reality. Feedforward methods make avatar reconstruction accessible by reducing inference time to a few seconds, but recent approaches rely heavily on scaling model capacity, training data, and computation. We ask whether such scaling is necessary. To this end, we introduce ARG-Avatar, an efficient feedforward framework with only 68M trainable parameters that achieves SOTA reconstruction quality. Our key insight is that 3D animation and rendering already provide strong geometric correspondences that existing methods largely attempt to learn from data. In light of this, we design the Foreground Avatar Coordinate RoPE attention (FACRoPE) and Intermediate Token Rendering (ITR) pipeline to guide avatar tokens to attend to their corresponding patches. Experiments across multiple datasets show that ARG-Avatar consistently outperforms prior methods when using two or more input images. Compared with LHM++, ARG-Avatar uses approximately 9$\times$ fewer trainable parameters, 4.8$\times$ fewer training sequences, and 14$\times$ less training compute, while running 6$\times$ faster and achieving a 2.7 dB PSNR improvement on the out-of-distribution NeuMan benchmark.
authors: Jianjin Xu;Soham Dasgupta;Fernando De la Torre

title: Flocking Time and Graph Volume in Nonlinear Cucker-Smale Models with Dynamic Networks
abstract: This study proposes a Cucker-Smale model incorporating dynamic networks and the discrete $p$-Laplacian ($p \in (1,2)$) and analyzes the relationship between flocking time constraints and graph connectivity from both theoretical and experimental perspectives. We establish that this model achieves flocking within finite time and derive a quantitative relationship between the lower bound of flocking time and graph volume. Based on these results, we observe that imposing sufficiently small flocking time induces an increase in network volume, and that larger initial velocity variance requires greater volume under the same time constraint. In our experiments, we trained a transformer-based PPO policy to select network structures at each time step. Under the most stringent time constraint, the maximum average number of connections increased sharply, confirming a threshold effect. The negative correlation between convergence time and average number of connections reflects the theoretical results well. This study provides quantitative evidence for the phenomenon that time constraints induce connection mobilization.

title: EGS: A Complementary Safety Framework for Educational LLMs
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer strong potential for personalized education, but adolescent-facing deployment raises risks of toxic, biased, misleading, or developmentally inappropriate content. We argue that educational safety should move beyond binary refusal: student queries are often ambiguous or curiosity-driven, requiring contextual guidance rather than simple blocking. We introduce the Educational Guardrail System (EGS), a lightweight, model-agnostic runtime framework that complements intrinsic alignment through query moderation, scenario-aware pedagogical guidance, and response moderation. EGS triages inputs by risk level, redirects gray-zone queries with category-specific educational interventions, and audits outputs before delivery. Experiments across general and education-specific benchmarks show that EGS improves moderation performance, refusal quality, and jailbreak robustness across diverse LLMs. These findings suggest that defense-in-depth guardrails can strengthen safety while preserving the pedagogical utility required in educational LLMs. Our code and model weights will be publicly available to support community adoption.
authors: Zexuan Fei;Zhengnan Guo;Yiming Luo;Kaiyi Huang;Aimin Zhou;Bo Jiang;Fei Tan

title: An Optimization Framework for Denoising Generation
abstract: Noise-unconditioned denoising learns a single score, so generation can be viewed as gradient ascent on a fixed log-density landscape. This optimization interpretation leaves two questions: do trajectories approach meaningful data, and do different initializations retain diverse outcomes? We establish both phenomena for empirical and population multi-scale Gaussian-mixture objectives. Under explicit posterior and landscape conditions, ascent converges almost surely within $O(mσ_{\min}^2/τ)$ of an $m$-dimensional reference manifold with reach at least $τ$. We derive a source--sink identity for the same fixed field and use it to prove finite-resolution regional coverage. In an affine construction, we further identify a positive-bandwidth regime where even empirical-score optimization can avoid training-sample memorization while preserving diversity at the training resolution. The same fixed objective naturally supports penalty-guided controllable generation. Experiments support our predicted mechanisms, show improved robustness under large-step guidance, and demonstrate downstream gains consistent with finite-data generative generalization.

title: MIRAGE: Motion Identity Reduction via Autoregressive Generative Encoding for Privacy-Preserving Skeleton-based Motion Data
abstract: Skeleton motion identifies people through body proportions and movement style, and skeleton streams are increasingly passed to third-party analytics that run action classifiers trained on raw data. A prior adversarial anonymizer adds a per-frame residual in the raw coordinate space but sees one frame at a time; motion retargeting needs a target skeleton and complete sequences, which rules out online use. We present MIRAGE, a target-free, causal anonymizer that adds an identity-reducing residual to each incoming frame in the raw coordinate space, computed by attention over past frames. One causal, optionally windowed mask governs every attention in a rotary-position encoder-decoder, and key/value caches let the trained function run frame by frame; on all 56,578 NTU 60 sequences, batched and streaming outputs differ by at most 7.2e-6 m. Reported results use an unbounded window, so per-stream state grows with stream length. We evaluate against a passive adversary that applies raw-trained identity models and an adaptive adversary that trains on the anonymizer's output, treating the adaptive adversary as the headline, on NTU RGB+D 60 over five generator seeds, alongside the per-frame residual anonymizer of Moon et al. trained identically. When consumers retrain on the released data, MIRAGE keeps 83.9% action recognition (raw 89.1%; Moon et al. 88.7%) while a retrained identity classifier reaches 43.4% re-identification (RI) over 40 subjects, against 69.4% for Moon et al. and 75.4% on raw data. The strongest adaptive attacker still reaches 49.3% (chance 2.5%), so MIRAGE reduces identity leakage; it does not anonymize. Against raw-trained (frozen) classifiers, MIRAGE lowers RI below the strongest retargeting baseline (10.36% vs. 22.09%), but frozen action recognition falls to 37.04% (vs. 75.82%), so at full residual scale it is not a drop-in replacement for raw input to existing frozen models.
authors: Thomas Carr;Xujun Che;Depeng Xu;Shuhan Yuan;Aidong Lu

title: Training Neural Networks to be Locally Adaptive
abstract: Deep neural networks fitted by global empirical risk minimization commit to a single model for the entire covariate space. In a regression problem, if the regression function $f_0$ is inhomogeneous --- varying rapidly in one region, while being nearly flat in another --- no single model can be appropriate everywhere, and the fit degrades where the function varies most rapidly. Here we study an alternative in which, instead of fitting the network globally, we fit it locally. For each query point $x$, a \emph{local neural network} is trained on the $k$ nearest-neighbours of $x$ alone, making the training sample and the fitted function query-dependent. We analyze the performance of the resulting estimator through a localization approach, establishing that the pointwise risk of the estimator with an appropriate choice of $k$ attains the rate $n^{-2α/(2α+d^{*})}$, up to logarithmic factors, when $f_0$ is locally $α$-Hölder with $α\in(0,1]$ and the covariates are supported on a $d^{*}$-dimensional manifold embedded in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$. A matching Le Cam lower bound shows that this rate is pointwise minimax optimal. However, the local rate-optimality requires $k$ to be calibrated to the smoothness of $f_0$, which is unknown in practice. We therefore provide a locally adaptive choice of $k$ that makes the neural network adapt to the local Hölder exponent of $f_0$ and to the intrinsic dimension simultaneously, both of which are potentially varying over the covariate domain. An extensive simulation study demonstrates the dominance of the locally adaptive neural network over a globally trained network and several state-of-the-art methods.

title: Grid-Responsive Pricing of Dynamic Wireless Charging with Coupled Residential Demand
abstract: Dynamic wireless charging (DWC) is an emerging technology that enables electric vehicles (EVs) to recharge while traveling. Its unique operational model creates two revenue streams for DWC operators through lane access tolls and electricity sales. However, these prices influence not only traffic flow and roadway energy delivery but also how much EV charging moves to homes instead, potentially within the same distribution network. Neglecting this coupling can underestimate grid loading and compromise pricing decisions. We develop a coupled traffic, EV energy, driver-response, and AC distribution network model with a model predictive control (MPC) framework that jointly optimizes DWC tolls and charging prices while explicitly accounting for displaced residential charging and network losses. Using 78 days of I-210 West traffic data, we show that conventional MPC exceeds feeder loading limits on 52 days, whereas the proposed residential load aware controller eliminates these violations with only 0.6% lower operator revenue. Under a more constrained feeder configuration, it eliminates 50 overloaded days with a 0.9% revenue reduction. Sensitivity analyses highlight the importance of accurate residential demand estimation and feeder loss modeling, while peak-aware pricing further reduces daily peak loading by 3.7% relative to the base load. These results demonstrate the value of coordinated pricing that captures the interaction between roadway and residential charging.
authors: Zhiheng Wang;Dipanjan Ghose;S. Sivaranjani;Junjie Qin;Qin Lv

title: Symmetry-selected entanglement death at Floquet resonances of parametrically coupled qubits
abstract: Periodic modulation of a qubit--qubit coupling is a standard way to engineer quantum interactions, but a strong modulation also reorganizes the transitions through which the qubits dissipate into a comb of Floquet channels. We study two identical, strongly coupled qubits whose transverse coupling is modulated anharmonically, as by a nonlinear coupler, with each qubit damped by its own reservoir. The modulation raises the ground-state concurrence of the cycle-averaged Hamiltonian from 0.45 to above 0.8, yet the steady-state concurrence stays close to its undriven value except at Floquet resonances selected by symmetry. There it undergoes entanglement death, vanishing at all times in the drive cycle over a finite range of modulation depths. Parity and exchange symmetry split the Floquet spectrum into an even sector, whose branches anticross at multiphoton resonances, and an exactly solvable odd sector, whose branches cross. Every dissipative channel connects the two sectors, so only the even anticrossings cause entanglement death, provided their gap exceeds the damping rate, whereas the nearby odd crossings leave the concurrence unchanged. Comparing time-independent and Floquet master equations, with and without the secular approximation, we show that the basis in which the dissipator is built changes the entanglement by up to 0.2 for an Ohmic bath and 0.5 for a flat one, whereas the secular approximation matters only near anticrossings with gaps comparable to the damping. The basis matters most when the bath has spectral weight at low frequency, where the drive moves dissipative channels through zero frequency. A transverse field that breaks parity lifts the selection rule.

title: RISA: Recoverable Sparse Attention for Block-Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Block-wise diffusion language models (DLMs) refine multiple tokens in parallel, offering an alternative to token-by-token autoregressive decoding. Their long-context inference, however, remains bottlenecked by memory-bound attention: every denoising step repeatedly reads a growing historical key--value (KV) cache. Directly applying sparse attention does not fully solve this problem, because different queries can select different pages, inflating the block's collective read set, while repeated support construction adds overhead and permanent eviction can discard information needed later. We present RISA, a recoverable sparse-attention method with shared read plans for block-wise DLMs. RISA exploits the fact that historical KV remains fixed within a block while queries evolve across denoising steps. Newly generated history is organized into exact priority and recovery tiers; seed queries then build a protected, bounded read plan whose indices are reused across the block while attention is recomputed with fresh queries and current-block KV. This separates history preservation from repeated reading and amortizes sparse-support construction without changing the backbone or decoder. On DreamReasoner-8B, RISA retains comparable task performance. At 32K, the default configuration speeds up attention by $2.67\times$ and fixed-trajectory requests by $1.36\times$ over dense, and attention speedup reaches $5.53\times$ at 128K. Across eight settings on three models, RISA decodes faster than the tested MAGE, QUEST, and LoSA budgets at matched KL.

title: SRED: Sparse Regional Evidence Distillation Across Magnifications in Whole-Slide Imaging
abstract: In computational pathology, high-magnification whole-slide image analysis preserves tissue detail but requires encoding many patches, whereas lower magnification reduces computation by covering a higher field of view per patch while sacrificing detail. Existing cross-magnification distillation matches features that often encode detail unreachable by low-magnification input, sometimes requiring slide-level labels that limit scalability. To address those issues, we introduce Sparse Regional Evidence Distillation (SRED), which transfers regional event occurrences that encode reachable high-level interactions between details without slide-level labels. We use a sparse autoencoder (SAE) to learn an event dictionary from 20x teacher features. Logical OR pooling records whether each event is detected in any spatially aligned patch, retaining both localized and shared evidence within the corresponding 5x region. A pretrained 5x encoder is fine-tuned to predict these regional targets without slide-level labels. Visual analysis identifies dictionary components responsive to recognizable histological patterns, supporting target interpretation. Compared with native 5x features, SRED improves average macro-F1 by 1.1 points across seven classification and grading cohorts and average C-index by 1.7 points across five survival cohorts. Runtime matches native 5x, with an average 11.58x speedup over 20x.
authors: Zhiyuan Yang;Jiahao Cheng;Vincent Quoc-Huy Trinh;Mahdi S. Hosseini

title: From Imperfective Paradox to Moorean Absurdity: Single-Chain Reasoning Lock-In and Multi-Candidate Verbalization Across Aspectual and Pragmatic Ambiguity
abstract: Natural language entailment and coherence judgments often depend on whether an event merely occurred, reached a telic culmination, satisfied a plan, or was evaluated under multiple pragmatic standards. We test observable consequences of the single-chain premature lock-in hypothesis across four preregistered, sealed formal experiments on Qwen3-8B-Q8_0 (16,640 formal units, temperature=0.0): 15 of 16 hypothesis slots retain confirmatory status (12 rejecting H0 under within-experiment Holm control at alpha_fam=0.05; E3_H3 demoted to descriptive status). In Experiment 1, Direct-CoT vs. MCU differs by 25.00 pp on telic high-confidence completion (Holm p=1.31239e-05), while NLI-CoT collapses by -91.25 pp on uninterrupted atelic items (Holm p=1.81805e-21). Multi-Candidate Verbalization (MCV) elicits K=5 weighted estimates in one call, separating the prompt from unweighted (MCU) and self-weighted (MCW) readouts. Mandarin (E2) and English (E3) expose an Interruption-Anchored Realis Paradox under NLI-CoT. In Experiment 4, MCU-CF raises perceived coherence on implicit Moorean sentences by 26.64 pp over Direct-CoT (Holm p=0.0006), alongside Direct-CF - Direct-CoT = 29.15 pp and MCU-CoT - Direct-CoT = 17.31 pp. A 1,800-call OpenAI ablation and a stage="dev" P16.7 cross-model extension (4,240 planned/collected units across five external models: 4,222 valid, 18 format-missing, 0 transport-missing; <2% missing per slice; OpenAI gpt-4o-mini at top_logprobs=20 achieves 1,000/1,000 valid units) show that discrete NLI-CoT and scalar Direct-CoT judgments dissociate across models. Confirmatory effects concern observable prompt-and-readout protocols; internal premature lock-in remains a hypothesis. All code, stimuli, preregistered analysis plans, and verification tools are available at https://github.com/asj252/llm-judgment-studies.

title: Is 4-Bit Quantization More Than Noise to a Chat Model's Safety Behaviour? Attributing Behavioural Shifts with Matched Perturbations
abstract: Chat models on phones and laptops are usually 4-bit copies of the model that was evaluated, and audits of such copies disagree about what quantization does to refusal. A 4-bit build is one of many weight perturbations of the same size, so a change in its behaviour could come from its specific rounding error or from any perturbation that large. In a pre-registered study of three 3-4B chat models, with paired tests, blind human labels and an 8-bit null, we find two 4-bit shifts of opposite sign: with a compliant reply prefilled, Qwen2.5-3B continues into harmful content more often, and on held-out jailbreaks Llama-3.2-3B complies 10.3 points less often. Matched perturbations separate the two. Shuffled and Gaussian versions of the error average close to zero, while scaling the real error, from its mirror image to twice its size, changes behaviour near-linearly. At half the real error, Llama's likelihood is almost unchanged, yet it already complies 5.8 points less often, and llama.cpp's Q4_K_M, at the same bits per weight, moves neither model. Refusal under 4-bit quantization depends on the specific rounding error, not on bits per weight or likelihood, so each build has to be compared with its original.

comment: 16 pages, 4 figures. Code and labels: https://github.com/egekaya1/qrefusal

title: Benchmarking a Grid Foundation Model for AC Optimal Power Flow: Feasibility and Warm-Start Results on Synthetic Texas and South Carolina Grids
abstract: Learning-based surrogates for alternating-current optimal power flow (AC-OPF) are often judged by the gap between their objective value and that of a nonlinear solver, which does not show that a prediction satisfies power balance and network limits. This paper tests whether predictions from the pretrained foundation model GridSFM-Open 1.1.0, recently released by Microsoft, are feasible AC-OPF operating points and whether they are useful initial values for a nonlinear solver. The model was evaluated zero-shot and after fine-tuning on 10, 100, and 1,000 labeled scenarios (FT10, FT100, and FT1000) on 500 scenarios for each of two synthetic grids, ACTIVSg2000 (Texas) and ACTIVSg500 (South Carolina), with Ipopt, MATPOWER MIPS, and pandapower PIPS as solver references. The lowest Texas median cost gap, 0.44\% for FT100, coincided with thermal violations in 24.1\% of cases and a median maximum bus power mismatch of 89 MW and 197 Mvar. Texas zero-shot predictions had a median maximum mismatch of 648 MW and 1,641 Mvar, and every South Carolina case violated a thermal limit for every model variant. Seeding Ipopt with FT1000 predictions gave geometric-mean solve-time speedups of 1.55x on South Carolina and 1.12x on Texas (p = 0.06, not significant at the 5\% level), while zero-shot seeds slowed South Carolina solves (0.26x). A small objective gap therefore did not indicate feasibility: although median zero-shot inference took only 1.32 s on Texas and 0.157 s on South Carolina on a shared host, every prediction still required a nonlinear solver, and fine-tuned predictions gave modest, grid-dependent warm-start speedups while zero-shot predictions slowed convergence on one grid. GridSFM may therefore be useful for initializing a nonlinear solver, but obtaining feasible AC-OPF solutions still required the solver.
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to the 2027 IEEE PES General Meeting

title: CueClash: Frontier Vision-Language Models Judge 3-D Relations Close to the Picture Plane
abstract: A vision-language model (VLM) can judge 3-D relations from the picture or from the ground layout. In photographs the two usually agree. We separate them with CueClash, rendered scenes in which the 2-D cue for each of five relations is right on exactly half the statements. The shortcut gap is accuracy when the cue is right minus accuracy when it is wrong. For Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.6 Flash at low reasoning effort it is +18 to +37 percentage points. It is +7 to +29 without two relations whose cue-wrong items are confounded with borderline cases or occlusion. Given ground coordinates and each relation's definition, they answer 99 to 100% correctly. Pixel measurements with camera depths remove most of the gap for objects fitting through openings. The failure lies in the step from the picture to the layout. The maps that the models draw of the scene from above mostly keep the depth order but, like the picture, shorten depth. GPT-5.5's maps stay close to a copy of the picture. Opus 5.5's and Gemini's maps undo about 0.6 of this shortening. Gemini's then shrink all depths by a further uniform factor. Opus 5.5 follows the picture mainly on fits, and its maps correct depth about as much as human observers of real scenes do. The three models also lose accuracy on CV-Bench photographs where a reliable 2-D cue misleads. In two open models the layout information reaches the language model, but their maps lose much of it.

title: RAG in a Trenchcoat: When Minimal Memory Is Enough for Agentic Systems, and When It Isn't
abstract: Agentic memory research has accumulated extraction, supersession, reflection, and graph synthesis on top of retrieval-augmented generation. However, we found that almost none of those primitives earn their cost in our tested memory benchmarks: we show this with BRIDGE, a deliberately minimal RAG memory with chained observation notes, hybrid BM25 with cosine retrieval, and chronological rendering, which reaches parity within bootstrap CI with the prior SOTA on LongMemEval-S and BEAM, and beats the best memory baseline on EverMemBench by 5.7-6.3 points at matched reader. It runs at ~5-7K reader-prompt tokens per query, using a single LLM call for each ingestion or query. We argue that this parity is itself the result: standard benchmarks score what memory retrieves, not what memory enables when the agent acts. To test the latter, we introduce five adversarial probes (Rule Application +-, Pattern Induction Style / Procedural, Dynamic Multiturn) judged at generation time by a cross vendor verification chain, where each query can only be solved by applying a remembered rule or pattern it never mentions. Across 5 probes x 20 scenarios, no architecture wins universally: atomic fact extractors (LangMem) win rule application, while BRIDGE's block-summary memory wins pattern induction. This result holds across four domains, three graders, and three reader families. Each design fails where the other wins, for reasons a recall benchmark cannot see: atomic-fact extractors discard the form a demonstrated pattern takes, while block-summary memory retrieves the rule but the reader does not act on it, a gap that presenting the rule more prominently largely closes. What separates memory designs is not what they retrieve but what they enable an agent to do, and that is what agentic memory should be evaluated on.
authors: Jingyu Liu;Zongze Li;Zach Xu;Zhanhui Zhou;Tahseen Rabbani;Dawn Song;Ce Zhang
comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026), Main Conference

title: CorrectCast: Selective Multimodal Context for Scale-Aware Residual Correction in Precipitation Nowcasting
abstract: Precipitation nowcasting models suffer from errors in intensity, location, and spatial structure. Addressing these errors by retraining nowcaster backbones can be computationally expensive and requires architecture-specific modifications. To overcome these limitations, we propose CorrectCast, a decoupled residual correction framework that refines completed nowcasts while keeping the base nowcaster frozen. By operating on predicted precipitation fields, CorrectCast requires training only a lightweight corrector, reducing computational overhead while providing a unified correction interface across different nowcasting models. Conditioned on the base nowcast and historical quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE) and precipitable water vapor (PWV) observations, the corrector selects multimodal context and employs scale-aware modulation to estimate residual corrections. On the Mississippi River Basin (MRB) and contiguous United States (CONUS) datasets, CorrectCast improves six base nowcasters spanning extrapolation-based, deterministic, and generative approaches, with absolute gains in mean CSI averaging 0.0233 and 0.0290 across the six models, respectively.

title: The Only Edge Was Memorized in Training: LLM Trading Agents Around Earnings and Bad News
abstract: Large language model (LLM) trading agents are tested on news, but news reaches stock prices within minutes, and a benchmark that replays headlines at their publication time finds no alpha in trading on them. Money can then remain in two places, before news whose date is known, such as earnings announcements, and after bad news, if the market's fall went too far. However, studies of LLMs and earnings read documents published with or after the announcement, and studies of reversal sort monthly portfolios, so neither tells whether an agent can trade these moments after costs. In this paper, we test LLM agents at both moments on the same look-ahead-free benchmark, before 598 earnings announcements and after 409 bad-news drops of large US stocks. Every input is cut at the decision close, staged agents are compared with single calls, simple rules and a logistic regression, and every decision is made with and without the stock's name. Across five models from four vendors, no agent beat the simple bets. Before earnings, the agents mostly bought and earned what buying before every announcement earned, and after bad news, a Gemini-based agent called almost every fall an overreaction while no agent picked better dips than buying them all. The only gains came from what the models had memorized in training. Given only the ticker and the dates, a GPT-based model called the direction of 59.2% of the announcements before its training cutoff and 53.3% after it. Agent builders should therefore compare an event agent with the simple bet and test it blind after the training cutoff.
comment: 21 pages, 9 figures, 12 tables. Original empirical study of LLM trading agents before scheduled earnings announcements and after bad-news drops, run on the rta-bench-1 benchmark (arXiv:2611.19530)

title: Decision Stability and Model Reduction for Hamilton--Jacobi Navigation in Multiscale Flows
abstract: Autonomous vehicles plan time-optimal routes through flow fields that are known only through reduced, finite-resolution models of an underlying multiscale flow. Classical Hamilton-Jacobi homogenization concerns convergence of the value function as the fine scale vanishes; but what a vehicle commits to is a route, and value accuracy need not imply route accuracy. We study this gap for a fixed-resolution reduction rather than in the homogenization limit. The committed route's dependence on the model-reduction error splits into two regimes. When the optimal route is a unique, nondegenerate minimizer with a regular value-function neighborhood, it depends Lipschitz-continuously on the reduction error, while the extra travel time from acting on the reduced model grows only quadratically with that error. When two routes are tied on the cut locus of the value function, the value remains stable, but an arbitrarily small change in the flow can switch the selected route, making route selection discontinuous in the reduction error. This dichotomy identifies where a reduced model must be accurate: not where the flow error is largest, but where the route choice is fragile. In the regular regime it yields a resolution-allocation principle, while an oracle marginal-regret benchmark illustrates the potential benefit of decision-aware resolution allocation relative to refinement based on flow-error magnitude.

title: Reconfiguring Procedural Knowledge for Compositional Robot Skill Adaptation
abstract: General-purpose behavior models increasingly internalize broad procedural knowledge during training, making their adaptation to new goals and skill interfaces less a problem of learning entirely new behaviors than of reconfiguring existing competence. We study this capability as reconfigurability, the ability to realize new behaviors by cost-efficiently restructuring existing components and relations under sparse governing information, where task specifications provide high-level goals and procedure specifications expose a limited set of reusable factors, leaving the concrete bindings and compositions required for execution underdetermined. We propose RecPo, a framework that represents skills task-agnostically through multiple procedure views and materializes executable skill sequences by composing stored transitions to realize task-specific changes. RecPo maintains a procedure knowledge base of skill-induced transitions, with each view exposing a reusable factor and preserving local skill connectivity. At deployment, it interprets task specifications through the same views and resolves the resulting compositional queries over the stored relations to bind skills for execution. On long-horizon tasks in an extended Franka Kitchen benchmark, RecPo achieves 91.9% ordered completion with 1.0 ms of task inference per episode across varying procedure support and task-record sparsity. Real-robot studies further demonstrate adaptation through local memory edits without task-specific retraining.
authors: Daehee Lee;Dongsu Lee;Sanghyun Ahn;Minjong Yoo;Honguk Woo

title: Towards Optimism-Pessimism Trade-off in Model-based Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Model-based offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) enables sample-efficient adaptation by leveraging offline pre-training for online fine-tuning. However, the distribution shifts between offline and online stages often hinder fine-tuning performance. Many existing methods encode the optimism-pessimism trade-off through a single-objective formulation. Selecting its trade-off coefficient through online fine-tuning can require costly bi-level optimization. We identify the balance established during offline training as a key challenge: in our motivating experiments, optimistic policies adapt better to novel tasks, whereas pessimistic policies perform better on the same online tasks. To address this challenge, we propose a bi-objective formulation that captures this trade-off, yielding a Pareto policy pool during offline training. This policy pool enables adaptive selection during online fine-tuning across diverse online tasks. To generate the pool, we introduce Multi-Objective Soft Actor-critIC (MOSAIC), which solves bi-objective problems and constructs diverse Pareto policies. After offline training, a contextual bandit algorithm hierarchically selects the most suitable policy for fine-tuning at each online interaction step. Empirically, our pipeline, Hierarchical Pareto Policy Pool (HiP3), achieves the strongest aggregate performance across both same and novel online tasks and maintains its advantage under stronger distribution shifts. Comprehensive ablations further clarify the roles of the policy pool, MOSAIC-based pool construction, and the online selection mechanism.
authors: Guochen Zhou;Yijun Yang;Qiqi Duan;Qing Su;Weiming Ou;Li Shen;Shihao Ji;Yuhui Shi;Zhisong Zhang

title: Readie: Low-Latency Code Sandboxes for AI Agents
abstract: From quantitative research to personal assistance, AI agents act by iteratively generating and executing code. To decouple the agent harness from code execution, many agents offload execution to dedicated systems called code sandboxes. However, existing code sandboxes suffer from slow startup. Whether they rely on custom snapshots or a single fat image, the root cause is the same: it is hard to build a compact, pre-warmed snapshot that can be shared across diverse agent-generated code while covering nearly all the artifacts (e.g., packages, datasets) it requires. In this work, we propose learned startup snapshots for low-latency code sandboxes. Our insight is that while it is hard for a single snapshot to be both compact and cover most workloads, a set of snapshots can achieve both. Each snapshot is small, initializes quickly, and covers a fraction of agent-generated code; together, the set covers most of it. We learn this set from a large training workload by formulating snapshot construction as an optimization problem and solving it with an approximation algorithm. Planned on 15K public and LLM-synthesized scripts, our system, Readie, reduces startup latency by 3-22$\times$ and end-to-end runtime by 1.3-3.3$\times$ compared to existing approaches at the same storage budget.
authors: Arjun Sivaraman;Zhaoheng Li;Alan Shi;Sanjay Malisetty;Eugene Wu;Yongjoo Park

title: Reconfigurable 2D Lateral Heterostructure Platform for Unified Detection, Emission, and Logic
abstract: Heterogeneous integration of sensing, light generation, communication, and computation typically requires specialized devices, resulting in complex interconnects, fabrication overhead, parasitic losses, and energy penalties. Developing a monolithic, reconfigurable device capable of controlling carrier generation, transport, and recombination remains a longstanding challenge. Two-dimensional (2D) lateral heterostructures offer a promising approach by combining spatially distinct domains of different charge polarity with a dynamically tunable electrostatic landscape. Here, multifunctional bilayer MoSe2-WSe2 lateral heterojunctions are demonstrated, integrating photodetection, reconfigurable electroluminescence (EL), and CMOS logic operation within a unified platform. The photodetector exhibits a responsivity of 35 A W-1, a specific detectivity of 5 x 10^13 Jones, and a noise-equivalent power of 6.3 x 10^-18 W Hz^-1/2, enabled by efficient charge separation and photoconductive gain. Under electrical injection, electrostatic gating dynamically switches the radiative recombination zone among the MoSe2 domain, lateral heterointerface, and WSe2 domain, enabling spatially programmable EL, optical multiplexing, and ternary optical logic. Furthermore, the complementary transport characteristics of the two domains enable CMOS inverter operation at 0.25 kHz. These functionalities originate from a common electrostatic framework in which the gate-tunable depletion region governs carrier extraction, recombination, and transport. This work establishes 2D lateral heterostructures as multifunctional building blocks for monolithically integrated electronic and optoelectronic systems combining light sensing, generation, and information processing.
authors: Purbasha Ray;Rupali Verma;Biswajeet Nayak;Suman Kumar Chakraborty;Shailendra K Varshney;Mayank Shrivastava;Prasana Kumar Sahoo

title: Not All Evidence Is Admissible: Evidence Governance for Tool-Augmented Medical Agents
abstract: Tool-augmented medical agents treat whatever their tools return as evidence. We show that this default is costly: medical tools fail silently, and a frozen reasoner cannot ignore what enters its context, so many cases it would have answered correctly are flipped to wrong once tool outputs are added. We call this evidence hijacking. $\mathcal{V}$-information explains the phenomenon: the reasoner has lost the option to ignore, so a tool output can carry negative usable information, and moving the decision of what to keep outside the reasoner restores that option. The theory further shows that part of any filtering gain comes merely from letting the reasoner see less, and only selection by content lets it see better. Building on this, we recast tool-augmented reasoning as evidence governance, which separates deciding what counts as evidence from the reasoner that answers, and propose context-independent evidence governance (CIEG), the first medical agent framework that rules, after acquisition, on whether each individual tool output may enter as evidence. Every tool output is written as a card that can be checked against the raw input; an independent checker that sees only the input and the cards decides which cards become evidence; and the reasoner answers from the admitted cards alone, with no training anywhere. On medical question answering, fundus glaucoma screening, and chest X-ray pneumonia classification, it achieves the highest accuracy among models of comparable scale, and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art tool-using agents and multi-agent systems built on the same backbone at lower cost.
authors: Runxun Zhang;Onofrio Antonio Catalano;Jinqiao Wang;Jingwei Wei

title: AI Agents Executing an RMS and EMT Ride-Through Workflow on a 2,000-Bus Synthetic Texas Grid: A Case Study with Open-Source Tools
abstract: This paper reports a case study of engineer-supervised AI agents executing a predefined RMS and EMT ride-through workflow on the 2,000-bus ACTIVSg2000 synthetic Texas grid with open-source tools. The test case is a 133 MW battery with a co-located 130 MW data-center load, assessed against ride-through criteria fixed before simulation and for loss of synchronism elsewhere in the grid. One agent ran 44 RMS cases and 15 without-project comparisons in ANDES; the other ran a 220-row EMT intake bench and an 84-row system study in DPsim and ParaEMT on a Kron-reduced area. Across the 44 RMS cases, 127 criterion cells fail, including loss of synchronism in all 44. Two findings concern the project plant. The battery keeps absorbing reactive power during sags on the light-load schedule (B3, as low as -19.8 Mvar on S4 T1), and the data-center load returns only at 5.00-5.56 s after long bolted faults (L3), which misses the ERCOT load-return requirement. In 13 of the 15 comparisons, which the authors selected after slips or speed-gate stops, the same machines slip without the project; the other 29 runs have no without-project comparison. RMS and EMT values differ in network, plant model, controls, operating point, and base, and so they are reported as separate, unaligned observations. The paper reports the errors the authors identified in the agent logs, 63 author messages, and 3.8 days from agent start to the integrated study report. The agents executed and documented the predefined ride-through and stability workflow, which covers one part of an interconnection study.
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. Submitted to the 2027 IEEE PES General Meeting

title: Demonstration of a Qubit Control Scheme Compatible with Superconducting Digital Signals
abstract: Superconducting quantum computing faces a critical scalability bottleneck arising from the escalating complexity of traditional analog control infrastructure. Single-Flux-Quantum(SFQ) systems operate at cryogenic temperatures and offer a potential route to addressing these challenges. Using microwave signals at qubit-dependent frequencies to trigger SFQ pulses requires many independent analog microwave sources, limiting the potential to reduce control wiring and increase integration density. A scalable SFQ control system therefore needs a scheme that can address qubits with different transition frequencies using a common clock. Here, we propose and experimentally demonstrate a control scheme for implementing both single- and two-qubit gates. The scheme uses guiding waveforms to rapidly generate bipolar high-speed pulse sequences on a common clock, providing a basis for future implementation in SFQ control systems. Numerically, this scheme achieves a simulated fidelity of 99.99% for 40ns $R(\varphi, \fracπ{2})$ gates with arbitrary initial phases and 99.9% for 100ns controlled-Z(CZ) gates. Experimentally, by utilizing an arbitrary waveform generator(AWG) operated at a fixed sampling rate of 25GSa/s to deliver the bipolar high-speed pulse sequences, we successfully demonstrate 40ns single-qubit gates with an average gate fidelity of 99.94% estimated using cross-entropy benchmarking(XEB) and 120ns CZ gates with 99.63% fidelity. These results demonstrate the feasibility of common-clock encoded pulse control for both single- and two-qubit gates.
authors: Chenyin Sun;Yu Xu;Zihua Chen;Dayu Li;Tianzuo Sun;Chen Zha;Yuan Li;Jin Lin;Lei Jiang;Tao Rong;Tao Jiang;Shaoyu Zhan;Xueshen Wang;Shijian Wang;Wenhui Cao;Yeru Wang;Xiaomin Wang;Ming Gong;Yulin Wu;Yuhuai Li;Gang Wu;Hui Deng;Kai Yan;Sirui Cao;Futian Liang;Fusheng Chen;Qingling Zhu;Yangsen Ye;Hao Rong;Shaojun Guo;Haoran Qian;Haibin Zhang;Yisen Hu;Shaowei Li;Jinjin Li;Cheng-Zhi Peng;Xiaobo Zhu;Jian-Wei Pan

title: HandRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement for Hand Pose Estimation
abstract: Egocentric 3D hand pose estimators still miss hands at the image border, misplace occluded hands and jitter. Such failures are usually fixed by hand-written inference refinements and by fine-tuning, two interdependent steps that are tuned separately. We present HandRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework for a hand pose system that consists of a video estimator and its executable inference harness. In each round, coding agents refine the harness, and a change is accepted only if it improves a composite of all ten benchmark metrics on held-out data without significantly regressing any of them. The accepted harness then guides the estimator through selective distillation, which supervises hand presence and temporal consistency on frames without ground truth, while ground truth supervises pose. Since the updated estimator may change which refinements remain useful, the harness is re-validated on it. Starting from the released ACE-Ego-Hand model, five rounds reduce MPJPE-p by 35% on HOT3D and 11% on ARCTIC and roughly halve jitter. On HOT3D, HandRSI's MPJPE-p is 16% lower than that of ACE-Ego-Hand fine-tuned on the same ground truth. Under a unified protocol, it outperforms nine re-run published methods on all ten metrics of both benchmarks. Hypervolume selection on the accuracy-speed front yields Lite, Medium and Heavy systems running at 20.7 to 41.1 FPS. This report gives the full method, every stage of every round and the complete protocol. Code, evaluator, harnesses and weights are public.
authors: Zhekai Wang;Luqing Luo;Wenhao Yao;Junjie Lu;Huanan Zhu;Feifei Gao;Yuhua Jiang
comment: Technical report. 25 pages, 17 figures, 18 tables. Code: https://github.com/GinKenneth/Hand_RSI

title: What RL on Expert-Built Tasks Teaches Nemotron 3.5 Super
abstract: We post-train NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super (120B total, 12B active parameters) with reinforcement learning (RL) on five expert-built task datasets, one at a time: real-world software engineering, complex constraints, long-horizon tool use, professional chart understanding and enterprise document reasoning. Each run trains a fresh rank-32 LoRA adapter with CISPO on Tinker, with no supervised stage, and each adapter is compared with the base model on the same tasks, harness and settings. On twelve headline benchmarks, eight built by other groups and four by Surge AI, the gains range from +4.5 points on IFBench to +13.8 on GDP_pdf, which rises from 10.4% to 24.2%; SWE-bench Pro V2 rises from 86.9% to 92.1%, Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 63.9% to 70.3%, MultiChallenge from 58.3% to 66.6%, AutomationBench from 14.8% to 27.5% and Chartography from 39.4% to 50.6%. The document adapter, trained without API tools, also gains +8.0 points on AutomationBench. In attempts read side by side with the base model's on tasks each adapter newly solves, the base model's failures recur in a few modes, and each adapter does more often what the base model missed: the tool-use adapter finds the data and the rules before acting, the coding adapter writes its own test or scratch files on SWE-bench Pro V2, the constraints adapter carries earlier turns into its answers, the chart adapter measures the marks in code, and the document adapter reads AutomationBench's spreadsheets.

title: Centroid Spectral Coupling: Implicit Alignment and Representation Diversity in Self-Supervised Learning
abstract: Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) aims to align augmented views while preserving representation diversity and preventing collapse. Existing non-contrastive methods often address these goals using multiple weighted loss terms. We introduce Centroid Spectral Coupling (CSC), a single-term SSL objective that implicitly couples view alignment, representation diversity, and collapse resistance. CSC constructs centroids from independently normalized augmented-view pairs and applies a ridge-based spectral objective to their uncentered second-moment matrix. Preserving centroid magnitudes encodes view agreement while encouraging balanced representation energy across spectral directions. We establish an exact decomposition into nonnegative alignment and spectral-imbalance components, characterize the geometry of global optima, and derive finite-loss guarantees for alignment and diversity. We also show that complete constant-output collapse is a strict saddle in normalized representation space. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Imagenette show that CSC achieves the highest linear Top-1 accuracy among the evaluated non-contrastive methods on all three benchmarks, and the highest kNN Top-1 accuracy on both CIFAR datasets. A ridge-parameter sensitivity study reveals an empirical alignment--diversity trade-off: increasing $κ$ strengthens view alignment but reduces representation effective rank. These results show that a unified spectral objective yields competitive visual representations without explicit contrastive negatives or separately weighted alignment and diversity penalties.
authors: M. Hadi Sepanj;Benyamin Ghojogh;Saed Moradi;Paul Fieguth

title: Quantum Causal Compatibility from Spatiotemporal Correlations
abstract: Which quantum causal structures can account for observed spatiotemporal correlations without access to an intervention-complete description of the underlying process? In particular, can such correlations distinguish a temporal chain, a common cause, and a common effect? Here, we address these questions using three-qubit pseudo-density operators constructed from experimentally accessible Pauli correlations. We derive necessary and sufficient conditions for pseudo-Markov compatibility with the chain, fork, and collider structures by relaxing complete positivity while preserving the corresponding quantum Markov constraints. Despite their distinct causal mechanisms, all three pseudo-Markov compatibility problems reduce to linear feasibility tests, without requiring full-rank marginal states. We further establish a unified semidefinite-programming approach to physical realizability and quantify the minimum violation of complete positivity through Choi negativity. Using a two-parameter family of pseudo-density operators, we demonstrate that different causal structures admit overlapping yet non-nested sets of correlations. Our results show that quantum causal explanations need not be unique, but experimentally accessible correlations can nevertheless distinguish and exclude candidate causal structures.
authors: Ya-Xi Ban;Zhu-Jun Zheng;Shao-Ming Fei;Chang-Yue Zhang;Mao-Sheng Li

title: Swift Heavy Ion Tracks in Polymorphs of Titanium Dioxide: The Effects of Electron Beam and Crystal Structures
abstract: Swift heavy ion (SHI) irradiation generates nanoscale damage in materials, offering opportunities for controlled modification of structural properties. Understanding the fundamental processes governing damage formation in altered regions remains a longstanding challenge. This work explores how crystal structure influences swift heavy ion-induced damage formation and evolution in rutile and anatase TiO2. Combining transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and molecular dynamics simulations, we investigate how differences in atomic arrangement govern track morphology and structural recovery. Although irradiation produces amorphous tracks in both polymorphs, their morphologies differ considerably. In rutile, tracks develop pronounced diameter variations, forming hourglass-like structures, whereas in anatase they retain a relatively uniform cylindrical shape. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that these differences arise from the distinct recrystallization behavior of the two crystal structures during rapid cooling, leading to different pathways of track evolution and recovery. Particular attention is paid to electron beam induced effects during TEM characterization, which can substantially modify the structure and apparent morphology of ion tracks. Prolonged electron beam exposure promotes the recrystallization of initially amorphous tracks and surface hillocks, accompanied by the development of Fresnel contrast. These findings highlight the importance of understanding beam-induced transformations for the reliable interpretation of TEM observations of radiation-damaged materials.
authors: Xiaoting Jia;Lijun Xu;Ruslan A. Rymzhanov;Wenqiang Liu;Peipei Hu;Shengxia Zhang;Jiande Liu;Jian Zeng;Jie Liu;Pengfei Zhai

title: Unsupervised Multi-modal Medical Image Registration via Invertible Translation
abstract: In medical imaging, the alignment of multi-modal images plays a critical role in providing comprehensive information for image-guided therapies. Despite its importance, multi-modal image registration poses significant challenges due to the complex and often unknown spatial relationships between different image modalities. To address this, we introduce a novel unsupervised translation-based multi-modal registration method, termed Invertible Neural Network-based Registration (INNReg). INNReg consists of an image-to-image translation network that converts multi-modal images into mono-modal counterparts and a registration network that uses the translated mono-modal images to align the multi-modal images. Specifically, to ensure the preservation of geometric consistency after image translation, we introduce an Invertible Neural Network (INN) that leverages a dynamic depthwise convolution-based local attention mechanism. Additionally, we design a novel barrier loss function based on Normalized Mutual Information to impose constraints on the registration network, which enhances the registration accuracy. The superior performance of INNReg is demonstrated through experiments on two public multi-modal medical image datasets, including MRI T1/T2 and MRI/CT pairs. The code is available at https://github.com/MeggieGuo/INNReg

title: EgoHandWAM: Probing the Role of Hand Motion in Egocentric World Action Modeling
abstract: How much does hand motion tell us about what a first-person camera will see next? EgoHandWAM forecasts three-dimensional wrist and fingertip trajectories and a future visual feature from the current image and recent hand states. We train on 751,065 EgoDex windows using a frozen DINOv2 encoder. On held-out development sessions, the action-only model reduces two-second wrist endpoint error from 60.26 to 56.48~mm relative to a stationary forecast. It still underestimates long reaches. Adding future-feature supervision gives nearly identical trajectory accuracy. With the recorded hand history, the visual head reduces smooth L1 error by 1.32\% relative to copying the current feature. Shuffling histories across sessions erases this gain. In a separate four-task probe, adding recorded future displacements to observed context and future tracking-validity masks reduces visual-feature error by 3.93\%. Masks alone give little improvement. A trajectory predicted from the same observations adds little. On two simulated RoboTwin tasks, substituting aligned human examples for an auxiliary batch of robot examples gives no consistent increase in task success across three training seeds.
authors: Kailin Wang;Haoxiang Jie;Yaoyuan Yan;Zhiyou Heng;Zhaosong Li

title: Long-Context Generation Is a Sampling Problem (When You Turn Up the Heat)
abstract: Open-weight language models are widely observed to get worse the longer they generate. Often, attempts to fix this involve more training. At high temperature, The sampler, i.e. the rule that picks the next token out of the model's probabilities, decides whether long and agentic generation survives and/or thrives. We test 29 open-weight models from 1B to 122B parameters on ten established benchmarks plus needle retrieval out to one million tokens, covering SWE-bench Verified coding agents, long chain-of-thought reasoning, long-form writing, long structured output and long-context reading. Samplers that keep their pool of candidate tokens small and steady as temperature rises don't lose accuracy. Samplers that let in low-probability tokens fall apart. At temperature 2, coding agents running top-p, top-k or Top-H resolve 0 of 100 GitHub issues, while the same agents running top-nsigma resolve 46 to 62 and win every issue the two samplers disagree on, on three Qwen3.5 models. Over all benchmarks top-nsigma keeps a median 100% of its temperature-1 score where top-p keeps 26%. Counting how many tokens each sampler lets through explains why. In one Llama-3.1-8B story, going from temperature 1 to 2 grows top-p's pool from 4 tokens to 51,845 while top-nsigma stays at 3. Across 133 combinations of sampler setting and temperature, the typical pool size predicts judged quality (Spearman correlation of -0.77), and when we pick the pool at temperature 1 and only apply temperature afterwards, Top-H, min-p and p-less stop collapsing. At the default temperature of 1 most samplers perform about the same, We release all code and data to the public.
authors: Allen G. Roush;Minh Nhat Nguyen;Ravid Shwartz-Ziv;Judah Goldfeder;Sanjay Basu
comment: 10 pages, accepted to the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Track on Evaluations and Datasets

title: When does deep reinforcement learning pay off in HVAC supervisory control? Four small Modelica case studies trained directly on FMUs
abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) is often proposed for the supervisory control of heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems. The reported gains are, however, difficult to interpret, because the baselines are often weak and the attainable optimum is seldom known. This paper examines four small, reproducible case studies based on an office building in Brisbane, Australia: pre-cooling under a time-of-use tariff; chiller staging with condenser water reset; chilled water supply temperature reset with a wet cooling coil; and chilled water storage under time-of-use prices and a demand charge. The plants were modelled with the Modelica Buildings library, and in three of the cases a soft actor-critic agent was trained directly on the exported functional mock-up unit (FMU). Each agent was compared with tuned rule-based controllers and, where practicable, with a near-optimal reference from hourly exhaustive search or dynamic programming with perfect foresight. In the two cases without storage the agent reached the near-optimal reference, but the margin above a well-chosen rule was small: 1.3% for condenser water reset and 0.18% for chilled water reset. In the latter case two common reset rules consumed more energy than a fixed set point. With a chilled water storage tank the margin was considerably larger. The agent outperformed both rules (-7.8%, compared with -3.9% and -6.3%) and adopted midday charging during the solar off-peak period, yet it obtained only about 45% of the saving achieved by the perfect-foresight schedule and did little to limit the demand peak. In the pre-cooling case a hand-tuned rule remained superior (-12.0% compared with -5.6%). These results suggest that studies of DRL for HVAC control should state the margin between the best rule and a near-optimal reference. Some practical difficulties encountered in training on co-simulation FMUs are also reported.
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Code, models and trained agents: https://github.com/Bingnan-Zhao/hvac-drl-lab

title: Finite sample guarantees of MPPI: suboptimality, sample complexity and closed-loop guarantees
abstract: This paper considers model predictive path integral (MPPI) control for nonlinear finite-horizon optimal control problems with bounded inputs, allowing nonconvex and nonsmooth costs. We prove theoretical guarantees that quantify the suboptimality caused by positive temperature and finite sampling on MPPI and establish their implications for closed-loop guarantees. Specifically, we derive a suboptimality bound for infinite-sample MPPI that characterizes the effects of temperature and prior coverage, followed by a high-probability finite-sample approximation error bound that reveals the dependence on sample size, temperature, and cost variability. By incorporating these bounds into a terminal-constraint-free MPC framework, we further establish semi-global practical recurrence of the closed-loop system. Numerical examples involving a four-link planar manipulator illustrate the temperature-sampling tradeoff and the influence of prior quality on approximation accuracy and closed-loop performance.

title: CEVA: Complementary Evidence Verification via Frame-Level Reorganization for Short-Video Fake News Detection
abstract: Short-video platforms are now a common way for the public to follow unfolding events. Their rapid, visually persuasive format also makes fake news easier to spread. Unlike text-image posts, short-video news interleaves multiple modalities and changing scenes, making it difficult to identify which frames verify a claim. Existing detectors either pool sampled frames homogeneously or select them by text-frame similarity. Both overlook that aligned frames may repeat a misleading claim, whereas less dominant context may challenge it. We present CEVA (Complementary Evidence Verification Approach), to our knowledge the first short-video fake news detection framework to explicitly organize frames by their evidential roles before multimodal fusion. Its Dual-Branch Complementary Reorganization (DBCR) module separates explicit-alignment frames from candidate complementary-context frames, and cross-modal fusion with bidirectional contrastive regularization operates on the reorganized evidence. On FakeSV and FakeTT, CEVA achieves the best overall results among the compared methods. Under fixed frame budgets and backbones, DBCR outperforms uniform, random, and similarity-based selection and improves two structurally different detectors. Together, these results establish pre-fusion evidence organization as an effective and transferable component of short-video fake news detection.
authors: Wenshen Yang;Junfeng Hao;Jing Li;Decheng Liu;Yangkunfei;Shuyu Jiang;Haizhou Wang

title: Synthetic Crystal Data Generation for Diffusion Pretraining in Material Property Prediction
abstract: Diffusion-based pretraining has emerged as a powerful strategy for learning transferable representations in graph neural networks for materials property prediction without requiring quantum-mechanical labels such as energies, forces, and stresses for every pretraining structure. However, the method retains a critical dependency: it requires structures residing near local minima of a potential energy surface, which have traditionally been obtained through costly DFT relaxations of known or physically synthesized compounds. This reliance constrains both the scale and the structural diversity of available pretraining data, leaving large regions of crystal structure space unexplored. In this work, we connect diffusion-based pretraining with synthetic structure generation to reduce this bottleneck. We introduce a synthetic data generation pipeline combining three complementary strategies: perturb-and-relax, generative sampling via MatterGen, and protostructure enumeration. Where structural relaxation is required, we use fast machine-learned interatomic potentials instead of performing a new DFT relaxation for each generated structure. We further compare a coordinate-denoising control with continuous-time variance-preserving (VP) and sub-VP diffusion objectives using a randomly initialized Orb-v2 backbone. The source comparison covers seven MatBench property-prediction tasks, and an eighth task, \texttt{mp\_gap}, is included in the protostructure scaling study. Every synthetic-pretraining condition numerically outperforms random initialization on all seven source-comparison tasks. Scaling the protostructure corpus from 20k to 165k under a fixed 400-epoch schedule numerically matches or exceeds MP-20k pretraining on most tasks; because this protocol increases both data diversity and optimization updates, the result reflects joint data-and-compute scaling.
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Accepted at the AI4Mat Workshop at NeurIPS 2026

title: RoboTeam: Benchmarking Vision-Based Multi-Agent Control of Many Robot Arms in Real Time
abstract: Multimodal agents can now control robot arms by calling tools and writing code. Existing benchmarks fall short in three ways: most test one or two arms on short tasks, many pause the world while the agent thinks, and many give it ground-truth object positions. We present RoboTeam, a simulated benchmark where agents control 4 to 16 robot arms in real time from camera images alone. Its 36 tasks are long jobs that the arms must do together, such as passing timbers or building a picture from hundreds of cubes. We start from the most flexible agent system, the adaptive system, where one agent decides when to fork delegates. With it, gpt-6.1-sol and opus-5.5 complete 28 and 27 tasks, and four other models at most 3. But at a high price: a typical task takes gpt-6.1-sol 3.5 hours and 218 million input tokens, and a third of its steps fail at least once and must be retried. We then compare it with three fixed systems: single-agent, hierarchical, and decentralized. All four complete a similar number of tasks but differ in time and tokens. The hierarchical and decentralized systems are faster but use up to 1.9 times the tokens, and the single agent uses fewer tokens but takes 1.6 times as long, so the adaptive system lies between them. Even so, no model or system is yet fast, cheap, and reliable at once. RoboTeam measures these limits where earlier benchmarks cannot: long multi-arm jobs, camera images only, and a world that never pauses.
