title: Auditable Authorization for LLM Agents: Empirical Evidence Across Model, Harness, and Workflow Layers
abstract: Human approval provides effective control only if rejected work stops and authorized work completes. We formalize refusal safety and bounded authorization completeness, and audit three execution boundaries: the model selects a call, the harness schedules and resumes it, and the workflow routes the decision to a protected effect. Paired decisions, exact traces, and native business-state witnesses support experiments with three models, five prompt arms, four runtime approval designs, two additional framework replays, and 100 public workflow sources. The paired model panel leaves seven of 300 approvals unfinished despite zero denied effects; parallel confirmation loses an approved branch in three tasks per model, restoration omits 336/672 CrewAI approvals, and four of 59 comparable n8n workflows execute after Reject. Comparing intent, generated calls, dispatch, and native effects identifies the first observable divergence and its repair target. This yields a practical audit contract that makes both refusal safety and authorization completeness independently verifiable, converting human approval from a procedural formality into an enforceable control boundary between intent and real-world effect.
authors: Bangjie Deng;Xiaoxuan Lu;Wenjun Chen;Chengge Wen;Yulin Wang;Jiayue Meng;Yao Yu;Liying Liang;Weijia Han;Ziwei Hong;Zidong Yu

title: Beyond Alignment: Supervising the Generator for EEG-to-Image Reconstruction
abstract: Visual brain decoding translates neural activity into human-interpretable images. While recent EEG-to-image reconstruction methods rely on aligning EEG signals with pretrained visual embeddings to condition an image generator, we empirically demonstrate that stronger cross-modal alignment do not translate into comparable gains in reconstruction quality. This indicates that improving the input condition alone is insufficient; the generative process itself requires explicit supervision. Although Representation Alignment (REPA) offers a solution by guiding diffusion transformers with pretrained vision encoder features, we find that EEG-conditioned generators struggle to follow these fixed targets. To address this mismatch, we introduce generation-derived supervision (GDS): an image-conditioned teacher that translates static image-encoder features into the internal representation space of a diffusion transformer. Our EEG-conditioned student generator closely tracks these dynamic targets during denoising, discarding the teacher at inference. Evaluated on THINGS-EEG and THINGS-MEG, our approach consistently outperforms conditioning-centric baselines, achieving state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity.

title: CompoundingKernel: Self-Improving from Zero to First
abstract: We present CompoundingKernel, a self-improving agent system that writes GPU kernels by search. As of 2026-11-11, its generated kernels rank #1 on the public L1, L2 and Quantization boards of SOL-ExecBench (NVIDIA B200). They have held #1 on L1 since 2026-10-27, albeit a short loss on 2026-11-07. All 235 problems have a site-verified correct kernel; on the 209 public-board problems they are 4.40x faster than the benchmark's reference baseline. The search starts from zero: agents get each problem's PyTorch definition but no reference kernels or official scores. A per-problem archive outside the model holds every correct kernel and its lineage. An LLM controller reads it, picks a parent or a new design, and gives each parallel child agent one direction. Checks outside the model decide correctness. At equal wall time, it beat a coded UCB style tree on 35 of 38 problems by making 2.4x as many correct attempts. Over a thousand agents ran at once, and one warm restart fix raised their evaluation rate 3.6x. We find that the rate of reliable measurements, not the number of agents, limits how far such a search scales. Our code and kernels are available on URL.
authors: Qian Qu;Hongyang Wang;Wenbo Chen;Yichuan Li;Jingguo Liu;Xian Li;Xuan Wang;Ruochen Wen;Leo Fan;Yiming Yan;Zheshen Wang;Benoit Dumoulin

title: Can an Agent Rethink What It Knows? Selective Scene Memory Updates in a Changing World
abstract: Task configurations in factories, warehouses, and everyday physical environments change over time. Physical AI systems therefore need to incorporate new facts into scene memory while preserving valid information about equipment, objects, and operating constraints. We study updates to this parametric semantic-memory layer and present a joint evaluation of correction and preservation under finite update budgets. At fixed current fact count and memory parameter count, the protocol combines independent single-fact updates, budget trajectories, old-to-new answer diagnostics, and first stable success. Using a frozen 4B language model with late-layer LoRA, we evaluate seven preparation conditions and six update budgets on four-field synthetic semantic configurations. In two exposure-matched history conditions, increasing the budget from eight to 32 updates raises joint success from 6.25% to 94.79% and 91.15%, respectively, while exact obsolete-value outputs fall from 174/192 and 166/192 to zero. Constant32, which matches preparation steps but repeatedly trains on unchanged content during the first 32 events, achieves higher early joint success at eight steps (53.65%); at 32 steps, it reaches 85.42%, below both changing-history conditions. These results distinguish rapid correction under a small budget from simultaneous correctness of the new fact and the other three facts after further training. For both changing histories, most cases remain jointly correct at all subsequent measured points from step 16 onward. Output analysis shows that short-budget failures primarily retain the old value; repeated training on the new fact together with the other current facts progressively replaces these obsolete answers.

title: Temporal Attention-Enhanced Mixture-of-Experts Guidance for Multi-Revolution Low-Thrust Rendezvous
abstract: Multi-revolution low-thrust rendezvous requires both long-duration orbital transfer and precise terminal control. This paper proposes a temporal attention-enhanced mixture-of-experts guidance law trained by deep reinforcement learning. A far-range expert acts on modified equinoctial elements, a terminal expert acts on the relative state in the target's local frame, and a learned gate blends their thrust commands. The terminal expert encodes its observation history with a Transformer to address partial observability, and the gate uses a separate encoder to account for the resulting history-dependent command. The experts are pretrained separately, the gate is trained with both experts frozen, and the complete guidance law is then fine-tuned end to end. On 600 test missions, it achieves rendezvous in every case at tolerances of 10 m and 1 m/s, reduces mean flight time and delta-v by 50.6% and 44.5% relative to distance-based hard switching, and remains successful without retraining under navigation errors, unmodeled orbital perturbations, eclipse-induced thrust outages, and thrust loss.
authors: Chenglong Wu;Yi Zhou;Hongxu Zhu;Jialong Song;Hexi Baoyin
comment: 27 pages, 11 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Aerospace and Electronic Systems

title: Revisiting What Makes a Good Context Subset: A Sparse Latent Basis Perspective
abstract: Selecting context subsets is increasingly important in modern LLM inference, yet what makes a subset effective remains unclear. We study this question in the controlled setting of few-shot demonstration selection. We examine a hypothesis that demonstrations should collectively provide task-relevant information needed by a target query. Assuming that the query representation provides a useful proxy for these requirements, we formulate selection as sparse reconstruction and instantiate it with Residual Explanation Search (RES), a Matching-Pursuit-style diagnostic procedure. Across seven benchmarks and eight open-weight LLMs, no retrieval objective is universally best. RES outperforms MMR in 34 of 56 model--dataset pairs, with its clearest advantage on sentiment tasks, suggesting that query-conditioned collective reconstruction may capture useful complementarity that pairwise dissimilarity misses. Relevance-based retrieval remains strong on template-heavy reasoning benchmarks, while all retrieval methods underperform zero-shot prediction on average on StrategyQA, where a solution-reconstruction analysis is consistent with the query not exposing the required external knowledge. Target-model hidden states further show that retrieval objectives interact differently with representation spaces: middle-layer representations generally favor similarity retrieval, whereas last-layer representations are often stronger for residual- and diversity-based selection. These findings support a conditional, representation-dependent account of context subset quality rather than a universally superior selector.
comment: 17 pages, 2 figures. The format of ACL rolling review

title: Neural Dual Bounds: Valid-by-Construction JGLP Warm-Starts for MAP and Constrained MAP
abstract: We present Neural Dual Bounds, a calibration-free framework that produces deterministic upper bounds for MAP inference in probabilistic graphical models using a single neural-network forward pass. The framework trains a network to output the edge messages of a mini-bucket style upper bound on a given join-graph decomposition in a self-supervised manner by directly minimizing a smooth dual objective. The output of this network can be used at test time to warm-start a standard JGLP optimizer. Across diverse benchmarks, this warm start yields dual gaps that are orders of magnitude tighter than those from zero initialization, with the largest gains in the early-iteration regime. We also apply our framework for the constrained MAP (CMPE) task, where neural warm starts with test-time adaptation are comparable to the adaptive baseline on Bayesian networks and achieve the tightest dual gaps, by one to two orders of magnitude, on the grid and segmentation families.
authors: Akshay Vyas;Shivvrat Arya;Brij Malhotra;Tahrima Rahman;Vibhav Gogate;Nicholas Ruozzi

title: Mem2Fair: Online Fairness Control for Text-to-Video Generation via Fair Memory
abstract: Text-to-video (T2V) generation models can produce systematically unfair demographic outcomes when prompts leave protected attributes unspecified. For example, prompts describing nurses without specifying gender may disproportionately generate videos depicting female nurses. Mitigating unfairness in T2V generation is particularly challenging: training-based methods that modify model internals require architecture-specific access and risk disrupting temporal consistency, while sampling-based methods often incur costly pre-deployment video generation. We present the first conditional online approachability formulation of attribute-level fairness for T2V generation. Building on this formulation, we introduce Mem2Fair, a plug-and-play framework that maintains concept-conditioned Fair Memory. Using generated videos at inference time as feedback, Mem2Fair selects prompt-level attribute interventions based on the deviation from each concept's prescribed fairness target, without training or separate pre-deployment sampling. Experiments demonstrate that Mem2Fair consistently improves fairness over the unmodified generator and existing baselines across multiple demographic attributes, prompt settings, and target distributions, while maintaining comparable prompt-video alignment and video quality. We further demonstrate its effectiveness on commercial black-box T2V models.
authors: Pengyu Chen;Jiaming Zhang;Xiaohua Feng;Yuyuan Li;Chaochao Chen

title: STaSBO: LLM-Guided Strategy Planning and Configuration Selection for Bayesian Optimization
abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) enables sample-efficient search for expensive black-box problems, but its performance depends strongly on surrogate-acquisition configurations whose suitability varies across problems and optimization states. We take a significant step toward LLM-driven strategic management of BO with STaSBO, a task-agnostic meta-controller that plans search behavior and jointly selects surrogate-acquisition configurations, while numerical BO retains responsibility for probabilistic modeling and candidate generation. STaSBO comprises two coordinated stages: strategy planning and strategy-guided configuration selection. A structured memory system connects prior plans, configuration selections, and candidate behaviors to optimization states, allowing the controller to revise its trajectory summary and behavioral plans during planning. To navigate the large joint configuration space, the selection stage shortlists configurations using surrogate fit evidence. Prospective BO-action diagnostics then expose the candidate behaviors, supporting final joint selection against the behavioral plans. Across 12 synthetic mathematical and 10 scientific and engineering application tasks, STaSBO achieves the best average rank against 11 baselines: 2.17 and 2.60, compared with 4.08 and 4.10 for the strongest baseline in each suite, respectively.

title: Incremental Learning of Vision-Language Models via Task Subspace Projection and Dynamic LoRA
abstract: Recent pre-trained vision-language models often encounter a Multi-Domain Task-Incremental Learning (MTIL) scenario in practice, where a set of classes of multi-modal tasks arrive incrementally. Due to privacy concerns and memory constraints, MTIL with pre-trained models encounters forgetting of knowledge from old tasks, degradation of zero-shot transfer capability, and underfitting of new-task knowledge. To overcome these challenges, previous MTIL methods attempt to learn a discriminative cross-task identification (CTI) module and an effective new-task adaptation (NTA) module. However, current CTI modules suffer from severe task confusion between seen and unseen tasks, and NTA modules cannot adaptively balance the performance and parameter cost while incorporating task-specific knowledge. To alleviate the above dilemmas, we propose an effective and efficient TSP-DLoRA method for MTIL, which consists of Task Subspace Projection (TSP) and Dynamic Low Rank Adapter (DLoRA) modules. Specifically, our TSP module includes a task identifier classifier based on task-specific subspaces and a feature projection strategy that can determine the identifier associated with samples from both seen and unseen tasks. Our DLoRA improves the knowledge adaptation from new tasks by dynamically assigning Low Rank Adapter (LoRA) across transformer layers based on the task distributions. Experimental evaluations across 11 datasets, using three performance metrics, demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method. Code is available at https://github.com/FerdinandZJU/TSP-DLoRA.
authors: Hao Fu;Qian Feng;Hanbin Zhao;Jiahua Dong;Xu Tan;Lina Wei;Chao Zhang;Hui Qian
comment: Pre-peer-review version of an article accepted for publication in the International Journal of Computer Vision (IJCV)

title: Site-Specific Cell Shaping: An Agentic Framework
abstract: An agentic framework is proposed for cell shaping in future sixth-generation (6G) wireless network planning. Cell shaping controls the coverage and interferences of base stations (BSs) through antenna parameters configuration, providing an important means of improving coverage. In contrast to conventional approaches that reply on costly performance evaluations, the proposed framework achieves intelligent and efficient antenna configuration through a perception-reasoning-reflection loop. Specifically, a Configuration Agent combines scene information, evaluation history, and reflection feedback to generate antenna configuration proposals. Then, a ray tracing(RT)-based evaluator assesses these proposals and returns a structured performance summary. Next, a Reflection Agent interprets these results to diagnose site-specific performance deficiencies, recommend feasible configuration adjustments, and accumulate conditional experience. Through this iterative process, the framework accumulates site-specific experience and progressively refines antenna configurations without human-in-the-loop intervention. Simulations in real-world urban scenarios demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves lower outage probabilities than the considered benchmark methods, highlighting the effectiveness of agentic reasoning and reflection in translating site-specific performance feedback and accumulated experience into adaptive antenna configuration decisions.

title: From Non-parametric Statistics to Images: Generating Galaxy Morphologies
abstract: Non-parametric statistics characterize complex galaxy morphologies but do not specify how to construct images that reproduce those statistics. We present Flow-VAE, which combines a variational autoencoder with a conditional normalizing flow to generate images conditioned on concentration, asymmetry, smoothness (CAS), Gini coefficient (G), and M20. A Gaussian mixture model completes unspecified descriptors and measures the training-distribution support of requested combinations. Using a dataset of 240,000 DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys r-band images, we evaluate fidelity by remeasuring morphological statistics from model outputs and comparing them with the inputs. With a tolerance of +/-10% of each descriptor's adopted range, descriptor-specific recovery rates are 96.62-99.97% for reconstruction and 87.81-99.83% for single-parameter generation among valid measurements. Generated descriptors show regression toward typical training values, while less-supported joint conditions produce broader residuals and systematic offsets. These results quantify the extent to which Flow-VAE can generate galaxy images consistent with prescribed non-parametric morphological statistics.
authors: Quanfeng Xu;Mi Chen;Renhao Ye;Siyuan Chen;Nan Li;Shiyin Shen
comment: 19 pages, 8 figures,accepted for publication in Universe

title: Martingale and signed diffusive optimal transport: geodesics and gradient flows
abstract: In signed diffusive transport, a path of probability densities $ρ_t$ on the circle and a momentum $m_t$ satisfy $\partial_tρ=\partial_{xx}m$, and the cost of the path is the action $\int_0^1\int m^2/(2ρ)\,dx\,dt$. The diffusivity $m/ρ$ is an unknown of this variational problem and can take either sign. On the real line, the constraint $m\ge0$ gives the martingale Benamou-Brenier problem of Huesmann and Trevisan. We study geodesics and minimizing movements, which discretize gradient flows. For signed geodesics, we prove the $Γ$-convergence of the time-discrete problems for all probability endpoints, and of the fully discrete Fourier-grid problems as the space and time meshes tend to zero independently, without a positive lower bound on the densities. For a modified Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) scheme on the torus, we prove convergence along subsequences to a weak solution of a fourth-order equation, the Derrida-Lebowitz-Speer-Spohn equation for the entropy in dimension one, under the assumption that the densities of the scheme stay above a positive constant on every finite time interval. In dimension one, the normalized minimum values of a discretization with nonnegative momentum and of a discretization by martingale couplings with a fourth-moment cost converge to the same martingale transport cost, and we identify the limit of the minimizing movements with nonnegative momentum for potential energies with bounded second and third derivatives. We compute geodesics and modified JKO trajectories by Douglas-Rachford splitting and by an interior-point method, and bound the optimization errors of selected solutions by dual lower bounds evaluated in interval arithmetic. The computed geodesics approach zero density near the points where the diffusivity changes sign, and along computed trajectories of the modified JKO scheme the density minimum can fall below its initial value.

title: Unit-Level Conformal Inference for Panel Counterfactuals
abstract: We develop conformal inference for panel counterfactual estimators using the exchangeability of prediction errors across units rather than over time. Existing conformal methods for panels with few treated units rely on temporal properties of treated-unit residuals, which are vulnerable to strong temporal heterogeneity such as nonstationarity. We instead hold out each control unit, hide its relevant outcomes, and predict them using the same rule applied to the treated unit. Target-date estimators, including difference-in-differences and synthetic control, use controls' pre-treatment and target-date outcomes to construct the counterfactual, allowing both full conformal confidence sets and Jackknife+ intervals. Full-path estimators, including factor-model imputation and matrix completion, also use controls' outcomes at other post-treatment dates; for these, we use the Jackknife+. Both procedures yield finite-sample, period-wise confidence sets under this across-unit exchangeability, without requiring stationarity or random assignment. We characterize when the coverage holds and show why a common prediction rule alone does not ensure it. For multiple treated units, a block Jackknife+ covers their average effect, while a relabeling test is exact for sharp nulls over all treated cells. We show that the synthetic control placebo test is a full conformal test of no effect that extends to full-path estimators. We also relate our procedures to a parametric bootstrap and classify common estimators by the inference they allow. We illustrate our procedures in three empirical applications.

title: On-policy distillation as a Backdoor Propagation Channel
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is emerging as an important paradigm for the post training of large language models, improving student models by leveraging supervision generated online by teacher models. However, whether this process also transfers latent security risks from teacher models to student models remains insufficiently studied. In this work, we reveal a new security risk in which an attacker first implants a conditional backdoor into the teacher model through supervised fine tuning (SFT), after which OPD can transfer the backdoor to the student model with only an extremely small proportion of trigger prompt exposure. More concerningly, we find that such backdoor transfer is substantially stronger under OPD than under conventional distillation methods, suggesting that OPD may provide an efficient channel for propagating backdoors across models. Our mechanistic analysis shows that the backdoor signal is primarily transmitted through anomalous differences in the conditional probabilities produced by the teacher model for triggered and clean inputs, and is gradually internalized into the internal representations of the student model during training. Furthermore, we investigate how to suppress such anomalous conditional probability signals at the source of distillation supervision and, based on this analysis, propose an OPD training method tailored to this conditional backdoor propagation setting to mitigate the risk of backdoor transfer induced by untrusted teacher supervision.
authors: Zane Fu;Yanzhao Zheng;Ziting Qin;Qianshan Wei;Yi Yu;Gongli Xi;Jihuai Zhu;Baohua Dong;Hangcheng Zhu;Ruohui Huang;Gang Yu

title: Fragmentation in Non-Hermitian Many-Body Systems
abstract: In non-Hermitian (NH) fermionic chains with spatially random imaginary gauge fields, single-particle eigenstates exhibit erratic NH skin localization with strongly fluctuating, subexponential decay, distinct from both conventional skin accumulation and Anderson localization. At finite filling, Pauli exclusion suppresses macroscopic accumulation and instead leads to fragmentation of the particle density, in sharp contrast to Hermitian disordered systems. Using exact free-fermion methods, we show that the density organizes into disconnected regions of high and low occupancy, forming spatially separated Fermi domains whose number $N_{\mathrm{FS}}$ scales subextensively with system size $L$. Remarkably, fragmentation is not only an equilibrium property but also emerges dynamically in the NH evolution, unlike in Hermitian systems where such structures are not dynamically selected. This behavior admits a Coulomb-gas description in a stochastic potential, establishing a direct link between erratic NH skin localization and real-space fragmentation of many-body states.
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures, accepted for publication in Phys. Rev.B, Supplemental document not included

title: Learning the Average Dose-Response Function with a Right-Censored Treatment
abstract: This paper considers estimation and inference for the average dose-response function under right-censored treatment duration and missing outcomes for censored units. Using the duration lower bounds provided by censored records, we construct a novel multiply robust estimator through augmented local estimating equations. Under suitable regularity conditions, the estimator remains consistent when any two of the outcome regression, treatment density, and censoring survival function are consistently estimated. We establish its convergence rate and asymptotic distribution within a cross-fitting framework under appropriate conditions on nuisance estimation. To address local smoothing bias that can distort confidence interval coverage, we further develop a debiased estimator that supports asymptotically valid pointwise inference without undersmoothing. Under additional uniform conditions, we construct simultaneous confidence bands using a Gaussian multiplier bootstrap. Simulation studies evaluate estimation accuracy, the validity of pointwise and uniform inference, and robustness to nuisance model misspecification. A semi-synthetic study calibrated to NHANES illustrates the proposed methods in a setting with a known dose-response function.

title: Omni-Workspace: Benchmarking Omni-Modal AI Assistants on Multimodal Workspace Tasks
abstract: Omni-modal agents are expected to move beyond multimodal understanding toward completing complex tasks in realistic multimodal environments. In these settings, information is distributed across heterogeneous files and modalities, with cross-file and cross-modal dependencies requiring agents to continually coordinate perception, reasoning, and tool use as newly gathered evidence informs subsequent actions. However, existing omni-modal benchmarks primarily focus on multimodal perception and understanding, leaving complex task completion through sustained interaction with multimodal workspaces underexplored. We introduce Omni-Workspace, a benchmark comprising 380 deep-research-style tasks across four multimodal workspace types and two difficulty levels. These tasks require agents to inspect and process workspace files, retrieve external information when needed, integrate evidence across files and modalities, and produce artifacts satisfying explicit requirements. Evaluating 18 representative models reveals limitations in long-horizon multimodal workspace execution, with the best model scoring only 65.93 on average. Further analysis identifies multimodal context inflation and task-state drift as recurring challenges. Motivated by these findings, we further propose OmniFocus, a lightweight approach combining multimodal working-memory management with explicit task-state tracking to improve performance and efficiency. Omni-Workspace advances the evaluation and development of omni-modal agents toward autonomous completion of complex tasks in multimodal workspaces.
authors: Yuhao Wang;Yucheng Zhao;Yiran Zhong;Feida Zhu;Hongcheng Liu;Qichao Wang;Ming Ma;Yu Wang

title: LogT: Logically Think with Images for Visual Search
abstract: Thinking with images empowers vision-language models (VLMs) to use an external Zoom-in tool for fine-grained visual search. Recent works employ supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) with tool-specific designs to enable such capabilities. However, achieving logical reasoning alongside accurate and efficient tool use remains a significant challenge. To address this, we shift the focus away from increasing RL complexity and instead identify SFT data quality as a key bottleneck. We then propose LogT (short for Logically Think with Images), a fully automated SFT data engine that explicitly enforces logic-chain-guided reasoning. LogT generates an SFT dataset featuring challenging, visually grounded questions and structured tool-use traces with human-like logic. We validate our approach by fine-tuning two base models, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3.5-8B, on the dataset and evaluating them across seven benchmark test sets. We show that LogT-SFT based on Qwen2.5-VL-7B outperforms the state-of-the-art trained with both SFT and RL, despite using 3.1$\times$ less data and $>120\times$ fewer GPU hours. Furthermore, applying a simple RL recipe without tool-specific design on LogT-SFT yields a model that surpasses prior methods with complex RL setups by a substantial 9.59-point margin. In addition to strong performance gains, our model exhibits higher tool-use accuracy and efficiency, as well as more structured and logically consistent reasoning traces, directly validating the effectiveness of our approach.
authors: Yanjun Fu;Quanzeng You;Jiadong Guo;Yujie Lu;Sai Charitha Akula;Haiping Wu;Miao Liu;Sanghamitra Dutta;Lu Yuan

title: What Moves a LoCoMo Score? Memory Context, Answer Prompts and Judges
abstract: LoCoMo is a widely reported benchmark for long-term conversational memory, but published scores mix memory quality with choices of answer prompt, judge and baseline layout that are rarely reported together. We measure how much these choices move a score, and evaluate Becos, a team memory system for coding agents, as a black box under all of them: ten conversations (1,540 questions), two answer models (gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4.1-mini), two answer prompts and three LLM judges, against a whole-conversation baseline rerun under identical conditions. Changing only the judge moves a score by up to 7.2 points and changing only the answer prompt by up to 9.3. A blind human check of 150 answers finds the judges reliable when they agree, and the primary judge's errors on disputed answers working against Becos rather than for it. Becos answers from a context with 90% fewer characters than the whole conversation. Its configuration was developed on LoCoMo itself, so there is no held-out set. With gpt-4o-mini answers it scores clearly higher than the whole conversation (79.7 vs 73.0 with the short prompt, paired 95% interval for the difference +3.8 to +9.5; 88.8 vs 77.5 with a step-by-step prompt). With gpt-4.1-mini answers the two score about the same (83.2 vs 83.1; 92.5 vs 92.1). We release every answer and verdict and the scoring script.
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures. Answers, judge verdicts, human-check grades and scoring script: https://github.com/becos-ai/locomo-results

title: Intersection Cuts for Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Programs via Decision-Diagram-Free Sets
abstract: We introduce a novel decision-diagram-based framework for generating intersection cuts to strengthen polyhedral relaxations of bounded mixed-integer nonlinear programs (MINLPs) with general nonlinear constraints. Building on decision diagrams (DDs) that provide outer approximations of MINLP feasible regions, we propose the concept of DD-free sets, which are convex regions whose interiors do not intersect the sets represented by the DDs. By exploiting the underlying graphical structure, we develop efficient methods for constructing these regions without requiring restrictive assumptions on the functional form of nonlinear constraints or access to distance oracles. We investigate the maximality properties of DD-free sets and devise algorithms for obtaining maximal forbidden regions within several structured classes. The resulting intersection cuts exploit geometric information retained in DD representations, enabling further strengthening of relaxations beyond what can be achieved through conventional DD-based convexification. We also introduce interval DDs to facilitate the representation of general nonlinear constraints and establish convergence results for intersections of constraint-specific DDs, providing a theoretical foundation for their integration into global optimization frameworks. Computational experiments on challenging open instances from MINLPLib, encompassing a broad range of nonlinear and nonconvex structures, demonstrate that the proposed approach can substantially improve dual bounds and achieve greater optimality-gap closure than state-of-the-art global optimization solvers. These findings highlight the potential of exploiting graphical representations of infeasible regions to develop stronger cutting planes for general MINLPs.

title: Generalization Testing of Grid Foundation Models for Power Flow and Optimal Power Flow
abstract: There is growing interest in foundation models (FMs) for power grids, particularly for power flow and optimal power flow. Their usefulness depends on generalization accuracy, which existing works test on their own benchmarks. We propose a three-axis framework to test their generalization limits: changed admittance matrices of training grids, load levels, and unseen grids. We test GENCO, LUMINA and GridSFM against the DC baseline, alongside their reported limitations, and discuss theoretical reasons for their failures. Experiments reveal that adding a line degrades all FMs more than removing one, and longer lines eventually make LUMINA and fine-tuned GENCO worse than DC. All three degrade beyond their training load range, where the loading-voltage curve steepens. On unseen grids, LUMINA degrades sharply even inside its training range, and GridSFM fails on the grid farthest from it. Thus, beyond training conditions, FMs behave more like meta-models requiring test-time fine-tuning data and compute.

title: Ref-MIL: Plug-and-Play Posterior Refinement for Multiple Instance Learning in QSM-Based Brain Disease Classification
abstract: Quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM) is a novel quantitative MRI contrast for studying tissue susceptibility changes in brain disorders, including Parkinson's disease (PD) and multiple sclerosis (MS). However, small cohorts and the lack of local annotations make developing deep learning models for QSM-based diagnosis challenging. In this work, we propose PoRef-MIL, a weakly supervised multiple instance learning (MIL) framework combining iterative slice relabeling and network retraining with a plug-and-play posterior refinement module (PRM). During training, a 2D dual-branch diagnosis network and a subject-level classifier were alternately trained for five rounds. The classifier was used to update slice pseudo-labels for retraining the diagnosis network. The PRM was applied during inference to refine slice probabilities through bidirectional posterior inference and calculate entropy-derived confidence from the refined probabilities, which was then used in sliding-window scoring to obtain subject-level predictions. PoRef-MIL was evaluated on an in-house PD cohort of 287 participants and a public MS cohort of 150 participants. Compared with eight classification methods, PoRef-MIL achieved the highest mean areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.942 and 0.872, and accuracies of 0.926 and 0.833, for PD and MS classification, respectively. Ablation experiments were conducted to validate the effectiveness of iterative relabeling and PRM, and the plug-and-play feature of the proposed PRM was also evaluated using four state-of-the-art MIL models. Overall, PoRef-MIL offers a promising approach to QSM-based disease classification in small cohorts without manual slice annotations.
authors: Ang Gaoa;Rui Jina;Yin Liu;Pengfei Rong;Feng Liu;G. Bruce Pike;Hongfu Sun;Yang Gao

title: Calibrating the Uncertainty of Self-Supervised Monocular Depth without Labels
abstract: Self-supervised monocular depth networks can predict a per-pixel uncertainty, which is mainly evaluated by how well it ranks pixels according to their error. Such metrics are insensitive to the magnitude of the uncertainty, so an uncertainty half as large as the actual error obtains the same score. In this paper, we investigate whether the predicted uncertainty is as large as the depth error, both on average (scale) and across confident and uncertain, near and far pixels (shape). On KITTI, the scale is miscalibrated for every uncertainty estimate we evaluate, and the error of MonoProb is nearly twice its predicted uncertainty. We propose MonoCal, which corrects both the scale and the shape without ground-truth depth. Scale calibration multiplies the uncertainty by a single constant measured from stereo pairs, requiring no retraining, and this constant closely matches the one fitted with ground truth. Since a constant cannot change the shape, we further retrain the uncertainty to predict where the depth of the network disagrees with that of a second self-supervised network. Experiments on KITTI show that MonoCal achieves better calibration across uncertainty levels and depth ranges than rescaling with ground truth, while still using a single image at inference. Code will be made publicly available.

title: A Unified Control Framework, Mathematical Model, and Five-layer Closed-loop Case Study for Embodied Intelligence Control Systems
abstract: Embodied intelligence holds that an agent develops cognition and behavior through real-time body-environment interaction, so its control system must tightly couple perception, decision making, learning, optimization, constraints, and physical execution. This report asks whether a unified framework exists, how its mathematical models unify, and how the framework is realized computably. Four conclusions emerge. (1) No single framework is accepted, but the field converges on a common skeleton: from operational-space and whole-body control to MPC, reinforcement learning, active inference, and diffusion/flow policies, all reduce to constrained sequential decision making on the configuration manifold. (2) Two languages describe it-deterministic optimal control (Euler-Lagrange plus constrained OCP, reduced in real time to a QP) and probabilistic inference (MDP/POMDP plus free-energy minimization)-rigorously bridged by control as inference and KL/path-integral control. (3) Engineering unification is already achieved by constrained optimization; the new frontier is cross-morphology, cross-task shared representation. (4) The hardest gap is provable stability and safety, the entry point for spectral, geometric, differentiable-optimization, and safe-learning methods. A single-link manipulator then runs through all five layers: L4 parses the instruction into a reference, L3 identifies a Koopman lifted linear world model, L2 solves a receding constrained QP, L1 adds torque saturation and a CBF, and L0 is the true nonlinear plant. Closed-loop tracking RMSE is 0.0218 rad with all constraints satisfied and a world-model error near 5 x 10^-6 rad, reported with curves and a 3D animation.
authors: Yiwei Zhou;Zhongcheng Lei;Xiaoran Dai;Wenshan Hu;Hong Zhou

title: Do VLMs Really Look at the Road? A Diagnostic Evaluation for Autonomous Driving
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly being evaluated for autonomous driving through question-answering benchmarks, yet high benchmark accuracy does not necessarily reflect visually grounded reasoning. We present a diagnostic evaluation framework that systematically probes whether VLMs base safety-critical driving decisions on visual evidence or instead rely on language priors, answer biases, and dataset regularities. Our benchmark comprises two task categories, Adverse Weather and Junctions \& Intersections, with a nuScenes spatial reasoning extension, and evaluates open-source (general, driving, and spatial-reasoning) VLMs along four diagnostic protocols: image versus no-image evaluation, counterfactual weather sensitivity, linguistic robustness under paraphrasing and negation, and spatial reasoning. All ground-truth labels are derived programmatically from BDD100K and DriveLM annotations, enabling reproducible evaluation without manual labeling. Across all models, we find that competitive overall accuracy conceals systematic failure modes, including strong affirmation bias, limited sensitivity to counterfactual scene changes, near-chance performance on negated questions despite high paraphrase consistency, and confident driving decisions even without visual input. These results demonstrate that current open-source VLMs remain insufficiently grounded for safety-critical autonomous driving and underscore the need for diagnostic evaluation beyond aggregate accuracy.

title: WA-JEPA: Goal-Aware Predictive Feedback Action Refinement for a World-Action Model
abstract: JEPA-based world models predict action consequences in latent space, but representative planning approaches rely on candidate-action search, requiring repeated evaluation of action sequences and incurring substantial online computational cost. Direct action generation avoids this search, yet how to leverage latent predictions to guide action generation given task goals remains a key challenge in translating learned physical dynamics into effective decisions. We introduce WA-JEPA, a world-action model that couples action generation, action-conditioned latent prediction, and goal-aware feedback. The model first generates an action proposal and predicts the resulting future scenes and proprioceptive states, then refines the proposal through two complementary feedback paths, using the task goal as a reference. Goal-discrepancy residual feedback (GDRF) uses differences between the latent representations of predicted scenes and the task goal to guide chunk-wise action refinement. Future-scene context feedback (FSCF) preserves fine-grained predicted scene representations to guide subsequent action refinement. Jointly learned from offline demonstrations, this process iteratively updates the same plan before execution, making future predictions directly participate in action generation without candidate-action search. We evaluate short-horizon goal reaching, long-horizon tasks, and full-task execution. The results show that goal-aware predictive feedback supports competitive task performance while maintaining a compact model and low online computational cost. Code is available at https://github.com/Dovisya/WA-JEPA.
authors: Tao An;Weihang Liang;Tianqi Wang;Chuqing Cao;Wenming Tan;Kai Zhang;Haibo Lei;Tao Xie;Lijun Zhao;Ruifeng Li
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures, including supplementary material. Code available at https://github.com/Dovisya/WA-JEPA

title: Advancing Quantum Reinforcement Learning with Differentiable Quantum Architecture Search and Adaptive Non-local Observables
abstract: Quantum Reinforcement Learning (QRL) using variational quantum circuits (VQCs) is constrained by fixed measurement protocols and hand-designed circuit ansätze. Adaptive Non-local Observables (ANO) and Differentiable Quantum Architecture Search (DiffQAS) address these issues independently, but to our knowledge have not been combined or compared in a single QRL framework. We present an ablation of ANO and DiffQAS within the Quantum Time-series Transformer (QTSTransformer), evaluated on a 2 x 2 factorial design across six environments--two classic-control tasks and four Atari 2600 games. Three findings emerge. First, the quantum agent outperforms a matched classical transformer baseline on five of six environments, with absolute scores ranging from 360.0 vs 304.0 (MarioBros) to 17.2 vs 2.5 (Breakout), while using approximately 12.5x fewer transformer parameters on the four Atari environments (more modestly so on the two classic-control tasks). Second, ANO and DiffQAS provide complementary benefits: ANO yields the largest gain on continuous-state CartPole (347.7 vs 223.2), while DiffQAS yields the largest absolute Atari gains (Breakout 17.2 vs 3.0; DonkeyKong 70.0 vs 37.0). Third, combining both innovations exhibits an asymmetric interaction: ANO-dominant tasks tolerate DiffQAS, whereas DiffQAS-dominant tasks degrade when ANO is added. These results provide design guidance for QRL agents: select between ANO and DiffQAS according to whether the bottleneck is the measurement basis or the gate topology, rather than applying both indiscriminately.
authors: Junghoon Justin Park;Kyumin Lee;Anna Jung;Samuel Yen-Chi Chen;Huan-Hsin Tseng;Shinjae Yoo;Jiook Cha
journal_ref: 2026 IEEE International Conference on Quantum Artificial Intelligence (QAI)

title: Scalable and Interpretable Quantum Mixture of Experts for High-Dimensional Spatio-Temporal Data
abstract: Quantum Mixture of Experts (QMoE) architectures offer a promising path toward scalable quantum machine learning, yet existing approaches remain largely confined to low-dimensional benchmarks and often rely on naive input partitioning that disrupts feature dependencies. We address these gaps by introducing Feature-Partitioned QMoE, which partitions high-dimensional spatio-temporal inputs into functionally coherent feature groups and assigns each group to a dedicated quantum expert. We further propose a hierarchical interpretability framework that leverages the modular structure of QMoE to produce circuit-level gating analysis, per-expert gradient saliency, and heterogeneity-based subtype discovery. Applied to ADHD classification from resting-state fMRI (N=4,458, ABCD Study, 180 brain ROIs, 363 timepoints), the proposed Theory-Driven QMoE achieves performance comparable to matched-capacity classical and quantum baselines while enabling circuit-attributable interpretation. The framework identifies FDR-corrected ADHD-associated biomarkers in executive-control and anterior default-mode networks and reveals three neurobiologically meaningful ADHD subtypes. These results position Feature-Partitioned QMoE as a scalable and interpretable methodology for applying quantum machine learning to high-dimensional biomedical data.
authors: Junghoon Justin Park;Anna Jung;Kyumin Lee;Samuel Yen-Chi Chen;Huan-Hsin Tseng;Shinjae Yoo;Jiook Cha
journal_ref: 2026 IEEE International Conference on Quantum Artificial Intelligence (QAI)

title: Isolating Perception for Multi-View Planning under Occlusion-Induced Partial Observability
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are beginning to saturate visual planning benchmarks, yet they fail to resolve depth ambiguity and degrade sharply with problem size under occlusion-induced partial observability (PO). We introduce BW-PO based on the Blocksworld domain, a controlled benchmark that reduces existing VLM planners and formalizers to near-zero performance, and propose VLM-as-perceiver, a paradigm that narrows the VLM's role to local perception while delegating cross-view evidence reconciliation and plan generation to external solvers. Across model-specific challenging subsets of BW-PO, this raises plan success from 1% to 97% for Gemma-4-31B, 0% to 95% for Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, and 3% to 84% for Gemini-3.1-Pro. Isolating perception in this way separates two bottlenecks that are otherwise entangled: reconciliation under depth ambiguity, and completeness of visual extraction under scene density.
authors: Kevin Nguyen;Ceyhun Efe Kayan;Feng Liu;Li Zhang

title: Alternative Computational Formulations for Testing Discrete-Choice Random Utility Models: Half-Space and Network-Flow Formulations
abstract: This paper develops computational algorithms for testing discrete-choice random utility models (RUM). The set of RUM-consistent choice probabilities forms a polytope, and existing computational methods rely on its vertex representation. We exploit alternative half-space (Block--Marschak inequalities) and network-flow representations to develop two methods based on the alternating direction method of multipliers and a flow-based column-generation algorithm. Compared with current vertex-based methods, our algorithms are better suited to GPU implementation. We establish convergence guarantees and provide optimality certificates for all three algorithms. The resulting algorithms achieve $100$--$600\times$ speedups over existing methods. The solver based on our methods is publicly available on Github at \href{https://github.com/mingxiz/d-rum-testing-gpu}{\texttt{d-rum-testing-gpu}}.

title: A Bag of Concepts? Testing Role-Filler Binding in the Verbalizable Workspace
abstract: Runtime alignment monitors built on a verbalizable workspace have been proposed as a way to surface a model's silent cognition before it produces output. Their value rests on the workspace carrying enough structure to distinguish safety-relevant propositions, most of which are relational: "the model plans to deceive the user" and "the user plans to deceive the model" share a concept set and differ only in role assignment. We ask whether the workspace carries the role-filler bindings (which entity fills which role) such a monitor would need, on three frontier language models (Qwen3.6-27B, Gemma-3-12B, Gemma-3-27B-IT), under two lens families (J-lens and R-lens), and with two methods for fitting the role direction (difference-of-means and LRE-gradient). We find a clean dissociation: the workspace carries directions that steer what the model outputs about roles but not the representations the model uses to compute them. Linear probes recover role at near-ceiling from the residual stream but score below a rank-matched random control when reading the workspace, and steering the model along the fitted role direction changes which entity it binds to no more than strength-matched control edits do. Ablating the workspace (zeroing the residual stream's projection onto its ten most active lens directions) damages binding on one of the three models (Gemma-3-27B-IT, holding across three lens variants) and shows no binding-specific damage on the other two, with a rank-matched random subspace as the control; this confirms our design detects binding when present, though scale and instruction tuning are confounded there. A workspace-lens monitor built on these directions would therefore miss a role assignment the model itself represents.
authors: Reya Dawlah;Elizabeth McMillin;Michael Shihong Zhang;Badrish Ananth;Rishi Adi Ruia;Ane Zuñiga;Thomas Jiralerspong
comment: Accepted at Interpretability as a Science Workshop, NeurIPS 2026

title: When Does Confidence Reveal Problem Difficulty?
abstract: While confidence signals are commonly evaluated for their ability to predict a model's own correctness, their relationship with problem difficulty remains less understood. In this work, we investigate a wide range of confidence-related signals and whether they can serve as indicators of problem difficulty across various task domains. We find that perturbation inconsistency, semantic entropy, and solution length exhibit strong associations with population difficulty than token-level uncertainty. Notably, these relationships persist even when restricting the analysis to problems correctly answered by the focal model, suggesting that such signals capture information about difficulty beyond their ability to predict the model's own correctness. We further explore applications of these signals, illustrating the potential and limitations of using confidence-related signals to guide inference-time decisions. Our findings highlight the utility of model-specific signals as imperfect but informative proxies for population-level problem difficulty.
authors: Xiyu Bao;Langyuan Cui;Hwee Tou Ng;Chun Kai Ling

title: EviRef: Evidence-Specific Memories for Logical Anomaly Detection across Capture Conditions
abstract: Logical anomalies arise when every component looks normal but their combination violates the scene rules. In practical inspection, these rules must hold under varying backgrounds, illumination, and imaging quality, with only a few dozen normal images per scene, whereas existing methods couple normality with appearance and merge different constraints into one reference. We model logical normality as decomposable constraints and propose EviRef, a training-free method that builds a separate reference memory for each family of evidence. Component prototypes built once per scene parse images under any capture condition into one label space, on which occupancy and relation constraints are verified. Semantic constraints are verified with whole-image embeddings independent of parsing, and additional evidence such as text is admitted through a task-level gate without modifying existing memories. On VID-AD, EviRef attains a mean image-level area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 92.1% (88.9% with visual evidence alone), the highest among the compared methods under each of five capture conditions, with a standard deviation of 0.5. Even with memories built from only 20 normal images per task, it surpasses all compared methods that use 50 normal images per task.
authors: Yaoting Huang;Wenqi Cai;Yijin Wei;Jianjian Qin;Chunzhi Gu;Haoran Xie;Chao Zhang

title: Executable Archaeology: Reanimating the Logic Theorist
abstract: The Logic Theorist (LT), created by Allen Newell, J. C. Shaw, and Herbert Simon in 1955--1956, is regarded by some as the first artificial intelligence program. It was originally simulated by hand and written in a pseudocode called the Logic Language (LL), which was later called Information Processing Language One (IPL-I). LT was revised many times. The first machine-executed version was written in IPL-II and ran on the JOHNNIAC, and a late version was published in 1963 by Einar Stefferud as a pedagogical document and written in IPL-V, the only version of IPL that was formally released to the public. We describe a reanimation of both the IPL-I (LL) version of LT and the 1963 IPL-V version. Comparing the two reanimations illuminates the process of the invention of early AI algorithms and computer languages.
comment: This paper builds upon a previous ArXiv paper of a similar name: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.13514. This paper is NOT a mere rehash of the previous paper; appropriate citations and comparison are provided in the discussion. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication.
