These features (along with improved performance at low temperature) position the newly discovered GaV$^-$ as a key resource for quantum sensing, networking, and computation.
authors: Adam D. Dodson;Tiamike Dudley;Luca Basso;Leopold Diaz;Jesse J. Lutz;Raj Patel;Matthew Markham;Jacob Henshaw;Andrew M. Mounce

title: Distribution-First Framework for Learning Risk-Sensitive Individualized Treatment Rules
abstract: Learning a risk-sensitive individualized treatment rule (ITR) with patient covariates is challenging when the treatment criterion depends on the full conditional outcome distribution rather than only its conditional mean. Existing methods are largely criterion-specific, making it difficult to compare multiple treatment criteria within a common pipeline, such as quantiles, conditional value-at-risk (CVaR), and complex preference-based objectives such as cumulative prospect theory. We propose a distribution-first framework for risk-sensitive ITR learning that first estimates treatment-specific conditional outcome distributions and then constructs the target ITR by plug-in criterion evaluation. The proposed framework unifies treatment rule learning across multiple criteria and accommodates hard-to-optimize objectives within the same estimation pipeline. On the theoretical side, it yields a general error propagation result for locally Hölder-stable criteria, linking first-stage distribution estimation error to downstream criterion estimation and treatment regret, together with sharper regret bounds under standard margin conditions. Empirically, we show that the proposed framework outperforms direct criterion-specific methods in multiple settings and further evaluate it on the ACTG175 HIV clinical trial, a randomized study comparing several antiretroviral regimens in HIV-infected adults.

title: Hierarchical Decoding for Quantum Error Correction
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires classical decoders that can keep up with syndrome data streams and supply correction information and logical measurement outcomes to the quantum control system. Meeting these requirements at scale requires high throughput while controlling the end-to-end latency from readout to usable correction. In this paper, we organize decoding algorithms, execution strategies, and code constructions using common classifications and examine their performance and trade-offs under the reported evaluation conditions. We distinguish decoder-level hierarchy, where multiple decoding stages or resources cooperate to decode a single code, from code-level hierarchy, where the code construction itself introduces multiple decoding levels. We first review single-code hierarchical decoders and their cascaded predecoding and windowed, streaming, and distributed implementations. We then study hierarchical and concatenated codes, focusing on how decoding is coordinated across code levels through hard decisions, soft reliability information, or syndrome information. We also examine how qubit modalities shape decoding workloads and timing requirements, and review how different decoding platforms meet these requirements, including central processing units (CPUs), graphics processing units (GPUs), field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), and cryogenic platforms. By assessing design trade-offs, this paper clarifies connections across the literature and provides a shared foundation for QEC design exploration. It also identifies gaps in performance reporting and system integration to guide future research toward practical quantum error correction.

title: SMIC: Shared Multiscale Input-Reference Conditioning across Transformer Layers for Natural Language Inference
abstract: Natural Language Inference models can be sensitive to localized lexical changes. We introduce Shared Multiscale Input-Reference Conditioning (SMIC), which constructs a single input-dependent multiscale reference and reuses it across Transformer layers. Each layer applies its own multiscale transformation to the shared reference and injects the resulting conditioning feature before the attention update. We instantiate SMIC in a token--context Transformer (TCT) and conduct from-scratch comparisons against decoder-based and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) baselines across all three ANLI rounds. TCT-SMIC attains the highest observed ten-seed mean accuracy on all three ANLI rounds. The ablations further support the contribution of SMIC. We evaluate a real-valued Llama-style plug-in and extend deletion/insertion diagnostics to pretrained ModernBERT encoder and Llama decoder models with and without SMIC. Across the evaluated perturbation protocols, TCT-SMIC exhibits comparatively low pooled-attention redistribution and smaller signed accuracy changes. We further establish a finite-sample bound on average subset-mass redistribution in terms of the mean Jensen--Shannon divergence between the restricted and renormalized attention distributions.

title: FlowIR: Depth-driven Rectified Flow for Resolving Thermal Ambiguity in Infrared Super-Resolution
abstract: Distinguishing different heat sources in low-resolution infrared (IR) images is inherently difficult, as multiple thermal emitters often collapse into ambiguous and overlapping responses. Existing super-resolution methods hallucinate structures from such ambiguous 2D evidence, leading to thermal drift, boundary merging, and unreliable restoration under infrared degradations. We propose FlowIR, a depth-driven rectified flow framework that resolves thermal ambiguity by injecting 3D geometric cues into the generation process. Pseudo-3D depth lifting and depth-guided 3D convolutions disentangle overlapping foreground objects, while cluster-wise inter-attention suppresses cross-source feature contamination. A Thermal-Geometry Consistency Loss further enforces geometric alignment during refinement. Built upon a lightweight rectified flow backbone, FlowIR restores IR images in only a few steps, producing sharply separated, degradation-robust, and geometrically faithful high-resolution results.
authors: Xingyue Zhu;Qinyun Mei;Zhexi Min;Yang Zou;Xingyuan Li;Zhiying Jiang;Jinyuan Liu
comment: Accepted to the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Multimedia & Expo (ICME 2026)

title: Causals: An Open Knowledge Graph for Research on Causal Reasoning
abstract: Applying causal knowledge to a new event requires connecting the event to relevant entities and the relationships through which its consequences may unfold. We present Causals, an open knowledge graph for research on this form of reasoning. Its initial release, constructed from news reports, contains 369,184 nodes and 1,272,418 edges linking reported events, organizations, commodities, financial instruments, and other entities. Structural relationships, observations, and attributed causal claims retain distinct semantics and links to source records. We describe the construction and representation of the resource and characterize its connectivity and multi-hop retrieval properties. Causals provides shared relational knowledge for studying how language models retrieve relevant context and apply mechanisms to particular events. The dataset is available under CC BY 4.0 at https://causals.org/, and we invite contributions to its ontology, records, and evidence.

title: Studying temperature-induced decrease of spontaneous polarization in PbTiO$_3$ from vibrational amplitude
abstract: PbTiO$_3$ is a typical ferroelectric polarization induced negative thermal expansion (NTE) material at a wide range of temperature. The elegant TiO$_6$ octahedron is used to study the polarization and NTE, whereas lacking its quantitative characterization. In this work, we propose a concise projection of vibrational amplitude to describe anisotropic distortion of atoms with temperature based on $ab$ $initio$ molecular dynamics simulations. We find that the huge negative mode Grüneisen coefficient is mainly from the different vibrational modes of the TiO$_6$ octahedral rotation at two boundary symmetry points in tetragonal phase along $c$ direction. The potential energy surface as a function of amplitude suggests the $c$-axis compression facilitates the TiO$_6$ octahedral rotation. We show that the vibrational mode of TiO$_6$ octahedral rotation around negative-expansion axis can promote spontaneous polarization reduction with increasing temperature, making transformation of PbTiO$_3$ from tetragonal to cubic phase occur, via the projected amplitude, potential energy surface, and forces of individual atoms.

title: Rectified Looped Transformer
abstract: Looped Transformers increase effective depth by repeatedly applying a shared block, offering a parameter-efficient approach to language modeling. However, most existing works directly reuse each loop's output as the next's input, which can lead to hidden-state scale growth and perturbation amplification as recurrence deepens. We propose Rectified Looped Transformer (RLT), which redesigns feedback between loops using an interpolation schedule inspired by flow-based modeling. At each loop, RLT forms the next input by linearly interpolating between the current state and its prediction. Such interpolation distributes state changes across loops, encouraging a smoother trajectory from the initial input to the final output. Theoretical analysis proves that, under appropriate assumptions, RLT keeps state magnitudes uniformly bounded across loops and reduces the worst-case perturbation amplification. We evaluate RLT on language modeling corpora and downstream benchmarks. At matched training and inference depths, RLT consistently achieves lower perplexity than a standard looped Transformer, while exhibiting greater robustness to input perturbations and variance in inference depth. Consistent with the theoretical results, latent trajectory analysis shows that RLT maintains more stable hidden-state norms across loops, which also facilitates extrapolation-based decoding strategies. Notably, RLT achieves these gains without requiring additional trainable parameters or extra recurrent block evaluations, thus providing a simple yet more stable feedback mechanism for looped Transformers.

title: Label-Efficient Document-Grounded Factuality Detection via Cross-Paraphrastic Invariance Learning
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent claims that are unsupported by a given source document, motivating accurate and efficient document-grounded factuality detection. Existing LLM-based evaluators often require repeated inference and incur high computational cost, whereas compact factuality detectors are efficient at inference time but commonly rely on large labeled or synthetically generated corpora. We propose CPIL (Cross-Paraphrastic Invariance Learning), a two-stage Siamese framework that converts a small labeled set into relational supervision without acquiring additional factuality labels. CPIL constructs positive pairs from distinct label-preserving paraphrastic views of the same document-claim instance and negative pairs from opposite-label examples associated with the same source document. It further introduces quantile-aware semi-hard negative mining, which derives a boundary from the positive-pair similarity distribution and balances informative negatives with broader coverage. In the two-stage training procedure, Stage 1 learns an encoder from these task-aware pairs, and Stage 2 jointly fine-tunes the encoder and a linear classification head for binary factuality prediction. At inference time, CPIL requires no paraphrase generation, pair construction, or Siamese comparison and uses only one encoder-classifier forward pass. On the 11-task LLM-AggreFact benchmark, CPIL-2% and CPIL-3% achieve macro-F1 scores of 81.04 and 81.60 while using only 2-3% of the FactCG-released labeled pool. Both settings outperform all compared compact detectors and two vanilla LLM references. Ablations and sensitivity analyses support the contributions of task-aware pair construction, dynamic negative mining, and multi-pivot paraphrasing.
authors: Chao Chen;Shanshan Lin;Dongsheng Hong;Sibo Ju;Wenjie Yang;Sihong Xie;Xiangwen Liao

title: Confident and Wrong: Structure Confidence Is a Poor Selection Filter for Protein Function
abstract: Structure-guided protein design can generate plausible candidates, but structural confidence does not predict function. We trained a function-guided model on measured metal-binding affinity with protein sequence, ligand identity, and assay conditions, and used it to design rare earth element (REE) binding variants of lanmodulin, a lanthanide-binding protein with four EF-hand domains. We screened 297 designs from three strategies against terbium and dysprosium, adjacent lanthanides among the hardest REE pairs to separate. Selection on structural confidence inverted the outcome it was meant to improve. The Structure-Confidence-Selected panel carried the highest pTM, complex ipLDDT, and composite confidence scores, and expressed at 97%, yet only 16.7% of its designs bound terbium (95% CI 10.4 to 25.7), against 83.3% (74.6 to 89.5) for the function-guided panel, whose confidence scores were the lowest. The odds of binding differed 25-fold between the two panels (Fisher exact $p = 1 \times 10^{-20}$). No structural-confidence metric separated binders from non-binders consistently across panels, whereas the function-trained model's predicted pKd gave the highest ROC AUC in every panel, 0.79 to 0.92, and ranked measured affinity among function-guided binders at Spearman $ρ= 0.98$. On the design objective, Tb/Dy selectivity, the function-guided designs also exceeded the natural lanmodulin family, outranking a randomly drawn ortholog 84% of the time across 149 orthologs. Structural confidence is a plausibility signal, not a selection criterion for function; direct supervision on measured function is what ranks designs.

title: Low Language Transfer Speech-to-Text
abstract: A multilingual speech recogniser has heard much speech in its own languages. We ask how much of that it brings to a language it was never trained on, when it is fine-tuned on the little that language has. We score 28 open multilingual models untouched on Low-Language-TTS, 50 low-resource languages in 11 writing systems, and fine-tune 24 of them on at most 1,000 clips a language, 82 hours in all, with a dev set choosing every epoch. Fine-tuning lowers every model's macro character error rate (CER), by 16.6 to 53.1 points, to 9.5 at best, and a word language model takes three CTC models 1.2 to 1.4 points lower; WER is still 34.4 at best. On the 12 languages that no model lists, every model starts at 46 or worse and the best ends at 11.7. The same architectures from random weights stay 60 points or more behind, so the gain is transfer, and an encoder left untouched already gives a Whisper or Qwen decoder most of what it needs. It is the language, not the corpus: on FLEURS recordings that ours do not share, the median model keeps 79% of its gain. It costs the languages the models knew, 5.7 points of CER on English, Spanish, French and German in the median model. Low-rank adapters on 4% of the weights come within 1.1 points of tuning everything, and on 2 of 3 models forget less. Seq2seq and language-model decoders are done within three to five epochs, while a new CTC head is still improving at twenty or thirty. Data beats epochs: 25 clips a language take Qwen3-ASR 0.6B from 60.9 to 39.3, and at equal clips presented, ten times the data is worth 9.7 points. A model that first learned forty of the languages learns the other ten no faster. On a public Malay benchmark, untouched Whisper large-v3 scores 8.9 when it detects the language and 14.9 when told the clip is Malay, because it then translates the English that speakers mix in; trained on the Scicom telephony dataset it scores 6.0.

title: Reconstruct What You Can: Distractor-free 4D Gaussian Splatting
abstract: Dynamic reconstruction from casual video must preserve valid subject motion while suppressing transient occluders, shadows, and volumetric effects. Existing methods either suppress valid motion through static-scene assumptions or model all observations jointly, producing ghosting and unstable geometry. We introduce ReCan-GS, a 4D Gaussian Splatting framework that separates coherent scene content from inconsistent observations. It derives a Jacobian-based deformation-sensitivity score from the learned deformation field, using it as an empirical proxy for reconstruction ambiguity. The score guides separation into dynamic Core Gaussians and per-view Distractor Gaussians, or post-hoc pruning of sensitive Core Gaussians. The same criterion supports removal of spatial occluders, photometric artifacts, and evolving smoke or fog without masks, pretrained segmenters, or medium-specific supervision. Experiments on synthetic and real dynamic scenes and synthetic smoke/fog scenes demonstrate its usefulness across the evaluated distractor regimes.
authors: Joel Julin;Liuyue Xie;Ananya Bal;Mose Sakashita;Koichiro Niinuma;Laszlo A. Jeni

title: Few-Shot Cross-Subject Neural--Image Retrieval via Stimulus-Anchored Latent Bias Calibration
abstract: In cross-subject neural--image retrieval, comparing the mean of a few stimulus-matched target observations with the global source mean conflates subject-specific representation shifts with stimulus-composition effects. To address this problem, we propose Stimulus-Anchored Latent Bias Calibration (SA-LBC), which estimates the first-order shift under fixed preprocessing and a frozen source-trained representation by averaging residuals between target responses and same-stimulus source-population anchors, then shrinks the correction using source-derived uncertainty. Under uniform sampling without replacement from a finite stimulus population, we derive exact finite-population MSE expressions for the unshrunk anchored and global-mean estimators, including residual--anchor cross-covariance, and establish a necessary and sufficient condition for anchoring to reduce MSE relative to global-mean estimation. In a 10-subject leave-one-subject-out evaluation on THINGS-EEG2, SA-LBC increases mean reciprocal rank (MRR) for the Attention--CLIP ViT-B/32 configuration from 0.1867 without calibration to 0.2013 and 0.2336 with M=2 and M=16 stimulus-level calibration samples, respectively. Across six neural--visual configurations and all calibration budgets, stimulus-matched anchors yield higher MRR than anchors with shuffled stimulus identities, but retrieval gains over no calibration remain representation-dependent. At (M=2), shrinkage improves MRR over the unshrunk anchored estimator in all six configurations, but its effects at larger budgets vary across representations; the relative ranking of translation and orientation corrections also depends on regularization strength. Thus, lower shift-estimation MSE does not guarantee higher retrieval performance. The source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/Xizhang-Yao/SA-LBC.

title: HybridCT: ML Accelerated Tomography for Climate Relevant 3D Cloud Observations
abstract: Low-level clouds are one of the largest sources of uncertainty in climate predictions, partly because we lack detailed three-dimensional (3D) measurements of their internal structure. Here, we present HybridCT, a cloud tomographic reconstruction scheme accelerated by machine learning (ML) that recovers 3D cloud extinction directly from passive multi-angle observations. An ML emulator maps radiances from multiple viewing angles to cloud optical thickness (COT), producing path-integrated projections, and a Simultaneous Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (SART) explicitly inverts these projections to retrieve 3D extinction. Training observations are generated from synthetic 3D cloud fields using radiative transfer simulations for nine viewing angles between $\pm$70$^{\circ}$. HybridCT reconstructs extinction with RMSE 13.3 km$^{-1}$ in 3.5 s, compared to 22.7 km$^{-1}$ in approx. 30 min for the state-of-the-art physics-based tomography framework AT3D, a speedup exceeding 500$\times$. HybridCT thus provides a scalable route toward large-scale observations of 3D cloud structure relevant to radiative-budget interpretation and evaluation of high-resolution cloud simulations.
authors: Linda Forster;Nicholas J. LaHaye;Marcin J. Kurowski;Anna Jungbluth;Bernhard Mayer;Anthony B. Davis

title: What Can a VLA Learn from the Agent That Calls It? Task-Level Experience Distillation for Embodied Navigation
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models drive the robot directly from camera views, yet a VLA alone shows three typical failures. It walks past the goal, stops before reaching it, and rarely recovers after going off track. Pairing a VLA with a large language model (LLM) planner fixes these failures, but queries the LLM throughout every episode, adding token costs and latency. We introduce Harness-to-Executor (H2E), a task-level distillation method that pairs an LLM planner and a frozen VLA as a heterogeneous training agent, keeps only sessions that reach the goal, and then trains a VLA alone on them so no LLM is used at test time. In these sessions, the planner gives sub-instructions and moves the robot with its own tools, detours are common, and the planner decides when to stop. H2E therefore labels every motion as a VLA action for the original task, whoever made it. It masks the loss on steps moving away from the goal and assigns end labels to states near it, so the VLA learns where the task ends. H2E sets a new state of the art on REVERIE-CE and NavRAG-CE. It raises an 8B VLA's success rate by 15.6% and 11.1% respectively, surpassing a method trained on 10M samples. The distilled VLA exceeds its agent on unseen episodes with zero LLM tokens and runs 3.7 times faster.
authors: Jinze Tao;Yuxiao Han;Kangkang Dong;Yancong Wei;Xiaojun Zhu;Bokui Chen;Houde Liu

title: A Sensitivity Framework for Assessing External Validity
abstract: Assessing the external validity of experimental results is a pervasive challenge in causal inference as internally valid findings need not generalize beyond sites in which the experiments were conducted. Since the number of sites is often smaller than the number of site-level variables that moderate causal effects, we develop a partial identification framework that lets practitioners assess external validity under a wide range of assumptions that allow extrapolation across site-level variables. Our optimization-driven approach can accommodate any affine family of parameter restrictions, such as interaction terms being dominated by direct effects (the "effect hierarchy principle"). Since standard estimating-equation arguments do not apply in our setting---underspecified parameter directions responsible for partial identification make the covariance matrix singular---we develop a novel debiasing approach for estimands given by constrained optimization problems, giving rise to semiparametrically efficient estimators for our flexible partial identification bounds. We illustrate our approach on multi-site microcredit experiments harmonized by Meager (2019), whose lending environments differ widely in interest rates, loan sizes, and promotion. Holding out one country at a time, we construct external-validity intervals for the held-out country from the remaining source sites and show how our framework connects different extrapolation assumptions to concrete partial identification bounds.

title: Optimal feature selection for firewall log analysis using Machine learning and Hybrid Metaheuristic algorithms
abstract: Firewall log classification is important to monitor network traffic. Machine learning classifiers using network-related features have shown good results for this task, but high-dimensional features slow down classification. In this paper, we apply feature selection using bee swarm optimization with Q-learning-based local search (QBSO-FS) to the UCI Internet Firewall Data Set, together with random forest (RF), k-nearest neighbor (KNN), and Bernoulli naïve Bayes (Bernoulli NB) classifiers. The first version of this preprint selected and evaluated feature subsets on the same 5-fold cross-validation of the full data set, which contains 12.8\% exact duplicates; the reported scores are therefore optimistically biased. In this extended version, we re-evaluate the method with a leakage-free protocol: the data are split into training, validation, and test sets, features are selected using the validation set only, and accuracy and macro-averaged scores are measured once on the untouched test set, for both the raw data and a deduplicated, preprocessed version. On a single stratified split, QBSO-FS selects 5--7 features. The selected subsets clearly improve Macro-F1 over all features for KNN on both data sets and for RF on the deduplicated data (by 8--19 percentage points). For RF on the raw data and for Bernoulli NB, the differences (0.2--1.5 percentage points) may not hold for a different split. RF with 7 selected features reaches 99.90\% accuracy and 94.88\% Macro-F1 on the deduplicated data. On the same split, this exceeds our re-implementations of the deep neural network configurations of previous studies and the feature subset selected by particle swarm optimization in one of them, while the run time saved on this low-dimensional data set is small. These results suggest that the method can support automatic firewall log analysis, while evaluation over multiple splits remains future work.
authors: Seungwoo Han;Gil Hong;Jewan Kim;Jeuk Yu;Sangjun Lee;Byeongok Cho;Jusung Jeon
comment: 13 pages. Revised version of engrXiv preprint (doi:10.31224/osf.io/pm3hy) with a corrected, leakage-free evaluation protocol; original results retained for reference

title: Anti-Kibble-Zurek behavior driven by dichotomous Markov noise in a quantum Ising chain: Generalized stochastic resonance in the defect density
abstract: The anti-Kibble-Zurek behavior may arise under noise, adding a noise-induced contribution to the defect density beyond the conventional Kibble-Zurek term. Most investigations of such behavior have so far been restricted to Gaussian noise. For Gaussian colored noise (GCN), the power spectrum dictates a monotonic variation of this term with the correlation time. Here, we focus on dichotomous Markov noise (DMN), a prototypical non-Gaussian colored noise, in the quantum Ising chain. We show that the noise-induced defect density, taken as the response function, exhibits generalized stochastic resonance: it is nonmonotonic in the correlation time, growing in the fast-noise regime and decreasing in the slow-noise regime. This resonance stems from the anomalous AKZ behavior in the slow-noise regime, where the DMN-induced trend is nonmonotonic, in contrast to the monotonic GCN case. The underlying mechanism lies in the sparse realizations of DMN in the slow-noise regime, a feature not captured by the power spectrum. Our work thereby reveals a fundamental distinction between Gaussian and non-Gaussian noises in the nonequilibrium critical quench dynamics of the quantum Ising chain.

title: ATune: Unsupervised Photo Retouching Through Image-Editor Controls
abstract: Photo retouching models are trained on pairs of original and retouched photographs, usually edited by experts. Expert edits are costly, so the two main public sets, FiveK and PPR10K, hold only 16,161 originals. Good photographs on their own are far easier to find: commercial stock collections and free ones such as Pixabay and Unsplash hold millions. We learn retouching from them alone: we damage each photograph the way a camera or a careless edit would, which gives a worse and a better version of the same photograph. From these pairs, our model, ATune, learns how 13 measured attributes, such as brightness, contrast and sharpness, should change to raise a photograph's quality. The edit is declarative: ATune sets target values for the attributes, and a simple search adjusts the sliders of an out-of-the-box photo editor until the photograph reaches them. Every edit is a list of slider values a person can read and adjust. The same model can drive any editor that makes those changes; we test RawTherapee and darktable. We train on 10M photographs from a commercial stock collection and test on FiveK, PPR10K and SPAQ. Nine quality judges score every edit, and in a user study 157 human raters made 9,253 choices between our edit and another method's edit of the same photograph. When Claude Opus 5 and GPT-6 Astra edit the same photographs in the same editor, raters prefer our edits to GPT-6 Astra's (54.3%) and rate them even with Claude's (50.5%). We also compare with supervised retouchers on their home ground: NeurOP on FiveK and AdaInt on PPR10K, each trained on that set's own expert edits. Raters chose our edits in 46.3% of those comparisons. ATune, a 54M-parameter model trained without a single expert edit, now matches frontier models at setting an editor's sliders.
comment: 27 pages, 12 figures, 18 tables. Main paper 8 pages plus supplementary material

title: High-Quality InSb Nanowires Grown by Molecular-Beam Epitaxy via Precise Catalyst Modulation
abstract: Semiconductor InSb nanowires are a major material candidate for topological quantum computation. The nanowires in current devices were mostly grown using metal organic chemical vapor deposition, incompatible with in situ growth of superconductor, a crucial requirement for low-disorder devices. Growth of InSb nanowires using molecular-beam epitaxy (MBE) can address this issue. So far, studies on MBE-grown InSb remain limited due to an extremely narrow parameter window for the growth and reproducibility. Moreover, the use of foreign catalysts can introduce deep-level impurities. Here, we report a self-catalyzed MBE growth of InSb nanowires without those foreign catalysts. We first grow GaAs nanowire stems, and then convert Ga catalyst droplets into In droplets in situ. Axial heteroepitaxial growth of InSb can be realized through the In droplets on top of GaAs stems. We further find that a low flux suppresses radial growth, enabling linear length tuning from 0.8 to 2.6 micrometer with growth time, while diameter stays nearly constant. These InSb nanowires have a pure zinc-blende structure free of twins, stacking faults. Transport measurement reveals an electron mobility near 19000 cm2 V-1s-1. Moreover, the observation of quasi-ballistic transport, quantum dots, and Kondo correlations demonstrates the coherent quantum transport capability of the MBE-grown InSb nanowires. Our work provides a substrate-independent, self-catalyzed route for the controllable synthesis of high-quality InSb nanowires, establishing a robust material platform for high-performance InSb-based electronic and quantum devices.
authors: Wenlong Yang;Jiaye Xu;Shuai Yang;Wenyu Song;Haiyan Shi;Donghai Li;Xiyu Hou;Sijun Chen;Ke He;Hao Zhang;Dong Pan

title: A Polynomial Bound on Split Rank
abstract: We prove that the split rank of a rational pure-integer polyhedron is polynomially bounded in its input length, resolving a conjecture of Basu, Conforti, Di Summa, and Jiang. If the defining system has dense binary encoding length $L$, then $O((L+1)^9)$ split rounds suffice to reach the integer hull in arbitrary dimension.

title: DER Aggregators in Wholesale Electricity Markets: A Hybrid Mean-Field Framework with Endogenous Price Feedback
abstract: The rapid growth of distributed energy resources (DERs), including rooftop solar and energy storage, is transforming the grid edge, where customer-side assets increasingly interact with the broader power grid. DER aggregators, entities that coordinate the actions of many small-scale DERs, play a key role in this transformation. This paper presents a hybrid Mean-Field Control (MFC) and Mean-Field Game (MFG) framework for integrating DER aggregators into wholesale electricity markets. Unlike traditional approaches that treat market prices as exogenous, our model captures the feedback between aggregators' collective actions and electricity prices. The MFC component optimizes DER operations within each aggregator, while the MFG models strategic interactions among multiple aggregators. To account for various uncertainties, we incorporate reinforcement learning, which allows aggregators to learn optimal bidding strategies in dynamic market conditions. We prove the existence and uniqueness of a mean-field equilibrium and validate the framework through a case study of the Oahu Island power system. Results show that our approach reduces price volatility and improves market efficiency, offering a scalable and decentralized solution for DER integration in wholesale markets.

title: Infinite or indefinite: the query cost of simulating the quantum switch
abstract: The quantum switch applies two operations in a coherent superposition of their causal orders and is a simple example of indefinite causal order. No quantum circuit that uses each operation once in a definite order can even describe it, yet photonic experiments have demonstrated its physical realization. We ask how many calls to the black-box operations a quantum computer in the circuit model needs to reproduce the switch. If one of the black boxes is known to be unitary, three calls suffice. For general channels on a $d$-dimensional system, we prove three results. In all three, circuits may use classical feed-forward and unlimited ancillary quantum memory. First, no finite number of calls suffices for exact simulation in the worst case. Second, approximation to any fixed error below $1/2$, measured in half the diamond norm, requires $Ω(d^{1/4})$ calls, exponential in the number of qubits. Third, an ordinary circuit can require exponentially many calls to obtain a single bit that the switch extracts with a few uses. We consider a device whose actual noise is dephasing in a fixed unknown basis and test it against a theoretical depolarizing model. The two channels have the same entanglement and average gate fidelities, so these figures alone do not distinguish them. At fixed noise strength, the quantum switch tells them apart with a number of device uses independent of $d$, whereas the circuit model requires $Ω(d^{1/16})$ calls. Noise characterization is needed for quantum error correction, and this gives a provable query advantage of the switch in a task relevant to practical quantum computing. We invite future work that extends such advantages to more practical computing tasks.
comment: 36 pages, 6 figures. Lean formalization and exact certificates available at https://github.com/dtlics/Indefinite-Causal-Order

title: Indic-Task Gains and Regressions after Reinforcement Learning
abstract: We run reinforcement learning (RL) with GRPO across four environments, starting from a supervised fine-tuned 30B-A3B mixture-of-experts model covering English and eight Indic languages. We compare the model before and after RL across 34 benchmarks in one evaluation campaign. MATH improves by 36.07 points, and most Indic benchmarks also improve. Yet XQuAD-Indic F1 falls 19.32 points as English answers rise from 8.7% to 91.7%; IndicQA falls 8.64, while English XQuAD gains 11.71 F1. A second RL run from the same supervised initialization adds an Indic environment together with language and repetition rewards. Compared with the released model, it improves both passage-answering and instruction-following benchmarks, along with preserving MATH performance. But it loses ground on reasoning and coding benchmarks. Several training choices changed together, so we cannot isolate the effect of any one of the reward terms. Script compliance remains unresolved. Adding a language reward did not ensure use of the requested script. Passage answering and script compliance therefore need direct evaluation, even when other benchmark scores improve.
authors: Sutanshu Saksena Raj;Daksh Maan;Avinash Benki;Parijat Chatterjee;Pasunuti Prasanjith;Purusharth Malik
comment: Accepted at the GlobalSouthAI Workshop, NeurIPS 2026

title: Disentangled Embedding Optimization for Diffusion-Based Dataset Distillation
abstract: Dataset distillation aims to compress large-scale datasets into compact synthetic subsets that enable efficient model training with comparable performance to the original data. Recent advances show that diffusion models are highly effective for this task due to their strong generative capability. Existing diffusion-based approaches typically perform class-wise clustering and use the obtained cluster prototypes as diffusion inputs to generate distilled samples. However, the uniformly distributed original samples in a category inevitably lead to entanglement near cluster boundaries, pulling the cluster prototypes closer and reducing the inter-cluster separation. Consequently, the diffusion model receives overly similar latent inputs, resulting in synthetic data with limited diversity. To address this issue, we propose Disentangled Embedding Optimization (DEO), a simple yet effective framework that replaces static clustering with trainable embeddings. These embeddings are optimized to match the Gaussian statistics (i.e., mean and covariance) of the original data distribution, while a diversity regularizer is designed to encourage separation among these embeddings to improve the intra-class variability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed DEO can generate more diversified and representative distilled data than existing cluster-based diffusion methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance and superior generalization across multiple datasets.
authors: Hongcheng Li;Yucan Zhou;Yibin Wang;Xiaoyan Gu;Bo Li;Weiping Wang
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures. Accepted at the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM 2026)

title: We Are What We Remember: Mental-State-Driven Memory for Long-Term Character Dialogue
abstract: Shared history in human dialogue is not merely a repository of facts, but the foundation of evolving relationships and mutual understanding. However, mainstream conversational memory systems rely on passive semantic similarity over external fact stores, frequently retrieving topically similar records while missing relationally pivotal experiences. Inspired by cognitive psychology's Self-Memory System (SMS), we propose MindMem, a mental-state-driven memory framework that asynchronously consolidates shared experiences into source-linked mental states of the character, the user, and their relationship. At each turn, a specialized mental-state reasoner (Mind) contextualizes these persistent states to anticipate latent user needs, form proactive intentions, and recover supporting episodic evidence that surface-level matching overlooks. To evaluate history-sensitive adaptation beyond factual recall, we introduce MemReal-Bench, a longitudinal benchmark grounded in month-long real-user interactions across dyadic and group scenes. By pairing Direct Question Answering (DQA) with Situated Memory Realization (SMR), it tests whether agents bridge the gap between knowing past facts and naturally using shared history, world rules, and relational trajectories. On MemReal-Bench, MindMem reaches 59.03% SMR and 82.58% DQA, exceeding the strongest memory baseline by 24.19 and 9.19 percentage points, respectively, and outperforming oracle target-memory injection on SMR. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/jiazhicheng7-ctrl/MindMem.
authors: Zhicheng Jia;Shuchen Wu;Zhuoshi Tong;Haisen Liao;Sicheng Zhou;Chao Yang

title: GridForge: A Tractable Network-Flow Method for Constructing Open, Continental-Scale Synthetic Power Grids
abstract: The goal of this paper is to construct open, continental-scale synthetic transmission grids with an optimization method that stays tractable. Security restrictions keep models of the real grid out of open research and machine-learning datasets, and optimization-based construction is hard at scale: the number of candidate lines grows combinatorially, so electrically faithful methods prune the candidates in advance. This paper presents GridForge, which keeps every bus pair within physical length limits as a candidate, selects lines with Garver's length-weighted network-flow linear program instead of binary decisions, and resizes them with a sequential direct-current (DC) power flow. Two stages of 13 regional networks are evaluated. Their node-degree distributions are nearly as strongly log-linear as those of the real Eastern and Western Interconnections ($R^2$ of 0.92 to 0.98 against 0.971 and 0.981), although the areas under the fitted lines differ from the real ones by 39.9% on average. On the upper Midwest and Tennessee Valley footprints, resizing lowers the DC power-flow loss from 5.89% to 4.14% and from 14.55% to 7.05%, and the DC optimal power-flow loss from 4.03% to 2.02% and from 5.54% to 2.47%. Without relaxing any line limit, the DC optimal power flow is feasible in 78.81% and 0.82% of the scenarios. Most lines are built at 69 kV. The models span 250 to 78,484 buses, were built on single machines, and are freely redistributable.
authors: Jonathan M. Snodgrass;Thomas J. Overbye;Christopher L. DeMarco;Bernard C. Lesieutre
