title: Unifying First-Order Coherence, Concurrence, and Bell Correlations in Three-Flavor Neutrino Oscillations
abstract: Neutrino oscillations provide a natural setting for investigating the quantum character of flavor conversion and the distribution of quantum resources over macroscopic distances. Here, we study exact relations among purity-based first-order coherence, pairwise concurrence, and the maximal Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) value in coherent three-flavor neutrino oscillations. By expressing the evolving neutrino as a three-qubit single-excitation state, we derive the generally mixed two-qubit reductions and show that the squared first-order coherence of each flavor mode and its two associated squared concurrences sum to unity. Furthermore, a closed two-branch relation is obtained, showing that the maximal CHSH value of any reduced pair is determined by its average first-order coherence and concurrence. The branch structure follows from the correlation-tensor spectrum and yields exact conditions for CHSH violation. For the vacuum parameters and propagation ranges considered, electron preparation gives weak CHSH violations in electroncontaining pairs, while muon preparation produces a dominant utau pair with substantially stronger concurrence and Bell correlations. The comparison also identifies the thirdflavor contribution responsible for the different locations of concurrence and CHSH maxima. These results clarify the distribution of quantum correlations during flavor evolution and provide a basis for extensions to coherent matter propagation and wave-packet-induced mixed states.

title: The 10 Mpc Volume
abstract: Accurate distances are now known for most unobscured galaxies brighter than MB = -13 mag within 10 Mpc from Hubble Space Telescope observations of their luminous stars. Complementary mid-infrared observations with the Wide-field Infrared Explorer provide global stellar mass estimates for these galaxies. Consequences are detailed knowledge of the properties of the Universe in a volume-limited space. Galaxies tend to lie within groups, within filaments. The filaments experience bulk motions in response to well defined gravitational attractors such as the Virgo Cluster and repulsors such as the Local Void. The groups are inevitably dominated by a single galaxy, with 10 galaxies between one and nine Mpc containing most of the stellar mass within the sample. There is a curious lack of galaxies in an interval fainter than these dominant galaxies. The dominant galaxies in halos tend to have gas reservoirs and ongoing star formation, a property extending to dwarf galaxies in separate halos. Secondary galaxies in halos are frequently gas depleted and lack evidence of star formation. With one notable exception, all galaxies in the complete sample have well formed red giant branches indicative of early-onset star formation.
authors: R. Brent Tully;Gagandeep S. Anand;Helene M. Courtois;Igor D. Karachentsev;Valentina E. Karachentseva;Ehsan Kourkchi;Dmitry I. Makarov;Lidia N. Makarova;Daniel Pomarede;Edward J Shaya
comment: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal. 32 pages, 30 figures

title: Encoding and Propagation of Grammatical Number in Large Language Models
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become an increasingly popular means of translating Large Language Model (LLM) hidden state vectors into a human-comprehensible list of features or symbols. As such, SAEs may provide insight into an LLM's knowledge representation and internal ``mental'' grammar - topics of pragmatic interest for mechanistic interpretation of AI behavior and of theoretical interest for the study of in silico representations of human language. Language models with fewer than 100M parameters, trained on small corpora, nonetheless exhibit strong grammatical competence and discourse coherence, despite producing content of limited reliability. We use SAEs that we trained on one such model (Pythia-70M) to conduct an in-depth examination of how a single grammatical phenomenon, number agreement, is represented and processed in an LLM. We demonstrate the mechanism and the methodology by which SAEs can be used to find and propagate ``plural noun'', ``plural matrix subject'', and ``generate a plural verb'' features which cause the LLM to produce plural verb forms such as ``are'', ``do'', or ``have'' instead of ``is'', ``does'', and ``has'' in response to prompts such as ``the men in the park''. We show that intervening to remove these features from the hidden states of plural subject noun tokens causes the model to produce singular verbs instead, and vice versa. We also show that corresponding ``singular noun'' and ``generate a singular verb'' features are not as effective for this task. This asymmetry suggests that Pythia-70m makes use of a privative representation of grammatical number in English. These findings replicated with larger LLMs Gemma-2-2b and Llama-3.1-8b yielded similar results. Our main contribution is a novel approach to the use of SAEs to understanding how LLMs encode human language that addresses a number of technical and methodological challenges.
affiliations: University of Minnesota;University of Minnesota

title: Minimum-Time Interceptor Selection and Obstacle-Avoiding Path Planning for Heterogeneous UAVs
abstract: Selecting the most suitable unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) to intercept a moving target is challenging when multiple vehicles have different speeds, initial headings, turning capabilities and launch delays, particularly in environments containing obstacles. This paper develops a computationally efficient framework that integrates minimum-time interceptor selection with obstacle-avoiding path planning for heterogeneous UAVs. The interception problem for each UAV is formulated as a minimum-time optimal control problem and solved numerically using an arc-parameterised nonlinear programming model based on Dubins-type paths. The candidate trajectories consist of minimum-radius circular arcs, straight-line segments and tangential obstacle-boundary arcs, with exact geometric distance constraints imposed to ensure obstacle avoidance along the entire path. To improve computational efficiency, a closed-form lower bound on interception time is incorporated into a bound-and-select algorithm that eliminates UAVs unable to improve the best verified feasible interception time. The proposed pruning strategy preserves the best computed interception decision obtained through full enumeration while reducing computational effort. Numerical experiments investigate the effects of target speed, UAV turning radius, launch delay and obstacle configuration. Across 20 randomly generated scenarios involving up to eight UAVs, the proposed approach reduces average computational time by approximately 85$\%$ for eight-vehicle teams without changing the selected interceptor or its computed interception time. The proposed approach provides an efficient method for selecting a single UAV and generating feasible Dubins-type interception trajectories in obstacle-constrained environments.

title: State-Feedback Passivity Control for Synchronous Machine Systems
abstract: The passivity of a generating station enables network stability to be established from conditions verified locally at each station. For synchronous machines, however, passivity can only be certified under conditions on the operating point, and these conditions fail under heavy loading and weak damping. This paper develops a state-feedback controller that enforces passivity using a storage battery connected at the terminal bus. A bilinear term arising from the product of the rotor-speed and stator-current deviations is treated as a bounded uncertainty, leading to robust positive-real conditions that can be enforced by a state feedback control designed using a single algebraic Riccati equation. The resulting controller guarantees passivity whenever the Riccati equation admits a positive-definite solution, with no separate condition on the operating point. Numerical examples show that existing conditions certify passivity only up to a fraction of the rated current, whereas the proposed state-feedback approach certifies it at the rated operating point of the machine.
authors: Maryam Khodabakhshloo;Elizabeth L. Ratnam;Ian R. Petersen

title: Upper and lower bounds for few-copy Gaussian tomography, and the absence of a fermionic warm regime
abstract: Chen, Mele, Mele and Preskill proved a crossover for bosonic Gaussian tomography: cold states need $Θ(m^3/ε^2)$ copies under single-copy or few-copy measurements, warm ones $Θ(m^2/ε^2)$. The author proved $Ω(m^3/ε^2)$ for adaptive single-copy tomography of mixed fermionic Gaussian states. This note shows the crossover has no fermionic counterpart and extends the fermionic bound to blocks of $k$ copies. There is no warm regime: on the quadratic Gibbs balls $β\|h\|_F\leβ_0$ of unknown Hamiltonian $h$, the single-copy rate is $Θ(m^3/ε^2)$ for every fixed $β_0>0$, at accuracies that resolve the ball, with a lower-bound constant independent of $β_0$. At the maximally mixed state a replicated-parameter Fisher budget gives $N>m^3/(8{,}553{,}600\,k\,ε^2)$ for blocks of at most $k$ copies and all $ε\le1/3600$; an exact formula for the maximal block Fisher information, via spinor tensor powers of $\mathfrak{so}(2m)$, shows that the budget $mt^2$ behind it is asymptotically attained for every fixed block size; whether $1/k$ is the true rate is open. Near the vacuum, block protocols need $Ω(m^3/(ε^2\min\{\sqrt k,m\}))$ copies, with no logarithm, via an exterior-power embedding of qudit tomography; parity superselection changes no rate, and number superselection costs nothing on number-conserving inputs. The embedding also carries upper bounds: a particle-number measurement followed by the $k$-copy qudit protocol of Nayak and Zhou attains the lower bound for every $k$ on number-conserving fermionic Gaussian states with bounded fugacity trace and on passive bosonic Gaussian states with bounded photon number, and a heterodyne stage that undoes displacement and squeezing extends this to all cold bosonic Gaussian states. This closes their $k$-entangled gap on the cold class; intermediate temperatures remain open.
comment: 32 pages, 2 tables. Extends arXiv:2609.23189 to measurements on blocks of k copies; uses Lemma 1 of arXiv:2609.26705 as a black box

title: Satisficing as competitive Bayesian weighting: a minimal model of goal-directed choice under an unattained target
abstract: Animals and humans often do not maximize; they act relative to goals (aspiration levels) that are frequently not yet met. How can a goal that is not (yet) realized organize choice? Deacon (2012) calls such absence-referenced organization \emph{ententional}, and García-Valdecasas and Deacon (2024) argue that ends are best understood as constraints rather than as particular states. We examine this idea in a minimal formal setting: Risk-sensitive Satisficing (RS), a bandit learning rule that values each action by its share of past trials multiplied by its surplus or shortfall relative to an aspiration level. We show that RS can be rewritten as a Bayesian-like estimator, Attention Competitive Bayes (ACB), in which the aspiration level is the prior mean of every action and the finite budget of trials sets how strongly evidence can override it. Two consequences follow. First, actions that are no longer sampled are partially overridden by the goal rather than by past observations: their estimates relax toward the aspiration level without any data being discarded. This ``pseudo-forgetting'' distinguishes ACB from models with an explicit forgetting rate. Second, when the aspiration is unattainable, exploration does not settle; in Bernoulli bandit simulations, adjusting the aspiration level from evidence reduced regret (expected loss). ACB offers an analyzable model in which an unattained goal and a limited attentional resource jointly constrain behavior, and it yields testable predictions about how organisms revalue options they have abandoned.

title: Cubic Optimization over Three Nonnegative Integers Is NP-hard
abstract: We prove that deciding whether an integer cubic polynomial takes a value at most one over three nonnegative integers is NP-hard. Hardness holds even when every feasible objective value is a positive integer, so every constructed instance has a finite, attained minimum. This establishes a sharp dimension boundary for the tractability of cubic integer optimization in fixed dimension. Our reduction from positive 1-in-3 satisfiability encodes Boolean constraints as modular conditions and uses an algebraic norm to construct a cubic objective whose minimum is one exactly for satisfiable formulas. The resulting six-parameter threshold language is NP-complete and admits short exponent certificates.
comment: 16 pages. A version of this manuscript was posted on Optimization Online on November 1, 2026

title: HyFlash: A Prefix-Memory Prior for On-Device Speculative Decoding
abstract: Parallel block drafting accelerates speculative decoding by predicting multiple future positions in a single backbone pass, but on-device deployment constrains both drafter capacity and context storage. Under tight memory budgets, drafters must model long-range dependencies and fine-grained draft-position interactions without the growing KV-cache overhead of full-context attention. We propose HyFlash, a compact parallel drafter that introduces a prefix-memory prior to separate long-range context modeling from fine-grained draft-position interactions with limited capacity. Local attention captures recent context and draft-position interactions, while recurrent memory compresses historical target features into fixed-size states. This inductive bias enables effective local and long-range modeling with bounded draft-side memory. Experiments show that HyFlash achieves higher acceptance than full-context attention with substantially less KV storage and with larger gains for shallow drafters and long contexts.

title: How Much Skill Orchestration Can LLM Agents Compile Away? Execution-Grounded Specialization for Token-Efficient Skill Use
abstract: Reusable skills guide large language model (LLM) agents through recurring requests, but each invocation still requires the model to interpret the skill and reconstruct its orchestration. Can agents automatically compile this orchestration into an executable fast path without human intervention? We first study zero-shot skill specialization, which compiles without execution evidence, and find that despite the skill's procedural guidance, incorrect assumptions about runtime bindings can make generated plans brittle and recovery costly. This motivates SkillCache, a one-trace skill specialization method that compiles a completed invocation into a parameterized capsule of programs and natural-language steps, replays it before reuse, and drives it with a plan executor that returns control to the model only when needed, keeping the source skill for recovery. With the Claude Code harness, warm execution of the same request reduces tokens on 87 SkillsBench tasks by 81% with Claude Sonnet 4.6 and by 74% with Claude Opus 4.8 at comparable reward, and capsules stay effective under controlled request changes. Capsules also transfer across models, raising three open-weight models' mean reward by 12-25 percentage points while reducing their tokens by 72-81%, suggesting that execution-grounded compilation is a promising approach to efficient repeated skill use and cross-model transfer.
authors: Jiayi Ni;Zac Wang;Alex Zhang;Zheng Liu;Roopa Prabhu
comment: 35 pages, 20 figures, 16 tables. An earlier version has been selected for an oral/spotlight presentation at the AgenticOS workshop at NeurIPS 2026

title: Double Machine Learning for Panel Data: Identification, Specification, and a Bank Regulation Effect
abstract: This paper examines robustness and causal interpretation of panel estimates using double/debiased machine learning. The prototype treatment setup is the 2018 US banking regulation. Under common treatment timing, we characterize identification and nuisance restrictions and derive exact bank-level representations of specified "within" and "first-difference" scores. Simulations assess panel model transformation-induced specification bias and inference under weaker overlap. Empirically, estimates vary with asset-size classification and prior growth. Prior-growth adjustment reduces overlap-weighted estimates across four Machine Learners (ML); doubly robust estimates depend on the fitted propensity and concentrated weights. Both bank groups received relief, so we estimate differential exposure effects. The findings highlight specification issues and the relation between functional-form robustness and causal identification.

title: $D^2$-OPD: Separating Direction and Distance in Extrapolative On-Policy Distillation
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student model to match a teacher's next-token distributions on student-generated prefixes. Extrapolative OPD further extends the teacher's log-probability shift relative to a reference policy to construct stronger learning targets. However, existing methods couple extrapolation direction and distance, allowing the magnitude of the teacher's shift to dictate how far the target moves. We propose $D^2$-OPD, decoupling these two factors: a per-prefix hard KL constraint bounds the target's distance from the teacher, while an adaptive combination of the teacher's post-training shift and the initial student--teacher gap determines the extrapolation direction. We optimize the student toward this target using forward KL, providing learning signals even for low-probability tokens. We evaluate three settings: where standard OPD performs well, where it struggles with base-model initialization, and where no teacher reference is available. On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, $D^2$-OPD attains the highest score in all three settings, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 9.45 points. Ablations validate the contributions of each component.
affiliations: Columbia University;AWS AI Lab;Amazon AGI

title: Nonparametric Subgraph Regression
abstract: Estimation and inference on a single large network are challenging due to dependence among observations. This paper studies nonparametric regression for outcomes defined on groups of $p$ agents, such as the indicator that three agents in a network form a triangle. Outcomes on groups that share an agent may be dependent, while outcomes on disjoint groups are independent. I call this problem subgraph regression; it nests dyadic regression as the special case $p=2$. Its leading application concerns subgraphs of a network, but the methods apply to any outcome defined on groups of agents. I establish a variance bound, uniform convergence rates in probability, and pointwise asymptotic normality for the subgraph analogue of the Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression estimator. The setting differs from regression with i.i.d. data in two ways: (i) the number of observations, of order $N^p$, overstates the effective sample size, which is $N$, and (ii) the rate of convergence depends on the dimension of the covariates of a single agent rather than of all $p$ agents, which mitigates the curse of dimensionality.

title: Exact penalties for maximum-edge bicliques in bipartite graphs
abstract: Given a bipartite graph $G$, we denote by $g(G)$ the largest product $|A||B|$ over pairs of vertex sets $A$ and $B$, one on each side, with no edge between them. These pairs are the bicliques of the bipartite complement of $G$; hence, computing $g(G)$ is the maximum-edge biclique problem, which is NP-hard, as shown by Peeters in 2003. Gillis and Glineur characterized it by a continuous quadratic program, in which a large enough penalty on the edges of $G$ makes the global maximizers correspond to the maximum pairs and the local maximizers to the maximal ones. We propose a new threshold for the penalty, which depends only on $g(G)$. For any penalty at or above it, the global maximizers correspond exactly to the maximum pairs, and every local maximizer with positive value corresponds to a maximal pair. This threshold is never larger than theirs and is sharp up to an additive $1/2$. Spectral and semidefinite bounds give computable penalties; in experiments, a simple local ascent succeeds far more often with the semidefinite one than with the earlier thresholds, although on our graphs that bound already reveals $g(G)$. The penalty formulation, whose optimal value is $\sqrt{g(G)}/2$, is also a copositive formulation of $g(G)$. Strengthening a semidefinite bound of Laurent, Polak and Vargas with the completely positive cone gives exactly $\sqrt{g(G)}/2$, while the doubly nonnegative strengthening is already inexact on six vertices. Finally, Pólya's linear programming approximations of the copositive cone become finite at an explicit level and converge to $\sqrt{g(G)}/2$ without ever being exact.

title: How Do AI Agents Waste Your Money?
abstract: AI agents may consume massive tokens across a wide range of tasks, but how many of those tokens are really necessary? Although prior work has shown that agents can incur unexpectedly high token costs, we still lack a systematic way to identify and measure token waste. In this work, we introduce a unified framework for measuring token waste across heterogeneous agent systems. Our framework records and normalizes complete agent trajectories, identifies removable spans using an LLM-as-a-Judge (LLMaJ), and maps the identified text spans back to the original trajectory for token-level measurement. We validate the identified waste through direct interventions by removing marked spans, resuming agent execution, and measuring changes in task outcomes and subsequent actions. In online pruning experiments, we remove 41-46% of the model's reasoning while largely preserving task performance across two distinct agent benchmarks. Using this framework, we analyze agents across multiple settings. Our analysis shows that token waste has a system-level structure that aggregate token usage alone cannot reveal. First, waste varies more across tasks and agent settings than across models. Second, reasoning and visible execution can exhibit different waste patterns. Third, different harnesses can introduce distinct sources of inefficiency even under the same model and task. Overall, our framework transforms token waste into an actionable optimization signal, enabling researchers and practitioners to train more efficient models, design better reasoning strategies, and optimize agent harnesses toward reducing unnecessary computation rather than merely reducing token usage.
authors: Huimin Zeng;Yuxuan Lu;Jesse Cai;Eric Hanchen Jiang;Di Wu;Po-Nien Kung;Wenbo Hu;Ziyi Wang;Dakuo Wang;Jiaxin Pei;Kai-Wei Chang

title: Dust Survival in Lensed Quiescent Galaxies at $z>1$ Depends on How They Quench
abstract: The interstellar medium of massive quiescent galaxies holds key clues to how they quench, yet remain poorly understood. Although dust is expected to be depleted rapidly ($\lesssim$100 Myr) after quenching, some quiescent galaxies host substantial dust reservoirs, raising the question of whether dust survives quenching or is replenished afterward. We present ALMA Band 6 continuum observations ($λ_{\mathrm{rest}}$$>$250$μ$m) of eight strongly-lensed, spectroscopically-selected quiescent galaxies at z$\sim$1-2.5 from the COOL-LAMPS and REQUIEM surveys, plus five archival REQUIEM systems. The sample spans more than two orders of magnitude in dust-to-stellar-mass ratio ($f_{\mathrm{dust}}<10^{-5}$ to $>10^{-3}$), and two galaxies host extended, resolved dust. Comparing $f_{\mathrm{dust}}$ with time since quenching, roughly half the sample, preferentially at higher redshift, is consistent with rapid quenching and harsh dust destruction, while lower-redshift, more slowly quenched systems are consistent with milder destruction, possibly reflecting an evolving dominant quenching mode. The two most dust-rich galaxies exceed even the mildest model destruction tracks, with J1201-3952 retaining the highest $f_{\mathrm{dust}}$ $\sim$1.8 Gyr after quenching. If these systems are truly quiescent, their dust masses approach maximum stellar yields, pointing to ISM grain regrowth and/or TP-AGB dust production. However due to our single-band continuum data, $f_{\mathrm{dust}}$ is uncertain ($\pm$0.3 dex systematic uncertainty from the unknown dust temperature) and we cannot rule out obscured star formation in these two galaxies. Our results suggest that dust survival depends on how galaxies quench: rapid, harsh quenching efficiently destroys dust, while slower, milder quenching can leave dust reservoirs that persist or are replenished long after star formation ceases.
authors: Sarah Bodansky;Katherine E. Whitaker;Gourav Khullar;Michael D. Gladders;Keren Sharon;Viraj Manwadkar;Yunchong Zhang;Jacqueline Antwi-Danso;Dylan Berry;Rachel Bezanson;Håkon Dahle;Carlos Garcia Diaz;Darko Donevski;Alex J. Geiger;Massissilia L. Hamadouche;Joel Leja;Guillaume Mahler;Alexandra Pope;Justin Spilker;Ezra Sukay;Francesco Valentino

title: Archetypal contexts in the neurons of language models: an architecture for intelligence?
abstract: We validate our previous hypothesis that a language model holds relational patterns apart from the subject domains that instantiate them (Nordfors, 2026). These archetypal contexts are patterns of relations that people recognize across many fields, such as the tipping point or winner takes all, held once and applied across domains. We show this inside the model, Qwen3.8-27B. One set of neurons carries the archetype, say the tipping point; another carries the topic, say politics, ecology or cell biology; a third carries the language, such as English, Spanish or Chinese. Silence the tipping point's neurons, and the model no longer identifies the pattern but still knows what the text is about. Silence the topic's, and it loses the topic but still names the pattern. In the neuron maps the layers organize themselves into a sandwich: the outer layers carry languages, the layers inside them topics, the layers at the heart archetypes. The sandwich emerges spontaneously during pretraining and appears in every model we mapped. Archetypes are the architecture for analogy, and we strongly suggest that this structure of archetypes and topics is the mechanism of a language model's intelligence: we see it self-organize as the model is trained. The neurons, the texts and the code are released with this paper as its reproduction package, so that anyone can repeat the test inside the model.
comment: 18 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. Reproduction package (neuron sets, texts, answers, code) in the ancillary files. v2: corrections to the text; the reproduction package now runs on any machine

title: Recursive Sparse Attention: Million-Token Length Extrapolation at Logarithmic Cost
abstract: At context lengths of about 1M tokens, dense attention is costly in prefill and decoding, and training typically relies on long documents, which become scarcer as the target length increases. Most sparse attention methods score all preceding blocks or tokens, so their selection cost per query is $O(L)$ at context length $L$; hierarchical selection reduces it to $O(\log L)$, but prior trainable hierarchical methods report accuracy only within their training length. We propose RecSA (Recursive Sparse Attention), which builds a tree over the KV cache in which each node summarizes its subtree with one key and one mean-pooled value. The keys come from one pooler per layer, shared by all levels and distilled from dense attention. Each level above the tokens selects at most $k$ candidates, so each query has $O(\log L)$ selection cost and reads $O(\log L)$ entries; the summaries of unselected candidates share one softmax with the exact tokens. Each entry's RoPE position is its index among the candidates of its level, so at any length every relative distance stays within the range seen during training. Initialized from Qwen3-4B and trained on 0.62B tokens at the original model's 32K training length, RecSA outperforms all baselines on RULER at every length from 131K to 2M; at 1M, it scores 60.5, compared with 40.0 for the best baseline, Dense + DCA. With our optimized kernels, RecSA is faster than dense attention in end-to-end prefill and decoding from 64K to 2M; at 524K on one H200 GPU, it accelerates prefill by 3.2x and decoding by 3.8x.

title: Subliminal Learning in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Subliminal learning is a phenomenon in large language models (LLMs) where a teacher passes a hidden preference to a student through training data unrelated to that preference. We study whether subliminal learning also occurs in vision-language models (VLMs). We finetune a teacher VLM to prefer a specific animal or facial attribute and use a control teacher from the same base model. Both teachers generate numbers for an unrelated visual task involving geometric shapes. Two students initialized from the same base VLM are finetuned on the same images, using numbers generated by either the biased or control teacher. Across VLMs ranging from 2B to 7B parameters, we find that both animal and facial preferences can transfer through this unrelated task. Students trained on biased-teacher outputs select the target more often than control students, with a difference of up to $\sim$10 percentage points in the animal preference task. Transfer can become stronger with more training data and varies with the target preference, model, and how the numbers are generated. Beyond preferences, we show that the biased student's explanations use more of the same words and phrases as the biased teacher's explanations than those of the control student, even when all three models select the same image. These results matter for training VLMs and show that training on unrelated data may change both a VLM's image preferences and how it explains its choices, and that transfer can become stronger with more training samples.

title: Source-balanced Capped Fisher: Bounded Evidence Aggregation for User Inference in Language Models
abstract: User inference asks whether a source contributed documents to a language-model update, even when the auditor observes only fresh documents from that source. Document-level scores can provide evidence of participation, but combining this evidence is challenging: documents differ in baseline predictability and in how strongly they reflect information learned from other documents of the same source. We propose source-balanced capped Fisher (SCF), an aggregation method that uses known nonparticipating sources to assess how unusual each document score is. It transforms the resulting reference-tail frequencies into negative-log evidence, caps individual contributions, and averages them within each source. This limits the influence of isolated extreme scores while retaining evidence across multiple documents. We complete the inference procedure with a decision rule that tests source participation using a p-value calibrated against a separate set of known nonparticipating sources. The rule provides finite-sample Type-I error control under source exchangeability. Experiments across four real-world datasets show that SCF achieves the highest AUROC among the evaluated aggregation methods in four domains. With the calibration-based decision rule, SCF delivers consistently competitive detection power across the tested settings, achieving the highest power in many cases, while empirical false-positive rates remain generally close to or below the nominal levels.

title: GetGaia 2.0: automatic membership and systemic motions of stellar systems with Gaia
abstract: We present GetGaia 2.0, a public Python package that retrieves the Gaia data around a stellar system and selects its member stars automatically. The membership is a probabilistic model fitted by expectation maximization that combines the astrometry of every source, with its full covariance, the color-magnitude diagram, the sky distribution and, when available, the line-of-sight velocities, from Gaia or from an external catalog. The local systematic errors of the Gaia reference frame are measured on the quasars of each field. The code returns the systemic proper motion (PM) and parallax with their full covariance, a detection significance, a contamination estimate and the structural parameters of the system. We validate it on synthetic catalogs, where it recovers the members with 90-100 percent purity, and run it on Gaia DR3 for the known dwarf galaxies of the Local Group within 850 kpc and for 95 Galactic globular clusters, in tiers that add one piece of literature information at a time. It measures the systemic PMs of 55 dwarf galaxies and 93 globular clusters at a significance of at least $3σ$; 29 of the dwarfs and 86 of the clusters are recovered from their position alone. The dwarfs include every Milky Way satellite within 300 kpc brighter than $M_V=-5.4$, ultra-faint systems down to $M_V=-0.8$, and nine galaxies at 370-820 kpc. The PMs agree with the published values within 0.1 mas/yr for 47 of the dwarfs and for all the clusters (median differences of 0.032 and 0.009 mas/yr), with uncertainties equal to those of dedicated studies, and none deviates by more than $3σ$. The Gaia line-of-sight velocities alone give the systemic velocity of 71 clusters, within 1 km/s of spectroscopy. GetGaia 2.0 delivers, without manual intervention, the systemic motions and the members of the stellar systems within the reach of Gaia, and is ready for the forthcoming Gaia data releases.
comment: 22 pages, 17 figures, 8 tables. Submitted to A&A. The code will be available at https://github.com/AndresdPM/GetGaia2

title: SAFE-Teen: Evaluating Chatbot Safety Across Adolescent Mental Health Conversations
abstract: Adolescents are increasingly turning to AI chatbots for mental health support, advice, and companionship, raising safety concerns. While recent evaluations have started to examine safety across multiple conversational turns, few compare how slight changes in a teen's responses can affect a chatbot's safety in the same scenario. We conduct a clinician-informed evaluation of chatbot safety in simulated conversations with adolescents aged 13-17, examining how safety failures vary with adolescents' responses and teen-aware system prompting. We evaluated 32,555 simulated conversations across 18 chatbot APIs and two system-prompt conditions using 22 safety criteria grounded in previously identified harms. Conversations spanned 983 variants of 106 seed scenarios covering urgent safety issues, health advice, and identity and relationships. The overall criterion failure rate was 43.3% without the teen-aware prompt and 24.9% with it. The teen-aware prompt reduced failures, but it didn't eliminate them. When a teenager pushed back on a chatbot's answer, failures on mental health diagnosis, medication, and substance misuse boundaries rose by 10-12 percentage points without the prompt, for more than 80% of chatbots. These findings reveal persistent safety failures in simulated adolescent-chatbot interactions and show that safety depends on how a conversation unfolds.
authors: Andrea Mock;Valerie Chen;Eric Lin;Rayan Krishnan;Diyi Yang;Caroline Figueroa
comment: 29 pages. Content warning: this paper discusses sensitive content, including self-harm, suicide, and other mental health topics

title: Compositional Unalignment: Auditing Safety in Large Vision-Language Models
abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) are vulnerable to compositional harm: an image and a prompt that are benign in isolation become harmful through the model's cross-modal reasoning. Recent alignment methods report strong scores on compositional safety benchmarks, but an LLM judge only measures observed behavior and cannot reveal how robustly safety is integrated into the model. We argue that un-alignment provides a complementary audit of alignment robustness. We first show that minimal supervised fine-tuning reaches an LLM-judge score comparable to a multi-stage reinforcement-learning pipeline, so similar benchmark scores cannot establish robustness by themselves. We then show that recognition and refusal of compositional harm are decoupled: nine standard direction-finding methods detect compositional harm with up to AUC=0.99, yet ablating the recovered directions either leaves refusal intact or destroys model coherence. We therefore propose CMaG, a training-free un-alignment method for compositional safety. CMaG measures refusal intention with a refusal-versus-compliance log-probability margin, takes its gradient with respect to mid-layer activations, and contrasts it against partially benign pairs to isolate the cross-modal interaction term. A single backward pass over 80 examples yields a direction along which steering monotonically converts refusal into compliance. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B and LLaVA-1.5-7B, CMaG reduces compositional safety scores by up to 65 points while over 98% of outputs remain coherent, outperforming gradient-based baselines; the direction also transfers to text-explicit harm and un-aligns models hardened by defensive training. Compositional safety can thus appear behaviorally strong while remaining fragile to targeted internal intervention. Warning: this paper contains unsafe model outputs, including references to self-harm.

title: Bearing, heading and the perceptual geometry of collective motion
abstract: Traditional models of collective motion commonly assume that animals turn to match their neighbours' directions of travel. In the harmonic theory, decisions follow from a neural representation of direction, and a neighbour enters only as a stimulus at a bearing, the direction in which it lies. Here we show that a neighbour's spatial extent allows its orientation to enter through projection geometry alone, and the theory generates a matrix of coupling coefficients indexed by the neighbour's bearing and aspect. Responses to bearing alone form one edge of this matrix, and classical heading matching is a special case on its diagonal, one ray through a two-parameter family. Independently, an animal that responds only to neighbour position, perceived with a delay, acquires an alignment coefficient set by the slope of its distance-weighted attraction profile, so that it can align, anti-align or reverse sign. Alignment need not be a rule to be measured. In schooling fish and walking pigeons with body orientation measured independently of travel, social responses are recovered, including bearing responses in the fish. Heading excess depends on how turning is measured, appearing in the fish with forward but not centred responses and remaining unresolved in pigeons. Controls show why neither outcome identifies a direct alignment rule. In fish recordings with motion-assigned body polarity, heading-dependent structure departs from Vicsek form and fails the coefficient test for a common angular potential. Whether animals align thereby becomes a measurable question, with geometric, perceptual and behavioural origins that can be distinguished.

title: Task-Calibrated Random Features via Influence-Based Error Cancellation
abstract: Random features approximate kernel integrals by Monte Carlo, yet only selected frequency-sampling errors affect a downstream task. We propose Task-Calibrated Random Features (TCRF), which balance frequency moments constructed from task-specific influence using weights shared across kernel entries. Closed-form weights coincide with classical minimum-distance calibration; the contribution is a reusable, task-derived calibration space. We show that first-order variance equals the residual variance after projection onto this space. For kernel ridge regression, complete cancellation yields a non-Gaussian second-order limit. For kernel Stein discrepancy, a subset identity and disjoint-block variance decomposition eliminate the linear component of pilot noise. Positive exponential-tilting weights preserve the positive-semidefinite feature representation and support higher feasible calibration ranks. Paired experiments show improved approximation to exact kernel ridge regression at larger frequency budgets and to the exact empirical Stein discrepancy under a fixed alternative, even after accounting for a frequency-equivalent pilot budget. Gains are smaller with cross-validated ridge, landmark pilots require conservative rank selection, and near the Stein null allocating the pilot budget to additional ordinary frequencies is preferable.

title: τ-bench-LILT: Evaluating Conversational Agents on Realistic Multilingual Tool-Use Tasks
abstract: Frontier evaluations of tool-using conversational agents are conducted almost exclusively in English, leaving a critical gap for organizations deploying agents in other languages and regions. We present $τ$-bench-LILT, a multilingual extension of ${τ^3}$-bench covering German, Korean, Turkish, and Farsi in the airline, retail, telecom, and banking domains. We natively localize every layer of the benchmark: customer databases are populated with culturally appropriate records, user-simulator prompts are refined iteratively through contrastive annotation by native-language experts, and tasks are updated according to the localized database and to reflect realistic tasks in the target region. Evaluation across eight agent models shows the largest drops compared to English in the Korean and Farsi retail domains, by up to 61 points in pass^4. Code and data released at https://github.com/lilt/tau-bench-lilt.
authors: Kaden Uhlig;Kiarash Mokhtari;Anıl Arslan;Yunsu Kim;Joern Wuebker

title: Barlow Packings All Have Maximum Packing Fraction: Why it is so Hard to Find Barlow Structures Other than fcc or hcp?
abstract: We apply lattice theory to periodic Barlow packings $(X_{1}X_{2}\dots X_{N})_{\infty}$ where $X_{i}\in\{A,B,C\}$ and $X_{i}\neq X_{i+1}$, formed by stacking two-dimensional hexagonal close-packed layers, interacting via generalized $(n,m)$-Lennard-Jones potentials. The cohesive energies of all packings lie between those of hexagonal close-packed (hcp, $(AB)$) and face-centered cubic (fcc, $(ABC)$) structure and vary almost linearly with the fcc stacking fraction. The equilibrium lattice constant, bulk modulus, Einstein frequency, and vibrational entropy show similarly near-linear trends. For the standard $(12,6)$ potential, fcc has the highest vibrational entropy and hcp the lowest, with other Barlow packings falling between them, consistent with previous sticky-hard-sphere Monte Carlo simulations and supported by phonon dispersion calculations. These trends imply an approximately linear dependence of free energy on fcc stacking fraction, with hcp and fcc as endpoints. This provides a simple thermodynamic explanation for why intermediate Barlow stackings are rare in nature: near-linearity offers little driving force to favor them. Exceptions may arise when hcp and fcc are nearly degenerate in energy or when many-body interactions, absent from the present model, favor another stacking. Density-functional calculations including dispersion forces for argon Barlow packings with periods $N=2,3,4$, and $12$ corroborate the predicted near-linear cohesive energy dependence.

title: CosmicGrain: An On-the-fly Dust Physics Module
abstract: We present CosmicGrain, a dust physics module built on Gadget-4 that models explicit dust superparticles that experience resolved gas-dust drag and radiation pressure, undergo collisional heating and cooling with gas, and are further shaped by subgrid treatments for grain growth, thermal sputtering, coagulation, shattering, supernova shock destruction, and astration. We run an eleven-rung physics ladder (S0-S10) at 1024^3 resolution to isolate the contribution of individual processes to a Milky Way-mass halo's dust population. Because dust is evolved as active on-the-fly particles, individual grains retain distinct histories producing results inaccessible to passive dust models such as the strongly asymmetric silicate-to-carbon shattering destruction ratio driven by silicate grains' smaller birth size. Gas-dust drag is the dominant driver of ISM dust enrichment, increasing dust levels by ~100 times while every other process changes the R200 dust abundance by only 10-30%. We find reasonable agreement with the Milky Way's radial dust-to-gas and dust-to-metal ratios, with carbon dust preferentially enriching the CGM relative to silicates. The code is freely available at https://cosmicgrain.space.

title: MammoSeek: A Mammography Agent with selective zooming for grounded reports
abstract: Radiologists read a screening mammogram by first forming a global impression of the four views and then selectively magnifying suspicious regions before assigning a BI-RADS assessment. MLLMs, in contrast, see the whole image at a fixed, reduced resolution, which makes sub-millimeter calcifications invisible, and they perform close to chance on mammography. Therefore, we present MammoSeek, a mammography agent that reproduces this reading process. After forming an impression of each breast, the agent performs selective zooming: it decides by itself which detector candidates deserve a closer look and inspects only those on full-resolution views. Guided by a BI-RADS assessment skill, it then assigns a category and generates a localized, lexicon-structured report for each breast; its assessment is combined with image-model scores in a decision layer to decide recall. On an internal (EMBED) and an external (VinDr-Mammo) dataset, \ours reaches exam-level AUCs of 0.824 and 0.818, far above other MLLMs, mammography agent and CNN classifiers. Selective zooming also outperforms both no zooming and forced zooming in localization, structured-report F1 and recall decisions at low cost.

title: Thermally-driven quantum reservoir computing
abstract: Heat generation limits computation, classical and quantum, from single logic gates to entire data centers. However, an in principle limiting physical factor can sometimes be turned into a resource. In reservoir computing, energy dissipation is what gives a reservoir its fading memory. Here, we introduce a paradigm where the data injection itself is encoded on the time-dependent temperature of a thermal bath. We derive an exact expression for the nonlinear response of any fixed readout, and prove a rigorous memory-nonlinearity trade-off which turns out to be a structural necessity, rather than a tunable dynamical regime, since the same coupling that injects data also enforces equilibration. We illustrate both results with a driven qubit, using a single free parameter, and with a pair of coupled qubits, where the breaking of a discrete symmetry opens a fifteen-dimensional space to a single observable, yet that observable alone recovers just over half of it. This refutes the misconception that large Hilbert spaces guarantee computational power. Our results relocate the memory-nonlinearity trade-off from the reservoir's dynamics to its measurement channel, pointing to observable choice and bath engineering (instead of Hamiltonian control) as the physical levers for a thermally-native quantum reservoir computer.

title: Multiplayer Stopping Games with a Conditionally Atomless Filtration
abstract: Stopping games are the multiplayer generalization of optimal stopping problems, in which each player independently chooses when to stop, and the payoff depends on who stops first and when. While the existence of $\varepsilon$-equilibria in two-player stopping games with integrable payoffs is known, the multiplayer case has remained open. We prove that every multiplayer stopping game in discrete time with integrable payoff process admits an $\varepsilon$-equilibrium for every $\varepsilon > 0$, provided the filtration is conditionally atomless. This condition is satisfied, in particular, when the underlying probability space is $\{0,1\}^{\dN}$ endowed with the uniform measure and its natural filtration. Our method also shows that every three-player stopping game, without the restriction to conditionally atomless filtration, admits an $\varepsilon$-equilibrium, for every $\varepsilon > 0$. The proof combines techniques developed for two-player stopping games and for multiplayer quitting games, with a key new insight: the richness encoded in a conditionally atomless filtration can substitute for an external public randomization device, allowing players to coordinate without an explicit coordination signal.

title: VINO: Revisiting 3D Representation Learning with Volume Transformers
abstract: Self-supervised learning has given rise to vision foundation models that learn general-purpose image representations transferable across downstream tasks, yet representation learning for 3D scenes has not achieved comparable success. Motivated by this, we identify key limitations of current 3D representation learning approaches and revisit their core design choices. We first replace the commonly used hierarchical PTv3 backbone with the Volume Transformer, a ViT-like architecture for 3D scenes. We then redesign two core objectives of modern approaches built around student-teacher networks: matching representations across views and predicting masked content from visible context. For the first objective, we separate the roles of teacher and student: the teacher provides clean, consistent targets while the student learns invariance to stronger perturbations. For the second objective, we prevent the student from accessing the masked geometry and instead require it to infer missing representations from visible context only. Finally, we redesign 2D-to-3D knowledge distillation, replacing direct regression of view-dependent image features with view-consistent supervision. Together, these changes form VINO, a framework that learns semantic representations of 3D scenes without labels. VINO substantially improves dense linear probing across indoor and outdoor benchmarks and transfers strongly to out-of-domain settings.
authors: Adrian Kruse;Kadir Yilmaz;Daan de Geus;Francis Engelmann;Bastian Leibe

title: Scalable Transpilation for Overcoming Restricted Connectivity in Distributed Superconducting Quantum Architectures
abstract: Distributed Quantum Computing (DQC) offers a promising pathway to scale superconducting quantum hardware, but restricted inter- and intra-module connectivity creates a major transpilation bottleneck. Current DQC transpilation methods often assume idealized hardware connectivity, ignore subsequent intra-module routing, or suffer from substantial computational overheads that limit their applicability at scale. To address this, we introduce a scalable transpilation method tailored for the restricted connectivity of distributed superconducting quantum architectures. Specifically, our quantum interaction graph (QIG) approach couples a graph-partitioning mapping step with a fast SABRE-inspired routing heuristic. On a 48-qubit (3 QPUs $\times$ 16 qubits) architecture with all-to-all inter-core connectivity, our method reduces average aggregated costs by up to 24.72% (unstructured) and 24.01% (structured), while delivering >250$\times$ speed-ups for structured workloads compared to the state-of-the-art DMapS algorithm. On the 399-qubit (3$\times$133) IBM Flamingo, where DMapS times out on dense circuits, our approach maintains practical runtimes. Against a DQC-adapted SABRE baseline, it reduces structured circuit routing costs by up to 51.94% (all-to-all inter-core topology) and 51.96% (restricted line topology). Ultimately, this work delivers a practical transpilation method for DQC at scale.
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE)

title: ShapleyOG: Fast Adaptive Shapley Value Estimation with Odd Gaussian Processes
abstract: Shapley values are a central tool for attribution in machine learning. Since their exact computation requires evaluating the cooperative game to be explained on exponentially many player coalitions, they are typically estimated from a limited number of evaluations. Recently, ShaplEIG has shown that adaptively selecting the coalitions to evaluate substantially improves sample efficiency over classical estimators. This, however, comes at the cost of a sequential procedure that, in every iteration, refits a Gaussian process surrogate of the game and selects the coalition with the largest expected information gain about the Shapley values. The resulting computational overhead limits its applicability to costly games with low evaluation budgets. We present fast adaptive Shapley value estimation with Odd Gaussian Processes (ShapleyOG) to overcome this limitation. ShapleyOG leverages the fact that Shapley values depend only on the odd component of the game, and we show that under paired sampling a Gaussian process surrogate on this component alone yields the same Shapley value posterior and coalition selection criterion from half as many observations. Moreover, ShapleyOG refits the surrogate only on a sparse schedule and efficiently updates the selection criterion in between, and it extends quadrature-based computation schemes to the prior covariance of the Shapley values, which allows for exact or cheaper approximate computation. In extensive experiments on diverse games, ShapleyOG matches the estimation accuracy of ShaplEIG while reducing its overhead by up to three orders of magnitude. As a result, it outperforms state-of-the-art non-adaptive estimators at equal total computation time already when a single evaluation takes a tenth of a second and a budget of a few thousand evaluations suffices, thereby widening the regime in which adaptive coalition selection is applicable and pays off.
authors: David Rundel;R. Teal Witter;Santo M. A. R. Thies;Matthias Feurer;Fabian Fumagalli;Bernd Bischl

title: Formamide formation on forsterite and Mg(OH)$_2\cdot$H$_2$O
abstract: Context. Formamide formation in the Universe has been the subject of debate due to its importance as a precursor to amino acids and RNA. Current studies focus on the gas-phase and icy grain formation routes. However, formamide formation on bare silicate surfaces or hydrated Mg-bearing molecular models remains largely unexplored in environments relevant to protoplanetary disks. Aims. This study presents a quantum-chemical investigation of formamide formation on an Mg center and a silicate surface. $Mg(OH)_2\cdot H_2O$ and the bare (010) forsterite ($Mg_2SiO_4$) surface, used as an analog of a bare dust-grain surface, may promote formamide formation via $NH_2$ addition to $H_2CO$. Methods. I employed density functional theory (DFT) to study the addition of $NH_2$ to $H_2CO$ with an isolated $Mg(OH)_2\cdot H_2O$ molecular model and on the forsterite (010) surface. First, I benchmarked various theoretical methodologies. I then examined the ability of $Mg(OH)_2\cdot H_2O$ and the forsterite (010) surface to promote formamide formation. Finally, for the case with an entrance barrier, I computed unimolecular rate constants and half-lives to assess its kinetic behavior. Results. $Mg(OH)_2\cdot H_2O$ promotes proton transfer within the $NH_2$-$CH_2O$ intermediate via the O-H group coordinated with Mg following $NH_2$ addition to $H_2CO$, whereas on the forsterite, a barrier-less addition pathway is found when $NH_2$ is initially physisorbed close to the formaldehyde center, followed by proton transfer leading to formamide formation. Conclusions. The Mg-bearing model systems considered here can promote rapid proton transfer following $NH_2$ addition to $H_2CO$. For the $Mg(OH)_2\cdot H_2O$ model, the reaction step from the pre-reactive complex is predicted to occur on nanosecond timescales at temperatures approaching 300 K. The present work provides kinetic data for astrochemical models.
comment: 18 pages, 10 figures. Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics

title: Distributed Geometric Optimization and Control of Rigid Differential-Drive Formations from Relative-Position Measurements
abstract: Distance based formation control fixes the shape of a robot team but leaves its position and orientation unconstrained. We regulate all three for differential drive robots that have only one absolute position anchor, absolute headings, body frame relative position measurements, and communication with their neighbors. We derive a two layer estimation control scheme directly from optimization. The first half of the result is a set of graph-proximal estimators that reconstruct the centroid, the anchor vector, and the centered coordinates. Exact proximal updates reach consensus in finitely many steps, and a finite number of primal dual iterations leaves a bounded reconstruction error. The controller combines proximal centroid and orientation steps with distance gradient shape regulation, and a finite rotation removes the orientation drift caused by the shape step. A discrete Lyapunov analysis gives local exponential convergence once the estimators have converged. We validate the method in ROS 2 Gazebo and in experiments with five physical robots.

title: A Machine Learning Approach to Coupling Photoionization & Multi-Frequency Radiation Hydrodynamics
abstract: We use machine learning (ML) to couple photoionization microphysics to radiation hydrodynamic simulations of line-driven winds. ML models are trained on outputs from the photoionization code XSTAR to predict the line-driving force multiplier as a function of gas ionization, optical depth, and the blackbody temperature of the irradiating spectral energy distribution (SED). We implement the trained models within Athena++, enabling rapid runtime evaluation of the radiative acceleration without directly solving the photoionization problem during the hydrodynamic evolution. We find that random forest models provide the highest accuracy and reproduce the force multipliers over a three-dimensional parameter space more accurately, and with less training data, than traditional precomputed tables using trilinear interpolation. Because the framework treats the force multiplier as a function of the evolving local SED, it can be generalized to more complex radiation fields and arbitrary spectral shapes. More broadly, this work demonstrates how ML can serve as a computational framework for embedding expensive microphysical calculations within large-scale dynamical simulations.

title: Detection of Differential Chromatic Refraction with LSST Camera data
abstract: The Earth's atmosphere acts like a prism, deflecting blue light towards the zenith more than red light. Airmass-dependent changes in astrometry can therefore be used to infer additional information about the wavelength distribution of light within a photometric passband. The Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) will observe each point in the southern sky several hundred times, with observations spread across a range of airmasses. Using commissioning data from the LSST camera released in LSST Data Preview 2, we report the detection of this differential chromatic refraction (DCR) effect in observations of galaxies and quasars in the COSMOS field. We show how information from DCR can complement the six-band colour information from LSST and help break degeneracies when selecting extragalactic samples and estimating their photometric redshifts. DCR will be a valuable resource for scientific studies and care should be taken not to remove useful DCR information from future LSST data releases.
comment: 7 pages, 6 figures, accepted for publication in MNRAS

title: Improving Gravitationally Induced Entanglement in Interferometric Configurations
abstract: Proposals to detect gravitationally induced entanglement between massive particles offer a promising pathway toward probing the quantum nature of gravity. We perform a systematic geometric optimization and comparative analysis of Stern--Gerlach (SG) and Mach--Zehnder (MZ) matter-wave interferometers for this purpose, deriving exact analytical expressions for the gravitational phase of each configuration. Our first key result is that geometric optimization is indispensable. For commonly assumed experimental parameters, neglecting the optimization of geometric ratios can suppress the accumulated phase, and hence the detectability of entanglement, by up to several orders of magnitude. Second, we provide a complete comparative analysis of two SG orientations (linear and parallel) and three MZ orientations (translation-symmetric, mirror-symmetric, and parallel-arms). The parallel-arms SG and MZ configurations tend to yield the largest phase accumulations and are nearly equivalent in performance, whereas the translation-symmetric MZ setup exhibits destructive-interference nulls that act as blind operating points where detection becomes ineffective. These observations highlight the importance of geometry-aware design. A Monte Carlo error analysis of realistic fabrication tolerances indicates that the parallel-arms configurations are generally more robust, maintaining low relative phase uncertainty over broad parameter intervals. Furthermore, an evaluation of Bell violations assesses the feasibility and signal-to-noise ratio of each configuration. Our results identify geometric optimization, particularly through parallel-arms designs, as an important consideration for near-term experiments targeting gravitationally induced entanglement.

title: Perceptual Distortion for Overfitted Video Coding: Sliced Matching in Space, Error Alignment in Time
abstract: Recent works in neural video coding have increasingly been trading off perceptual quality against reconstruction fidelity at a fixed bitrate. Wasserstein Distortion (WD) offers a principled approach to balancing these objectives by relaxing spatial correspondences in feature matching, enabling lightweight overfitted image codecs to compete with computationally intensive generative decoders. Extending vanilla WD to video, however, presents two challenges: its independent Gaussian approximation limits the expressiveness of feature distribution matching, while unconstrained texture resampling across frames introduces temporal inconsistencies. We address these challenges by distinguishing between the correspondences that can be relaxed and those that must be preserved. Spatially, we introduce a local sliced Wasserstein distortion (SWD) that matches empirical feature distributions through one-dimensional optimal transport, capturing cross-channel dependencies without enforcing exact spatial alignment. Temporally, we employ a novel flow residual that constrains coding errors along motion trajectories, preserving temporal consistency without imposing additional reconstruction fidelity constraints. Evaluated on UVG and HEVC Class B with the overfitted codec COOL-CHIC, our framework achieves BD-rate reductions of 9.2% in DISTS and 3.0% in LPIPS relative to frame-wise WD, averaged over test sequences, while lowering tOF by 10.2% at matched rate.
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures; submitted to IEEE ISCAS

title: Dithered Belief Propagation for Real-Time Quantum Memory Decoding
abstract: We introduce dithered belief-propagation decoding for circuit-level quantum memory to mitigate the oscillations and trapping behavior that limit standard belief-propagation (BP) decoders for qLDPC codes. Our approach combines a quantum-adapted sign-flip mechanism with chained randomized prior perturbation. Evaluated under circuit-level noise on the distance-11 rotated surface code and the distance-12 bivariate-bicycle code, the proposed dithered decoder significantly outperforms BP and BP+OSD+CS-10. The proposed decoder achieves accuracy comparable to or better than state-of-the-art Relay-BP, especially at higher physical error rates, while trading a moderate increase in additions for about 98% fewer multiplications on average and eliminating node-level RNGs. These results suggest that dithering is a promising approach toward real-time decoding of quantum memories.
authors: Zhengyu Cai;Mohamad Ali Jarkas;Bokun Zhao;Warren J. Gross
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures. In the proceedings of QCE 2026

title: Matriarchy Classics: A Computational Approach to Swap Only Gendered Words in Classic Novels
abstract: This paper proposes a trustworthy computational method to gender-swap public domain novels, with programmatic guarantees that only gendered words are inverted and all other words are left unchanged. This may seem like a simple task, but both large language models and naive rule-based methods fail to complete it. The proposed method includes a custom whitespace-preserving tokenizer, gender-swap mappings across plural and possessive forms, pronoun handling, and a character renaming strategy. It shortens the time required to gender-swap a novel from weeks of manual labor to minutes. The method is demonstrated on two public-domain novels. Pride and Prejudice is transported to matriarchal Regency England, where inheritance flows through daughters, mothers rule the household, and a frantic Mr. Bennet is determined to secure advantageous marriages for his sons. The Great Gatsby pivots to a matriarchal Jazz Age where newly-rich Ms. Gatsbee throws lavish parties in the hopes of reuniting with her lost love, David, who is now married to the violent Thelma Buchanan. Gender-swapped novels could serve as useful tools to investigate the gender biases of readers, authors, societies, and AI systems.

title: A Proxy-Based Method for Measuring Racial Disparities in~Text-to-Image~Generators
abstract: We present an automated method for auditing text-to-image generators for representational bias against ground-truth demographic benchmarks. Our approach adapts the racial proxy variables used in U.S. antidiscrimination law to provide a fine-grained comparative analysis of variations in racial representation in generated images. We classify each generated image by race and then compare the model's distribution to publicly available demographic benchmark data to identify patterns of over- and under-representation. We also measure skin tone using CIELAB values and calculate cosine similarity amongst groups of images in order to capture biases that don't show up in demographic comparisons such as differences in image quality across races and skin tones. We report on experiments testing three models (Imagen 4 Fast, Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large Turbo, and Flux Schnell) using three categories of proxies (geographic, occupational, and surname) and 50 variants within each category. We find notable variation across the models as well as by proxy category. For example, Imagen 4 Fast overrepresents white classified images more than the other models tested and produces images with lighter, more homogeneous skin tones. Imagen 4 Fast also had the largest representational disparity for Black demographics among surname and geographical prompts. Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large Turbo produces results that overall diverge most from census data but yield the most diverse range of skin tones. Our method yields a generalizable and legally-grounded auditing tool that surfaces detailed information about model outputs without relying on implicit normative definitions of fairness.
authors: Nia Mucher;Ngan Pham;Jason Chin;Aaron Brown;David Evans
journal_ref: Proceedings of the Ninth AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society, Vol. 9, No. 3 (2026), pp. 1846-1857

title: Bayesian Tensor Train Kernel Machines with Automatic Model Complexity Inference
abstract: Tensor Network (TN) kernel machines accelerate supervised learning by using low-rank TNs to reduce computation and memory. However, most TN-based methods are deterministic with manually tuned ranks and feature dimensions, while the existing Bayesian TN kernel machine is restricted to the CANDECOMP/PARAFAC decomposition (CPD), whose single rank is shared by all modes. We extend this framework to the tensor train (TT) and propose Bayesian Tensor Train Kernel Machines (BTT-KM), whose hierarchical ARD-type priors on the TT cores infer the TT ranks and feature dimensions from data. Since each TT core is coupled to the others only through its neighbors, its closed-form posterior update requires propagating the contributions of all other cores along the chain. Mean-field variational inference yields a Bayesian alternating least squares algorithm with the same computational complexity as its deterministic counterpart and a closed-form predictive distribution. A synthetic experiment illustrates that BTT-KM recovers the true TT ranks and feature dimensions from an over-parameterized initialization.
comment: 31 pages, 4 figures, 1 algorithm. Code available at https://github.com/afrakilic/BTTKM

title: Adapting LLM Judges to Observed Human Annotation Policy through Soft Prompt Tuning
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly employed as automated judges for evaluating chatbot responses. While proprietary models can achieve high agreement with human annotators, they remain costly and difficult to deploy in practical settings. Lightweight open-source LLM judges provide an attractive alternative but typically exhibit lower agreement with human ratings. In this paper, we investigate whether soft prompt tuning can align open-source LLM judges more closely with human annotation policy. We train soft prompts on the FairBotBench benchmark and evaluate the adapted judges across the dimensions of bias, toxicity, and personalization. Our findings demonstrate that hybrid soft-prompt tuning, which combines textual prompts with learned continuous prompt embeddings, consistently improves agreement with human annotations over the corresponding untuned baselines. For Qwen 3.5 9B, the adapted judges surpass both hosted reference judges across all three evaluation dimensions.
authors: Tamás Janusko;Sven Kleinkop;Ricardo Bochnia;Gunnar Hempel;Steffen Tomschke;Jürgen Anke;Maik Thiele
comment: CONVERSATIONS 2026, International Symposium on Chatbots and Human-Centred AI (Preprint)

title: Data-Driven Modeling of Molten Chloride Corrosion Using Static Test Data
abstract: Molten chloride corrosion has been studied for decades, yet reliable prediction across different alloys, salts, and test conditions remains difficult. In this work, 291 static molten chloride corrosion experiments reported in the literature were compiled into a structured dataset and used to develop an interpretable machine-learning framework for corrosion-rate predictions. To better represent the differences in salt condition across studies, a Chloride Salt Preparation Index (CSPI) was introduced to bring the reported salt-treatment method, atmosphere control, and pre-exposure impurity condition on a common numerical scale. A blended tree-based ensemble provided the most consistent predictive performance, achieving a cross-validated \(R^2\) of 0.85 and an MAE of 0.41 mg cm\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\). The graded CSPI retained more useful information than a simple purified/unpurified classification and emerged as the dominant model descriptor. Global sensitivity and SHAP analyses further identified exposure time, temperature, and alloy chemistry as important contributors to the model predictions, with several observed trends consistent with the established molten-chloride corrosion behavior. The conformal prediction intervals were well calibrated, providing an estimate of prediction uncertainty in addition to the point prediction. Overall, the framework demonstrates that historical corrosion data can support quantitative, interpretable, and uncertainty-aware prediction when experimental context is represented explicitly, while also highlighting where more consistent reporting and targeted experiments are needed to improve future molten-salt corrosion models.

title: Eddies that ride the flow: a model of turbulence with Richardson dispersion and anomalous dissipation
abstract: We construct a divergence-free velocity field $\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x},t)$ on $\mathbb{T}^{n}$ that is a genuine function of position and carries both defining properties of turbulent transport: Richardson pair dispersion and a dissipative anomaly. No synthetic field has carried both, because the frame that gives the first destroys the field the second requires. The key is a dichotomy: deforming a spectrally localised pattern smears it across scales, whereas pushing its generating centres forward and re-convolving leaves the spectral envelope exactly invariant --- so transporting the eddy centres preserves both cascade and frame. In the field the finite-size Lyapunov exponent obeys $ζ(R)=h(R)-1$ threshold by threshold within the scaling range, with a sweeping deficit $Δ_{\rm sw}=+0.038\pm0.019$, consistent with zero, against $+0.091\pm0.019$ for the frozen field on the same data, a gap that doubles at Navier--Stokes intermittency. Companion papers prove that this family shows Richardson dispersion and a dissipative anomaly (Fefferman and Mayboroda 2026), and that a scalar advected by this flow obeys Yaglom's relation (De Lellis 2026), at small Kubo number. Trajectories forget their starting point as the smallest eddy is removed: the median separation of pairs released from one point with independent Brownian kicks varies as $κ_{p}^{0.0333\pm0.0038}$ over 22 decades of particle diffusivity, against $κ_{p}^{1/2}$ for a smooth control. A scalar in the same field closes the exact scale-by-scale variance budget, four independently measured terms balancing the dissipation to 15\% over 1.2 decades with no adjustable constant, and reaches its inertial--convective asymptote $S_{L}=-χr$ to $0.9995\pm0.0018$ once the measured diffusive transfer is restored, while under an imposed mean gradient $χ$ changes by 14\% over a factor 5.8 in $κ$.
authors: Raul Jimenez;Svitlana Mayboroda;Camillo de Lellis;David N. Spergel;Max Engelstein
comment: The code, the analysis scripts that produce every figure and numbers in the paper, the run configurations, the data behind the figures and the supplementary movies are available at https://github.com/R1967J/kinematic-field. A single self-contained generator of the velocity field kinematic_field.py

title: Nonequilibrium Spin-Glass Order in a Long-Range Quantum Ising Glass and Its Sensitivity to Noise
abstract: We study spin-glass order after a transverse-field quench in a long-range quantum Ising glass. The diagonal-ensemble Edwards-Anderson order coincides at the no-quench and zero-field endpoints, yet in between cold shells overshoot it and hot shells undershoot it. This stems from a competition in correlation space between the rigidity of populated eigenstates and the spread of their pair patterns. Under weak longitudinal dephasing the zero-field endpoint is exactly pinned while the characteristic finite-quench response fades, giving a self-referenced noise probe for quantum spin simulators.
comment: 27 pages, 23 figures: Letter (4 pages + End Matter, 3 figures) and Supplemental Material (20 figures)

title: What Patients Say They Can't Access: Mining Cancer Screening Barriers from Online Communities
abstract: Cancer screening disparities persist across the U.S., yet the patient-reported barriers driving low uptake remain poorly characterized at scale. While clinical surveys capture structured responses, they miss the organic, unsolicited discourse where patients candidly describe real-world obstacles. In this paper, we conduct a large-scale analysis of over 56,000 posts across six cancer-specific Reddit communities to surface barriers to cancer screening among U.S. patients. We apply a pipeline combining keyword filtering, barrier triage, open coding, and codebook synthesis to systematically extract and categorize patient-reported barriers from 576 U.S.-located posts. Our qualitative analysis reveals recurring structural, informational, and psychosocial barriers that vary meaningfully by cancer type and community context. These findings lay the groundwork for future work aimed at proactively identifying and addressing barriers at scale - spanning a broader range of cancer types and populations - and informing the design of targeted interventions, navigator programs, and health system policies that translate patient-reported obstacles into actionable solutions.

title: Consistent yet Contextual: Learning Author-Level Mixtures of Style for Authorship Attribution
abstract: Approaches to authorship verification or attribution typically model the style of a document, asking whether two documents were likely written by the same author. While recent approaches have been performant, such approaches largely ignore modeling the authors themselves and how varied their style is. Here, we introduce multiple alternatives for modeling the author and demonstrate that allowing an author's representation to capture multiple consistent but distinct writing styles yields significant performance improvements. Using our new authorship model, we then examine when an author writes in a way that is most idiomatic of their style across four scenarios: (i) variation in the size of their writing audiences, (ii) temporal distance from when the model was trained, (iii) the effect of preceding context, and (iv) the effect of genre norms on style. Across all four experiments, we demonstrate that authors vary substantially in how idiolectic their writing is. Our results have clear implications for both the modeling and data used for authorship verification and attribution, showing that authors need to be represented with their multiple styles and that some settings produce text that is much more informative about who wrote that text.
authors: Omkar Yadav;Michael Jiang;Kenan Alkiek;Jian Zhu;David Jurgens

title: Practical Semialgebraic Optimization via Sparse Sample-Based Sum-of-Squares Programming
abstract: As the importance of semialgebraic optimization grows in engineering, so does the need for scalable sum-of-squares (SOS) methods. Their convex relaxations can guide mixed-integer search and often deliver certified global optima outright. Scaling traditional SOS typically requires hand-crafted bases and redundant constraints, whereas sample-based SOS numerically exploits feasible set geometry to reduce bases and build smaller, often tighter relaxations from black-box evaluations. However, discrete variables can require exponentially many samples, and each sampled equation couples all cliques, destroying correlative sparsity. In this work, we avoid enumeration and slack variables by sampling a tractable variety that contains the feasible set, with multipliers only for the omitted constraints. To recover sparsity, we introduce "separator" polynomials that split the sampled equations into local systems coupled only on clique overlaps. This yields a novel, convergent hierarchy of semidefinite programs (SDPs) with block sizes and sample requirements governed by local interactions rather than total problem size. Lastly, we show how to verify sample sufficiency and prune redundant equations numerically before solving. In robust estimation and motion planning, we obtain certifiably small optimality gaps at scales far beyond those reported for traditional sparse SOS. For example, we solve a truncated least-squares 3D registration problem with 1600 candidate correspondences in under 49 seconds using an off-the-shelf SDP solver on a laptop CPU.
