title: FlagRot: Selective Rotation for Low-Bit KV Caches
abstract: Long-context inference is bound by the KV cache, which 2-bit codes could shrink about sixfold if their error stays in check. The usual remedy rotates keys before quantizing, assuming rotation always helps. However, we observe that it does not: rotation flattens a spiky piece of a key but can give a flat one a new peak, and both coexist within one key. We therefore propose FlagRot, which stores each 32-channel piece rotated or as is, whichever has the smaller calibrated attention error, and rotates the query instead when reading. We further show that how often to decide follows the quantization axis: per-channel caches such as KIVI need one decision per head, at no write cost, while per-token caches decide per key, with the choice stored in existing sign bits. At 2.5 bits per value, FlagRot lowers the twelve-model KL divergence of KIVI from 18.7 to 12.4 x 10^-3, below RotateKV on 9 of 12 models. Served as a vLLM plugin, it raises RULER at 128k tokens by +2.9 points and the LongBench v1 mean by +0.4 to +1.9 points on the three of four models where 2-bit KIVI loses accuracy. It also lowers the error of 4-bit integer and FP4 caches.
authors: Kunming Shao;Xijie Huang;Jierun Chen;Jiaqi Shao;Yanli Wang;Jiangnan Yu;Qiwei Li;Wei Zhang;Kwang-Ting Cheng;Chi Ying Tsui

title: Peer Memory Changes Who LLM Agents Consult Without a Detected Gain in Answer Accuracy
abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems often reuse the same agents across tasks, creating an opportunity to draw on past interactions when deciding whom to consult. We study this form of memory with PeerMem, which saves MACE's LinUCB state and reuses it when the same agents return. Using six agents, a fixed set of 80 HotpotQA questions, and 12 paired lineages per model, we compare cold, warm, and shuffled initialization in an answer-exchange protocol with reference-answer feedback. Under stable evidence access, warm memory lowers pooled hindsight regret and increases consultation of other evidence holders on Qwen3-32B and Gemma-4-31B-it, while final token F1 differences remain uncertain. Qwen interaction traces further show that warm agents more often encounter peer answers that score above their own prior answers. We extend the evaluation to Qwen3.5-9B using freshly learned memory to compare warm and cold initialization under reassigned and paired stable roles. The primary changed-minus-stable final-F1 interaction is -1.38 points, with a 95% interval of [-3.50,+0.73]. Together, these experiments trace the effects of peer memory through consultation, answer revision, and final task performance.
authors: Jeffrey Chu;Anjali Joseph;Rivan Mandot;Feker Demere;Vincent Li
comment: 27 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Personalized, Aligned, Long-Term Memory for AI Systems (PALM)

title: Adaptive Qubit Encoding for Continuous-Variable Quantum Optimization
abstract: Optimizing continuous-variable functions on qubit-based quantum hardware requires a finite representation of the search space and a solver-compatible representation of the objective function. Fixed-grid discretizations provide a direct encoding, but restrict the search to a predefined range and resolution; at the same time, constructing a compact Hamiltonian for a general continuous-variable objective can be impractical. Here, we introduce a framework for continuous-variable optimization tailored to qubit-based quantum architectures. The method combines an adaptive discretization with an iterative local mapping of the objective function onto an effective spin-glass Hamiltonian. We assess the approach on unconstrained and constrained instances of the $n$-dimensional Gramacy-Lee benchmark, and on a proof-of-concept inverse-planning problem in intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) for cancer treatment. The results show that this framework can produce competitive solutions, supporting its use as a flexible mapping strategy for continuous-variable optimization in qubit-based quantum and quantum-inspired pipelines.
authors: Samuele Cavinato;Marco Tesoro;Gianluca Morettini;Marta Paiusco;Alessandro Scaggion;Simone Montangero;Ilaria Siloi

title: Thinking Fast, Trading Late: System One Decision Models vs the Market
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) read company news at scale, and backtests suggest that their readings predict stock returns. We ask how much of that predictability survives a test that rules out look-ahead, memorization and selection. We propose OLIVIA, a protocol for such tests: point-in-time inputs with company identities masked, selection on validation data only, an analysis plan frozen by cryptographic hash, and a test period unblinded once through a logged lock. We apply it to AI decision models, non-generative language models that return probabilities for typed questions, reading news about S&P 500 stocks: an open-weights model we fine-tuned on 2024-2025 data, three commercial models and standard baselines. The fine-tuned model's signal replicated on two validation quarters (daily information coefficients 0.055 and 0.065) but fell to 0.020 (t = 1.7) on the blinded January-July 2026 test. The commercial models' readings line up with the overnight move to the open (information coefficient 0.074 to 0.077) but not with the move after it, so the news is priced by the time a trader can act on it at the open. No model can tell over- from under-reaction, and no pre-registered strategy survives costs and a deflated Sharpe ratio. Commercial models identify masked companies in 62% to 74% of cases against a 28% baseline: masking hides names, not companies. The market reads the news first.
authors: Amir Dehkordi;Alireza Kargarzadeh;Nariman Khaledian;Navid Parvini;Sid Ghatak;Arman Khaledian
affiliations: Independent Researcher;TailState Intelligence Ltd;Independent Researcher;Zanista AI Ltd;Increase Alpha, LLC;Zanista AI Ltd
comment: 40 pages, 12 figures, 12 tables; pre-registered (analysis plan frozen by hash before the test period was unblinded); code at https://github.com/AmirDehkordi/NewsAction

title: The Impact of Internal Electric Fields on Accurate Diamond Magnetometry
abstract: Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center spin ensembles are a promising platform for accurate vector magnetometry, as they offer measurements referenced to a spin Hamiltonian in an anisotropic crystal with native vector sensing capabilities. However, charged dopants within the diamond produce random internal electric fields (RIEFs) that shift NV spin-transition frequencies, and their impact on the accuracy of NV magnetometry has not been investigated. Here, we characterize RIEFs' effect on NV spin-transition spectra and propose an analytical fitting function to improve accuracy in their presence. We build a Monte Carlo RIEF model that reproduces the asymmetric lineshapes observed in experimental optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) spectra, and use it as a testbed to quantify RIEF-induced errors by simulating ODMR spectra including RIEFs and comparing reconstructed magnetic fields to the known model input. With standard analysis approaches, we observe systematic errors exceeding the g-factor uncertainty in fields below $\sim$ 5 mT, while the proposed fitting function reduces the error by nearly an order of magnitude. Our results demonstrate that RIEFs can play a significant role in the systematic error budget for NV magnetometry, and offer a path towards improved accuracy in NV quantum sensing.
authors: Jack Faller;Daphne Freda Gavras;Andrew Lowther;Romain Ruhlmann;Lilian Childress

title: SLATE: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Long-Horizon API Selection in E-commerce Tool Use
abstract: Enterprises increasingly want LLM agents to automate standard operating procedures over their software stacks -- mapping each step of a procedure to the right call among thousands of internal APIs, without hand-authored step-to-API mappings. The core difficulty is API selection at scale: choosing and composing the correct tools over a long horizon, judged only by whether the overall task succeeds. Current tool-use benchmarks do not test this regime -- they expose only a handful of tools, evaluate single-step invocation, or grade multi-step behavior with subjective LLM-as-a-judge scores that penalize valid alternative trajectories. We introduce SLATE (Synthetic Large-scale API Toolkit for E-commerce), a large-scale benchmark that tests large-toolset, long-horizon API selection in a realistic enterprise domain. SLATE couples (i) queries decomposed into hierarchical, tool-grounded procedures over a ~1,000-tool e-commerce library, (ii) a deterministic, context-aware simulator that returns recorded outputs for matching calls and default responses otherwise, and (iii) an end-to-end task-success metric -- a task succeeds when it reaches every reference outcome -- that credits diverse-but-valid trajectories while remaining fully automatic and reproducible. Experiments with six open decision models and the language models they are built on, from 3B to 12B parameters, show that even the best model completes only 5.0% of the tasks, establishing SLATE as a challenging testbed for reliable enterprise tool use. We release SLATE, its simulator, and the evaluation harness at https://geshijoker.github.io/slate/
authors: Rongzhe Wei;Ge Shi;Min Cheng;Sarthak Ghosh;Vaibhav Gorde;Leman Akoglu;Pan Li;Na Zhang

title: Must AI Spell It Out? Pragmatic Comprehension of Alerts in a Time-Critical Task
abstract: Assistive systems typically tell users everything, often spending time and attention on what a user already knows, leaving less for what happens next. People, on the other hand, leave out what they expect the listener can supply. Can people use their prior knowledge to understand an incomplete message when the speaker is a machine though? We studied this pragmatic comprehension in a monitoring task controlling users' prior knowledge and the available time to detect critical situations. In a preregistered study (N=114), we compared a pragmatic planner that reasons over a model of the listener's knowledge to decide what to say, when, and how explicitly, with a baseline specifying problems fully in onset order. Participants resolved underspecified alerts almost as reliably as fully specified ones and sooner, detected more problems, and rated the pragmatic assistant helpful more often, with no increase in reported mental demand. Our findings show that people can recover what the system left implicit and that pragmatic communication can support effective assistance under the constraints of a changing world.

title: Parametrization of unitary matrices, parametrizing the symmetric $S$ matrix and the $NN$ $S$ matrix above the inelastic threshold
abstract: None of the $S$-matrix representations used in analyses of nucleon-nucleon ($NN$) scattering above the inelastic threshold is implicitly unitary, general, and connected to low-energy (Stapp) parameters, and hence correspondingly related to the physical properties of the scattering. Such a representation is also needed to solve the corresponding inverse scattering problem. I present an $S$-matrix representation which satisfies these requirements. As a by-product, I derive a parametrization of an $n$-dimensional unitary matrix.

title: Mass-Metallicity Relation of the Fossil Disk in Six Nearby Galaxies using JWST RGB Stars
abstract: We here present the first ever mass-metallicity relation (MZR) of fossil disk populations using the resolved stellar populations in the James Webb Space Telescope Near-Infrared Camera (JWST/NIRCam) images of six nearby galaxies. Both the mass and metallicity were determined using the Red Giant Branch (RGB) stars, employing methods that have been well established to study the halo populations of nearby galaxies using the Hubble Space Telescope images. Specifically, we obtained the mass and metallicity by comparing the color, magnitude and number density near the tip of the RGB (TRGB) stars in the F115W$-$F200W vs F200W color-magnitude diagrams (CMDs) with that of the PARSEC isochrones of 4 and 13~Gyr. The RGB metallicities of the disks of nearby galaxies closely match those found in galaxies at redshifts $z>8$, with the metallicity range following a power-law relation with the fossil disk mass. The power-law index of the fossil disk MZR, $γ\approx0.26$, compares well with the typical value found in MZRs obtained using gas metallicities across redshifts. Through this work, we illustrate the utility of JWST/NIRCam images for obtaining the mass and metallicity of the fossil disks of nearby galaxies at precisions that were not possible earlier, which opens up a new method to carry out the near-field cosmological studies.

title: A Modular Open-Source Python Framework for Small Satellite Attitude Determination and Control
abstract: Advanced attitude determination and control (ADCS) techniques can be difficult for small satellite teams to adopt: tightly coupled implementations require substantial code changes to evaluate different actuators, sensors, orbits, mission goals, and control laws. Existing tools often emphasize orbit mechanics or flight software rather than closed-loop ADCS. This paper presents an open-source, modular ADCS framework in pure Python for rapid development, repeatable testing, and flight-oriented integration across heterogeneous spacecraft. The package supports torque- and command-level control, bound-respecting allocation, and full- and reduced-attitude objectives. Interchangeable estimation, control, planning, and actuator/sensor modules are reconfigured through configuration changes. Integrated simulation includes attitude and orbit propagation, sensor and actuator bias and noise, and environmental disturbances. An actuator-aware planner supports underactuated architectures, while hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) capability enables testing on mission-representative computers. Case studies include a 3U CubeSat with three magnetorquers and one reaction wheel, a magnetorquer-only 1U, and a 6U with three reaction wheels and thrusters. These demonstrate actuator and sensor failures, full- and reduced-attitude goals, and momentum management. HIL testing on a Raspberry Pi uses the same package. Adapting a published control law to a new actuator configuration requires fewer than five lines of configuration changes. The framework underpins flight software for an Earth-observing CubeSat with visible and long-wave infrared imagers, three magnetorquers, and one reaction wheel, without star trackers or propulsion.

title: Balancing Chain-of-Thought and Answer Supervision for Small Language Models on Medical Question Answering
abstract: Small language models (<=9B parameters) can support local medical question answering (QA) while reducing privacy and latency concerns, but effective fine-tuning remains challenging. This paper compares two chain-of-thought (CoT) supervised fine-tuning methods: Uniform-across-Sequence (UaS), which applies equal loss weighting to the full CoT-and-answer sequence, and Segment-weighted (SwS), which separately weights CoT and answer losses. We evaluate six general- and medical-domain models on multiple-choice QA (MedQA and EMS-MCQA) and free-text QA (Med-O1). Results show that neither method is universally best: on multiple-choice QA (MedQA and EMS-MCQA), SwS generally performs better, with general-purpose models benefiting most; notably, Qwen3.5-4B improves by up to 44.8% over its zero-shot baseline on MedQA. In contrast, medical-domain models show smaller or even negative gains on MCQs. On free-text QA (Med-O1), UaS performs best for nearly all models and provides consistent improvements across both model types, with the 3B Llama-3.2 model approaching the performance of much larger 7B medical-domain models. We also find that excessively long CoT generation is associated with lower performance in some models on either multiple-choice or free-text QA tasks, suggesting that limiting the CoT length during training may benefit selected models. Overall, the results show that CoT loss weighting should be matched to the task format and the knowledge already encoded in the base model, rather than using a single fine-tuning strategy for all clinical QA tasks.

title: The Complexity of KKT Points of Quadratic Programs with Polynomially-Bounded Coefficients
abstract: Computing a Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) point of a quadratic polynomial over the unit hypercube is known to be $CLS$-complete, when the coefficients of the polynomial are encoded in binary. We prove that the problem remains $CLS$-complete even when the coefficients are encoded in unary. This is the first problem proven to remain $CLS$-hard when the input is given in unary.

title: Pump quantization changes optimal measurements for quantum sensing
abstract: Standard analyses of quantum phase sensing often neglect the overhead of generating squeezed-light by treating the pump as an undepleted classical resource. Realistically, the pump is a quantum object that undergoes significant depletion and entangles with the produced squeezed light, raising the question of how the crossover from a classical to a quantum pump limits the quantum advantage in sensing. Contrary to prior analyses, we show that quantum advantage persists despite pump quantization, but depends critically on the nonlinear $(χ^{(2)})$ source dynamics. In particular, we demonstrate that Heisenberg scaling emerges in the regime of strong pump depletion, rather than maximum signal squeezing. At maximum squeezing, the quantum Fisher information (QFI) for interferometric sensing of an unknown phase scales as $N^{3/2}$, where $N$ is the pump photon number, surpassing the shot-noise limit but establishing that squeezing itself is insufficient to attain Heisenberg scaling of $N^2$. At maximal pump depletion, where the signal flux is maximized, the QFI scales as $N^2$. In this regime, standard photon counting is suboptimal, while a joint nonlinear measurement of the entire pump-signal system is shown to achieve Heisenberg scaling. Our work shows that pump quantization changes both the optimal operating point and the measurement strategies required to preserve a realistic quantum advantage in phase estimation and, more broadly, many-body quantum dynamics.
authors: S. A. Wadood;L. Bello;T. Ilias;J. W. Fleischer

title: Early-age formation of MgO-SiO$_2$ binders and the effect of hydromagnesite and dehydrated hydromagnesite: An in situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction and pair distribution function study
abstract: MgO-SiO$_2$ binders are promising low-CO$_2$ alternatives to Portland cement that can permanently store CO$_2$ by incorporating magnesium carbonate phases. Adding a magnesium carbonate such as nesquehonite or hydromagnesite is known to change the initial hydration product from crystalline brucite (Mg(OH)$_2$) to disordered hydrous carbonate-containing brucite (HCB), yet how these binders evolve during the initial hours of reaction remains largely unknown. Here, in situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction (XRD) and pair distribution function (PDF) analysis follows an MgO-SiO$_2$ paste with and without hydromagnesite (HY, Mg$_5$(CO$_3$)$_4$(OH)$_2$$\cdot$4H$_2$O) or dehydrated hydromagnesite (DHY, HY heated at 325 °C to remove water) over the first 24 h, with ex situ measurements to 42 days. Real space phase quantification reveals that magnesium-silicate-hydrate (M-S-H) is detected in the first scan (~45 min) of every paste, before formation of any brucite or HCB. The PDF results also show that in the neat MgO-SiO$_2$ paste, half of the M-S-H present at 42 days has formed by 24 h, while no M-S-H is detected by XRD at any age due to the intrinsic disorder present in this phase. Both carbonate sources (HY and DHY) are found to increase the extent of MgO dissolution, where no unreacted MgO is detected at 24 h in contrast with >7 days for the neat paste. However, DHY is seen to slow the initial stages of MgO dissolution (prior to ~6 h) compared with the neat paste, a period during which significant DHY rehydration is seen to occur without any HCB formation. Hence, this investigation shows that the onset of HCB precipitation in MgO-SiO$_2$-(D)HY paste is influenced by the hydration state of the DHY phase, where precipitation is delayed while DHY is rehydrating.

title: Exact penalty methods with adaptive discretization for nonsmooth semi-infinite optimization
abstract: The paper considers a nonsmooth semi-infinite optimization problem in which the constraints are reformulated through a value function. Stationary points of the cutting surface approximations are studied, showing that stationarity is preserved in the limit under boundedness of the associated sequence of multipliers. Building on these results, an algorithm that combines the cutting surface approximations with a penalty scheme is devised, together with some proximal variants. An exact penalty result is established under suitable global conditions, and numerical results are reported to compare the methods with existing exact penalty and cutting surface algorithms.

title: Non-Hermitian effective dynamics from post-selection protocols
abstract: Multiple seemingly distinct frameworks are commonly proposed to explain the emergence of effective non-Hermitian dynamics in quantum systems coupled to an environment. Furthermore, it remains contested how to properly calculate expectation values or whether thermal equilibrium states exist in non-Hermitian systems. In this work, we show that Feshbach projection, the Lindblad master equation, and the ancilla approach can all be understood through the Kraus map formalism, leading to non-Hermitian time evolution if an appropriate post-selection procedure is enforced. After first deriving an exact expression for the conditional system dynamics, we discuss the approximations employed in each approach and the classes of non-Hermitian Hamiltonians that can be obtained. Within this framework, we physically justify the consistency of the right-right formalism (as opposed to the biorthogonal one) for calculating expectation values. Finally, we demonstrate that the traditional notion of thermodynamic equilibrium is not applicable to general non-Hermitian systems. Consequently, stationary states are characterized as non-equilibrium steady states, which should not be conflated with system-projected thermal states of the system-environment composite.

title: Analog quantum simulation of paraparticle statistics
abstract: Bosonic and fermionic quantum statistics describe all known elementary and emergent particles in three dimensions, although many attempts have been made to discover other valid quantum statistical frameworks. One recent formulation proposes "$R$-paraparticles," indistinguishable particles with nonlocal internal degrees of freedom governed by generalized exchange rules [Wang and Hazzard, Nature 637, 314 (2025)]. Here, we emulate a species of paraparticle that exhibits a generalized Pauli exclusion principle using a superconducting qubit lattice. We confirm its unique quantum statistics by measuring a $180^\circ$ phase shift under paraparticle exchange, observing antibunching independent of internal degrees of freedom under two-particle interference at a beamsplitter, and finding a thermal occupation inconsistent with both Bose-Einstein and Fermi-Dirac statistics. These results demonstrate that parastatistics are observable on quantum simulation platforms, further motivating their use to explore theorized new phases of matter.
authors: Gyunghun Kim;Cora N. Barrett;Sarah E. Muschinske;Junyoung An;Helin Zhang;Ilan T. Rosen;Rabindra Das;Michael A. Gingras;David K. Kim;Bethany M. Niedzielski;Meghan Schuldt;Jonilyn L. Yoder;Mollie E. Schwartz;Kyle Serniak;Jeffrey A. Grover;Max Hays;William D. Oliver

title: EpiLoRA: Fusing Many LoRA Adapters into Low-Precision GEMMs for Serving and RL
abstract: Low-rank adapters (LoRA) let one base model serve many fine-tuned variants: multi-tenant engines keep a single copy of the base and batch the requests of many tenants, each with its own adapter. As base models move to 8-bit (FP8) and 4-bit formats, their general matrix multiplications (GEMMs) become cheaper, but the adapters do not: engines run them as separate small GPU kernels beside the GEMM, whose latency takes a growing share of every decoding step. An adapter projects its input down to a low rank and back up, and our key observation is that the GEMM needs the down-projection only in its epilogue, the final stage in which it writes its output. EpiLoRA, a plugin for the vLLM engine, therefore launches the down-projection first and the low-precision GEMM as a dependent kernel that streams its weights meanwhile and adds every tenant's up-projection in its epilogue. On NVIDIA Hopper GPUs, EpiLoRA decodes for a single adapter with up to 24% lower time per token than vLLM's fastest configuration, and faster than SGLang and TensorRT-LLM; with many tenants, its adapter kernels deliver more throughput than vLLM's on most GPU-model pairs we tested. The same low-precision base also trains: a LoRA reinforcement-learning trainer that computes on the engine's FP8 weights needs no 16-bit copy, so a 27B model trains on one 48 GB GPU, and an engine that then keeps activations in 16 bits removes most of the remaining mismatch between the model generating training data and the one trained.

title: Fly Whiskers Meet LiDAR: Robust Navigation under Sensor Failure
abstract: We extend FLYNN, a leaky integrator recurrent network wired on the Drosophila melanogaster connectome, with a 32-ray 2D LiDAR interface that requires no learned fusion layer beyond a scalar input gain. A 270 degree frontal scan at 8 m range is injected as inverted proximity into the 37 BM Vib head-bristle neurons. Across 24 paired comparisons in a four-state vision matrix with LiDAR on or off, FLYNN-LiDAR has 17 significant wins, 5 nonsignificant comparisons, and 2 significant losses against three LiDAR-capable baselines. Both losses are to MobileNet with the left eye off. With full vision, FLYNN-LiDAR reaches 96.6% success. Under total vision loss, the scan raises success from 45.2% to 64.6%; the baselines reach 44.6% to 56.6% with the scan on. Under out of distribution textures, it is the only LiDAR-capable model whose success improves with the scan (44.2% to 58.4%); both CNNs score 0%, and SmallWorld declines from 26.8% to 7.4%. Under periodic vision dropout, FLYNN-LiDAR achieves 93.6% and 89.6% success at 25% and 50% duty with fewer collisions. Profiling the evaluated forward paths gives 3.93M multiply accumulate operations per step; EfficientNet and MobileNet require 4.60x and 2.94x as many. Final-state analysis shows near-linear sensory superposition (cosine 0.9955).

title: Unital qubit channels are $3$-noisy
abstract: The algebraic and environmental characteristics of mixed unitary quantum operations are investigated. It is established that the composition of two uniformly n-mixed unitary channels is itself n-noisy, and this n-noisy property is shown to be an invariant under unitary equivalence. Furthermore, by utilizing majorization and the divisibility of Kraus rank-four unital qubit channels, we demonstrate that any unital qubit channel can be physically simulated using a three-dimensional maximally mixed environment. Together, these results advance the classification and physical realization of noisy quantum channels.

title: Hardware-Aware Design and Layout Selection in Quantum Reservoir Computing for Insurance Claims Forecasting
abstract: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) processes temporal information through quantum dynamics, but it remains unclear whether small QRC models can forecast real data competitively with classical models and whether their predictions survive the transfer from ideal simulation to noisy hardware. We address both questions for a six-qubit gate-based reservoir that forecasts next-day motor-insurance claim counts. Five reservoir candidates were selected and frozen using hardware-native interaction graphs, Trotterized Ising dynamics, memory and measurement-robustness criteria, circuit cost, and calibrated-noise screening. On 232 held-out test days, the ideal candidates reached root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) of 5.66-6.12 claims/day, compared with 5.36 for ridge regression. For four of the five, the difference from ridge was not significant under a 95% block bootstrap, and their accuracy was comparable with classical recurrent and reservoir baselines. On the 156-qubit IBM Kingston processor, we ran 63 evaluations in 21 paired rounds, comparing hardware-aware, random-native, and Qiskit optimization level 1 layouts. Hardware-aware placement gave lower RMSE than Qiskit in every round, with a maximum transfer distortion of 7.59 claims/day (11.84 for Qiskit), and avoided the severe transfer failures seen for some random layouts. Most of the hardware distortion appeared as a systematic forecast shift, which a short hardware probe on training inputs detected before the test runs. Longer replay windows raised circuit cost without a consistent gain in forecasting accuracy or hardware transfer. Small QRC models can thus reach competitive accuracy on this task, and hardware-aware layout selection makes their transfer to IBM Kingston more consistent.
authors: Renáta Rusnáková;Eugen Šlapak;Gaurav K. Pandey;Juraj Gazda

title: Timely Ground-Station Status Delivery via UAV-Assisted Data Collection and Hierarchical RL
abstract: We consider a UAV-assisted status-update system in which a rotary-wing unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) collects updates from multiple sensors, stores the newest update of each sensor, and forwards selected buffered updates to a ground station (GS). We minimize a weighted sum of the time-average GS-side age of information (AoI) and UAV energy consumption over a finite horizon. The optimization is subject to half-duplex operation, sensor and UAV energy-causality constraints, transmission-rate and power limits, and a terminal-location constraint. Because collection changes the information age at the UAV but does not reduce the GS-side AoI until the buffered update is forwarded, mobility, collection, and forwarding decisions are coupled over time. We use a hierarchical AoI-energy actor-critic (HAE-AC) controller in which a coarse-timescale actor selects return-feasible UAV movements, while a deterministic per-slot scheduler constructs feasible collection or forwarding sets and assigns the minimum transmit power required for each scheduled transmission. In a 100-sensor deployment, HAE-AC reduces the average GS-side AoI by about 22% relative to an adaptive staleness-gated benchmark. Compared with forward-upon-collection, selective buffered forwarding reduces the number of downlink bursts by roughly 30% while increasing the number of collections per sensor by more than 23%.

title: Liouvillian Kramers Degeneracy
abstract: The Kramers theorem generally guarantees the spectral degeneracy of time-reversal-invariant Hamiltonian operators with half-integer spin, underlying a variety of physical phenomena. Despite its fundamental significance, the Kramers degeneracy has been argued to be absent in Liouvillian superoperators acting on mixed states because of the double structure of the Hilbert space. Here, we instead demonstrate that the interplay of time-reversal symmetry$^†$ and parity symmetry enforces the Kramers degeneracy in Liouvillians. We explicitly construct dissipative many-body models of interacting fermions and spins exhibiting the Kramers degeneracy and show that their complex spectral statistics follow those of non-Hermitian random matrices in the corresponding symplectic symmetry classes. Of the three fundamental universality classes of non-Hermitian random matrices, the symplectic class has never been realized in symmetry-resolved many-body Liouvillians. Our constructions provide its explicit realizations and spectral signatures of nonintegrability in symplectic open quantum systems.

title: EvoGroup: A Self-Evolving Harness for Group Agents in Shared Contexts
abstract: With the rise of Group Agent such as Claude Tag, agents increasingly serve as digital workers for long-term team collaboration. These agents operate over shared contexts that continuously accumulate through multi-user interactions. However, existing agent memory systems are mainly designed for individual users and struggle to capture group-level knowledge in shared contexts, including group relationships and collaboratively formed knowledge. Manual memory strategies further limit adaptation to diverse and evolving shared contexts. To this end, we propose \textbf{EvoGroup (EvoG)}, a self-evolving harness for group agents that starts from a minimal six-tool cold start and adapts through interaction with shared context. EvoG uses confidence and task outcomes to select informative trajectories, while also eliciting self-reflections on uncertainty in low-confidence cases. The analysis agent then examines selected trajectories through adaptive progressive disclosure, followed by bucketed analysis to synthesize high-level findings that guide the evolve agent in revising the Harness. Empirically, pass@1 on held-out split of EverMemBench improves from 71.07\% to 89.58\%, surpassing both self-evolving memory and human-designed harnesses, including Claude Code (85.83\%). To evaluate generalization, we freeze the evolved harness and evaluate it on the unseen GroupMemBench, where, with GPT-5.5, it demonstrates effective generalization and outperforms both memory baselines and human-designed harnesses.
authors: Xinyi Xu;Xiaoyang Li;Yucheng Feng;Wenqing Chen;Youliang Yuan;Wei Shi;Rongxiang Weng;Zibin Zheng

title: Interstellar and intergalactic medium in the ultraviolet band
abstract: This article presents an overview of key scientific challenges in the astrophysics and astrochemistry of the interstellar and intergalactic media. Addressing many of these challenges will become possible with the Russian space observatory Spektr-UF, which is currently being prepared for launch. The ultraviolet (UV) spectral range is critically important for studying the evolution of the Universe, as it contains fundamental absorption and emission lines of most chemical elements and the most important molecules. These lines make it possible to reliably determine the physical conditions and chemical composition of various astrophysical objects, as well as the characteristics of the processes occurring within them. The article examines the prospects for UV observations across a broad range of scientific problems, from investigating the epoch of helium reionization and the thermal history of the Universe to mapping ongoing star formation in galaxies. Dedicated sections address the study of the chemical evolution of galaxies at intermediate redshifts, the distribution of "hidden" baryons and metals, the small-scale structure of interstellar clouds, the physics of photodissociation regions and protoplanetary disks, and the modeling of UV emission from nebulae surrounding fast-moving pulsars. The high sensitivity and spectral resolution of the Spektr-UF instruments are expected to provide fundamentally new data across all these research areas, filling existing gaps in our understanding of the interstellar and intergalactic media.
authors: M. S. Kirsanova;S. A. Balashev;M. V. Barkov;E. O. Vasiliev;D. S. Wiebe;I. I. Zinchenko;A. V. Moiseev;M. S. Murga;I. N. Nikonorov;M. E. Sachkov;I. S. Khrykin;B. M. Shustov;Yu. A. Schekinov;A. D. Yarovova

title: Factorized approximate inverse preconditioners in the tensor train format
abstract: We present a preconditioning pipeline that accelerates Tensor Train (TT) linear solvers for symmetric positive-definite problems. Extending the Factorized Sparse Approximate Inverse framework to tensor networks, we construct a preconditioner as the product of a TT operator and its transpose. This formulation is positive semidefinite for any bond dimension and truncation, and definite whenever the factor is non-singular, satisfying the mathematical requirements of the Conjugate Gradient method. We detail the construction of this preconditioner and its integration into Density Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG)-like linear solvers. Performance evaluations show consistent iteration reductions for anisotropic diffusion and Poisson problems across various configurations, leading to net speedups of up to 25% in ill-conditioned settings of time stepping schemes that can reuse the approximate inverses. These benchmarks were performed with the open-source Julia library DifferenTT.jl, which we also introduce in this work to provide out-of-the-box access to these preconditioned pipelines.
authors: Pau Torrente Badia;Daniel Pérez García;Artur Garcia-Saez;Stefano Carignano

title: Why Pay for Long Reasoning When Rewrite Do Trick? Causal Effects of Reasoning History Compaction on Future Generation and Agent Cost
abstract: Reasoning substantially improves language models' ability to solve difficult problems, but long reasoning traces make these gains expensive. Efficient reasoning should express useful analysis in fewer tokens by reducing repetition and text that adds little value to solving the problem. Progress in proprietary models motivates this goal, yet their hidden scratchpads limit direct study of how it is achieved. We investigate whether open-weight models can generate less verbose reasoning by changing the form of their own earlier thoughts, without retraining. Our intervention rewrites prior reasoning into compact state records before pending tool results are revealed, then compares continuations from original and compact histories. Across the tested models, accepted compact histories usually shorten future reasoning; a coding case study also shows less repeated verification after a shared candidate solution. In software-agent deployments, compaction can reduce total spending, although task quality and rewrite-inclusive time depend on the target and compressor. These findings identify reasoning history as one way to reduce future reasoning-token use and motivate model-specific compaction policies evaluated for both efficiency and retained capability.
journal_ref: Proceedings of the Second Workshop for REsearch on Agent Language Models (REALM 2026), pp. 1213-1228, 2026

title: High-fidelity quantum gate learning via physics-informed neural networks
abstract: We propose a physics-informed neural network (PINN) approach for high-fidelity quantum gate learning in both one- and two-qubit systems. We train a PINN using the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, where smooth control fields with fixed boundary conditions are obtained by minimizing a loss function that considers model dynamics, gate error, physical constraints, regularization terms, and multiple initial conditions. Training considers pairs of mutually unbiased bases, while independent validation combines Haar-random input states with the average gate fidelity. Unitary simulations yield an average gate infidelity of $8.49\times10^{-8}$ for Hadamard and values between $3.39\times10^{-7}$ and $4.96\times10^{-6}$ for controlled-NOT under $XX$, $YY$, and $ZZ$ interactions. We examine how the learned control fields depend on the coupling, training configuration, and available local fields, including five exchange-type dipolar scenarios. We test the learned control fields under the Lindblad master equation with dephasing and amplitude damping, theoretically reproducing the expected first-order fidelity loss in the weak-dissipation regime. Finally, boundary-adapted Chebyshev expansions represent 139 learned controls with a minimum common count of $K_\ast=24$ coefficients per control for all eleven family-averaged mean squared errors to fall below $10^{-6}$. Separately, square-pulse and Strang propagation at $K=30$ preserve all 31 continuous polynomial references within infidelity $10^{-5}$ at $N=128$ and all larger tested resolutions, under both sampling rules. These results connect multi-state gate synthesis, control-resource characterization, and compact square-pulse playback.
authors: Luis Fabra;Cristian E. Susa;Alcides Montoya;Ariel Norambuena

title: Evidence for strong shocks in the ISM of small radio sources
abstract: Radio jets deposit energy into the interstellar medium of their host galaxies, and while a jet is still confined within the host it is expected to drive shocks through the gas. Broad [OIII] 5007 profiles trace ionized gas that has been disturbed, the [OI]/H-alpha versus [OIII]/H-beta diagram helps distinguish gas photoionized by an AGN from gas excited by shocks, and the high ionization [NeV] 3426 line traces the hard UV continuum of the accretion disk, which shocks only reproduce at very high velocities. We have selected two samples of radio-loud AGN from a cross-match of the VLA Sky Survey with DESI Data Release 1, at 0.15 < z < 0.5 and with [OI] 6300 detected at > 5-sigma: one with projected radio sizes of 10-15 kpc, whose jets are still inside the host, and one with sizes greater than 25 kpc, whose jets have broken out. We fit the [OIII] and [OI] profiles, measure W80, and classify each source on the BPT diagram. The confined sources have broader [OIII] lines, sit systematically closer to the LINER region, and are detected less often in [NeV], and the [NeV] difference is not explained by redshift or dust. The broad components are not systematically blueshifted, so the confined sources are distinguished by line width rather than by outflow velocity. We then discuss how these results indicate that the jets of the confined sources are driving strong shocks through the interstellar medium of their hosts.

title: Entanglement-Aware Quantum Circuit Optimization through Globally Optimal Partitioning
abstract: We introduce a scalable framework for globally optimal quantum-circuit partitioning and entanglement-aware block resynthesis. The partitioning problem is formulated as an integer linear program over qubit-feasible convex subcircuits, supporting objectives such as minimizing the number of partitions or a weighted execution cost. The resulting partition selection is exact over the enumerated feasible candidates and their computed costs when the ILP is solved to proven optimality. The selected partitions are resynthesized using an operator-Schmidt rank (OSR) based synthesis technique, which exploits their internal entanglement structure. We compare the end-to-end integer linear programming (ILP)--OSR workflow with BQSKit while identifying their different routing methods, and separately compare local OSR and BQSKit synthesis on matched three- and four-qubit unitaries. On the frozen sample of 772 local unitary targets, OSR produces 741 verified syntheses versus 617 for BQSKit, and matches or improves the CNOT count in all 617 jointly verified pairs. These results demonstrate that globally optimal partition selection combined with entanglement-aware resynthesis improves circuit quality and extends block-based optimization to problem sizes that are impractical for existing optimization workflows.

title: Possibility of Potts Spin-Ice in Rare Earth Twisted-Kagome Layers: an Example of DyAgGe
abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) spin-ice compounds, predominantly based on the pyrochlore or spinel structure, have been attracting considerable interest in the last two decades. A two-dimensional (2D) analogue is the spin-ice consisting of kagome planes. So far, only Ising spin ice has been discovered in any material, and only one 2D material, the kagome compound HoAgGe, has been identified as a spin ice. In this Letter, we show that another rare-earth twisted Kagome magnetic compound, DyAgGe, is in fact a Potts spin ice (or color ice), where at each site not two but four spin directions are allowed. We argue that an 8-state spin ice may also exist in this class of systems. We present a first-principles calculation of magnetic interactions in DyAgGe, and confirm the 4-state Potts structure of this material by matching our model predictions with the available experimental data.

title: Evolved Spiking Neural Networks for EEG Seizure Detection: Calcium Dynamics and Delay Mechanics
abstract: Neuroevolution can discover compact network designs that are hard to specify by hand. The EONS framework evolves the topology, weights, thresholds and delays of neuromorphic spiking networks without gradients. We tested whether giving integrate-and-fire (IF) neurons an activity-dependent calcium current (Ca-IF neurons) improves evolved networks for EEG seizure detection, with calcium parameters fixed, shared across a network, or evolved for each neuron. On 10 held-out CHB-MIT patients never seen in training, per-neuron calcium raised the record-level Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) from 0.592 to 0.726 over 20 independent runs (p = 0.008) and lowered the false-alarm rate from 0.17 to 0.10. Fixed or per-network calcium gave no significant benefit. IF networks with evolved synaptic delays of 1-3 ticks gave a similar gain (p = 0.005), whereas axonal delays did not. On Siena, with unchanged settings, per-neuron calcium gained +0.096 MCC over IF in one patient-disjoint split (p = 0.011) and +0.059 in the other (p = 0.052). These results suggest that calcium and delays may make the evolutionary search more effective, and motivate testing on more data and in neuromorphic hardware.

title: A Conditional Mutual Information Analysis of Response Variety in Language Models
abstract: Large language models provide a variety of responses at inference (generation) that conventionally depend on a temperature parameter. Using a conditional mutual information approach, a quantitative, entropy based analysis of response variety is given. Three limiting behaviors are defined: arbiter, independent (conditionally) and neutral (deterministic) that span no to maximal mutual information. We give examples of each behavior and suggest their application to: temperature analysis, language analysis, prompt compression, and knowledge graphs.

title: Estimating LuSEE-Night's Sensitivity to Cα Radio Recombination Lines
abstract: Carbon radio recombination lines (CRRLs) arising from the cold neutral medium (CNM) of the interstellar medium are potential foregrounds in the 1-50 MHz band that LuSEE-Night will observe from the lunar far side. CRRLs are sensitive probes of the temperature, density, and radiation field of the CNM, and LuSEE-Night will provide sky-averaged measurements in a poorly explored frequency range. We model CRRLs across this band, accounting for doppler, collisional, and radiation broadening, and we estimate line strengths using two independent methods - fixing either the peak or the frequency-integrated optical depth - applied both uniformly across the sky and with region-dependent values informed by prior low-frequency observations. We simulate LuSEE-Night's expected response to these CRRLs and further convolve the beam-diluted spectra with LuSEE-Night's polyphase-filter-bank spectrometer response, including its zoomed-mode frequency resolution of $\sim$390 Hz, to obtain the expected observed brightness temperature. Using these simulated spectra, we estimate the integration time required to detect individual CRRLs at SNR=5 across the six sky models considered. Required integration times range from as short as 30 hours (in the most optimistic model where the optical depth across the sky is $\sim$10$^{-3}$) to 27.6 years (in the most conservative models where the optical depth across the sky is $\sim$10$^{-4}$). Stacking the 361 simulated C$α$ lines between 10 and 50 MHz reduces the integration time needed for an SNR=5 detection to $\sim$11 minutes and $\sim$151 hours respectively, indicating that LuSEE-Night has realistic chances of making a stacked detection of C$α$ RRLs within a realistic mission lifetime, even under the most conservative optical-depth assumptions.

title: Rethinking Next-Visit Diagnosis Prediction Beyond Aggregate Metrics: Retrieval--Memory Multi-Agent Adjudication
abstract: Next-visit diagnosis prediction forecasts the diagnoses documented at a patient's next encounter, turning retrospective electronic health records into prospective clinical prediction. However, conventional aggregate evaluation obscures its multifaceted nature: distributionally, models must handle variable-size diagnosis sets and long-tailed labels; temporally, they must distinguish persistent, newly recorded, and recurrent diagnoses; and both vary with observed history depth. We introduce an evaluation framework along these dimensions and apply it to rule-based heuristics, LLM-based prompting, retrieval, memory, and multi-agent approaches. This reveals that repeating the last visit outperforms most LLM-based approaches overall despite predicting no new or recurrent diagnoses, and that retrieval and memory exhibit distinct profiles whose relative strengths vary across temporal transitions and backbones. Motivated by this, we propose LONGINUS, a retrieval-memory multi-agent adjudication framework combining evidence retrieved from patient records with structured memory of the patient trajectory. Using cross-view agreement as a reliability heuristic, it preserves shared predictions and adjudicates disagreements without revealing their source. Across MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV with four LLM backbones, LONGINUS achieves the best transition-specific performance among LLM-based methods in nearly all settings while remaining competitive with them on aggregate metrics.

title: A Tutorial on Shape Servoing of Deformable Objects-Part II: Advanced Concepts
abstract: In robotics, shape control, or shape servoing, refers to the automatic manipulation of a deformable object toward a desired shape. This article is the second of a two-part tutorial on data-driven, Jacobian-based shape control, in which the deformation Jacobian, a local model of how robot motion changes the measured shape, is estimated from measurements. Part I built the shape-servoing loop and derived a local stability condition. This paper starts by using the singular value decomposition of the deformation Jacobian to identify shape changes that can be produced by small robot motions, those that require large robot motions, and those that are locally unavailable. It then analyses how the choice of shape features determines how the controller regulates the object's shape and, therefore, how much the object deforms on its way to the target. It then describes three ways in which the shape control loop can fail: loss of controllability, loss of observability, and occurrence of mechanical instabilities. It closes with shape-control extensions to time-varying targets, secondary tasks, and three-dimensional objects.

title: He I $λ$10830 Resonant Scattering in M17: Toward a Diagnostic of Optical Depth and Gas Kinematics
abstract: The lower level of the He I $λ$10830 transition is metastable and therefore well populated. In H II regions, the line can become optically thick, and its photons then undergo resonant scattering. Draine (2026) predicted that scattering splits the profile into several peaks. We present Magellan/WINERED spectra ($R \approx 70{,}000$) at six pointings along a line from the ionizing source CEN 1 across the southwestern bar of M17, with He I $λ$10830 and Pa$γ$ in the same exposures. Every He I $λ$10830 profile is multi-peaked, while the Pa$γ$ profiles are single-peaked. Because Pa$γ$ does not undergo resonant scattering, it traces gas kinematics; its single peak argues against a purely kinematic origin of the He I peaks, and the shared exposures exclude an instrumental origin. We therefore attribute the He I peaks to resonant scattering, as predicted. We compare the profiles quantitatively with the static, spherically symmetric models of Draine (2026), using width and asymmetry measures independent of the systemic velocity. At two pointings far from CEN 1, no static model of any optical depth reproduces width and asymmetry together: both profiles are more red-weighted than static models of comparable width. Such profiles cannot arise from uniform motion but are expected from scattering in expanding gas. We argue that the profile is shaped by both the kinematics and the optical depth of the He$^{+}$ zone, and resolved He I $λ$10830 profiles could therefore provide a new diagnostic of these properties in H II regions.

title: Coexisting Kondo and Weyl-like transport in kagome heavy-fermion metal, Yb$_y$Co$_3$G$e_{3-x}$Sn$_x$
abstract: Strong electron correlations and topology offer complementary routes to controlling electrical conduction, as correlations can make electrons heavy (e.g. Kondo lattices) whereas topology can make them behave as massless particles (e.g. Dirac or Weyl systems), and having both in one material is rare. In Kondo lattice systems, Kondo hybridization between localized 4$f$ and conduction electrons strongly enhances the quasiparticle mass, where in Weyl-Kondo systems these Kondo-renormalized bands form Weyl states, and simultaneous signs of both Kondo and Weyl states in one material have not been observed in transport. Here we report signs of both in the kagome metal \ce{Yb_yCo3Ge_{3-x}Sn_x} by combining magnetotransport, heat capacity, magnetization, angle-resolved and X-ray photoemission spectroscopy, and DFT+U calculations to reveal Yb-dependent Kondo scattering developing into lattice coherence, with extrapolated Sommerfeld coefficient of approximately 2 ~Jmol$_{\mathrm{Yb}}^{-1}$K$^{-2}$. Transverse magnetoresistance (MR) follows single-ion Kondo scaling, whereas longitudinal transport contains an additional negative response proportional to B$^2$ and remains unsaturated up to 32 T, consistent with a chiral anomaly. These findings support a picture of Kondo and Weyl-like conduction arising from distinct electronic states without external Fermi-level tuning, suggesting a possible route to combining correlated and topological functionality in a bulk material.

title: X-rays from Low-mass Active Galaxies in the Galaxy And Mass Assembly (GAMA) Survey
abstract: We present new Chandra observations of seven broad-line AGNs in low-mass galaxies ($M_\star < 5 \times 10^9\,M_\odot$) selected from the GAMA sample of Salehirad et al. (2022). X-ray emission is detected in six galaxies, with luminosities spanning $\log(L_{\rm 0.5-8\,keV}/{\rm erg\,s^{-1}})\approx40.5$--43.8. Their X-ray luminosities generally exceed predictions for X-ray binary populations, and their proximity to the optical galaxy nuclei favors accreting massive black holes as the dominant emission source. Spectral fits for four sources yield photon indices $Γ\approx1.7$--2.2, with little evidence for intrinsic absorption in most cases. Virial black hole masses and hard X-ray bolometric corrections imply nominal Eddington ratios $λ_{\rm Edd}\approx0.004$--1.1, although uncertainties are substantial. Optical tracers generally imply higher bolometric luminosities and Eddington ratios, particularly for the X-ray-undetected galaxy. The X-ray-bright sources are broadly consistent with optical AGN scaling relations involving H$α$ and [O III], whereas most lie below the established X-ray--mid-infrared relation, potentially reflecting host-galaxy contamination. Four sources are consistent with the expected UV-to-X-ray spectral slope relation, while three show evidence for relative X-ray weakness. These results reveal diverse X-ray properties among broad-line AGNs in low-mass galaxies and highlight the importance of multiwavelength diagnostics for understanding black hole accretion and interpreting broad-line AGN candidates at high redshift.

title: Reconstruction of the conformal algebra from a critical groundstate on the (fuzzy) sphere
abstract: Recently, we found a method to reconstruct the dilatation operator (sphere Hamiltonian) from a regulated conformal field theory groundstate. In this paper, we explore methods to construct the whole global conformal algebra, and test our construction using fuzzy sphere regularization. Starting from a groundstate of the same Hamiltonian, these methods perform better than constructions of the conformal generators based on a Hamiltonian density, are model-independent, require no additional tuning, and improve with system size. One purpose of reconstructing the conformal algebra is to identify conformal primary states, which we do with some success. We also find further evidence supporting the model of the short-distance corrections to the entanglement Hamiltonian proposed earlier and use it to make systematic improvements.
authors: Rolando Ramirez Camasca;Xiang Li;Ting-Chun Lin;John McGreevy

title: H 0557$-$385: A Candidate Missing Link Between Radio-Quiet Seyferts and Young Radio Galaxies
abstract: The Seyfert 1 galaxy H 0557$-$385 (z = 0.034) has long been classified as radio-quiet on the basis of its radio-to-optical flux ratio, yet its radio properties are physically inconsistent with this designation. We present a broadband ($0.076 - 258.8$ GHz) radio spectral analysis combining new Australia Telescope Compact Array (ATCA) observations with archival Murchison Widefield Array (MWA), Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP) and Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) data. The spectrum requires a two-component model: a compact, self-absorbed component with a stratified gigahertz-peaked (GPS)/high-frequency-peaked (HFP) spectral shape (turnover at $9.4^{+0.6}_{-0.5}$ GHz), superposed on an extended, optically thin power-law lobe ($α_{\rm pl} = -0.78$) that dominates below ~1.6 GHz. The derived parameters $-$ a source size of ~15 pc, an equipartition magnetic field of 2.8 mG, a synchrotron age of $\lesssim1.8\times10^{3}$ yr, and a time-averaged jet power of ${\sim}5\times10^{41}$ $-$ $5\times10^{44}$ erg s$^{-1}$ $-$ are characteristic of compact steep-spectrum and GPS young radio galaxies, not of canonical radio-quiet AGN. The two-component structure admits two interpretations that the present data cannot distinguish: the extended emission may be the growing lobe of a genuinely young, expanding radio galaxy, or relic plasma from an earlier episode of a transient or recurrent jet. Under either, H 0557$-$385 is better understood as an intermediate object: optically a Seyfert, but with the radio-physical properties of a newly ignited or recently re-triggered radio galaxy. It is therefore a candidate missing link between radio-quiet AGN and large-scale radio galaxies. Distinguishing these scenarios will require high-resolution imaging and multi-epoch monitoring

title: Revisiting the Missing Baryon Problem: Baryon Redistribution Across Halo Evolution
abstract: The baryon fraction provides a fundamental diagnostic of baryonic matter distribution within dark matter halos and the baryon cycle. While its cosmic value is well constrained, the baryon content within halos on nearly all scales is significantly lower than the cosmic mean; this is called the ``missing baryon problem.'' Using the high spatial, mass, and temporal resolutions of the NewCluster simulation, we investigate the baryon fraction evolution by tracing halo assembly histories from merger trees and gas tracer particles. We identify three distinct evolutionary phases: an early growth phase driven by cold accretion in low-mass halos, a suppression phase likely dominated by supernova feedback, and a recovery phase in massive halos enabled by deeper potential wells and hot-mode accretion. We further find that the redshift dependence of baryon fraction, particularly in low-mass halos, is influenced by the thermal state of the intergalactic medium, with suppression emerging after the surrounding gas becomes persistently hotter than the halo virial temperature. In addition, the scatter in baryon fraction at fixed halo mass correlates with the large-scale environment, with baryon-rich halos preferentially residing closer to filamentary structures. Overall, our results highlight that baryon fraction evolution is governed by the interplay between feedback and environment, requiring a time-resolved perspective on the baryon cycle.

title: The STARfall pathway: forging intermediate-mass black holes through stellar collisions in dense star clusters
abstract: Intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs, $10^2 < m_{\rm BH}/\mathrm{M}_{\odot} < 10^5$) are elusive objects bridging the gap between stellar-mass and supermassive black holes, whose origin remains uncertain. They may form from the collapse of very massive stars (VMSs, $m_*\geq150\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$) assembled through repeated stellar collisions in compact and fast evolving star clusters. We investigate the formation of VMSs and IMBH seeds via repeated mergers and collisions as a function of cluster initial conditions, assessing the implications for globular clusters and dense high-redshift system. We develop STARfall, a semi-analytic tool that follows the evolution of a massive stellar binary via binary-single interactions, mergers, collisions, and stellar evolution, while consistently accounting for the host cluster evolution. Our results show that clusters with central densities above $10^6\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}\,\mathrm{pc}^{-3}$ can undergo a catastrophic sequence of stellar collisions, or "starastrophe", within $3$ Myr. Through this process, VMSs rapidly grow in mass and collapse into IMBHs with masses of up to $10^3-10^4\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$, despite the effects of intense stellar winds. Applying our models to observed systems, we find that compact clusters in the Cosmic Gems Arc and Milky Way globular clusters could have hosted VMSs that collapsed into IMBHs in this mass range. Despite their longer core-collapse timescales, the inferred central densities of Little Red Dots may also support IMBH formation in the same mass interval. Our models show that VMS assembly requires two essential ingredients: short core-collapse times and large central densities. Compared to observed systems, our models suggest that clusters in the Cosmic Gems Arcs and several Galactic globular clusters could have nurtured VMSs that directly collapsed to IMBHs with masses $10^3-10^4\,\text{M}_{\odot}$.

title: Long-range entangled criticality from coherent errors
abstract: We find that coherent error can induce a phase transition from the clean surface code phase into an extended long-range entangled critical regime with diverging Markov length. To demonstrate this, we establish two general results of independent interest. The first relates topology and quantum information to mixed-state entanglement: we show that when a noise channel acting on a topological code preserves a higher-form symmetry and nonzero coherent information, the noisy state for generic logical input is long-range entangled. The second generalizes the local recovery construction based on finite Markov length to any locally parameterized family, thus encompassing local Lindbladian evolution, coherent errors followed by syndrome dephasing, and thermal states. We apply these results to the honeycomb surface code, in which we find an extended long-range entangled critical regime that is a quasi-long-ranged counterpart of 1-form strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking. As a byproduct of these studies, we relate the conditional mutual information to conductance in a Majorana network model.
authors: Amir-Reza Negari;Subhayan Sahu;Jan Behrends;Benjamin Béri;Timothy H. Hsieh

title: Galactic-Scale Distribution of 10Be and Its Implications for the Early Solar System 10Be/9Be
abstract: Meteoritic inclusions indicate that the early Solar System contained a substantial abundance of the short-lived radionuclide 10Be. Whether it was inherited from the parent molecular cloud or requires local irradiation or late injection remains debated. Here we present the first three-dimensional simulations of a Milky Way-like disc that follow the multi-phase interstellar medium, cosmic rays (CRs), and the production and transport of 10Be by galactic CRs (GCRs) and in supernova remnants (SNRs). Nearly all 10Be is produced by GCR interactions; SNRs contribute at most about ten percent of the 10Be inherited by newly formed stars. The 10Be/9Be ratio traces the CR energy density, declining smoothly with galactocentric radius, and because stars form where supernovae inject CRs, their natal gas is CR-enriched roughly fivefold relative to the mean interstellar medium, which one-zone estimates miss. Accounting for a possibly higher Galactic star formation rate 4.6 Gyr ago, inheritance of GCR-produced 10Be can then explain the early Solar System's 10Be/9Be in our models, without late injection or local irradiation. Even when GCR-induced 10Be production in dense gas is reduced tenfold, the meteoritic value is reached in the innermost disc and missed by only a factor of a few elsewhere, so the main conclusion is robust to uncertain low-energy GCR penetration. The inferred birth radius of the Sun depends strongly on the CR diffusivity, ranging between 3 and 8 kpc, suggesting that improved modelling of low-energy CR transport could sharpen constraints on the birthplace of the Solar System.

title: Isophotal signatures of the brightest cluster galaxy - intracluster light transition
abstract: The distinction between brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs) and intracluster light (ICL) remains ambiguous, with inferred cluster properties depending strongly on the adopted definition and measurement methodology. We report the presence of a common inflection feature in the radial profiles of surface brightness, ellipticity, and position angle of BCG+ICL systems, indicative of a structural transition in the underlying stellar distribution. Using a combination of low redshift clusters (z < 0.1) observed with the Wendelstein Wide Field Imager, deep Hyper Suprime-Cam observations of clusters at 0.2 < z < 0.4, and cosmological hydrodynamical simulations from Horizon-AGN and Hydrangea, we consistently identify a common inflection at radii of 60-85 kpc. We interpret this feature as a characteristic transition in the combined BCG+ICL light distribution, that may reflect the hierarchical assembly of the cluster. The persistence of this feature across multiple photometric bands, redshift ranges, and simulations supports its robustness. To identify these transitions, we employ an automated second derivative based approach that does not rely on parametric decompositions or arbitrary surface brightness thresholds. This framework provides a physically motivated and scalable means to characterise the BCG-ICL transition, and it will be of paramount importance for forthcoming large scale surveys such as the Legacy Survey of Space and Time and the European Space Agency's Euclid mission.
authors: Giulia Golini;Sarah Brough;Louisa Canepa;Garreth Martin;Matthias Kluge

title: A full chemical network treatment of supermassive black hole seed formation from dark matter annihilation or decay
abstract: The recent discoveries of high-redshift quasars at $z\sim6-10.1$ present a challenge to conventional supermassive black hole (SMBH) formation scenarios: their central SMBHs are too large to have grown from early stellar remnants, even under efficient super-Eddington accretion. An alternative approach is the direct collapse of primordial, dust- and metal-free gas clouds into black hole seeds as early as $z\sim20$. To prevent fragmentation from highly efficient molecular hydrogen cooling and allow such a collapse, a strong flux of UV photons is required to photodissociate molecular hydrogen, suppressing star formation. We investigate whether the decay or annihilation of dark matter with masses below $\sim200$ eV can produce sufficient UV radiation, both from the cosmological background and within early dark matter halos. Using thermal simulations of a one-zone primordial gas cloud model with the Grackle chemistry and cooling library, we map the resulting gas behavior across a range of dark matter lifetimes, cross sections, and masses. From this, we determine regions of parameter space where direct collapse into an SMBH is possible and the corresponding maximum halo mass required.

title: Ly$α$ in Compact Broad-Line Emitters, Including Little Red Dots, Is More Closely Linked to the Host Galaxy than to the Broad-Line Nucleus
abstract: JWST has found many faint broad-line AGN at $z>4$, but it is unclear whether the Ly$α$ we see from them comes from the accreting black hole or from its host galaxy. The answer matters for how these sources are interpreted and for how many ionizing photons they release. We use deep JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy from the DIVER program to measure Ly$α$ in 12 compact broad-line emitters (CBEs) at $z=4.2$--5.5 in GOODS-N. CBEs include little red dots (LRDs), little blue dots, and other broad-line AGN. Six are detected in Ly$α$. Every source shows a broad-line region, yet Ly$α$ does not follow it: the sources with the strongest H$α$ relative to the UV include weak detections and nondetections, and every detected Ly$α$ line (FWHM $\approx300$--1000~km~s$^{-1}$) is narrower than broad H$α$ (1100--3300~km~s$^{-1}$). Instead, Ly$α$ appears to track the host galaxy. We model the AGN-subtracted host with a dust-attenuated SED fit. Including the upper limits, the observed Ly$α$ follows the Ly$α$ production in this host model more closely than it follows H$α$/UV, in both equivalent width and luminosity. Every detection exceeds its host-model value by a factor of 1.5--18, leaving room for a nuclear contribution. The black hole is visible in these sources, but the Ly$α$ we observe is more closely tied to its host. The median effective Ly$α$ escape fraction of the detections is only 0.09, which suggests that ionizing escape from CBEs is typically modest and varies widely.

title: Tiny Galaxies, Mighty Nitrogen: Linking Chemical Anomalies to Compact Galaxies at High Redshift using JWST/JADES
abstract: The origin of anomalous chemical enrichment in high-redshift galaxies discovered by JWST remains a key question in galaxy evolution. Enhanced nitrogen abundances have been identified in several galaxies at early cosmic times, but the physical conditions driving this enrichment, and their connection to galaxy morphology, remain unclear. We test whether morphologically compact galaxies at 4 < z < 7 show stronger chemical anomalies than extended systems. Using JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopic data, we construct samples of compact and extended galaxies and analyse their rest-frame spectra. We stack the spectra of each population and measure key UV and optical emission lines. We detect nitrogen emission in the compact galaxy stack, including NIV], and [NII], while also detecting key carbon and oxygen lines. The detection of [OIII]λ4363 enables a direct-Te determination of the oxygen abundance. From these measurements, we infer chemical abundance ratios, including log(N/O) and log(C/O). We find that compact galaxies exhibit elevated log(N/O) (by ~ 0.7 dex) and log(C/O) (by ~ 0.5 dex) abundance ratios relative to extended systems. The abundance patterns of compact galaxy stacks are comparable to those of previously identified individual nitrogen-enhanced galaxies at high redshift and second-generation globular-cluster stars in the Milky Way. These results suggest a possible link between galaxy compactness and chemical enrichment pathways in the early Universe. Deeper JWST NIRSpec IFU observations of compact high-redshift galaxies will be crucial for determining the origin, spatial distribution, and evolutionary significance of these abundance patterns.
