title: CREDO: Evidence-Conditioned Credit Assignment for Temporal Reasoning Agents
abstract: Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering (TKGQA) requires language model agents to retrieve evidence, select relevant facts, and perform multi-step temporal reasoning. However, the trajectory-level outcome signal in GRPO does not explicitly distinguish the quality of intermediate decisions: downstream failures can penalize useful evidence acquisition, while identical rewards in all-failed groups eliminate the relative outcome signal despite differences in intermediate progress. We propose Credit Redistribution with Evidence-Driven Opportunities (CREDO), which uses intermediate evidence to recover local supervision, including in all-failed groups, and determine where outcome supervision acts. CREDO assigns positive stage-level credit through comparisons among rollouts of the same question and uses retained answer overlap as an opportunity proxy to shift part of the outcome-policy weight toward reasoning and answering. The framework preserves terminal rewards and trajectory-level advantages, while redistribution conserves total outcome-policy weight per trajectory. Following the public evaluation protocol of prior work, CREDO raises Overall accuracy from 78.0% to 82.4% and Multiple accuracy from 55.0% to 65.6% on MultiTQ relative to the strongest published baseline in our comparison. On TimelineKGQA, it raises cross-KG accuracy from 30.9% to 36.4% relative to our reproduced baseline via direct transfer to ICEWS Actor under matched training and evaluation settings.
authors: Yue Leng;Shengtao Wen;Xiang Chen;Xinyi Zeng;Yu Tian;Sheng-Jun Huang

title: Sharp Generalization for Nonparametric Regression in Interpolation Space by Shallow Over-Parameterized Neural Networks with Channel Attention
abstract: We study nonparametric regression using an over-parameterized two-layer ReLU neural network with fixed covariance-based channel attention, trained by gradient descent with both layers updated simultaneously. The spherical covariates follow an arbitrary fixed non-atomic distribution, and the target function lies in an interpolation space with spectral bias widely studied in the statistical learning literature. We prove that early-stopped training achieves regression risk $\cO(\eps_n^2)$, where $\eps_n$ is the critical population rate of the attention kernel $\Kattn$. Its positive eigenvalues are $λ_j^{s'}$, where $λ_j$ are those of the ReLU feature covariance kernel $K$ and $s'=2s+3$ for $s\ge1$. Under polynomial eigenvalue decay $λ_j\asymp j^{-2α}$ with $α>1/2$, the regression risk bound $\cO(\eps_n^2)$ specializes to the minimax optimal rate $\cO(n^{-2αs'/(2αs'+1)})$. Our analysis is based on two new technical results on the optimization and generalization of the attention network. First, the neural network function after every gradient descent iteration admits a decomposition into a function with bounded Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) norm and a uniformly small residual. Second, local Rademacher complexity converts this decomposition into a regression risk bound. Kernel gradient descent on the same ball attains the same rate, while our theorem gives explicit sufficient width and auxiliary-sample conditions for simultaneous network training. Our analysis is further extended to covariates supported on $\RR^d$ through a novel normalization method. Under a sub-Gaussian covariate distribution, the attention network achieves a nearly optimal regression risk $\cO((\log n)n^{-s'(d+3)/(s'(d+3)+d)})$ without a density assumption.

title: BanglishDepYT: Depression Detection in Native Bengali Social Media with Emotion-Preserving Preprocessing and Domain-Adaptive Pretraining
abstract: Depression affects millions of Bengali speakers across South Asia, yet automated detection systems have relied almost entirely on datasets translated from English. Such datasets cannot capture the emoticons, romanized Bengali words, and elongated spellings that characterize real expressions of distress. We introduce BanglishDepYT, a Bengali depression dataset collected natively from YouTube, comprising 191,000 unlabeled comments and 1,000 samples verified through dual bilingual annotation. We propose EPH (Emotion-Preserving Hybrid preprocessing), which converts emoticons to semantic tags, preserves Banglish tokens, protects negation words, and normalizes emotional elongation. A key finding is that preprocessing choice substantially affects performance on informal text: standard cleaning reduces the Banglish Survival Rate to zero (SVM F1: 0.7062), while EPH preserves signals (CESS: 0.9996 vs. 0.6694) and raises SVM F1 to 0.8570, an improvement of 0.1508. We further apply domain-adaptive pretraining (DAPT), continuing SahajBERT pretraining on unlabeled in-domain comments. DAPT-SahajBERT achieves the highest mean F1 (0.8161) and MCC (0.6272), significantly outperforming the baseline (F1: 0.7805, p = 0.0013, d = 1.450) and matching MuRIL (p = 0.589). These results suggest that targeted domain pretraining is a competitive alternative to large-scale multilingual pretraining. LLM-assisted annotation using Qwen2.5-7B achieves substantial human agreement (kappa = 0.611), enabling pseudo-labeling of 96,071 comments. Semi-supervised training improves AUC from 0.8499 to 0.8731 (p = 0.044), offering a scalable path to expanding annotation. All code, models, and datasets are publicly released to support reproducible research.

title: A Planar Switching Neuron Shares Logarithmic First-Spike Latency with Its Three-Dimensional Parent But Not Its Onset Mechanism
abstract: Can a reduced neuron model reproduce first-spike latency scaling while changing how a stimulus initiates sustained firing? We compare a piecewise-linear planar Neurosimilator with its three-dimensional parent. Both exhibit logarithmic latency dependence over the investigated input intervals, with different fitted coefficients. The mechanisms differ. In the parent, sustained spiking and a stable resting focus coexist in a spiking--rest bistability regime. An abrupt step accesses spiking, while slow stimulation can retain rest at the same final input. Its step-induced firing threshold is therefore an operational basin-access threshold below the saddle-node limit point, not a loss of equilibrium stability. In the planar model, the resting equilibrium instead reaches a switching boundary while its subthreshold eigenvalues remain negative. We derive the planar latency law from this boundary approach. The model generates repetitive excursions without an imposed reset and admits exact trajectories within six switching regions. Similar measured latency scaling thus coexists with different mechanisms of access to firing. Validating a reduced model's mechanism of excitability requires examination of stimulus protocol and attractor access alongside equilibrium structure and spike timing.

title: OCP-Based Nonlinear Model Predictive Control for Quadrotor Trajectory Tracking
abstract: Fast online optimization is essential for nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) on resource-limited aerial platforms. This paper presents an analytical-derivative NMPC solver for quadrotor trajectory tracking. For the state-affine translational model with held thrust and attitude commands, fourth-order Runge--Kutta integration yields an exact discrete-time prediction map. Forward--backward difference equations provide the gradient and exact Hessian of the finite-horizon cost condensed over the input sequence. These derivatives drive a nested optimal-control-based direction recursion, while a shifted warm start reuses the preceding solution. The resulting solver addresses the unconstrained tracking problem without a general-purpose nonlinear programming package. Gazebo experiments show comparable tracking accuracy to iLQR and two acados SQP configurations, with mean solver-time speedups of $1.97$--$2.30$. In onboard flight tests, the mean solver time is $0.3121$\,ms, corresponding to speedups of $3.37$--$5.77$ over the same baselines. The largest measured solver time is $3.7754$\,ms within a $20$-ms control period. These measurements cover the numerical solver and exclude estimation, communication, and command publication.

title: FinForesight: A Diagnostic Backtesting Benchmark for Deep Research Systems in Financial Forecasting
abstract: Anticipating financial outcomes requires synthesizing evolving evidence and reasoning under uncertainty, making deep research systems promising tools for forecasting. Yet evaluating forecasting ability is challenging because historical backtests may reward memorized outcomes or information retrieved after the forecast date. Live forecasting avoids direct access to realized outcomes, but feedback arrives only after events resolve. To obtain timely feedback and assess historical scores, we introduce FinForesight, a diagnostic backtesting benchmark for financial deep research systems. Across the Chinese, U.S., and Hong Kong markets, the benchmark evaluates four forecasting tasks: valuation, return ranking, event direction, and future financial fundamentals. Two capability diagnostic tasks assess counterfactual reasoning and financial calculation, scored separately from forecasting performance. Our harness-compatible framework restricts retrieved evidence to information available at the forecast date. We compare pretraining-era, resolved post-cutoff, and live evaluations to test whether controlled backtests approximate future performance. Pretraining-era scores exceed post-cutoff scores in most temporal comparisons, and stronger retrieval controls narrow the gap between post-cutoff backtests and live results. Forecasting attribution and robustness analyses reveal how scores respond to retrieval policy and how predictions respond to prompt rewrites and numerical perturbations. The code and benchmark data are publicly available.
authors: Fengyuan Liu;Mukai Li;Jieshun You;Yilin Zheng;Chenjia Min;Yizhou Zhang;Harper Chen;Qi Liu

title: Mean Field Game Problem with Kantorovich Potential Coupling: An Attrition model
abstract: In this work we address a class of Mean-Field Game (MFG) systems on the flat torus $\mathbb{T}^{d}$ in which individual agent incentives arise from macroscopic, distribution-dependent objectives governed by the Wasserstein-2 ($W_{2}$) distance. Taking the first variation (Lions derivative) of the Wasserstein-based macroscopic functional yields a coupled forward-backward system of Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman (HJB) and Fokker--Planck (FP) equations featuring a nonlocal coupling driven by the Kantorovich optimal transport potential. As a primary case study, we formulate a large-scale attacker-defender attrition model aimed at protecting High-Value Units (HVUs). By defining population-wise attrition rates via the $W_{2}$ metric and casting the defense strategy as a Pareto-optimal McKean--Vlasov control problem, we derive a concrete HJB--FP system with a Kantorovich potential coupling. We prove the local-in-time existence of classical solutions for this system using Schauder's fixed-point theorem. Finally, we compute the MFG dynamics by combining the Sinkhorn algorithm with ResNet-based Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), and simulate two-dimensional attacker-defender engagements across diverse attrition parameters, control costs, and multi-HVU configurations.
authors: Avetik Arakelyan;Davit Alaverdyan;Naira Hovakimyan;Isaac Kaminer;Tigran Bakaryan

title: LLM-Enhanced Multimodal House Price Prediction using Structured, Textual, and Visual Features
abstract: Accurate house price prediction is essential for real estate buyers, sellers, agents, and financial institutions. Traditional methods rely primarily on structured data, e.g., number of bedrooms, bathrooms, parkings, but they overlook rich contextual information embedded in textual descriptions and property photos. Previous deep learning approaches for house price prediction have fused multimodal data but they fall short to extract structured spatio-temporal and contextual features from texts and semantic visual information from images. In this paper, we introduce a novel multimodal framework that addresses these limitations by systematically integrating structured attributes, textual descriptions, and visual images of properties to achieve higher prediction accuracy while maintaining interpretability. We use a large language model to derive domain-specific spatio-temporal and contextual features from text, and an unsupervised vision-language approach to automatically group photos into meaningful classes like indoor, outdoor, mixed, or floorplan, that are commonly present in real-world house listings. These categories are created without manual labeling by aligning image clusters with carefully designed pseudo text prompts. We fuse all features into a unified representation and use an optimized regressor to predict prices. Experiments on a large real-world property dataset demonstrate that our method outperforms traditional methods and existing multimodal baselines. Ablation studies confirm that the novel textual feature extraction and categorized visual embeddings substantially contribute to more accurate and reliable price predictions.
authors: Khandokar Md. Rahat Hossain;Souvik Das;Tahsina Hashem;Mohammed Eunus Ali;Tanzima Hashem

title: Surrogate Losses for Fairness-Aware Classification: Fisher Consistency and Calibration
abstract: Fairness-aware classification seeks to balance predictive accuracy and fairness across demographic groups. Although surrogate losses facilitate the optimization of fairness-aware objectives, it remains unclear when minimizing these losses yields optimal decisions under the original fairness-aware risk. This paper investigates the statistical validity of surrogate-based fairness-aware classification under demographic parity and equal opportunity, considering both attribute-blind and attribute-aware settings. We introduce fairness-aware Fisher consistency and characterize it through conditions on the derivatives of the surrogate losses. The characterization shows that consistency depends not only on the individual loss functions but also on their interaction within the fairness-regularized objective. We further establish a calibration inequality that relates the excess fairness-aware risk to the excess surrogate risk, providing a quantitative connection between surrogate optimization and the original classification objective. Numerical experiments illustrate how deviations from the consistency conditions affect fairness-aware excess risk and how the regularization parameter influences the well-posedness of surrogate optimization. An application to consumer credit default prediction demonstrates that appropriately calibrated fairness regularization can substantially reduce demographic disparities while maintaining predictive performance.
authors: Changcheng Song;Yi Yang;Xiangyu Chang;Xiaoling Lu;Yufeng Liu

title: Halal-NeSyNet: Clause-Scoped Neuro-Symbolic Cross-Attention for Automated Food Ingredient Auditing and Risk-Aware Halal Logistics Triage
abstract: Verifying that a packaged food is Halal requires reading ingredient declarations and E-number additives before goods enter certified warehouses. Dual-origin additives such as E471, E422, E441 and E920 are Mushbooh (doubtful) unless a botanical, microbial or certified-Halal qualifier appears in the same ingredient clause, so a plant-based qualifier on one clause must not clear an unqualified additive in another. We call a failure to respect this scope cross-clause modifier confounding and build a benchmark of 3,199 items (277 Open Food Facts records and 2,922 template-generated clause-swap items, labelled by an explicit 50-code rule base rather than by a certification authority) with a 540-item counterfactual suite. We propose Halal-NeSyNet, which couples a DistilBERT encoder with a 16-dimensional rule-derived symbolic vector through cross-attention and gated fusion, trained with an asymmetric false-Halal risk loss. Over five seeds, text-only TF-IDF baselines reach 86.25-86.71 % accuracy with 13.42-21.73 % false-Halal leakage and 6.33-26.00 % counterfactual triad consistency, whereas Halal-NeSyNet reaches 97.04+/-0.34 % and 99.67+/-0.50 %. Gradient boosting given the same symbolic vector reaches 96.25+/-1.24 % (+0.59 points from Halal-NeSyNet, 95 % CI [-1.11, +2.28]), so most of the gain comes from clause-scoped symbolic features and not from the network, and the risk loss did not help. Holding out whole template families, text-only models fall to 61.91-78.35 %, Halal-NeSyNet to 90.87+/-11.76 % and logistic regression with the symbolic vector to 91.11+/-2.88 %, with far more spread for Halal-NeSyNet. A three-lane receiving simulation auto-clears 49.33 % of cargo at 0.76 % green-lane contamination. Because labels and features come from one rule engine and 91.3 % of the items are templated, the results measure fidelity to a rule policy, not religious certification.

title: When Does Sparse Routing Help? The Geometry of Expert Separation in Mixture of Experts
abstract: Sparse mixtures of experts combine multiple prediction models while evaluating only a small subset for each input. Although this architecture reduces computation, how expert separation and routing sparsity jointly govern expert recovery remains an open problem. In this paper, we address this question for location Gaussian mixtures of experts with a fixed number of experts by establishing how expert separation and spatial arrangement determine recovery rates. For dense models, our results reveal that when experts form well-separated clusters, the separation geometry is governed by the size of the largest cluster; without a prescribed cluster structure, this geometry is instead driven by the total number of experts. For sparse models, the separation geometry on retained routing regions is determined by the number of active experts, while the contribution of omitted regions is controlled by their total probability. Consequently, activating fewer experts reduces the separation complexity in these bounds. Furthermore, Top-1 routing yields a particularly striking result: experts can be recovered at a rate independent of the separation quantity. Our technical approach combines polynomial interpolation and Gaussian reproducing-kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) test functions with quantitative restriction inequalities that extend pointwise comparisons to expert functions.

title: QFabric: Guarded Cross-Domain Task Recovery and Its Limits on a Linux-RTOS Board
abstract: Heterogeneous embedded boards pair a Linux application processor with a real-time microcontroller (MCU), which suggests moving a task between the two domains when its timing degrades. We present QFabric, a prototype that treats cross-domain placement as guarded recovery from a violated empirical soft real-time contract: a bounded task is compiled for both domains, monitored in windows with hysteresis, switched only after semantic and capacity admission at a quiescent epoch boundary, and committed or rolled back after probation. On an Arduino UNO Q (Cortex-A53 Linux and a Cortex-M33 running Zephyr), we characterize the stock Bridge RPC interconnect and measure five workloads in both domains under idle, CPU-load, and higher-priority SCHED_FIFO contention, with ordinary and real-time callers. Each MCU invocation costs about 19 ms of dispatch regardless of compute, the MCU runs the heaviest kernel 34x slower, and because every call traverses Linux userspace, Linux contention inflates the MCU path far more than the Linux path (p99 up to 400 ms versus 17.0 ms). Across 30 cells of a four-node chain, Linux meets every contract within 0.8% misses and QFabric correctly never migrates; a controller without hysteresis migrates in 7 cells, raising p95 by up to 177x, and probation rolls back 5 of those moves. On Linux-dispatched heterogeneous boards, migration therefore cannot isolate a task from Linux interference, and recovery guards matter chiefly by preventing harmful moves. This paper supersedes an earlier artifact release whose reported improvement arose from measurement defects that we identify. All source, raw traces, and generators are public.
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 8 tables. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23692354

title: Physically Motivated Stellar Populations for Galaxies at Cosmic Dawn with a Temperature-Dependent IMF
abstract: The first few years of James Webb Space Telescope observations have identified previously undetected galaxies at $z>12$ and provided new constraints on galaxies at $z>8$. Many of these objects have stellar masses that are difficult to reconcile with $Λ$CDM, inferred from models not calibrated for the high-redshift Universe. This necessitates new, more astrophysically plausible stellar population models for estimating stellar masses of galaxies at cosmic dawn. We introduce a simple stellar population (SSP) library, Simple Stellar Populations with Temperature (SSPT), computed using a temperature-dependent stellar initial mass function and its implementation in the public code CIGALE. When used in a configuration designed for high-redshift galaxies that requires young stellar population ages, the new models predict stellar masses that are ~0.3-0.5 dex lower than estimates from similar CIGALE analyses using models calibrated to the local Universe, and nearly 2 dex lower than estimates from analyses using other codes and softer constraints on stellar ages. Application of these physically motivated stellar populations suggests that stellar masses of early star-forming galaxies are not in tension with $Λ$CDM, and that galaxy formation from virialized halos remains a reasonable hypothesis at the highest redshifts. The SSPT SSPs and their CIGALE implementation are released publicly.

title: Access Resources and Stability of Error-Correction Capabilities in Continuous Strategic Codes
abstract: Continuous quantum error correction depends on which parts of a measurement record remain available to the controller at recovery. We study this temporal access using continuous strategic codes, formulated as open continuous process tensors contracted with causal instruments and conditional recovery. For monitored stabilizer codes, a common-optimal-correction criterion identifies when records can be merged without loss and yields a factorization for separated CSS inference. Terminal decision labels and causal persistent memory carry different costs: five persistent classical states reach the complete-record optimum in a finite-strength counting model, whereas its two-window diffusive counterpart has nine terminal decision labels and requires unbounded memory for exact causal recovery. Uniform lower and constructive upper bounds establish an optimal fidelity deficit of order $m^{-2}$ for $m$ persistent states in the diffusive model. Counting and diffusive stability bounds translate open-process approximation into guarantees for deployed-controller performance and retained access advantages, quantified by explicit quantizers and model-mismatch curves. The same process--instrument framework connects storage with persistent environments and irreversible noise to spacetime interrogation and record-selected paths for a logical $T$ gate. These results specify which record distinctions recovery needs, the memory cost of approximating them, and the logical protection retained under model error.

title: Smoothed analysis of stability radii for the assignment problem
abstract: Every linear program can tolerate small changes to its costs and still yield a solution of the original problem. The size of this tolerance measures how robust an optimal decision is to noise or numerical error, and how much regularization the problem can support. Classical sensitivity analysis can determine this tolerance only from an optimal solution. This paper provides a priori lower bounds on two measures of this tolerance -- the optimality gap and the $\infty$-norm stability radius -- for the $n$-by-$n$ linear assignment problem over the Birkhoff polytope. The bounds derive from a smoothed analysis, which adds Gaussian noise with standard deviation of at least $σ$ in every direction to an arbitrary base cost. At every fixed confidence level, uniformly over the base cost, both quantities are at least of order $σ/(n\sqrt{\log n})$. The radius bound is asymptotically sharp. Under isotropic noise, the worst case occurs when every assignment has equal cost, and in this case, a scaled stability radius converges in distribution to a standard exponential variable.

title: Fredholm approximations to the Bethe-Salpeter equation with spherical-Bessel kernels for Wannier-Mott excitons
abstract: We develop a deterministic radial approximation to the static Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE), designed for rapid preliminary screening of Wannier-Mott exciton binding across direct-gap bulk materials. The approximation replaces the electron-hole transition problem by small radial eigenvalue problems that require no stochastic sampling. Starting from the four-point BSE and its matrix representation in a Bloch electron-hole basis, we retain one valence and one conduction band in the effective-mass limit within the Tamm-Dancoff approximation. We introduce a central projection of the screened direct interaction and omit bare electron-hole exchange. The resulting model applies to spatially extended excitons whose envelopes vary slowly on the scale of the unit cell, provided that the effective-mass description and central screened interaction adequately represent the exciton of interest. A partial-wave decomposition separates the angular-momentum channels and expresses their interaction kernels as spherical-Bessel transforms of the real-space screened Coulomb interaction. Nyström discretization produces real symmetric radial matrices suitable for standard eigensolvers. Their dimension is set by the radial grid independently of the Brillouin-zone sampling used to calculate screening. We implement the formulation in the all-electron, full-potential code $\texttt{exciting}$. For bulk GaAs, the compact radial problem reproduces the corresponding conventional matrix-BSE binding energy within $(1~\mathrm{meV})$ at matched sampling. Further refinement achieves finite-mesh stability within the same tolerance on denser screening meshes without increasing the radial matrix size.

title: Principled Human-AI Collaboration in Agentic Workflows
abstract: Organizations adopting AI face the challenge of deciding which outputs can be released without human review while meeting the quality standards of human experts. We develop a statistical framework for delegating tasks between experts and black-box generate-verify workflows, in which AI-generated answers are verified and revised over multiple rounds. Before deployment, human experts evaluate selected outputs, and their judgments are used to calibrate the verifier threshold and number of attempts. Our method selects the policy with the highest estimated automation rate among statistically approved candidates, without modifying the generator or verifier. We establish finite-sample control of the error rate among released outputs, characterize the expert evaluations sufficient to attain a target automation rate, and derive a minimax lower bound establishing rate optimality in the quality margin and required confidence. In a MultiHiertt financial question-answering case study, average held-out automation increases from 2.50% to 24.17% as expert evaluations accumulate, while released-output error rates remain around 1.20%. In contrast, heuristics that release answers after consistently high verifier scores either violate the 5% error tolerance or automate at most 1.30% of tasks. Synthetic experiments further examine these theoretical predictions under controlled settings.
comment: 44 pages, 4 figures. Includes supplementary material with proofs and experimental details

title: Distributionally Robust Optimization over Incomparable Spaces
abstract: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) provides a principled framework for making decisions under uncertainty when the underlying distribution may be incorrectly specified. A widely used approach builds on ideas from optimal transport (OT) as a means of measuring differences between distributions. However, this depends on these distributions residing in the same space. In certain settings, the reference data distribution we have and the space on which we make our decision may be different, which renders classical OT techniques impossible. In this paper, we provide a new DRO formulation in which ambiguity sets are defined through the Gromov-Wasserstein distance, which is an extension of OT to pairs of distributions residing in incomparable spaces. We show that several seemingly unrelated optimization formulations, including conditional value-at-risk minimization, group distributionally robust optimization, robust graph $k$-median, and $k$-median with outliers, can be recovered as special cases of our formulation. We describe the computational aspects of solving the proposed formulation based on the doubly-nonnegative relaxation. Last, we illustrate the framework through experiments on clustering over incomparable spaces and stochastic graph $k$-median.

title: Can Large Language Models Extend Their Agentic Capabilities to Goal Pursuit in Open-Ended Multi-Turn Interaction?
abstract: Goal pursuit in open-ended dialogue requires agents to adapt their actions to interaction feedback across successive exchanges. We investigate whether agentic capabilities developed for multi-step tool use carry over to dialogue organized through the model's native tool interface, and how this changes interaction behavior. We define Tool-Mediated Interaction (TMI) as a training-free protocol that represents dialogue actions as tool calls and counterpart responses as tool results, maintaining a continuous reasoning-action-observation loop with retained reasoning and interaction history. We evaluate TMI across social interaction, emotional support, persuasion, and price negotiation using two models and 15,678 main-experiment episodes. Across both models, TMI improves social goal attainment, emotional-support preference, donation amounts, and buyer negotiation margins over conversational baselines with and without thinking. A Qwen ablation further shows that TMI outperforms ordinary conversation with retained reasoning on all four primary outcomes. Behavioral analyses associate the improvements with task-specific patterns in initial proposals and responses to interaction feedback. Alongside these gains, TMI reduces mean reasoning tokens per decision by 42.0-81.5% relative to the thinking baseline and lowers mean cross-turn phrase reuse across all eight model-environment pairs. These findings show that interaction organization shapes both goal attainment and reasoning across dialogue turns.
authors: Mingyu Chen;Jingkai Lin;Xiaofen Xing;Liankai Huang;Ruiqi Xiong;Xiangmin Xu

title: Revisiting LLM Homogeneity Through a Multidimensional Lens
abstract: Concerns about LLM homogeneity are typically quantified with embedding similarity, which reduces two texts to a single score. We revisit homogeneity with 25 interpretable metrics spanning five dimensions: semantic, lexical, syntactic, structural, and stylistic & presentational. A human study shows that perceived similarity depends on both content (what responses say) and form (how they say it), yet embedding similarity correlates less with human meaning judgments than sentence-level matching ($ρ=0.417$ vs. $0.606$) and not significantly with form judgments ($ρ=0.140$). Across 18 contemporary LLMs, models say similar things in different words: they share global semantics and broad linguistic profiles but remain distinct in lexical characteristics, structural patterns, and interactional conventions. Across releases from 2024 to 2026, models become more like themselves but not more like one another: among significantly changing metrics, intra-model distances decrease for 17 of 22, and inter-model distances increase for 14 of 21. Across two post-training pipelines, model-specific conventions emerge during SFT and are selectively reshaped by preference optimization. These results suggest that homogeneity is multidimensional and evolving, and that embedding similarity alone can overstate cross-model homogeneity while concealing diverging intra- and inter-model trends.

title: The Structure of Disagreement in Emotion Annotation
abstract: Calculating inter-annotator agreement is an established practice in NLP, and disagreement-aware work increasingly retains the distribution of human judgments rather than reducing annotations to a single gold label. Keeping the distribution, however, does not explain why annotators disagree. This paper examines the types of disagreement that occur in emotion annotation, starting from multilabel annotations of 1,677 sentence-level units from Ernest Hemingway's The Old Man and the Sea and testing the patterns they reveal against individual-level annotations from BRIGHTER and GoEmotions. Across the three datasets, we find three main recurring disagreement structures. Emotion categories overlap systematically; annotators differ both in how broadly they apply labels and in how they treat particular category boundaries, while sparse participation and explicit abstention can look like disagreement. Where intensity is rated, disagreement over whether an emotion is present can be separated from disagreement over its intensity once recognized. Similar aggregate disagreement can therefore arise from qualitatively different annotation processes. Hard aggregation removes most of this structure, while annotator vote-share representations keep marginal label frequencies but not the co-occurrence, annotator-specific, or procedural patterns that produced them. We argue that disagreement should be understood in terms of its underlying patterns before it is summarized, aggregated, or used as a modeling target, and propose a vocabulary for disagreement structure.

title: Strong convergence of a slowly damped primal-dual dynamical system with general time-scaling, Tikhonov regularization and implicit Hessian damping
abstract: This paper proposes a novel mixed-order inertial primal-dual dynamical system with general time-scaling and Tikhonov regularization coefficients, together with implicit Hessian damping, for solving convex optimization problems with linear equality constraints in Hilbert spaces. The proposed dynamical system incorporates slowly vanishing viscous damping and is developed based on a time-dependent Tikhonov-regularized Lagrangian. Under suitable assumptions, we establish fast convergence rates for the objective residual, the feasibility violation, and the primal-dual gap using a Lyapunov analysis. Moreover, we prove that the generated primal-dual trajectory converges strongly to the minimum-norm primal-dual solution. Numerical experiments illustrate the theoretical results and indicate improved convergence performance relative to the comparison dynamical systems.

title: Learning Gradients of Homogeneous Functions
abstract: Homogeneous gradient functions have widespread significance, including applications in maximum energy subspace selection and retrieval problems. Euler's homogeneous function theorem specifies how the potential associated with a positively k-homogeneous gradient field can be recovered directly from the field itself. We use Euler's theorem to build on GradNets and propose a homogeneous gradient network architecture that is guaranteed to correspond to the gradient of a homogeneous function. Then, we describe how monotone homogeneous GradNets universally approximate the gradients of k-homogeneous convex functions. The inductive bias of homogeneous GradNets enables them to outperform baseline ICNNs by up to 7dB in our max energy subspace projection experiment and by up to 13% higher accuracy, 98% fewer parameters, and 70% fewer FLOPS in our amortized inner product search experiment.
authors: Mayur S. Gowda;Srinivasa Pranav;Shreyas Chaudhari;José M. F. Moura

title: InformedXRD: Reproducible Benchmarks and Physics-Informed Evaluation for Powder Diffraction Symmetry Classification
abstract: Machine learning for powder diffraction (PXRD) symmetry classification is being trained at scale, yet the field lacks a common evaluation standard: papers report results on different subsets of experimental archives, with different target taxonomies, preprocessing, and metrics, and published models are rarely released in a form that permits rescoring. We present InformedXRD, an evaluation framework with three parts: (i) a machine-readable mapping from 230 space groups to 99 extinction groups, the finest classes powder diffraction can identify from systematic absences alone; (ii) a benchmark-construction method whose inclusion rules are specified as code and reproduce from a frozen snapshot, instantiated as RRUFF-473, RRUFF-325, and, as a small example, opXRD-98; (iii) a reporting protocol with prior-only frequency baselines, a label-permutation test, a hierarchy-aware error metric on the condensed translationengleiche subgroup graph, and stratified evaluation. We build on the mapping, RRUFF benchmarks, subgroup graph, and four ViT checkpoints released in our earlier work (Baggett et al., 2026). Using these checkpoints, a 1D residual CNN, and six architectures trained under the XRDBench recipe (Cao et al., 2025), we show that evaluation design changes what conclusions are justified: paired tests point in different directions at Top-1 and Top-5; paired Top-k tests do not separate the three leading XRDBench models, while hierarchy-aware analysis describes error distance and direction across all six; an input-blind frequency predictor matches the models on aggregate Top-k, yet a label-permutation test still detects pattern-specific evidence; and stratified analysis exposes a label-entropy confound that aggregate accuracy hides. All mapping tables, benchmark code, scripts, and checkpoints are released as shared infrastructure for PXRD-ML evaluation.
authors: Edward G Friedman;Elizabeth J. Baggett;Abhishek Shetty;Derrick Chan-Sew;Vanellsa Acha;Harshitha Dwaracherla;P. A. Kienzle;William Ratcliff

title: From Ghost SICs to SIC-POVMs: A Galois Reduction of Zauner's Conjecture
abstract: Symmetric informationally complete positive operator-valued measures (SIC-POVMs, or SICs) are optimal minimal measurements for quantum state tomography. Problem~1 of Horodecki, Rudnicki and Życzkowski's open problems in quantum information asks for SICs in infinitely many dimensions. By work of Appleby--Flammia--Kopp and Radchenko--Wheeler, ghost SICs, which satisfy the SIC equations with Hermiticity up to parity, exist unconditionally for $d\ge4$. We study the passage from ghosts to SICs. We compute all isolated points of the complexified SIC variety for $d=4,5,6$; exactly half are SICs. We prove that no symmetry of the SIC equations maps a ghost to a SIC, so the step is purely arithmetic, and that a SIC exists in dimension $d$ whenever the ghost overlap units satisfy a place law: each Galois conjugate is real or unimodular according to the infinite place of the real quadratic field $F$ below it. If the unit field is abelian over $F$, the place law is the Stark relation $c_-=κ$; equivalently, a Galois conjugate of an associated near-group fusion category is unitary exactly when it is pseudo-unitary. For $d$ a power of a prime $p\equiv5\pmod 6$ or of $3$, an infinite family, we prove that under the algebraic part of Stark's conjecture $c_-=κ$ is equivalent to the triviality of $κ$ on the Hilbert-class-field part of the unit field. That condition involves no complex conjugation, and it follows from a sign-free multiplet hypothesis. We state an explicit $GL_2$ reciprocity law for the squared ghost overlaps that implies $c_-=κ$, and we prove it for the computed algebraic overlaps in $d=5,7,11,15$ by Artin reciprocity and a check in every ray class. Zauner's conjecture remains open: the algebraic part of Stark's conjecture and the multiplet hypothesis are not proved here.
comment: 100 pages, 1 figure, 18 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/hassankhodaiemehr/ghost-sic-galois

title: Variance Reduction Note 3: The Convergence of PAGE
abstract: The probabilistic gradient estimator (PAGE) alternates randomly between an accurate gradient refresh and a cheap recursive correction. This third expository note on recursive variance reduction explains the algorithm and gives a self-contained convergence proof for smooth nonconvex optimization. A Lyapunov function combines objective decrease with estimation error, turning the refresh probability into an explicit contraction parameter. The resulting expected oracle complexity is $O(n+\sqrt n\,ε^{-2})$ for finite sums and $O(ε^{-3})$ for online problems, with the other problem parameters fixed. Initialization, refreshes, and both evaluations in each gradient difference are counted. The presentation is pedagogical and makes no claim of a new algorithm or convergence rate.

title: Near-Optimal Learning of Quantum Many-Body Systems from Gibbs and Thermal Metastable States via the Stationarity Test
abstract: We study the problem of learning a finite-range quantum Hamiltonian on an $n$-qubit $D$-dimensional lattice from copies of its Gibbs states at a known inverse temperature $β$ or its thermal metastable states. Existing efficient algorithms at arbitrary temperature have sample guarantees with an $e^{\poly(β)}$ dependence, leaving open whether the exponent can be made linear in $β$. We achieve this improvement: for $β\ge1$, our algorithm learns all Hamiltonian coefficients to $\ell_\infty$-error $ε$ with probability at least $1-δ$ using $\tO\bigl(e^{O(β)}ε^{-2}\log(n/δ)\bigr)$ copies and total time $\tO\bigl(n e^{O(β)}ε^{-2}\log(n/δ)\bigr)$. The measurements act on individual copies and are supported on balls of radius $O\bigl(β^2+β\log(1/ε)\bigr)$. Our sample complexity achieves the optimal exponential order in $β$, with optimal $ε^{-2}$ dependence up to logarithmic factors. Building on the stationarity-test framework \citep{Bergamaschi2026Stationarity}, we prove a unified Fisher-information coercivity bound showing that errors in the candidate Hamiltonian produce a detectable signal with only an $e^{-O(β)}$ loss in sensitivity. The key is a smooth frequency filter whose bandwidth remains independent of temperature, together with sharper estimates relating this signal to the Hamiltonian coefficients. For thermal metastable states, the guarantee holds under local drift $ζ\le e^{-Cβ^{2D+1}}$, for a geometry-dependent constant $C>0$, and above an accuracy floor $\tO(e^{O(β)}ζ)$. The argument applies to both Gibbs and thermal metastable states and, combined with local measurements and projected stochastic gradient descent (SGD), yields both learning guarantees.

title: Write Facts the Way Models Read Them: Lifting the Two-Hop Curse
abstract: A language model that learns a new fact by fine-tuning can repeat it but cannot reason with it: taught that a person is a citizen of a new country, it still cannot say, without chain-of-thought, who the head of state of that person's country is. This two-hop curse is widely treated as a reasoning deficit, and the strongest knowledge editors answer it with synthesized reasoning data. We show that the reasoning is intact and the writing is wrong. Fine-tuning writes a new fact as an answer to be said, whereas the second hop reads the bridge ("that person's country") as an entity, from the middle layers on: patching the model's own representation of the entity into the bridge at those layers largely restores the second hop, yet after fine-tuning the bridge there is no closer to the new entity than before the edit. We therefore propose read-equivalent writing (Legible): one loss term makes the bridge phrase, at the layer where the second hop finishes reading it, match the model's own reading of the new entity, and keeps the same relation's other subjects unchanged. Phrases and targets come from the edited model itself, and no multi-hop training data is used. Across Qwen2.5, Llama-3 and Qwen3, Legible (I) composes learned facts more often than the model composes its own knowledge, on MQuAKE's two-hop-curse questions; (II) reaches 1.8-2.6x the bridge accuracy of CaKE, whose reasoning data composes no better than plain fine-tuning, and has the best average over composition, accuracy and locality against four families of writers; and (III) lifts the curse on RippleEdits, on the benchmark of Balesni et al., who named the curse, and at 14B.

title: VLMs Read Aloud: The Gap Between Recognizing and Using Visual Text
abstract: Visual-text compression renders long contexts as images and is engineered around how much of the text a vision-language model (VLM) can recover. Yet recovered text is not usable text. VLMs can transcribe the text in an image word for word and still fail to answer from it; given back their own transcript, they answer nearly as well as from the original text. We call this difference the read-use gap. Recognizing and using visual text have different resolution requirements: Qwen3-VL-8B's recognition saturates at 15-pixel characters while use catches up only at 24 pixels, and scaling from 2B to 32B raises recognition without narrowing the gap. Putting the evidence into words closes it: thinking VLMs recite the evidence in their thinking, and their own transcript, written without seeing the question, recovers most of what thinking adds. In a preregistered held-out test, the gap ranks how much eight VLMs gain from their own words over pixels (Spearman $ρ$ = 0.86), which recognition rates do not. We propose ALOUD, which spends visual resolution on finding and recognizing evidence and language tokens on using it. Without keeping the source text, it doubles the accuracy of a frozen Qwen3-VL-8B on long documents compressed 5x and 10x: at 5x, from 27.7% to 54.8%, near the original text's 58.5%, with a context smaller than the compressed pages themselves. For less than the cost of reading the original text, it leads at equal budget every method that does without it, at every level, and beats AGAR and VERA, which paste the original text back; at 5x it also beats LensVLM-9B, which is trained and keeps the original text. Visual-text compression is limited not by how much text a model can recover, but by how much it can use.

title: Superradiance fingerprints of moiré exciton-biexciton condensates: path-entangled biphoton vs. supercurrent-enabled one-photon channel
abstract: Hybrid moiré excitons form a dense array of electrically tunable single-photon emitters, entailing cooperative optical responses with intriguing consequences. With the strong dipole-dipole interaction, they also realize Bose-Hubbard quantum simulators of emergent correlated matter such as Bose-Einstein condensates (BEC). Here we reveal the characteristic cooperative radiation from condensates of hybrid moiré excitons in twisted MoTe$_2$ bilayers. In each individual moiré trap, the layer hybridization selection rule dictates that the ground-state exciton is a quantum emitter of orbital-angular-momentum photons, with an exceptionally long radiative lifetime. Ground-state emission becomes pronounced only upon forming condensates, where inter-sublattice dipole attraction and intra-sublattice repulsion together lead to the coexistence of exciton and biexciton BEC with comparable weights. The biexciton (molecular-type) BEC decays through superradiance of path-entangled biphotons, whereas the exciton (atomic-type) BEC is dark at rest and becomes superradiant when it carries a supercurrent. Our findings not only uncover a novel source of entangled light but also establish unique fingerprints for exploring the cold chemistry of atomic-molecular condensates with moiré excitons.
authors: Haochen Wang;Shengxian Li;Hongyu Lu;Mingxing Chen;Wang Yao

title: Abstention Spends Its Budget on Local Label Variance More Than on Novelty: Auditing Conformal Calibration and Selective Prediction under Molecular Scaffold Shift
abstract: Selective prediction with split conformal calibration promises a post-hoc fix for molecular property prediction: abstain on the least reliable compounds, ideally out-of-distribution chemistry, and the retained set becomes trustworthy without retraining. We audit this recipe for a gradient-boosted fingerprint model on lipophilicity (regression) and BBBP (classification) under a Bemis-Murcko scaffold split, holding the fitted model and evaluation molecules fixed while varying only the calibration fold (18 replicates). (i) On lipophilicity, coverage depends on calibration provenance: calibrating on held-out training-scaffold molecules falls below nominal (PICP 0.841 at a 0.90 target), while novel-scaffold calibration recovers it (0.904); on BBBP, coverage stays above nominal in every regime. (ii) For split conformalized quantile regression (CQR) the conformal correction is a constant, so conformalization does not change what is abstained on. (iii) The abstention score (CQR width; effectively ensemble variance on BBBP) tracks local label variance more than chemical novelty: controlling for local label variance largely explains away the novelty association (partial Spearman 0.067 and 0.047). (iv) At a fixed assay budget, gating on interval width or ensemble variance never improves hit precision over ranking by point prediction, at the pre-specified operating point or across 20 exploratory settings; a plain novelty gate shows small, uncorrected gains at the smallest budgets. (v) In an exploratory analysis, exact conformal selection exceeds its false discovery rate target under training-scaffold calibration (0.303 at q=0.2) and is consistent with it under novel-scaffold calibration, contributing a data-driven batch size rather than a better ranking. Conformalization earns its keep through guarantees whose validity hinges on calibration provenance, not by choosing what to abstain on.

title: Theoretical Prediction of Superconducting 2D Hydrogenated Janus V2CSH and Nb2CSH MXenes
abstract: Two dimensional hydrogenated Janus MXenes represent a new frontier in superconducting materials, where asymmetric surface terminations enable tunable electronic and vibrational properties. In this work, we present the first comparative study of hydrogen or sulfur terminated V2CSH and Nb2CSH monolayers using density functional theory and density functional perturbation theory. Both compounds are structurally and thermally stable, exhibiting isotropic in plane elasticity and nonmagnetic multiband metallic states dominated by transition metal d orbitals. The asymmetric S or H terminations generate nonequivalent surface potentials and intrinsic out of plane dipoles. Electron phonon coupling constants of 0.39 (V2CSH) and 0.53 (Nb2CSH) yield superconducting transition temperatures of 2.36 K and 5.27 K, respectively, within the Allen Dynes framework. Low energy lattice vibrations, primarily involving metal and sulfur atoms, account for 77% of the coupling in both MXenes. These findings establish metal substitution as a design principle for tuning superconductivity in Janus MXenes and highlight Nb2CSH as a promising candidate for low temperature superconducting applications.
authors: Jubair Hossan Abir;M. R. U. S. Shapon;Md. Sharear Aman;Md. Kamrul Hassan;A. K. M. Azharul Islam;Saleh Hasan Naqib

title: Sweep Less, Steer More: Using Activation Steering Geometry for Reduced Hyperparameter Search
abstract: Representation steering methods like difference-in-means (DIM) offer a lightweight approach to controlling LLM behavior, but their effectiveness varies widely across concepts, datasets, and layers, making principled deployment costly without exhaustive hyperparameter sweeps. We build on the discriminability index $d'$, a compute-cheap geometric measure of how well contrastive training activations separate along the steering direction. Across five behaviors on 3 models, we demonstrate uses beyond its established role as a dataset-level steerability predictor. First, in the multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) setting, we show that $d'$ reliably identifies performant layers at which to steer, eliminating the need for a layer-wise sweep. Second, we extend this analysis to open-ended multi-token generation, and find that $d'$ remains successful for layer selection across different settings. Lastly, we test whether the position of a generated token's representation on the DIM line predicts steering success on that individual example. In the MCQA setting, this works for high-$d'$ datasets but is inconsistent across behaviors, models, and training-token choices in open-ended generation. This highlights that methods developed and conclusions drawn in single-token MCQA settings do not necessarily transfer to open-ended generation.

title: TopoSteer: Topological Layer Selection for Activation Steering in LLMs
abstract: Activation steering controls large language models at inference time by adding a vector to their internal representations. Most work asks how to build that vector, and far less attention has gone to where to add it, even though steering at a poorly chosen layer can be worse than not steering at all. Prior selectors choose a layer without ever steering the model to test it: they score how separable the target behavior is at that layer, and how consistently the individual examples point along the steering direction. We argue that what matters is not the separability of the two activation clouds, nor the alignment of individual displacements with their mean, but the extent of the cloud of per-example displacements that mean-difference steering averages. We propose a topology-based layer selection method, called TopoSteer, which scores a layer by the total H_0 persistence of its displacement cloud, computed as the length of the cloud's Euclidean minimum spanning tree. We show that the score focuses on the displacement cloud's relative geometry, while class separation affects it only through standardization. We also provide a theoretical explanation for our method by proving that, as example-level variation increases, TopoSteer and discriminability move in opposite directions, so the two criteria can rank layers in opposite ways. Across multiple language models and steering tasks, TopoSteer provides a principled alternative to discriminability- and separability-based layer selection and yields more effective steering without requiring held-out validation.
authors: Tuc Nguyen;Marcos Gutiérrez-del-Pozo;Eduardo Paluzo-Hidalgo;Yifan Hu;Adaku Uchendu;Thai Le

title: Purity maxima, absolute separability, and spectral volumes of absolutely PPT states
abstract: For $m\otimes n$ systems with $n\ge m\ge3$, we determine the exact maximum purity of absolutely positive partial transpose (APPT) states and the unique maximizing ordered spectrum when $n\ge2m^2-4$ for even $m$ or $n\ge2m^2-m-4$ for odd $m$. Under these dimension assumptions, absolutely separable states have the same maximum purity, attained at the same unique ordered spectrum. The proof uses an outer polytope defined by two linear head--tail inequalities, each comparing a sum of the largest eigenvalues with a sum of the smallest. Under explicit multiplicity assumptions, we derive an exact matrix criterion for APPT membership of full-rank spectra with three distinct eigenvalues. For every $m\ge10$, this criterion gives explicit APPT boundary spectra at $n=4m-2$ and $n=4m$ that disprove both cases of the maximum purity conjecture of Ahiable, Kothakonda, and Winter. We also determine the exact completely absolutely separable (CAS) purity maximum and its unique maximizing ordered spectrum in every bipartite dimension. We prove that the inner APPT polytope consists entirely of absolutely separable spectra. The resulting linear sufficient condition for absolute separability strictly improves the reduction-map and eigenvalue-ratio tests. Finally, we compute the exact relative volumes of the CAS set and an outer polytope defined by a single head--tail inequality. Under the uniform measure on spectra, the CAS, absolutely separable, and APPT volumes have the same asymptotic order $\sqrt n\,e^{-κ_m n}$ for every fixed $m\ge2$, with explicit $κ_m>0$.

title: Long-time behavior of first-order Hamilton-Jacobi equations in the Wasserstein space
abstract: We establish the long-time behavior of solutions $U$ to first-order Hamilton-Jacobi equations in the Wasserstein space $\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb T^d)$. For a class of Hamiltonians with quadratic growth, including non-convex ones, we prove that there exist a unique ergodic constant $λ$ and a solution $V$ of the associated ergodic problem such that $U(t,m)-λt$ converges to $V(m)$, uniformly on $\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb T^d)$, as $t\to+\infty$. Finally, we provide applications to mean field control problems and zero-sum differential games.

title: Robust Appointment Scheduling with Heterogeneous Costs
abstract: Designing simple appointment systems that under uncertainty in service times, try to achieve both high utilization of expensive medical equipment and personnel as well as short waiting time for patients, has long been an interesting and challenging problem in health care. We consider a robust version of the appointment scheduling problem, introduced by Mittal et al.\ (2014), with the goal of finding simple and easy-to-use algorithms. Previous work focused on the special case where per-unit costs due to under-utilization of equipment/personnel are homogeneous i.e., costs are linear and identical. We consider the heterogeneous case and devise an LP that has a simple closed-form solution. This solution yields the first constant-factor approximation for the problem. We also find special cases beyond homogeneous costs where the LP leads to closed form optimal schedules. Our approach and results extend more generally to convex piece-wise linear costs. For the case where the order of patients is changeable, we focus on linear costs and show that the problem is strongly NP-hard when the under-utilization costs are heterogeneous. For changeable order with homogeneous under-utilization costs, it was previously shown that an EPTAS exists. We instead find an extremely simple, ratio-based ordering that is 1.0604 approximate.

title: Accounting for Irregular State Transitions through Belief Estimation in Online Medical Consultation
abstract: While online medical consultation broadens access, unprompted patient disclosures and topic shifts frequently disrupt clinician inquiry, leaving clinical states progressively revealed. We characterize these dynamics using both existing evaluation metrics and task-specific interaction metrics designed in this work. Through an empirical study across 16 medical dialogue datasets, we show that authentic online interactions exhibit substantially lower contextual continuity and higher unpredictability than offline and simulated benchmarks. We propose PRISM (Policy Reasoning with Inferred States for Medicine), a framework inspired by partially observable Markov decision processes that decouples latent state estimation from action selection to address drifting dialogue trajectories. Specifically, PRISM factorizes clinical triage into belief estimation, policy optimization, and response realization. By maintaining an evolving posterior belief over consultation states and conditioning action selection on the maximum a posteriori state, PRISM advances clinical goals while accommodating patient-initiated shifts. Extensive evaluations show that PRISM substantially outperforms frontier LLMs and clinical agents, achieving a 22.40 percentage point gain in clinical decision accuracy alongside decisive improvements in response generation, surpassing the strongest baseline by 5.51 points in BERTScore_F1. Furthermore, ablation studies show that providing oracle consultation states consistently boosts response quality across all evaluated baselines by guiding their action reasoning, yielding average gains of 5.58 points in BERTScore_F1.
authors: Mingzhe Lu;Xiangru Chen;Jian Qin;Yunpeng Li;Xihan Gao

title: Dynamically defined bulges reveal that early-type galaxies with compact bulges host more massive black holes
abstract: We revisit the $M_{BH}-M_{bulge}$ relation for early-type galaxies by introducing a uniform bulge defined by dynamical decomposition. From the set of nearby galaxies with accurately measured black hole masses, we select 30 early-type galaxies that have been observed with wide-field integral-field unit instruments (MUSE, ATLAS3D, or PPAK). For each galaxy, we construct an orbit-superposition Schwarzschild model and obtain its stellar orbit distribution. In this framework, we define the bulge uniformly as comprising stellar orbits with circularity $λ_z < 0.7$ (or, in an alternative definition, $λ_z < 0.2$) and lying within $r < 3$ kpc. From these orbits, we reconstruct the spatial density distribution of the bulge and measure its mass ($M_{bulge}$), size ($R_{bulge}$) and surface density slope ($γ_{bulge}$). We find that the dynamical bulge defined by $λ_z < 0.7$ yields masses that are systematically consistent with the photometric bulge masses. Comparing to the bulge from photometric decomposition, using this dynamical bulge definition slightly decreases the scatter around the best-fitting from 0.56 to 0.47. More interestingly, we identify a clear trend: at a given bulge mass, galaxies hosting more compact bulges (i.e. smaller bulge sizes or steeper bulge density slopes) systematically contain more massive black holes; eight outliers show overmassive BHs together with ultra-compact bulges. We interpret this as direct observational evidence that the $M_{BH}-M_{bulge}$ relation evolves over a galaxy's merger history, with that history imprinted in bulge compactness. Incorporating compactness via an $M_{BH}-M_{bulge}-R_{e, bulge}$ (or $γ_{bulge}$) relation brings the outliers into agreement and reduces the overall scatter of the sample to $\sim 0.3$.
authors: Hanjing Shi;Ling Zhu;Sabine Thater;Yong Shi;Ana L. Chies-Santos;Luis Gabriel Dahmer Hahn;Zhengya Zheng

title: See, Think, Use: Diagnosing Perception and Reasoning Failures in VLMs
abstract: We present See, Think, Use, a protocol that traces each answer of a vision-language model to perception, reasoning or the use of perception. The diagnosis shows a developer which stage to improve and directs test-time compute to the stage that fails. Benchmarks score the final answer, and an answer that rests on the image earns the same credit as a guess or a memorized prior. The protocol asks the model two extra questions per item and needs no access to its weights. A localization probe asks for a box around every instance and measures seeing, and a text-replacement probe answers from a description and measures thinking. Use is the rate at which the answer follows the model's own perception across counterfactual image pairs. The rate needs no answer labels, because the question and its prior are the same on both images. On two model families and six datasets the protocol shows that the knob that helps follows the task family. Answers follow the model's perception except on images that contradict a common prior, and asking the model to localize first repairs this failure when its boxes are right. Allocating compute by the measured stages comes close to the best uniform policy at lower cost and beats a random allocation of the same compute wherever a knob raises the short stage. We will release the code, the prompts and the per-question outputs.
comment: The authors request withdrawal of this preprint. The manuscript has been substantially revised for submission to a conference, and this early version no longer reflects the scope and content of the current work

title: Can Large Language Model Agents Learn by Watching Tutorial Videos?
abstract: Humans continuously acquire knowledge from carefully crafted materials such as books and tutorial videos, carrying that understanding into future tasks. Millions of such instructional videos are uploaded online every day, yet LLM agents remain unable to exploit this ever-expanding wealth of human teaching. Their capabilities are frozen after training, while parameter updates at scale remain prohibitively expensive. This raises the central question: can LLM agents learn from this vast instructional resource without parameter updates? We introduce Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL), a nonparametric continual-learning paradigm that consolidates tutorial videos into a persistent, structured tutorialbook memory through a two-stage adversarial process that harvests hard, video-grounded questions and uses them to refine the memory. At inference time, TAL retrieves through a Table-of-Contents (TOC) tree, tying retrieval directly to the model's reasoning rather than to embedding similarity. To study this setting, we introduce VidLearn, a multimodal QA benchmark built from 72 chess tutorial videos spanning 12 openings. On VidLearn, TAL outperforms all evaluated baselines and improves monotonically as more videos are consumed, achieving up to 113% and 91% relative gains over the corresponding vanilla MLLMs on the training and test splits, respectively. In actual gameplay, TAL reaches a stronger opening-phase position than its vanilla counterpart in 69% of head-to-head games. Evaluation in a second domain further demonstrates the generality of TAL. Together, these results highlight instructional videos as a scalable resource for parameter-update-free agent continual learning.

title: Correctness and Predictive Uncertainty in Bayesian TSK Fuzzy Regression: A Reproducible Evaluation on Tabular and Building-Meter Data
abstract: Uncertainty estimates from fuzzy regression are informative only when the implementation is correct and the comparison protocol makes the sources of variation visible. We revisit a first-order Takagi--Sugeno--Kang (TSK) regression implementation and rebuild its dense, conjugate Bayesian, BIC-based, and rule-level spike-and-slab estimators using corrected code. The corrected pipeline freezes the Gaussian membership partition at training time, uses a scaled conjugate prior, evaluates firing strengths in the log domain, and reports direct posterior-predictive quantiles for Bayesian methods. Across 30 outer 80/20 splits on three targets from two UCI regression datasets, corrected TSK-LS obtains $R^2=0.957$, $0.923$, and $0.786$ on Energy-Heating, Energy-Cooling, and Concrete, respectively; rule-level Gibbs sampling with Bayesian model averaging obtains $0.957$, $0.922$, and $0.784$. We then evaluate the same workflow on a bounded chronological sample of the Building Data Genome 2 meter data that covers 158 buildings across 17 sites. In a common-unit evaluation, every method is scored on the same 47,400 test rows and every trained model uses 94,800 train--validation rows. Persistence has RMSE $27.710$, compared with $29.083$ for both TSK-LS and Bayesian TSK; the pre-specified building-level mean RMSE difference between Bayesian TSK and persistence is $+0.0447$ with a 95% site-cluster bootstrap interval of $[-1.5536,1.5665]$. The Bayesian TSK 90% intervals have PICP $0.980$ and MPIW $116.469$. Taken together, the evidence supports a narrower conclusion: spike-and-slab model averaging is a reproducible implementation option, but it does not provide a demonstrated accuracy or calibration advantage across the tested tabular and building-meter settings.

title: Dual Path Following for an Aerial Manipulator Under State and Input Constraints via Transverse Feedback Linearization
abstract: This paper studies dual path following for a quadrotor carrying a three-degree-of-freedom arm. The center of mass of the combined system must follow a vehicle path and the end effector must follow a second path, while the arm respects its joint limits and avoids its singular postures. The vehicle and the arm are mechanically coupled, so one controller must handle both paths. With the center of mass and the end-effector path coordinates as outputs, and a dynamic extension of the thrust, the system admits a normal form without internal dynamics. We characterize the states where this normal form fails. We formulate the transverse feedback linearizing controller as a quadratic program that relaxes only the speed of the end effector along its path and imposes safety and actuator limits as inequality constraints. The program reduces to a scalar problem with a closed-form solution. If it remains strictly feasible for all time, the feedback is locally Lipschitz, both paths are invariant and attractive, and every constraint holds. In the physics engine Drake, the controller resolves a conflict between the two speed references by slowing the end effector while both paths remain invariant. By contrast, a cascade with a safety filter leaves both paths. Code and animations are available at https://gradslab.github.io/am_dual_pf-/

title: Transport for Conditional Sampling: Foundations and Applications
abstract: Conditional sampling is central to Bayesian inference, generative modeling, and causal inference: given a joint law for random variables $X$ and $Y$ and an observation $Y=y$, one seeks to sample from the conditional law of $X\mid Y=y$. Even when the joint distribution is accurately represented, this task can be computationally difficult as it may require evaluating intractable normalizing constants or solving a new inference problem for each observation. Measure transport provides an approach to this problem by identifying a map with triangular structure that directly pushes forward a reference to the conditional of a joint distribution for any observation. This article reviews the theoretical, methodological, and algorithmic foundations of triangular transports, with the Knothe-Rosenblatt rearrangement as a canonical construction. We discuss methods for estimating triangular maps from finite samples, as well as their use in simulation-based inference and causal inference. While our primary aim is to review existing formulations, we also present new ideas and open questions for conditional sampling using transport.

title: Boson sampling is fragile to loss
abstract: Boson sampling experiments aim to demonstrate quantum computational advantage with increasing numbers of interfering photons. A central question is whether their computational hardness survives under photon loss. We show that even an arbitrarily small nonzero uniform loss rate permits efficient classical sampling in the average case when the rate remains fixed as the system grows. We exploit how loss suppresses correlations involving many photons to approximate the full output distribution using low correlation orders. The resulting samplers run in time polynomial in system size and inverse total variation error, with the error averaged over Haar random interferometers. The results apply to Fock state boson sampling with single-photon states in distinct input modes and arbitrary additional vacuum inputs, and to Gaussian boson sampling with equal squeezing of bounded strength in every input mode. Classical sampling is efficient even when the mean detected photon number grows linearly with system size, showing that large photon counts alone do not ensure computational hardness.

title: Variational learning of energy-stable macroscopic flow equations from microscopic laws
abstract: We present a generalized variational approach for constructing energy-stable macroscopic partial differential equations (PDEs) directly from microscopic physical laws. Rather than fitting the PDE evolution for prescribed variables from macroscopic trajectories, we construct an extendable variational structure by adjoining auxiliary variables to seek autonomous reduced dynamics in an enlarged state space. By defining these variables as micro--macro encoders with explicit microscopic counterparts, we cast the learning problem as the sample-wise joint identification of the reduced state representation and the variational ingredients from time-discrete data, enabling systematic law-level transfer across scales. The resulting PDEs preserve frame indifference, physical constraints, and energy stability by construction, and admit a fluctuation--dissipation-consistent stochastic extension. Numerical results for the non-Newtonian hydrodynamics of polymeric fluids show that the learned models capture the viscoelastic responses induced by nonlinear and heterogeneous molecular interactions beyond empirical closures.

title: Longest-Queue Policies in Dynamic Matching with Abandonments
abstract: We study a dynamic two-way matching market in which agents of heterogeneous types arrive over time, wait to be matched according to a compatibility network, and abandon the system if their random patience expires. The decision maker collects match rewards and pays holding and abandonment costs, and seeks to maximize the expected net value over a finite horizon. We evaluate policies by their approximation ratio against a fluid benchmark, the optimal value of a linear-programming relaxation that upper bounds the expected net value of every policy. Under a general position gap (GPG) condition, which requires the unique optimal dual solution of this linear program to remain optimal under small perturbations of the arrival rates, we propose a longest-queue policy. The policy first uses this dual solution to identify a set of good match types and a set of critical agent types. Upon each arrival, it considers only good matches and matches the arrival to the critical partner with the longest queue subject to availabilities. In the high-volume regime, in which arrival rates are scaled by s, we prove that the policy attains an approximation ratio of at least 1-O(1/s) at every scale s >= 1 and every horizon T >= 1, so the ratio tends to 1 as s goes to infinity.

title: When Should an Agent Refresh? Adaptive Index Reuse for Efficient Long-Horizon Reasoning
abstract: Language agents read code, tool output, and dialogue in contexts that grow at every step. Dynamic sparse attention lets a small indexer choose the earlier tokens each query attends to, but the indexer still scores the whole prefix at every layer. Cross-layer reuse methods such as IndexCache rerun the indexer at only some layers, with one fixed pattern for every input. In an agent, the relevant evidence can change abruptly when a traceback or test result arrives, so fresh selections matter more at some steps than at others. We propose Adaptive Index Reuse (AIR), which keeps IndexCache's execution and learns, for each segment of an agent episode, how many layers refresh their selection. A small controller reads signals from completed computation and the latest tool event, chooses a pattern from a nested library, and learns from terminal task reward under an expected compute budget. On Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with a 128K context, AIR improves success over the strongest static schedule at matched cost on SWE-bench Verified (27.0% to 32.4%), Terminal-Bench 2.0, and three $τ^2$-bench domains, and it lowers time per successful task on all five. Across 50 backbone, context, and benchmark settings, it matches or exceeds that schedule in 44.

title: Towards Fine-grained and Robust Detection of Human-AI Co-authorship
abstract: The widespread adoption of large language models (LLMs) is reshaping how textual content is produced, complicating text provenance, and raising concerns for misinformation, plagiarism, and intellectual property. While prior work on AI-generated text detection has progressed, one-dimensional human-AI co-authorship scores lack signals directly relevant to ``AI involvement''. It remains unclear how adversarial paraphrasing distorts detection signals. In this work, we formulate a discrete-class text provenance detection framework. This framework allows an abstraction of realistic co-authorship scenarios into distinct degrees of AI involvement, differentiating the AI polishing on the surface level from the AI updating the discourse structures. This framework reveals the mechanisms of how adversarial paraphrasing blurs the decision boundaries for co-authorship detectors. To improve robustness of the detectors, we augment training data with adversarial paraphrases generated by the state-of-the-art paraphrasing attack model, exposing detectors to challenging meaning-preserving rewrites. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and generation models demonstrate that adversarial paraphrasing substantially degrades detectors trained only on benign data, while adversarial data augmentation leads to consistent robustness gains and good cross-generator transferability. Overall, our findings highlight the value of discrete-class formulation and principled data augmentation for building reliable detectors of human-AI co-authorship.
authors: Ziruo Zhao;Jie Fu;Wendy Hui Wang;Zining Zhu

title: FlyWheel: Attention Kernels Built for the TPU
abstract: Attention kernels on Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) often underutilize their matrix units (MXUs) because of repeated matrix operand loads, vector-intensive computation, and dependencies that leave MXUs idle. We present FlyWheel, a set of fast TPU kernels for both softmax and linear attention. FlyWheel reformulates softmax and triangular inversion to reduce vector work, while coordinating data layouts to improve matrix operand reuse. It then overlaps independent computation to hide execution latency. We apply these techniques to both softmax attention and Gated DeltaNet on TPU v6e and v7x. FlyWheel speeds up softmax attention by up to $4.14\times$ over the state-of-the-art RPA kernel and $1.80\times$ over Splash Attention, reaching 81% of peak BF16 throughput on v6e. It also speeds up Gated DeltaNet prefill by up to $3.61\times$. Integrated into vLLM serving Qwen3.8-27B, FlyWheel improves prefill throughput by up to $1.56\times$ while maintaining comparable accuracy.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Joint Generative Modeling of Fault Event Sequences and Sensor Time Series in Solar PV Plants
abstract: This paper presents a multimodal generative model designed to simulate a solar energy plant system for predictive maintenance and fault prediction. We propose a novel approach to enhance system generation through conditional generation by leveraging both event sequences and time-series data and improve next event prediction. The framework employs a Transformer Hawkes Process (THP) to encode event data and an iTransformer to encode time-series data, integrated via a co-attention mechanism that effectively captures cross-modal dependencies between discrete events and continuous signals. From these integrated representations, we employ two specialized decoders for simulation: a Conditional Latent Diffusion Model (CLDM) for modeling future sensor trajectories and the Score Matching-based UnceRtainty quantiFication for Transformer Hawkes Process (SMURF-THP) for high-fidelity event prediction. This dual-decoder strategy supports uncertainty-aware, history-conditioned simulation by rolling the model forward for a specified number of generation iterations, producing finite stochastic scenarios rather than deterministic extrapolations over the full observational record. Evaluated on a comprehensive dataset from the Red Rock Solar Site in Arizona, our approach improves aggregate event-prediction F1 relative to baselines and supports applications in predictive maintenance, fault detection, and energy optimization for solar power systems.
