title: LF-VideoQA: Evaluating Long-Video Understanding with Long-Form Theory-of-Mind Questions
abstract: The hardest part of understanding a long video is not pinpointing any one moment but synthesizing many, e.g., answering a question that requires tracking what develops across hours of content and articulating how the pieces fit together. To date, most long-video QA datasets require only a short answer or a multiple-choice selection, oversimplifying the long-video understanding task to retrieval. We introduce LF-VideoQA, a dataset for long-form, open-ended question answering over long narrative videos built on theory-of-mind questions: a character's belief depends on everything they have seen or been told, so each question demands assembling and reasoning from evidence distributed across the video. The dataset contains more than 6,300 questions on 94 recent films; each requires reasoning over scenes spanning an average of 23 minutes and comes with a question-specific rubric for recall and precision scoring. The dataset is created entirely automatically by annotating screenplays with scene events and each character's first-order beliefs and meta-beliefs, then generating (question, answer, rubric) triples through LLM-based question generation and verification; human studies validate their quality. We evaluate four families of state-of-the-art open-source VLMs across three settings and find the task highly challenging: (i) even an oracle with access to the screenplay falls well short of complete answers; (ii) the best non-oracle model attains barely half of the recall level of the oracle; (iii) unlike on prior long-video benchmarks, captions and subtitles underperform the video itself, indicating that the questions need visual evidence; and (iv) recall is the predominant bottleneck, with answers omitting many required rubric claims.
authors: Shaden Shaar;Bradon Thymes;Majd Aldaye;Claire Cardie;Bharath Hariharan

title: Dysfunctional Functionals and their Therapies in Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory
abstract: The exchange-correlation functional in Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory (TDDFT) is known to have dependence on past densities and initial states, and yet this memory-dependence is ignored in practical calculations which almost always use an adiabatic approximation. We discuss the dysfunction that arises due to this deficiency and point to therapies that go beyond the adiabatic approximation. Still, adiabatic TDDFT has had success in a wide range of systems for response properties and for fully non-equilibrium dynamics, and why this is so is only partially understood. This, together with the rigorous foundation of the exact theory and its favorable system-size scaling, provides tremendous impetus for continuing to strive towards improved approximations to the exact functionals, and a deeper understanding of the impact of approximations in applications.

title: Unlearning by Extrapolating a Shrink-and-Heal Lookahead
abstract: Unlearning aims to make a large language model behave like one retrained without its forget set. Prevailing likelihood-suppression objectives, however, lack an explicit forgetting target: they continually reward lower forget-set likelihood, making forgetting sensitive to the optimization budget. We address this limitation by estimating the direction toward the oracle without training it. Our key idea is to shrink the fine-tuned model toward its pre-fine-tuning weights and briefly re-learn the retain set, thereby removing the forget-specific contribution; in the linearized regime, this shrink-and-heal lookahead moves the model a fixed fraction of the way to the retrained model, its unique fixed point. Our method, SHIFT, extrapolates the lookahead's per-token changes into distillation targets and iteratively refines them. Evaluated against eleven baselines under a unified OpenUnlearning protocol, SHIFT achieves the highest aggregate score across all TOFU settings and the closest oracle alignment, 3.7x closer on average than the next-best method; on MUSE, it preserves the most retain knowledge. Under larger optimization budgets, baselines overshoot the oracle, while SHIFT remains near it, even under relearning attacks.

title: Modeling CO Line Luminosity with FIRE simulations: II. Comparison With Observations, CO Luminosity Functions and Redshift Evolution
abstract: We present predictions for the CO(1-0) and CO(2-1) luminosities of 765, 850, 887 and 915 galaxies at z=0, 1, 2 and 3, respectively, drawn from the Feedback in Realistic Environments (FIRE-2) simulations and post-processed with SKIRT radiative transfer and CLOUDY line emission calculations. We compare our CO line luminosity predictions with existing observations. At z=0, our predictions reproduce the observed scatter and mean relation between star formation rate (SFR) and CO(1-0) luminosity for both massive star-forming galaxies and low-metallicity dwarf galaxies. We also reproduce the observed superlinear power-law slope between CO(1-0) luminosity and metallicity. At z=1, our CO(2-1) predictions scatter to much lower luminosities than observed, which likely reflects the limited sensitivity of current surveys. At fixed SFR, our CO(1-0) luminosities decrease by roughly an order of magnitude per unit increase in redshift. This decline is likely driven by the decrease in metallicity with increasing redshift, since FIRE-2 galaxies with comparable SFR and metallicity produce similar CO(1-0) luminosities regardless of redshift. At fixed stellar mass, the predicted luminosities show no redshift dependence. These results show that our FIRE-2 predictions reproduce the observed scaling relations between CO(1-0) luminosity and galaxy properties wherever the observed galaxies are robustly detected. This gives us confidence in our predictions for the regime where no observational data exist, and suggests that our luminosity predictions can be used to build predictive models for CO line intensity mapping experiments.
authors: Doğa Tolgay;J. Richard Bond;Norman W. Murray;Dongwoo Chung;Robert Feldmann;Andrew Wetzel

title: Humanized but Still True? Auditing Facts and Detection in AI-Text Humanizers
abstract: AI "humanizers" rewrite machine-generated text so that detectors classify it as human-written. Public leaderboards score evasion and embedding similarity, but not whether checkable details survive. We check whether numbers, dates, person and organization names, and quoted spans survive each rewrite, using a rule-based checker validated by two AI annotators (precision 0.84-1.00, recall 0.93-0.95; no human annotation). In the October 2026 cycle of a public humanizer leaderboard, all 11 commercial tools changed or dropped at least one of these units in 35-65% of the documents that contained one. Most changes were to quoted spans; counting numbers and names alone, 10 of the 11 tools still altered at least one in 20% or more of the documents. The September 2026 cycle was similar (19-50%). An open 12B humanizer kept at least 97% of numbers and names in fact-dense U.S. federal agency text, but reworded 67-78% of the quoted spans, against its own prompt. Unit retention and detector evasion were not clearly related across tools (Spearman rho = -0.46, 95% CI -0.65 to 0.08), and the open model's four released files (two of them quantization-aware low-bit files) did not show the pre-registered monotone trade-off. On federal texts with matched human, AI-styled and humanized versions, a general-purpose decision model, Jev, asked a single zero-shot question, separated human originals from humanized rewrites with AUROC 0.864 (0.827-0.902), 0.18-0.22 higher than Binoculars, Fast-DetectGPT and the adversarially trained RADAR, while calling 24% of the human originals AI at a 0.5 threshold. On the AI-styled rewrites by 2026 models, both perplexity-based detectors scored below chance (AUROC 0.37 and 0.39), also with line breaks removed. Hypotheses, data rules and analyses were frozen before the main runs; two earlier data contacts are disclosed. We release the checker and the per-item results.
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/zwang-devv/humanizer-fact-audit

title: Cross-Prompt Reuse of Entity-Replacement Responses
abstract: With model weights fixed, we measure how much of an entity-replacement response transfers between English factual questions, beyond whether answers change. We add the hidden-state change from two source questions to a target question about the same entity, comparing the predicted log-probability shift between two relations' published answers, given known answer prefixes, with the measured one. Hidden reuse injects the aligned change at 50% depth before the target's remaining layers; direct reuse adds source output-score changes. With other-relation sources, hidden reuse removes 45% and 49% of no-change error on 0.5-1B Qwen and Llama. Gemma-2-2B removes 22% and passes one of three comparisons in plain text without its default beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token. A later protocol restoring it yields 58-68%, passing every comparison on three cohorts. Larger checkpoints, chat format and new entities show replication and format- or cohort-dependent failures. On small plain-format checkpoints, other-relation hidden reuse mainly reproduces the shift both relations' questions share, without reliably lowering relation-selective error. With target-relation sources, hidden reuse's post hoc advantage over direct reuse is 0.2-0.9 nats outside chat format, unconfirmed and not replacement-specific. The same relation-neutral change at both questions' entity tokens lowers relation-selective error more than random or other-replacement changes, indicating receiving-question dependence.

title: Robustness of Median-based Splitting Rules for Causal Trees
abstract: Causal forests (Athey and Imbens, 2016) are a widely used method for the estimation of heterogeneous treatment effects. Standard implementations use mean-based splitting criteria, which perform well when the outcome distribution is well-behaved and free of contamination, such as outliers or heavy tails. However, real-world data are rarely clean. Outcome perturbations can affect the tree structure selected by mean-based splitting rules and lead to unreliable treatment effect estimates. In this study, we systematically examine the robustness of causal forests to irregularities in the outcome distribution. Building on the median-based splitting criteria introduced by Maßmann and Gliszczyńska-Schroeder (2026), we empirically investigate three median-based splitting criteria: Median Absolute Deviation (MAD), Least Median of Squares (LMS), and Median Squared Deviation (MSD). We conduct Monte Carlo experiments and apply the methods to empirical benchmark datasets from the causal inference literature to compare the performance of the median-based approaches with standard causal forests. We additionally examine pointwise confidence interval coverage using the Bootstrap of Little Bags and the infinitesimal jackknife. The results indicate that median-based splitting criteria can reduce sensitivity to outcome irregularities in specific scenarios, particularly in the presence of extreme heavy-tailed noise and nonlinear treatment effect heterogeneity. However, these benefits are scenario-dependent and do not consistently lead to more accurate conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimates.

title: Queering the Audits: Community-Based Auditing of AI Harms to Queer Communities
abstract: AI systems embed majority-group defaults into training data, evaluation metrics, and category definitions, producing documented harms for queer communities including erasure, misclassification, and discrimination. Standard technical audits often rely on aggregate measures and cannot detect harms that be come visible only through the lived experience of affected communities. We conducted a participatory auditing workshop at EurIPS 2025 where 16 queer community members audited four case studies using the 4Cs harm taxonomy (Content, Conduct, Contact, Contract) applied across the AI lifecycle. Participants used structured worksheets and plenary synthesis to classify harms and trace them to their origins in the development pipeline. Across all four cases, participants traced harms to problem definition and data collection, and they identified contractual structures that extract value from vulnerable populations while providing minimal recourse. These findings illustrate that community-informed auditing surfaces concrete, identity-specific harms that aggregate evaluation methods risk overlooking.

title: SPARK: Self-Correcting Embodied Memory via Physical Re-Observation
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems have seen growing adoption in embodied settings as language-queryable memories of the environment. However, existing approaches often assume a reliable single-episode knowledge base (KB) or accumulate observations across episodes without correcting prior errors. Such errors can persist through incorrect semantic labels, inaccurate object positions, and inconsistent spatial relationships. To address this, we present SPARK, a corrective multi-episode framework for embodied RAG. After the first episode, a semantic critic flags regions of the KB, a targeted planner generates revisits, and a selective merge adds, removes, or replaces KB information based on the new observations. We evaluate SPARK on four outdoor AirSim maps under two degraded viewpoint conditions, using perception-built KBs, a visibility-constrained oracle used only for evaluation, and a fixed set of 158 embodied question answering (EQA) questions scored before and after correction. A single corrective episode improves downstream EQA on every map under both conditions while storing 13-41% fewer objects than append-only updating, with gains up to 2.7x on one map-condition pair. Extending correction through Episode 4 brings every map above the EQA performance of its undegraded reference. Ablations show that the critic's three signals each contribute to performance, that targeted revisits achieve a larger mean gain than untargeted ones under the same budget, and that selective merging achieves gains comparable to append-only updating with a smaller KB. Overall, SPARK demonstrates the value of correcting embodied memory through targeted re-observation, particularly as embodied systems scale and the risk of accumulated errors increases.

title: Reading the Count: Prediction Markets and Brazil's 2026 Presidential Election
abstract: We rebuild the public count of Brazil's 2026 presidential runoff minute by minute from the electoral court's section-level records and compare it with every trade on Kalshi and Polymarket. A projection published live on the night gave the eventual winner, Lula, a probability of 0.998 from 19:15, with 1.6% of sections counted. The markets reached 0.9 at 20:24, with 46% counted. Read as the projection's central estimate with a wider uncertainty, their prices imply a standard deviation of the final margin about four times the live projection's, and about twice that of a section-level projection calibrated on the 2018 runoff, the earlier night with the largest errors. Valued at these projections, takers' purchases of Lula after the count resumed had an expected profit of 4 to 18 cents per Kalshi contract after fees; valued at a state-level extrapolation of the count, it was zero. During a two-hour suspension of the count the markets gave Lula 0.25 to 0.44, below every reading we compute afterwards from the sections then public, none of which was available live. On the first-round night, when the headline count showed the eventual leader ahead from its first file, the same markets were faster than our projection.
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Code and results in the ancillary files

title: The L1157 filament as traced in HNCO by the LMT
abstract: Context. The L1157 outflow is a prototype of chemically active outflows where to look for molecular species linked to complex chemistry. Aims. With the aim of imaging the large (parsec) scale structure of key prebiotic molecules, we have mapped the whole blue-lobe of the L1157 outflow with the Large Millimeter Telescope (LMT), proving the potential of this facility to detect weak and extended molecular emission. Methods. Isocyanic acid, HNCO, an important precursor of complex chemistry, was chosen to be observed in its (4_0,4-3_0-3) transition at 87.925 GHz with the SEQUOIA focal-plane array, covering an area of 3x3 arcmin2 centered at the position of the main shock L1157-B1, which included a large portion of the vicinity of the protostellar region. Results. The HNCO emission was detected not only from the outflow but it also was found tracing a structure of about 0.3 pc in length, corresponding to the filament from which the protostellar system was born. Conclusions. The HNCO molecule was found to be a tracer of the densest part of filaments in molecular clouds, and given its importance in the formation of more complex molecules, its presence in the cold, quiescent filamentary gas indicates that the building blocks of complex chemistry are already well established in stages prior to protostellar warming or shocks. By allowing the detection of structures related with the filament, these observations proved the LMT potentialities to map weak and extended components in molecular clouds.
authors: A. I. Gómez-Ruiz;C. Codella;O. S. Rojas-García;R. Bachiller;D. Sánchez-Arguelles;M. Chavez Dagostino;G. Narayanan;A. Batta;V. Gómez-Rivera;I. Rodríguez-Montoya;E. E. Martínez-García;R. Naranjo-Romero

title: Optimistic Gradient Algorithms with Randomized Coordinate and Variance Reduction Strategies for Composite Inclusions
abstract: In this paper, we consider a class of possibly nonmonotone finite-sum composite inclusions in which evaluating all components or updating all coordinates at every iteration can be computationally expensive. We develop two optimistic gradient frameworks that combine variance reduction with randomized block-coordinate updates. The first framework applies under a blockwise average Lipschitz continuity condition and the existence of a weak-Minty solution. It achieves an $\mathcal{O}(1/k)$ convergence rate for the expected squared residual, and its iterates converge almost surely under mild additional conditions. The second framework relies on a backward-forward reformulation under average co-coercivity and co-hypomonotonicity. It achieves faster $\mathcal{O}(1/k^2)$ and $o(1/k^2)$ rates for the expected squared residual, as well as $o(1/k^2)$ almost-sure rates. For both frameworks, we provide a generic condition on the stochastic estimator that covers mini-batch, loopless SVRG, and a generalized JacSketch-type estimator, and we derive the corresponding oracle complexities under importance-based block sampling. In particular, in highly heterogeneous regimes, the L-SVRG and JacSketch variants attain $\mathcal{O}\big(n + n^{2/3}ε^{-2}\big)$ and $\mathcal{O}\big(n + n^{2/3}ε^{-1}\big)$ oracle complexities for the nonaccelerated and accelerated methods, respectively. Numerical experiments illustrate the effects of variance reduction and block-coordinate sampling, and compare the proposed methods with existing baselines.

title: One Waveform, Two Stories: Benchmarking Speech-Acoustic Conflict in Audio-Language Models
abstract: Audio-language models (ALMs) are evaluated on their understanding of both speech and environmental sounds. What remains underexplored is how they respond when spoken claims contradict acoustic evidence within the same recording. We introduce SAC-Bench, a benchmark of intra-audio speech--acoustic conflict comprising 616,031 unique clips from 188 sound-event classes across seven semantic, temporal, and spatial tasks. It pairs environmental recordings with compatible or contradictory synthesized spoken claims and includes audio-only controls where applicable. Across five open-weight ALMs evaluated on semantic and temporal tasks, high audio-only accuracy often coexists with large losses under conflicting claims; Event Identity accuracy is 24.8--46.5 percentage points lower in conflict than compatible conditions. Temporal Order failures persist even when speech follows the complete event sequence, so simultaneous speech--event masking cannot fully explain them. A spatial case study with Spatial-Omni finds lower motion accuracy associated with both spoken claims and the speech source's physical trajectory. Prompt interventions sometimes restore acoustic accuracy, but can also reduce claim-aligned answers without improving grounding or worsen performance. SAC-Bench thus separates acoustic competence, conflict robustness, and intervention effects.

title: GAVAGAI: Referential Alignment for Infant-Scale Vision-Language Models via Balanced Optimal Transport
abstract: A child learns which words name which things from roughly 100 million words of input. Vision-language models trained at a comparable scale bind words to referents far less reliably, and we argue that part of the gap is structural: the usual next-token captioning objective has no variable standing for "this word refers to that region," so training applies no direct pressure to ground words. We add such a variable by treating each scene as a small assignment problem between the content words heard and the regions seen, solved as entropic optimal transport under two constraints. First, a word may be assigned to a special NOTHING column instead of any region, which matters because most content words in caregiver speech do not name anything visible. Second, no region may receive more than a bounded share of the assignment mass, a capacity constraint that encodes mutual exclusivity. The alignment step costs about eight Sinkhorn iterations, small next to the vision encoder. In controlled simulation, the naive version of the idea, a row-wise softmax that forces every word onto some region, collapses to 0.000 word-to-picture accuracy under realistic non-reference rates, below the 0.058 of captioning alone, while our two constraints reach 0.075 in that regime and 0.700 on clean input. A one-parameter version of the model reproduces adult cross-situational learning accuracy across three ambiguity conditions (RMSE 0.024). On the SAYCam infant video corpus, adding the alignment loss to a next-token captioning model raises word-to-picture accuracy from 32.4% to 48.7% and localization IoU from 0.18 to 0.38. A contrastive model trained on the same child's data remains stronger on its own benchmark, so our claim is that the loss improves a captioning objective under high non-reference rates, not that it sets a new best.

title: Variance-reduced First-order Methods for Finite-sum Function Constrained Convex Optimization
abstract: This paper studies finite-sum convex optimization with convex function constraints, where both the objective $f(x)=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x)$ and the constraint mapping $g(x)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n g_j(x)$ may have a large number of components. We propose a variance-reduced anchored constraint extrapolation method (VaRAn-ConEx), which combines stochastic component sampling with primal--dual extrapolation for nonlinear function constraints. Relative to stochastic approximation schemes such as ConEx, VaRAn-ConEx~method reduces gradient complexity by using epoch-wise full-gradient correction and variance-reduced estimators for both the objective and constraint components. In the semi-finite case where $n=1$, the method attains gradient complexities $O(\sqrt m/ε)$ under constant steps and $O(m/ε^{1/2}+1/ε^{3/2})$ under nonconstant steps. In the fully finite-sum case, we establish boundedness of the Lagrange multiplier sequence and derive convergence and gradient-complexity bounds for constant and nonconstant step-size policies. Under these policies, we then prove similar gradient complexity with $m$ replaced by $\max\{m,n\}$. We also show acceleration when the finite-sum objective $f$ is strongly convex, irrespective of components $f_i$.

title: Decentralized Multi-Agent Coordination and Communication in Shared Codebases
abstract: Coding agents working in shared repositories may receive separate, independently-motivated requests from human developers, creating a setting that is multi-agent by necessity. When this scenario happens, their individual implementations may work separately but conflict when combined. To study this setting, we introduce ParallACT, a benchmark of orchestrator-free multi-agent coding tasks. ParallACT contains both complementary and contradictory tasks. In complementary tasks, each agent's task is separately useful and implementations must share an interface to be productively combined. In contradictory pairs, both agents' tasks require editing the same code in incompatible ways, and naively combining independent solutions fails to produce a useful implementation. We compare a single-agent oracle given the combined set of tasks against multi-agent settings that vary execution order, visibility, awareness of other agents, and access to a communication channel. We find that the oracle solves most tasks while parallel agents perform substantially worse. Their performance drop is notable for complementary tasks, and particularly sharp for contradictory tasks (e.g., from 62% to 16% for Claude Code with Claude Opus 4.8) where merged code typically satisfies only one specification, and the same gap appears in all six further configurations pairing two agent harnesses with three open-weight models. Simply telling an agent that a peer exists does not help significantly, and giving agents access to a communication channel recovers only a small part of the performance, at an additional token cost. ParallACT thus identifies and isolates a core challenge that will become more common as multi-agent coding by independent principals becomes standard, and provides a controlled test of which coordination strategies help, and at what cost.
authors: Rishabh Mediratta;Lingyun Xiao;Peter Stone;Joydeep Biswas;Elias Stengel-Eskin

title: Evidence for topological flat band magnetism in Co$_3$Sn$_2$S$_2$
abstract: Correlations and topology are central pillars in the study of emergent electronic phases. Topological flat bands near the Fermi level unite these concepts, providing a route towards correlated topological phenomena and unconventional magnetism. Despite theoretical predictions, momentum-resolved observation of a topological flat band at the Fermi level has remained elusive. Using angle resolved photoemission spectroscopy, we observe a flat band at the Fermi level within the topologically non-trivial electronic structure of the magnetic kagome Weyl semimetal Co$_3$Sn$_2$S$_2$. We further uncover a strong temperature dependence in which the flat band shifts across the Fermi level, accompanied by a reconstruction of the Fermi surface. Strikingly, this evolution occurs on the same temperature scale as previously reported anomalies in the magnetic response. Together, these results provide evidence for topological flat band magnetism in Co$_3$Sn$_2$S$_2$, establishing a microscopic setting in which topology, electronic correlations, and magnetism become intertwined.
authors: Ola Kenji Forslund;Andrzej Ptok;Chun Lin;Aksel Kobialka;Wan Yu Chen;Ugne Miniotaite;Martin Månsson;Yasmine Sassa;Timur Kim;Cephise Cacho;Jian Rui Soh;Chin Shen Ong;Vladislav Borisov;Olle Eriksson;Johan Chang

title: Zero mode, Zero influence: Spatial-derivative coupling in particle detectors
abstract: It is common in particle detector models in cavity QED to often omit zero modes or assume their state, compromising causality or introducing ambiguity in their predictions. We show that spatial-derivative coupling eliminates both problems. For free massless scalar fields in static periodic or Neumann cavities of any spatial dimension, cavity-frame spatial derivatives annihilate the zero-mode operator while preserving microcausality. Detector dynamics and entanglement harvesting then depend only on the reduced detector-oscillator state, nonperturbatively and even with initial correlations with the zero mode. Time derivatives and moving-detector rest-frame spatial derivatives can retain zero-mode state dependence not compromising causality. Realized through current coupling in superconducting circuits, spatial-derivative coupling thus makes zero-mode state assumptions unnecessary.

title: Quantum dynamics of ultrasmall magnetic skyrmions in atomic-defect landscapes
abstract: Magnetic skyrmions are prime candidates for future information technology, and their fate in devices is settled by the defects they encounter. In ultrathin films, skyrmions can be as small as a couple of nanometers, carrying only a few tens of magnetic moments, while atomic defects reshape their energy landscape on the atomic scale. Here, we demonstrate that such ultrasmall skyrmions can behave quantum mechanically and that their quantum dynamics is unusual. Since the gyrotropic force dominates, the two coordinates of a ferromagnetic skyrmion are canonically conjugate and the skyrmion behaves as a particle in the lowest Landau level of an effective magnetic field, with a magnetic length of 0.6~Å. Utilizing skyrmion-defect interaction profiles of Cr and Fe adatoms and dimers in PdFe/Ir(111), obtained from atomistic spin simulations parametrized from first principles, we unveil quantized gyrotropic orbits with level spacings of 20--85~$μ$eV, bound not only by pinning defects but also, counter-intuitively, by repulsive ones. Saddle points of the energy landscape act as quantum beam splitters for skyrmions, and quantum depinning reaches rates of 1--100~Hz below the critical current. Embedded impurities, in contrast, bind the skyrmion so strongly that it ceases to behave as a rigid particle, defining a strong-coupling regime. For the Gilbert damping typical of ultrathin films, the quantized levels remain well resolved. The thermal-to-quantum crossover lies between 40 and 160~mK, which is within reach of millikelvin scanning tunneling microscopy, where tip-induced escape statistics and electron spin resonance STM can reveal the quantized gyrotropic motion of skyrmions pinned at defects crafted atom by atom.

title: Application a quantum machine learning algorithm to the applied problem of modeling the thermal regime of a servers
abstract: Quantum computing is a rapidly developed field of science. In the NISC era, quantum machine learning stands out, potentially outperforming classical machine learning. In this paper, we explore the applicability of quantum machine learning to a real-world application. We solved the problem of prediction of the temperature of GPUs in a high-performance computing cluster. We trained a quantum circuit to predict the temperature of each of the eight GPU of each cluster node based on 16 physical parameters. We demonstrated that quantum machine learning performs on this task just as well as classical machine learning. Furthermore, using model problems, we demonstrated that quantum machine learning can potentially outperform classical machine learning.

title: Cross-Lingual Persona Effects in LLM Negotiation
abstract: Tell an LLM negotiator to be "headstrong" and it should hold firm on price, but does that instruction retain the same behavior in every language? To test this, we use identical buyer and seller instances of Gemini 3.6 Flash to negotiate the same 12 CraigslistBargain scenarios in English and Korean. The pilot-scale 2 x 2 x 3 design crosses interaction language, seller urgency (none or strong), and buyer persona (cooperative, neutral, or headstrong), yielding 432 attempted negotiations. We call this property cross-lingual social-policy fidelity: whether a prompt-defined social policy produces the same behavioral effect regardless of interaction language. It often does not. Korean negotiations reached agreement far more often than English (77.3% vs. 52.5%, a 24.8-point gap, Holm-adjusted p = .0039), but only for neutral and headstrong buyers; cooperative buyers were already near-ceiling in both languages. Buyers' opening offers barely differed by language; the gap instead emerged later, through larger seller concessions and a smaller final gap in Korean, and agreed prices were also lower in Korean. Repeating the full design with Qwen3.7 Flash as both agents gives directional support: agreement was again higher in Korean (+13.9 points vs. Gemini's +24.8, with an interval whose lower bound is near zero), and sellers again conceded more. Pragmatic analysis reveals why: while both languages frequently featured face-threatening acts like rejections and counter-offers, Korean dialogue softened these threats with substantially more politeness mitigation, especially among sellers (11.7% vs. 3.6%). These results show that such a policy can produce different simulated negotiation behavior, not just different wording, when only the interaction language changes.

title: Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots
abstract: Collaborative robots (cobots) are designed to be safer and more interactive than traditional industrial robots, share the same workspace as humans, and assist them in a range of shop-floor tasks such as palletization, joint assembly, and part inspection. Many of these tasks involve repetitive workflows that may evolve with changes in production environments and task specifications. These requirements motivate the need for intuitive interfaces that allow workers to modify workflows on the shop floor and generalise these routines for future use. This work introduces the Teach-Abstract-Apply (TAA) framework, which enables human operators to (a) teach new workflows to cobots in natural language, (b) abstract the taught workflows into skills for later use, and (c) apply these skills in different settings. As a case study, we apply the TAA framework to a collaborative structure-building task and evaluate it with both open-weight (Qwen3-Coder) and closed (GPT5.2-Codex) models in self-play and cross-model configurations. Our results show that skill abstraction improves task success rates and reduces interaction cost. Beyond automated evaluation, a preliminary human-in-the-loop study suggests that the pipeline also works with human instructions.

title: Phase-space dynamics and multicomponent wave-packet structures in the Dunkl anharmonic oscillator
abstract: We study the phase-space dynamics and multicomponent wave-packet structures of the Dunkl anharmonic oscillator (Kerr medium). Starting from the time-evolved state, we derive analytical expressions for the Dunkl-Husimi $Q$-function and a normalized angular Husimi profile. The Dunkl parameter modifies the coherent-state excitation weights and the parity-dependent phase accumulation, producing angular anisotropy and asymmetric phase-space separation. For the half-integer deformation $μ=0.5$, the dynamics generate asymmetric multicomponent Husimi patterns with unequal peak heights and an early reconstruction at $t=π/λ$. For the deformation $μ=1.0$, the Husimi distribution exhibits broadening while retaining its multimodal structure and unitary evolution. At the fundamental nonlinear revival time, the wave packet is reconstructed for the selected parameter ratio. The standard Kerr dynamics are recovered in the limit $μ\rightarrow 0$.

title: Finesse evolution in a bichromatic cavity under blue and red resonant illumination in vacuum
abstract: The long-term performance of high-finesse optical cavities depends on the stability of their mirror coatings under vacuum and under continuous exposure to high circulating power. In cavities supporting multiple wavelengths, a central question is whether degradation at one wavelength compromises performance at another. Understanding this interplay is essential for those cavity quantum electrodynamics experiments that need diverse optical fields for cavity stabilization, trapping, and light--matter coupling. Here, we investigate wavelength-dependent degradation and recovery of a bichromatic cavity with high-reflectivity coating at 455 nm and 671 nm in vacuum. Cavity ring-down measurements reveal a decrease in the 455 nm finesse from 7.7*10^3 to 1.9*10^3 after 11 hours of continuous exposure to high circulating power. Simultaneous measurements show no measurable degradation at 671 nm. Continuous operation at 671 nm, instead, produces no measurable degradation at either wavelength under the tested conditions. Comparison of oxygen depletion and Avrami-type loss models indicates kinetics compatible with nucleation and growth, without uniquely identifying the microscopic mechanism. We demonstrate partial recovery of the finesse with illumination at 455 nm in air. Our results indicate a wavelength dependence of laser-induced optical damage in bichromatic cavities and provide an estimate of the blue light intensity that can be safely used in such cavities.
authors: M. S. Caracas Nuñez;A. Kadakkavattathu;G. Gatta;L. Duca;N. Mizukami;C. Sias

title: Triple descent in quantum linear regression
abstract: Quantum linear regression models, such as quantum extreme learning machines and quantum fidelity kernels, are trained on features that can only be estimated from finitely many measurement shots. Sampling noise is usually treated as a nuisance that more shots suppress; we show instead that it can fundamentally reshape the instabilities of the learning problem. As the number of measurement outcomes grows, the prediction error displays a triple-descent profile, with two peaks of fundamentally different origins. The first, classical, peak occurs when the measurement first becomes informationally complete, is a direct analogue of double descent in classical linear regression, and is caused by ill-conditioning of the measurement itself. This peak affects predictions only through their variance, and is thus suppressed by increasing the number of shots at inference. The second, quantum, peak occurs beyond informational completeness when the number of outcomes matches the number of training states: shot noise populates unphysical outcome combinations and the regression fits these pure-noise features with large weights, corrupting the learned model itself. More training or test shots cannot remove this quantum peak, which disappears only in the ideal limit of exact training features. Using random-matrix theory, we derive the shape of both peaks analytically, accounting also for ridge regularization. Our results show that treating quantum features as exactly known overestimates classical instabilities while missing genuinely quantum ones.
authors: Gabriele Lo Monaco;Salvatore Lorenzo;Alessandro Ferraro;Mauro Paternostro;G. Massimo Palma;Luca Innocenti

title: Outstrumental Variable Regression
abstract: Estimating the causal effect of a treatment $X$ on an outcome $Y$ from observational data in the presence of unobserved confounding requires additional structure or assumptions. Existing identification strategies such as instrumental variable regression exploit exogenous variation in only the treatment. We show that the causal effect can also be identified if the outcome mechanism varies across a finite set of environments, even if the treatment distribution is unchanged. Concretely, we introduce Outstrumental Variable Regression (OVR), which proceeds in three steps: (i) compute the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X$ in each environment; (ii) form the vector of differences in these conditional expectations between all environments and a reference environment (we call this vector contrast); and (iii) regress $Y$ on $X$ while adjusting for the contrast and environment. We prove that this yields the true causal effect if the following two conditions hold: inclusion restriction, i.e., the contrast determines the conditional confounding bias; and positivity, i.e., the treatment varies sufficiently strongly after adjustment. We prove that a finite-sample version of OVR is consistent under regularity conditions and demonstrate the procedure's effectiveness on synthetic and real-world data.
authors: Felix Schur;Linus Kühne;Julius von Kügelgen;Jonas Peters

title: KINDER: Kernel-based Independence for Fair Representation Learning via Prototype-space Erasure
abstract: Concept erasure is a prominent approach to achieving fairness in machine learning through the removal of sensitive attributes from learned representations. Prior concept erasure methods typically define debiasing indirectly through the failure of a chosen adversary, probe, or fairness penalty, which makes the target of erasure dependent on a particular decoder family or optimization setup. We introduce KINDER, which directly removes sensitive-attribute information from intermediate representations with respect to a chosen family of prototype functionals, and is compatible with any deep model containing an intermediate feature space, independent of the architecture, task type, or training paradigm. KINDER operates in a random Fourier feature space, where it estimates a sensitive subspace from protected group prototypes and projects representations onto its orthogonal complement. Thus, it forms an explicit representation cleaning mechanism distinct from prior fairness control studies. We conduct extensive experiments across diverse settings and show the effectiveness of KINDER on (i) supervised and self-supervised settings, (ii) classification, regression, and image segmentation tasks, and (iii) diverse data modalities, including visual, textual, and tabular data. Code and trained models are available at: https://github.com/abtinmU/KINDER
authors: Abtin Mogharabin;Alp Toykan Kaplan;Jiaee Cheong;Sinan Kalkan

title: Short-Circuit Current Calculation in DC Shipboard Microgrid Using Operational Admittances
abstract: The increasing adoption of DC shipboard power systems is driven by the need to integrate energy storage systems seamlessly onboard. In this context, accurate calculation of short-circuit current transients is critical for sizing fast-acting protection devices. This paper proposes a methodology to calculate short-circuit current transients based on operational admittance modelling of network elements and power converters. The superposition principle is then applied to calculate current contributions and voltage time profiles. The methodology is validated with a detailed EMT model of a notional LVDC shipboard microgrid section consisting of an active front end, a bidirectional buck-boost converter and two special loads. Results demonstrate that the methodology accurately tracks nodal voltages and the fault current contributions dynamics up to the prospective fault current peak, thus providing a computationally efficient tool for fault analysis and protection coordination in LVDC microgrids.

title: Model Collapse Is Avoidable Even as Real Data Vanishes: A Sharp Criterion for Iterative Gaussian Estimation
abstract: Large generative models are commonly trained on data collected from the open web, which may contain data produced by previous generations of the same model. Previous work has shown that recursively training on model-generated data can progressively degrade model performance, a phenomenon known as model collapse. Yet, generative models continue to improve dramatically over time. Existing theory suggests that this is enabled by the availability of new real data at each iteration, kept separate from generated data. However, exact separation is not realistic, and uncurated data is still commonly used. We bridge this gap by considering a more realistic setup in which real and generated data are not handled differently during training. Specifically, we present a comprehensive theoretical study of iterative estimation of the mean and covariance of a multivariate Gaussian distribution. At each iteration, samples are drawn from a mixture of the real data distribution and the estimated distribution from the previous iteration, but are used indistinguishably. We provide a single equivalent condition for consistency of the mean and covariance estimators in Euclidean norms, and convergence to zero of the expected squared 2-Wasserstein distance between the estimated and true distributions. Using this result, we show that consistency holds, i.e., model collapse is avoided, for any fixed real data fraction above zero, and even for a fraction that vanishes across iterations, provided it does not vanish too quickly. However, more real data (or data curation) remains important at practical finite times: the convergence rate of the mean estimator deteriorates as the real data fraction approaches zero. We support our results with an empirical investigation of the theoretical setup, and with experiments on iterative training of a diffusion model on CIFAR-10 that correlate with our theory.

title: Porteous Meets Walsh: Counting Critical Points for $\mathcal{H}_2$-Norm Model Order Reduction Using Algebraic Geometry Behind Multiparameter Eigenvalue Problems
abstract: Several polynomial systems arising in systems and control have been shown to exhibit a partially linear structure, which allows them to be reformulated as a multiparameter eigenvalue problem (MEP). In this work, we show how such MEP formulations can be leveraged to obtain refined information about the solution set of the polynomial system. We demonstrate, in the setting of single-input single-output $\mathcal{H}_2$-norm model order reduction, how the Thom--Porteous formula can be used to derive an exact count of the complex solutions of the critical equations derived from Walsh's theorem. We prove, under suitable genericity assumptions, that their set of complex solutions is finite and that all solutions occur without multiplicity. Moreover, we derive an explicit formula for the total number of complex solutions as a function of the model orders. Throughout, we provide a self-contained and application-oriented exposition of the algebro-geometric tools required for our analysis, with the aim of making them accessible to the broader engineering community.

title: Benchmarking Quantum Convolutional Neural Networks and their classical surrogates on long-range strongly correlated models
abstract: We benchmark quantum convolutional neural networks (QCNNs) and their classical surrogates for phase differentiation in one-dimensional strongly correlated systems with beyond-nearest-neighbour terms. Using an anisotropic Heisenberg spin chain and an extended $t$-$t'$ Fermi-Hubbard model as representative spin and fermionic testbeds, we train QCNN classifiers on labelled ground-state datasets and map out finite-size phase diagrams. In hybrid setups, we employ Pauli backpropagation to express the QCNN measurement as a weighted sum of Pauli-string expectation values to be evaluated directly on input states, and study how truncation parameters control the trade-off between approximation accuracy and the size of the resulting Pauli expansion. Robust convergence is achieved for the Heisenberg model under aggressive truncation, whereas the Fermi-Hubbard model requires substantially looser thresholds, resulting in a sharp growth in retained Pauli strings and evaluation cost. Our results contribute to charting where hybrid quantum-classical training is viable for learning strongly correlated quantum states, and provide practical guidance for choosing truncation regimes in Pauli backpropagation-based surrogates.
authors: Tatiana A. Bespalova;Réka Schwengelbeck;Laura Mismetti;Johannes Schachenmayer;Ivano Tavernelli;Francesco Tacchino

title: Costate Estimation and Covector Mapping for Bernstein Polynomial Direct Methods in Optimal Control
abstract: Bernstein polynomial approximation of continuous functions has a slower rate of convergence as compared to other approximation methods. ``The fact seems to have precluded any numerical application of Bernstein polynomials from having been made. Perhaps they will find application when the properties of the approximant in the large are of more importance than the closeness of the approximation.'' -- has remarked P.J. Davis in his 1963 book Interpolation and Approximation. This paper presents a direct approximation method for nonlinear optimal control problems with mixed input and state constraints based on Bernstein polynomial approximation, in which the dynamic and path constraints are imposed at the Bernstein coefficients (control points). We provide a rigorous analysis showing that, under convergence assumptions on the control polygons, the proposed method yields consistent approximations of time continuous optimal control problems and can be used for costate estimation of the optimal control problems. In particular, multipliers satisfying a relaxed Karush Kuhn Tucker system of the resulting nonlinear program, scaled by the quadrature weight, approximate the costate and the multipliers of the optimal control problem. Owing to the structure of the Bernstein differentiation matrix, the discrete transversality conditions are contained in the relaxed Karush Kuhn Tucker system, and no additional closure conditions need to be added to it. This result leads to the formulation of the Covector Mapping Theorem for Bernstein polynomial approximation.
authors: Venanzio Cichella;Isaac Kaminer;Claire Walton;Naira Hovakimyan;Antonio Pascoal

title: A Preconditioned Semismooth Newton Method for Box-Constrained Elliptic Optimal Control Problems with Random Coefficients
abstract: We consider the optimal control problem of an elliptic PDE with random diffusion under pointwise box constraints on the control. The constraints make the optimality conditions nonsmooth, with an active set that is not known in advance, and the random diffusion couples the state and the adjoint across all stochastic modes. To design a solution algorithm for this problem, we rely on the Fenchel duality viewpoint. Fenchel duality absorbs the box constraint into the objective and yields an exact reduced problem in the elliptic adjoint variable alone. After a stochastic Galerkin--finite element discretization, eliminating the state leaves a strongly monotone, piecewise smooth equation, which we solve directly by a matrix-free semismooth Newton method with the box projection retained exactly and with no outer iteration, penalty or smoothing parameter. Next, we introduce and analyze a current-set preconditioner, which adds the active-set correction of the current Newton step to a mean-diffusion reference operator and is inverted exactly by a rank-1 update. For implementation, we use a cheaper preconditioner that keeps only a fraction of free control values. Numerical experiments show second-order convergence of the state, and Newton and PCG counts that stay bounded under mesh refinement and growth of the stochastic dimension.

title: MEMENTO: Learning Context Management for Long Context Processing Agents
abstract: LLM agents that operate over long inputs must perform context management: deciding what to retain in a fixed-size context window. A common approach is compaction, where the model replaces its history with a self-generated note. Yet off-the-shelf agentic models, including GPT-5.5 and GLM-5.3, often write ineffective notes, and reinforcement learning (RL) alone rarely discovers useful note-taking behavior. We present MEMENTO, a long-context agent built on Qwen3-8B and trained to manage its context through compaction. We first bootstrap note-taking by fine-tuning on synthetic trajectories annotated with notes generated in hindsight, then reinforce it with RL using a reward that combines answer correctness, note-quality heuristics, and confidence calibration. Although trained only to compact into a fresh window, MEMENTO extends at test time to strategies such as context folding and confidence-based backtracking. On book-level question answering across four benchmarks, with books of up to 2.5M tokens, MEMENTO raises Qwen3-8B's accuracy from 36.9% to 67.8% while never holding more than 20K tokens in context. It outperforms GPT-5.5 agent in the same harness (13.1%) and full book context (56.7%) at less than 1/50 the cost. It also nearly matches a ~100x larger GLM-5.3 agent (69.3%) at 1/9 the cost, and comes within 6.4 points of GLM-5.3 full context at 1/26 the cost.

title: ProLand: A New Infeasible Manifold Optimization Method for LoRA Fine-Tuning
abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning but can suffer from redundant basis directions. Constraining the basis factor to the Stiefel manifold addresses this redundancy through orthonormality. Landing methods allow temporarily infeasible iterates to explore a neighborhood of the manifold while progressively restoring orthogonality without per-step retractions. To improve optimization efficiency while retaining this flexibility, we introduce ProLand (Product-space Landing), a retraction-free optimizer that combines coordinated factor updates with Muon-style spectral directions. By designing the updates in the space of the represented weight increment, ProLand separates objective optimization from orthogonality restoration, supporting efficient feasibility recovery. This coordinated construction also enables Muon-style directions to guide objective optimization while preserving that separation. Experiments cover four GLUE validation tasks on DeBERTa-v3-base and seven language benchmarks on Qwen2.5-3B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Moonlight-16B-A3B across multiple adapter ranks. Across these 11 tasks, ProLand achieves the highest average score among the compared methods in every tested encoder and decoder model-rank configuration.
authors: Chenyu Zhou;Yuxuan Zeng;Qi Deng;Dongdong Ge;Yinyu Ye

title: Distance to integrability and complexity
abstract: We consider nearest-neighbour interactions on spin-1/2 chains. We find the full set of integrable models of this form and apply a numerical algorithm to determine the "closest" integrable model for a given Hamiltonian. This allows us to define a model-independent distance to integrability. We show that standard measures of chaos interpolate between integrable and chaotic values with increasing values of this distance. However, there is a large variation across models and the distance to integrability provides additional information not directly provided by these diagnostics.
authors: Sean Casey;Marius de Leeuw;Tristan McLoughlin;Sergiy Zhuk

title: Spectral and Conformal: Neural Network Methods for Calibrated Trajectory Prediction and Control-Point Intervals
abstract: Autonomous systems that navigate their environment need methods to quickly assess the feasibility and safety of desired trajectories. Traditional solutions that rely on numerical integration can be computationally heavy, while fast data-driven surrogates lack the formal guarantees that numerical approaches provide. This work demonstrates a framework that uses (1) a neural network with a spectral backbone to learn trajectories and quantile bands with built-in constraints (initial conditions and stability); (2) a modified conformal quantile regression to provide calibrated, joint trajectory-level coverage; and (3) interval arithmetic to extend noise-free coverage guarantees to control points. After refactoring the network for inference, the trajectory inference time for a quadrotor under a closed-loop linear quadratic regulator is 3.45~ms on a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. The total pipeline time, including trajectory inference time, is 9.81~ms, or approximately 100~Hz, consistent with typical control rates.

title: Parameter-Free First-Order Method for Constrained Variational Inequalities
abstract: Constrained variational inequalities (VIs) provide a general framework for modeling and solving complementarity and equilibrium problems with functional constraints. In this paper, we propose a parameter-free accelerated operator sliding (PFAOS) method for solving monotone VIs with convex smooth constraints. For a single constraint, PFAOS achieves an operator evaluation complexity of $\mathcal{O}(1/\varepsilon)$ and a constraint gradient evaluation complexity of $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{\varepsilon})$, without requiring prior knowledge of the Lipschitz constant of the VI operator or the smoothness constant of the constraint function. We further extend PFAOS to multiple constraints by incorporating a primal-dual hybrid gradient update, yielding a multi-constrained PFAOS (MC-PFAOS) method that preserves the same evaluation complexities. Finally, numerical experiments are conducted on large-scale games with coupling constraints to validate the efficiency and effectiveness of the proposed algorithms.

title: In the age of big data and AI: do we still need chemical bonds?
abstract: Chemical bonding is the language through which chemistry rationalizes materials structure, stability, properties, and reactivity. Meanwhile, modern deep-learning models achieve remarkable predictive performance using representations based largely on compositional and structural information, raising the question of whether explicit bonding concepts remain necessary. In this work, we argue that artificial intelligence does not render chemical bonding obsolete but provides a new framework for evaluating and refining bonding concepts. We show that, through linear probing, Allegro and MACE embeddings recover bonding descriptors with (R^2 > 0.95), indicating that bonding emerges naturally from Allegro's and MACE's latent spaces. We also show that bonding descriptors provide information beyond bond distance in our electronic-structure-featurized MEGNet (ESF-MEGNet) model, reducing prediction error for properties including bulk and shear moduli by 15%. We discuss implications for interpretable machine learning, synthesizability prediction, and generative materials design, and suggest joint-embedding approaches for learning more general bonding representations. More broadly, we propose that chemical bonding can be understood as a learnable representation of electronic structure. From this perspective, different bonding models represent alternative compressions of the underlying electronic information and can be evaluated through their predictive power, dimensionality, and complexity. The age of machine learning shifts the focus from whether a bonding model is physically motivated to whether it captures the information required to explain and predict materials behavior. If a materials genome exists, it should be encodable through a representation of chemical bonding. If no bonding representation can capture this information, our understanding of the chemical bond may require revision.
authors: Mohammed Al-Fahdi;Aakash Naik;Katharina Ueltzen;Luc Walterbos;Tom Demeyere;Philipp Benner;Janine George

title: Euclid Quick Data Release (Q1). Mass-to-light ratio of elliptical galaxies: constraints from strong lensing
abstract: Mass is among the most fundamental properties describing a galaxy. The relation between the luminosity and the total mass of a galaxy contains information on the efficiency of the star formation process and on the distribution of dark matter. We used strong gravitational lensing data from the Euclid Quick Data Release 1 (Q1) to constrain the total mass enclosed within an aperture of $5\,h^{-1}$kpc, $M_5$, of elliptical galaxies. Our analysis is based on a sample of 95 lenses, which we built by ensuring that their selection function is reproducible. This enabled us to correct our inference for selection effects. The average $\log_{10}{(M_5\,h\,M_\odot^{-1})}$ for a galaxy with an $r$-band luminosity of $10^{10.7}L_{\odot}\,h^{-2}$ at $z=0.5$ is $11.30\pm0.02$. The mass $M_5$ scales with luminosity to the power $β_\mathrm{L}=0.71\pm0.07$, and decreases with increasing redshift at fixed luminosity. Assuming a scenario in which galaxies grow by mergers and stellar populations evolve passively, these correlations imply that $M_5$ increases with time for individual galaxies. These measurements provide a useful benchmark for testing models of galaxy structure and evolution that make predictions on the distribution of total mass on the scales of $5\,h^{-1}$kpc.

title: A VLT/CRIRES+ study of helium 1.083$μ$m absorption features towards the inner Orion Nebula
abstract: JWST NIRCam F115W observations towards the inner Orion Nebula revealed a diverse array of previously unknown dark features. The most likely cause was absorption or suppressed emission of the helium 1.083$μ$m triplet which lies in that filter. We have obtained VLT/CRIRES+ high-resolution spectrographic observations over a selection of different dark targets, confirming that the features are indeed explained by a reduction in the flux of the helium 1.083$μ$m triplet, a reduction that is fairly uniform across the line. The Orion Nebula is a blister HII region, with a dense, bright ionised layer on the far side from the observer near the Orion A molecular cloud and lower density gas elsewhere. Using a simple radiative transfer model, we show that dark features arise when emission from the dense layer is absorbed by intermediate density helium (e.g. in clumps, globules, or winds from objects like proplyds) on the near side of the dense layer.

title: Quantum Simulation of Hadronization: From String Breaking to Event Generation
abstract: High-energy collisions produce large numbers of quarks and gluons that are bound into hadrons by the confining interactions of quantum chromodynamics (QCD). This hadronization process is intrinsically real-time and non-perturbative. Event generators describe hadronization using phenomenological models with parameters fitted to data rather than calculated from QCD. Uncertainties in these models limit the precision of certain measurements at the Large Hadron Collider. Quantum computers could enable first-principles simulations of these dynamics. Existing quantum simulations of gauge theories have demonstrated string-breaking dynamics. This white paper summarizes the conclusions of the InQubator for Quantum Simulation workshop \textit{From String Dynamics to Event Generation with Quantum Simulation}. We develop a roadmap for extending these simulations to inform phenomenological models of hadronization. A sequence of toy models is proposed for connecting current quantum simulations to QCD. The observables that should be extracted are listed, and the challenges that separate present simulations from quantitative predictions are identified. We propose a staged program in which quantum simulations first provide qualitative modifications to event generators and later provide quantitative input.

title: The MAGPI Survey: the evolution of galaxy spin-filament alignments since z~0.3
abstract: We present measurements of galaxy spin-filament alignments at 0.20<z<0.42 using the MAGPI Survey, exploiting resolved stellar and ionised gas kinematics to reconstruct 3D spin axes. Cosmic filaments are identified using a stellar mass-matched constant-number-density population from the GAMA, MAGPI Redshift Survey and DESI datasets. We detect a flipping of the statistical alignment signal at z~0.3 as a function of M*: low-mass galaxies preferentially exhibit spins parallel to the direction of their host filaments, while high-mass galaxies tend towards perpendicular orientations. The transition mass is measured to be log(M{*,t}/Msun)~10.8, approximately 0.6 dex higher than the value for the SAMI Galaxy Survey at z~0.05. Bootstrap analysis gives 99.5% confidence that the transition mass is higher for MAGPI than SAMI. At fixed stellar mass MAGPI galaxies exhibit stronger parallel alignments than their SAMI counterparts, suggesting evolution of spin-filament alignments over the past ~3 Gyr. The gaseous component in MAGPI galaxies is more closely aligned with filaments than the stellar component, relative to a M*-matched SAMI sample. This indicates a stronger coupling between ionised gas and the large-scale structure at z~0.3, consistent with coherent gas accretion onto filaments remaining efficient at higher M*. At z~0 we detect a transition toward perpendicular alignments at lower M*, while the gas and stellar components exhibit similar alignments relative to filaments, likely due to the cumulative effects of mergers and secular evolution.

title: Dust-induced reversal of the optical wavelength dependence of spiral-arm pitch angles
abstract: The classical density-wave scenario predicts a blue-to-red age--colour gradient across the spiral arms of disc galaxies as a consequence of shock-induced star formation. However, observations of spiral-arm pitch angles at different wavelengths sometimes suggest the opposite trend, namely a red-to-blue ``colour jump''. The origin of this apparent contradiction remains unclear. In this work, we investigate the effects of dust attenuation on post-shock stellar emission, together with the streamline motions of gas and stellar populations. We find that dust attenuation in regions with relatively high optical depths, $\hatτ_{V} \gtrsim 0.2$, can produce an apparent red-to-blue spatial sequence, with respect to the shock location, by reversing the relative positions of the flux maxima of stellar populations observed in different bands. Moreover, streamline motions confine post-shock stellar populations near the spiral arms for longer than in a circular-orbit model, thereby modifying the spatial distribution of the emitted light. We conclude that the apparent red-to-blue colour jump does not necessarily contradict the classical density-wave scenario. Instead, it can arise from the same post-shock stellar populations that intrinsically produce a blue-to-red age--colour gradient if their emission is modified by dust attenuation.

title: Intranight optical monitoring of eight quasars with superluminal jets and low optical polarization: Probing the mechanism of rapid flux variability
abstract: Intranight optical variability (INOV) of blazars whose emission arises predominantly from a relativistic jet, has been widely linked to a combination of two key observational diagnostics: the fractional optical polarization ($P_{opt}$) and the Doppler boost arising from relativistic beaming of the jet's emission. To discern which of these two factors plays the dominant role, we investigate INOV of a well-defined representative sample of 8 flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs, which are `low-synchrotron-peaked' blazars) whose jets exhibit a low degree of polarization ($P_{opt}$ < 3$\%$) but a large superluminal motion with c$β_{app}$ = 5c $-$ 31c (median = 10c). We report sensitive optical monitoring of these 8 `low-polarization superluminal quasars' (LPSQs) using a 1.3-metre telescope, in 20 sessions of minimum 3-hour duration. These data were supplemented with similarly high-quality monitoring data/results available in the literature for this sample, thus adding another 19 sessions. Duty cycle (DC) of strong INOV (amplitude $ψ> 5\%$) is found to be zero, applying the normally used $F_η$ test, and $\sim 7\%$ using the more powerful `enhanced $F$-test'. The small DC, despite the strong Doppler boost expected from the observed high superluminality, shows that strong INOV is much rarer among LPSQs, compared to high-polarization quasars, for which DC $(ψ> 5\%$) is found to be around 30%, even using the $F_η$ test. This provides the first compelling evidence that optical polarization is the primary diagnostic of INOV, while relativistic beaming plays a supportive role. Possible implications for the proposed mechanisms for INOV are pointed out.

title: Exhaustive Construction of Generalized Parent Hamiltonians for Matrix Product States
abstract: Characterizing local Hamiltonians that host interesting many-body states as eigenstates has been an important problem in quantum many-body physics. For matrix product states (MPS), there is a well-known construction of parent Hamiltonians that have the MPS as the frustration-free ground state. However, recent results on quantum many-body scars have shown that such a construction does not exhaust all possible Hamiltonians that have the MPS as an eigenstate. In this work, we develop an exhaustive construction of generalized parent Hamiltonians that have a given translation-invariant MPS as an eigenstate. These go beyond the conventional projector-based construction of frustration-free parent Hamiltonians, where each local Hermitian term has the MPS as an eigenstate, by allowing non-Hermitian telescoping terms that cancel out with periodic boundary conditions (PBC). We derive a local tensor equation that establishes a correspondence between inequivalent classes of generalized parent Hamiltonians, i.e., those that cannot be related using linear combinations with frustration-free Hamiltonians, and the MPS transfer matrix spectrum. We illustrate the connection to intrinsic physical properties, including non-Abelian symmetries and zero correlation length, and further extend this construction to block-injective MPS. Our framework hence provides a systematic bridge between generalized parent Hamiltonians and the local structure of quantum states.

title: Quantum simulation of real-time Yukawa dynamics with qubits and qumodes
abstract: Real-time quantum simulation of field theories offers access to scattering and decay dynamics, circumventing the limitations of Euclidean lattice methods. However, representing bosonic fields on qubits requires a finite-dimensional approximation and can entail costly multi-qubit operations. Hybrid qubit-qumode architectures avoid this by encoding bosonic fields directly in oscillators. We formulate scattering in the (1+1)-dimensional Yukawa theory for such a device, with staggered fermions on qubits and the scalar on qumodes. Trapped ions are a natural candidate, with the fermions on the internal states of the ions and the scalar on their collective motion, so that the Yukawa coupling becomes a native spin-dependent displacement. Emulating the device with tensor networks, we study the decay of a single scalar particle and fermion-antifermion scattering around the resonance region, using observables that can be measured on the device natively. We compare the results with those obtained using lattice perturbation theory. The emulation is able to resolve corrections beyond the Dyson summation of the one-loop self-energy.

title: A Supermagnified Little Red Dot with a Resolved Host
abstract: Little red dots (LRDs) are an intriguing new class of sources in the early universe discovered by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) characterized by V-shaped spectra and extremely compact sizes. Their underlying mechanisms still remain the subject of ongoing debate. We present JWST observations of a gravitationally lensed LRD nicknamed "Best Friend" at $z_{\rm spec} = 8.297\pm0.002$. Its high magnification factor of $μ= 36^{+8}_{-12}$ makes it the highest magnified LRD reported to date and unveils both the resolved structure of its host and a central engine less than 7 pc in size. The spectrum of the central engine, in which broad lines are not detected, possibly owing to the limited S/N and spectral resolution, is better interpreted as black hole activity rather than a dense star cluster. The latter cannot be fully excluded, but if true, the resulting lower limit on stellar density would be $>1.25^{+0.4}_{-0.3}\cdot10^6 \mathrm{M_{\odot}/pc}^2$, which is around 2 orders of magnitude higher than stellar densities of typical clusters at high-z. By performing a spatially resolved analysis of NIRCam photometry and NIRSpec/PRISM spectroscopy, we find that the host stellar mass is $\log(M_\star/M_{\odot}) = 7.3^{+0.2}_{-0.8}$. Best Friend demonstrates the power of lensing to reveal the morphologies of LRDs.

title: Hidden Neutrino Active Galaxy Candidates: Prospects for Catalog and Stacking Searches with IceCube, IceCube-Gen2, and KM3NeT
abstract: In high-energy neutrino astrophysics, the identification of high-energy neutrino sources is a central goal, and jet-quiet active galactic nuclei (AGNs) have emerged as promising candidates. For this purpose, we present a theory-guided, intrinsic X-ray selected sample of hidden neutrino AGN candidates consisting of $28$ X-ray bright AGNs (X-HiNAC), combining the {\em Swift}/BAT and BASS surveys with dedicated {\em NuSTAR} observations and spectral analyses. We compile their intrinsic X-ray fluxes, spectral properties, luminosity distances, and supermassive black hole masses, to provide a coherent sample for neutrino source searches. The sample is physically motivated but remains model independent given that the neutrino flux is proportional to the intrinsic X-ray flux. Using the magnetically powered corona model, we also demonstrate the prospects for individual-source and stacking searches with IceCube-Gen2 and KM3NeT. We identify promising individual targets and find that stacking the remaining sources, excluding NGC 1068, could yield a $5σ$ detection within $\sim 5-15$ years under favorable model assumptions at the current and upcoming neutrino observatories. We highlight systematic uncertainties in the adopted source parameters, particularly the black hole masses, for which different measurement techniques can yield estimates differing by up to an order of magnitude. Such uncertainties can significantly affect the predicted neutrino emission, motivating more precise black hole mass measurements and improved broadband X-ray observations. Our findings motivate improved multiwavelength characterization of nearby AGNs and provide a guide for investigating their role as high-energy neutrino sources.

title: MARTA: An overmassive black hole hidden in a young, clumpy, and metal-poor galaxy at z~3.8
abstract: JWST has extended the search for accreting black holes into the high-redshift, low-mass regime. We report a low-mass black hole candidate in MARTA 3887, a clumpy, metal-poor galaxy at $z=3.7694$, combining deep JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy, HST and JWST imaging, and archival VLT/MUSE data. We detect a broad H$α$ component with $L_{\rm Hα,b}=2.35\times10^{41}$ erg s$^{-1}$ and FWHM $=1270^{+260}_{-250}$ km s$^{-1}$, with no [O III] counterpart of comparable width. Under a broad-line-region interpretation, virial calibrations give $\log(M_{\rm BH}/M_\odot)=6.52^{+0.18}_{-0.23}$ and $λ_{\rm Edd}=0.07$, or up to 0.38 for alternative calibrations. The host comprises at least three compact clumps, with $\log(M_\star/M_\odot)=8.16^{+0.09}_{-0.10}$. If stellar photoionization dominates the narrow lines, the gas is highly ionized and metal poor, with $12+\log({\rm O/H})=7.68\pm0.04$ ($\simeq0.10\,Z_\odot$). The inferred $M_{\rm BH}/M_\star=2.3\%$ lies about 2 dex above the extrapolated local relation, suggesting that black-hole growth has outpaced the assembly of the observed host. If growth began only when the first 10% of the observed stellar mass had formed ($t_{10}=92$ Myr ago), a $10^2\,M_\odot$ seed would require a lifetime-mean Eddington ratio $\simeq5.7$; earlier growth or a more massive, e.g. direct-collapse, seed would allow sub-Eddington mean accretion. MUSE reveals extended Ly$α$ emission ($\simeq6.5$-6.9 proper kpc), offset by $+64^{+10}_{-8}$ km s$^{-1}$ from systemic, with a provisional escape fraction of $\simeq0.44$. Together with a Mg II doublet ratio close to the optically thin limit and a high [O III]/[O II] ratio, this makes MARTA 3887 a laboratory to study black-hole growth, stellar assembly, and ionizing-photon escape jointly.

title: EMBER: A Little Red Dot Candidate at $z_{\rm spec}=10.36$ in the Seed Black Hole Era
abstract: Little red dots (LRDs) are a newly discovered population that may trace rapidly growing black holes (BHs) and provide a link between seed BHs and luminous active galactic nuclei (AGNs). However, no LRD had previously been spectroscopically confirmed at $z>10$, leaving this earliest phase observationally unexplored. Using JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy from the EMBER program, we measure a spectroscopic redshift of $z_{\rm spec}=10.361^{+0.003}_{-0.002}$ for \target, the highest-redshift LRD candidate known to date. The redshift is constrained by a prominent Ly$α$ break and multiple tentative emission lines, including C\,{\sc iv}\,$λ\lambda1549,1551$ and [O\,{\sc iii}]\,$\lambda4363$ detected at $S/N=3.9$ and $3.6$, respectively. Its extreme NIRCam-MIRI color of $m_{\rm F444W}-m_{\rm F770W}=1.82\pm0.1$, characteristic V-shaped continuum with a turnover near the Balmer limit, and continuum slopes of $β_{\rm UV}=-2.26^{+0.11}_{-0.11}$ and $β_{\rm opt}=1.17^{+0.74}_{-0.70}$ all support its LRD nature. A possible iron complex at $λ_{\rm rest}\sim0.24$--$0.25\,{\rm μm}$ and a possibly high $\log\left([{\rm O\,III]\,\lambda4363/\rm Hγ}\right)=0.17^{+0.24}_{-0.22}$ further support an AGN-like interpretation, as seen in previously known LRDs. Tentative detection of Ly$α$ emission may indicate enhanced Ly$α$ transmission at $z\sim10$. Our findings extend the observational frontier of BH growth into the seed-BH formation era, and upcoming MIRI spectroscopy will further establish the physical nature of the source.
