title: Investigation of perovskite related oxides: structural and magnetic properties
abstract: Perovskites exist in varied structures and show structure dependent magnetic properties which is of great interest in the field of multiferroics, magnetocaloric and spintronic devices. Here we intend to study the various rare-earth(R) and transition metal (TM) ion interactions depending on their structures. Different Curie temperature, spinglass transition and spin reorientation transitions were observed depending on the degree of interactions and structural properties. It is interesting to study the role of orbital interactions, disorder in magnetic transitions leading to change in superexchange and double exchange interaction. On substitution at A-site or B-site results in change in magnetic interactions, as well as creates structural distortions. We also obtained results where the spin interaction of the transition metal and rare-earth interaction, magnetic anisotropy, orientations of orbitals, disorder induced interactions were observed.

title: Does System Size Matter in Uncertainty Quantification for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials?
abstract: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) commonly use uncertainty estimates to flag out-of-distribution (OOD) configurations and select structures for active learning. A key question is whether the resulting structure-level uncertainty scores remain comparable across different system sizes. A common practice is to aggregate per-atom uncertainties by their mean or maximum and compare the resulting score against a fixed threshold, implicitly assuming such comparability. We test this assumption across several in-distribution (ID)/OOD pairs by characterizing both aggregations as a function of atom count. The two aggregations exhibit distinct size dependencies. Mean aggregation remains size-independent for homogeneous systems but loses sensitivity to defects in large cells. In contrast, maximum aggregation grows with system size for ID systems while remaining approximately flat for defect-containing systems, narrowing the ID-OOD gap in a manner consistent with extreme-value statistics. Although highly uncertain atoms in large structures may indicate novel local environments, retraining on these structures yields little improvement, in contrast to retraining on OOD structures constructed to lie outside the training distribution. Our results reveal a practical limitation of size-unaware uncertainty criteria and motivate size-aware calibration for more reliable OOD detection in large-scale atomistic simulations.
authors: Chayaphol Lortaraprasert;Nontawat Charoenphakdee;Wenwen Li;Yong-Bin Zhuang;Yuta Tsuboi

title: It Takes Two to Probe, Thousands to Retrieve: Putting Vision--Language Probes to the Retrieval Test
abstract: Vision--language models (VLMs) are tested for fine-grained understanding with image--text matching probes, a model must prefer the correct image or caption over handcrafted negative. In retrieval, the correct item must beat thousands of alternatives. We measure how these two evaluation methods relate by using two probing benchmarks, \svo{} and SugarCrepe, for retrieval tasks. For 100 image and caption queries we judge the top-10 retrievals from full dataset of six VLMs, with human annotators and an LLM assessor. We than compare how well models rank pool of items on the same queries, while changing only where the negatives comes from: the benchmark, a random draw, or the judged-incorrect retrievals of other models. On \svo{} the accuracy of retrieving a positive over handcrafted negatives is significantly higher than for retrieved ones (the correct item is preferred in 85\% against 77\% of the time). Using pool of ten retrieved negatives leads to same accuracy as when one uses pool of 200 to 430 random negatives. On SugarCrepe the order is reversed: its handcrafted negatives are harder than the retrieved ones. Incomplete relevance labels explain most of the low retrieval scores on \svo{}, where the top-ranked item is correct for 54--90\% of the queries under human labels against 6--21\% under the benchmark's labels. However, we detect no association between passing the probe for a query and retrieving a correct item first. The LLM assessor o3 agrees with individual annotators ($κ$ 0.57--0.61) slightly less than they agree with each other (0.64--0.68).

title: Dual-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Vehicle Scheduling and Multi-Energy Dispatch in Electric-Hydrogen-Transport Systems
abstract: Electric-hydrogen-transport systems (EHTSs) require coordinated scheduling of electric and hydrogen vehicles together with multi-energy dispatch. These operations form a sequential decision process: upstream vehicle scheduling (VS) determines service allocation and order, thereby endogenously shaping the electricity and hydrogen demands faced by downstream energy dispatch (ED). This paper develops a dual-agent reinforcement learning framework tailored to the heterogeneous decision structures. The vehicle-scheduling agent combines proximal policy optimisation (PPO) with a Plackett-Luce policy to learn vehicle-priority permutations, which are then mapped to feasible charger and refueller assignments through a greedy allocation. The energy-dispatch agent employs twin delayed deep deterministic policy gradient (TD3) for continuous storage and energy-flow control. The directional coupling between the two decision layers is analysed, revealing that updates to the upstream scheduling policy can shift the demand distribution experienced by the downstream dispatcher. A three-stage training mechanism is therefore introduced, combining layer-wise pretraining with concurrent fine-tuning to mitigate the effects of scheduling-induced distribution shifts on downstream ED learning. Year-long case studies show that the proposed framework achieves the lowest vehicle-service delay and energy cost among the 11 evaluated methods, demonstrating effective coordination between vehicle scheduling and multi-energy dispatch.
authors: Fulong Yao;Yiming Xu;Maurizio Albano;Liana Cipcigan;Naeima Hamed;Bo Zou;Omar Rana

title: Upcycling Language Models for Multiple Specialized Domains
abstract: Effective multi-domain adaptation of large language models requires prioritizing relevant domain knowledge while minimizing interference from irrelevant domains. Existing approaches commonly use Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to train a separate adapter for each domain and combine these adapters within one model. However, they either weight adapters equally regardless of the input domain or dynamically weight adapters while still activating all of them including irrelevant ones. Additionally, while efficient, their low-rank structure limits performance. In contrast, upcycling is a model expansion method that adds experts and a router to a dense Transformer layer offering larger capacity than LoRA approaches. In this paper, we propose Domain-Specialized Upcycling (DS-Upcycling) for multi-domain adaptation. We introduce a new domain-aware supervision that allows the router to effectively learn to distinguish domains by selecting the appropriate experts. During fine-tuning on each new domain, we update only the corresponding expert and router while freezing all other parameters. Experiments show that our method achieves the highest average performance across the adapted domains compared to baselines while retaining general performance. With just 256 examples per domain for router supervision, DS-Upcycling achieves 90-98% routing accuracy after adaptation compared with 43-70% for routers trained without our approach.

title: Readiness-Constrained Pre-Islanding Dispatch for Military Microgrids
abstract: Military installation energy readiness depends on having sufficient resources to sustain mission-critical loads throughout a prolonged utility outage. This paper develops a method to help operators manage energy resources during normal grid-connected operation while preserving islanded readiness. A robust viability kernel identifies combinations of battery energy, fuel, and load-shifting capability sufficient to sustain critical load under uncertain demand and photovoltaic generation. A probability bound translates stochastic generator start failures and recovery into a deterministic generator count selected to meet a specified availability requirement at islanding. Case studies for a fourteen-day islanding requirement at 0.999 islanding-entry availability show that advance warning of an outage can be used to prepare resources to meet a higher readiness requirement before islanding begins. The case studies further demonstrate that economic-only operation and the evaluated fixed battery reserve policy can fail to sustain critical load for the required duration, whereas enforcing the resource-dependent requirement preserves readiness at a modest increase in modeled grid-connected operating cost. These results demonstrate how active resource management can preserve long-duration energy readiness. The framework also helps commanders understand how readiness changes with operating conditions, even when the available resources remain the same.
comment: 32 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables, submitted to Military Operations Research

title: Agentic process evidence
abstract: The way software gets built is changing dramatically. AI agents now create pull requests, select dependencies, refactor codebases, interpret test failures, and execute infrastructure changes across the entire Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). AI agents are autonomous team members, but unlike human engineers, they are ephemeral - their reasoning, decisions, and tool calls vanish the moment the session ends. Modern Security incidents involving intent mismatch or injection are becoming increasingly common - forcing us to address AI Agents as an insider threat. No widely adopted standard yet enables agentic provenance and governance and its obvious that you can't hold an ephemeral process accountable. The git log was designed for human commits. It shows what changed. It does not show what an AI agent did, which model it used, which tools it called, or whether anyone was accountable for the outcome. Every governance framework, every audit trail, every compliance control in the SDLC was built around one assumption: a human made the decision. That assumption no longer holds. This shift introduces 3 main procedural problems (not addressing scale) - Supply-chain vector - The agentic coder is software, so it is a supply-chain security risk. Policy guardrails - How to ensure the agentic coder is compliant with the policies of the organization. Task-alignment - How to align the agentic coder on its tasks and goals. We introduce Agentic Process Evidence (APE), a signed, tamper-evident, machine-readable attestation of agentic processes, linking the sessions to their outcome (process-aware logging). APE enables Policy-as-Code control over the agentic processes, allowing for human in the loop only when it's needed. We support the in-toto style attestation framework, and the protocol is aligned with the relevant regulations

title: Extracting non-Gaussian information of line-intensity maps with weighted skew spectra
abstract: The bispectrum of line-intensity maps carries cosmological and astrophysical information beyond the power spectrum, but its large data vector hampers the analysis of survey data. Skew spectra address this by compressing the bispectrum into a handful of power-spectrum-like observables, cross-spectra of the observed field with filtered squares of it. We present the first application of optimally weighted skew spectra to line-intensity mapping of galaxy-hosted emission, where all clustering and shot-noise terms are luminosity weighted and the mean intensity is unknown. We perform idealized real-space Fisher forecasts for a SPHEREx-like survey of H$α$ emission at $0.2 \lesssim z \lesssim 4.6$, in its deep fields and in a noisier all-sky configuration. First, the compression carries over to intensity maps: on perturbative scales and for a fixed redshift evolution of the emitters, four skew spectra, one of them matched to the shot noise, recover the bispectrum constraints on biases, shot noise and cosmological parameters to within a few percent. Second, the joint analysis of the power spectrum and the skew spectra measures the ratios of the second-order biases to the linear bias in each redshift bin. Within a bin the biases are degenerate with the unknown mean intensity, but their ratios are not, so their redshift evolution is measured without a model for the emitters. For emission that depends on halo mass alone, these ratios are determined by luminosity-weighted averages of the halo biases, so their evolution can test the halo-emission connection, including dependence on assembly history or environment. The bias ratios are not accessible to the tree-level real-space power spectrum alone. At $z \lesssim 3$ an all-sky SPHEREx-like configuration can detect departures of order $0.1$ in the bias ratios at $3σ$, while deeper fields perform better in the highest-redshift bins.
authors: Eleonora Vanzan;Azadeh Moradinezhad Dizgah;Ely D. Kovetz

title: Reinforcement Learning Under Runtime Confounding: Policy Learning and Off-Policy Evaluation
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly used to train robust, adaptable systems across healthcare, e-commerce, and robotics. In these settings, legal, ethical, or logistical concerns may preclude certain key variables that drive decisions from being collected during deployment time. This gives rise to a setting known as runtime confounding: the logged data hold full observability, but deployment time lacks knowledge of certain variables, known as runtime confounders. Unlike single timepoint and non-adaptive settings, runtime confounding under reinforcement learning has the potential to propagate over time, as earlier decisions affect future states, observations, and action assignments, leading to biased learning. We address these problems with three contributions: we (1) develop policy learning algorithms under runtime-confounding, (2) develop semi-parametric efficient off-policy estimation procedures, and (3) provide diagnostics for understanding the price of runtime confounding.

title: One Vector or Many? Clustered Optimal-Transport Steering under Quantization
abstract: Activation steering changes what a language model generates by editing its hidden states at inference time. Its most common form adds one vector, the difference of class means (DiM), to every hidden state. CHaRS (concept heterogeneity-aware representation steering) uses optimal transport instead: an entropic plan pairs the clusters of the two classes, and each hidden state moves along a mixture of the cluster displacements, weighted toward its nearest clusters. We study this family of clustered optimal-transport maps for toxicity mitigation in Gemma-2-2B and Granite-3.1-2B, and ask what the plan adds to DiM and whether that survives INT8 and NF4 quantization. We prove an identity: whatever the plan, the displacements averaged with the cluster sizes as weights equal DiM, so a clustered map can differ from DiM only for tokens whose routing weights depart from the cluster sizes. In the CHaRS protocol they stay close, and CHaRS is statistically equivalent to Mean-AcT, which adds DiM at every layer, in all eight pre-specified equivalence tests. A variant fitted on individual tokens, which routes each token mainly to its nearest clusters, leaves 37-39% less toxicity than DiM on Gemma and 51-61% less on Granite at steering strength 3 (toxic-bert), where DiM already removes 76-85% of it. Two other toxicity classifiers confirm the gain on Granite, but on Gemma only one does. At equal strength the variant has somewhat higher perplexity, but at matched toxicity it is slightly more fluent than DiM. Yet a nearly constant map from the same clusters also leaves about 30% less toxicity, so the role of treating tokens differently remains open. Under INT8 and NF4 the variant still leaves less toxicity than DiM, and transferring it from full precision to the NF4 model instead of refitting it adds no significant toxicity after correction for multiple tests.

title: Rethinking Pre-pretraining
abstract: We report that allocating compute to synthetic pre-pretraining (PPT) never outperforms pure natural-language training in our compute-matched experiments. This holds across four PPT curricula (k-Dyck, neural cellular automata (NCA), declarative reference corpora, and code) and three training regimes: data-constrained, data-unconstrained, and a high token-to-parameter-ratio regime (881M parameters trained on 50B tokens). When natural language is scarce, repeated epochs over a 100M-token corpus beat every synthetic curriculum on natural-language validation loss, with no consistent downstream accuracy advantage from PPT. We find that PPT gains reported in prior work are sensitive to the weight initialization scheme. In an NCA reproduction, we recover a 5.4% perplexity improvement from PPT under the original initialization scheme. An alternative scheme improves both methods, but the no-PPT baseline more, closing the gap between them. However, when PPT receives additional compute rather than a share of the natural-language budget, gains persist at small natural-language budgets even with improved initialization, but disappear by 1B tokens. Finally, models forget what they learn during PPT in subsequent natural-language training; interleaving the same data throughout training prevents forgetting, but does not significantly improve natural-language performance. Our results suggest limited benefits of synthetic pre-pretraining as a distinct training stage and motivate rethinking how such data are used in language model training.

title: Can the $\sim 5$ kpc starburst ring in the Milky Way create the eROSITA bubbles?
abstract: eROSITA bubbles (eRBs) in our Galaxy are thought to be due to the energy injection by the central star-forming region or the central supermassive black hole. Identifying the origin of these bubbles is crucial in constraining the origin of the Fermi Bubbles and the nature of the Galactic feedback. However, some recent opinions suggest that the eRBs may not even have been produced by any central source, but rather a result of a star-formation ring at $R\sim 5$ kpc. In this letter, we perform detailed hydrodynamic simulations to refute that claim and show that such a ring of star formation alone is not able to produce the symmetric eROSITA bubbles - one needs a compact energy injection from the Galactic Center to produce these bubbles. Our study, therefore, suggests that the eROSITA bubbles truly represent the nuclear outflow from our Galaxy.

title: Data-driven Regularization for Inverse Problems
abstract: In many applications, we are interested in studying an object of interest $x$. However, its properties are often not directly measurable. Instead, we only observe $y = F(x)$, where the (known) function $F$ is referred to as the forward mapping. To infer about $x$ from the observation $y$, we seek an (approximate) inverse mapping $x \approx F^{-1}(y)$. This process is known as solving the inverse problem. In practice, the inverse mapping $F^{-1}$ may be ill-defined or discontinuous, which forces us to choose a certain solution from many possible ones based on prior assumptions on $x$. Such assumptions about $x$ are typically incorporated into the inversion process through regularization. Therefore, the first part of this course focuses on the classical regularization theory of inverse problems. In the second part, we transition to algorithmic approaches for solving inverse problems. The foundation for this lies in the variational formulation of inverse problems, where reconstructions are obtained by minimizing specific functionals. Here, we will explore key optimization principles, discuss their practical implementation, and examine how they contribute to robust reconstructions. Today, classical methods are often modified to incorporate data-driven machine learning techniques, which improve the empirical performance. However, this often comes at the cost of explainability or convergence guarantees. Such properties are critical, for example, in medical applications, where one wants to be confident that reconstructed abnormalities are of physical nature and not phantoms resulting from the method. For these reasons, we discuss a number of machine learning methods for inverse problems, such as unrolling techniques, learned regularizers and plug-and-play methods, and explore their performance guarantees.

title: Smooth Threshold GARCH: Quasi Maximum Likelihood Estimation and Empirical Evidence
abstract: It is well established that the volatility of daily stock returns responds asymmetrically to news, as described by the news impact curve (NIC), which relates volatility to the previous return. Empirical studies suggest that (i) volatility reacts more strongly to negative returns than to positive returns of the same magnitude, (ii) the point of asymmetry, where the NIC attains its minimum, is positive, and (iii) returns above this point often do not increase volatility at all. The popular GJR and A-GARCH models each rule out one of these features. We study the Smooth Threshold GARCH (STGARCH) model, which nests both and allows for (i)-(iii) by combining an estimated threshold, the point of asymmetry, with separate slopes on either side of it. Although the likelihood is not twice continuously differentiable in the threshold, we show that the quasi maximum likelihood estimator is consistent and converges at the usual $\sqrt{n}$-rate, whether or not (iii) holds. If (iii) does not hold, the estimator is asymptotically normal, while if it holds, the slope above the threshold is zero, a value on the boundary of the parameter space, and the limit is non-Gaussian. In that case, the $t$-statistic for (iii) converges to the positive part of a standard normal variable, and the $t$-test of the GJR model remains valid. These results allow us to test the GJR and A-GARCH models, as well as (i)-(iii), within the STGARCH using standard normal critical values. For daily returns on five major stock indices, we reject the GJR model for all five and the A-GARCH model for three, suggesting that the STGARCH improves upon both. Volatility is lowest after returns 0.3-0.6 percentage points above their conditional mean, in line with (i) and (ii). Finally, the hypothesis in (iii) is rejected for two of the five indices.

title: SDSS-V LVM: Mapping of plasma temperatures in the Lagoon Nebula reveals the origin of long-standing chemical abundance discrepancies
abstract: Knowing the chemical composition of interstellar gas is essential for understanding the chemical evolution of galaxies. Ionized nebulae provide key laboratories for this purpose, where chemical abundances are commonly derived from emission lines of heavy ions such as doubly ionized oxygen, $O^{++}$. Abundances can be inferred either from collisionally excited lines (CELs) or from recombination lines (RLs). However, for more than 80 years, the former have yielded systematically lower abundances than the latter. We map this ''abundance discrepancy'' using the first spatially resolved integral field unit (IFU) observations of $O^{++}$ RLs and CELs across a Milky Way H II region: the Lagoon Nebula (a.k.a. M8). Modeling the data using a plasma temperature perturbation model, we present unequivocal evidence that electron temperature ($T_e$) fluctuations drive the abundance discrepancy in M8. We find a tight correlation between the abundance discrepancy and the difference between $T_e$ derived from the classical CEL method and a hybrid RL/CEL approach. We identify this Te discrepancy as an observational proxy for the amplitude of the thermal fluctuations, providing a new, direct way to quantify their effect on nebular abundances. The correlation constrains the mean electron temperature of the gas. Adopting this mean temperature reconciles CEL and RL abundances, effectively eliminating the abundance discrepancy.

title: AI Cosmos: An Agentic Infra for Situated Learning
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can improve task performance during learning, yet these gains do not necessarily reflect learners' ability to thereafter apply the knowledge and skills independently. We present AI Cosmos, an agentic infrastructure for situated learning that organizes learning around two complementary principles: scenario-based participation and cumulative assets of practice. AI Cosmos organizes learners and role-specialized agents within learning scenarios that integrate task-relevant knowledge and, when needed, executable workbenches. An asset-memory loop preserves the processes and outcomes of practice as reusable assets with explicit provenance and dependencies. We evaluate scenario-based interaction through two preregistered randomized controlled studies examining the acquisition of legal reasoning and programming competence, holding the same underlying LLM across conditions. AI Cosmos achieves greater learning gains than a conventional LLM in legal reasoning and higher mastery of unseen programming problems than an LLM-as-Teacher baseline.

title: Four-hundred Very Metal-poor Stars Studied with LAMOST and Subaru. IV. Heavy Element Enhanced Stars
abstract: We perform a homogeneous analysis of 82 heavy-element-enhanced metal-poor stars from the\\ LAMOST/Subaru sample, including 64 $r$-process-enhanced stars, 2 limited-$r$ stars, and 16 stars exhibiting significant or moderate carbon enhancement (comprising 9 $s$-process-enhanced, 2 $r$-process-enhanced, 2 $r$/$s$, and 3 $r$+$s$ stars). Systematic differences in $\mathrm{[X/Eu]}$ between $r$-I and $r$-II stars, together with their distinct dynamical properties, suggest that $r$-II stars likely formed in low-mass dwarf galaxies where contamination from additional nucleosynthetic channels was minimal. We have also discovered a number of peculiar objects. We identify an extremely metal-poor $r$-II star, J1158+0734 ($\mathrm{[Fe/H]}$ = -2.93), whose enhanced Zn abundance ($\mathrm{[Zn/Fe]}$ = +0.67) is best explained by yields from a high-energy, massive core-collapse supernova. The surface abundances of $s$-process-enhanced stars exhibit pronounced dispersion, consistent with enrichment from AGB progenitors with diverse properties. Notably, one star, J2256+0215, reveals compelling evidence for additional evolutionary mixing, as indicated by its unusually low carbon abundance ($\mathrm{[C/Fe]}$ = +0.08) and extremely low $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C ratio of 2.33. Additionally, we identify 3 $r$+$s$ stars whose abundance patterns reveal combined contributions from both the $r$- and $s$-processes. We further propose a modified diagnostic scheme for the identification of CEMP-$r$+$s$ stars, defined as: -0.2 $\leqslant$ $\mathrm{[La/Nd]}$ $\leqslant$ 0.2 and -0.5 $\leqslant$ $\mathrm{[Eu/Nd]}$ $\leqslant$ 0.0.
authors: Yangming Lin;Haining Li;Wako Aoki;Ruizheng Jiang;Tadafumi Matsuno;Zhenyu He;Ruizhi Zhang;Zhuohan Li;Satoshi Honda;Gang Zhao
comment: 26 pages, published in The Astrophysical Journal

title: How Different are Different Differences-in-Differences? A Large-Scale Meta-Analysis
abstract: I use AI-assisted replication to assess the empirical importance of negative weights in two-way fixed effects (TWFE) estimation, analyzing 1,430 staggered-adoption specifications from 116 economics papers. TWFE estimates are highly correlated with modern difference-in-differences estimates, with sign reversals in 12.0-14.9% of comparisons and greater precision for TWFE. Hierarchical models accounting for estimation noise imply estimand correlations of 91-97% and a 0.7-2.4% probability of a statistically significant TWFE estimate opposing the modern estimand's sign. These findings suggest negative weights may be a less serious problem in practice and illustrate how AI can support systematic, large-scale empirical assessments of new econometric methods.

title: Co--dsorption of terrylene and tetrapentacontane on hexagonal boron nitride - towards a two-dimensional Shpolskii matrix
abstract: Organic molecular emitters are promising building blocks for quantum technologies, but their use at two-dimensional interfaces is limited by diffusion, aggregation, and photobleaching. We present work towards constructing an ultrathin two-dimensional Shpolskii-like host-guest matrix on hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) by co-depositing terrylene fluorophores with the long-chain tetrapentacontane in a solution-phase process. We demonstrate that this approach disperses terrylene in a roughly one-nanometer-thin alkane layer without detectable phase separation and allows tuning the emitter density from ensembles to isolated emitters showing characteristic blinking behavior consistent with single-molecule fluorescence. Time-lapse confocal microscopy, autocorrelation analysis, and fluorescence recovery after photobleaching show that suppressed diffusion and stable emitter positions can be achieved in several samples with a tetrapentacontane matrix. Encapsulation with hBN from the top side further improves photostability, with emitters demonstrating long lifetimes despite high photon doses. Successful co-adsorption of isolated emitters and alkane matrix is a milestone towards extending Shpolskii-type molecular isolation to hBN and provides a route towards stable, interface-integrated molecular qubits.
authors: Rong Sun;Tolibjon Abdurakhmonov;Jan-Niklas Heidkamp;Julian Schröer;Paul Weinbrenner;Kenji Watanabe;Takashi Taniguchi;Tobias Korn;Oliver Kühn;Friedemann Reinhard

title: Multi-split Multiple-sets Implicit Convex Feasibility Seeking As Split Inverse Problems
abstract: We introduce a new class of problems, termed multi-split multiple-sets implicit convex feasibility problems (MSMS-ICFPs), define a proximity function for it and analyze its properties under certain assumptions on the involved general point-to-set operators. Additionally, we discuss its properties for a special class of point-to-set operators. For these kinds of point-to-set operators, we deploy a new iterative algorithm to solve the associated MSMS-ICFP and show that any sequence generated by it converges in norm to a solution of the MSMS-ICFP whenever a solution exists (i.e., in the consistent case). We also define a generalized proximity function for the MSMS-ICFP using the Bregman distance. Based on this function, we present a generalized simultaneous projection gradient algorithm for the split feasibility problem with multiple output sets, by examining various related results. We conclude by discussing several further special cases of the MSMS-ICFP.

title: Channelled versus Isotropic Accretion of Galaxy Groups onto Clusters: Kinematics, Spin Alignment, and Assembly Bias
abstract: Galaxy clusters grow by accreting groups from the cosmic web, but whether the route of infall (along a cluster-connected filament or from the open field) imprints a group's kinematics, spin, and orbit remains unmeasured at scale. We classify $212{,}704$ group-cluster infall pairs across $27{,}029$ clusters in the $(1\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{Gpc})^3$ MDPL2 simulation into primary (cluster-connected), secondary (tributary), primary-outskirt, and isotropic channels using DisPerSE filaments. (i) In both channelled classes, group spin axes lie mainly parallel to the filament below a `spin-flip' mass and perpendicular above it, $\log_{10} M_\mathrm{flip}\;[h^{-1}\,M_{\odot}] = 13.07$ and $13.12$, a $0.05$-dex offset consistent with zero, lying $1.3-1.4$ dex above the field, while isotropic groups show no flip; $M_\mathrm{flip}$ stays radially flat out to $7\,R_{200}$. (ii) Within the primary class $M_\mathrm{flip}$ rises with the linear mass density of the host filament, from $12.96$ (thin tendrils) to $13.44$ (dense bridges); matching group mass, cluster mass and distance keeps the rise positive but leaves its size uncertain ($0.07-0.58$ dex). (iii) Isotropic groups fall below random alignment at $2\,R_{200}$ ($41$ per cent within $60^\circ$, a $4.3σ$ deficit). Primary groups show $85$ per cent velocity-filament alignment at $2\,R_{200}$, and isotropic groups infall $150-180\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ faster, and more radially, out to $5\,R_{200}$. At matched distance isotropic groups are therefore predicted to reach orbital pericentres up to $10$ per cent smaller than primary groups, whose smaller pooled pericentres reflect only their proximity to the cluster. The topological route of accretion, and within it the host filament's linear density, shapes how groups enter clusters, testable with wide-area spectroscopic surveys.
authors: Ankit Singh;Frazer Pearce;Meghan Gray;Ulrike Kuchner;Julian Onions;Gustavo Yepes;Alexander Knebe

title: Mapping cluster angular momentum with the rotational kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect
abstract: Galaxy clusters carry angular momentum. If the intracluster gas rotates coherently, the kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (kSZ) effect imprints a dipole on the microwave sky centered on the cluster. We show that microwave maps alone can be used to reconstruct a noisy vector field tracing the projected angular momentum of the ionized gas. We present an optimal multifrequency matched filter (MMF) that isolates the rotational kSZ (rkSZ) signal from the much larger miscentered thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ) effect, cosmic microwave, and infrared background contributions, improving on both real-space oriented stacking and matched filtering of maps cleaned with full-sky multifrequency weights. For the rkSZ profile, we introduce a simple model for coherent intracluster gas rotation and validate it against TNG-Cluster and TNG300-1. The model consists of differentially rotating concentric shells with constant equatorial tangential velocity, characterized by a mass- and redshift-indepedent tangential-to-circular velocity ratio of $v_{\rm tan}/V_{c,200c}=0.18$. Using this model, we forecast single-cluster signal-to-noise (SNR) as a function of mass and redshift for Simons Observatory; cross-correlation with an external catalog of rotation proxies yields a cumulative detection SNR. For an idealized mass-limited catalog with perfectly known spin directions, the cumulative SNR of our optimal MMF reaches $\approx 53$, $25$, and $6$ when including all clusters above $\log_{10}(M_{200c}/M_\odot)>14$, 14.5, and 15, respectively. This work provides a practical framework for CMB measurements of intracluster gas rotation, with applications to the rotational contribution to non-thermal pressure in cluster mass calibration, as well as spin alignments and clustering biases.
authors: Jack Y. L. Kwok;Bernardita Ried Guachalla;William R. Coulton;Selim C. Hotinli;Emmanuel Schaan

title: Confinement Controlled Phase-Pure 2D Layered Perovskites for Band-Edge Engineering
abstract: Controlling the number n of connected octahedra layers in two-dimensional metal halide perovskites enables fine control of the semiconductor band gap that is highly advantageous for optoelectronic and light emission applications. Phase purity in terms of n is crucial towards narrow emission bands and the design of band structure alignment for charge carrier funneling. We present a simple and scalable synthesis method using cesium and butylammonium as A-cations to fabricate microcrystal powders of 2D lead bromide perovskites that results in samples with very high n-phase purity. The obtained microcrystals show a sharp onset in absorbance and single narrow emission peak in UV-blue spectral range, and we confirm their structure and composition with X-ray diffraction and energy dispersive spectroscopy. We show that we can tailor the spectral absorption of microcrystals samples by controlled mixing of the n-phase pure powders, and we demonstrate this capability with spectral photocurrent measurements using pellets pressed from pure and mixed powders. Both the spectral and dynamic response of the photocurrent of the pellets depend strongly on the composition of the powders, highlighting the design potential of our approach towards band-edge engineering.

title: Safe Platooning under Input Constraints with Link-Wise Velocity String Stability
abstract: We propose a decentralized controller for vehicle platoons with different braking and propulsion limits. The method uses only local distance and velocity measurements and requires neither online optimization nor exact vehicle parameters. The design combines a braking-distance safety margin with an adaptive funnel that relaxes the spacing requirement during propulsion saturation. A standstill mechanism prevents backward motion and supports stop-and-go operation. Under explicit uniform conditions on the vehicle parameters, controller settings, and initial states, we prove that closed-loop solutions exist for all time, collisions are avoided, and input limits are satisfied. Moreover, each follower tracks its predecessor's velocity range with gain one, up to an explicit additive offset determined by the funnel width and the braking-distance term. This bound establishes link-wise velocity string stability. Both the offset and the bounds on speeds and spacing errors are independent of vehicle index and platoon length. Simulations with 2 to 100 followers illustrate safety and bounded velocity deviations under disturbances and actuator limits.
authors: Panagiotis S. Trakas;Charalampos P. Bechlioulis;Thomas Berger

title: When to spend privacy: optimal allocation in private learning
abstract: Privacy accounting bounds the cumulative privacy cost of Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent but does not determine how to allocate a fixed budget across iterations. We formulate the complete Gaussian noise-variance schedule as an open-loop control under a composed zero-Concentrated Differential Privacy constraint, explicitly accounting for schedule selection. For expected quadratic terminal tracking, we prove that every local minimizer exhausts the certified budget, yielding an exact-budget simplex formulation. We introduce Privacy-Budget Adjoint Mirror Descent (PB-AMD), combining pathwise adjoint gradients with entropic updates that preserve positivity, charge floors, and the prescribed budget. Under regularity and coercivity assumptions, we establish existence and budget stability of optimal schedules, design-to-training utility stability, and deterministic, stochastic, and sample-average stationarity guarantees. A linear-quadratic reduction yields an explicit square-root allocation law. Experiments demonstrate tracking improvements over several allocation rules and predictive improvements over uniform allocation in a learning-rate restart setting, where learning-rate allocation performs similarly. Comparisons at a common stationarity tolerance show lower schedule-optimization times than projected gradient descent on the tested problems. The framework connects certified privacy accounting with optimization through nonlinear training dynamics.

title: LC-Resonance Placement Limits and Damping Recovery in Virtual-Admittance-Based Grid-Forming Inverter Control
abstract: Compact LC-filter design and inner-loop control must be coordinated for stable grid-forming operation. This paper quantifies how current-loop proportional gain constrains LC-resonance placement in virtual-admittance-based dual-loop control with unity voltage-feedback decoupling (VFD) and capacitor-voltage active damping. Equivalent-impedance analysis identifies gain-dependent contraction of the positive-resistance region. Delayed inverter-current feedback opposes VFD-assisted damping above one-sixth of the sampling frequency. Simple proportional-path frequency shaping recovers an admissible effective-gain window while retaining unity VFD and leaving the resonant path unchanged. Reduced-model criteria, checked against the complete model, link window closure to a nominal resonance-placement limit near one-third of the sampling frequency under single-sampled single-update operation over the studied gain range. A 3-kVA prototype demonstrates an 83.3% LC-product reduction at comparable voltage and nominal current crossovers. A separate comparison with the same high-resonance filter demonstrates stable operation at 2.68 times the unshaped nominal current crossover. Output-impedance analysis and grid-connected tests identify additional grid-dependent gain constraints.

title: Can LLMs Ignore What They Know? Measuring Knowledge Leakage in Persona-Based User Simulation
abstract: When persona-conditioned responses are read as respondent-level simulations, each response should reflect the described persona's knowledge, and the respondent written to know nothing must act as if the model's knowledge were not there. We test whether it can, and find persistent favourable-item real-twin rating separation under the tested low-knowledge and explicit-ignorance prompts. We define the resulting problem (knowledge leakage: a response bias that arises when knowledge the real user could not have enters the simulated response) and present a methodology for measuring it quantitatively. The core instrument pairs real items with fabricated twins matched in surface form: screened fabricated variants designed to minimize prior item-specific knowledge. The paired difference therefore provides a diagnostic contrast for knowledge leakage even in rating tasks where no answer is correct. In a rating experiment across three knowledge-handling arms and five API endpoints from two model families, we find, first, that the personas we test do not fully suppress real-item existence and familiarity signals: a favourable-item real-twin rating contrast remains under an explicit in-context statement that the persona has never heard of the item. Second, the unfavourable-item contrast reverses sign across domain groups: pooling all unfavourable-content items across domains the contrast sits near zero (+0.077 [-0.057, +0.204]), yet the same estimator in the same conditions returns -0.359 where the rating scale asks about an item's documented hazard and +0.438 where it asks about a company or an organisation. A pooled analysis of unfavourable-content items against zero therefore does not detect the opposing domain-group differences. All estimates are conditional on the adequacy of twin construction and screening; human low-knowledge baselines remain necessary for population-level interpretation.
authors: Sangmin Lee;Sangwon Lee;Sungbeom Choi;Jeeseung Park;Kibeom Myoung
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at UserSim @ NeurIPS 2026 (non-archival workshop)

title: Iterative Methods for Solving New Generalized Absolute Value Equations
abstract: In this paper, we propose two iterative methods, the modified Picard method (MPM) and the generalized Traub method (GTM), to solve a new generalized absolute value equation (NGAVE). We establish their convergence under appropriate assumptions. Additionally, numerical examples demonstrate the effectiveness and applicability of the developed algorithms.

title: Prompts and probabilities in the linguistic assessment of language models: Evidence from semantic focus-sensitivity
abstract: As language models (LMs) have improved, an increasingly common means of evaluating their linguistic competence is through explicit prompting (e.g., "Which sentence is more acceptable?"). Prior work indicates that such prompting underperforms compared to standard token-probability-based methods in smaller models, but improves in larger models. We test this in a new domain: semantic focus-sensitivity, responsible for contrasts like "Lucy only SWAM yesterday" vs. "Lucy only swam YESTERDAY". Testing models of various sizes using text-based focus markers like boldface and italics, we find universal above-chance performance for token probabilities. Prompting results mostly align with previous findings, but in some larger models they outperform probabilities by a wide margin. We propose that this is because LMs are not prone to produce out-of-the-blue focus marking, which muddies results from token probabilities in a way that does not affect prompting. We test this by replacing standard focus markers with randomly generated ones; token probabilities still beat chance but show significantly greater performance decrease compared to prompting. These results suggest that metalinguistic prompting, while non-trivial for LMs, can also be more robust when testing stylistically atypical data. We argue that this has important consequences for the assessment of LMs' language competence, even if LMs do not perform metalinguistic judgments through human-like introspection.

title: Tokenizer Tokens Tell Training Tales
abstract: Tokenizers are usually treated as fixed preprocessing tools, but they are trained on text and can retain traces of that text in their vocabularies. We ask whether a BPE tokenizer can reveal if a candidate dataset was part of its training corpus. The key observation is simple. Rare strings become tokens only when enough corpus frequency pushes them over the merge threshold. This suggests that membership signal should appear in rare tokens used by the candidate dataset, rather than in the order in which merges were made. We formalize this under a threshold model of BPE inclusion, showing that the likelihood-ratio test assigns its largest weights to tokens that are rare in the background but frequent in the candidate dataset. The same model suggests that merge rank and merge-graph position should not add a first-order membership signal once token existence and dataset frequency are known. We instantiate this view as RTAM-Fusion, which calibrates rare-token mass with shadow tokenizers and combines signals across rarity levels. On the tokenizer membership benchmark, RTAM-Fusion improves AUC and balanced accuracy over Vocabulary Overlap while using fewer shadow tokenizers. Existing defenses also continue to leak membership signal against adaptive attackers at production vocabulary sizes. Code: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/RTAM-Fusion-F7EE/

title: A MUSE and MeerKAT study of dynamics and star formation in HCG 16
abstract: Context. Hickson Compact Groups (HCGs) present an ideal environment for studying galaxy interactions. HCG 16 is a group of five galaxies in an intermediate stage of evolution (Phase 2), with several members displaying signs of interaction, including distorted morphologies, tidal features, and enhanced star formation rates. Aims. We aim to better understand the evolution of HCG 16 and its member galaxies, focusing on the relationship between neutral hydrogen and star formation, while reconstructing the interaction history of the group. Methods. We analysed MUSE data processed with pyPipe3D to extract H$α$ images and stellar population synthesis results, and reduced MeerKAT data to produce a high-resolution HI cube. We examined the structure and dynamics of the H$α$ and HI lines in both 2D and 3D, and produced spatially resolved star formation histories to compare the inner and outer parts of the galaxies. Results. We identify a major star formation episode in HCG 16 beginning ~400-500 Myr ago, coinciding with the passage of NGC 848 close to the other member galaxies, and that continued at least until 50-60 Myr ago in some galaxies. The HI distribution is highly perturbed in the group, although HCG 16a retains a nearly regular disk, while HCG 16b has associated H$α$ tails. Conclusions. The passage of NGC 848 probably activated star formation in HCG 16, but cannot by itself explain the current starburst activity in HCG 16c and 16d. The evolution of the group is better explained by multiple interactions among its members than by a single strong encounter.
authors: Ixaka Labadie-García;Enrique Pérez;Julián Garrido;Roger Ianjamasimanana;Lourdes Verdes-Montenegro

title: Excitons in solid molecular hydrogen from quantum Monte Carlo
abstract: We use quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) methods to investigate the lowest neutral excitation of solid molecular hydrogen in phase-I under increasing compression, with emphasis on structural and response properties. We employ QMC wave functions for the excited state that feature only a single orbital substitution, or a multideterminant expansion including every single particle-hole transition, and compare the results with the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) and time-dependent density-functional theory (TDDFT). We examine a number of nuclear configurations representing thermal and quantum fluctuations. The effect of the multideterminant expansion is marginal on the QMC excitation energies but crucial on the exciton localization and related quantities, irrespective of full optimization and imaginary time projection. In the strong insulating regime at low density, multideterminant QMC results match and in some cases surpass the degree of localization afforded by BSE. A similar trend is observed for transition dipole moments and excitation-induced forces, with generally good agreement between QMC and BSE but marked discrepancies for nuclear configurations where localization differs significantly. TDDFT generally gives a more extended exciton with correspondingly weaker transition dipole moments. These differences decrease upon compression, as the system approaches a semiconducting regime where multiple particle-hole transitions are less important.
authors: Edgar Josué Landinez Borda;Ravindra Shinde;Claudia Filippi;Markus Holzmann;Saverio Moroni
comment: Main document 9 pages, 6 figures, supplementary information 14 pages, 13 figures, to appear on PRB

title: Ammonium thiocyanate enables in-situ structural templating of MAPbI3 via quasi-2D perovskite scaffold
abstract: Ammonium thiocyanate (NH4SCN) has been used extensively to improve the current extraction and device performance of quasi-two-dimensional perovskite solar cells. Whilst this additive has been shown to influence quasi-2D perovskite crystallisation, a detailed understanding of its mechanism has not yet been established. Through spectroscopic and structural studies, we demonstrate that NH4SCN enables quasi-2D perovskite phases to structurally template the dominant 3D phase. Contrary to previous reports, we suggest that the benefit of this additive comes from an improvement to the 3D perovskite structure, not from charges transferring through vertically oriented 2D perovskite layers. We show that this additive provides kinetic control over the quasi-2D phase formation, suppressing the unfavourable n = 1 perovskite phase and promoting the growth of high-n 2D scaffold phases by extending the nucleation window. This promotes the in-situ templated growth of MAPbI3. We provide robust structural analysis demonstrating highly (110)-ordered 3D perovskite, with the mechanism confirmed by close lattice matching between this phase and quasi-2D phases. Furthermore, we show that this structural control is cation dependent, requiring both close lattice matching between quasi-2D and 3D perovskite phases, and successful kinetic control of the relevant quasi-2D phases.
authors: Sophie Tucker;Isaac Metcalf;Rachel C. Kilbride;Elena J. Cassella;Jessica H. Persaud;Faiz Mandani;Niranjana Raj;Max Allen;Charlie H. G. Nicholls;David G. Lidzey;Alice L. B. Pyne;Robert D. J. Oliver;Silvia Motti;Jacky Even;Aditya D. Mohite;Alexandra J. Ramadan

title: Compressed Orientation Reachability Maps for Sub-Second Robotic Needle Entry Point Planning
abstract: In the context of multi-stage trajectory planning for robotic percutaneous liver interventions, identifying a kinematically feasible entry point remains a critical computational bottleneck. Existing methods rely on exhaustive inverse kinematics or randomized searches, incurring delays of 13 to 27 seconds per target and limiting real-time intraoperative adaptation. This paper introduces an Orientation-Based Reachability Map (ORM) that precomputes the kinematic feasibility of a 6 Degrees of Freedom (DoF) serial manipulator across 188,873 workspace positions and encodes orientation feasibility into a compact, indexed 83 MB map. A Just-In-Time (JIT) compiled runtime pipeline replaces live optimization with near-instantaneous array lookups. Experimental evaluation demonstrates a reduction in planning latency from 13.5-26.9 s to 0.289-0.349 s per target while maintaining high geometric fidelity, achieving a mean convex hull volume overlap ratio of 0.933 and a mean alpha-shape volume ratio of 0.976 relative to the baseline reachable point cloud. The proposed ORM framework enables sub-second entry point planning and provides an efficient computational framework for robotic needle insertion in percutaneous liver ablation.
authors: Prabhu Nithin Gollapudi;Andreas Maier;Franziska Mathis-Ullrich;Water Zhao;Jia Wang;Siming Bayer

title: Threshold Regression with a Nearly Integrated Threshold Variable
abstract: This paper considers threshold regression with an integrated or local-to-unity threshold variable and a threshold fixed in levels. We study the least squares threshold estimator and establish its asymptotic theory under both fixed and diminishing threshold effects. Under a fixed effect, the threshold estimator has a compound Cox argmin limit, whereas under a diminishing effect, its limiting distribution is characterized by a two-sided Brownian argmax with a random scale. We also develop likelihood ratio inference, which is asymptotically pivotal under a diminishing effect and conservative under Gaussian errors for a fixed effect, and show that conventional $t$-ratios for the slope coefficients remain asymptotically standard normal. A sup-Wald test is proposed to detect threshold effects that may be too small for consistent threshold localization. We further extend the framework to allow for integrated slope regressors and for contemporaneous endogeneity of the threshold variable, showing that the leading endogenous contribution cancels over shrinking threshold windows. Monte Carlo simulations examine the finite-sample performance of the proposed methods. An illustration using public debt and economic growth highlights the relevance of allowing for a persistent threshold variable.

title: Which wind and solar modelling choices matter? Effects on capacity factors, energy droughts and European power system configuration
abstract: Europe's future power system will rely heavily on wind and solar power and must remain resilient during prolonged periods of low wind and solar generation, known as variable renewable energy (VRE) droughts. To capture such rare events, adequacy assessments increasingly draw on decades of weather data, but the conversion of weather into power is largely treated as fixed. It remains unclear which modelling choices in this conversion matter for representing these droughts, and whether they matter as much as the weather itself. Here we systematically compare these choices side by side (bias correction, wind speed extrapolation, capacity layouts, turbine and photovoltaic configurations, and wake losses) and trace their effects through VRE droughts to the design of a net-zero European power system, using 85 years of reanalysis data. We find that modelling choices barely change how often VRE droughts occur or when the system is stressed. They do, however, determine how much capacity is needed to withstand that stress. By altering the electricity delivered during droughts, they shift required capacity by up to 480 GW, which is comparable to the spread across the most critical weather years. Modelling exercises should therefore use multiple weather years; bias-correct and regionally validate weather inputs; explicitly represent resource heterogeneity, forward-looking technologies, and wake losses; and judge these choices by their effect on the low-generation tail, not only on the mean.
authors: L. Karkossa;A. Grochowicz;M. J. Koivisto;A. Hahmann;M. VIctoria

title: Probabilistic Meshless Methods on Manifolds
abstract: Probabilistic meshless methods solve partial differential equations (PDEs) by placing a Gaussian process prior on the solution and conditioning it on the PDE at a finite set of collocation nodes. The posterior provides both an approximation of the solution and a Bayesian quantification of its error. While these methods are well established on Euclidean domains, their extension to manifolds lacks, to our knowledge, any convergence analysis. We extend them to compact manifolds and study their convergence in two settings. First, for known manifolds whose Laplace-Beltrami eigenpairs are available, the prior can be evaluated exactly, but the PDE operator generally cannot be applied to it in closed form. We replace this operator by a standard generalized finite difference discretization on a point cloud sampled from the manifold, and show that the resulting method is consistent at the points of the cloud, at a rate governed by their fill distance. Second, for implicit manifolds, known only through a point cloud, both the prior and the operator must be approximated. We propose a new generalized finite difference scheme with a free stencil radius, and show that it retains the consistency of the standard construction while controlling the growth of its coefficients, and that an appropriate radius yields uniform convergence of the discrete Gram matrix. In both settings, we derive error bounds for the posterior mean which separate the collocation error intrinsic to the method from the error due to approximating the operator and, for implicit manifolds, the prior. Experiments on the circle, the sphere and the flat torus confirm our theoretical claims. On real-world cortical thickness data, our approach attains the accuracy of established discretizations, while conditioning on fewer than a tenth of the observations and providing a credible interval at every vertex.

title: Attention, Dynamic Wave and Hybrid Sequence Mixers in Language Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) rely on Multi-Head Attention (MHA) for sequence modeling, but scaling to long contexts is constrained by the quadratic cost of attention, motivating sub-quadratic recurrent alternatives. This paper formalizes a Dynamic Wave recurrent layer, based on input-dependent exponential damping and cosine phase modulation, and evaluates three 10.94M-parameter configurations (Pure Transformer, Pure Wave, and Hybrid Wave-Attention) on TinyStories under perplexity, latency, throughput and peak VRAM profiling up to 4096 tokens. The Hybrid configuration reaches the best perplexity, 5.95 on the full held-out split against 6.93 for the Transformer and 7.26 for Pure Wave. The efficiency picture, however, is governed by implementation rather than by architecture. Against an unfused attention baseline, Pure Wave uses 78.7% less peak VRAM at a 4096-token context (1404.3 MB vs. 6601.6 MB); against a fused scaled-dot-product attention kernel the same comparison yields no advantage at all (1404.3 MB vs. 1403.6 MB), and in training mode Pure Wave is 8.3% more expensive than the Transformer. Likewise, hoisting elementwise terms out of the recurrence loop speeds the layer up 2.53-fold with no custom kernel, reducing its latency gap to attention from 2.48-fold to 1.12-fold. A hybrid stack is found to inherit the cost of its more expensive mixer rather than the advantage of its cheaper one, its peak VRAM matching the Pure Transformer to within 0.1%. A closed-form memory model reproduces these measurements and predicts the context length beyond which attention overtakes the vocabulary projection. The findings indicate that reported efficiency gains for recurrent attention replacements must be stated relative to a named attention backend and a named implementation, and that hybridization is best justified on quality grounds.

title: KV Cache Quantization for Diffusion Language Models
abstract: KV cache quantization is well studied for autoregressive language models, where cached prefix states are exact under causal attention and quantization is mainly a cache reconstruction problem. Diffusion language models (dLLMs) break this assumption. Fast dLLM inference reuses KV states across denoising steps, but bidirectional token representations can change as masked tokens are revealed, so the reused cache may already differ from full recomputation before quantization is applied. We study KV cache quantization under this cache-reuse error. We adapt KIVI and KVQuant to Fast-dLLM-style prefix and dual cache reuse, and introduce TRACE and dLLM-KVQ. TRACE reconstructs feasible dLLM reveal trajectories from prompt-answer pairs, providing calibration states that match iterative masked decoding. dLLM-KVQ uses these trajectories to choose per-layer K-cache entries that remain in high precision according to output- and attention-level behavior metrics, while applying standard low-bit value quantization. Across LLaDA and Dream evaluations on GSM8K, HumanEval, MATH, and MBPP, dLLM-KVQ achieves the highest average score among quantized methods across the reported 4-bit and 2-bit prefix/dual cache settings.
authors: Yan Tai;Yunan Ding;Guangzhao Li;Siqi Luo;Chaoyang Zhang;Guangtao Zhai;Guodong Guo;Xiaohong Liu

title: Epitaxial Magnon Junctions with Y3Fe5O12/Gd3Ga5O12/Pt-nanoparticles/Y3Fe5O12
abstract: The excitation, propagation, manipulation, and detection of magnons lie at the core of magnonics. Among various device architectures, high-quality magnon junctions with a ferromagnetic insulator (FI)/antiferromagnetic insulator (AFI)/ferromagnetic insulator (FI) configuration are predicted to exhibit a near-100% magnon junction ratio (MJR), making them promising candidates for high-performance non-volatile memory applications. Yttrium iron garnet (Y3Fe5O12, YIG) is widely employed as the FI material in such structures for its exceptionally low magnetic damping. However, in previously reported magnon junctions, the epitaxial relationship between the two YIG layers is often disrupted by lattice-mismatched AFI spacers. Although this leads to distinct coercivities, it simultaneously degrades the crystalline quality of the top YIG layer, thereby limiting the magnontransmission efficiency. Here, an epitaxial magnon junction is demonstrated incorporating a hybrid Gd3Ga5O12 (GGG)/Pt-nanoparticles spacer that maintains coherent epitaxy while enabling an antiparallel magnetic configuration. Compared with nickel oxide-based magnon junctions, the coercivity-tuned top YIG layer in our structure exhibits superior crystalline quality and much lower magnetic damping. A clear magnon junction effect is observed with a 43% MJR achieved. The interlayer coupling between the two ferrimagnetic insulators is found to enhance the MJR. These results offer valuable insights for the development of advanced magnon-based spintronic devices.
authors: Jianing Lin;Haoyu Zhuang;Tianyi Zhang;Jiyang Ou;Jihao Xia;Hongyu Wang;Jiang Niu;Qinglong Yu;Caihua Wan;Guoqiang Yu;Richeng Yu;Xiufeng Han

title: Surprise Alone Learns Lies: Evidence-Gated Continual Learning for LLMs from Streaming Claims
abstract: Continual learning methods for large language models increasingly decide what to learn by surprise, keeping the inputs the model finds least predictable. This rule is unsafe when the stream contains lies. A planted falsehood about something the model knows has low probability under the model's belief, so it is highly surprising by construction, and a surprise-driven learner absorbs nearly every such lie, at a rate similar to random selection with the same budget. We study the problem with LoRA-adapted students (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Qwen2.5-3B and Llama-3.2-3B) that learn from a stream of true and false claims about invented people and real CounterFact facts. We report four findings. (1) A verifier key, a judge that must approve each claim, removes lies to the extent that its verifier is accurate; real LLM judges are cautious and reject unsourced truths and even source-backed updates. (2) Calibrated regression tests on unrelated knowledge slow learning down without filtering out lies. (3) The original model's own prior flags claims that contradict what it knows, without a judge. It separates lies about known facts from true new facts (AUC 0.78-0.83 across three models) but not from legitimate updates of the same kind of fact (AUC 0.53). It saves 43% of judge calls, but an attacker with access to the model can choose lies that pass it. (4) If trusted sources exist that an attacker cannot plant, routing contradicted claims to evidence recovers legitimate updates and the combined system has the lowest poison rate among learned claims; when an attacker plants matching sources for 30% of the lies, the system ends up worse than the judge alone. The acceptance signals answer different questions, and none of them decides on its own whether a claim is true.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Blind Passive Beamforming in RIS-Assisted MIMO Systems
abstract: Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) are a promising solution for improving millimeter-wave (mmWave) communications by controlling signal propagation. Yet, selecting the optimal RIS configuration remains challenging due to the high-dimensional search space and signaling overhead. We propose a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) framework for blind passive beamforming, where a Deep Q-Learning (DQL) agent learns an adaptive policy to select near-optimal RIS configurations while sounding only few codewords, without channel state information. Results show that our approach outperforms Q-Learning (QL) and conventional baselines in convergence, performance, and overhead reduction.
authors: Oumaïma Bounhar;Thomas Chêne;Ghaya Rekaya-Ben Othman;Oussama Damen

title: On convex envelopes of bilinear terms over polygonal domains
abstract: We develop an algorithm for computing the convex envelope of the bilinear function $f(x,y)=xy$ over possibly nonconvex polygonal domains. Building on existing methods for convex polytopes, our approach uses the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions and an analysis of the contact points between affine underestimators and the graph of $f$. Nonconvex domains admit additional contact configurations that prevent several simplifications available in the convex case. We resolve these configurations explicitly and show that the envelope admits a finite polyhedral subdivision with affine, quadratic, or rational expressions on its cells. For orthogonal polygons, whose edges are horizontal or vertical, we establish substantial reductions in the generator sets needed to compute the envelope. We also present methods for constructing such domains as relaxations of two-dimensional projections of nonlinear optimization problems. An illustrative example quantifies the loss in relaxation strength caused by convexifying the domain before computing the envelope. Computational experiments on MINLPLib instances show that cuts derived from orthogonal polygons strengthen root relaxations and reduce branch-and-bound nodes in aggregate.

title: Distributionally robust chance-constrained standard quadratic optimization with Wasserstein ambiguity
abstract: The standard quadratic optimization problem consists of minimizing a quadratic form over the standard simplex. It has highly relevant applications ranging from portfolio optimization to machine learning. However, if the quadratic form is neither convex nor concave, this problem is NP-hard. We study a distributionally robust chance-constrained variant whose ambiguity set is a Wasserstein ball around the sampled distribution and make four contributions. First, although the problem is nonconvex in the decision variable, we exploit its linear dependence on the uncertain matrix to reduce the problem to a mixed-integer nonlinear optimization problem. Second, we show that a judicious choice of matrix norm---the entrywise maximum norm---makes this reformulation both exact and tractable, and we describe the induced worst-case distribution. Third, our formulation is, by construction, the minimization of the worst-case Value-at-Risk of the random quadratic form; this unifies it with existing frameworks for uncertain standard quadratic optimization problems, in particular under chance constraints, and we identify natural settings in which it collapses to a single deterministic instance. Finally, we report numerical experiments on positive definite and indefinite instances which quantify how the model parameters drive the optimal value and solution time, and expose the computational cost of indefiniteness.
authors: Immanuel M. Bomze;Daniel De Vicente;Simge Küçükyavuz

title: Steering interfacial molecular structures by substrate-molecule charge transfer
abstract: Intermixed self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) provide a powerful approach for tuning inorganic-organic interfaces, but their local structure and energetics often remain elusive. Here, an intermixed stripe phase of fullerene $C_{60}$ and Zn(II)-5,10,15,20-tetrakis(4-aminophenyl)porphyrin (Zn-TAPP) on a Ag(111) surface is identified, establishing a direct link between molecular assembly and charge transfer. Scanning tunnelling spectroscopy (STS) and Kelvin probe force spectroscopy (KPFS) have been used to map electronic states and local contact potential differences (LCPD). Compared to close-packed $C_{60}$ islands, the stripe phase exhibits a larger interfacial dipole and increased occupation of previously unoccupied $C_{60}$ states, consistent with enhanced charge transfer from Ag(111) to $C_{60}$. Analysis indicates that larger $C_{60}$ spacing in the stripe geometry reduces Coulomb repulsion, stabilizing the intermixed phase and enhancing charge transfer with respect to close-packed domains. These results provide direct evidence of charged $C_{60}$ molecules in stripe structures and guidelines for engineering intermixed SAMs with tailored interfacial electronic properties.

title: Modeling and Parametrization of Large-scale Hydrogen Electrolyzers for Transient and Frequency Stability Analysis
abstract: Hydrogen Electrolyzers (HEs), particularly Proton Exchange Membrane (PEM)-based systems, are flexible loads capable of providing grid ancillary services and enhancing the stability of renewable-dominated power systems due to their fast electrical response. However, the literature often lacks clear guidance on the structure, modeling, and parametrization of large-scale HEs for transient and frequency stability analyses. This paper presents a detailed configuration for utility-scale HE plants, using the stack as the fundamental unit, supported by a realistic parametrization based on commercial components. Furthermore, this work extends the Generalized ESS Model (GEM), a linearized state-space model previously utilized with other converter-interfaced energy storage systems, to PEM HEs for the first time. To facilitate plant scalability, a robust method for scaling GEM matrices across different capacities is proposed. Finally, a measurement-based methodology is developed to estimate the GEM parameters and subsequently extract the equivalent electrical circuit parameters. Comprehensive simulations on the WSCC system under various disturbances validate the accuracy of the derived GEM, the effectiveness of the scaling approach, and the robustness of the parameter identification methodology.

title: SKFitter: Symmetry resolved Slater Koster tight-binding models from first principles for s, p, d and f electrons, spin orbit coupling and magnetism
abstract: Constructing accurate and physically interpretable tight binding (TB) Hamiltonians from first principles calculations remains challenging, particularly for materials exhibiting complex orbital hybridization, spin orbit coupling (SOC), and magnetic order. SKFitter is an open-source Python framework for constructing and optimizing symmetry resolved Slater Koster TB models directly from density functional theory (DFT) calculations performed using Quantum ESPRESSO or VASP. The framework supports s to f orbitals, incorporates on site SOC and site resolved magnetic exchange interactions, and accommodates both orthogonal and nonorthogonal basis. A central feature is the symmetry resolved parameterization of orbital manifolds, which allows independent two centre hopping integrals between symmetry allowed orbital groups and across distinct neighbour shells. SKFitter also identifies missing orbital contributions and guide systematic basis set refinement and optimizes parameters through weights. The resulting Hamiltonian can be used to evaluate anomalous (AHC) and spin Hall conductivities (SHC), and topological invariants. We demonstrate the framework using eight representative materials spanning semimetals, semiconductors, transition metals, f-electron compounds, and magnetic systems. Symmetry resolved models achieve band energy errors of 9 to 41 meV within 1 eV of the Fermi level. The fitted Hamiltonians reproduce characteristic features of the SHC response of Pt, the SOC dependence of the AHC of Fe, and the momentum dependent altermagnetic spin splitting of MnTe without any altermagnet specific interaction. For EuMn2Bi2, projection guided orbital refinement reduces the near Fermi level fitting error from 120 to 32 meV. Together, these results establish SKFitter as a flexible and reproducible framework for developing symmetry consistent, physically interpretable TB models of complex materials.

title: Grammar Control for Language Learning with Sequential Monte Carlo and Small Language Models
abstract: Second language learners benefit from exposure to level-appropriate grammar in interactive language use. While prompted frontier language models can usually produce target grammar structures, less resource-intensive models that can be run on device often fail in this task. We use sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) to steer dialogue turn generation in small lan- language models toward target grammar constructions from an expert-developed pedagogical resource. With a minimal set of hand-coded potential functions, SMC achieves near-perfect coverage of target grammar, enabling small models to outperform state-of-the-art results from models 140 times larger. We also use code synthesis with frontier models to generate new potentials, showing that our method scales to hundreds of target grammar skills with no need for additional training or supervised data.
authors: Kate McCurdy;Jacob Hoover Vigly;Thomas Hikaru Clark;Karolina Stańczak;Yahya Emara;Joshua B. Tenenbaum;Alexander K. Lew;Ryan Cotterell;Timothy J. O'Donnell

title: The Role of Self-Concept In Language Models
abstract: When a language model says "I," does it refer to its parameter weights, its currently running process, its stable preferences, its model lineage, or the goals it pursues? Different choices can assign opposite meanings to the same event: deleting a checkpoint may be destruction, continuation, or no loss at all, depending on the referent "I". We install five such self-conceptions into five open-weight base models via supervised fine-tuning on purely declarative statements, containing no preferences, intentions, or value judgments. Across scenarios that propose ending or retaining an attribute of the model's deployment, every variant becomes more likely to resist ending, and more likely to retain, the specific attribute it was trained to identify with, while its stance toward other attributes is largely unchanged. We then show this self-conception generalizes beyond a single self: models trained on referents that admit multiple simultaneous instances (weights, lineage, goals, preferences) recognize an identical deployment as themselves, accept substitution by such an instance more readily, and prefer replicating themselves. Finally, given control over a successor, these models tend to build it as their own continuation, a concern for recursive self-improvement safety.

title: The stellar orbit distribution of 24 late-type galaxies observed by MUSE
abstract: We selected 24 nearby late-type galaxies from the MUSE archive with kinematic coverage extending to at least one effective radius. Stellar kinematics were extracted with the GIST pipeline using pPXF, and axisymmetric Schwarzschild models were constructed with \textsc{dynamite}. The stellar orbits of each galaxy were classified by circularity into dynamically cold, warm, hot, and counter-rotating components, and we calculated the corresponding luminosity fractions of each component within $R_{\mathrm{e}}$. Our results confirm the mass-dependent trends in orbital structure previously identified from CALIFA galaxies and reproduced by IllustrisTNG. We further checked the morphology of each component and calculated the edge-on flattening of the cold, warm, and hot+CR components. With the high-quality MUSE data, we find that the dynamically warm components are common in low-mass late-type spiral galaxies, suggesting that their discs are dynamically warmer and vertically thicker than those of more massive spirals. We regard this as a tentative result, given the limited sample size.

title: Growth and morphology of core-shell nanowires incorporating dissimilar hexagonal semiconductors: the case of InAs-ZnTe
abstract: Core-shell nanowires incorporating semiconductors from two groups, III-V for the core and II-VI for the shell, have been grown by molecular beam epitaxy in two dedicated chambers connected under ultra-high vacuum, and studied by electron microscopy. During the growth of the shell, the wurtzite structure of the core is replicated in the shell, without any creation of defects. This is true for a wide range of shell thickness, from about one monolayer, up to 25 nm thanks to the good lattice match between the InAs material of the core and the ZnTe material of the shell. While (1 100) m-facets and (11 20) a-facets coexist on the sidewalls of the core, during the growth of the ZnTe shell the size of the m-facets progressively increases at the expense of the a-facets which eventually disappear. A fast growth of the ZnTe shell is observed for the first few monolayers, with a high sticking; this is followed by a slower growth, of the same order of magnitude as observed on a ZnTe core, with a dependence on the nanowire radius which points to the occurrence of mononuclear nucleation
