title: Topology and regularity of small sub-Riemannian balls under an index condition
abstract: We study the topology and regularity of small sub-Riemannian balls under an index condition on length-minimizing curves in the metric tangent space. We prove that sufficiently small spheres are Lipschitz hypersurfaces homeomorphic to Euclidean spheres, while closed balls are homeomorphic to Euclidean closed balls, and open balls are diffeomorphic to Euclidean open balls. These results improve the known ones and extend them beyond two-step distributions. The proof relies on uniform Lipschitz estimates for the distance, of independent interest.

title: Efficient Agentic Audio-Visual Question Answering through Toolset Pruning and Modality Consolidation
abstract: Fine-grained audio-visual question answering (AVQA) requires models to resolve complex cross-modal correspondences and temporally grounding from sparsely distributed evidence. Omni-modal agents, which autonomously orchestrate perception tools to actively collect evidence, achieve strong performance, but it remains unclear whether active perception from both audio and visual modalities depends on broad specialized toolsets, especially audio or visual modality-specific tools. Such systems may also introduce long execution trajectories and substantial inference cost. We investigate whether comparable performance can be retained with a compact workflow exposing only essential perceptual capabilities. Starting from the specialized-tool OmniAgent, we conduct staged controlled experiments that prune the toolset and progressively consolidate modality-specific tools into omni-modal tools, motivating a two-tool agent comprising only Omni-modal captioning and Omni-modal QA. Across three widely used AVQA benchmarks, our compact agent achieves comparable or better accuracy than the specialized-tool agent while reducing inference cost by around 70%.

title: Comment on "Is there a density-gradient expansion for the electronic exchange energy?"
abstract: Perdew et al. [arXiv:2610.07201 (2026)] dispute our finding [Phys. Rev. B 113, 115136 (2026)] that the separate exchange ($b_x$) and correlation ($b_c$) contributions to the $q^2$ coefficient of the long-wavelength proper polarization function depend on the infrared regularization of the Coulomb interaction, although their sum $b_{xc}=b_x+b_c$ does not. We question their claim that the conventional exchange coefficient is uniquely determined. In Qian's [J. Math. Phys. 56, 111901 (2015)] derivation, which Perdew et al. cite in support of their claim of a unique exchange-gradient coefficient, an integral of the form $\int_{-a}^{b}dx/x$ crosses a singularity and does not exist as an ordinary improper integral. Its finite Cauchy principal value (which is a particular way of regularizing the integral) is obtained only by excluding equal intervals on the two sides of the singularity; unequal exclusions give different answers. Independently, Sham's calculation with the screened interaction $e^{-λ_0 r}/r$ gives an exchange-gradient coefficient different from the bare-Coulomb calculations of Svendsen--von Barth [Int. J. Quantum Chem. 56, 351 (1995)] and Engel--Vosko [Phys. Rev. B 42, 4940 (1990)]. The discrepancy remains when $λ_0>0$ is so small that $1/λ_0$ is comparable to the size of the observable universe, making the two interactions experimentally indistinguishable on laboratory scales. Why should the exactly unscreened result be preferred, even if its calculation is accepted as valid? Our calculation shows that the ambiguity of the separate contributions cancels in the combined, regulator-independent coefficient $b_{xc}$.

title: Optimization-based lane-changing trajectory planning in mixed traffic with embedded input convex neural networks
abstract: Lane-changing (LC) maneuvers are highly challenging vehicle interactions, with substantial implications for traffic safety and efficiency. Developing effective LC strategies for connected and automated vehicles in mixed traffic is complicated by the uncertainty associated with surrounding-vehicle behavior and the computational burden of embedding realistic prediction models within optimization schemes. To capture these complex interactions while retaining tractability, this study proposes a data-driven optimization framework that embeds neural network (NN) surrogates for safety and lateral comfort within a Bézier-curve-based trajectory planner. Specifically, the safety cost during the LC process is quantified via a surrogate composed of an input convex recurrent neural network (ICRNN) encoding the planned trajectory, a fully input convex neural network (FICNN) embedding the LC duration, and a partially input convex neural network (PICNN) decoder fusing them with historical traffic states; separately, another FICNN surrogate approximates the optimal lateral comfort cost as a function of the LC duration. Both surrogates are embedded via linear programming (LP) formulations, avoiding the binary variables required by conventional mixed-integer programming (MIP) approaches for NN-embedded optimization. We further theoretically establish their exactness at optimality and extend the framework to problems with additional analytical objective terms and multiple surrogates. Experiments on a hybrid dataset combining real-world and simulated trajectories demonstrate that the proposed method achieves surrogate accuracy competitive with unconstrained baselines while substantially improving optimization efficiency over conventional MIPs. Closed-loop simulations further show that the proposed planners markedly reduce the weighted planning cost and consistently outperform baseline methods.
authors: Yuanxiang Yang;Yu Liu;Fabricio Oliveira;Yu Han;Claudio Roncoli

title: Memorization Capacity of Invariant Convolutional Neural Nets
abstract: Neural networks are powerful memorizers which are often able to interpolate their training data even when the labels have been randomized. While there exists an extensive literature on the memorization capacity of fully connected networks, in practice more specific architectures with problem-dependent properties are preferred, such as convolutional networks for image classification. In this paper we consider convolutional networks which are invariant with respect to a given arbitrary finite group of orthogonal transformations, which may include translations, reflections, and/or rotations of images and invariances of higher order tensors. We prove upper bounds on the size of an invariant convolutional neural network with threshold activations that is required to interpolate a given dataset with two classes. Our bounds are formulated in terms of a complexity measure that takes the invariant structure into account and is instance-specific, i.e., it is related to the mutual arrangement of the classes in the given dataset and their geometric properties rather than the number of samples. Our proof is constructive: for given input data, instances of an interpolating network can be computed via a randomized algorithm with high probability. In numerical experiments we investigate the practical effectiveness of this algorithm.

title: Development and application of a machine learning potential for diamond surfaces and their sliding interfaces with silicon nitride and silica: effect of passivation, orientation and load
abstract: Friction and wear of diamond are controlled by its surface chemistry, which determines whether covalent bonds form across the sliding interface. First-principles simulations have explored the role of surface orientation and passivation, but are limited to a few hundred atoms and tens of picoseconds. To bridge this gap, we develop a reactive machine learning interatomic potential for the C/H/N/O/Si chemical space, covering diamond, silicon nitride, silicon oxide, their surfaces, interfaces, and environmental molecules. The potential is trained on a large dataset of diverse structures and is tested on multiple physical properties, including ab initio reaction barriers on diamond surfaces, and structural/mechanical properties of amorphous Si$_3$N$_4$ and SiO$_2$. We then simulate sliding of diamond-Si$_3$N$_4$ interfaces with four surface orientations, clean and H/OH-passivated terminations, and normal loads from 0.1 to 23 GPa. We identify two different regimes: one where sliding is localized at the interface, and shear stress is proportional to the interfacial bond density, and another where shear is distributed inside the softer material, and adhesion due to full interfacial bonding dominates. These results show how passivation, surface orientation and load together determine interfacial bonding and friction, with implications for the environmental sensitivity of diamond wear. More broadly, the potential enables reactive simulations of diamond, silicon nitride and silica with near-ab initio accuracy at length and time scales beyond first-principles methods, providing a useful tool for future studies of wear at plowing asperities, chemical-mechanical polishing, and properties of amorphous ceramic films.

title: Variable Metric Three Operator Splitting
abstract: To minimize the sum $f + g + h$ of three convex functions when $f$ is differentiable with a Lipschitz-continuous gradient, we present a proximal algorithm, variable-metric three operator splitting (VMTOS), a generalization of the three operator splitting (TOS) scheme of Davis and Yin. We establish convergence guarantees by controlling changes in the metric. The smallest saddle-point residual among the first $k$ primal-dual iterates is $\tilde{O}(k^{-1/2})$. When $f$ and the convex conjugate $h^*$ are strongly convex and the accepted metrics and their inverses are uniformly bounded, the rate improves to $\tilde{O}(β^k)$ for some $β\in (0,1)$. We develop a practical Barzilai--Borwein update for diagonal metrics that satisfies our bound on metric changes. Under the same strong convexity assumptions, this update guarantees the required uniform metric bounds, yielding R-linear convergence. Numerical experiments on benchmark optimization problems show that VMTOS is competitive with other proximal algorithms.

title: 3-Methoxy-1-propanol Rotational Spectroscopy and Radio Astronomical Search toward NGC 6334I
abstract: The methoxy functionalized alcohol species methoxymethanol and 2-methoxyethanol have recently been identified toward the MM1 protostellar source in the NGC 6334I massive star-forming region. Here we report measurements of portions of the centimeter, millimeter, and sub-millimeter regions of the rotational spectrum of the most stable conformer of 3-methoxy-1-propanol in order to probe the presence of even larger methoxylated alcohols toward the source. The experimental rotational parameters determined from these spectra were used to simulate the rotational spectrum of 3-methoxy-1-propanol under the physical conditions of the MM1 source and compared to the same ALMA observational dataset of the source in which 2-methoxyethanol was first discovered. No 3-methoxy-1-propanol transitions are identified in the data, and an upper limit on its column density toward the source was determined to be $7.5 \cdot 10^{15} \text{ cm}^{-2}$. When considering the series of these three methoxy alcohols, the decrease in column density going from 2-methoxyethanol to 3-methoxy-1-propanol is consistent with how the column density of 2-methoxyethanol decreases compared to methoxymethanol.
authors: D. Archie Stewart;Laurent Margulès;Roman A. Motiyenko;Brett A. McGuire
journal_ref: D. Archie Stewart et al 2026 ApJ 1010 146

title: Controllability of Nonlocal Partial Differential Equations
abstract: This chapter provides a short survey of recent developments in the controllability of nonlocal partial differential equations. We first review controllability results for evolution equations involving nonlocal spatial operators. Particular attention is devoted to unique continuation properties, observability inequalities, and Carleman estimates in establishing controllability properties. We then discuss controllability issues for partial differential equations with memory terms, highlighting how memory effects influence reachable states, null controllability, and exact controllability. We review and compare various analytical techniques developed to overcome the difficulties arising from the nonlocal structure. We also provide a critical assessment of some of these methods. Throughout the chapter, we emphasize the interplay between controllability and observability, the adaptation of classical control methods to nonlocal settings, and the distinctive phenomena that arise in comparison with local equations. We then discuss geometric inequalities and their role in the controllability of diffusion models. The chapter concludes with a discussion of current challenges and several open problems, aiming to provide directions for future research.
authors: D. Cardona;S. E. Chorfi;F. Et-tahri;L. Maniar

title: Selective Sliding Mode Control Enhances Robustness of Aerial Robots Under Disturbances
abstract: Quadrotor control under disturbances such as wind gusts and payload variations remains challenging. First-order sliding mode control (SMC) and matched/unmatched uncertainty distinction are classical approaches; however, neither tells a practitioner which loops in a cascaded controller should be made robust to sustain disturbances, how to tune those loops, nor what the additional costs are on an embedded processor. Applying robust control uniformly across all axes addresses disturbances indiscriminately, adding tuning effort on axes where no disturbance acts. On inherently underactuated vehicles, disturbances along some axes cannot be opposed directly at all. We propose a principled methodology for deciding where robust control belongs in a cascaded architecture, with all control running onboard the vehicle. We recover the acting disturbance from PID hover flights under disturbance by inverting the equations of motion, use the recovered signal to identify and quantify the excited axes, and deploy robust control where it counts. Experiments on a Crazyflie 2.1 quadrotor under slung-payload and oblique-wind disturbances show tracking improvements concentrated on the axes the rule selects, and gain sweeps confirm that the switching gain reduces error on matched axes but has no effect on an excited unmatched axis, as the analysis predicts.

title: Collective sliding relaxor ferroelectricity across thousand-layer van der Waals superstructures
abstract: Relaxor ferroelectrics are among the most important electromechanical materials owing to their exceptionally large electrostrictive responses. However, conventional relaxor behavior is generally associated with chemical complexity and structural disorder, where local compositional fluctuations generate polar nanoregions, making the microscopic origin of this behavior difficult to control and engineer. Here we report sliding relaxor ferroelectricity (S-RFE), a previously unknown relaxor state in which engineered stacking-phase heterogeneity enables cooperative interlayer sliding to generate collective relaxor behavior. Through stacking-phase engineering in rhombohedral boron nitride, we create sliding domains that act as structural analogues of polar nanoregions and cooperatively align under an electric field through interlayer sliding. This collective state produces reversible electromechanical deformation of up to approximately $-1.6\%$ with negligible hysteresis in approximately 300-nm-thick crystals, corresponding to approximately 1000 atomic layers. The resulting electrostriction coefficient ($Q_{33}$ of approximately $1200\,\mathrm{m}^{4}\mathrm{C}^{-2}$) exceeds those of most crystalline electrostrictors by orders of magnitude. Unlike conventional relaxors, whose electromechanical response is often suppressed by dipolar freezing at low temperatures, S-RFE remains active down to 1.6 K and maintains giant electromechanical functionality. Our results establish sliding relaxor ferroelectricity as a new route to relaxor behavior and reveal how atomic-scale interlayer motion can be amplified into collective mesoscale functionality across approximately one thousand layers, providing a materials-by-design platform for electromechanical, photonic, and quantum technologies based on van der Waals materials.
authors: Nianze Shang;Cuiju Yu;Yucai Lin;Juan C. Arias-Muñoz;Jiajie Qi;Quanlin Guo;MD Gius Uddin;Youqiang Huang;Tuomas Pajunpää;Christopher P. Edwards;Rodolfo E. Canet-Albiach;Faisal Ahmed;Andreas C. Liapis;Yaoqiang Zhou;Zhibin Zhang;Hao Hong;Qing Dai;Andrea Alù;José L. Lado;Kaihui Liu;Zhipei Sun

title: Detailed chemo-dynamical characterization of four elusive Milky Way star clusters
abstract: A variety of faint and observationally challenging stellar systems has been discovered in the Milky Way in the last decades. Unveiling their kinematic and chemical properties is crucial to understand their nature and to assess their role in the history of our Galaxy. In this paper, we present a chemo-dynamical analysis of four elusive stellar systems (BH 140, Garro 01, BLISS 1, and Kim 3) using spectra collected with the X-shooter medium-resolution spectrograph at the VLT. We derived precise line-of-sight velocities and chemical abundances for all targets. Specifically, we provide the first spectroscopic characterization of metallicity and α-element content for BH 140, the first comprehensive chemical characterization for BLISS 1 and Garro 01, and the first spectroscopic metallicity determination for Kim 3. BH 140, Garro 01 and BLISS 1 are relatively metal-rich systems with [Fe/H] ~ -0.7 dex and have enhanced α-element abundances, whereas Kim 3 is notably metal-poor with [Fe/H] ~ -1.8 dex. We also performed an orbital analysis to investigate their origin as accreted or in situ systems. We found that Garro 01 and BH 140 have orbits confined within < 1.5 kpc from the Galactic plane, the former having also a remarkably circular orbit. They were likely born in situ, although the high orbital eccentricity of BH 140 and its mild deficiency in α-elements leave other possibilities open. Although undoubtedly accreted, BLISS 1 does not exhibit a clear dynamical association with any known progenitor, lying in a high energy (E) - high vertical angular momentum (LZ ) prograde orbit reaching a maximum height from the Galactic plane of zmax ~ 8 kpc. Its chemical properties seem to favor an in situ origin, which might be connected with the Aleph sub-structure. Finally, we tentatively link the high energy and low LZ orbit of Kim 3 to the Elqui stream.
authors: D. A. Alvarez Garay;E. Ceccarelli;D. Massari;M. Bellazzini;A. Mucciarelli;M. Libralato;E. Pancino;A. Avdeeva;M. Echeveste;E. I. Leitinger;S. Nedhath;S. Rani;E. Reggiani;N. Sanna;S. Saracino;L. Steinbauer;A. Turchi;E. Dodd;E. R. Garro;C. Zerbinati

title: Interventional Training Reduces Causal Bypass in In-Context Introspection
abstract: Introspection, the ability of a system to access and reason about its internal signals, is crucial for language model (LM) self-consistency and scalable interpretability. Prior work argues that LMs possess introspective capabilities, and that training (SFT) could enhance such behavior. However, most setups leave open the possibility of "causal bypass," in which the self-report relies on signals that are correlated with the self-report's subject, while being causally unrelated to it. Although high-level concepts are difficult to intervene on, lower-level signals (such as a single neuron activation) allow precise interventions. Understanding such signals can serve as a minimal prerequisite before understanding more complex introspection. In this study, we train hundreds of introspectors across three low-level signal types and eight LMs. We find that straightforward SFT training leads to causal bypass, and propose interventional training, an alternative where we train the model to report on counterfactually perturbed values. This method enables more accurate introspection of endogenous $\textit{and}$ injected signals, particularly in out-of-distribution (OOD) data. The mechanism generalizes across token positions and scales with more data. Our results demonstrate that while causally grounded introspection is possible, it is not guaranteed -- emphasizing the need to train on mechanisms, rather than behaviors alone.
authors: Zilu Tang;Jongin Kim;Kerem Sahin;David Atkinson;Aaron Mueller;Derry Wijaya

title: HEDGE: Gated Hypergraph Memory for Scalable Multi-Agent Debate
abstract: Multi-agent debate systems require agents to retain and revisit arguments across multiple rounds, yet limited context windows and unstructured memories make relevant information increasingly difficult to recover. Existing flat and pairwise-graph memories also struggle to capture higher-order relations, including multi-agent agreement, conflicting evidence, and evolving consensus. We introduce HEDGE, a selective memory framework that represents debate trajectories as semantic hypergraphs. Hyperedges connect related claims across agents, while intra-hyperedge relational graphs preserve fine-grained argumentative structure. A learned memory selection module (MSM), trained through supervised learning and reinforcement learning, routes each memory candidate to STORE, BACKUP, or OMIT, retaining useful information while limiting redundancy. Across seven diverse benchmarks, HEDGE consistently outperforms strong single-agent, multi-agent, and memory baselines, improving accuracy by 5.0 points on average over the strongest multi-agent system with GPT-4o-mini. The gains reach 8.2 points on conflict-heavy tasks, while HEDGE reduces memory usage by 48% and the number of debate rounds by 34%. Code is available at: https://github.com/AmirAbaskohi/HEDGE.

title: The Hidden Value of Soft Infrastructure for Urban Flood Adaptation
abstract: As sea level rises and flooding events become more frequent, cities are tapping into a range of engineering and planning solutions to reduce flood losses. Beyond traditional ``hard'' infrastructure (e.g., sewage, seawalls), ``soft'' infrastructure that supports and empowers the role of citizens in preparedness has been hailed as a promising avenue for improving adaptation. Despite its promise, there have been very limited attempts to quantify its effectiveness in reducing losses relative to hard infrastructure, particularly in urban environments. This study fills this knowledge gap using generative AI to quantify the effectiveness of a range of hard and soft infrastructure in urban areas. We demonstrate, for the first time, that soft infrastructure can significantly reduce flood losses, with an impact on par with hard infrastructure. Our results open the door to novel ways of confronting adaptation challenges in cities. Soft infrastructure is a viable alternative, especially when budgetary or time constraints make hard infrastructure unattainable. Policymakers should also couple soft and hard infrastructure to maximize resilience.

title: Inertial Steering and Motion Prediction of Tracked Vehicles on Low-Adherence Surfaces
abstract: Tracked vehicles are widely used in off-road applications, but their conventional motion models often rely on no-slip assumptions that become inaccurate on low-adherence surfaces. Rather than treating inertial effects arising from slip as a disturbance to be minimized, this work investigates how inertial effects arising from a moving mass can be deliberately exploited for steering on low-friction surfaces. A dynamic model for an articulated tracked vehicle with a passive trailer is developed, allowing inertial effects from trailer motion to be captured. The approach is experimentally evaluated on ice, where our dynamic model outperforms the kinematic baseline. We also propose a mixed dynamic-kinematic model to adapt predictions to both surface and situation by exploiting predictions from both methods. Finally, we demonstrate inertial steering on a mono-track vehicle without a conventional steering mechanism, showing that controlled movements of an internal mass can generate turning motion on ice. The resulting behavior can be predicted using the proposed dynamic model by representing the internal mass as a frictionless trailer, revealing the analogous dynamics between the two configurations. These results demonstrate the feasibility of inertial steering as an alternative steering mechanism for tracked vehicles operating in low-adherence environments.
authors: Mathis Turgeon-Roy;Mohamed Ounally;Veronica Vannini;Olivier Roy;François Pomerleau

title: Odds Estimation for Supermassive Black Hole Binaries in Local Core Galaxies
abstract: Supermassive black hole binaries (SMBHBs) are expected products of massive galaxy mergers, but identifying binaries in nearby galaxies remains challenging. We combine simulated massive-galaxy assembly histories from IllustrisTNG with a semi-analytic core-scouring model to connect observable core galaxy properties to the probability of hosting a bound SMBHB at z=0. We (i) construct a core galaxy population using an observationally motivated galaxy stellar mass function, (ii) model binary evolution through dynamical friction, stellar hardening, and gravitational-wave emission, and (iii) perform logistic regressions with five observable predictors: stellar mass deficit, stellar mass, central density, central velocity dispersion, and effective radius. The resulting models perform well on simulated systems, achieving a pseudo-$R^2$ of $0.51\pm0.03$, accuracy $0.95\pm0.01$, precision $0.92\pm0.03$, and recall $0.82\pm0.04$. Uncoalesced binaries are typically compact, with separations peaking near 0.3 pc, though only $\sim0.3\%$ emit in the pulsar timing array band. Applying the model to observed core galaxies, we identify eight nearby galaxies more likely than not to host SMBHBs. Of those eight host candidates, we note Messier 86 (NGC 4406) as a particularly likely example that was similarly identified using independent means and therefore warrants future follow-up.
comment: 18 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables, submitted to AAS Journals

title: Continuous Envy-Free Allocation via Reciprocal Preference Matrices: An Alternative to Sperner-Based Discretization
abstract: Fair allocation problems on a continuous simplex are often approached through Sperner-type discretizations: agents label mesh vertices according to their preferences and a fully labelled elementary triangle gives a discrete localization of a fair outcome. We develop a continuous alternative for three agents and three alternatives by representing preferences with multiplicatively consistent reciprocal pairwise-comparison matrices. Two independent ratios per agent induce exact linear indifference boundaries and turn envy-free allocation into a finite-dimensional feasibility problem. For the six possible assignments, we introduce an assignment score $Φ$ built from the agents' consistent priority vectors and prove that an incentive solution component is nonempty if and only if its assignment is the unique minimizer of $Φ$, whereas a disincentive solution component is nonempty if and only if its assignment is the unique maximizer. Consequently, the strict solution region is either empty or a unique convex preference region whose closure lies in the interior of the simplex. The weak solution set is never empty and degenerates exactly when $Φ$ has ties. We also compare the exact continuous formulation with Sperner-based discretization, including the boundary convention required in the disincentive model. Under exact consistency, the model uses six independent pairwise thresholds, whereas a regular triangular mesh with resolution $m$ contains $(m+1)(m+2)/2$ vertices. The method therefore exchanges a stronger parametric preference assumption for an exact continuous solution set and a resolution-independent elicitation stage.
authors: Luis Ángel Calvo Pascual;Susana Merchán Rubira;Diego de Pereda Sebastián;Javier Rodrigo Hitos

title: Learning Between the Lines: Interaction Interpolation in a Multi Element Machine Learning Interatomic Potential
abstract: The continuous development of machine learning inter-atomic potentials (MLIAPs)has greatly accelerated materials research in recent years. However, the need to con- struct custom MLIAPs for each unique problem remains a bottleneck which raises the question of the transferability of MLIAPs. While foundation MLIAPs can achieve transferability due to the broad coverage of chemical space represented in their training sets, their size and computational cost limits their routine use. We address this gap by developing a lightweight general-purpose MLIAP for metal alloys spanning twelve elements (Al, Sc, Ti, V, Cu, Zn, Zr, Nb, Mo, Hf, Ta, W). Here, we utilize a step-wise active learning (AL) approach to develop a compact yet diverse dataset and model that generalizes well by interpolating from previously seen interactions. The resulting potentials transfer effectively to unseen, higher body-order alloys systems, requiring only unary and binary training data to capture ternary and quaternary systems. The model also transfers well to new elements via an alchemical extrapolation within the network, requiring only unary data for the new element and its alloys. These findings suggest that MLIAPs trained on targeted, diversity-driven datasets provide transferability at a relatively low computational cost, offering a practical path toward general-purpose, resource-efficient MLIAPs for materials modeling.
authors: Ademola Soyemi;Kipton Barros;Timothy C. Germann;Benjamin T. Nebgen;Brenden W. Hamilton

title: A morpho-kinematic view of the Necklace nebula
abstract: We present a morpho-kinematic study of the Necklace Nebula based on spatially resolved spectroscopic observations and 3D modeling performed with the SHAPE software. The nebula is characterized by an equatorial disrupted ring accompanied by bipolar outflows. The geometry and velocity field of these different components are derived from the comparison between observed and synthetic images and position-velocity diagrams. The best model successfully reproduces the main morphological and kinematic features of the nebula, allowing us to constrain its 3D structure. We confirm that the disrupted ring is tilted about 60° from the plane of the sky, but the bipolar outflows are inclined by 46° with respect to the line of sight. This situation might indicate that the bipolar structures are not simple extensions of the equatorial ring, but instead correspond to a distinct mass-ejection event. The slight misalignment between these two components suggests either precession of the ejection axis, a temporal change in the dominant mass-loss geometry, or a misalignment in the magnetic field. Given that the Necklace Nebula hosts a close binary central star and is a well-established post-common envelope planetary nebula, our results support a scenario in which binary interaction plays a central role in shaping its morphology, even before the common envelope phase.
authors: E. Santamaría;J. A. Toalá;L. Sabin;M. A. Guerrero;G. Ramos-Larios
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures and 2 tables. Accepted in MNRAS

title: A Retrospective-Approximation Interior-Point Method
abstract: An algorithm is proposed, analyzed, and tested for solving nonlinearly constrained continuous optimization problem instances wherein the objective function is defined by an expectation over a random variable argument and the constraints include inequalities (and perhaps equalities) involving functions that may be nonconvex. The algorithm combines a retrospective-approximation strategy for handling the objective and an interior-point approach for handling the constraints. In each iteration of an outer loop, the objective is approximated by an empirical average over a set of realizations of the random variable argument and the resulting sampled problem is solved with an interior-point method that allows inexact search-direction computations for computational flexibility. Termination conditions for the interior-point method are tailored for those needed for convergence guarantees by the outer loop. Over the outer loop, the sample set is updated adaptively in such a manner that convergence guarantees for solving the original optimization problem can be assured. The results of numerical experiments are presented, which show that the proposed algorithm can outperform competing methods that have comparable theoretical guarantees.
authors: Frank E. Curtis;Zahra Khatti;Daniel P. Robinson

title: Contextual Embeddings Beyond the Gold Chunk
abstract: Contextual embeddings represent chunks of a document with respect to the document's global context. These models are typically trained and evaluated under the assumption that a relevant document contains only a single relevant chunk. In this work, we argue that in real-world use cases a retriever should not only find answers spread over several chunks but also surface the evidence needed to verify them. To address this, we introduce pplx-embed-v2-context, a family of contextual embedding models trained by distilling graded chunk-level relevance from a query-aware context compression model. This removes the need for gold-chunk labels and makes the training targets independent of the chunking. We utilize a vision-language backbone for training and release pplx-embed-v2-context in 9B and 0.6B sizes with compatible embedding spaces. On the evaluation side, we introduce two benchmarks that label both the chunks that answer a query and the evidence needed to verify the answer. Context-bench is a controlled diagnostic, and Q2D-Chunk is built from real-world search queries. To encourage further research, we also publish Q2D-Chunk as a public leaderboard. Our 9B model sets a new state of the art on both benchmarks and ConTEB. We find that the visual retrieval capabilities of our 9B model transfer from its vision-language base model and propose to extend chunking to image inputs. We demonstrate that our models achieve state-of-the-art performance among dense retrievers on visual ViDoRe-V3 and that performance improves with granular image chunking.
authors: Sedigheh Eslami;Markus Krimmel;William Barber;Antoine Chaffin;Maximilian Schall;Jonas Golde;Louis Milliken;Ekaterina Glazkova;Denis Bykov;Bo Wang

title: Autonomous Quantum Measurement with Agentic AI
abstract: Quantum materials exhibit diverse electronic and functional phenomena, but their characterization requires extensive experimental expertise, iterative decision-making and accumulated laboratory knowledge that is difficult to document and transfer. Here we introduce Quantum Agent (QUANTA), an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) framework for autonomous quantum-materials characterization. Using a widely adopted Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS) as an experimental platform, QUANTA combines retrieval augmentation using scientific literature, experimental protocols and prior measurements with specialized agents for experimental planning, troubleshooting, and data interpretation. A separate deterministic control layer validates instrument actions. Guided by incoming data, QUANTA evaluates measurement quality, revises experimental plans and selects subsequent measurements. We demonstrate these capabilities through transport measurements of the topological Weyl semimetal TaP, as well as investigations of nonlinear responses in magnetic material Co2MnGa. These results establish QUANTA as a generalizable framework for evidence-driven, safeguarded and closed-loop quantum-materials characterization.
authors: Eunbi Rha;Abhijatmedhi Chotrattanapituk;Mouyang Cheng;Chung-tao Chou;Shenyong Ye;Ashley S. Dale;Long Ju;Luqiao Liu;Mingda Li

title: A Feasible-Direction-Type Method for Nonconvex Optimization with Infeasible Starts
abstract: We develop an infeasible-start extension of the Topkis--Veinott feasible-direction method for nonconvex composite optimization. At each main iteration, a strongly convex local model is used to obtain objective descent while limiting increases in constraint violation. A separate feasibility-reduction step is invoked when feasibility improvement is needed. Under a feasibility-reduction condition, we establish the standard first-order rate for reducing the Fritz John residual and constraint violation. We then verify that both proximal-gradient and regularized Gauss--Newton methods applied to minimizing the squared constraint-violation function satisfy the required feasibility-reduction property under a Polyak--Łojasiewicz condition. Numerical experiments compare the reduction methods, including an experimental prox-linear variant, and compare the scalar-regularized and curvature-enhanced subproblem formulations.

title: Environmental Quenching of Satellite Galaxies out to z~0.4 with GAMA and DEVILS
abstract: While numerous studies have shown that satellite galaxies experience declining star formation rates after infall, direct comparisons across different surveys and redshifts are complicated by varying sample selections, environmental metrics, and techniques used to derive galaxy properties. In this work, we select satellite galaxies from the highly complete Galaxy and Mass Assembly (GAMA) Survey and the Deep Extragalactic VIsible Legacy Survey (DEVILS) to investigate environmental quenching out to z~0.4. These surveys derive galaxy properties and environments in a consistent manner, minimizing systematic biases and enabling a robust comparison across redshift. Using projected phase space as a proxy for infall time, we quantify the evolution of the quenched fraction and trace how satellites evolve relative to the star-forming main sequence (SFMS). We find consistent trends between GAMA and DEVILS, with satellites exhibiting a steady decline in star formation relative to the SFMS at a rate of ~0.14 dex/Gyr following infall. Extending this analysis to include visual morphology, we find similar declining trends for both early- and late-type systems. Overall, we find no significant redshift evolution between GAMA and DEVILS, indicating that group and cluster environments have a comparable impact on the star formation activity of satellite galaxies over the past ~4.5 Gyr.
authors: Megan Oxland;Matías Bravo;Laura Parker;Luke Davies;Sabine Bellstedt
comment: 22 pages, 10 figures, 3 tables. Accepted for publication in ApJ

title: What to randomize matters: a controlled study of volume, axis and representation in low-data molecular generation
abstract: Chemical language models can struggle to generate new molecules when trained on small datasets, where a model may reproduce training examples rather than learn a useful generative distribution. Randomized SMILES augmentation varies atom traversal, whereas Sequential Attachment-based Fragment Embedding (SAFE) also allows the order of fragment blocks to vary. How these distinct sources of representational variation affect low-data molecular generation has not been clearly studied. Here, using 1,000 seed molecules to train an autoregressive sequence model, we compare canonical SAFE with randomized SAFE at increasing corpus sizes, isolate atom-order and fragment-order axes of SAFE randomization, and compare fully randomized SAFE with randomized SMILES at molecule-by-molecule matched training corpora. Three findings emerge. First, randomization of SAFE alone raises the genuine yield of novel molecules more than 450-fold, turning a model that merely reproduces its training set into a practical molecular generator. Second, the two axes of randomization act jointly rather than additively: atom order alone reaches a tenth, and fragment order alone a seventh, of the genuine yield obtained when both vary, which is four times their combined contribution. Third, at matched corpus size and compute, randomized SAFE delivers 2.8 times the genuine yield of randomized SMILES. Welch tests with Games-Howell post-hoc comparisons resolve every difference on the primary outcomes. In the low-data regime, thus, what one randomizes rather than only how much determines whether augmentation produces new molecules or merely new spellings of the training set.

title: The Bochum Survey of the Southern Galactic Disk: IV. Multi-Band Photometry
abstract: The Southern Galactic Disk Survey (GDS) monitored a mosaic of 268 fields along a $6^\circ$-wide stripe in the southern galactic disk from September 2010 to September 2019. These fields were observed between 21 and 407 times simultaneously in $r'$ ($8\,\mathrm{mag} \lesssim r' \lesssim 18\,\mathrm{mag}$) and $i'$ ($7\,\mathrm{mag} \lesssim i' \lesssim 17\,\mathrm{mag}$), supplemented by between 2 and 147 observations in each of the bands $U$, $B$, $V$, and $z'$. Here we present the matched multi-band catalogue, which integrates photometry and light curve data from all bands, containing photometry for almost 21.7 million Gaia DR3 sources, of which $113\,449$ are identified as variables. We give an overview of the survey's variable content with respect to its main characteristics and known variability type classifications. The comparison with the cross-match catalogue of Gaia DR3 sources with variables from the literature compiled by Gavras et al. (2023) and the International Variable Star Index (VSX) indicates that approximately $40\,\%$ of the variable sources remain unclassified in terms of variability type. Light curves for all of these sources are contained in the GDS data catalogues, available via the German Astrophysical Virtual Observatory (GAVO), and can contribute to their classification.
authors: Julia Blex;Dominik J. Bomans;Kerstin Weis;Markus Demleitner;Moritz Hackstein;Anna Franckowiak;Michael Ramolla;Christian Westhues;Christofer Fein;Rolf Chini

title: Efficient MPC for LC-Filtered Three-Level NPC Inverters in Vehicle-to-Load Applications
abstract: Finite control-set model predictive control (FCS-MPC) offers fast, modulator-free voltage regulation but is sensitive to the fidelity of its internal model. This sensitivity is usually countered by algorithmic augmentation, disturbance observers, adaptive weighting, or learning-based estimators, at the cost of extra tuning and computation. This paper instead improves fidelity at the source. For a three-level neutral-point-clamped (3L-NPC) inverter with an LC output filter in vehicle-to-load operation, a coupled alpha-beta-frame predictive model carries the capacitor voltage and filter current jointly through the state vector, so that the second-order LC coupling is retained without enlarging the 27-candidate search. The cost function additionally regulates dc-link neutral-point balance and switching effort. One-step prediction accuracy, parametric sensitivity, and computational cost are bounded in closed form. Simulation of a V2L system yields a voltage total harmonic distortion of 0.72%, a steady-state tracking error of 1.6%, and transient recovery within one fundamental cycle, meeting the applicable IEEE power-quality limits with margin, without observers, parameter estimation, or learning-based augmentation.

title: CopyLoop: Fast Looped Transformer Decoding via Context Copying and Shallow Screening
abstract: Looped Transformers increase computational capacity through the repeated application of shared blocks, but their recurrent depth makes conventional full-depth decoding expensive. While existing speculative pipelines accelerate generation by processing consecutive token positions at varying depths, they are typically limited by sequential decoding overheads. We introduce CopyLoop, a training-free decoding algorithm that combines low-cost context-copy proposals with shallow screening and continuous recurrent scheduling. Rather than step-by-step generation, CopyLoop proposes multi-token suffixes from repeated context. It then evaluates them early at a shallow recurrent depth to efficiently filter out incorrect branches, processing newer blocks concurrently while earlier blocks are still progressing toward full-depth verification. We evaluate CopyLoop across six model checkpoints from the Ouro, Raven, and Huginn families, covering code generation and multi-step mathematical reasoning. CopyLoop achieves decoding speedups of 2.98x--10.70x over full-depth autoregressive decoding on Base models and 2.74x--3.52x on Thinking models, consistently outperforming or closely matching all competing baselines across evaluation tasks. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm a strong synergy between shallow screening and continuous scheduling, while our analyses show that CopyLoop requires only lightweight model calibration and yields greater speedups on longer generations with reusable contexts.

title: Computationally Constrained First-Order Prediction-Correction Approach for Time-Varying Convex Optimization
abstract: Time-varying optimization methods often predict the locations of time-varying optima, then sample the objective function being minimized, and then compute corrections to those predictions. However, existing methods typically do not account for settings in which the number of computations is limited. Therefore, in this work we formulate a prediction-correction algorithm that is designed to obey a budget constraint on the total number of iterations it can execute over a given time horizon. We first identify a threshold on the average number of computations between samples of the objective, above which a bound from prior work certifies contraction of iterates toward a minimizer. Below this threshold, we introduce a finite-horizon contraction certificate, which we use to give budget conditions under which the tracking error admits an explicit bound that decays at a prescribed rate. We also present an algorithm to determine how many prediction and correction steps should be executed for each sample of the objective, while obeying a given budget on the allowable number of computations. Empirically, we show in a simulation that our approach reduces cumulative tracking error by 45.5 % relative to a comparable baseline approach.
authors: Negin Musavi;Oscar Jed R. Chuy;Melkior Ornik;Matthew T. Hale

title: UnEZ: A Fully Unsupervised Self-Templating Neural Network for Redshift and Line Strength Estimation
abstract: As spectroscopic surveys grow, estimating galaxy properties such as metallicity, star formation rate, and redshift becomes computationally cumbersome. Methods of estimating such properties rely on template spectra or curated redshift catalogs, which fail to represent the diversity of objects seen in large-scale surveys. We present UnEZ, a fully unsupervised, physics-informed machine learning model that can predict spectroscopic redshifts and line strengths with no prior redshift or line strength labels. An encoder predicts emission and absorption line amplitudes/widths, and a fixed deterministic decoder constructs a unique template, estimated redshift, redshift confidence curve, and spectral model. UnEZ was tested on the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) Data Release 18 due to its large dataset and thoroughly vetted redshift catalog which serves as an independent benchmark. Despite the lack of templates, line strength labels, or redshift labels, UnEZ's performance competes with modern redshift estimation algorithms. At SNR > 10, UnEZ achieves an outlier fraction of 0.459% and a normalized median absolute deviation (NMAD) of $1.237 \times 10^{-4}$. At SNR > 3, UnEZ achieves an outlier fraction of 3.89% and an NMAD of $1.471 \times 10^{-4}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate how UnEZ's line strength and redshift predictions can be utilized for various purposes such as constructing template spectra required in traditional redshift estimation algorithms. UnEZ illustrates how a fully unsupervised neural network can allow redshift, among other galaxy properties, to emerge naturally from the spectra themselves, providing a template-free, label-free approach that scales to the demands of future surveys.

title: The extragalactic science of the KMOS VVVX-GalCen spectroscopic survey II: Discovery of a galaxy cluster at z = 0.089 behind the Galactic plane
abstract: The Zone of Avoidance (ZoA) continues to represent the most significant incompleteness in the extragalactic census of the Local Universe. It is evident that photometric surveys alone are insufficient to establish whether the galaxy overdensities detected therein are physical systems or projections along the line of sight. We present the first spectroscopic results of the extragalactic science area of the KMOS VVVX-GalCen Spectroscopic Survey, demonstrating how near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy can reveal and dynamically characterise galaxy clusters hidden by the Milky Way. A photometric overdensity of 19 galaxy candidates was identified in the VVV NIRGC III catalogue, centred at $(l,b)=(274.05^\circ,+2.85^\circ)$ with a mean interstellar extinction of $A_{K_s}=0.2$ mag; 16 of these candidates were observed with VLT/KMOS in the $HK$ grating and yielded spectra with reliable cross-correlation radial velocities. A total of 14 galaxies form a compact structure with a mean redshift of $\langle z \rangle = 0.089 \pm 0.001$, which corresponds to a mean radial velocity $\langle cz \rangle = 26660 \pm 170$ km/s, while two are foreground galaxies. The rest-frame line-of-sight velocity dispersion is $σ_v = 560^{+110}_{-120}$ km/s, implying an indicative dynamical mass of $M_{200} = 1.9^{+0.7}_{-1.1} \times 10^{14} M_\odot$ (based on members within the cluster core $\sim 0.4 r_{200}$) and placing the system in the poor-cluster regime. Of these 14 cluster members, 13 also lie within the $2σ$ scatter of the fitted near-IR red sequence. The other two galaxies are foreground objects that lie outside this range.

title: Pinpointing Pivot Points: The DECIDE Framework for Data Analysis Decision Importances
abstract: Human judgment calls made throughout the data science life cycle can change the conclusions drawn from data. Independent analysts often make different choices when given the same data, leading to often unacceptable variations in results and contributing to the ongoing reproducibility crisis across scientific disciplines. The rapid adoption of agentic tools threatens to amplify this crisis. Several approaches have been developed to address this variation by following the same strategy: repeating an analysis under different combinations of analytical decisions and inspecting the distribution of outcomes. Examples include multiverse analysis, specification curve analysis, and vibration of effects. More broadly, the Predictability-Computability-Stability (PCS) framework assesses how documented judgment calls across the data science life cycle affect conclusions, with predictability serving as a reality-check that a model captures signal. Each of these approaches results in a "multiverse" object. While the distribution of outcomes reflects the overall variability of conclusions, estimating the influence of each individual decision requires additional tools. A common heuristic is to train a model to predict the outcome from these decisions and treat its coefficients or feature importances as proxies for each decision's influence. Although this strategy may work in certain cases, it assumes the model is correctly specified and accurately predicts the outcome, which we show is not always the case. In this work, we introduce DECIDE, a model-free framework that quantifies each decision's importance from the actual outcomes across the plausible decision space, avoiding issues of predictability by design. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DECIDE by applying it to real-world multiverse analyses. We further provide what is, to our knowledge, the first formal definition of the multiverse.
authors: Zachary T. Rewolinski;Jan Simson;Frauke Kreuter;Christoph Kern;Bin Yu

title: Safeguarded Neurally-Accelerated Preconditioning (SNAP) framework for Nonlinear Optimization
abstract: We introduce the Safeguarded Neurally-Accelerated Preconditioning (SNAP) framework for hybridizing nonlinear optimization methods with pre-trained neural operators (NOs). SNAP targets parametric optimization problems arising from variational formulations of nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs), where many parameter instances require repeated solves. Inspired by multilevel line-search methods, SNAP operates in cycles, combining classical optimization steps with a search direction generated by a pre-trained NO. Since NO-generated search directions carry no a priori descent guarantee, SNAP employs an a posteriori safeguard by accepting only corrections that satisfy prescribed descent and acceptance conditions. We prove global convergence of the SNAP algorithm and show that it preserves the convergence rate of the underlying optimization method independently of the employed NO architecture. Moreover, we also show that when the NO corrections are sufficiently accurate, SNAP converges faster, with the improvement directly related to the NO training error. To demonstrate SNAP's efficiency in practice, we run numerical experiments on a diverse set of nonlinear parametric optimization problems, including parametric minimal surface, Allen--Cahn, and nonlinear Helmholtz problems. The efficiency of SNAP is demonstrated by comparing two NO architectures, Fourier neural operator (FNO) and Transolver, and by using SNAP as a standalone solver and as a nonlinear preconditioner. Our numerical results show a substantial reduction in the number of required iterations, while demonstrating robustness and generalization across a wide range of problem parameters and mesh resolutions.

title: Gold vs.~Translation: Are We Measuring Language, Knowledge, or Locality in Translated Benchmarks?
abstract: Translated versions of English-origin benchmarks such as MMLU are widely used to evaluate large language models in non-English languages, yet it remains unclear whether they measure the same constructs as natively created benchmarks. We frame this as a proxy validity question and compare DeepL-translated MMLU proxies against six native benchmarks in seven pairings across five Nordic and Baltic languages, evaluating 29 models on each pairing. Beyond ranking agreement, we test incremental proxy validity: does the translated score add predictive value for native performance after controlling for model size and language proficiency? Proxy validity varies substantially across benchmark pairings. Applying the same robustness criteria to all seven pairings, we find four robust effects, two marginal effects, and one null result. The strongest evidence occurs for curriculum-overlap benchmarks such as Skolprov ($ΔR^2$=.128, 95% CI [.038,.253]), whereas translated MMLU provides no significant incremental value for Sweden-specific factual knowledge in SwedishFacts (p=.242). Because SwedishFacts is also the only open-ended benchmark, we cannot fully separate the effects of local content and response format. Overall, the results indicate a clear pattern: translated benchmarks provide a better proxy when their source content overlaps with the native evaluation target, while locally anchored knowledge is less reliably captured.

title: Multiscale evaluation of the elastic response of polycrystalline NiAl using molecular statics, EBSD-based finite element and analytical homogenization methods
abstract: The presented work proposes a multiscale framework for the numerical and analytical determination of the elastic constants of the intermetallic nickel aluminide (NiAl) at the microscopic scale. Molecular dynamics (MD) calculations have been employed to evaluate the stiffness tensors of a single NiAl monocrystalline body with cubic Pm$\bar{3}$m symmetry. The atomistic results were transferred to the upper scale as an input to micromechanical models. Here, finite element modeling (FEM) and analytical homogenization methods were used to simulate the elastic behavior of polycrystalline NiAl, with special attention to grain anisotropy and its morphology. The microstructural features of the heterogeneous body were evaluated experimentally using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) and subsequently used to generate a 3D polycrystalline geometric model that preserves realistic distributions of grain orientations and grain sizes. The reconstructed NiAl polycrystal was subjected to uniaxial tensile test simulations using FEM to evaluate the effective Young's modulus ($E$) and Poisson's ratio ($ν$). The numerical results were confronted with the experimental values of $E$ and~$ν$. With these model assumptions, a very good agreement between numerical and experimental results was achieved. Finally, the experimental results were compared with classical analytical estimates. Among the analytical approaches, the Hashin-Shtrikman upper bound and self-consistent approximation reproduced the experimental Young's modulus with minor deviations.
authors: Szymon Nosewicz;Marcin Maździarz;Paweł Hołobut;Witold Chromiński;Katarzyna Kowalczyk-Gajewska;Grzegorz Jurczak

title: From Local to Global: Sheaf-Theoretic Control Barrier Functions on Manifolds
abstract: Control barrier functions (CBFs) provide formal safety guarantees for dynamical systems by rendering a safe set forward-invariant via pointwise-optimal feedback control. While the CBF framework is well established for dynamical systems in Euclidean space, there exist gaps for systems evolving on non-Euclidean manifolds. For systems modeled as constrained control differential inclusions, we introduce the Sheaf-CBF: a sheaf-theoretic framework for CBFs on smooth manifolds and vector bundles. The differential inclusions are formulated intrinsically on the control bundle, and analogous regularity properties in the Euclidean case are established fiberwise under local trivializations. Regularity conditions are given under which a pointwise-optimal feedback law is single-valued and continuous over local charts. Framed as a local-to-global optimization problem, sheaf-theoretic restriction and gluing compatibility conditions on overlapping charts are shown to uniquely determine a continuous global section of the control bundle, thereby guaranteeing forward invariance of the safe set. Numerical simulations on a nontrivial M{ö}bius strip demonstrate that failure of sheaf compatibility results in violations of safety, whereas the Sheaf-CBF maintains forward invariance.
authors: Keith A. Currier;Wilmer Leal;Brandon C. Fallin;James Fairbanks;Warren E. Dixon

title: ARRAKIHS: The observability of tidally stripped satellites in a Milky Way-like halo
abstract: Deep imaging surveys are revealing increasing numbers of low surface brightness stellar streams around Milky Way-like galaxies. These streams trace the orbital evolution and internal structure of their disrupted dwarf galaxy progenitors. We investigate the evolution and observability of tidal features from dwarf galaxies consistent with the $Λ$CDM framework and Local Group observations. We performed high-resolution $N$-body simulations of dwarf galaxies orbiting in a static Milky Way-like potential comprising a disc, bulge, and dark matter halo. Each dwarf comprised a Plummer stellar distribution embedded in a cuspy or cored generalised Navarro--Frenk--White dark matter halo. Idealised integrated surface brightness maps were constructed every 0.5 Gyr over 10 Gyr, and detectability was quantified through the projected area of stellar light brighter than limiting surface brightnesses, $μ_{\rm lim}=29$--$32$ mag arcsec$^{-2}$, chosen to span depths relevant to ARRAKIHS, LSST, and Euclid. The detectability of tidal features depends most strongly on progenitor stellar mass, orbital configuration, parameterised by the eccentricity proxy $e_0$, and evolutionary stage. Across this range, extended tidal debris is predominantly recovered for initially more radial configurations, mainly those with $e_0 \gtrsim 0.75$. In the simulated grid, detectable area is dominated by $M_\star=10^8$--$10^9 M_\odot$ progenitors, whereas $M_\star=10^6$--$10^7 M_\odot$ systems can undergo stripping without detectable debris. The detectable area evolves non-monotonically with time, reflecting the competition between stream formation, phase mixing, and the fading of diffuse debris below the adopted surface brightness limits. Cuspy and cored progenitors show similar evolution of the detectable area, with differences smaller than the scatter induced by orbital diversity.

title: Rennala NSGD: Asynchronous Stochastic Optimization Beyond Euclidean Geometry
abstract: The empirical success of matrix-aware optimizers, such as Muon (Jordan et al., 2024) and Shampoo (arXiv:1802.09568), highlights the potential of non-Euclidean geometry for deep learning, including large language model (LLM) training. Despite this progress, the theoretical understanding of stochastic optimization in general normed spaces remains limited, particularly in distributed settings. We analyze minibatch stochastic gradient descent (SGD) for smooth nonconvex optimization with respect to an arbitrary norm on a finite-dimensional space. Using the framework of $κ$-regular normed spaces (arXiv:0809.0813), we derive high-probability oracle complexity bounds under a light-tail condition stated directly in the dual norm induced by the update norm. The bounds make the dependence on geometry explicit through the regularity constant $κ$ of the dual space. In the Euclidean case, our bound recovers the standard minibatch SGD rate up to logarithmic factors. For some non-Euclidean geometries and noise models, it is sharper than bounds obtained by converting a Euclidean noise assumption, reducing a linear dimension dependence to a logarithmic one. Building on this framework, we introduce Rennala NSGD, a semi-asynchronous distributed algorithm, and establish wall-clock time complexity guarantees under fixed, heterogeneous worker computation times. In the Euclidean case ($κ=1$), our bound matches the parameter dependence of classical Rennala SGD up to logarithmic factors.

title: The coupled evolution of nuclear star clusters and intermediate-mass black holes in a dwarf-galaxy merger
abstract: Nuclear star clusters (NSCs) and intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) are expected to coexist in low-mass galaxies and might together facilitate the coalescence and growth of IMBHs. We simulate an equal-mass, gas-rich dwarf-galaxy merger in which each progenitor hosts a $10^3\,\rm M_\odot$ IMBH embedded in a $10^6\,\rm M_\odot$ NSC to study their co-evolution. The simulation model combines the multiphase interstellar medium and fully sampled initial stellar mass function of GRIFFIN at $4\,\rm M_\odot$ gas resolution with the regularised post-Newtonian black hole dynamics of KETJU. Black holes are modelled as accreting sink particles without feedback. Without NSCs, $10^3$-$10^4\,\rm M_\odot$ IMBHs sink only to separations of $50$-$200\,\rm pc$ and capture no gas. With NSCs, the clusters coalesce within ${\sim} 500\,\rm Myr$, the IMBHs form a binary within a few Myr, and scattering of mainly old NSC stars drives them to merger ${\sim} 340\,\rm Myr$ later. The NSCs also promote gas capture, growing the black holes to $1.1\times10^5$ and $4.1\times10^4\,\rm M_\odot$. Gas capture is suppressed during the merger-induced starburst by stellar feedback and the motion of the NSCs relative to the gas, and proceeds in brief supernova-regulated episodes once the NSCs have settled in the centre. Scattering by the IMBH binary and the merger recoil of ${\sim} 175\,\rm km\,s^{-1}$, which removes the remnant from the NSC but not from the galaxy, leave a larger, rotating NSC with a flat core. The stellar tidal disruption rate rises towards coalescence, and the merger is detectable with LISA out to high redshift. NSCs thus remove the delivery and hardening bottlenecks of IMBH mergers in low-mass galaxies.
authors: Christian Partmann;Rachel S. Somerville;Michaela Hirschmann;Antti Rantala;Natalia Lahén

title: A Luminescent Organic Triradical as an Optically Addressable Qudit
abstract: Luminescent molecular trityl radicals provide options for optically-addressable electron spins and are promising for quantum sensing. Here, we present a luminescent triradical comprising three trityl groups covalently attached to a central phenyl ring. We find two distinct photoluminescence bands at 633 nm and 690 nm with different temporal evolutions, which we attribute to excited quartet and doublet states respectively. The ground state quartet is 1 meV (11.5K) lower in energy than the doublet, resulting in near-equal population of doublets and quartets at room temperature. We demonstrate optically initialized spin polarization, coherent control of the ground state quartet, and optical readout. Potential for optical quantum sensing is shown via optically detected magnetic resonance at room temperature and magneto-photoluminescence up to 3% at 5 mT. This material is a candidate optically addressable molecular qudit, providing opportunities to leverage larger state spaces than qubit systems.
authors: Kueyoung E. Kim;Avik Bhanja;Alistair Inglis;William K. Myers;Sam L. Bayliss;Richard H. Friend;Petri Murto

title: Metropolized backward sampling for conditional sequential Monte Carlo
abstract: Particle Gibbs samplers with backward sampling are widely used for sampling the smoothing distribution of state-space models, but, with few particles, the new trajectory often coincides with the current one at many time steps. A known but rarely used remedy replaces the random selection of the final particle by a Metropolis--Hastings move which avoids the current particle. We show that, with backward sampling, this remedy only helps at the last time steps, because its effect on the update rates decays geometrically with the distance to the final time. We propose instead Metropolized backward sampling, which makes such a move at every step of the backward pass, forcibly switching trajectories whenever possible. Additionally, we introduce a coupled version which prevents proposing the current trajectory, maximizing the chances of an actual switch versus the current trajectory and performing perfect sampling when the state-space model has no observations, a feature not shared by backward sampling. We prove that, at every time step, both methods dominate backward sampling as they update the state more often and have smaller lag-one autocorrelations than it does. Our methods are drop-in replacements for backward sampling, and can be used to improve any particle Gibbs sampler.

title: AtomTree: A Hierarchical Framework for State-Aware Embodied Instruction Following with LLMs
abstract: Embodied instruction following in interactive environments requires agents to interpret natural language commands and complete long-horizon tasks. Existing planners either rely on large labeled trajectories, or use few-shot and zero-shot LLM prompting that produces a whole plan in a single serial reasoning process. These approaches depend on linguistic common sense, commit to a plan from the initial instruction, and only update after failures, which weakens robustness and state awareness. We present AtomTree, a hierarchical framework for state-aware task planning with LLMs. AtomTree incrementally builds a tree of subgoals and actions, where the LLM decides at each step, from the current symbolic state, whether to further decompose or to output a grounded low-level action. A lightweight memory module summarizes past outcomes for reuse in later decisions. When a low-level action stalls, AtomTree triggers hierarchical backtracking replanning to return to the parent node and regenerate the subtree plan from the latest state, preventing continued drift along an incorrect trajectory. In zero-shot evaluation on the ALFRED benchmark, AtomTree outperforms prior LLM-based planners. Project page: https://zhaihaotian.github.io/atomtree-website/.

title: Integrating multi-source local information for global undirected graph reconstruction via integer programming
abstract: Graphical models are widely used to represent conditional independence structures, but learning them is challenging when data are fragmented across sources that measure different subsets of variables and may not be directly shareable. We develop a general framework for reconstructing a shared global graph from heterogeneous, partially observed sources. Our framework permits both the observed variable sets and source-specific distributions to differ. Under a source-wise faithfulness condition, local conditional independence graphs correspond to latent projections of the shared global graph, which is identifiable up to the equivalence class induced by the observed variable sets. The framework integrates raw data, estimated source graphs, or a combination of both, accommodating settings with restricted access to individual-level data, such as privacy constraints. We develop mixed-integer optimization formulations and scalable approximate algorithms for several classes of graphical models. Unlike standard high-dimensional analyses, our guarantees are governed by new combinatorial notions of signal strength that capture how information propagates across partially observed sources. Extensive simulations further show that integration can substantially improve estimation of source-specific projected graphs relative to separate source methods. Real-data application illustrates the framework's use with partially-observed sources of fatty acid measurements.

title: The Quine Test: How Much of a Model's Self Survives Its Own Description?
abstract: Frontier language models express coherent preferences, but behavioral evidence alone cannot say whether these belong to the model or to a character it portrays. Following Hofstadter's view of the self as a self-description, we ask whether a model's description of itself works as a portable specification of its preference profile, a quine test: can the text a model writes about itself regenerate its behavior elsewhere? Ten models from nine labs write self-descriptions; we place each one in the prompt of other models (receivers) and of fresh instances of the author, and measure how closely their choices on a 110-item preference battery match the author's. First, the tested native self-descriptions (native: the profile measured under a generic assistant prompt) show no average reconstruction gain across variations in length, framing, wording and prompt placement: on a 0 to 1 fidelity scale where a model's fidelity to a fresh instance of itself is 0.979 and to unrelated models about 0.89, the one-sided 95% upper bound on the pooled gain is below +0.01 in every tested system-prompt condition, and descriptions based on the author's observed choices do no better. Second, the channel itself is strong: explicitly listing the author's answers lets receivers reproduce its profile at fidelity 0.955 to 0.960 across three model grids, within 0.03 of same-model repeatability. Third, self-descriptions written under an explicit preference policy transfer the assigned preferences almost as well as the policy text itself. Fourth, reading its own self-description shifts even the author away from its baseline, modestly more than unrelated prose of the same length. For the preferences measured here, native self-descriptions influence behavior without reliably specifying how to reproduce it in another model. We release the pipeline, battery, raw call logs, and 198 model-written descriptions.

title: Learning Scientific Trajectories to Predict Future Biomedical Discoveries
abstract: AI co-scientists have expanded the use of large language models for generating scientific hypotheses and guiding experimental investigation. Here we investigate whether temporal patterns in the semantic representations of complete biomedical conclusions can guide hypothesis generation. We introduce ForeSCITE, a framework that identifies thematic clusters of published conclusions, estimates a direction separating earlier from more recent findings within each cluster, and projects existing conclusion embeddings along these directions. An embedding language model trained to reconstruct conclusions decodes the projected coordinates into natural-language hypotheses. Across 407 clusters derived from approximately three million pre-cutoff conclusions, we identify temporal structure and illustrate its retention after decoding. In retrospective, time-sliced evaluations, ForeSCITE increases semantic coverage beyond the historical corpus, biomedical entity-pair novelty and post-cutoff pair re-observation relative to five prompt-based and retrieval-augmented baselines. Expert review of prioritized CAR-T hypotheses identified 37 candidates as both novel and biologically plausible, and expert justifications for five selected hypotheses illustrate their biological rationale and subsequent literature support where available. These findings support temporal guidance in semantic space as a scalable mechanism for proposing biomedical hypotheses for subsequent scientific evaluation.
authors: Chia-Hsuan Chang;Brian Ondov;Jiang Lv;Lan Jiang;Yunmai Wang;Haerin Song;Xueqing Peng;Qiaozhu Mei;Xiaolei Su;Hua Xu

title: cuPDQPx: A GPU-Accelerated Restarted Halpern PDHG for Large-Scale Convex Quadratic Programming
abstract: We present cuPDQPx, a GPU-accelerated, factorization-free first-order solver for large-scale convex quadratic programming (QP). Building on the restarted reflected Halpern primal-dual framework of cuPDLPx, we introduce an auxiliary-variable splitting that yields explicit updates without linearizing the quadratic objective or solving inner quadratic subproblems. A preconditioned proximal point interpretation yields both sublinear and linear fixed-point residual convergence guarantees. For practical efficiency, cuPDQPx integrates diagonal preconditioning, step-size selection, adaptive restart, and adaptive primal and quadratic weight updates. cuPDQPx is implemented in C and CUDA with optimized sparse matrix-vector products, kernel fusion, and CUDA Graphs. Numerical experiments on the Maros-Mészáros collection, a convex subset of QPLIB, and synthetic large-scale QPs demonstrate that cuPDQPx has strong numerical performance at both $10^{-4}$ and $10^{-8}$ tolerances.

title: On The Scaling Relations Between Black Holes And The Galaxy/Bulge Mass And Their Connections With The Black Hole Occupation Fraction
abstract: We investigate the black hole (BH)--host galaxy scaling relations predicted by the semianalytic model \texttt{FEGA25}, focusing on their dependence on BH mass threshold, galaxy morphology, and redshift, and on their connection with the BH occupation fraction (BHOF). Using the YS200 cosmological simulation as our reference volume, we study the $M_{\rm BH}$--$M_{\star}$ and $M_{\rm BH}$--$M_{\rm bulge}$ relations for different BH mass selections and compare their redshift evolution with the hydrodynamical zoom-in simulation \texttt{NewCluster}. We find that BH mass cuts primarily affect the low-mass regime, while the selected relations progressively converge toward the intrinsic no-cut relations at higher host masses. The $M_{\rm BH}$--$M_{\star}$ relation also depends systematically on galaxy morphology, with increasingly bulge-dominated systems preferentially occupying higher stellar masses. Over $z=0$--$3$, FEGA25 shows no clear systematic evolution of either scaling relation, consistent with a broadly preserved statistical connection between BH and host-galaxy growth. NewCluster shows no clear monotonic evolution either, although it exhibits larger scatter, particularly toward high host masses. We further show that BHOF and BH--host scaling relations encode complementary information. A low BHOF generally corresponds to a stronger selection-induced offset, but the mapping is not unique: substantially different occupation fractions can yield similar median scaling relations, and at fixed BHOF the bias depends on the host property and underlying BH mass distribution. At $z=0$, \texttt{FEGA25} is consistent with available observational constraints for both stellar- and bulge-mass relations, while predicting increased scatter and bending toward lower host masses.
authors: Emanuele Contini;J. K. Jang;Jinsu Rhee;Changjo Seo;Sukyoung K. Yi

title: Beyond fabrication: Misattributed numbers in papers written by AI research agents
abstract: Verifying numerical claims in research written by AI agents is an important but challenging problem. Recent benchmarks show that many agent-written papers fail integrity checks, but such verdicts, often produced by a single LLM judge, identify failure without explaining its nature, and existing checks either test a paper for internal consistency or test whether a reported value appears somewhere in an agent's output. We re-analyze all 540 released judgments from a recent public benchmark of AI research agents (nine agents, fifteen open research problems) and manually label 256 numerical claims from 18 submissions. Failures concentrate on alignment between the paper and the underlying work rather than overt cheating, and about four in five unsupported claims correspond to values in the agent's own files that come from the wrong experiment, metric, or run. We introduce a deterministic claim-to-evidence checker that scores whether the surrounding context identifies the claimed result and calibrates each claim against numerical decoys. With its rules fixed before labeling, it certifies claims with over 90% precision against blinded annotators (78 of 85; Cohen's kappa = 0.89), while verifying only a subset of claims; most claims it cannot verify are nevertheless traceable, so failure to verify is not evidence of falsehood. An LLM verifier given the same evidence recovers more traceable claims but accepts about three times as many misattributed ones, so the two are best used together. Applied to 99 submissions, the checker reveals large differences in traceability across agents, and on 30 submissions a second judge configuration, with a different model and harness, orders the agents' vendor groups as the official judge does while passing twice as many papers. These findings motivate provenance-first auditing of AI-produced research.
