title: Game-Theoretic Foundations for Undiscounted Bisimulation Metrics
abstract: Bisimulation metrics offer a principled notion of task-relevant state similarity in reinforcement learning, but existing constructions and methods are largely confined to discounted MDPs, where contraction arguments ensure well-defined fixed points and downstream guarantees. We develop a unified foundation for bisimulation metrics in undiscounted settings, that is total- and average-reward problems, by replacing the standard operator-centric view with a game-centric one: we interpret prior metric operators as Bellman-Shapley operators of zero-sum turn-based games and define metrics as the corresponding game value functions, yielding unique definitions even when $γ=1$. This game-theoretic foundation facilitates transfer of dynamic-programming theory and algorithms. We also use this game-centric perspective to characterize how metric finiteness depends on structural properties of the underlying MDP and motivate certain directed metrics that remain finite in weakly communicating MDPs. We further introduce an abstract framework for modifying the games' action spaces, allowing general transition coupling sets, that recovers many existing metrics and guides new constructions. Finally, we prove that these metrics bound total-reward and, when the optimal gain is state-independent, optimal relative value differences. We also provide error and suboptimality guarantees for aggregation-based planning in total- and average-reward settings.

title: Robust LLM-Generated Text Detection through Matched Conditional-Response Probing
abstract: Reliable detection of large language model (LLM)-generated text must remain effective under meaning-preserving text revisions, such as rewriting, polishing, and expansion. In practice, LLM outputs are often rewritten, polished, expanded, translated, or lightly edited before publication, weakening the lexical, syntactic, and local discourse cues used by many existing detectors. We introduce \textbf{M}atched \textbf{C}onditional-\textbf{R}esponse \textbf{P}robing (\textbf{MCRP}), a frozen-LLM probing framework that measures how a candidate text responds when a semantically matched condition is introduced, removed, or replaced. For each candidate, the frozen probe LLM first generates a short semantic condition and then compares token-level losses and prompt--target attention measurements under matched, null, and control conditions. It aggregates bidirectional conditioned alignment, counterfactual sensitivity, and internal attention coupling into a probe representation, on which it trains a lightweight supervised random-forest classifier while keeping the probe LLM frozen. Across standard detection, robustness to meaning-preserving text revisions, multilingual, and multidomain evaluations, MCRP achieves consistently strong performance. Under rewriting, polishing, and expansion, it reaches 93.97\% F1 and 96.24\% ROC-AUC, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 19.50 and 25.77 percentage points, respectively. Component ablations show that the response feature groups make complementary contributions to predictive performance. In the condition-control study, matched conditions consistently outperform random, mismatched, and corrupted alternatives, demonstrating a measurable incremental benefit from semantic matching.
authors: Junfeng Hao;Wenxian Wang;Tao Leng;Xingshu Chen;Hao Ren;Haizhou Wang

title: Tight Stationarity Transfer and Repeatability for Inexact Proximal-Gradient Methods
abstract: Proximal-gradient methods are widely used for composite optimization, but inexact proximal updates introduce a residual in the proximal optimality condition, complicating the analysis of how stationarity changes across a step. We study this question for composite objectives consisting of a smooth convex term and a possibly nonsmooth weakly convex term, focusing on the relationship between the directional-stationarity measures at the input and output points of an inexact proximal-gradient step. We first establish separate input and output bounds, but their combination can yield a conservative estimate because their worst-case residual directions may differ. By exploiting the magnitude and orientation of this shared residual, we establish tight joint bounds and derive an exact one-step stationarity-transfer factor that strictly improves the estimate from separate bounds in the short-step regime. We also identify the precise residual-tolerance threshold for finite uniform stationarity transfer. A further distinction emerges over multiple steps: endpoint worst cases can repeat over arbitrarily many iterations, whereas interior worst cases cannot persist across two consecutive steps, yielding strict two-step submultiplicativity. These results also provide principled tolerance-selection rules, descent estimates, and stationarity-complexity guarantees for inexact proximal-gradient methods.

title: Finite-Temperature Magnetism and Longitudinal Spin Transport in Compensated Half-Metal Ferrimagnets with Near-Zero Magnetization
abstract: Fully compensated ferrimagnets, characterized by nearly vanishing magnetic moments at zero temperature, perfect spin-polarized electronic structures, and ultrafast spin dynamics, represent a highly promising materials platform for next-generation spintronic devices. By minimizing stray magnetic fields and reducing switching currents, FCFs enable a viable path toward high-speed, low-power spintronic devices. In this work, we present a systematic investigation of the electronic structure, finite-temperature magnetism, and spin-dependent transport properties of the Heusler-type fully compensated half-metallic ferrimagnet Mn3Al in magnetic tunnel junctions. We demonstrate that Mn3Al is a half-metallic FCF with 100% spin polarization and fully compensated magnetization at 0 K. Combining density functional theory with Monte Carlo simulations, we characterize its finite-temperature magnetic properties and show that Mn3Al exhibits a net magnetization below 11.6 emu/cc at 300 K, confirming the robustness of its nearly compensated ferrimagnetic order at room temperature. Furthermore, we predict that the Mn3Al/MgO/Mn3Al MTJ yields a giant tunneling magnetoresistance effect at 0 K, which remains as high as 232% at 300 K. Our results establish Mn3Al and related half-metallic FCFs as excellent candidates for magnetoresistance-based spintronic applications.
authors: Jiahao Shentu;Jie Li;Jianting Dong;Meng Zhu;Chen Wang;Qing Zhang;Yizhuo Song;Wenqi Sun;Jia Zhang

title: EPSBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Earnings Forecasting
abstract: Quarterly earnings forecasting requires an agent to connect financial evidence to the income-statement line items that produce a company's reported earnings. We introduce EPSBench, a benchmark for studying this ability across 149 firm-quarters from 86 US companies. Agents read a fixed collection of filings, earnings-call transcripts, and news, then estimate company-specific income-statement drivers with cited evidence. A shared accounting calculator converts these estimates into GAAP diluted earnings per share (EPS), providing a common basis for comparing forecast assumptions. We evaluate six models under a common harness, assessing point forecast error relative to date-matched analyst consensus and checking whether their prediction intervals achieve the stated coverage. Three models show no detectable paired difference in point forecast error from consensus, and three have higher error. Across all six models, nominal 80% intervals contain reported EPS in only 37--70% of runs that return an interval, and most misses fall above the upper bound because the forecasts run low. The driver records trace most of the error gap between models to operating-income estimates.
authors: Yanbin Yin;Chuyu Xu;Liqin Ye;Jing Peng;Chao Zhang

title: Human Evaluation with Automatic Scores: Separating Sampling and Estimation Gains
abstract: Automatic judges offer inexpensive information about model outputs, but an evaluation team must decide how to turn that information into fewer human annotations. Scores can guide sampling, correct an estimate, or support adaptive acquisition, and these uses may capture overlapping gains. We compare their incremental value on fixed evaluation pools from three preference datasets, and 19 attributed-question-answering systems. Matched comparisons use the same scores, account for pilot labels and budget rules, and separate acquisition from estimation. Score stratification is a strong reference: after ten-bin stratification, the best fixed local linear correction offers only 1.00--5.27% further MSE reduction in the primary configurations. Unequal allocation offers larger gains in some pools, but can increase error when confident scores conceal variable human outcomes. Comparison on AttributedQA, shrinking learned quotas toward score-only quotas lowers pooled MSE for 17 of 19 systems relative to the score-only procedure, but ordinary pooled 95% intervals cover only 88.09--93.54%. The same shrinkage improves on the score-only reference in only one of eight preference configurations. Ranking experiments further show that lower individual MSE need not improve system selection. These findings support a simple starting procedure, proportional sampling within score strata followed by a stratified human mean, and identify what additional evidence is needed to justify correction or adaptation for the intended evaluation output.

title: Cross Lingual Abstractive Summarization for Marathi
abstract: Text summarization is an important task for advancing natural language processing (NLP) research and applications in Indic languages. Despite progress in extractive and abstractive summarization, both monolingual summarization (MS) and cross-lingual summarization (CLS) remain relatively underexplored for these languages. Recent advances in Transformer architectures, pretrained language models (PLMs), and dataset availability offer new opportunities to address this gap. In this work, we construct cross-lingual training data from the monolingual Marathi MahaSum corpus and combine it with the smaller cross-lingual PMIndiaSum dataset to fine-tune IndicTrans2, an Indic neural machine translation model. We evaluate the resulting models using ROUGE, chrF and chrF++ metrics, focusing primarily on Marathi-to-English summarization due to computational constraints. We also discuss the applicability of our approach to the English-to-Marathi direction. Our experiments demonstrate that leveraging a pretrained translation model yields substantially better summarization performance than the IndicBART and mBART-50 based baselines reported in previous work on cross-lingual summarization.

title: Damped stochastic mirror descent for non-smooth ill-posed problems in Banach space
abstract: We introduce a damped variant of the stochastic mirror descent method for systems of non-smooth nonlinear ill-posed operator equations in Banach spaces. At each iteration, the method samples a random subset of the equations, performs a mirror-descent step in the dual space with an adaptive step size derived from the discrepancy principle, and applies a damping term that prevents the iterates from drifting away from the initial guess. The scheme accommodates non-smooth forward operators through a family of bounded linear surrogates, admits general $p$-convex penalty functionals which also includes trained convex penalty, allows the noise level to differ from equation to equation, and dispenses with two classical requirements, namely reflexivity of the image space and Gâteaux differentiability of the forward operator. We study its regularization properties under an \textit{a posteriori} stopping rule by proving first that the iteration terminates after finitely many steps almost surely, and then that the mean-square error of the iterates tends to zero as the noise level vanishes. Numerical experiments on a system of non-smooth semilinear inverse source problems and the identification of a diffusion coefficient confirm the theoretical analysis and shows improved convergence results.

title: Belief-Driven Search in Connectivity-Constrained Mobile Sensor Networks with Convergence Guarantees
abstract: Multi-agent search and coverage is critical to autonomous exploration, search-and-rescue, and defense applications. This paper investigates settings where a mobile sensor network is tasked with coordinating to discover the position of a stationary target within a bounded region. We develop a Bayesian update scheme where agents iteratively combine local uncertainties derived from their sensor measurements through inverse variance weighting to get a better global understanding of where the target may be located given some prior belief. Network agents' trajectories are governed by a primal-dual gradient update rule that simultaneously minimizes the expected sensing uncertainty and enforces network connectivity among the agents. We prove that the belief converges to the target under mild planner conditions, with an explicit exponential rate of false-hypothesis rejection and a bound on expected search time. Simulation results show that we can successfully find the target and collapse belief to the ground truth target location while ensuring connectivity of our sensor network. They also empirically confirm our theoretical bounds and planner conditions. Finally, we compare against a naive lawnmower sweeping strategy, showing that our method locates the target more quickly when the prior is informative.
authors: George J. Ziavras;Ziqiao Zhang;Shreyas Sundaram;Christopher G. Brinton
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Extended version with full proofs

title: A New Formulation of the Elastica Model with Application to Image Inpainting
abstract: Curves and interfaces play a central role in computer vision and image processing, and Euler's elastica energy is one of the most successful tools to model and manipulate them. The elastica energy is usually computed through a level-set or a phase field representation of the curve, in which the curvature term makes the energy nonlinear, non-convex and, in the level-set case, non-differentiable, so that its minimization is notoriously difficult. In this paper, we propose a new formulation of the elastica model based on a binary representation of curves. The key ingredient is a very simple formula for the curvature: if $φ$ is the $\pm1$ binary function associated with a curve $Γ$, then along $Γ$ the curvature is given by $-\frac{1}{C_0ε}\left(R_ε*φ\right)+O(ε)$, where $R_ε$ is a radial kernel supported in a ball of radius $ε$ and $C_0$ is an explicit constant. No derivative of $φ$ is involved and the convolution is evaluated by FFT. The resulting energy is a weighted total variation, so that formally the new formulation is a generalization of the well-known ROF model; a phase field type model is obtained from the same curvature formula. Combining FFT with the split Bregman iteration, which for the present problem coincides with an augmented Lagrangian method (ALM), we obtain efficient algorithms whose subproblems are either linear systems solved by conjugate gradient or explicit pointwise formulas. Numerical experiments on the inpainting of binary images are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms.

title: Keepace.ai: A Technical Report on a Large Language Model for Sports and Health
abstract: Large language models hold promise for delivering safe, scientifically grounded, and personalized exercise guidance at scale, yet the sports-and-health domain still lacks curated training corpora and rigorous evaluation benchmarks. Keepace (Keepace.ai) is a domain-specialized LLM built on Qwen3.5-27B through post-training, currently optimized for Chinese-language exercise guidance across three tasks: workout plan generation, sports-and-health knowledge QA, and personal sports data analysis. In internal rubric-based evaluations designed with domain experts, Keepace outperforms its base model and larger general-purpose baselines, with the most pronounced improvements in exercise safety, boundary compliance, structured output completeness, and scientific accuracy. This report summarizes the current design, data pipeline, safety-first evaluation framework, and evaluation results of Keepace.
authors: Keepace. ai Team;Bowen Wu;Heng Wang;Jufeng Mi;Kang Liu;Kun Li;Long He;Manling Han;Suli Fan;Xiaosen Jiang;Yi Wang;Ying He;Yu Tang;Yunhan Li;Zifang Liu

title: Necessary and Sufficient Structural Conditions for the Validity of Lyapunov-Type Exponential Stability Criteria
abstract: Whether the exponential decay of a Lyapunov function along trajectories implies exponential stability of the state---an inference we call migration---is long assumed in Lyapunov's second method but never characterized at the criterion level. We formalize stability criteria over trajectory families, distinguish admissibility of a criterion (its structural condition suffices for its conclusion) from tightness (its necessity), and establish the necessary and sufficient structural conditions for validity. In logarithmic coordinates the theory reduces to a single two-sided displacement function of the comparison pair: in discrete time, migration holds if and only if a regularity package (excluding failure by infinitely many steps of finite displacement) and a joint lower bound (excluding failure by a single step of unbounded expansion) hold simultaneously. Continuous time strengthens the latter; the two criteria are separated exactly by the minimum step size. Written without its inverse-function formulation, the Panteley--Lor'ia criterion coincides with our continuous-time conditions on every nondecreasing pair, and loses soundness beyond: it was already complete on the classical regularity class. An envelope construction shows that regularization costs no discriminative power, and radial unboundedness, a standing assumption since Hahn, is dispensable.

title: Nearly Minimax Optimal Regret for Adversarial Linear Bandits with Strong Corruptions
abstract: We study adversarial linear bandits with strong corruption, in which an adaptive adversary chooses the reward vectors and a strong adversary corrupts each observed reward after seeing the learner's action, subject to a known total corruption budget $C$. Strong corruption breaks the importance-weighted reward estimates used by adversarial bandit algorithms: by corrupting only the rounds in which a rarely sampled action is drawn, the adversary amplifies each unit of corruption by the inverse of its sampling probability. The best known bound for this problem, $\tilde O(\sqrt{d^3T} + dC)$ by Liu et al. (2024), is a factor $\sqrt{d}$ above the corruption-free rate in its leading term, and whether $\tilde O(d\sqrt{T} + dC)$ regret is achievable was left open. We propose CRW-FTRL, which runs follow-the-regularized-leader with a radius-weighted entropy regularizer and estimates rewards with a normalized kernel estimator whose sensitivity to corruption is governed by per-action radii instead of inverse sampling probabilities. The radii are nondecreasing and are chosen jointly with the sampling distribution through a monotone log-determinant barrier problem, so that a negative linear term in the regularizer cancels both the corruption bias and the estimation error of every comparator. For $K$ actions in $\mathbb{R}^d$, CRW-FTRL achieves $\tilde O(\sqrt{dT\log K} + dC)$ regret with high probability against an adaptive adversary, which matches the best known corruption-free rate and the $Ω(dC)$ lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Applied to a discretization of a general compact action set, it yields $\tilde O(d\sqrt{T} + dC)$ regret, which settles the statistical rate of corrupted adversarial linear bandits under strong corruption.

title: A domain-specific atomistic model for Earth's core materials
abstract: Understanding Earth's core requires accurate descriptions of multicomponent iron alloys under extreme conditions. Here, we develop the Earth's Core Atomistic Model (ECAM) for Fe-Ni-S-Si-O-C-H alloys through sampling with a foundational atomistic model, targeted ab initio simulations, and iterative exploration. A compact dataset selected from nearly half a million configurations is consistently labeled using high-accuracy first-principles calculations and used to train a lightweight model. The model explicitly includes thermal electronic contributions and runs nearly two orders of magnitude faster than the original foundational model. ECAM corrects artifacts in the foundational model's description of core materials and reproduces the density, seismic velocity, Gibbs free energy, and phase diagrams of Fe and binary alloys in agreement with previous ab initio calculations. ECAM is expected to enable more realistic modeling of chemical partitioning and crystallization in Earth's core. Our workflow also provides a practical route from foundational-model sampling to efficient domain-specific simulation.
authors: Tianqi Wan;Liangrui Wei;Zepeng Wu;Renata M. Wentzcovitch;Yang Sun

title: Age-Resolved Vertical Motions in the Milky Way Warp: A Localized Enhancement in Intermediate-Age Populations
abstract: Determining how the Milky Way warp evolves provides constraints on the formation and dynamical evolution of galactic disks. Using Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment Data Release 19 (APOGEE DR19) spectroscopy, we estimate ages for 222,355 red giants. With Gaia astrometry and geometric distances, we analyze 168,824 of these stars in five age bins spanning $0$--$10$ Gyr. The warp-related radial vertical-velocity ($V_Z$) profile of young red giants ($0$--$2$ Gyr) is broadly consistent with those of classical Cepheids and young open clusters. Over $9\leq R<12$ kpc, we find that the mean $V_Z$ values of the intermediate-age red giants ($2$--$4$ and $4$--$6$ Gyr) are $1.48\pm0.46$ and $1.49\pm0.52$ km s$^{-1}$ higher than that of the young population, respectively. By contrast, at $R\simeq12$--$13$ kpc, the $V_Z$ profiles of the $0$--$6$ Gyr red giants are consistent within their uncertainties. The intermediate-age enhancement persists across our robustness tests and may reflect smaller effective kinematic warp onset radii for the intermediate-age populations. The observed velocity differences may arise from the combined effects of earlier perturbations and the present-day warp, or from differences in vertical structure among stellar populations.
authors: Xiaoyue Zhou;Xiaodian Chen;Haifeng Wang;Shu Wang;Zhihong He;Licai Deng
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, 1 table, accepted for publication in ApJL. Online Dataset: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23308202

title: 3DCodeEdit: Benchmarking Instruction-Guided 3D Program Editing
abstract: Language models increasingly create 3D content through code, with practical workflows often relying on editing existing programs rather than regenerating them, for speed and precise control. Such edits require understanding what a program builds and foreseeing how a change reshapes it, yet prior benchmarks mostly evaluate generation or simple edits against a reference. In this paper, we introduce 3DCodeEdit, a benchmark of 2,592 instruction-guided editing tasks over 108 Blender programs that construct objects entirely in code. Its edits range from parameter to structural changes, style redesign, and scene composition, and are judged from renders against human-reviewed checklists. Across 17 models, the average success rate is only 37%, and even the strongest models complete fewer than 60% of structural and style edits. As models become more capable, their failures shift to geometric foresight, where the code runs but builds the wrong shape. We therefore study whether multi-turn feedback can compensate for this missing foresight. Feedback from a separate reviewer model that describes how the renders differ from the request helps most, more than maximum reasoning effort or an agent harness, and can let a 27B model surpass the single-shot rate of a 2.8T-parameter model.
authors: Binjie Wang;Xinran Zhao;Shoubin Yu;Xiang Li;Silong Yong;Chenyang Yang;Tianyu Chen;Ruofei Du;He He;Chen Zhao;Tongshuang Wu

title: Data Center Load Reductions: Attribution, Measurement Limits, and Estimation
abstract: Hundreds of gigawatts of data center loads are seeking interconnection in the United States given the massive growth of artificial intelligence and cloud computing. In recent years, several incidents of data centers reducing their loads by hundreds to thousands of megawatts have been documented, raising grid reliability concerns. U.S. regulators have since ordered reliability standards for the integration of computational loads, and the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) now calls on transmission owners to install disturbance recorders at these facilities to support root cause analysis. Such recorders usually observe only electrical quantities at the point of interconnection (POI). A sudden load reduction can be caused by a change in workload or a switch to backup supply. This work shows when POI measurements can distinguish the two mechanisms. It is established that they can produce identical POI voltage and current in a quasi-static constant power model, and during the transient their separation depends on the reduction relative to measurement noise, the clearing time, the dynamics through which workload reaches the POI, and the recorder bandwidth. When POI data are insufficient, an estimator that uses workload data is proposed to determine how much of the facility stayed connected. The results of this work identify the measurements and grid information utilities need to determine why data center load dropped.
authors: Abdallah Alalem Albustami;Ahmad F. Taha;Mohammad Alwahdanee;Zuhaib Shakeel Muhammad

title: Scalable Bayesian Quadrature via Operator-Adapted Features
abstract: Kernel methods face two recurrent bottlenecks: the cubic cost of inverting an $n\times n$ kernel matrix, as in kernel ridge regression, and the evaluation of kernel integrals, as required in kernel quadrature. Existing low-rank kernel and Gaussian process approximations primarily address the former bottleneck, but do not control the downstream quadrature error when both the kernel matrix and kernel mean are approximated, particularly when the integrand lies outside the kernel reproducing kernel Hilbert space. We address both challenges through an operator-adapted finite-feature approximation. Specifically, we construct a finite-dimensional working kernel from the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of a second-order differential operator. We establish convergence guarantees for the resulting finite-feature estimators in kernel quadrature, with extension to other related kernel methods. Our results show that, with $m \lesssim n$ basis functions, the truncated estimator attains the corresponding benchmark statistical rates. The theory covers fixed/random designs, noisy/noiseless observations, oversmoothing/undersmoothing regimes, and Matérn/Gaussian-type weights. We provide explicit error bounds that quantify the roles of the spectral cutoff, regularization parameter, lengthscale, sampling geometry, and operator boundary condition. We verify the convergence results in numerical experiments.

title: Two Birds with One Stone: Skill-Augmented Generation via Unified Retrieval and Utilization
abstract: Skills, as reusable external knowledge, have demonstrated substantial potential to enhance the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to solve complex tasks. However, existing skill-augmented generation methods typically rely on separate models for skill retrieval and skill utilization, resulting in disconnected optimization of these two processes. To address this gap, we propose Skill-Uni, a unified reinforcement learning framework that jointly optimizes skill retrieval and utilization. Specifically, we adopt a generative skill retrieval paradigm that enables a single model to both learn how to retrieve relevant skills and leverage them for task solving. To effectively train this unified framework, we introduce a two-stage training strategy consisting of warm-up instruction tuning and GRPO, allowing the model to progressively improve its skill retrieval and utilization capabilities. Extensive experiments on five skill-related benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of Skill-Uni, yielding average performance gains of 66.59% and 34.82% over the base Qwen3-4B and LLaMA3.1-8B models, respectively. Besides, Skill-Uni is compatible with various skill retrieval engines, demonstrating its flexibility and generalizability. Additional in-depth analyses also provide insights into the effectiveness of Skill-Uni.
authors: Zihan Luo;Jiahui Kang;Wei Zhou;Qilin Fan;Mingyan Li;Chao Chen

title: Convex-SKM-Net: Low-Latency Block Halfspace Corrections for Neural Convex Constraint Satisfaction
abstract: Fast inference and strict constraint satisfaction are essential for learning-based decision-making. Existing methods often rely on constraint-specific projections or feasible-set parameterizations, while iterative repair can be costly. We introduce Convex-SKM-Net, a convex constraint-satisfaction layer that forms linearization halfspaces from residual and (sub)gradient oracles without constraint-specific inequality projectors. It applies fixed-depth dual projected-gradient descent (dual PGD) to minimum-displacement block problems using GPU-friendly matrix operations. We jointly learn the predictor and a positive-definite mobility, adapting the correction geometry to improve objective quality. We prove convergence of the outer iterates at fixed dual depth and linear convergence in distance under Slater's condition and bounded subgradients. All our test outputs on three second-order-cone model-predictive control (SOC-MPC) horizons and six power-system convex relaxations satisfy a $10^{-3}$ feasibility tolerance. Comparisons with the latest constraint-satisfaction methods show inference speedups of up to $144.3\times$ on SOC-MPC and $7.7\times$ on a convex quadratically constrained quadratic programming (QCQP) benchmark with joint training. On QCQP, the mean objective gap is $0.012\%$, with full test feasibility at $10^{-4}$. Learning mobility reduces the five-seed affine-task mean gap by $22.4\%$ and improves gaps in matched power-system comparisons.

title: Crystoria: A Large-Scale Crystal Dataset Linking Thermodynamic and Dynamical Stability for Materials AI
abstract: Large-scale crystal databases have transformed materials discovery by making millions of structures and thermodynamic properties accessible to materials informatics. Yet dynamical stability remains sparsely characterized at a comparable scale because its evaluation is substantially more computationally demanding than conventional structure and energy calculations. This mismatch creates a critical gap between the rapidly expanding crystal-structure space and the physical information available for materials research and machine learning. Here we introduce Crystoria, a large-scale crystal dataset designed to bring dynamical stability to the scale of modern materials data. We construct Crystoria by systematically curating low-energy and metastable inorganic crystals, standardizing their structural identities, and combining machine-learning-accelerated structural relaxation with phonon-based dynamical screening. The resulting dataset contains 2,649,640 crystal structures, spanning 89 elements, 219 of the 230 space groups, and primitive cells containing 1-48 atoms. Among them, 1,793,353 structures (67.68%) are classified as dynamically stable, revealing substantial variation in dynamical stability across chemical and crystallographic space. By bringing dynamical stability to the scale of millions of crystal structures, Crystoria provides a physically grounded foundation for materials artificial intelligence (AI) and enables systematic exploration of the dynamical crystal landscape.
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures, 1 table; 6 pages of Supplementary Information with 4 supplementary figures included

title: Unveiling the Shock-Excited Molecular Environment in the Orion Protostar HOPS 370
abstract: We present near-infrared K-band ($1.94$--$2.52~μ$m) spectroscopy of the deeply embedded protostellar source HOPS\,370, obtained with the TIFR--ARIES Near Infrared Spectrometer (TANSPEC) on the 3.6-m Devasthal Optical Telescope (DOT). The spectrum is dominated by prominent molecular hydrogen ($\rm H_2$) ro-vibrational emission, with multiple transitions detected from the $1$--$0$ S, $2$--$1$ S, and $1$--$0$ Q branches. Using the intrinsically linked $\rm H_2$ $1$--$0$ Q(3) and $1$--$0$ S(1) transitions, which arise from the same upper energy level, we derive a visual extinction of $A_V = 23.24 \pm 1.25$ mag, corresponding to $A_K = 2.50 \pm 0.13$ mag, consistent with the embedded Class~0/I nature of the source. The diagnostic line ratio $F(2$--$1~{\rm S}(1))/F(1$--$0~{\rm S}(1)) = 0.12 \pm 0.01$ is consistent with thermal excitation and disfavors ultraviolet fluorescence as the dominant excitation mechanism. Assuming optically thin emission and local thermodynamic equilibrium, we derive an $\rm H_2$ excitation diagram that yields an excitation temperature of $2078 \pm 215$ K and a molecular hydrogen column density of $(1.93 \pm 0.93)\times10^{20}$ cm$^{-2}$. We further derive an ortho-to-para ratio of $2.45 \pm 0.21$, indicating substantial shock-driven thermal processing while remaining below the high-temperature equilibrium value of 3. Taken together, these diagnostics indicate that the molecular hydrogen emission in HOPS\,370 originates predominantly in warm, shock-heated gas most likely associated with its protostellar outflow. Our results demonstrate the diagnostic power of combined S- and Q-branch $\rm H_2$ spectroscopy for constraining the physical conditions and excitation history of deeply embedded protostellar systems.
authors: Somnath Dutta;Koshvendra Singh;Devendra K Ojha;Saurabh Sharma;Tarak Chand;Manojit Chakraborty;Kartik Gokhe;Joe P. Ninan;Jyotirmoy Dey

title: Component Translation and Judge-Labelled Refusal: A Multilingual Safety Evaluation
abstract: Whole-prompt translation evaluates a request in different languages but does not compare which component carries a language. We introduce a paired reversal: translate the complete request component or the complete operation component into the same target language, holding behaviour, English frame and translated-span count fixed. Component identity and non-English text quantity change together. Assigning English, Chinese and Spanish independently to the two components yields nine configurations on 190 of 300 sampled harmful behaviours retained after consensus annotation and automatic gating. Refusal scored by language-model judges is the primary outcome; unsafe compliance is reported separately. On Gemini 2.5 Flash and DeepSeek, three refusal swaps are about 5.3 percentage points and the fourth is -0.5; none survives the pre-specified six-test Holm correction. In an exploratory extension, Mistral Small 4 has a 13.7-point Spanish swap (95% interval [8.4, 18.9]), which survives the twelve-test Holm sensitivity correction under the primary judge, and 12.1 points under a second judge. GPT-5.4-mini estimates are within 2 points of zero. Component assignment supplies an additional evaluation dimension. Evaluations should record component languages and translated text quantity, comparing matched behaviours at equal translated-span count while interpreting refusal and unsafe compliance separately.
comment: 12 pages, 1 figure. Ten-page manuscript prepared for the 4th Workshop on Large Language and Foundation Models (WLLFM 2026) at IEEE BigData 2026, plus appendices A-E. Replication archive included as ancillary files

title: Machine learning-guided real-time AC optimal transmission switching
abstract: The operation of power grids has substantial economic consequences, affecting generation costs and, ultimately, electricity prices. The Optimal Transmission Switching (OTS) problem seeks to reduce these costs by selectively switching off transmission lines. However, OTS gives rise to a challenging mixed-integer nonlinear optimization problem that is difficult to solve at operationally relevant timescales, particularly as rapidly changing loads create a need for real-time switching decisions. To address this challenge, we develop a machine learning-guided method that identifies high quality line switching decisions in real time. Specifically, we construct a grid-specific switching-value model that rapidly estimates the generation-cost reduction associated with opening transmission lines by fine-tuning a pretrained model for AC optimal power flow (AC-OPF). The switching-value model provides signals to guide promising switching decisions, and topologies proposed by the model are evaluated using exact AC-OPF solvers to verify feasibility and obtain the actual generation cost. We develop multiple strategies that use the ML surrogate to efficiently explore the combinatorial space of transmission topologies, including Fixed-Rank Search, Adaptive-Rank Search, and Swap-Enhanced Search. Across multiple benchmark networks, our proposed algorithms identify line switching decisions that significantly reduce generation cost within a 50s computational budget. In particular, under a realistic data center buildout scenario on the 2,000-bus synthetic Texas grid, our approach reduces generation costs by 31.97% and gross nodal load payments by 94.34%. More broadly, our results demonstrate that a fine-tuned surrogate can effectively guide search even without guaranteeing feasibility, enabling classical optimization methods to tackle large nonlinear combinatorial problems on operationally relevant timescales.
authors: Weimin Huang;Weiwei Yang;Bistra Dilkina;Konstantina Mellou;Ishai Menache;Marco Molinaro;Chris White;Baosen Zhang

title: DecompGym: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Designing Decomposition Algorithms
abstract: Benders decomposition and column generation solve large optimization problems by passing cuts, columns, and dual values between a master problem and subproblems, and are hard to implement correctly. Large language models now automate parts of algorithm design, which points toward agents that build decomposition solvers for new problems. As a first step toward such agents, we study how well current coding agents design and implement these two algorithms, and how they fail. We introduce DecompGym, 81 instances from nine problem families (five Benders, four column generation), in which an agent writes a solver for a prescribed method. Each solver must meet three criteria: execution within a 60-second time limit; numerical feasibility together with a method audit, in which an LLM judge reads the solver's code; and an objective within 1% of the stored optimal objective. We evaluate 12 GPT, Claude, and Gemini models running in coding-agent tools. Over up to ten attempts, we compare independent regeneration with reflection, which first diagnoses the failure. On the first attempt, two models solve every instance and seven solve more than 90%. Most Benders failures (48 of 62) are missing or suboptimal solutions. The most common column-generation failure is a method-audit rejection. Output checks alone would accept 93 of the 108 attempts that fail the method audit. The most common rejection, an optimalif, occurs 96 times, 92 of them in one model.Reflection turns 66% of retries into successes, compared with 39% for regeneration, and it repairs method-audit failures, for which the judge names the defecective gaps. Agents for decomposition therefore need checks on how a solver reaches its answer and feedback that locates the error. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/SIKAI-C/DecompGym.
authors: Sikai Cheng;Tinghan Ye;Arnaud Deza;Xiaonan Qi;Miao Li;Litong Liu;Changkun Guan

title: Scaling Lean Theorem Proving for Real-World Code Verification
abstract: We present EasyProver, a Lean proving system built from recursive agents with isolated contexts, asynchronous search, parallel tactic probing, and an elastic elaboration service. Using an off-the-shelf frontier model with no additional training, it proves 669/672 PutnamBench problems and all six IMO 2026 formalizations and resolves 597/600 NTP4VC verification conditions and all 189 VERINA tasks by proof or refutation. Because these benchmarks are close to saturation, we also introduce Aegis, which converts competitive programming problems into much harder verification tasks over real implementations. The pipeline writes safe Rust solutions, translates them into Lean with Aeneas, generates specifications, and labels each frozen statement with a kernel-checked proof or refutation. It produces 2,045 differentially validated Rust-Lean program pairs and 11,533 candidate specifications. Unlike hand-written benchmarks, these tasks carry implementation-level obligations from fixed-width arithmetic, explicit failure, generated loops, casts, and functionalized mutation. On a stratified sample of 2,000 statements, EasyProver proves 1,054 (52.7%) within a 30-minute budget per statement. The same tasks can also be used to benchmark other provers and as rewards for reinforcement learning.
authors: Debargha Ganguly;Divya Raghunathan;Dejan Jovanović;Vikash Singh;Soonho Kong;Aaron Tomb;Aman Goel;Ferhat Erata;Sam Bayless

title: Data Amount Heterogeneity Improves Performance in Federated Learning for Neuroimaging
abstract: Federated Learning (FL) allows for secure analysis of distributed data without data sharing. We and others have successfully applied FL to neuroimaging tasks, such as Alzheimer's disease classification from structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). FL trains a deep learning model locally at each site, encrypts the local model parameters and sends them to a federation controller that aggregates the local models under homomorphic encryption, the resulting community model is sent back to the sites for further training, and the process repeats for a number of rounds. FL often achieves learning performance (e.g., accuracy) close to centralized training, but no data leaves the sites and model parameters are protected through encryption and other measures. In this paper, we show that federations composed of sites with heterogeneous amounts of data (1 large site plus small sites) perform better than homogeneous (same data per site) federations, particularly in low data regimes, while reaching performance close to centralized training. Having a big site often results in faster convergence and higher final accuracy. Heterogeneous federations better exploit sites with small amounts of data, a common situation in large consortia such as ENIGMA.
authors: Paul Kurian;Tamoghna Chattopadhyay;Abhijith Shaji;Greg Ver Steeg;Paul M. Thompson;Jose Luis Ambite

title: ATI-OPD: Adaptive Teacher Intervention for Stable Long-Sequence On-Policy Distillation
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own responses using token-level feedback from a teacher. As responses grow longer, the student's prefix can depart from the teacher's own reasoning, weakening its feedback on later tokens. Updates based on this feedback can reinforce the same deviations in later responses and destabilize training. Prior approaches such as length control and loss reweighting limit learning from problematic responses but leave their prefixes unchanged. Fixed cutoffs can also discard later reasoning. We propose \textbf{Adaptive Teacher Intervention for On-Policy Distillation (ATI-OPD)} to improve subsequent teacher guidance by revising the student's reasoning prefix. ATI-OPD replaces the earliest high-disagreement segment with a short teacher segment, then lets the student resume its own reasoning from the revised text. To handle renewed disagreement, it excludes persistently divergent suffixes from the distillation loss while retaining useful student continuation. Training diagnostics show less teacher-student disagreement, fewer gradient spikes, and fewer extremely long responses. Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two teacher-student pairs, ATI-OPD improves average student-only accuracy over standard OPD.

title: Turbulent gas-rich discs at high redshift: Chaotic orbits and rapid bulge formation at high gas fraction
abstract: Using the \nexus\ N-body/hydrodynamic framework, we show that stellar bars that emerge in high-redshift disc galaxies are different in their orbital characteristics compared to their low-redshift counterparts. We identify bar-supporting orbits and, among them, find the fraction of chaotic orbits compared to regular orbits ($f_{\rm chaos}$). This fraction rises above 60\% for models with $f_{\rm gas} > 60 \%$; for $f_{\rm gas} \lesssim 60\%$, we observe chaotic fractions close to zero. The emerging bars seen in the $f_{\rm gas}= 80\%$ and $100\%$ simulations collapse in $\lesssim$1 Gyr to form central bulges supported by rotation, and this collapse follows soon after the chaotic fraction starts to dominate ($f_{\rm chaos} \gtrsim 50\%)$. Moreover, the gravitational potential in those simulations steepens rapidly over that period, and by integrating the chaotic orbits, we find that orbits that deviate from the evolving mean field are more likely to be chaotic. Hence, we argue that the irregularity associated with the rapidly evolving, central potentials drives higher chaotic fractions in these gas-rich bars. As a result, the emergent bars collapse through `violent relaxation' to form oblate rotating bulges. Supporting evidence for this picture comes from the fact that particles of different mass share identical radial profiles, a natural consequence of the rapid relaxation process.
authors: Johan M. Villa-Alatorre;Joss Bland-Hawthorn;Thor Tepper-Garcia;Oscar Agertz;Christoph Federrath

title: Incoherent dark excitons extend Floquet-like physics across time and momentum
abstract: Floquet phenomena - where a coherent, time-periodic drive hybridizes the conduction band with energy-replicated copies of the valence band - have been demonstrated with intense optical fields and, more recently, other bosonic excitations. However, within mean-field approximations and the current understanding of Floquet phenomena, these effects survive only for the coherence time of the drive, limiting practical use and current demonstrations to the sub-picosecond regime. Here, consistent with recent theoretical predictions beyond the mean-field picture, using time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy in WSe$_2$/MoS$_2$ heterostructures, we show that incoherent, dense populations of dark interlayer excitons hybridize the conduction band with energy-replicated copies of the valence band, mimicking Floquet-like phenomena - now persisting for nearly a nanosecond. With increasing interlayer exciton density, the valence band and its replica evolve from an inverted-parabolic to a Mexican-hat dispersion, a signature of the predicted non-zero static coupling that hybridizes the bands and scales linearly with the exciton density. By tuning twist angle, we further show that dark excitons with net momentum create replicas that hybridize with bands offset not just in energy but also in momentum, providing another powerful degree of freedom beyond conventional Floquet engineering. These results establish a robust, long-lived route to engineering electronic states, beyond a coherent, zero-momentum drive.

title: Estimating Implicit Expected Log Density Ratios
abstract: When exact probabilities cannot be computed, \emph{density ratio estimation (DRE)} is a key subroutine in the wide range of applications where density ratios appear, from experimental design to generative modelling and reinforcement learning. In this paper, we introduce the concept of an \emph{expected log density ratio (ELDR)}: log density ratios that are integrated under some third, possibly distinct measure. We show many problems with implicit densities where DRE is naïvely used are actually ELDR estimation tasks, and prove fundamental limitations on finite-sample ELDR estimation. Based on these results, we argue that the typical DRE-based approaches are unsuitable for ELDR estimation, and provide some foundational motivation towards bespoke ELDR estimators. To demonstrate, we propose a simple modification to some DRE methods that allows samples convergent to the integral distribution to appear in training data. We show through benchmarks that this can improve ELDR estimation error.

title: Physics-Guided Inferencer-in-the-Loop Digital-Twin for Real-Time Adaptive Emulation of Nonlinear PMSMs
abstract: A real-time digital-twin (RTDT) of a permanent magnet synchronous machine (PMSM) allows drive controllers to be tested in hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) before they meet the real machine. Its machine model rests on identified parameters or flux look-up tables (LUTs) from finite-element analysis (FEA) or characterization tests; the maps are regenerated offline when the machine changes, and online estimators track a few parameters such as resistance and PM flux. This article makes the executed model learnable from reference data. A physics-guided machine learning (PGML) network advances the currents and predicts torque in one step, trained with analytical one-step labels. In the proposed Inferencer-in-the-Loop (IIL) architecture, a GPU retrains the network while a field-programmable gate array (FPGA) executes the last accepted weights. For damper circuits, shifted parameters, and an FEA-calibrated saturated machine, one kernel form reaches average normalized mean absolute errors (NMAEs) of 0.19%-0.67% at measured FPGA kernel latencies of 0.30-0.34 $μ$s, and retraining for a shifted machine nears its final loss within 94 s. On a magnetically linear 200-W drive, a residual form corrects the analytical step and learns its physical parameters from operating data; each step takes under 2.5 $μ$s, 20 times faster than real time and ahead of the physical drive's measurements even at 20-kHz sampling. On six held-out runs (1193 s), its $i_q$ error is 5.9%-9.4% of measured RMS, against 10.4%-13.2% for an independently fitted grey-box model, and over 30 min of loaded heating its online-updated heads track a 4.1% winding-resistance rise with an RMS error of 0.44 m$Ω$.

title: Emergent higher-order optical nonlinearity in self-assembled polar supertextures
abstract: Giant optical nonlinearities enable advanced materials control and bridge exotic light-matter phenomena to next-generation photonics. However, materials exhibiting strong higher-order optical nonlinearity beyond the second order are typically rare. Here, we report the discovery of a giant and ultrafast second-harmonic generation (SHG) in self-assembled polar skyrmions under mid-infrared excitations. The transient SHG intensity exhibits a distinctive power dependence originating from higher-order nonlinearity. More generally, we show that large higher-order nonlinearity emerges across diverse domain structures in polar superlattices. Phase-field simulations demonstrate a strong and periodic local permittivity variation within each polar texture at equilibrium, and further confirm the fast polarization oscillation in polar skyrmions with mid-infrared excitations. This intense local permittivity modulation can satisfy epsilon-near-zero conditions, unlocking dramatically enhanced nonlinear optical responses without photonic engineering. Consequently, the self-assembled polar topologies with strong inherent optical nonlinearity could establish a platform for quantum information processing and high-speed optical communications.

title: Passive Identification of Unequal Phase Grid Impedances by Phase-Domain Source Cancellation
abstract: Passive grid impedance estimators that return a single resistance--inductance pair cannot represent a grid whose phase impedances are unequal. This paper identifies a separate pair for each phase from recorded point-of-common-coupling (PCC) voltage and current without injected perturbations. In each phase, the unknown grid-source voltage is cancelled by a periodic difference (PD) or by a second-order-generalized-integrator notch difference (SOGID), and moving-window integration (MWI) replaces the current derivative by an integral and an endpoint feature. The resulting two-parameter regression requires a period or notch-frequency estimate but no phase-locked-loop angle. A voltage-balance analysis gives the source residual left by frequency mismatch and bounds the parameter error by the ratio of this residual to the conditioning of the two features. In the unequal-phase interval (8.3--9.8~s) of a 10-s EMTP grid-forming record, SOGID-MWI attains phase-averaged R/L errors of 5.09/0.33\%; a shared value has a minimum error of 41.67\% for the phase ratio 1:0.5:2. On a 50-s constant-impedance grid-following record, the errors are 0.56/0.06\% over the 20--30-s synchronization disturbance. In a controlled 40-dB noise study, a noise-referenced update rule reduces the white-noise GFL error from 55.9/65.0\% to 12.3/11.5\%.

title: Minimum-Time Escape from the Conic Field of View of a Reeds--Shepp Pursuer: the Faster Evader
abstract: We continue the study of minimum-time escape of an omnidirectional evader from the forward conic field of view of a Reeds--Shepp pursuer, now for a faster evader, and solve the game for every speed ratio $ν>1$ and every half-angle $0<α<π/2$: the escape time is characterized by explicit characteristics and the selection of roots of a scalar equation, and it is the value of the game in nonanticipative strategies at every state. Above the end $E$ of the evader's dispersal line on the front axis, the evader chases the reversing pursuer along a universal line fed by tributaries. The characteristic from the boundary of the usable part is an involute of a circle of radius $ν$ ending at a cusp, and two explicit thresholds decide whether it reaches the axis before the cusp and whether the jump of the escape time across it ends before the cusp or runs to it; in the latter case primaries fold back next to the barrier. The pursuer's optimal strategy is the relay of the slower case. The evader follows the tributaries and switches once to a primary, or commits in advance to a heading certified by the scalar equation of the primaries. Level-set and semi-Lagrangian computations are compared with the value.

title: MiniMMD: Minimization of MMD for Sampling, Inference and Integration
abstract: Many problems in computational statistics and machine learning can be formulated as approximating a target distribution by minimizing a discrepancy over a restricted class of candidate distributions. This minimum-discrepancy viewpoint appears, for example, in numerical integration, sampling, generative modelling, and statistical inference, but these instances are often studied separately in the literature. This thesis develops the first unified treatment of these many problems through the minimization of the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), a kernel-based discrepancy between probability measures. The central theme is that MMD is not only a statistically meaningful distance between probability distributions, but also a tractable optimization objective to design practical and efficient algorithms. This thesis summarizes the recent theoretical and empirical advancements of such minimum-MMD based algorithms.

title: Safety of layered control systems via control barrier morphisms
abstract: Layered control architectures provide a powerful paradigm for synthesizing controllers for complex systems. Yet, translating guarantees at each layer to system-level guarantees is challenging due to the interactions between layers. To address this problem, this paper presents a categorical perspective on layered control architectures. Individual systems are represented as control coalgebras, their interactions are specified as morphisms to mediators, and system-level behaviors are obtained via composition defined categorically as a pullback. To analyze the safety of these systems, we formulate control barrier morphisms (CBMs), the categorical generalization of control barrier functions. We prove that feedback controllers satisfying a CBM condition render the associated safe subobject forward invariant. It is through CBMs that we can establish the safety of layered systems: given a CBM at each layer subject to compatibility conditions, the universal property of the pullback implies the existence of a CBM for the composed system. Safety of a full-order model being safety filtered by a reduced-order model is recovered as a specialization of the categorical framework.
authors: Aaron D. Ames;Joe Moeller;Massimiliano de Sa;Paulo Tabuada

title: Same Label, Different Interface: Beyond Action-Space Labels in Robot Learning
abstract: Robot-learning studies often compare position and velocity actions as though each label identified a single experimental treatment, yet the label alone does not determine what the robot executes. Before affecting robot motion, bounded policy output passes through filtering, physical scaling, reference construction, feedback, timing, and effort limits. We study how these omitted properties affect attribution under one shared learner and training budget. Across three contact-rich Factory tasks (PegInsert, GearMesh, and NutThread), we compare five joint-space interfaces, with ten independently trained policies per condition. We first remain within the same position-feedback law and vary the executed interface: substituting only the physical action scale as the directly modified component changes sample-median evaluation success by 0.645-1.000 across tasks, while removing an exponential moving average produces task-dependent changes. We then move to a cross-law comparison and choose a velocity scale that exactly matches the position interface's local raw-torque command gain. This calibration raises the sample median on GearMesh and NutThread, with no median change on PegInsert. Yet clear residual sample-median gaps remain on PegInsert and GearMesh, while the NutThread interval includes zero. Thus, even this explicit equality leaves feedback and held-action dynamics unmatched and does not establish position-velocity trained-outcome equivalence. Action-interface comparisons should therefore report the executed pathway and state the physical quantity they match.

title: Calculation and rejection diverge in language models tested at known mechanical limits
abstract: When a language model returns engineering quantities with the status "solved", software that trusts it passes them on, even when the requested design is physically impossible. Such failures could reflect poor calculation, how the answer is requested, or a failure to judge feasibility. We set beam loads and disk speeds at known percentages above or below plastic collapse or burst, measured each model's limit calculation separately and tested 12 models in 4,860 calls, including follow-up experiments on new designs. We find that a model can recognize an impossible design when asked only whether it is feasible, yet accept the same design, reporting "solved", when asked for a full answer. Three models accepted beams 10 to 30% beyond collapse despite precise limit calculations in separate questions, and many accepted replies stated the violation. Asked only about feasibility, Opus 5 and Gemini 3.8 Flash rejected every impossible new design they were given, including those accepted in full answers, without false alarms. Rewording when to decline or changing the answer format raised rejection on the original beams, but not consistently on new designs. Software and benchmarks using a model's status should test feasibility judgment and full-answer rejection separately, and report the exact prompt.
comment: 94 pages, including Supplementary Information. Data and code: https://github.com/nbbllxx0/Certified-feasibility-margins

title: Nemotron 3.5 Super and Lightning: Open, Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Models for Agentic AI
abstract: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Super and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, open and efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer models designed for reasoning, long-context understanding, and agentic workloads. Super is a 120B-parameter, 12B-active multimodal model, while Lightning is a smaller 30B-parameter, 3B-active text model; both designed for efficient deployment. Both models combine large-scale distillation, long-context training, and native speculative decoding, while Super further incorporates Indic continued pretraining and agentic software-engineering mid-training. We develop a comprehensive post-training pipeline spanning supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RLVR and RLHF), complemented in Super by specialized teacher training and multi- teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). This transforms Super from a text-only base model into a multimodal agent capable of reasoning over text, images, video, and interactive tool environments. We further explore test-time scaling through parallel agent execution and self-verification. Across training and deployment, we jointly optimize capability and efficiency. Indic continued pretraining improves Indian-language benchmarks by up to 9.82 percentage points, while agentic mid-training strengthens software-engineering capabilities and robustness across agent harnesses. The post-trained Super model achieves 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro, surpassing Nemotron 3 Ultra despite using approximately 4.6x fewer active parameters. Post-training MTP boosting improves speculative- decoding acceptance length by up to 21.8% under probabilistic draft sampling, while NVFP4 quantization achieves 99.62% median accuracy recovery relative to BF16. Inference optimizations enable up to 4,856 output tokens/s/GPU on GB200 while sustaining at least 50 tokens/s/user.

title: PyPSA-Libya: An Open-Source Energy System Model for National Decarbonization and Hydrogen Export Pathways
abstract: Libya possesses significant renewable energy potential that remains largely untapped. This paper presents PyPSA-Libya, a national-scale model built on the PyPSA-Earth framework, designed to explore optimal transition pathways for the Libyan power sector. We present two primary studies: (1) an electricity-only capacity expansion analysis comparing a zero-emission constraint against an unconstrained baseline at 36-cluster resolution, and (2) a sector-coupled hydrogen export study evaluating the levelized cost of exporting 70 TWh/year of hydrogen to Europe under three technological scenarios and a 100 EUR/tonne CO2 carbon tax regime. Results indicate that while solar PV dominates the domestic capacity mix, integration of hydrogen production significantly alters grid storage requirements. Furthermore, under carbon pricing, steam methane reforming with carbon capture (SMR-CC) frequently out-competes pure green electrolysis, establishing a lower-cost compliance pathway for cross-border export. The model, data, and configuration files are released under an open-source license to support transparent energy planning in Libya.

title: Boxing Problem
abstract: We study the \textit{Boxing Problem}, which seeks a subset of points in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) maximizing the total reward of a selection of points minus the width of its axis-aligned bounding box. We also investigate the associated \textit{Boxing Set}, defined by the epigraph of the width function over binary selection variables. Although the width function is not submodular in general, we restore submodularity by fixing an anchor point. After anchoring, we establish a connection to the intersection of mixing sets with a linking constraint, which yields a polynomial-time optimization algorithm and a polynomial-size extended formulation. We then study the polyhedral structure of the Boxing Set and show that its facets admit laminar families of tight sets and can be obtained by sequential lifting. For the one-dimensional case, we provide a complete description of facet-defining inequalities together with a strongly polynomial-time separation algorithm.

title: Interpretable Feature Discovery from Unstructured Data Using LLMs and Statistical Choice Models
abstract: Feature extraction from unstructured data typically relies on opaque embeddings unsuited to interpretable decision-making. Interpretable features, on the other hand, typically require costly, and often infeasible, hand-engineering. Large language models (LLMs) offer a natural bridge, as they can read raw data and describe it in interpretable terms. One could simply ask an LLM to extract features from a large sample of the dataset, but context limitations and diluted attention can lead to unsatisfactory results. We introduce a method that automatically discovers interpretable, decision-relevant features from unstructured data. Our key idea is to perform pairwise comparisons between items, asking an LLM to articulate, in interpretable terms, the features distinguishing each pair. We treat these explanations, or rationales, as data: we develop a statistical choice model that combines these rationales across the comparisons to identify relevant features and estimate per-item, per-feature scores. We first test our method on a synthetic hiring dataset of cover letters with known ground-truth features and show that it significantly outperforms direct LLM feature extraction in feature recovery. We then apply it to the ChangeMyView (Reddit) debate dataset, where it discovers several interpretable features associated with persuasion while reaching predictive accuracy comparable to established baselines. We also show how the same rationales can be used to audit LLM decisions, yielding a holistic score whose decomposition over interpretable features reveals what the LLM rewards.

title: Neural Compression of Long ADMM Trajectory for Multiparametric Quadratic Program
abstract: Solving large-scale multiparametric quadratic programs (mpQPs) in real time often requires thousands of iterative optimization updates, creating a major computational bottleneck in model predictive control and learning-enabled systems. This paper proposes TQPNet, a self-supervised neural compression framework that learns to compress long ADMM optimization trajectories into a compact neural warm start followed by a few refinement iterations. We derive a low-dimensional ADMM scheme operating on the primal-dual variables $(x,β)$ and show that its iteration admits an equivalent ReLU-layer representation, termed ADMM(ReLU). Building on this insight, TQPNet combines a multilayer perceptron with ReLU activations (MLP(ReLU)) and a small number of unrolled ADMM(ReLU) refinement layers. The network is trained offline using an optimality-condition-informed residual loss, eliminating the need for solver-generated labels. The proposed residual-based framework enables both self-supervised training and online solution certification through adaptive ADMM(ReLU) refinement. Experiments on large-scale mpQPs and real-time MPC applications demonstrate that TQPNet achieves high accuracy, strong generalization, and substantially faster inference than conventional optimization-based methods.
authors: Liang Wu;Honghui Zheng;Bo Yang;Xu Yang;Yilin Mo;Ján Drgoňa

title: Prompt Lottery in LLM-as-a-Judge: Measuring and Mitigating Sensitivity to Syntactic Rephrasing
abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge has become a standard for evaluating large language models, yet most approaches implicitly assume that a single judge prompt functions as a stable evaluation instrument. Prior work has primarily explored deliberate prompt modifications such as scoring rubrics, role descriptions, or chain-of-thought reasoning in order to optimize accuracy. In contrast, we investigate whether validated prompt variants intended to preserve evaluation semantics while differing in surface realization (\textit{paraphrastic rephrasings}) yield consistent judgments under a fixed evaluation task. We introduce \textit{Prompt Lottery}, a phenomenon in which paraphrastic rephrasings produce different LLMaJ judgments. Across a large-scale study spanning diverse evaluation tasks, judge families, and model backbones, we find that these variations can alter evaluation outcomes and, in some settings, reverse relative model rankings. A user study with 10 human annotators shows that LLMaJ judges exhibit 6-9$\times$ larger agreement degradation under prompt rephrasings than humans, falling below the generally accepted threshold in usability studies. This indicates that single-prompt evaluation is insufficiently robust for model ranking. Finally, we show that multi-prompt aggregation substantially improves robustness by emphasizing judgments that remain consistent across prompt variants.
authors: Ilija Subasic;Brett Levert;Andrew Rabinovich;Sajjad Pakdamansavoji;Zhao Chen

title: Thermal laser evaporation of superconducting Nb films
abstract: Thermal laser evaporation (TLE) is an emerging physical vapor deposition (PVD) technique that uses continuous-wave lasers to evaporate even the most refractory elements. The deposition and characterization of superconducting refractory elements are of interest to assess the quality of films deposited by TLE. Here, we report the deposition of niobium (Nb) on c-plane sapphire using a home-built TLE system equipped with a 1070 nm continuous-wave fiber laser. A deposition rate of 0.19 Å/s was achieved with 533 W of laser power focused to a diameter of approximately 500 $μ$m on a Nb target. A film with a thickness of $22.47 \pm 0.05$ nm and a root-mean-square (RMS) roughness of $0.23 \pm 0.02$ nm exhibited a room-temperature resistivity of $21.60 \pm 0.05$ $μΩ\mathrm{cm}$ and a residual-resistivity ratio (RRR) of 5.71. The superconducting transition temperature, $T_\mathrm{c}$, of the film was measured as 9.24 K, only 10 mK below the bulk value, with a transition width of 29 mK. Among films deposited without substrate heating, the electrical and superconducting properties of the present films meet or exceed those deposited by other techniques. This work contributes to the emerging consensus regarding TLE as a versatile PVD method for refractory elements and compounds.
authors: Yifei Yan;David S. Catherall;Finley B. Donachie;Dorsa Najafipanah;Austin J. Minnich

title: From Error Prediction to Causal Influence: Auditing SAE Features in Multiple-Choice QA
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can predict internal features associated with model errors, but association alone does not establish causal influence. We study this distinction in multiple-choice question answering, where answer preference can be measured by the logit margin between the correct answer and the competing choices. Across eight datasets, we analyze Gemma~3 1B and 4B with Gemma Scope SAEs. We propose a pipeline to filter out the features that have high correlation with format and content artifacts, such as prompt and answer permutation, and evaluate the remaining ones with causal feature interventions. Our results show that SAE activations contain predictive signals about wrongness and uncertainty across models and datasets. After filtering artifact-contaminated features, selected features for causal intervention at question and option spans produce larger absolute margin shifts and a higher wrong-to-correct rate than randomly selected features, indicating greater causal leverage. However, answer flips are rare, and we do not observe stable effect directions across meaning-preserving changes in prompt format and answer order. An adapted HalluSAE baseline produces larger final-token margin changes, but relies on substantially contaminated features and does not significantly improve correction rates. Therefore, the identified features reflect context-dependent answer competition rather than the mechanism of incorrect answer errors.
authors: Aria Nourbakhsh;Adelaide Danilov;Oleksandr Marchenko Breneur;Salima Lamsiyah

title: Cosmic rays in galaxy halos I: the circumgalactic transport rate and a dynamically significant cosmic-ray reservoir
abstract: Fermi-LAT observations imply that most of the cosmic rays (CRs) produced in normal star-forming galaxies escape from the discs where they are accelerated into the circumgalactic medium (CGM), but the subsequent evolution of those escaping CRs is unclear. Here we construct a simple semi-analytic model for their transport and loss, which we constrain by confronting the model with a series of observations: limits on CR energy densities in the outer Milky Way from Fermi-LAT, the isotropic gamma-ray background (IGRB), stacked CGM X-ray emission from eROSITA, and the requirement that the accumulated pressure of CRs in galaxy CGMs not be so large as to render them unstable. We show that these constraints can be jointly satisfied in only two scenarios: one where CRs diffuse quickly through the CGM and freely escape beyond it into the IGM, and another where the CR diffusion time out of halos is of order the Hubble time. In the latter scenario CRs accelerated by star formation naturally explain both the IGRB and the heat input required to maintain the temperature of the CGM against X-ray cooling, and their relatively slow transport means that roughly half of the CR energy injected into the CGM of an $L_\star$ halo over its star-formation history remains there at $z \simeq 0$. This makes CR pressure dynamically significant, and also means that a non-negligible part of the IGRB is produced by CRs in the Milky Way's own halo. We argue that this latter scenario is the more likely one, as it avoids the need to posit a second source for the IGRB that is coincidentally very close in both power and spectral shape to the contribution from star-forming discs.
