title: Dynamics of Hidden Learning Structure
abstract: A learner's present predictions do not fully determine how it will learn next. We study the dynamics of hidden learning structure through two related operations. Fiber Regulation Theory (FRT) describes protected repair of existing function and the learning responses left available after repair. Fiber Acquisition Theory (FAT) describes the formation and renewal of trainable structure, distinguishing neutral installation, access to a learning signal, and additional functional directions. The two operations also constrain one another. A repair obligation can force a change in a learning channel, while acquired features can make new protected repairs feasible or reduce the minimum coefficient cost of existing ones. We characterize joint admissibility and response reachability, and give a finite supervised-learning construction in which the two operations together produce a favorable response absent from either operation alone. We implement protected head repair and fixed-capacity LoRA renewal in Qwen2.5-32B with AdamW, under replay and output distillation. Across two training trajectories differing in seed and within-task example order, the coordinated policy achieves higher teacher-forced Exact than either separate policy in all four comparisons. It also has the lowest macro NLL under both learning rules on the second trajectory. The implementations realize structure-conditioned self-regulation within specified information and action constraints: accessible state readouts and arrived evidence guide repairs and structural renewals, and ordinary learning continues from the modified state.

title: Vagus nerve stimulation strengthens beta- and gamma-rate auditory steady-state responses in rat cortex
abstract: Background: Gamma entrainment using sensory stimulation (GENUS) is under study as a treatment for neurological disease, but cortical engagement is variable. Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) modulates cortical state and sound-evoked beta-gamma activity, suggesting that it may strengthen responses to rhythmic sensory input. Objective: To determine whether VNS strengthens auditory steady-state responses across beta and gamma rates and whether the effect depends on cortical region and sensory drive. Methods: Electrocorticography (ECoG) was recorded from core and belt auditory cortex, insular auditory field (IAF), and anterior insular cortex (AIC) in seven isoflurane-anesthetized rats before and 90 min after initiation of 30-Hz cervical VNS. Responses to 500-ms click trains at 20 and 40 Hz were quantified using inter-trial phase clustering (ITPC), event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP), and debiased weighted phase-lag index (WPLI). Results: VNS increased click-evoked P1-N1 amplitude. During 40-Hz trains, 40-Hz ITPC and ERSP increased only in auditory core. During 20-Hz trains, 20-Hz ITPC increased in core, belt, and IAF, whereas ERSP increased only in core; 40-Hz harmonic responses increased only in core. AIC showed no change. Within auditory cortex, WPLI increased selectively at frequencies present in each click train and not in the alpha band. Conclusions: VNS strengthened beta- and gamma-rate stimulus-locked responses in auditory-driven cortex without globally increasing synchrony. VNS may therefore enhance auditory cortical target engagement during GENUS, although effects on disease pathology or clinical outcomes remain untested.
authors: Shinichi Kumagai;Tomoyo Isoguchi Shiramatsu;Karin Oshima;Yohei Ishishita;Kenji Ibayashi;Yoshiyuki Onuki;Naoto Kunii;Kensuke Kawai;Hirokazu Takahashi

title: A Jump-Modified Wasserstein Gradient Flow for Maximum Mean Discrepancy with Energy Kernels
abstract: We study a jump-modified Wasserstein gradient flow of the squared maximum mean discrepancy generated by the energy kernels $K(z)=-|z|^q$, $0<q<2$, in every dimension $d\ge2$ as well as the one-dimensional range $1\le q<2$. Under subcritical density and finite-moment assumptions, we prove global well-posedness. The added jumps transfer mass toward smaller values of the first variation and dissipate the same MMD energy as the transport term. Under our hypotheses on the target and jump rates, every Borel probability measure with finite MMD energy and zero jump dissipation is equal to the target. Combining this rigidity with compactness and a second-moment identity yields convergence to the target from finite-second-moment data, without additional uniform-in-time density or moment assumptions. We also construct a global collision-free particle process whose energy is nonincreasing along each path. A quantitative mean-field estimate applies to general initial empirical approximations, including deterministic configurations; propagation of chaos for exchangeable data and long-time target approximation follow as consequences.

title: Hereditary Effective Atom Theory for Large-Scale Atomic Structure Prediction
abstract: Predicting the atomic structure of large systems requires simultaneous exploration of atomic positions, species, and, generally, the number of atoms. The combinatorial growth of possible arrangements can make this search difficult even for standard global optimization methods. We introduce Hereditary Effective Atom Theory (HEAT), which integrates Effective Atom Theory (EAT) into a genetic algorithm. HEAT combines EAT's continuous relaxation of atomic positions, species, and population with the global search capabilities of genetic algorithms. Central to the method is a crossover scheme that directly superimposes two parent structures and relaxes the combined structure. HEAT outperforms conventional genetic-algorithm baselines in recovering a missing 240-atom H sublattice, predicting a 364-atom edge-dislocation core, and reconstructing a 1150-atom interior region of twisted-bilayer $\mathrm{WSe_2}$ from experimental ptychographic constraints. These results demonstrate how continuous effective-atom relaxation improves the exploration of large combinatorial structure spaces.
authors: Justin Tahmassebpur;Chia-Hao Lee;Cristóbal Méndez;Shake Karapetyan;Zixiao Shi;David A. Muller;Tomás Arias

title: Anytime-Valid Inference in Conjoint Experiments
abstract: Choosing an appropriate sample size is a fundamental challenge in experimental design. This challenge is particularly salient in conjoint experiments, where researchers simultaneously target many estimands whose inferential goals may be reached at different sample sizes. Conventional sample-size calculations address this challenge in an ex ante manner. In large online studies, including many conjoint experiments, data often arrive continuously, allowing researchers to dynamically stop data collection. In such settings, the relevant practical question is not "what sample size should I choose in advance?" but rather, as data accumulate, "have I learned enough yet?" A naive response is to repeatedly inspect conventional confidence intervals and $p$-values, but doing so invalidates their inferential guarantees. We address this challenge by developing a general anytime-valid framework for conjoint experiments that allows continuous monitoring and data-dependent stopping. This framework equips many common conjoint estimands with asymptotic $e$-processes, confidence sequences, and anytime-valid $p$-values, and provides a general recipe for any estimand that can be expressed as a linear contrast of population OLS coefficients. Across common conjoint settings, we demonstrate that anytime-valid inference can yield substantial sample savings relative to fixed-sample designs. The probability of early stopping frequently exceeds 50%, with mean sample savings often surpassing 25%.

title: From Common Information to Canonical Correlation Analysis and Beyond: Bridging Information Theory, Signal Processing, and Machine Learning
abstract: Many problems in signal processing, machine learning, and neuroimaging provide several jointly observed measurements of one process, each mixing a component common to all of them with a component private to itself, and require the common component to be recovered without supervision. This problem has been studied in several communities, largely independently. Statisticians proposed canonical correlation analysis (CCA), introduced by Hotelling in 1936. Information theorists proposed two notions of common information, due to Gács and Körner and to Wyner. Engineers developed subspace methods for sensor arrays and multiuser communications to design multiview receivers. This tutorial presents the main results and tools each community developed for this problem in a single exposition, and explains the connections that emerge where they meet, distinguishing exact equivalences from special cases and analogies. We develop the information-theoretic foundation from first principles. We then introduce CCA and its extension to several views, followed by the engineering thread from blind multiuser detection to CCA as a blind receiver. Next, we turn to nonlinear CCA, covering kernel, deep, and probabilistic formulations, the conditions under which the common factor is identifiable, and connections to self-supervised learning. We conclude with a discussion of further extensions and open directions. The exposition is self-contained, so that readers from each of these communities can follow the parts developed by the others.
comment: Tutorial, 100 pages, 11 figures. Accepted for publication in Entropy, Special Issue "Foundations and Frontiers of Information Theory" in honor of H. Vincent Poor's 75th birthday

title: Is In-Context Reinforcement Learning A Posterior Sampler? An Empirical Study
abstract: In-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) exploits the impressive in-context learning ability of large language models to zero-shot generalize to new, unseen tasks at inference time without any parameter updates. Among many approaches, the Decision-Pretrained Transformer (DPT) is particularly appealing for its theoretical grounding: under idealized assumptions such as a sufficiently expressive model and infinite pretraining data, DPT can perform Bayesian posterior sampling. Whether this characterization survives in practice remains open. Therefore, we ask: \textit{is ICRL, specifically DPT and our proposed DPT variants, a Bayesian posterior sampler in practice?} To approach this question, we establish two necessary conditions that a Bayesian posterior sampler must satisfy: \textit{sufficient-statistic invariance} and the \textit{martingale property}. We then construct statistical hypothesis tests to statistically assess if practically-trained ICRL models satisfy these conditions. Applying these tests in Gaussian, Bernoulli, and linear bandit settings, we find that both conditions are consistently violated, suggesting that ICRL may not behave as Bayesian posterior samplers in practice. Beyond this negative result, our tests provide a principled toolkit for testing the Bayesian behavior of ICRL.

title: The H IX galaxy survey IV: What does the molecular gas reveal in HI eXtreme galaxies
abstract: Galaxies with extreme amounts of neutral atomic hydrogen (HI), known as HI-eXtreme (HIX) galaxies, paradoxically exhibit normal or low star formation rates. To investigate the bottleneck in their star formation, we present ALMA CO(1-0) observations for five HIX survey galaxies: ESO208-G026, ESO378-G003, ESO381-G005, ESO417-G018, and ESO055-G013. While these systems possess massive, extended HI discs, their molecular gas discs are compact with normal H$_{2}$ masses relative to their stellar mass. Dynamical modelling with 3DBarolo reveals that the HI and molecular gas are kinematically consistent. Both gas phases show high velocity dispersions, indicating enhanced turbulence compared to regular late-type galaxies. We calculate the specific angular momentum for the stellar, atomic, and molecular components alongside the global stability parameter ($q$). Most of the system angular momentum is stored in the HI discs, rendering them globally stable against collapse. This stability suppresses the atomic-to-molecular gas conversion, as evidenced by extremely long HI depletion times contrasted with typical H$_{2}$ depletion times. The high angular momentum and HI excess likely originate from past gas accretion or recent tidal interactions; this is especially apparent in ESO378-G003 and ESO381-G005, which exhibit extended HI structures and positive tidal indices.
authors: V. A. Capa;H. Dénes;K. A. Lutz;T. H. Brown

title: Strain-Induced Interfacial Bond Evolution and Facet-dependent Strain Response of Electronic Properties in Oxidized Silicon Nanowires
abstract: Silicon nanowires (Si NWs) have emerged as promising candidates for next-generation nanoelectronic devices due to their tunable electronic properties, and compatibility with aggressive scaling requirements. The integration of strain further enhances their performance by modulating carrier mobility, band structure, and transport behavior without altering material chemistry. Within the NW, the silicon-silicon dioxide (Si-SiO$_{2}$) interface serves as a critical region where strain redistribution and suboxide bonding collectively influence the mechanical and electronic response. Here, we combine reactive force field molecular dynamics and first-principles calculations to investigate how oxidation-induced interfacial structure and crystallographic facet orientation govern strain-dependent bond evolution and facet-dependent strain response of electronic properties in oxidized Si NWs. Simulated dry thermal oxidation generates chemically realistic Si-SiO$_{2}$ interfaces, enabling direct characterization of bond order redistribution and stress gradient development across the interface under tensile strain. Interfacial Si-Si bonds exhibit elongation and reduced bond order associated with partial oxidation states, leading to localized stress concentration and preferential bond rupture. Complementary density functional theory calculations on facet-specific models reveal that orientation-dependent interfacial bonding modulates facet-dependent strain response of electronic properties. Together, these results establish a direct coupling between interfacial suboxide chemistry, mechanical deformation, and electronic structure, providing atomistic insight into strain-modulated behavior at oxidized silicon interfaces in faceted NWs.
authors: Yasir Mahmood;Daniel Wines;Viviana Dovale-Farelo;Kamal Choudhary;Lucas M Hale

title: HyperDrone: Simulation-to-Reality Transfer at Millions of Frames per Second
abstract: We present HyperDrone, an extremely fast quadrotor simulator focused on high-performance batch rendering that is more than 20x faster than existing state-of-the-art batch quadrotor simulators. HyperDrone combines highly optimized multirotor dynamics with HyperLux, a new ray-tracing engine that supports Nvidia OptiX, Vulkan, Apple Metal and WebGPU backends that takes full advantage of modern ray-tracing hardware, capable of running both components entirely on the GPU. HyperLux renders RGB, depth, semantic/instance segmentation, surface normals and optical flow observations at configurable levels of fidelity, including reflections, realistic lighting, motion blur, anti-aliasing, and Physically Based Rendering (PBR). Even in the highest-fidelity settings, HyperLux achieves millions of Frames Per Second (FPS) on consumer-grade GPUs while rendering realistic 3D scenes. We demonstrate the merits of HyperDrone by training a vision-based yaw-control policy purely in simulation and transferring it to a real small-scale quadrotor (Crazyflie) with a camera, running completely onboard.
comment: Accepted at Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026)

title: Auditing Conformal Prediction for Language Models Under Inference-Time Model Shift
abstract: Conformal prediction (CP) for language models is typically evaluated under a matched protocol, in which calibration and deployment use the same post-training inference configuration, such as quantization mode and inference temperature. In deployment, these choices often differ from those used at calibration to meet memory or throughput constraints or serving policies. We argue that this exposes a limitation in current CP evaluation protocols for language models. We formalize the underlying phenomenon as inference-time model shift: a change in the conformal score distribution induced by inference configuration rather than by the input--label distribution, and theoretically characterize how it breaks split-conformal exchangeability even when the task distribution and trained model are unchanged. We then evaluate its consequences across 8 language models, 4 finite-label benchmarks, and 12 inference configurations. We find that matched evaluation can substantially overstate deployment-time coverage, and that the effect is heterogeneous across models and datasets. We argue that inference configuration should be reported as a first-class experimental axis in CP evaluations for language-model systems.
comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Track on Evaluations and Datasets

title: Kinetic Mean-Field Planning via Schrödinger Bridges: Existence, Penalization, and Consistency Bounds
abstract: We study a mean-field planning problem for a swarm of interacting, non-cooperative agents whose dynamics are stochastic and kinetic. The noise acts on the velocity only, and the interaction (of Cucker-Smale type for instance) enters through the drift. For a fixed flow, the problem reduces to a Schrödinger bridge problem, and we first prove the existence of an equilibrium by a Schauder fixed-point argument. Then we replace the hard terminal constraint by a penalty function and show that equilibria of the penalized problems converge, along subsequences, to an equilibrium of the original problem. Since equilibria are not unique in general, we instead quantify the consistency error, which measures how far an equilibrium of the penalized problem is from being an equilibrium of the original one. The rate is of order $n^{-1/2}$ for the relative-entropy penalty. The proof relies on the quantitative stability of entropic optimal transport and on a pointwise linear growth bound on the score of the degenerate reference dynamics, which is of independent interest.

title: Experimental Characterization of SMD Inductors for Cryogenic Power Conversion at 4 K
abstract: With the increasing complexity and scalability demands of cryogenic electronic systems, such as quantum computing platforms, conversion of power within the cryogenic environment has become a primary concern. Magnetic inductors are among the key components affecting converter performance, as their electrical and magnetic properties can change significantly at low temperatures. In this paper, five commercially available Vishay SMD power inductors are experimentally characterized down to 4 K: DC resistance is measured continuously during cooldown, while frequency-dependent AC inductance and resistance are measured up to 2 MHz at both room temperature and 4 K. The results show substantial DC resistance reductions of 25x-58x at 4 K, while the inductance degrades by only about 5-5.5%. Although cryogenic operation slightly increases the AC resistance (due to the intensified skin effect) and raises core losses, converter-level analysis shows an inductor-only efficiency improvement of approximately 5.3-6.9 percentage points at 1 A, and up to 22.8 points at 3 A. The measured frequency-dependent impedance of each inductor is imported into Cadence and a complete single-phase 24 V-to-1 V buck converter with GaN power devices is simulated at 1, 2, and 3 A at 4 K. The full-converter efficiency at 4 K is shown to improve by 3.0-5.2 percentage points at 1 A and by up to 22.5 points at 3 A for the AC-characterized devices. These findings indicate that commercially available off-the-shelf power inductors remain operationally viable under cryogenic conditions and can simultaneously increase inductor efficiency and reduce the overall power loss in cryogenic power conversion systems.
authors: Rami Rasheedi;Umeshkumar Patel;Jonathan Baldwin;Antonino Miceli;Inna Partin-Vaisband

title: KROME-X: a GPU-ready library for chemistry and microphysics in astrophysical simulations
abstract: KROME is a Python pre-processor that writes a complete Fortran solver of chemistry and microphysics for each chemical network, widely used in astrophysical simulations. We introduce here KROME-X, a complete rewrite of KROME in modern C++, which incorporates updated physics. A code generator translates a declarative network description into a compact core (rates, right-hand side, analytic Jacobian, thermal terms, and tables), which a fixed, header-only runtime integrates with a C++ port of the `backward differentiation formula' method of CVODE (SUNDIALS). The physics is validated against legacy KROME and independent references. On the legacy test cases KROME-X reproduces legacy KROME to the accuracy of the solvers, wherever the physics is the same, and is up to 13.5 times faster at equal tolerance. On NVIDIA A100 GPUs, it can outperform its share of a computing node from a few thousand cells per call, with the highest throughput (5 to 30) obtained for $10^5$ cells per batch. Networks of hundreds of species still run faster on the CPU due to the GPU's limited memory capacity. The new version also includes, among other changes, on-the-fly co-evolution of a photon field alongside chemistry, which conserves photons exactly; the secondary ionizations using the photoelectron energy of each absorption; dust evolution in size and temperature with a true grain energy equation; line cooling rates rebuilt from current atomic and molecular data, and incorporating optical thickness effects. KROME-X therefore represents the natural successor of KROME and provides a portable, extensible framework for astrochemical kinetics on both CPUs and GPUs for future hydrodynamic simulations.
comment: 12 pages (+ 7 of appendix), 14 figures, submitted to A&A

title: A Model-Free Continuous-Time RL Algorithm from Discrete-Time Off-Policy Data with End-to-End Guarantees
abstract: In this paper, we study continuous-time reinforcement learning, where the state follows an unknown stochastic differential equation but only a fixed off-policy batch of discrete-time transitions is available. Standard discrete-time Q-learning becomes problematic as the sampling interval shrinks, because differences between action values vanish. Continuous-time alternatives, such as Deep Advantage Updating and martingale q-learning, preserve the action signal but jointly learn a value function and an action-dependent critic. Building on the PhiBE-Q formulation (arXiv:2606.21925), we develop a model-free PhiBE policy iteration (PhiBE-PI) framework that uses a single state-action critic while preserving the continuous-time action-ranking scale. At each iteration, the framework learns the critic directly from sampled increments and uses it to improve the policy. The same batch is reused throughout, without explicitly estimating the drift or diffusion. We further develop an implementation under linear function approximation and establish a local end-to-end suboptimality guarantee for the learned policy. Our analysis quantifies how errors from time discretization, function approximation, and finite-sample policy evaluation propagate through policy iteration. It accounts for the dependence of successive policies on the reused data, so the guarantee does not require a fresh batch at each iteration. Moreover, we identify a bias-variance trade-off: smaller sampling intervals improve the approximation to the continuous-time problem but can increase statistical error at a fixed sample size. Thus, finer time discretization does not necessarily lead to better policy performance.
authors: Chaorui Yao;Yuming Paul Zhang;Lin Yang;Yuhua Zhu

title: Backtracking Direct, Indirect and Total Effects
abstract: Natural direct and indirect effects are defined through cross-world interventional counterfactuals. We propose an alternative construction based on backtracking counterfactuals. Rather than intervening on the treatment or mediator and change the structural equations, we use a backtracking conditional distribution to construct an alternative exogenous state satisfying a desired treatment-mediator constraint and then evaluate the unchanged structural equations on that state. This yields the backtracking direct and indirect effects, and also the backtracking total effect. Likewise, we adapt the population intervention effects.

title: Not so Fast: Revised Calibration of SIDM Core Collapse
abstract: Self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) haloes undergo gravothermal evolution whose late-time behaviour is central to predictions for dense substructure and black-hole seed formation. We revisit the calibration of this evolution using a new spherical Direct Simulation Monte Carlo code, SphDSMC, which follows spherically symmetric SIDM systems without force softening and to substantially higher central densities than standard N-body simulations. We compare SphDSMC calculations with conventional N-body simulations and with one-dimensional gravothermal fluid models. We show that N-body results converge to SphDSMC only for softening lengths significantly smaller than those normally adopted for collisionless simulations, and that allowing multiple scatterings per particle per time step does not introduce significant errors when implemented appropriately. Calibrating the gravothermal fluid equations against SphDSMC, we find that the commonly used harmonic interpolation between the long- and short-mean-free-path conductivities is inaccurate. A gentler transition, however, yields excellent agreement for NFW haloes over a range of concentrations and truncation radii, with a single long-mean-free-path conductivity parameter. The revised calibration gives a long-mean-free-path collapse time that is somewhat shorter than previous estimates, but we show that collapse slows dramatically once the core becomes optically thick. We provide fitting functions for the late-time evolution and argue that black-hole seed formation by SIDM gravothermal collapse has generally been underestimated in duration, making it unlikely to explain the massive high-redshift black holes inferred from JWST observations without additional physics.
authors: Frank C. van den Bosch;Yarone M. Tokayer
comment: 25 pages, 16 figures, accepted for publication in MNRAS

title: Physics-Informed Mixed Integer Programming Methods for Optimal Patch Antennas
abstract: Antennas come in various shapes and sizes, as their performance characteristics are very much dependent on their exact shape. Coming up with a shape that matches desired design characteristics has, up until this moment, been largely the domain of metaheuristics and local optimization methods. While these methods are convenient, they generally provide no performance guarantees and rarely allow to enforce hard design constraints. In this paper, we show how Mixed-Integer Programming (MIP) can be used to optimize the shape of so-called patch antennas. The methodological focus is to show how underlying laws of physics allow to derive effective bounds on variables as well as new cutting planes. These greatly improve the effectiveness of the underlying basic MIP model, enabling the automated design of practically relevant patch antennas for a wide variety of applications.
authors: Ruben Hoeksma;Jesse van Rhijn;Marc Uetz;Wick Wijnholds

title: Actually, All Learnable Distribution Classes Are Privately Learnable
abstract: We show that every class of distributions that is learnable up to arbitrarily small target error in total variation distance with finitely many samples is also learnable under ($\varepsilon, δ$)-differential privacy up to arbitrarily small target error with finitely many samples. This proves a conjecture of Ashtiani. Previous work by Bun, Kamath, Mouzakis, and Singhal [arXiv:2402.00267] gave a weak refutation of this conjecture, showing that this implication is not true when learnability is defined with respect to a fixed target error. In contrast, we show that, under the standard definition of learnability, the conjecture is true.
authors: Mohammad Afzali;Hassan Ashtiani;Alex Bie;Gautam Kamath;Peihan Liu;Argyris Mouzakis;Vikrant Singhal

title: Ultrafast and Anisotropic Exciton Transport in Layered NbOI$_2$
abstract: Ferroelectric layered semiconductors provide a unique platform for exploring coupled excitonic and electronic phenomena in reduced dimensions. Here, exciton transport in layered NbOI$_2$ is investigated using transient absorption microscopy. Ultrafast and strongly anisotropic exciton diffusion is observed. The diffusion coefficient of about 160 cm$^2$ s$^{-1}$ along the nonpolar crystal axis is among the highest reported for van der Waals semiconductors. The transport exhibits an approximately twofold in-plane anisotropy between the polar and nonpolar directions, reflecting the intrinsic low-symmetry crystal structure of NbOI$_2$. The environmental stability of NbOI$_2$ is further investigated, and fabrication and encapsulation conditions required to achieve long-term sample stability are identified. These results establish NbOI$_2$ as a promising platform for studying anisotropic exciton transport and highlight the critical role of interface protection in air-sensitive van der Waals materials.

title: Self-Supervised Tuning of Low-Fidelity Optimization Models via High-Fidelity Feedback
abstract: Low-fidelity (LF) optimization models are widely used in large-scale operations because they can be solved efficiently and reliably, but they often exhibit systematic errors relative to high-fidelity (HF) formulations that better capture physical and operational constraints. Existing learning-based approaches typically rely on supervised or semi-supervised training with HF solutions, which are expensive to compute and may not align with HF operational objectives. We propose a self-supervised framework that parameterizes LF optimization models directly from HF feedback. The low-fidelity problem is embedded as a differentiable optimization layer and trained end-to-end, while a HF correction problem evaluates its solution and provides gradient information through its dual variables, without requiring HF solution labels. We evaluate the framework on optimal power flow, optimal gas flow, and pooling problems, spanning different sources of low- and high-fidelity mismatch. Across all three applications, the self-supervised approach improves objective quality and feasibility over untuned LF models and generally outperforms semi-supervised training. The learned parameterizations also generalize to unseen operating conditions and, for network applications with up to 30,000 nodes, to systems not encountered during training.
authors: Gonzalo E. Constante-Flores;André H. Quisaguano-Paredes;Asha Ramanujam;Rishabh Gupta;Can Li

title: Paramagnetic phase of MnTe$_2$: complete one phonon Raman spectrum
abstract: In this study we present a complete first-order Raman scattering spectrum of paramagnetic phase of MnTe$_2$- a material, where new type of spin texture induced by noncoplanar antiferromagnetic ordering below the Néel temperature ($T_N \approx 90$ K) gives rise to unconventional scenario of magnetism. Basic properties of all five phonon modes ($A_g$, $E_g$ and three $T_g$) predicted by the group theory have been successfully approached through polarization, excitation and temperature dependent measurements. In particular, the ever-missing phonon mode of $T_g$ symmetry has been unambiguously resolved in the room temperature Raman spectrum at approximately 107 cm$^{-1}$, just 1.5 cm$^{-1}$ higher in frequency compared to the $E_g$ mode. Density functional theory calculations reproduce the observed Raman-active phonon spectrum and support the assignment of all five first-order Raman modes, including the near-degeneracy of the $E_g$ and one of the $T_g$ vibrations. The calculations further reveal a dense manifold of low-energy antiferromagnetic spin configurations, separated from the ground state by only a few meV per formula unit. Furthermore, strong signals of inelastically scattered light from the paramagnetic (PM) phase of MnTe$_2$ were acquired with long wavelength excitations, i.e. 633 nm and 785 nm, revealing the $2A_g$ overtone at approx. 360 cm$^{-1}$. The enhanced absorption of the light in the near infrared range could be a putative reason behind the anomalous angular dependence of scattered intensity of the highest frequency $T_g$ phonon mode (183 cm$^{-1}$) measured in PM MnTe$_2$ with parallelly aligned polarizers. Finally, upon cooling just below the $T_N$, the measured properties of phonons remained basically unperturbed by the incipient long-range antiferromagnetic ordering.
authors: Taras Palasyuk;Dominik Kurzydłowski;Ashutosh S. Wadge;Rajmund Bacewicz;Madhavi H. Dalsaniya;Michał Wierzbicki;Daniel Jastrzebski;Andrzej Wiśniewski;Wojciech Szuszkiewicz;Igor Antoniazzi;Bruno Camargo;Maciej R. Molas;Adam Babiński;Krzysztof Zberecki;Cezariusz Jastrzebski

title: Funnel-Precompensated Disturbance Observer for Uncertain Minimum-Phase SISO Linear Systems of Arbitrary Relative Degree
abstract: Disturbance observers (DOBs) recover nominal behavior, but fast filters risk peaking. We propose a funnel-precompensated DOB for uncertain minimum-phase single-input single-output linear systems of known relative degree. A stable-factor residual yields a minimum-phase channel. At relative degree two, gain conditions require positive plant high-frequency gains and one positive common design gain; for higher degrees, the common-design result also uses a plant-gain interval and mismatch condition. Global boundedness, practical nominal-output recovery, and open-funnel initialization are established.

title: Spatial-Frequency Control Authority of Grid-Forming Inverters over Voltage Waveforms in Distribution Feeders
abstract: This paper develops a spatial-frequency framework to quantify the impact of distributed energy resources with grid-forming inverters (GFMs) on voltage waveforms at different locations along a feeder. An analytical authority function is formulated to characterize how controllability varies with both electrical distance from the point of common coupling (PCC) and frequency. It is shown that the GFM control authority generally decays with both distance and frequency, reflecting the limited ability of inverter actions to influence voltage waveforms at distant points. To better capture controllability near resonance, a relative dominance metric is introduced to compare the influence of inverter-induced and grid-induced voltages at a given location and frequency. These results highlight that waveform controllability is fundamentally a spatial-frequency phenomenon along the feeder. Simulation studies validate the analytical findings by demonstrating both the spatial decay of control effectiveness along the feeder and the frequency-dependent trends in control authority in a realistic electromagnetic transient setting. The proposed framework provides insights into the placement and coordination of GFMs to enable effective waveform-level voltage control across electrical distance along the feeder.
comment: Accepted at the 2027 IEEE PES Grid Edge Technologies Conference & Exposition, Salt Lake City, Utah, April 19-22, 2027. 5 pages

title: Brittle by Design? Multi-Scenario Reinforcement Learning for Robust Mission Coordination in Systems of Systems
abstract: As systems engineering (SE) shifts from monolithic systems to Systems of Systems, Mission Engineering (ME) has emerged as a new line of thinking in SE. Mission environments are uncertain and dynamic, and outcomes depend on how mission assets interact with them, rendering static architectures brittle and calling for flexible yet analytically rigorous ME approaches. We propose an intelligent mission coordination methodology integrating high-fidelity digital mission models with Reinforcement Learning (RL) for adaptive task allocation. Using a Digital Engineering (DE) infrastructure comprising a digital mission model and agent-based simulation, we formulate mission tactics management as a Markov Decision Process and train an RL coordinator with Proximal Policy Optimization to map mission states to tactical actions from realized outcomes. An aerial firefighting mission with three scenarios demonstrates the approach. First, all trained coordinators significantly outperform random and heuristic baselines. Second, single-scenario coordinators can be brittle: the coordinator trained on the more forgiving scenario degrades to random tactics performance in more demanding scenarios, whereas the demanding-scenario coordinator retains most of its advantage when transferred. Third, within the same training budget, a coordinator trained on both scenarios concurrently matches the scenario-specific coordinators in their own scenarios and significantly outperforms every other policy. Sensitivity analyses on ignition location, weather, scenario, and training curricula show that the variability represented during training shapes post-deployment performance. This proof of concept shows DE-enabled mission simulations combined with RL offer a reusable methodology for improving ME practice, which can be extended to fleet design and selection from a mission-first perspective.

title: Polymer-Mediated Hotspot Evolution in Shock-Induced Pore Collapse in 1,3,5,7-Tetranitro-1,3,5,7-tetrazocane (HMX)-based Explosives
abstract: The initiation of detonation in high explosives (HEs) under shock loading is strongly influenced by the collapse of porosity and the subsequent formation of hotspots. As these materials are widely integrated with polymer binders to form polymer-bonded explosives, the collapse of pores at explosive-binder interfaces has received significant interest. Recent molecular dynamics (MD) simulations revealed that the shock-driven expansion of soft polymers (e.g. polystyrene) into a void produces greater pressure-volume (PV) work during recompression and higher local temperatures compared to pore collapse in neat HEs, ultimately expediting the onset of chemical reactions. Yet how pore collapse, interfacial phenomena, and binder chemistry jointly affect initiation remains insufficiently understood. We provide deeper insights into the role of polymer in hotspot evolution through reactive MD simulations, specifically characterizing its chemical behavior during the shock-induced collapse of voids at sizes approaching experimentally relevant length scales. We consider the HE 1,3,5,7-Tetranitro-1,3,5,7-tetrazocane (HMX) in a crystal-gap-crystal stack with polystyrene along the upstream surface. In the hydrodynamic collapse regime, hotspots nucleate at the material interfaces, with void length-dependence in PV work, shock temperature, and the onset of self-sustaining chemistry. Driven by shock-induced deformation and HMX decomposition, the binder undergoes backbone chain scission followed by extensive aromatic-backbone cross-bonding, akin to a graphite to diamond transformation. These reactions act as heat sinks, suppressing deflagration and ultimately inhibiting hotspot growth and coalescence between crystals. The simulations further link the polymer's chemical response to the shock-to-detonation transition in polymer-bonded explosives.

title: Deflation-Based Spectral Preconditioning for the Conjugate Gradient Method on Perturbed Systems
abstract: We consider sequences of large symmetric positive-definite linear systems in which spectral information from a reference matrix $A$ is reused to accelerate the solution of a nearby system with perturbed matrix $A(t)=A+tE$, where $E$ is symmetric, $\|E\|_F=1$, and $t\geq0$ is the perturbation size. We compare deflated conjugate gradient (deflated CG) with preconditioned CG (PCG) equipped with a scaled spectral preconditioner constructed from the same spectral information of $A$. First, we derive an energy-norm error characterization of deflated CG. We then use perturbation analysis to show that, after one additional PCG iteration, the squared PCG error is bounded, up to terms of order $t^2$, by an explicit multiple of the squared deflated CG error. This result clarifies the role of the scaling parameter in the preconditioner. Experiments show that the scaled spectral preconditioner recovers much of the convergence improvement provided by deflation while requiring fewer products with $A(t)$.

title: Hybrid PPO-Based Multi-Objective Optimization for UAV-mounted STAR-RIS with Energy Harvesting
abstract: This paper investigates a multi-objective optimiza tion framework for UAV-mounted reconfigurable intelligent sur face (STAR-RIS)-assisted Sixth Generation (6G)-enabled Internet of Things (IoT) systems. The considered framework jointly supports communication enhancement and radio-frequency (RF) energy harvesting (EH) through adaptive STAR-RIS transmission and reflection control. A weighted multi-objective optimization problem is formulated to jointly optimize the base station (BS) beamforming vectors, STAR-RIS transmission and reflection coefficients, RF power-splitting factor, and UAV trajectory under quality-of-service (QoS), power, and mobility constraints. Due to the strong coupling among the communications, EH, and UAV mobility variables, the resulting problem is highly non convex and difficult to solve using conventional optimization methods. To address this challenge, a hybrid proximal policy optimization (H-PPO) framework is proposed. The developed hybrid actor-critic architecture combines a categorical policy for discrete UAV movement decisions with Beta-distributed policies for continuous communication-control variables. In addition, a two-stage reward mechanism is introduced to enforce QoS feasibility while balancing system sum rate, energy efficiency, and harvested energy. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed H-PPO framework achieves faster convergence and more stable training behavior than proximal policy optimization (PPO) and twin delayed deep deterministic policy gradient (TD3) baselines. In particular, H-PPO achieves approximately 66% and 60% faster convergence than PPO and TD3, respectively, while maintaining more stable training behavior. Furthermore, the proposed framework effectively balances communication performance and EH under different QoS requirements, STAR RIS sizes, transmit power levels, and user densities.

title: Robust Procurement Planning for Community Choice Aggregators: Managing Market Price Uncertainty
abstract: Community Choice Aggregators (CCAs) play an important role in the energy transition by procuring renewable electricity for local communities while balancing affordability, resource adequacy, and clean-energy requirements. In California, these long-term procurement decisions are coordinated through integrated resource planning (IRP). However, conventional IRP frameworks typically represent wholesale electricity prices deterministically, even though price uncertainty can expose CCAs to substantial financial risk by affecting the cost of market imports and, particularly, the value of export opportunities. This paper develops a robust optimization framework for CCA resource procurement that hedges against uncertainty in wholesale import and export prices. We extend the open-source GenX capacity expansion model with a budgeted robust optimization formulation that protects procurement decisions against adverse price realizations while remaining computationally tractable for large-scale, multistage planning studies. Using data from a California CCA, we show that market price uncertainty can materially change optimal procurement strategies. Rather than aggressively expanding renewable capacity based on expected export revenues, robust portfolios reduce dependence on uncertain market revenues, leading to more conservative renewable investments and less reliance on market exports. We demonstrate that moderate uncertainty budgets provide most of the risk-reduction benefits of robust planning at limited additional cost, whereas higher robustness levels yield diminishing benefits as portfolio conservatism increases. These findings provide guidance for selecting uncertainty budgets in IRP studies and demonstrate how robust optimization can support affordable and resilient procurement decisions as CCAs contribute to the transition toward low-carbon electricity systems.

title: Depth Separation for Neural Networks under Gaussian Measure
abstract: We revisit the problem of depth separation for neural networks, as studied by Eldan and Shamir, Daniely, and others. Specifically, we consider the natural setting of $L^2$ approximation of radial functions under the standard Gaussian measure in $d$ dimensions. We show that there is a radial function in $L^2$ under the standard Gaussian measure that can be approximated to a fixed sufficiently small $L^2$ error by a depth-3 ReLU neural network of polynomial size in $d$ but can only be approximated by depth-2 networks with subexponentially bounded weights if their size is at least exponential in $d$. For that, we prove a general result showing that if a radial function has substantial mass in the high frequencies of its Hermite expansion, then it cannot be well approximated by a depth-2 neural network with small width and bounded weights. All theorems, lemmas, propositions, and corollaries are verified in Lean~4.

title: FAUST XXXII. Chemically layered structures and ionisation in the disk and envelope of NGC 1333 IRAS 4C
abstract: Recent molecular line observations with high spatial resolutions have revealed vertical chemical stratification in Class I/II disks (i.e. chemical composition changing with height in the vertical direction of the disk), as well as a radial variation of ionisation rates. However, such chemical layered structures in Class 0 disk and envelope systems have been investigated only for limited objects, such as L1527. In the context of the ALMA Large Program FAUST, we report the results of molecular line observations toward the disk and envelope around the low-mass Class 0 protostar NGC 1333 IRAS 4C in the Perseus Molecular Cloud. Previous observations have shown that the disk rotation axis of this object is largely tilted to the line of sight, making it suitable for studying the molecular abundance distribution as a function of disk height. We found that the molecules known as gas density tracers such as C18O and H2CO are distributed around the disk midplane. In addition, molecules known as tracers of photochemical reactions such as CCH and c-C3H2 are distributed in the low-density upper layers of the disk, unlike the distribution in L1527. Moreover, the column density ratio of HCO+/CO derived from the H13CO+ and C18O line emission suggests that the ionisation degree and the ionisation rate vary with the disk radius and they are larger in the outer region of the disk and envelope.

title: ReAPO: Retry-Aware Policy Optimization for Efficient Exploration in LLM Reasoning
abstract: RLVR improves language-model reasoning, but commonly relies on independent stochastic rollouts for exploration, which can repeatedly sample similar failed strategies. Prior work has seen success with approaches that guide exploration by introducing dependence into the sampling process by including incorrect solutions in the context for subsequent attempts. Still, these methods introduce the additional question of how to assign credit to each attempt. We propose to view the credit assignment through the lens of Stochastic Shortest Paths, a framework in classical reinforcement learning that seeks to minimize the expected cumulative cost to reach a terminal state (in our case, a verified successful response). We show that, under suitable simplifying assumptions, this perspective naturally leads to a simple modification to GRPO, which we call Retry-Aware Policy Optimization (ReAPO). ReAPO allocates additional generation to failed trajectories, allowing successful retries to be reinforced without rewarding preceding failures, and assigns credit in a theoretically principled way to each attempt. Across Qwen3 and OLMo-2 models from 0.6B to 4B and eight mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks, ReAPO improves first-attempt performance over GRPO as well as natural recent baseline algorithms, while additional ablations demonstrate the utility of both serial sampling and ReAPO's credit assignment. On Qwen3-0.6B, ReAPO also outperforms GRPO with twice the group size or twice the training steps, reaching their peak accuracy with 39% and 31% fewer generated tokens, respectively. Taken together, our results suggest that ReAPO is a simple yet effective approach for improving LM reasoning performance through improved exploration and retry-aware credit assignment.

title: Constraints on Reionization from Planck Low-$\ell$ EE Polarization and the Lyman-Series Forests
abstract: CMB measurements tightly constrain the Thomson scattering optical depth ($τ_{\rm es}$), but they still permit a broad range of degenerate reionization histories. Incorporating Lyman-series forest constraints on the end of reionization can alleviate the degeneracy and narrow the range of allowed histories. We explore this effect using forest measurements combined with full Planck likelihoods. We apply upper limits on the neutral fraction at $4.9\lesssim z\lesssim6.9$ derived from the dark pixel fraction, as well as a lower limit at $z=5.8$ from damping-wing-like features on the edges of long dark gaps in stacked forest spectra. We find that neither the choice of parametric vs. non-parametric reionization model, nor the choice among different forest data combinations, produces a significant shift in $τ_{\rm es}$ or the other cosmological parameters. Instead, forest constraints primarily redistribute $τ_{\rm es}$ in redshift. Combining dark pixel, damping-wing-like, and CMB measurements, we find $z_{50}=7.7^{+0.7}_{-0.8}$ and a 95\% upper limit of $Δz_{90}<11.4$ for the midpoint and duration of reionization, respectively. The asymmetry of the reionization history ($A_z$) is not well constrained by these data. Stronger constraints can be obtained using Ly$α$ forest measurements of the mean IGM photoionization rate, at the cost of requiring more detailed modeling. Using a new semi-analytic reionization model, we obtain (model-dependent) constraints of $z_{50} = 7.4^{+0.2}_{-0.3}$, $Δz_{90}=6.0^{+0.8}_{-1.0}$, and $A_z = 2.4^{+0.3}_{-0.7}$. We also find evidence that the ionizing emissivity of reionization sources declines after $z=7-8$, perhaps signaling a decline in the escape fraction and/or the onset of a feedback process. Our results motivate the development of forest likelihood products and fast forward models for its transmission statistics.

title: PIANISTpy: A JAX-based Python package for velocity-anisotropic astrophysical equilibrium models
abstract: The hierarchical assembly of dark matter haloes and galaxies via mergers and anisotropic mass accretion naturally imprints non-trivial velocity anisotropy onto haloes and galaxies, an empirical fact emerging from cosmological simulations. However, dynamical studies based on idealised numerical simulations typically assume isotropic velocity distributions for the systems studied. This is mainly because no tools exist to construct anisotropic initial conditions with fully self-consistent (i.e., physical and instability-free) truncation boundary conditions for finite spatial extents. Here we present the first such analytical framework that performs truncation in phase space, with two distinct approaches to guarantee either the monotonicity of output distribution functions or identical truncated density profiles. We additionally present the open-source JAX-based GPU-accelerated Python package PIANISTpy (Particle Initial conditions with ANISoTropy) for constructing spherical, non-rotating initial conditions, supporting arbitrary double-power-law analytical radial density profiles and a library of analytical anisotropy profiles. This framework further permits the construction of systems with non-analytical anisotropy profiles via an arbitrary linear superposition of all implemented analytical anisotropy models as basis functions. PIANISTpy also outputs 3D velocity profiles and line-of-sight-integrated observables with end-to-end differentiability for rapid gradient-based Monte Carlo inference, and self-consistent local dark matter velocity distributions of anisotropic haloes beyond the unphysical Maxwell-Boltzmann simplification adopted in terrestrial detection experiments. We discuss use cases and demonstrate PIANISTpy's orders-of-magnitude higher numerical solver accuracy and superior dynamical stability of particle initial conditions relative to existing tools, including galpy and AGAMA.

title: The MIni-Halos in MIni-Clusters (MIMIC) project: New insights into the origin of mini-halos from a LOFAR, uGMRT, and MeerKAT study of diffuse radio emission in Abell 496 and ZwCl 235
abstract: We aim at investigating the presence of diffuse radio emission in low-mass (M$_{500}\leq3\times10^{14}$ M$_{\odot}$), relaxed galaxy clusters. We present a pilot study for the MIMIC (MIni-halos in MIni-Clusters) project, focusing on Abell 496 and ZwCl 235, using LOFAR (54, 144 MHz), uGMRT (400, 650 MHz), and MeerKAT (1.28 GHz) data, as well as Chandra X-ray data. We detect diffuse radio emission in the central 100 kpc of both Abell 496 and ZwCl 235, spatially confined within sloshing-induced cold fronts seen in X-ray images. The diffuse sources satisfy the classification criteria for radio mini-halos and represent the least powerful known to date, with 1.4 GHz radio powers of $(2.2\pm0.2)\times10^{22}$ W/Hz in Abell 496 and $(1.3\pm0.3)\times10^{22}$ W/Hz in ZwCl 235. The mini-halos have steep spectra ($-1.9\leqα\leq-1.4$), and in Abell 496 we find outward steepening of the spectral index. In both clusters, the radio and X-ray surface brightness are correlated over the diffuse source extent, with sub-linear or nearly linear slopes depending on frequency. Separately, we present the properties of two extended (>200 kpc) tailed radio galaxies in both clusters. The steep spectra, sub-linear radio-X-ray correlations, and confinement within cold fronts suggest that contribution from fossil plasma advected from the central radio galaxy and plausible turbulent re-acceleration are at play in Abell 496 and ZwCl 235. These two systems allow us to extend mini-halo scaling relations toward the low-power regime. We confirm a strong correlation between the mini-halo radio power and the cool core X-ray luminosity, with $P_{1.4} \propto L_{X,70}^{1.5\pm0.2}$. We find, for the first time, tentative indications that mini-halos with steeper radio spectra may preferentially be associated with lower core X-ray luminosities and lower radio power. (abridged)

title: Link between the properties of circumgalactic outflows and the recent star formation history of their host galaxies
abstract: Galactic outflows play a key role in galaxy evolution, yet their connection to the star formation history of their host galaxies remains poorly constrained. Building on previous work modeling extended Mg II emission of galaxies observed with VLT/MUSE to infer outflow properties, we investigate how these properties depend on the recent SFH. We derive non-parametric SFHs by fitting spectroscopic and photometric data with linear combinations of single stellar population models, and compute star formation rates over different timescales sensitive to recent stochastic bursts. We find moderate correlations between these SFRs (and sSFRs) and the kinematic properties of the outflows, namely maximum velocity and radial acceleration rate. Such correlations are not recovered using SFR tracers based on [O II] luminosity or parametric SFHs, highlighting the importance of capturing bursty star formation on timescales consistent with the traveling time of ejected gas into the circumgalactic medium. Using the extent and kinematics of the Mg II halos, we estimate each galaxy's outflow launching time and compute the SFR averaged over the relevant timescale. We identify a correlation between this SFR and the maximum outflow velocity, although it is not significantly stronger than those obtained using fixed averaging timescales. This suggests that the properties of Mg II halos are shaped by a series of star formation events rather than by a single dominant burst. Lastly, we find faster outflows in galaxies whose recent star formation is dominated by one or a few concentrated episodes, whereas galaxies with star formation spread more evenly over time exhibit slower outflows. These results indicate that the circumgalactic medium acts as a dynamical archive of recent star formation, linking bursty galaxy growth to outflow kinematics and providing a direct observational constraint on feedback models.

title: A Reverse-Gold Theorem: Positive-Data Identification by Substrate-Bounded Contrastive Learners
abstract: Gold's theorem shows that no learner can identify an arbitrary language in a superfinite class from positive presentations alone. We prove a positive result of a different shape. Fix an innate \emph{recursive contrast operator} $R$ mapping any string to a finite set of structurally bounded perturbations of it, and a discriminative scorer of bounded capacity trained by InfoNCE-style contrastive estimation \citep{vandenoord2018,macollins2018} on self-generated perturbations. Under a faithfulness condition relating operator, scorer, and target, the trained scorer achieves \emph{PAC conditional identification} from positive data alone: with high probability it ranks all but an $\varepsilon$-fraction of positives above every out-of-language perturbation in their own orbit, with sample complexity polynomial in the capacity, the orbit size, the score bound, and $1/\varepsilon$. The negatives are constructed by the learner, not supplied by an oracle, and no global normalizing constant over strings is ever computed. The misranking bound follows from the geometry of the contrastive loss---per-example loss floors plus a definite loss increment under misranking---yielding an $\varepsilon^{-2}$ rate, together with an explicit approximation gap that quantifies the cost of in-language (``colliding'') perturbations and vanishes for orbit-pure operators. The ranking guarantee lifts to a global membership classifier under a margin condition, and the same operator composed with the learned scorer is a normalization-free Metropolis--Hastings generator. We instantiate the hypotheses for substitutable context-free languages \citep{clarkeyraud2007} and the subregular classes \citep{heinz2010,hayashikamigaito2025}, and state an open conjecture locating the construction in the mildly context-sensitive hierarchy.

title: Ammonia Fitting of Multiple Velocity Components in High-Mass Star-Forming Regions
abstract: We perform a multiple velocity component analysis of ammonia (NH$_3$) gas from KEYSTONE, a Green Bank Telescope survey covering 11 giant molecular clouds (GMCs) at distances from 0.7 to 2.7 kpc. We extend existing codes to enable simultaneous fitting of up to three velocity components in NH$_3$ (1,1) with radiative transfer. Using our multiple component fitting technique, we produce the best maps of the centroid velocity and velocity dispersion in these clouds to date. Over the entire survey, multiple velocity components were seen in 13% of pixels where we detect and fit NH$_3$ emission, primarily in clusters at the heart of the GMCs. In these multiple component pixels, the median measured NH$_3$ linewidth decreased by a factor of 1.4 compared to equivalent single-component measurements, but there are also significant cloud-to-cloud variations. Regions with multiple velocity components tend to be found in the densest zones of the GMCs and at the sites of high-mass star formation, indicative of multiple filaments, cores, or complex velocities associated with the formation of massive stars. Disentangling these velocity features will allow future quantitative analysis of coherent motions, such as infall and outflow, in these complex environments. The multi-component data products are available on the CADC.

title: Unveiling the correlation between the UV 2175 Å dust attenuation bump, PAH emission, and gas-phase metallicity at cosmic noon
abstract: The UV 2175 Å attenuation bump is one of the most prominent yet poorly understood features of galaxy attenuation curves. Its main candidate carrier is polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) molecules, which are more prevalent in high-metallicity environments. We present the first systematic study of the relationship between PAH abundance and the UV bump in 49 galaxies at cosmic noon (1.5 < z < 2.7), examining its dependence on stellar mass, star formation rate (SFR), and V-band optical depth. For 19 galaxies, we also investigate gas-phase metallicity using oxygen abundances. We measure the bump amplitude from VLT/MUSE spectroscopy and derive galaxy properties, including the PAH-to-dust mass fraction $q_{\rm PAH}$, through spectral energy distribution fitting with Prospector, combining JWST/NIRCam and JWST/MIRI photometry. Oxygen abundances are derived from strong-line diagnostics using Keck/MOSFIRE and JWST/NIRSpec data. We find a positive correlation between bump amplitude $E_{\rm bump}$ and $q_{\rm PAH}$ (Spearman $ρ= 0.60$). UV bumps are rarely detected at low $q_{\rm PAH}$, supporting PAHs as their primary carriers. Both $E_{\rm bump}$ and $q_{\rm PAH}$ correlate with stellar mass, oxygen abundance, and optical depth, and anticorrelate with specific SFR, suggesting that PAHs and the UV bump are suppressed in low-metallicity, dust-poor, and/or intensely star-forming environments. This is consistent with PAH destruction in environments with limited dust shielding and/or strong radiation fields. A principal component analysis of $E_{\rm bump}$, $q_{\rm PAH}$, optical depth, specific SFR, and oxygen abundance explains 97% of the variance, suggesting that previously reported correlations with stellar mass reflect an underlying dependence on metallicity. Finally, variations in dust geometry may explain the wide range of bump amplitudes (0-0.5 mag) at high $q_{\rm PAH}$.

title: A combined HST and JWST analysis of the stellar population in Draco II
abstract: Draco II (Dra II) is one of the faintest and most metal-poor Milky Way satellites known, yet its nature as either an ultra-faint dwarf galaxy or an extended globular cluster remains debated. We perform a photometric analysis of the stellar population of Dra II reducing deep multi-band observations from the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). We select Dra II member stars based on their proper motions and photometric quality criteria. For the first time, optical and infrared photometry are combined to produce a stellar catalogue reaching 50 percent completeness at $F814W = 26.5$ mag (corresponding to the absolute magnitude $M_{F814W} = 10.1$ mag). The colour-magnitude diagram confirms that Dra II hosts an old stellar population with an age of $13.5_{-1.5}^{+1.7}$ Gyr at a distance of $19.2\pm0.9$ kpc. We measure an $α$-enhanced stellar population with a low mean metallicity of $[\rm Fe/H]_{CaHK} = -2.38 \pm 0.17$ dex and confirm the presence of an intrinsic metallicity spread of $σ_{[\rm Fe/H]} = 0.85 \pm 0.13$ dex. We identify 10 unresolved main-sequence binary stars in the HST catalogue with mass ratios $q > 0.5$ in the mass range $0.43<M_1/M_\odot<0.71$, corresponding to a binary fraction of $f_{bin}^{q>0.5} = 0.21 \pm 0.07$. This value is higher than those typically observed in globular clusters and lies near the upper range measured in open clusters. The stellar mass function is best modelled by a single power law with a slope of $1.53\pm0.26$ over the mass range $0.13$--$0.77\ M_\odot$. We find no evidence of mass segregation. Consistent results are obtained independently from the JWST catalogue. Combining these findings strongly suggests that Draco II is best classified as an ultra-faint dwarf galaxy rather than a globular cluster.

title: Discovery of a Broad-Line Active Galactic Nucleus at $z = 9.98$
abstract: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has uncovered a previously unexplored population of faint active galactic nuclei (AGNs) in the early Universe. We present MoM-BL-z10 at $z=9.9837\pm0.0009$, identified through a systematic search for broad-line AGNs at $z\geq6$ using public JWST/NIRSpec PRISM spectra from the DAWN JWST Archive. The PRISM spectrum exhibits a broad component in H$β$ at 5.35 microns. A narrow+broad Gaussian fit yields a broad H$β$ detection at S/N = 3.87, with FWHM = $3480^{+2040}_{-950}$ km s$^{-1}$ and $L_{{\rm H}β,{\rm broad}}=1.25^{+0.33}_{-0.31}\times10^{42}$ erg s$^{-1}$. The detection of [Ne III] $\lambda3870$ and the high [Ne III]/[O II] and [O III]/H$β$ ratios further support the AGN interpretation. Its rest-frame UV and optical continuum slopes, compact NIRCam morphology, and a tentative MIRI F770W detection suggest similarities to Little Red Dots (LRDs). The broad H$β$ detection enables the first virial SMBH mass estimate at $z\sim10$. We derive $M_{\rm BH}=3.6^{+5.8}_{-1.7}\times10^7 M_\odot$ and $λ_{\rm Edd}=0.11^{+0.10}_{-0.07}$ using the standard single-epoch virial calibration and quasar bolometric correction. We also consider an alternative scenario adopting the LRD-specific bolometric correction and assuming $λ_{\rm Edd}=1$, which yields $M_{\rm BH}=2.1^{+0.6}_{-0.5}\times10^6 M_\odot$. Under either scenario, the inferred SMBH mass at a cosmic age of only 470 Myr highlights the challenge of rapid BH growth in the early Universe, suggesting super-Eddington accretion from a stellar-mass seed or a more massive seed. As the highest-redshift broad-line AGN identified to date, MoM-BL-z10 provides a new observational benchmark for understanding the early growth of supermassive black holes.

title: Simulation-Informed High-Velocity Dark Matter in the Effective Theory of Direct Detection
abstract: The interpretation and reach of direct detection (DD) experiments depend sensitively on the local dark matter (DM) velocity distribution, particularly its high-velocity tail. This tail is crucial for elastic scattering at low DM masses or large momentum transfers, and for inelastic upscattering, where additional kinetic energy is needed to overcome the mass splitting. In practice, however, phenomenological studies typically rely either on the Standard Halo Model (SHM) or, when an enhanced high-velocity tail contributes to the scattering rate, on the single simulation that includes a large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) analogue, Au-25, whose debris reaches ~ 950\kms. In this work, we instead build on a previously presented empirically-motivated reconstruction method, to construct the local DM velocity distribution, using stellar kinematics from the Gaia space telescope. We combine this reconstructed Milky Way component with the best LMC analog in the FIRE-2 simulations, and find no local DM faster than ~ 900\kms. We compare the resulting distribution with the two commonly used benchmarks, the SHM and Au-25. We then study how these different velocity distributions affect the interpretation of DD searches across all operators of the non-relativistic effective field theory of DM--nucleon interactions, for both elastic and inelastic DM. As an illustrative application, we consider the high-energy event observed in the LUX-ZEPLIN extended search. Requiring the event to remain compatible with the absence of signal in the surrounding energy sidebands, we observe the inferred inelastic DM mass splitting can be shifted by up to $\sim 130$~keV depending on the assumed high-velocity tail. Higher-resolution simulations of the high-velocity DM population reaching the detector will therefore be crucial for interpreting a future signal and setting robust limits on DM interactions.

title: Arepo-CD: Coupling Collisional $N$-Body Dynamics with Moving-Mesh Magnetohydrodynamics
abstract: Star formation is a hierarchical, clustered process in turbulent giant molecular clouds (GMCs), where close stellar encounters can strongly affect cluster evolution and feedback. However, gravitational softening in many hydrodynamic simulations of GMCs limits the treatment of these encounters. We present Arepo-CD (Collisional Dynamics), a framework that couples star-by-star collisional $N$-body dynamics to the moving-mesh magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) code Arepo. Star-star interactions use unsoftened gravity, while interactions involving gas or collisionless components remain softened. Compact stellar subsystems are identified on the fly and evolved with a fourth-order forward symplectic integrator and slow-down algorithmic regularization coupled to the native Arepo timestep hierarchy. Benchmark tests against the collisional $N$-body code PeTar show good agreement in cluster core collapse and subsequent expansion, radial density profiles, and stellar velocity distributions. Coupled to the Rigel star formation and feedback model, Arepo-CD follows cluster formation and early evolution in radiation MHD simulations of a $10^5~M_\odot$ turbulent molecular cloud. In the fiducial GMC comparison, the collisional and softened-gravity runs yield similar star formation histories and integrated star formation efficiencies. Nevertheless, close gravitational encounters during the embedded phase generate a substantial runaway population, with a velocity tail extending beyond 100 km/s. Ejected massive stars redistribute radiative feedback into the surrounding lower-density medium and produce a more extended distribution of heated gas. Arepo-CD provides a practical and computationally efficient framework for studying collisional stellar dynamics and its coupling to gas evolution and feedback during star cluster formation in realistic galactic environments.
authors: Chuizheng Kong;Hui Li;Long Wang;Yunwei Deng;Elizabeth Moreno-Hilario

title: Chemical abundance patterns at z=1-7: Carbon, Nitrogen, Neon, Sulphur, and Argon abundances from JWST spectroscopy
abstract: The relative abundances of chemical elements in the interstellar medium (ISM) trace the history of star formation and chemical enrichment in galaxies. We investigate the abundance patterns of carbon (C), nitrogen (N), neon (Ne), sulfur (S), and argon (Ar) in star-forming galaxies at z=1-7, combining ultra-deep JWST/NIRSpec observations from the MARTA survey with archival spectroscopy. We assemble 244 galaxies with [OIII]4363 detections and derive direct Te-based abundances. New empirical strong-line calibrations for N/O, Ne/O, S/O, and Ar/O extend the analysis to an additional 514 galaxies. We find distinct abundance-metallicity trends. N/O is enhanced by 0.18 dex in median relative to local galaxies, with a stronger enhancement at low metallicity. Direct measurements reveal decreasing S/O and Ar/O with increasing metallicity, while strong-line measurements suggest a flattening at higher metallicities, especially for S/O. We also identify a stellar-mass dependence in the O/Ar-Ar/H plane, with lower-mass galaxies exhibiting lower O/Ar at fixed Ar/H, consistent with differences in star-formation efficiency and delayed SNe Ia enrichment. Ne/O remains approximately constant up to 12+log(O/H)=8.2, with a mild increase at higher metallicities and no significant redshift evolution. C/O tentatively increases with metallicity, broadly following the local relation. Finally, a forward model shows that observational selection affects the abundance ratios differently: it mainly restricts the accessible metallicity range for Ne/O and Ar/O, but preferentially selects galaxies with enhanced N/O at low metallicity, with a weaker effect for S/O. These results provide new constraints on chemical enrichment at high redshift and highlight the importance of accounting for selection effects when interpreting abundance-metallicity trends.

title: The Balmer Absorber Strength Problem of Little Red Dots
abstract: Little Red Dots (LRDs) commonly show Balmer absorption features. Some observed LRD spectra have weaker absorption in H$α$ than in H$β$, in apparent contradiction to atomic physics according to standard attenuation models. This tension is naturally resolved when one considers emission from the absorbing medium itself, which is ignored in the standard model: when the Balmer absorption is optically thick, a non-negligible source function could fill in the H$α$ absorption trough and reduce its observed absorption equivalent width (EW). With proof-of-concept photoionization models we show that the source function of H$α$ could be systematically stronger than that of H$β$. This is due to radiative trapping preferentially populating the $n=3$ level of neutral hydrogen, which operates efficiently when the medium is optically thick to H$α$ but not very optically thick to Paschen-$α$. Such line-dependent source functions could lead to significant corrections to the expected EW and selectively weaken H$α$ absorption, consistent with observations. Quantitatively, this depends on the distance of the absorbing medium and its internal structure, providing a new diagnostic of the environment around LRDs. Future modeling of the absorbers may also potentially open a new avenue for estimating the mass of the central engine.
authors: Hanpu Liu;Eliot Quataert;Bingjie Wang;Jenny E. Greene;Yan-Fei Jiang

title: Mechanistic discovery in grain boundary structure and deformation driven by agentic AI
abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems hold immense potential for automating complex workflows in materials discovery and design, but extending these capabilities to domain-intensive mechanistic studies remains challenging. General grain boundaries (GBs) exemplify this challenge, as their structural complexity complicates experimental characterization and atomistic modeling. Here, we present GBClaw, an agentic AI framework for investigating the structure and deformation of general GBs, which are common in real polycrystals yet remain understudied. By integrating large language models into a modular architecture, GBClaw effectively combines systematic simulations with targeted mechanistic analysis through iterative workflow refinement and dynamic replanning. Applied to 14 general asymmetric tilt GBs in nickel, the framework characterized interfacial defect structures and deformation modes across these incommensurate boundaries. It established a general approach to identify previously unobserved, widely spaced secondary GB misfit dislocations (SGBMDs) alongside closely spaced primary GB misfit dislocations (PGBMDs) in simulated atomic configurations and experimental images. Comparisons of GB sliding with and without SGBMDs revealed substantial differences in shear strength, underscoring the critical role of misfit-dislocation hierarchies in sliding resistance. Researcher-guided follow-up calculations further elucidated the structural origins of shear asymmetry and an anomalous shear response. This work demonstrates that combining agentic AI with domain expertise bridges high-throughput computational screening and deep mechanistic discovery at complex material interfaces.
authors: Yazhuo Liu;Kunqing Ding;Xiaoguo Gong;Zifeng Wang;Yichen Yang;Yifeng Che;Wen Chen;Josh Kacher;Olivier Pierron;Shigenobu Ogata;Ting Zhu

title: Adaptive Multi-Token Prediction: How far should we go?
abstract: Multi-token prediction (MTP) can accelerate language-model decoding by drafting several tokens and verifying them in a single target-model pass. However, the best speculation horizon changes with context: longer drafts offer greater amortization when reliable, but can waste compute on suffixes discarded after a rejection. Unlike autoregressive drafting, where a stopping rule can decide token by token, MTP must fix the horizon before drafting, as all heads fire in the same forward pass. We therefore formulate horizon selection as an online control problem, using verification feedback to learn how far the draft can be trusted in each context, and introduce Adaptive Multi-Token Prediction (AMTP): a lightweight controller that requires no retraining and leaves the exact verifier unchanged. To guide horizon selection, we characterize the expected number of tokens committed at each horizon via acceptance survival, the probability that a draft prefix is fully accepted. Before each round, AMTP predicts how far the draft is likely to survive and picks the horizon with the highest expected tokens per second, learning freely from every verification pass. Theoretically, we show that any online learner's prediction error translates into throughput regret against the best horizon for each context, and in turn into a bound on wall-clock completion time. With online gradient descent, this regret is sublinear. Across five draft-target pairings built on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with Medusa heads, Meta's MTP models, and Qwen3-4B-Inst-2507-MTP, evaluated on AIME 2025 and GSM8K, AMTP decodes up to 4.1x faster than standard decoding and matches or outperforms the fixed window in 8 of 10 settings, with throughput gains of up to 10%.

title: Resolving the extended interstellar medium of infrared galaxies I. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon emission
abstract: We investigate spatial variations in polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) properties and photoelectric heating efficiency in 67 nearby luminous infrared galaxies from the Great Observatories All-sky LIRG Survey (GOALS). Using mid-infrared spectroscopy from Spitzer and far-infrared cooling-line maps from Herschel, we extract spectra in concentric annuli and matched aperture grids out to about 14 kpc. PAH features are measured with the CAFE spectral decomposition tool. We trace photoelectric heating efficiency by combining PAH emission with cooling lines after isolating the neutral-gas contribution. In starburst galaxies, the PAH 11.3/7.7 ratio rises out to about 5 kpc while 6.2/7.7 remains nearly constant, indicating predominantly large, neutral PAHs. Between 5 and 8 kpc, 11.3/7.7 continues to rise while inferred PAH sizes decrease. Beyond 8 kpc, 11.3/7.7 falls and 6.2/7.7 rises, indicating smaller, more ionized PAHs. These trends are consistent with PAH photodestruction near the central starburst. Strong active galactic nucleus (AGN) systems show more neutral PAHs and harder radiation fields in their nuclear and inner regions. Beyond about 5 kpc, PAHs become more ionized and approach the starburst locus as the radiation field weakens. Strong AGNs influence average PAH charge states at 6-14 kpc as effectively as moderate AGNs at 1-6 kpc. Photoelectric heating efficiency increases with radius in both starburst and AGN-hosting galaxies as the radiation field weakens. In starbursts, higher efficiency is associated with more neutral PAHs, while AGN-dominated systems show the opposite relation. These results provide quantitative, spatially resolved constraints on the extent of AGN effects on dust properties in a population of luminous infrared galaxies.
