title: The Solar System through dust maps. Encounter statistics with interstellar gas
abstract: During its orbit around the Milky Way, the Solar System crosses different environments, including dense ISM regions. These encounters increase dust influx, leave geological signatures, and affect the heliosphere. For the local ISM, we estimate crossing frequencies and durations, the fraction of time spent above gas density thresholds, and how Solar vertical motion and ISM stratification influence these statistics. We quantify gas influx and dust exposure. We use Gaia-based 3D dust maps of the Solar neighborhood, sampled by integrating the Solar System along its Galactic orbit while rigidly translating the maps. From the resulting density time series, encounter statistics and fluxes are derived. We find that the Solar System spends most of its time in low density environments, while crossings of dense gas become rarer with increasing density threshold. For nH>=1cm^-3, the crossing frequency is above 600Gyr^-1, whereas thresholds around 200cm^-3 are crossed once per Gyr. Individual crossings last tens of kyr and become shorter at higher density thresholds. The inferred durations soon become nearly constant, reflecting the finite spatial resolution of the maps. The Sun spends 18 to 47% of the sampled time above 1cm^-3, and 1 to 10% above 10cm^-3. The residence fraction can be reproduced by combining the vertical volume filling factor of gas with the fraction of time spent by the Sun at each height. Within the current vertical range sampled by the Sun, we find no clear enhancement of crossing statistics during midplane passages, suggesting that these do not necessarily lead to periodic perturbations of the Solar System. About 50% of the gas influx is contributed by gas with nH<=3-4cm^-3, and about 90% by gas with nH<=48cm^-3. Our results provide a first order, data driven estimate of ISM encounter statistics, gas influx, and dust exposure along the Solar System's Galactic orbit.
authors: E. Maconi;J. Alves;S. Hutschenreuter;S. Ratzenböck;M. Pantaleoni;C. Zucker;C. Levy;G. Edenhofer

title: Magnetoelectric Bulk Photovoltaic Effect in Centrosymmetric Solids
abstract: It is commonly believed that a bulk photovoltaic current requires broken spatial inversion symmetry. However, in this work, we demonstrate that dc photocurrents can arise in centrosymmetric solids from the bilinear coupling between the electric and magnetic components of light. This magnetoelectric bulk photovoltaic effect (MBPE) has a quantum-geometric origin in the dipole moments of the Zeeman quantum metric and Zeeman Berry curvature. We identify four distinct MBPE mechanisms, including time-reversal-even and time-reversal-odd injection-like and shift-like photocurrents driven by linearly or circularly polarized light. Our symmetry analysis shows that the MBPE is allowed in broad classes of two-dimensional centrosymmetric nonmagnetic and magnetic materials under normally incident light. As representative examples, we predict sizable MBPEs in centrosymmetric monolayer Pt$_2$HgSe$_3$ and altermagnetic RuF$_4$, with current densities on the order of $1~\mathrm{mA/m}$. Notably, the injection-like photocurrent in RuF$_4$ reverses sign upon switching either the light helicity or the Néel vector. Our results extend the bulk photovoltaic effect to centrosymmetric solids and open new opportunities for electrical readout of altermagnetic order.

title: Every minute counts: Wind farm power control during imbalance settlement using distributional soft actor-critic
abstract: Wind farms can provide flexibility by curtailing their output during periods of excess generation in the power grid. One way to achieve this is through implicit balancing, where curtailment is performed in anticipation of a negative imbalance price. By doing so, the wind farm helps reduce system imbalance while also lowering its own costs. However, implicit balancing is challenging, since imbalance prices are hard to predict and can also be affected by the control actions taken by the farm. To address both challenges, we use distributional soft actor-critic (distSAC) to learn a control policy that adjusts the power setpoint every minute. Using real data of the Belgian grid and an offshore wind farm, we show that our method can turn the imbalance costs caused by forecast errors into a small revenue. Moreover, distSAC outperforms a price threshold controller, often used in industry, and performs slightly better than soft actor-critic (SAC). Unlike SAC, distSAC can also learn risk-averse policies by optimizing a risk measure, such as conditional value at risk. These risk-averse policies were found to better account for their price impact, reducing overshoots by 16-27% while achieving similar cost savings. Last, we find that 1-minute setpoints lead to lower imbalance costs than 15-minute setpoints, regardless of the control policy.
authors: Max Bruninx;Seyed Soroush Karimi Madahi;Timothy Verstraeten;Jan Decuyper;Chris Develder;Ann Nowé;Jan Helsen

title: Tailoring Dielectric Relaxation and Charge Transport in Amorphous Ge-Te-Se Phase-Change Materials through Yttrium Incorporation
abstract: The Te(1-x)(GeSe0.5)Yx (x = 0.05, 0.10, 0.15) alloys were prepared by a melt-quenching method and characterized using dielectric spectroscopy. The dielectric parameters and electrical conductivity were evaluated to assess their potential for phase-change memory and other electronic applications. The temperature and frequency dependence of the dielectric constants, ac conductivity, and dielectric loss of prepared chalcogenide glassy alloys were investigated over the frequency range 1 Hz - 1 MHz, and the temperature range 302 - 422 K, below the glass transition temperature. Both dielectric loss and dielectric constant were found to decrease with increasing frequency and decreasing temperature. The observed dielectric loss change was interpreted using the Guintini model of dielectric dispersion, correlated barrier hopping (CBH) model, and orientation polarization. The Cole-Cole analysis confirmed a distribution of relaxation times and yielded activation energies consistent with the CBH conduction mechanism. The frequency dependence of the ac conductivity follows the power law (Aωs), where the frequency exponent (s < 1) decreases with increasing temperature, further supporting the CBH conduction mechanism. The incorporation of Y increases the density of localized tail states, resulting in enhanced ac conductivity. These findings suggest that the investigated materials are promising candidates for future phase-change memory and other electronic device applications.

title: Truncate or Not? A Scaling Study of Looped Transformers with Truncated Backpropagation
abstract: Looped transformers reuse a shared block of layers to increase computational depth without increasing the number of trainable parameters. They are trained with backpropagation through time (BPTT). To save training compute, BPTT is often truncated to the last few loops, but truncation yields biased gradients that may weaken the benefit of looping. In this work, we study the value of truncation in looped transformer training in a systematic way: we jointly vary model size, training tokens, and forward and backward loop counts across nearly 600 training runs and fit a unified scaling law that captures the effects of looping and truncation through effective parameters. Despite the training-compute savings of truncation, our fitted law favors full BPTT when forward and backward loop counts are jointly optimized. In matched-compute runs, full BPTT through fewer loops consistently outperforms truncated settings of the same compute. The law further shows that at fixed model size, the compute-optimal loop count and training-token budget both grow with compute. When model size is also free, the law identifies two fully trained loops as the best looped setting. Experimentally, this setting achieves lower validation loss than the compute-optimal non-looped model with about 27% fewer non-embedding parameters and only 8% more training compute.
authors: Xuyuan Xiong;Siyu Chen;Zihan Shao;Yue Su;Weiyang Jin;Ping Luo;Zhuoran Yang;Xihui Liu

title: Towards instance-dependent regret optimality in Episodic MDPs with Posterior Sampling
abstract: We study regret minimization in finite-horizon episodic Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). While minimax-optimal algorithms are known, tractable approaches to instance-dependent optimality are still lacking. Motivated by this gap, we introduce $π_0$-PSRL, a variant of PSRL that uses posterior samples to decide when exploration is needed, while following a fixed reference policy $π_0$ during exploration episodes. This decouples the test for exploration, triggered when the sampled and empirical MDPs have different optimal policies, from the choice of the policy used to gather information. The resulting design addresses a limitation of standard PSRL, where the sampled optimal policy may not be the optimal choice for exploration. We prove instance-dependent regret bounds for $π_0$-PSRL, identifying the logarithmic exploration cost induced by $π_0$ and taking a step toward matching asymptotic lower bounds for episodic RL. Our proof techniques showcase a novel proof structure to derive problem-dependent regret bounds in episodic MDPs, and concentration results for Dirichlet random variables, that may be of independent interest.
authors: Victor Boone;Cyrille Kone;Waris Radji;Odalric-Ambrym Maillard;Dorian Baudry

title: Mediation and moderation in distance-based regression with triangular fuzzy data: simulation evidence and an application to academic performance
abstract: We study mediation and moderation in the distance-based regression model for triangular fuzzy responses, in which the center and transformed spreads of the response are linear in the components of fuzzy and crisp covariates. With a common design, componentwise least squares minimizes the unconstrained quadratic extension of the Yang--Ko distance on the transformed scale, for any choice of its shape parameters. Direct, indirect and total effects are defined separately for the center and the spreads of the response as plug-in contrasts on the fitted equations; when the mediator spreads are transformed and carry part of the indirect association, the product-of-coefficients rule no longer holds for the center. Moderation is modeled through triangular interaction regressors and tested with a Freedman--Lane permutation test. In simulations calibrated on real data, percentile bootstrap intervals for the indirect effects had coverage between 0.905 and 0.975, the empirical size of the indirect-effect tests did not exceed 0.085, and ignoring the paths through the mediator spreads biased the indirect effect on the center by 16 to 20\% at every sample size. The fuzzy model predicted better than a centers-only model only from $n=250$. In data on 91 university students collected in 2014, the indirect contrast through a course indicator accounted for about half of the model-based association between prior knowledge and the center of academic performance, the interactions of prior knowledge with sex and with motivation remained after a Holm adjustment, and the spreads of the covariates did not improve leave-one-out prediction.

title: Federated Community Detection in Bipartite Networks
abstract: We study federated spectral estimation when a large matrix is horizontally partitioned across servers that cannot share raw data. We propose FLICKER, a target-specific gradient-based power iteration that recovers a singular direction associated with a prescribed spectral target using only matrix-vector products on local blocks. Different target directions can be recovered independently and in parallel. We establish non-asymptotic convergence guarantees and provide a recursive grid-search procedure for spectral target selection. Building on FLICKER, we develop BiFLICKER for federated community detection in bipartite networks, together with a sequential projected variant for nearby or repeated singular directions. Under a sparse bipartite stochastic block model, we show that properly rescaled leading singular values from a reference server provide valid global targets, and that Sequential BiFLICKER achieves a vanishing misclustering rate and exact recovery under stronger sparsity conditions. Simulations show that BiFLICKER remains close to centralized spectral clustering and is more robust than existing federated spectral baselines when local sample sizes are small. On a LastFM user-artist network naturally partitioned by country, Sequential BiFLICKER attains an overall ARI of 0.94 against centralized clustering while revealing cross-country communities with distinct listening profiles.

title: Kinematic structure and age of a Scorpius--Centaurus subcomponent: implications for PDS 70 planetary system
abstract: PDS~70, the only system with two directly imaged protoplanets embedded in their natal disk, is a benchmark for giant-planet formation theory. Interpreting the planetary luminosities requires a precise age for the host star, but the widely adopted isochronal age of $5.4\pm1.0$~Myr is substantially younger than ages inferred for the Upper Centaurus--Lupus (UCL) population with which it is associated. We address this discrepancy by determining a new kinematic age for PDS~70 using radial velocities for 405 candidate members of the Scorpius--Centaurus T subcomponent from the Wide Field Spectrograph (WiFeS) on the ANU 2.3~m telescope, reducing uncertainties by a factor of $\sim5.5$ compared to \textit{Gaia}. %We supplement these measurements with H$α$ and lithium equivalent widths as youth diagnostics. We combine these with \textit{Gaia} DR3 astrometry in the \texttt{Chronostar} kinematic reconstruction framework to derive a posterior-weighted kinematic age of approximately $10$--$15$~Myr for all the T subcomponent stars, with a kinematic age of $\approx 12$--$16$~Myr for PDS 70, ruling out ages as young as the published isochronal estimate. At this kinematic age, PDS~70~\textit{b}'s (and to a lesser extent, PDS~70~\textit{c}'s) luminosity is incompatible with warm-start cooling tracks under current dynamical mass constraints. The most natural interpretation is that PDS~70~\textit{b} formed $\approx10.5$ Myr after its host star, and no less than $\approx7.7$ Myr after it.

title: Tuning-Free Tests for Treatment Effect Heterogeneity via Expectile Processes
abstract: This paper develops tuning-free tests for treatment-effect heterogeneity. By characterizing the null hypothesis as constancy of the expectile treatment-effect curve, we construct test statistics as continuous functionals of the mean-centered sample expectile process. We establish a uniform Bahadur representation, derive the asymptotic properties of the test statistics under the null and fixed alternatives, and show nontrivial power against local alternatives approaching the null at the $n^{-1/2}$ rate. For feasible inference, we develop a fast multiplier bootstrap that consistently approximates the nonpivotal null distribution while capturing the first-order effect of estimating the unknown common shift. The procedure is tuning-free, requiring no density or score-function estimation, bandwidth selection, or repeated refitting. The framework further incorporates a pointwise-studentized refinement and a covariate adjustment that reduces asymptotic variation without altering the population discrepancy. Monte Carlo comparisons with existing methods show generally reliable size control, competitive power, and substantial computational savings. An application to a large-scale water-conservation experiment illustrates the proposed tests.

title: Timing Skew Estimation of Time-Interleaved ADC based on Inter-Channel Correlations without Computing Derivative of Input Signal
abstract: Time-interleaved analog-to-digital converters (TI-ADCs) enable multi-gigasample-per-second throughput in high-speed applications, but sub-picosecond timing skews among interleaved channels introduce large spectral artifacts that degrade dynamic performance. To continuously track parametric drifts without interrupting normal operation, background calibration is required. However, extracting timing skews under unknown inputs is challenging, and many existing correlation-based methods rely on resource-heavy derivative filters that restrict input bandwidth. This article proposes a novel background timing-skew estimation technique for two-channel TI-ADCs that overcomes these limitations. Closed-form timing-skew expressions are derived using: (a) adjacent-channel cross-correlation combined with single-channel auto-correlation for sinusoidal inputs, and (b) adjacent-channel cross-correlation for Wide-Sense Stationary (WSS) inputs, specifically bandpass-filtered wideband noise and Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexed (OFDM) signals. The derived analytical models are validated through comprehensive simulations, offering an efficient framework for real-time background calibration in high-speed data converters.

title: Interfacial origin of magnetic compensation and topological-like Hall effect in crystalline lutetium iron garnet thin films.
abstract: Ferrimagnetic oxides such as rare-earth iron garnets (REIG) have emerged as essential components of spin-based devices owing to their high Curie temperatures, low Gilbert damping, and excellent insulating properties. Recently, REIGs have attracted immense interest for hosting robust chiral spin textures that can be potential information carriers in next-generation spintronic devices. Here we investigate the structural, chemical, and magnetic behaviour of single-crystal Lu3Fe5O12 (LuIG) thin films for different film thicknesses on a Gd3(Mg,Zr)Ga5O12(111) or SGGG(111) substrate. Our results demonstrate the presence of a 3 nm-thick Gd-rich LuIG layer at the LuIG/SGGG interface, which gives rise to a magnetic compensation temperature around 50 K. We further probe the anomalous Hall effect (AHE) in LuIG layers with an adjacent platinum ultrathin film. In addition to the magnetic compensation point, the AHE loops show pronounced nonmonotonic features, often attributed to the spin Hall topological-like Hall effect (SH-THE) and non-collinear spin textures arising from the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI). LuIG thickness-dependent AHE measurements reveal that the composition variation due to Gd diffusion breaks the inversion symmetry and could contribute to DMI. These findings shed light on fundamental understanding and engineering of the different interfaces of magnetic garnets for advanced spintronic device applications.

title: Ferroelastic domain wall driven glassy dynamics and photoresponse in a SrTiO$_3$ (111) two-dimensional electron gas
abstract: The (111) orientation of SrTiO$_3$ (STO)-based heterostructures has emerged as a versatile platform for two-dimensional electron gases (2DEGs), yet the influence of STO's polar ferroelastic domain-wall (DW) network on charge transport remains largely unexplored. Here we study AlO$_x$/STO (111) interfaces hosting 2DEGs of different carrier densities. In the lower-density 2DEG, low-temperature transport exhibits thermal hysteresis, slow resistance relaxation, cooling-rate dependence, and memory effects, signaling glasslike electron dynamics. The relaxation is strongly non-monotonic in temperature, increasing below $\sim$80 K, peaking near 25 K, and vanishing below $\sim$12 K, tracking the established evolution of the ferroelastic DW state of bulk STO rather than any electronic energy scale, which identifies the DW network as its origin. These signatures are absent in a second, more metallic interface with much higher carrier density, demonstrating that the electron-DW coupling can be tuned. We further show that polar DWs govern the photoresponse: the persistent photoconductivity rises sharply below $\sim$80 K, coinciding with the onset of DW polarity. Together, these results establish polar ferroelastic DWs as a carrier-density-tunable electronic degree of freedom in STO (111)-based 2DEGs, opening routes to manipulate 2DEG properties through topological defects.
authors: Jyotirmay Maity;Manav Beniwal;Pranab Hazra;Sumit Tomar;Srimanta Middey

title: Single-level reformulations for network pricing under Wardrop equilibrium with separable affine costs
abstract: We consider the problem of setting tolls on a subset of the arcs of a congested network so as to maximize the revenue of a network authority, anticipating that users route according to a Wardrop equilibrium. This problem is naturally cast as a bilevel program in which the leader sets tolls while the followers respond by choosing an equilibrium routing. We focus on the important special case of separable affine arc cost functions. Under this assumption, Wardrop equilibria admit Beckmann's convex characterization, from which we derive three new single-level reformulations of the bilevel problem, exploiting both Beckmann's formulation and its dual: an arc-based formulation, which we solve exactly, and two path-based formulations, solved by column-and-constraint generation. Beyond the reformulations, we further derive from Beckmann's potential an upper bound on the optimal revenue that can be used to certify optimality gaps across all formulations. An extensive computational study on instances derived from the Sioux Falls and Eastern Massachusetts networks compares our formulations with the recent mixed-integer nonlinear formulation of Beck, Labbé and Schmidt. The arc-based formulation solves substantially more instances to proven optimality (within a time limit of 1800 s) than this formulation and, unlike it, returns a feasible solution on every instance. It remains effective on the largest, 74-node network, on which the formulation of Beck et al. solves none. The magnitude of the upper bounds on the tolls proves to be a major driver of tractability: the genuinely hard core of the benchmark emerges once the regulatory cap on tolls is removed. The two path-based formulations, used as heuristics, return a solution within one percent of the optimum on every instance whose optimal value is known, often in seconds where exact formulations reach the time limit.

title: Keep the Lineages Alive: Diversity-Preserving SMC for Diffusion LLM Decoding
abstract: Inference-time sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) decoding can improve the reasoning accuracy of masked diffusion language models (diffusion LLMs) without post-training by resampling a population of partial generations according to a reward. Its effectiveness therefore depends on the resampling step, which must concentrate computation on promising candidates while retaining enough diversity to explore alternative reasoning paths. The reward can be internal, the decoder's own confidence on the committed prefix, or external, a process reward model scoring that prefix. Under either reward, multinomial resampling can disrupt this balance by duplicating high-weight particles and discarding lineages that may still reach a correct solution. The effective sample size (ESS) does not register this loss: multinomial resampling resets it to its maximum even as distinct lineages disappear. To retain such lineages, we introduce lineage-preserving SMC (LP-SMC), which combines Chopthin resampling with an input weight floor. Instead of equalizing weights, Chopthin bounds the ratio between the largest and smallest weights it returns and carries the unequal weights forward. The floor limits how far below the maximum a weight may fall before resampling so that lineages with low early weight keep a chance to recover. Across mathematical-reasoning and code-generation benchmarks on two base models, LP-SMC raises oracle coverage, the fraction of problems with at least one correct particle, in every setting, by 1.8 to 25.6 points, and raises end-to-end accuracy under a common reward-model selector in eleven of twelve settings, by up to 7.9 points on LLaDA-1.5 and 18.3 on Dream-7B. The coverage gain persists under the external reward model, which suggests that diversity-preserving resampling and the guidance signal contribute separately to inference-time search.

title: A Stress-Induced Tetragonal Distortion in K2OsCl6 under Pressure
abstract: The structural behaviour of cubic (Fm-3m) K2OsCl6 under compression was investigated to 35.4 GPa using angle-dispersive synchrotron powder X-ray diffraction. Upon increasing pressure, K2OsCl6 undergoes a sequence of structural transformations from the ambient-pressure cubic phase to a tetragonal (P4/mnc) phase above 9.5(3) GPa, followed by a transition to a monoclinic (P21/n) phase beginning at approximately 14.2 GPa. The tetragonal and monoclinic phases coexist over the pressure range 14.2-17.2 GPa, while the monoclinic phase is observed as the sole phase at 17.9 GPa and remains stable up to the maximum pressure investigated. Analysis of the diffraction profiles and unit-cell parameters indicates that the intermediate tetragonal structure is likely associated with stress-induced symmetry lowering rather than a distinct thermodynamic phase. This distortion, which is adequately described by the tetragonal P4/mnc space group, is attributed to non-hydrostatic deviatoric stresses arising from the pressure-transmitting medium. Equation-of-state analysis reveals a pronounced reduction in compressibility across the structural transitions, with the bulk modulus increasing from 26(2) GPa for the cubic phase to 71(3) GPa for the monoclinic phase. The pressure-induced structural sequence is analogous to that reported for related compounds such as K2IrCl6, although the transitions in K2OsCl6 occur at lower pressures. All structural transformations are reversible upon decompression.
authors: Neha Bura;Peije Zhang;Ganesh Bera;Catalin Popescu;Caleb J. Bennett;Brendan J. Kennedy;Daniel Errandonea

title: HP-GSBS: Accelerating greedy state boundary search with reusable interval statistics
abstract: Greedy State Boundary Search (GSBS) identifies transitions between relatively stable neural activity patterns in continuous recordings. Repeated template reconstruction and correlation evaluation make analyses across recordings and parameter settings computationally expensive. We present HP-GSBS, an open-source implementation that expresses the matching objective as additive interval contributions and computes t-distance from reusable correlation statistics. Streaming candidate reduction, sequential local refinement, and active-block reuse complement CPU, PyTorch CUDA, and Triton execution paths. Across seven controlled workloads with two input realizations each, median same-input speedups range from 154 to 1,730. All 168 optimized executions reproduce complete reference boundary histories and selected state counts, with a maximum absolute t-distance difference of $1.88\times10^{-11}$. Four publicly supplied BBBD EEG analysis matrices provide complementary cross-backend validation. A naturalistic fMRI application segments 4,230 angular-gyrus voxels in a group response and 16 participants; the 17 CPU fits total 213.10 seconds. Mean pairwise boundary alignment exceeds a circular-shift baseline, illustrating cohort-level use of the saved segmentations. Versioned results, recording-level parallelism, and optional low-memory execution support varied analysis scales. HP-GSBS connects an explicit mathematical reformulation of repeated computation to efficient and reproducible neural-state analysis.

title: A high-Galactic-altitude scattering screen: scintillation from Globular Cluster pulsar M53A
abstract: While known interstellar scattering screens are largely confined to the Galactic disk, the scattering properties of the circumgalactic medium (CGM) in the deep Galactic halo have remained unexplored. Using observations from the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST), we report the first detection of scintillation arcs in the secondary spectra of the high-latitude pulsar J1312+1810A (M53A). Under the 1D anisotropic and 2D isotropic thin-screen models considered here, the inferred scintillation screen distances are $12.8_{-3.5}^{+2.6}$ and $11.7_{-3.5}^{+2.8}$\,kpc, respectively. These model-dependent estimates correspond to Galactic heights of $12.6_{-3.5}^{+2.6}$ and $11.5_{-3.5}^{+2.7}$\,kpc, placing the candidate screen among the highest-altitude scattering structures inferred to date. The strong, time-variable scintillation asymmetry suggests substantial electron-density inhomogeneity within the screen. We speculate that this screen is associated with small-scale structures near the shock boundary of the northern eROSITA bubble. These results support the presence of discrete, inhomogeneous scattering structures deep within the Galactic halo, far beyond the regions where localized stellar feedback is typically concentrated, and highlight pulsar scintillation as a promising probe of small-scale ionized structures in the CGM.

title: Distributed Algorithm for Linear Least Squares Problems via Iteratively Preconditioning by Successive Over-Relaxation
abstract: This paper focuses on a novel distributed optimization algorithm for solving multi-agent linear least squares problems within a server-agent framework. Distributed methods are particularly suited to large-scale systems. The computational tasks can be partitioned across agents, while local data of one agent remain inaccessible to others. The proposed approach employs an iterative preconditioning scheme with the successive over-relaxation technique, leading to a substantial reduction of the number of iterations required for convergence, which presents a critical advantage where server-agent communication is costly. Theoretical convergence proof of the proposed algorithm is presented. Finally, benchmark problems are tested to demonstrate the performance comparison of the proposed approach over several prominent distributed methods.

title: Statistical Learning Theory for Direct Preference Optimization
abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) learns from pairwise preferences through a logistic objective whose score-difference parameterization follows the Bradley--Terry model. We study how failure of this modeling assumption limits DPO, distinguishing structural misspecification from limited model capacity and finite-sample estimation. Our main contribution is a characterization of structural approximation error through the triangle-curl of the preference log-odds, which vanishes exactly when preferences admit a Bradley--Terry representation. We upper bound the achievable excess logistic risk by a score-class approximation term and a triangle-curl term, and establish a lower bound proportional to triangle-curl under additional boundedness assumptions. For ReLU score models, including clipped models, we derive explicit approximation rates showing that increasing capacity can eliminate the score-approximation term while leaving the structural obstruction unchanged. We further establish finite-sample bounds for clipped empirical risk minimizers that separate network approximation, structural misspecification, and estimation error. We place these results within a surrogate-risk framework by identifying contextual preference accuracy (CPA) as a natural measure of agreement between preference judgments and changes in pairwise probability ratios relative to the reference policy. Standard logistic consistency and calibration results connect DPO's objective to this policy property and transfer our excess-risk upper bounds to CPA, without treating CPA as a complete measure of generated-response quality.

title: The Exact Boundary of Linear Optimality in Witsenhausen's Counterexample
abstract: Witsenhausen's counterexample has resisted a closed form solution for decades. However, it has remained unknown whether a mathematically tractable representation exists or not. In this paper, we solve this open problem, showing that the optimal policies are either linear or not tame and characterizing the exact regions where the two properties hold. Moreover, in the linear optimal region, we give an essentially unique closed form solution for the optimal policy, and show that no optimal first-stage policy is definable in any $o$-minimal expansion of the ordered real field in the nonlinear optimal region.

title: Dynamic Dual-Feedback Conformal Inference for Time Series Forecasting
abstract: Quantifying uncertainty in time series forecasting is particularly demanding because sequential data exhibit temporal dependence and are prone to distributional changes. Conformal inference has emerged as a powerful uncertainty quantification approach through the construction of prediction sets. Recent advances have introduced online conformal methods that adaptively adjust prediction thresholds through feedback mechanisms. However, the existing feedback mechanism typically relies solely on miscoverage indicators (actual feedback), whether the true label falls within the interval at each time step, while overlooking the empirical prediction threshold (estimated feedback) that is derived from the oracle conformal method. In this paper, we propose Dynamic Dual-feedback Conformal Inference (DDCI), which incorporates a dual-feedback mechanism consisting of actual feedback and estimated feedback. The former drives the primary adjustment of the intervals based on true observations, while the latter dampens excessive expansions or contractions by leveraging empirical thresholds from conformal inference during updates. By balancing these two signals, DDCI achieves more stable and narrower prediction intervals in sequential settings while maintaining near-nominal coverage in practice.

title: Adaptive Long-range UAV Flight Planning using Monte Carlo Search Trees
abstract: Long-range fixed-wing UAV missions require energy-efficient, dynamically feasible trajectories that can adapt online to evolving wind and airspace constraints. We present a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based framework that addresses this challenge by formulating mission planning as a finite-horizon Markov decision process incorporating aircraft kinematics, onboard energy dynamics, forecast wind fields, terrain, and time-varying no-fly zones. The MCTS planner searches over waypoint references generated by pre-stabilizing feedback controllers and a constraint-aware navigation field, yielding dynamically feasible trajectories. Simulation results from medical delivery scenarios show that the MCTS planner outperforms baseline geometric planners and population-based optimization algorithms. Moreover, the MCTS planner can be used in closed-loop to rapidly compute safe diversion trajectories under evolving constraints.
comment: Authors' accepted manuscript. Published in AIAA, DOI: 10.2514/1.G010042

title: Fair Regression under Approximate Demographic Parity
abstract: Exact demographic parity requires the same prediction distribution across sensitive groups. In regression, this can be too restrictive and reduce predictive accuracy. We instead bound every pairwise Wasserstein distance between group-specific prediction distributions by a chosen tolerance, allowing the groups to differ while keeping fairness tunable. On the real line, the prediction and constrained transport problems have the same infimum. If the transport problem attains this value and suitable Monge maps exist, a deterministic transport-form predictor realizes it. Under a standard one-dimensional condition, the problem becomes a bounded quantile optimization that is convex when the conditional expected loss is convex in prediction. Under squared loss with two positively weighted groups, the $W_1$, $W_2$, and $W_\infty$ constraints yield soft-thresholding, shrinkage, and clipping. Under the stated conditions, we establish rates for the known-cost plug-in estimator. When the cost is unavailable, we describe an observed-loss computational proxy. Synthetic and California 2018 ACS studies illustrate the tunable fairness-accuracy trade-off and distinguish calibration feasibility from held-out fairness and accuracy.
authors: Weiwei Wang;Xianyang Zhang;Raymond K. W. Wong

title: Computation of Free Boundary Minimal Tori via Extremal Steklov Eigenvalues
abstract: Fraser and Schoen showed that the first Steklov eigenfunctions of a metric maximizing the length-normalized first eigenvalue of a surface with boundary define a free boundary minimal immersion into a Euclidean ball. We develop a method for this extremal problem on surfaces of genus one with $b$ boundary components and use it to compute free boundary minimal tori for $b \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 8\}$. By uniformization, the problem is a nonsmooth maximization over the modulus of a flat torus, the centers and radii of $b$ removed disks, and a boundary weight. The eigenvalues are computed with doubly periodic layer potentials, all derivatives follow from a single formula for the underlying pencil of boundary integral operators, and the coalescence of eigenvalues at a maximizer is handled by a two-stage nonsmooth method. The Lagrange multiplier matrix that certifies first-order stationarity rescales the eigenfunctions into the free boundary minimal immersion. For $b=1$, the supremum is the Fraser--Schoen bound $4π$, attained by branched double covers of the disk; the embedded torus with connected boundary of Carlotto, Franz, and Schulz is a saddle point, which answers their question whether it maximizes the eigenvalue in the negative. For $b \geq 2$ the largest values correspond to free boundary minimal tori in \mathbb{B}^5 and \mathbb{B}^6; the surfaces of Folha, Pacard, and Zolotareva, two disks joined by a central neck and $b$ equatorial necks, are maximizers within their symmetry class but saddle points of the full problem, with values increasing toward $4π$ as $b \to \infty$.

title: The DARWIN Project: Cosmological Simulations of Galaxy Formation down to Dwarf Scales in Diverse Environments
abstract: We present the DARWIN project, a suite of cosmological simulations with RAMSES to study dwarf-galaxy formation and evolution across diverse environments. DARWIN-1 is a full-box simulation in a cubic volume of $(65.5\,{\rm cMpc})^3$ with a minimum cell size of 500pc, while DARWIN-2 comprises zoom-in simulations of 24 field regions and a Milky Way analog connected to a filament, reaching 62.5pc resolution. The simulations employ baryonic physics tailored to their aims. For DARWIN-2, we include radiative transfer in three photon energy bands to trace hydrogen and helium ionization. DARWIN-1 reproduces the cosmic star formation rate density and galaxy stellar mass functions reasonably well at $z>1$. Both simulations broadly reproduce observed stellar mass-halo mass relations, chemical abundances, star-formation surface densities, and black hole-galaxy scaling relations. At lower redshift, DARWIN-1 shows an excess in the number density of massive galaxies, although the inferred stellar content of massive halos depends on the definition of galaxy stellar mass. Other systematic differences arise from spatial resolution, feedback efficiency, and environmental selection. To facilitate comparison with observations, we generate mock images using the radiative transfer codes SKIRT and Powderday. We also explore a machine-learning approach to mitigate resolution-driven biases in the dwarf galaxy properties of DARWIN-1 using the higher-resolution DARWIN-2 simulations. The DARWIN simulation suite therefore provides a comprehensive numerical framework for studying the formation, evolution, and internal physics of dwarf galaxies in a cosmological context.

title: Detection Augmented Learning In Non-Stationary Bandit Environments
abstract: We study the problem of non-stationary bandits without knowledge of the environmental changes. We propose Detection Augmented Learning (DAL) a black-box paradigm that comprises three modular components: a bandit algorithm, a change detector, and a forced exploration schedule. This modular design enables its applicability across a broad spectrum of bandit problems, from classical to highly structured settings. First, we provide theoretical insights into DAL's strong empirical performance: a single regret bound shows that DAL transfers the regret of its stationary input to the piecewise stationary setting, attaining or improving the best known bounds in every setting considered. We further identify conditions under which DAL performs well in drifting environments. Then, we showcase DAL's practical performance and versatility through extensive experimentation in which DAL consistently surpasses all state-of-the-art methods, both prior-free and prior-based, across diverse non-stationary scenarios in nine bandit settings. Finally, we investigate the effectiveness of the forced exploration and show that a bandit-driven strategy improves performance and shortens detection delay.
authors: Argyrios Gerogiannis;Yu-Han Huang;Subhonmesh Bose;Venugopal V. Veeravalli

title: Crystal Structure Based Graph Neural Network And LLM Multi-Modal Approach for Material Magnetic Ordering Prediction
abstract: AI/ML models are useful for the prediction of materials' properties. Recently, there has been great progress in developing Neural Network models to predict the properties of solids, molecules, and crystals, avoiding expensive and time-consuming laboratory testing. This study presents a novel AI/ML-based multi-modal approach to predict material magnetic ordering using material crystal structure information as input to a Graph Neural Network model (GNN) and semantic text descriptions of the material's properties and structure as input to a Large Language Model (LLM), before performing information fusion of the GNN and LLM outputs to predict material magnetic ordering in four classes (Non-magnetic, Ferromagnetic, Antiferromagnetic, Ferrimagnetic). The model is trained, validated, and tested on a dataset which is a combination of Materials Project dataset, Magndata dataset, and a set of uranium compounds with magnetic ordering determined in laboratory testing, with an 80/10/10 (training/validation/testing) data split. The proposed GNN and LLM multi-modal approach achieves better overall accuracy than both the standalone GNN and LLM approaches with three fusion strategies.

title: A Benders decomposition approach for hierarchical k-medoids
abstract: We study a hierarchical clustering problem formulated as a sum of k-medoids objectives. This problem is related to the multi-period p-median problem, but instead of having nested facilities, we consider a hierarchy of nested assignments. We present two Benders formulations from the p-median literature and show how the obtained nested p-median solutions can be converted into hierarchical k-medoids solutions. We validate our methods on various instances. First, we show on small-scale instances that a standard Benders decomposition approach achieves speedups of up to three orders of magnitude over an existing branch-and-price method, while producing hierarchical k-medoids solutions that are at most 5% away from optimality. Second, we present an aggregated Benders heuristic that can handle instances with more than 13,000 observations.

title: Corrected Block Sparse Spectral Optimization: Exact Models, Finite Identification, and Local Dynamics
abstract: The block generalized-power method pairs threshold-based support selection with inexpensive Stiefel updates, but the standard block formulation conflates two nonequivalent objectives and leaves inactive components, threshold ties, and post-selection refitting ill-specified. We rebuild the model from the primal. Eliminating each loading column from the normalized loading-ball problem gives a sum of soft-thresholded Euclidean norms (A-SUM); the squared-threshold objective in common use arises from a quadratic lift (A-SQ). We prove both identities, exhibit a two-component instance whose maximizers disagree, and specify explicit conventions for zero-response columns, ties, rank deficiency, and mask-before-refit. For A-SQ we separate the historical full-polar iteration from a safeguarded Riemannian ascent and prove, for the latter, whole-sequence convergence via a sufficient-ascent lemma, a relative-error lemma, and the Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz property, which applies because the soft-threshold objective and the Stiefel constraint are semi-algebraic. A strict threshold margin then forces finite identification of the support and sign pattern. The post-identification map is ordinary power iteration on the active covariance for a rank-one hard threshold, and the Frechet derivative of a coupled polar map for component-specific supports; a radius-based safe-screening rule follows from the same local analysis. Planted-spike experiments match the predicted identification time and local rates. On modern-AI panels (GPT-2 residual stream, ViT CLS stream, Pitprops) the thresholded block-sparse components match dense PCA on reconstruction and improve on it in monosemanticity and class specialisation. On three native-label scRNA datasets (Zheng17 FACS-sorted PBMCs, 68k donor-A with FACS-correlated labels, Tabula Muris) A-SQ beats dense PCA on cluster-recovery AMI by +0.023 to +0.044 at matched sparsity.

title: Velocity-resolved Ionization Mapping of the Broad-line Region. II. Signatures of Eccentric Broad-line Regions from a Quantitative Photoionization-Based Model
abstract: Velocity-resolved reverberation mapping (RM) is one of the most powerful tools for probing the geometry and kinematics of the broad-line region in active galactic nuclei. However, its interpretation may be non-unique, as similar velocity-delay signatures can arise from different combinations of BLR geometry and kinematics. To address this degeneracy, this series of studies develops velocity-resolved ionization mapping (IM) as a complementary technique. In this second paper of the series, we construct photoionization-based BLR models to quantitatively demonstrate the diagnostic power of the joint RM+IM framework. We calculate local \ha\ and \hb\ emissivities with Cloudy, couple them with disk-like BLR models, and generate synthetic velocity-dependent line fluxes, lags, and Balmer decrements. The model reproduces the observed anti-correlation between the integrated BD and the incident ionizing continuum, with scatter naturally introduced by reverberation delays. We show that a virialized elliptical BLR can produce diverse velocity-delay maps and velocity-resolved lags that mimic RM signatures commonly attributed to virialized motion, inflow, or outflow. In contrast, the velocity-resolved BD is sensitive to the symmetry of the BLR gas distribution, providing a key diagnostic for distinguishing eccentric geometry from non-virial motions. Through proof-of-concept comparisons with one double-peaked and one single-peaked AGN, we show that an elliptical-disk BLR can simultaneously reproduce the observed line profiles, velocity-resolved lags, and velocity-resolved BDs. These results provide a quantitative basis for IM, support the presence of eccentric BLR structures in AGNs, and demonstrate the potential of joint RM+IM analyses to break the BLR geometry-kinematics degeneracy.
authors: Jiancheng Wu;Hai-Cheng Feng;Sha-Sha Li;Qingwen Wu;Xinwu Cao

title: Zeeman Quantum Geometry of the Layer Pseudo-spin
abstract: Two-dimensional layers coupled by position-dependent interlayer tunnelling host a layer pseudo-spin whose polarization is a controllable internal degree of freedom. We introduce the quantum geometry of this layer pseudo-spin: a mixed tensor formed from the interband Berry connection and the layer matrix element, which governs the response to an oscillating in-plane electric field. Because the layer pseudo-spin is an Ising-type scalar invariant under threefold rotation, its selection rules differ from those of a pseudovector spin. In a minimal two-band model, the layer-pseudo-spin quantum metric and Zeeman--Berry curvature are nonzero, while their zone integrals vanish. An in-plane drive therefore leaves the spatially averaged polarization unchanged at linear order but imprints a moiré-periodic intracell pattern, directly imageable by layer-resolved tunnelling. For twisted MoTe$_2$ bilayer, we quantify the local dipole modulation and identify the rectified, helicity-odd, and third-harmonic channels through which a net response appears at higher order.

title: A Unifying View of Distributionally Robust Optimization for Probability Smoothing via Maximum Entropy
abstract: The probability smoothing problem seeks estimators that assign positive probability to all categories, including those unobserved in a finite sample. In our previous work, we established that the estimator derived from distributionally robust optimization (DRO) with a $q$-norm ambiguity set ($q$-DRO) satisfies the axioms of Positivity, Symmetry, and Order Preservation, while relaxing the rigid Ratio Preservation axiom characterizing Laplace smoothing. In this paper, we observe that Symmetry itself imposes a strong constraint: it forces all unobserved categories to receive identical probability regardless of their relation to observed categories. Motivated by this observation, we study DRO with an optimal transport ambiguity set (OT-DRO), which incorporates inter-category dissimilarities through a cost matrix and thereby enables structure-respecting smoothing. We derive a tractable dual reformulation of OT-DRO as an empirical cross-entropy minimization with a Lipschitz-type penalty on the log-probability vector, and we identify an explicit threshold on the robustness radius at which the optimal estimator reduces to the uniform distribution, paralleling the threshold established for $q$-DRO. We then show, through Sion's minimax theorem, that DRO for probability smoothing over any compact convex ambiguity set that contains a strictly positive distribution is equivalent to entropy maximization over that set. This unifying perspective explains the parallel threshold structure in $q$-DRO and OT-DRO.

title: Fully First-Order Optimization for Implicit Multilevel Compositions via Recursive Perturbations
abstract: We study optimization over a finite composition of implicit response maps generated by smooth potentials with strongly monotone signed gradients. This class includes chains mixing strongly convex minimization and strongly convex--strongly concave saddle responses. We propose a fully first-order method based on recursively perturbed response solves. The central issue is stability under inexact response solves: a downstream adjoint error changes the perturbation vector of the next upstream perturbed problem. We establish coupled bounds for the forward response errors and backward errors in the scaled response differences whose coefficients remain bounded as the perturbation parameter $δ$ decreases. A triangular Lyapunov construction combines these bounds with the $O(δ)$ bias of the exact perturbation estimator. For the warm-started method with finitely many inner iterations, this gives $\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\|\nablaΦ(x^k)\|^2 \leq O(K^{-1})+O(δ^2).$ Thus, for fixed problem data and finite depth, $δ=O(ε)$ yields an $O(ε^{-2})$ outer-iteration dependence. For strongly convex minimization chains, we also derive condition-number-dependent first-order oracle complexity bounds.

title: A LATE-Targeting Experimental Design for Multi-Arm RCTs
abstract: We study the design of multi-arm experiments that identify local average treatment effects under imperfect compliance. With three or more arms, conventional randomization fails to identify margin-specific effects even under strong extensions of monotone compliance. A choice-theoretic analysis unifies these extensions and motivates a two-stage design: subjects report a preferred arm and are randomized conditional on it. If treatment is confined to the assigned or reported arm, one-sided noncompliance is restored conditional on the report, identifying the effect between the two arms for their compliers. Any tilt of assignment toward the reported arm makes reporting the favorite strictly optimal, and no assignment lottery can strictly elicit the ranking below the favorite. We then discuss the design's applicability and feasibility in relation to the choice model.

title: The Forward/Inverse Duality of Controlled Emergence:A Computational Design Program from Explanation to Engineering
abstract: The macroscopic capabilities of intelligent systems arise from the local interactions of many simple units. When such systems are deployed in the real world, their behaviour must nevertheless be constrained, leaving designers caught between releasing adaptability and preventing loss of control, yet without formal tools to resolve the dilemma. This paper proposes a unified research program for controlled emergence that restates this tension as a pair of dual problems: the forward problem explains macroscopic behaviour from local rules, and the inverse problem solves for controllable rules and readout mechanisms from a desired target. We take an augmented quintuple as the formal object shared by both ends, and decompose ``engineering'' into three independently measurable coordinates: controllability, reproducibility, and degree of formalizability. On this basis we give three testable working hypotheses (critical scale; the cooperation and trade-off between constraint and adaptability; minimal constraint) and one feasibility criterion, which reduce inverse design from unconstrained optimization to interval checking. The program takes explicit failure boundaries as its premise, does not pursue complete control, and always preserves the system's room for self-organization. The reduced pilot experiment attached to this paper serves only to verify the executability of the research protocol and does not constitute a statistical test of the working hypotheses. This design language generalizes to multi-agent artificial intelligence, the industrial internet, and emergency response systems, all of which must confront emergence and controllability at once.

title: Autonomous adaptive spectral analysis with an LLM agent for self-driving laboratories
abstract: Self-driving laboratories accelerate materials exploration through autonomous closed-loop integration of synthesis, characterization, and next-experiment selection. However, characterization does not always directly provide the target property; measured spectra or images often require automated analysis to extract quantitative descriptors based on physically motivated assumptions and predefined criteria. Such procedures can fail for measurements outside these criteria, requiring a decision on whether a reliable value can be recovered or no numerical value should be reported. Here, we implemented an autonomous adaptive spectral-analysis agent using a large language model (LLM) to supervise a deterministic numerical-analysis routine. For each spectrum, the agent executes the predefined analysis script and assesses the result using the measured spectrum and fitting diagnostics. Valid results are accepted unchanged, recoverable failures are reanalyzed through bounded adjustments of predefined fitting parameters, and NaN (not a number) is returned when no scientifically defensible value can be obtained. We evaluated the workflow on optical transmittance spectra from 203 epitaxial beta-Ga2O3 films grown during a previously reported self-driving thin-film growth campaign. The predefined optical analysis script returned Urbach energy, an optical-quality metric, for 183 spectra and failed for 20. The agent retained those 183 values and evaluated 20 exception cases, recovering 16 through bounded parameter adjustments and returning NaN for 4 when the spectral evidence did not support a reliable Urbach tail. The audit records captured spectral features, parameter changes, and rationale for each decision. These results demonstrate autonomous scientific exception handling by an LLM agent while leaving quantitative property extraction to deterministic numerical analysis.

title: Upper bounds on the number of images produced by point-mass lenses at different distances
abstract: If a light source is sequentially lensed by $n$ intervening point-mass lenses at distinct distances, the number of isolated images for a generic source position cannot be greater than $2\cdot 3^{n-1}$. If lensing shear is present in each lens plane, the image counts could be as large as $4^n$, however. For a general multi-plane point-mass lens system, we also devise the recurrence for the BKK bound on the image counts, which is strictly less than Perry's bound due to the resultant degree for $n\ge 2$. None the less, this bound is still quadratic in the number of lenses on each plane, so is likely to overestimate the true sharp bound, which is expected to grow linearly with the number of lenses.

comment: 9 pages (including 2 separate pages for two appedices); no figure

title: Linear Regression with Common Unobserved Heterogeneity
abstract: We study inference on common slope parameters in linear panel models with two-way unobserved heterogeneity. In linear regression, bias arises from unobserved heterogeneity that is shared between the residual and the covariates. Our common unobserved heterogeneity (CUH) estimator targets this common variation directly: it searches over functionals of the residualised outcome for variation that also resides in the covariates, and seeks to further project out only bias-inducing variation. This makes the estimator less sensitive to weak outcome factors while avoiding the complete removal of exogenous variation in covariates that is unrelated to the confounding heterogeneity. We develop a weak-factor theory based on a singular-value strength index and establish $\sqrt{NT}$-asymptotic normality of the cross-fitted CUH estimator. Under homoskedastic errors, its asymptotic variance is no larger than that of a common correlated effects factor estimator. Simulations and empirical applications illustrate the resulting bias--variance trade-off and the gains from selectively removing common variation.

title: Divergence based Ranked Preference Alignment for LLMs
abstract: Alignment of large language models typically relies on pairwise preference feedback, though ranked feedback can capture more comprehensive information across multiple responses within a single annotation. However, ranked-preference alignment is underexplored in practice compared to simpler pairwise approaches, potentially resulting in suboptimal behavior. Concurrently, recent research has conceptualized large language model alignment objectives as divergence estimators between aligned (preferred) and unaligned (less-preferred) response distributions, resulting in a family of objectives with an interpretable theoretical foundation and strong empirical performance. This work unifies these perspectives by introducing $f$-RPO, a $f$-divergence objective for ranked preference optimization that extends divergence-based alignment to ranked feedback and recovers pairwise preference alignment as a special case. Our theoretical analysis establishes rank-order consistency, showing that $f$-RPO preserves the underlying preference ordering at convergence. Empirical results indicate that total-variation and reverse-KL variants of the proposed objective consistently outperform ranked-alignment baselines in both ranking and generation quality across Qwen, Llama, & Gemma models ranging from 0.5B to 8B parameters.

title: Reading Between the Lines: How Much Information Remains After Fitting a Stellar Spectrum?
abstract: What if we could model 100% of a stellar spectrum? Modern surveys infer stellar properties by comparing observed spectra with synthetic models, yet even the best fits leave structured residuals. We analyse 7087 GALAH survey spectra and ask what information remains after subtracting each best-fitting model. Across 13927 pixels, 4.5% of residuals exceed $3σ$, far above 0.3% expected from Gaussian noise. We map the amplitude, significance, sign, and recurrence of these residuals and identify 380 significant regions. Comparison with stellar atlases, line lists, diffuse interstellar bands, and sky diagnostics links most regions to plausible causes: 62% are candidate line-strength or line-profile mismatches, while others trace missing or unidentified lines, interstellar absorption, sky emission, or broader reduction structure. We then train data-driven models on the residual spectra themselves. Residual-only models recover $T_\mathrm{eff}$ to 80-150 K and [Fe/H] to 0.059-0.086 dex, depending on sample quality, and retain weaker, partly indirect information about elemental abundances. Extinction-related coefficients recover the strongest known interstellar features, whereas chromospheric activity leaves plausible Balmer-line signatures but is not recovered robustly out of sample. Most strikingly, the residual flux in 6% of wavelength pixels that were synthesised but excluded from the GALAH DR4 optimisation recovers stellar labels almost as well as the full residual spectrum and better than the remaining 94% alone. Residuals are therefore not merely imperfections to discard: they map missing line data, incomplete physics, unfitted astrophysical components, and observational systematics. Reading between the lines turns one spectroscopist's trash into another one's treasure, and provides a practical route towards extracting more of the information already present in stellar spectra.

title: Reinforcement learning on the EPRI AI-ccelerating Unit Commitment benchmark: diagnosing over-commitment and guiding MILP with learned policies
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly proposed as a fast solver for unit commitment (UC), but standalone agents remain far more expensive than mixed-integer linear programming (MILP). In the first study of RL on the 51-generator, 72-hour benchmark of the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) AI-ccelerating Unit Commitment competition, we trace this gap to the agents' own exploration, close most of it, and show that the resulting policy can accelerate an exact solver. In every configuration tested, Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) and an action-branching Deep Q-Network (DQN) trained from scratch committed about twice the units of a thermal-only MILP optimum, at 39-64% higher cost, whereas a merit-order rule came within 1.6-7% (10-24% when unserved energy is priced). When each unit's decision is sampled independently, spare units insure against random de-commitments. Consistent with this, injecting exploration noise during fine-tuning enlarged a lean policy's fleet, a reward without shaping terms did not remove the over-commitment, and under their training noise the agents outperformed the rule subjected to comparable noise. Imitating the MILP solutions and fine-tuning conservatively brought PPO within 2.6% of the optimum, and these policies had the lowest penalised cost of any evaluated (about 5%). Fixing the fine-tuned policy's confident decisions made the MILP 3.8-8.5 times faster within 0.10-0.25% of the best solution, with a smaller worst case than an imitation-only policy fixing as many variables (1.1% against 8.9%). Because dispatch method and benchmark scope alone shift the reported optimality ratio by up to 3.6% and 9%, we propose a reporting protocol.

title: Stability and Stabilization of Kronecker-Sum-Coupled Multilinear Systems
abstract: Coupled dynamical systems with multi-dimensional state structures arise in many applications such as spatiotemporal processes and large-scale interconnected systems. However, existing studies primarily focus on matrix-based coupled systems or tensor-based dynamical systems without couplings. The properties of coupled tensor-based systems remain largely unexplored. In this article, we study Kronecker-sum-coupled multilinear systems under the transform-based tensor product framework. We establish fundamental tensor spectral properties showing that stability can be characterized through lower-dimensional subsystem dynamics together with slice-wise matrix stability in the transform domain. We further develop optimization conditions for state-feedback stabilization and show that the stabilization problem can be decomposed into independent subsystem problems. Finally, we analyze the computational complexity of the proposed framework and demonstrate its substantial computational advantages over unfolding-based approaches using both synthetic systems and multi-inertia motor systems.
authors: Ziqin He;Ruoying Wang;Shenghan Mei;Yidan Mei;Xin Mao;Can Chen

title: The Next Generation Virgo Cluster Survey (NGVS). XXIX. Demography of Nuclear Star Clusters
abstract: Nuclear star clusters (NSCs) provide insights into processes shaping galaxy cores. We use deep $u^*giz$ CFHT imaging from the Next Generation Virgo Cluster Survey (NGVS) to study NSCs in Virgo cluster galaxies. Our parent sample consists of 3680 certain, likely or possible cluster members spanning more than six orders of magnitude in stellar mass. Using a self-consistent classification framework, we identify 1144 candidate nucleated galaxies: 804 high-confidence NSCs and 340 lower-confidence candidates. This is the largest and most uniform NSC catalog for any environment studied to date. We explore the nucleation fraction, $f_{\rm nuc}$, as a function of stellar mass, morphology and environment. Consistent with previous studies, we find stellar mass a key factor driving nucleation probability. However, host-galaxy morphology is also important, with the peak of the $f_{\rm nuc}$ distribution occurring at progressively lower masses as one moves from later to earlier morphological types. We interpret this shift as evidence that the more extended structures of late-type galaxies reduce the efficiency of GC inspiral at fixed stellar mass, while gas-rich secular processes and central star formation may contribute increasingly to NSC growth at higher masses. Environment plays a smaller role, with only a slight enhancement in high-density regions. We characterize the nonlinear relationship between NSC stellar mass and host-galaxy mass, and assess the role of selection effects. We conclude that NSC formation is best explained by a hybrid scenario, with inspiraling star clusters and in situ star formation contributing, and their relative importance dictated primarily by galaxy mass.
