title: New Modelling and Solution Frameworks for Multiple Objectives, Decomposability and Impulsivity in Continuous-time Markov Decision Processes
abstract: Impulsive control, in the context of continuous-time Markov decision processes (CTMDPs), refers to actions that instantaneously update the state of the process, leading to theoretical complications. Previous work has overcome these complications, but at the expense of approachability and ease of implementation: those models are mathematically complex and incompatible with pre-existing solution methods. This paper presents an alternative formulation of impulsive control for CTMDPs that is easier to employ in the modelling of real-world problems and can be solved by pre-existing solution methods. This formulation is then extended to allow for multiple objectives and decomposability. A decomposition-based heuristic method is developed that leverages Dantzig-Wolfe decomposition to find approximate Pareto fronts for large multi-objective decomposable impulsive CTMDPs. The modelling framework and solution methodology are applied to a dynamic maintenance problem to demonstrate their computational efficiency, solution space coverage, and solution quality.

title: Uncovering the origin of complex velocity distributions in edge-on disc galaxies
abstract: Stellar line-of-sight velocity distributions are a powerful tool for studying galaxy kinematics and formation history, with multiple-peaked LOSVDs often indicating the presence of complex kinematic components. We extract stellar LOSVDs across the disc of a simulated spiral galaxy viewed edge-on, and study how often and why we see multiple-peaked LOSVDs. We find that the multiple-peaked LOSVDs are mainly found close to the midplane because they result from the presence of spiral arms. This is not because the spiral arms have significantly different kinematics to the disc, but because they correspond to over-densities. Variations in the number of arms present along a line-of-sight create variations in the number of peaks in LOSVDs. This can be used to quantify the strength of the spiral arms above the midplane, and how the thickness of spiral arms vary across the disc. We find that the commonly used fourth order Gauss-Hermite moment, $h_4$, is negative in the regions where there are multiple-peaked LOSVDs, and hence traces spiral arms. Finally, we discuss the observability of the multiple-peaked regions and their associated $h_4$ measurements with current integral field spectrographs. We find that the spectral resolution of MUSE might not be high enough to uncover multiple peaks in LOSVDs when they result from spiral arms, but should allow for identification of the regions of negative $h_4$. On the other hand, higher resolution spectrographs like KOALA and WEAVE may be able to recover multiple peaks in LOSVDs, representing a promising avenue for characterising spiral arms in edge-on disc galaxies.
authors: Sophie Townson;Marie Martig;Robert J. J. Grand;Prashin Jethwa;Jesús Falcón-Barroso;Timothy A. Davis

title: The Cost of Executability: Temporal Margins for Continuous-Time Multi-Agent Path Finding under Closed-Loop Control
abstract: Multi-agent path finding (MAPF) solvers are evaluated on the schedules they produce, not on how well those schedules can be executed. Specifically, continuous-time optimal solvers can achieve even lower cost than their discrete counterparts by scheduling agents with near-zero temporal/spatial separation, and by exploiting graphs with higher connectedness; however, such schedules may prove hard to execute under a realistic controller. We integrate AOC-CBS, an anytime-optimal continuous-time MAPF solver, into a fleet coordination framework in which each agent tracks its timed path using model predictive control, and we evaluate the resulting system on congested MovingAI benchmark instances with 21 to 40 agents. Without intervention, only a fraction of the instances complete execution. We then apply T-robustness by adding a time-margin, i.e., a minimum temporal gap between agents at shared locations, as well as spatial inflation of the agent footprint. Increasing either margin raises execution success, for a relatively small increase in the schedule's sum-of-costs; it also improves how closely agents adhere to the schedule: when tracking each agent's position throughout execution and comparing it against the position it should occupy according to the schedule, the mean discrepancy falls significantly as the margin increases. In general, the two margins have different effects; temporal margin decreases deviation, giving the controller room to stay on schedule. Spatial margin affects deviation less and instead increases the clearance between agents, so that the same deviation no longer leads to a blocking stall. They are nonetheless substitutes rather than complements: spatial inflation is almost free in schedule cost, but its effect on execution success is small and does not compound with a temporal margin already in place.

title: Synergistic Self-Driven Nanoconfinement and Dynamical Heterogeneity in Deeply Supercooled "No Man's Land" Water
abstract: The 150--235 K ``no man's land'' (NML) of deeply supercooled water is a highly debated regime where rapid crystallization hinders experimental observation of the hypothesized liquid-liquid phase transition. Using TIP4P/2005 molecular dynamics simulations, we uncover a structurally and dynamically heterogeneous state at ambient pressure that exhibits novel physical features. Our results demonstrate that this low-density state ($ρ\approx 0.925$ g/cm$^3$) is a unique supercooled liquid, distinct from both glassy and spinodal states. Specifically, it emerges as a stable, structurally arrested phase driven by a self-generated ``soft skeleton'' of nanoclusters. This network forms an intrinsic nanoporous structure that imposes nanoconfinement on the remaining fluid, proving that NML confinement can be an entirely self-driven phenomenon. Finally, we resolve the temperature-dependent, nonlinear behavior of density and compressibility, highlighting a structurally driven anomaly that clarifies the thermodynamics of deep supercooling. Collectively, this work provides a transformative structural framework for understanding the anomalous nature of water within the NML.

title: Polaritonic self-hybridized critical coupling by Brillouin zone folding induced quasi-bound states in the continuum in bulk WS2 metasurfaces
abstract: Maximizing the absorption of exciton-polaritons in transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) under critical coupling conditions is crucial for developing high-efficiency polariton-based photodetectors, solar cells, and perfect absorbers. Here, we propose a polaritonic critical self-hybridized coupling between Brillouin zone folding driven quasi-bound states in the continuum (BZF-QBIC) mode and A excitons in a bulk WS2 metasurface. This polaritonic critical coupling shows robust behavior with respect to the asymmetric parameters of the involved BZF-QBIC mode, in contrast to the asymmetry-sensitive conventional QBIC-based critical coupling. By changing the height of WS2 metasurfaces, we observe a typical anti-crossing behavior with a Rabi splitting of 246.5 meV. Moreover, the maximum absorption value of 0.5 for exciton-polaritons is achieved at the polaritonic critical coupling condition. The large population of excitons provided by bulk WS2 is essential for achieving polaritonic critical coupling and can further enhance polaritonic absorption. This work enables the realization of robust, high-absorption self-hybridized polaritonic critical coupling in TMDCs, and further expedite their applications in high-absorption low-dimensional polaritonic devices.
authors: Kuidong Wang;Xiongwei Guo;Fu Liu;Jinhai Si;Xun Hou

title: Radial-Angular Resolution Framework for Near-Field Communications
abstract: Near-field beamfocusing confines radiated power into a localized three-dimensional focal spot, making the analytical characterization of radial and angular resolution critical for sixth-generation (6G) multi-user systems, yet existing models treat the focal resolution as a fixed geometric outcome rather than a tunable design variable. Based on the Angular Representation (ASR) approach, this paper presents a resolution framework to design contiguous focal regions across both the radial and angular domain for steered multi-user systems. By extending the definition of a tunable inter-beam overlap $ρ$, we derive closed-form expressions for the radial and angular focal boundaries and extents, alongside the steering-dependent minimum focal distance $d_{0,\text{min}}$ and maximum steering angle $θ_{\text{max}}$. Using these boundaries, iterative synthesis algorithms are developed to construct uniform and non-uniform radial and angular beam arrangements. Finally, by analyzing both isolated and joint radial-angular configurations, we quantify the fundamental trade-offs between $ρ$, achievable user capacity, inter-user interference, and system sum-rate across varying steering angles.

title: Routes planning in a condominium company using mathematical optimization
abstract: This work focuses on planning daily routes for a group of employees of a condominium company. Given a set of employees and a set of customers with pre-scheduled visits, we want to build doubly-open routes to guarantee visits to all customers, ensuring that each customer is visited by an employee with the appropriate skills to carry out the required activity. The travel times between customers and the service time in each customer are known. The problem includes time windows for visiting customers, each employee has a maximum working time, and the daily working period is between 9 AM and 6:30 PM. The routes respect the lunch break period if they extend from morning to afternoon, which means that lunch break can be avoided if the route is fully completed in the morning or in the afternoon. The aim is to minimize the distance covered by all routes with a penalty for including lunch breaks. The distances and times between customers are collected via an API to Microsoft Azure; and the solutions are then displayed on Bing Maps. The results obtained show the operational advantages of an efficient and effective vehicle routing planning in a specific condominium management company. The model can be extended to other service provider companies.

title: A Large-Dimensional Analysis of Least-Squares Federated Learning via Generalized Total Variation Minimization
abstract: Federated learning over decentralized networks inherently trades off the suppression of local finite-sample noise through collaboration against the bias that collaboration introduces between heterogeneous nodes. We study this tension by performing a large-dimensional analysis of Generalized Total Variation Minimization with least-squares models. Using tools from random matrix theory, we show that Lipschitz observations of the global GTVMin solution concentrate in large dimensions, universally for any underlying network structure. We provide exact analytic expressions for the asymptotically precise performance under both i.i.d. and non-i.i.d. Gaussian mixture distributions on a fixed network. For the latter, these expressions quantify how regularization balances local adaptation against collaboration. Our theoretical results are confirmed by experiments on synthetic and real-world data.

title: Sorption Molecular Dynamics of Point Defects in 2D Materials with a Machine Learning Potential
abstract: Defect engineering is a crucial tool for tuning and tailoring the properties of two-dimensional (2D) materials. A key challenge is identifying which defects are kinetically stable at room temperature and sufficiently promising to warrant further investigation. However, identifying stable defects with suitable properties using first-principles calculations, such as density functional theory (DFT) is computationally demanding, effectively limiting the scope of high-throughput studies. In this work, we investigate whether the machine learning interatomic potential MACE can reproduce sorption trends (adsorption vs. absorption) previously obtained from high-throughput DFT calculations and extend the analysis to elevated temperatures. A total of 17,624 defect structures from the ADAQ database are simulated using MACE-accelerated molecular dynamics (MD) at both 0 K and 300 K. The results show that MACE successfully reproduces the overall sorption trends observed in DFT calculations at 0 K at a fraction of the computational cost. Simulations performed at 300 K further indicate that the qualitative sorption trends remain largely the same when including finite-temperature effects. These findings demonstrate that MACE-driven MD can be used as an effective high-throughput prescreening tool for defect-related studies in 2D materials, specially related to sorption. While conventional first-principles methods, such as DFT, remain necessary for accurate and quantitative validation, the use of MLIPs enables MD simulations of finite-temperature defect behavior at a fraction of the computational cost of DFT-based MD.
authors: Nils-Ruben Skogemyr;Albin Sjöstedt;Isak Wernroth;Isak Häggqvist;Isac Ljungwald;Hans-Ove Åkesson;Henricus R. A. ten Eikelder;Rickard Armiento;Joel Davidsson

title: Transverse magneto-gyrotropy driven by spin-induced ferroaxiality
abstract: Photon chirality is inherently sensitive to structural handedness and magnetism, which break spatial inversion and time-reversal symmetries, respectively. Ferroaxial order, by contrast, hosts two-dimensional chirality while preserving both symmetries, thereby precluding its direct coupling to photon chirality. Intertwining ferroaxiality with magnetic order, however, may lift such constraints and enable unconventional coupling to photon chirality. Nevertheless, the optical response arising from such intertwined order has yet to be demonstrated experimentally. Here, we demonstrate transverse magneto-gyrotropy arising from spin-driven ferroaxiality in the Weyl magnet EuCd2Sb2. Whereas the conventional polar magneto-optical Kerr effect is governed by magnetization parallel to the light-propagation direction, we observe a gyrotropic response associated with magnetization transverse to the light-propagation direction. The optical rotation exhibits a characteristic 120-degree periodicity upon rotation of the in-plane magnetic field, reflecting the threefold symmetry of the emergent ferroaxial state and revealing the ferroaxial origin of the transverse gyrotropic response. This coupling to photon chirality enables vectorial control of the gyrotropic response through the magnetic field direction. Our findings establish an interaction between photon chirality and transverse magnetization enabled by intertwined ferroaxial and magnetic orders, demonstrating a novel form of multiferroicity with functional light-matter interaction.
authors: Yoshihiro Okamura;Takumi Kagawa;Ayano Nakamura;Shinichi Nishihaya;Masaki Uchida;Susumu Minami;Ryotaro Arita;Youtarou Takahashi

title: Sequential Learning-Based Physics-Informed Neural Network Modeling for Parameter Estimation on a Power Converter
abstract: A staged physics-informed neural network (PINN) is proposed for identifying the inductance, capacitance and parasitic resistances of a DC buck converter from time-domain data. Gradients are released in the order of L to C to rL to rC, a sequence derived from sensitivity analysis. The five-stage schedule recovers L and C to within 5% and the series ESR to 10%, while a three-stage variant attains the same accuracy 11% faster. An 84 factorial sweep confirms that the trained PINN remains accurate for simultaneous 8% perturbations of all four components, achieving a waveform RMSE of 2.6 x 10-2 over 5 ms-an order-of-magnitude better than a simultaneous-training baseline.

title: Topology-adaptive Estimation of Maximum Voltage Unbalance for Distribution Networks with Finite-sample Guarantee
abstract: High penetration of single-phase distributed power production and frequent topology changes can significantly increase voltage unbalance in distribution networks. Reliable probabilistic power flow (PPF) assessment for the network, therefore, must account for topology-dependent power-flow equations, numerical error in the voltage unbalance factor (VUF), and finite-sample uncertainty in power measurements. In this paper, we propose Topology-Adaptive Certified Quantile Estimation (TACQE) to estimate the maximum VUF across monitored electric buses. Following a local network change, TACQE updates the cross-couplings among power-flow sequences, and certifies candidate PPF solutions against the updated nonlinear equations. The resulted power-flow state enclosures provide rigorous bounds on the maximum VUF. Furthermore, we derive independent reference-solver evaluations to calibrate discrepancies from the reference PPF solution. This leads to a uniform sampling bound that yields simultaneous upper-tail probabilities and quantiles, which provides a finite-sample guarantee for the estimated maximum-VUF distribution over an entire range of VUF thresholds. From our numerical simulations across 101 fixed-topology quantiles, it demonstrates that the designed TACQE can provide a fast candidate post-change power flow solution where it reuses most of the previous network model and modifies only the affected bus blocks.
authors: Jinbao Wang;Jun Liu;Shiliang Zhang;Xuehui Ma;He Zhang

title: Weighted Adjoint Matching: Finetuning Flow Matching Models with Time-Dependent Control Cost
abstract: We introduce Weighted Adjoint Matching, a method to finetune a pretrained diffusion or flow matching model given a differentiable reward. We derive it from Adjoint Matching, which reformulates finetuning as a stochastic optimal control problem with a quadratic control cost. Building on the observation that these models generate coarse features before fine details, we place a time-dependent weight on the control cost. A high cost early in the generative process preserves balance and diversity in the coarse features, which carry most of the semantics, while a low cost at the end lets the model increase the reward by refining details. We prove that our method is equivalent to maximizing the reward under time-varying Kullback--Leibler regularization on the generative paths. Experiments on Gaussian mixtures and on MNIST show a better tradeoff between reward and mode balance than Adjoint Matching.

title: A particle swarm optimization with a reduced-subspace trust-region safeguard for contact-rich controller tuning
abstract: Contact-rich robotic insertion is challenging because uncertainty in alignment, friction, and contact conditions can lead to unsuccessful assembly, excessive contact forces, and jamming. Designing a reliable controller therefore requires balancing insertion performance, robustness, and recovery from unexpected contact. In this paper, we propose PSO+TR, a derivative-free optimization (DFO) method that combines the exploratory search of particle swarm optimization (PSO) with a trust-region (TR) procedure for local refinement to improve the search process when progress stagnates. We apply the method to derivative-free policy optimization of an interpretable robotic insertion controller, jointly tuning its motion, feedback, and recovery parameters while preserving its predefined control structure. The proposed approach is evaluated on 93 eligible benchmark problems from the bound-constrained programs (BCP) collection and a synthetic contact-rich planar insertion task under uncertain operating conditions. Three random seeds per benchmark problem yield 279 matched problem--seed instances per method. PSO+TR reaches the prescribed target on 228 of these instances (81.72\%), the highest observed target-attainment rate among the five compared methods, which also include PSO, randomized black-box optimization (VRBBO), matrix adaptation evolution strategy (MAES), and differential evolution (DE). Across eight robotic optimizer seeds, the deployed controller-selection pipeline achieves 97.78\% completion under development conditions and 58.00\% under withheld stress conditions, compared with 91.22\% and 31.12\%, respectively, for the fixed staged controller. The stress violation rate is reduced from 20.69\% to 2.19\%. These findings support combining global and local search for DFO and structured contact-rich controller tuning. The synthetic planar results require validation on physical robots.

title: Ergodic and Metastable Behavior of Stochastic Popularity Dynamics in Social Networks
abstract: This paper studies popularity dynamics in social networks, where users' engagement with competing channels is driven by intrinsic content quality, social influence, and popularity feedback. We introduce a stochastic model in which users interact through a directed influence network and channel exposure depends jointly on these three mechanisms. We first characterize the resulting dynamics in the absence of intrinsic quality, showing that popularity concentrates asymptotically on a single channel, leading to a winner-takes-all regime. When all channels have positive intrinsic quality, we establish ergodicity of the popularity process and characterize its long-run behavior. We further show that, when intrinsic quality is small, the system exhibits metastable behavior: it can remain for long periods near configurations dominated by a single channel before transitioning to another. These results highlight how weak quality differences can coexist with strong path dependence induced by popularity feedback. We then investigate platform-level interventions and propose controls that compensate for network-induced exposure biases and mitigate excessive concentration. Analytical results are illustrated through numerical simulations and an empirical analysis of YouTube data, whose observed popularity dynamics are consistent with the proposed stochastic framework. The results provide a mathematical framework for understanding the interplay between quality, social influence, and reinforcement in online popularity dynamics.

title: MCMC Can See Can't See
abstract: It is folklore that passing "convergence" diagnostics does not guarantee that a Markov chain has converged. We prove this as an impossibility for any finite checklist of diagnostics. Running more chains, longer chains, and smarter diagnostics does not avoid this impossibility in certifying convergence. Under regularity assumptions, we determine how the worst-case undetected non-convergence decays as more diagnostics are added, and how to choose diagnostics optimally. Folklore suggests that the sampler's slowest mixing modes are the "dangerous" ones that must be monitored; we prove that the slow modes yield nearly optimal diagnostics as sampling proceeds. Given a source class, we also give an anytime-valid bound on the remaining discrepancy and show how undetected bias caps the effective sample size that a finite checklist can certify.

title: Outperforming 1000 Euclidean Layers With Hyperbolic Goal-Conditioned RL
abstract: Scaling self-supervised contrastive reinforcement learning (CRL) to 1000-layer Euclidean neural networks has enabled state-of-the-art goal-reaching performance, yet wall-clock time scales linearly with depth. We find that changing the geometry achieves stronger performance with far shallower networks. This matters in complex navigation environments, where walls can make route distance deviate substantially from Euclidean distance. In a U-shaped maze, we show that the longer the route, the more it deviates from Euclidean distance. Hyperbolic CRL addresses this mismatch by replacing Euclidean distances in CRL's contrastive objective with geodesic distances in hyperbolic space. On hard navigation tasks, inductive bias beats scale: depth 64 hyperbolic agents outperform 1024-layer-deep Euclidean networks while training more than $12 \times$ faster and using about $13 \times$ fewer parameters. We observe that hyperbolic agents behave qualitatively better in hard humanoid mazes, where they follow corridors to reach goals, whereas Euclidean agents try straight-line shortcuts over walls. Our results show that matching the representation geometry to the task can substitute for substantial network depth. Code is at https://github.com/Probabilistic-and-Interactive-ML/HypGCRL .
authors: Timo Klein;Thomas Lang;Andrii Shkabrii;Lukas Miklautz;Yllka Velaj;Sebastian Tschiatschek

title: Minimax estimation of the pseudo-spectral gap of continuous Markov chains, with applications to empirical concentration bounds
abstract: We study the minimax estimation of the pseudo-spectral gap $γ_{ps}$ of a Markov chain from the observation of a single trajectory. Extending earlier works on finite-state space chains by Wolfer and Kontorovich (2024), we provide an estimator in the case of a compact, continuous state-space. Our estimator appears to be minimax-optimal on the class of chains with a transition operator with Lipschitz density, up to logarithmic terms. Our estimator, combined with Paulin's version of Bernstein inequality, allows to derive empirical concentration inequalities for Markov chains. This unlocks many applications, from confidence intervals, to active learning and generalization bounds. In particular, for rested bandits with Markov rewards, we provide a version of UCB with a regret bound similar to the one in the iid case, without assuming any knowledge on the pseudo-spectral gap of the chains.

title: Nova shells in 3D: I. A catalog of integral field spectroscopic observations
abstract: Classical novae eject material during thermonuclear eruptions on accreting white dwarfs, forming expanding shells whose structures and kinematics provide insights into the eruption mechanism and binary interaction. However, their intrinsic three-dimensional (3D) structures remain poorly constrained. We present the first 3D catalog of nova shells based on integral field spectroscopy, enabling us to investigate their structures beyond projection effects. We compiled observations of 19 nova shells obtained with MUSE at the VLT, complemented by new MEGARA observations at the GTC and WEAVE observations at the WHT. We constructed 3D visualizations of selected emission lines to explore the diversity of shell morphologies and kinematics. The shells reveal a wide variety of structures, including ellipsoidal or spherical shells, rings, bipolar features, and clumpy or irregular components, many of which are not apparent in 2D projections. Approximately 60% of the sample exhibits predominantly ellipsoidal or spherical shapes, while about 30% shows ring-like or bipolar structures. Several objects display strong line-dependent morphological differences, with [O III] or [N II] tracing distinct kinematic components from those seen in H$α$. Compared with imaging studies, integral field spectroscopy reveals a larger fraction of bipolar or toroidal shells. The differences between emission lines highlight the diverse excitation mechanisms and physical conditions within the ejecta. Finally, comparing expansion velocities in the plane of the sky and along the line of sight suggests low intrinsic aspect ratios, consistent with estimates from projected shell shapes.
authors: Janis B. Rodríguez-González;Edgar Santamaría;Martin A. Guerrero;Jesús A. Toalá
comment: 23 pages, 22 figures and 2 tables. Accepted in A&A

title: New spherical codes by tuning an annealing solver
abstract: The spherical code problem asks how to place $N$ points on a unit sphere in $D$ dimensions to maximize the smallest distance between two points. It is a non-smooth and non-convex max-min problem, where few problem sizes have known optimal solutions, some have constructions, but most still only have numerically obtained solutions. We use a simple solver, with seven parameters, that anneals a LogSumExp surrogate, minimizes with L-BFGS, applies a random perturbation between anneals, and repeats with no acceptance test until a fixed limit is reached. We search the solver parameters for every instance with $N \le 1024$, $3 \le D \le 32$, and $N > 2D$, a total of 29,670 instances, using 32 parameter trials. We then run the solver for 60 seconds with the best parameters for each instance, without utilizing any symmetries or existing solutions. After enforcing monotonicity of the results and numerically polishing the solutions, we improve the best known code in 4,577 instances. When a single set of solver parameters is used for all instances, with one 60-second episode, the number of improvements is still 3,649. From our records, we find 24 codes with an exact algebraic cosine. Among our ablations, we find that 1) the repeated anneal contributes most to improvements, 2) at our $32 \times 60$-second budget only fitting one parameter per-instance is better than fitting all seven, and 3) good parameters can be predicted from the instance size. We provide the solver code, the fitted parameters, and the codes.

title: EEG Correlates of Verbal and Perceptual Reasoning
abstract: Identifying the neural underpinnings of intelligence is one of the major goals of modern intelligence research. However, few imaging studies explore the high extremes of intelligence, and most use only a single composite IQ score. This study used quantitative EEG recordings to investigate correlations between the EEG variables of individual alpha peak frequency, relative power, and coherence, and scores on verbal and perceptual reasoning tests in participants with IQs from the low-average to exceptionally gifted ranges. Overall, the results did not reveal any pattern of significant relationships between these EEG measures and the two psychometric tests. Since this study had only a small sample, heavily skewed towards the high-IQ end of the scale, no definitive conclusions about the EEG measures and verbal and perceptual reasoning can be drawn. Nevertheless, it reveals many opportunities for further research, and suggestions are made for progressing this topic in the future.

title: L1 Minimum Energy Estimation of Positive Systems
abstract: We present a novel class of minimum energy estimation problems for positive linear systems with linear costs subject to coupled process and measurement disturbances, where the latter is bounded by the state and the former is bounded by the noise. Through dynamic programming we show that the problem admits explicit solutions. Remarkably, the Luenberger observer structure of the optimal estimator emerges from the optimization itself, with a switching gain that inherits the sparsity of the disturbance constraints, and it is obtained from a differential equation in the finite horizon case. In the infinite horizon case, an algebraic equation characterizes the limit of the finite-horizon solution and yields a stationary estimator with a static gain. We introduce two distinct notions of detectability to characterize when the static gain stabilizes the error dynamics while preserving their positivity, and analyze under which conditions the stationary solution can be formulated as a linear program. We further establish that a disturbance perturbation of finite L1-norm yields an estimation error of finite L1-norm. The framework is illustrated on a large-scale irrigation network.

title: High-Harmonic Generation Probes Quantum Nuclear Fluctuations in Liquid Water
abstract: Nuclear quantum effects are essential for an accurate description of the hydrogen-bonded structure of liquid water, yet their spectroscopic signatures can be subtle and difficult to measure. Moreover, probing these effects in solution on femtosecond timescales (or below) is an open challenge that is pivotal for optical control of hydrogen bonds and ultrafast spectroscopy of proton transfer. Here, we combine path-integral molecular dynamics with real-time time-dependent density-functional theory to explore high-harmonic generation (HHG) in liquid water from first principles, rigorously accounting for quantum nuclear delocalisation. Relative to classical-nuclei simulations, quantum sampling suppresses the harmonic yield around certain harmonics by up to an order of magnitude, inducing local structural minima. By analysing the ab initio simulations and reproducing the key effects with a simplified model Hamiltonian, we trace the physical origins of the interference minima to the broadening of valence-band states induced by hydrogen-bond fluctuations, a mechanism expected to generalise to other hydrogen-bonded structures. Our work shows that nuclear quantum effects are indispensable for capturing ultrafast electronic dynamics in liquids, and demonstrates the power of liquid HHG spectroscopy for attosecond probing of nuclear fluctuations.
authors: George Trenins;Nicolas Tancogne-Dejean;Angana Mondal;Angel Rubio;Hans Jakob Wörner;Aaron Kelly;Ofer Neufeld;Mariana Rossi

title: Alignment-driven binary evolution in warped circumbinary discs: 3D moving-mesh hydrodynamics of eccentric and inclined binaries
abstract: We present three-dimensional moving-mesh hydrodynamical simulations (\arepo{}) of equal-mass binaries in circumbinary discs, spanning binary eccentricity ($e = 0.0,\,0.3,\,0.6$) and inclination ($i = 0^\circ$--$60^\circ$), using a locally isothermal $α$-disc ($H/r = α_{\rm visc} = 0.1$) with fixed Keplerian orbits. Discs above the critical inclination $i_{\rm crit}(e)$, decreasing with $e$, drive their interiors near-polar, so eccentricity alone alters the outcome at fixed $i$. Discs reach polar alignment ten times faster than they align toward the binary plane, settling long before the binary's orbit responds. Alignment dictates how the disc acts on the binary. First, a disc tilting back toward the binary plane spends nearly all its torque reorienting the binary's orbit, whereas a disc driven polar redirects it into the orbit itself, which shrinks 10--20 times faster. Second, at $e = 0.6$ the turn to polar is a single transient reshaping the accretion flow, cavity and orbit, with accretion enhanced ($i = 45^\circ$) or suppressed ($i = 60^\circ$). Third, misalignment suppresses coplanar eccentricity pumping: the attractor at $e \approx 0.4$ survives only below $i \approx 15^\circ$, so misaligned binaries circularise and may enter the gravitational-wave regime less eccentric than coplanar models predict. Around a circular binary, the familiar $\approx 4.5$-orbit accretion modulation vanishes while the disc is strongly warped, returning as it realigns, a time-domain signature of misaligned massive black-hole binaries. Finally, observed polar discs around stellar binaries, such as HD~98800~BaBb's, are likely in their final state; intermediate misalignments reflect slower alignment toward the binary plane.
comment: 25 pages, 15 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to MNRAS

title: Galactic Morpholography: Linking present-day galaxy compactness to assembly history and relic formation in the COLIBRE simulations
abstract: Compactness is widely used to identify candidate relic galaxies, the largely untouched survivors of the first compact massive galaxies. Yet relicness is an evolutionary rather than structural property. Using the COLIBRE cosmological hydrodynamical simulations, we test whether present-day structure traces galaxy formation and assembly histories. Six complementary tracers (stellar age, metallicity, [Mg/Fe], sSFR, velocity dispersion and ex-situ mass fraction) vary coherently across the stellar mass-size plane and independently identify a characteristic compactness scale of $\log_{10}(Σ_{1.5,\mathrm{crit}}/(\mathrm{M}_\odot\mathrm{kpc}^{-1.5}))=9.75\pm0.10$. We term this mapping between present-day structure and assembly history morpholography. Combining this threshold with the Degree of Relicness ($\mathrm{DoR}>0.6$), which quantifies early and rapid star formation, we distinguish compact from ancient galaxies and identify 267 relic candidates at their intersection. Ancient galaxies span nearly the full ex-situ-fraction range, from predominantly in-situ formation to substantial merger-driven growth. Relic candidates are concentrated at stellar masses of $\approx 10^{10}$-$10^{11}$ solar masses, host black holes that lie $\approx 0.25$-$2.5$ dex above the median black-hole-stellar-mass relation, and are predominantly satellites (76%), preferentially in cluster environments. Only $\approx 3$% show evidence of strong tidal stripping, suggesting that environment primarily preserves rather than creates relic-like systems. Approximately one third (87/267) are direct descendants of the $z=2$ massive quiescent galaxies identified in COLIBRE. Present-day structure thus retains a statistical fossil record of assembly history, supporting morpholography as a link between nearby galaxies and the early Universe.
authors: Maximilian Zemsch;Claudia D. P. Lagos;Chiara Spiniello;Michele Cappellari;Ángel Chandro-Gómez;Katy L. Proctor;Evgenii Chaikin;Johanna Hartke;Filip Huško;Sylvia Ploeckinger;Alexander J. Richings;Mahsa Sanati;Joop Schaye;James W. Trayford

title: Reciprocity coordinates a three-way trade-off in recurrent neural circuits
abstract: Biological neural circuits contain both unidirectional and reciprocal connections, but how reciprocity affects circuit computation remains unclear. We varied reciprocity \r{ho} across 21 levels in recurrent-network simulations while holding network size, connection density, and directed-edge count fixed. Low-reciprocity networks produced more diverse stimulus-driven activity and performed better on four continuous-input tasks, whereas higher reciprocity generally improved performance on three delayed-memory tasks. Increasing reciprocity reduced online memory capacity and accelerated recovery from perturbations. A post-cue noise experiment showed that higher reciprocity suppressed internal noise propagation but made cue-evoked states less distinguishable, and component matching separated the contributions of cue separation and within-cue dispersion to readout robustness. Within this ensemble, reciprocity thus mediates a three-way trade-off among representational capacity, local stability, and task-state separability: higher reciprocity lowers capacity, strengthens stability, and compresses separability. Whether it improves behaviour depends on whether the stability gain outweighs the lost separation between task states. Connectome and microcircuit datasets from five species showed intermediate reciprocity, while reciprocity varied substantially across adult Drosophila brain regions, providing compatible structural context and motivating circuit-specific functional tests.
authors: Xiaoyu Zhang;Mingyi Huang;Yixuan Cui;Xin Lu;Yuguo Yu

title: Recursive Gradient Retraction Methods for Stochastic Nonconvex Optimization on Stiefel Manifolds
abstract: Nonconvex optimization on Stiefel manifolds underlies many problems in machine learning and deep learning. However, existing stochastic Riemannian retraction methods often rely on stepsizes that require prior knowledge of the gradient Lipschitz constant, a prescribed iteration horizon, or restrictive batch-size choices. We develop {\sf RGR}, a recursive gradient retraction method for stochastic nonconvex optimization on Stiefel manifolds. Instead of recursively updating gradient estimators in changing tangent spaces, {\sf RGR} constructs them in the Euclidean space and subsequently maps them to tangent space, thereby avoiding vector transport. The method comprises three variants: {\sf RGR-SPIDER} for finite-sum optimization and {\sf RGR-SRM} and {\sf RGR-EMA} for online stochastic optimization. {\sf RGR-SPIDER} is Lipschitz-free and horizon-free, as its adaptive stepsize requires neither prior knowledge of the gradient Lipschitz constant nor a prescribed iteration horizon. {\sf RGR-SRM} and {\sf RGR-EMA} are mini-batch and horizon-free methods whose convergence guarantees do not rely on prescribed large batch sizes and whose parameters can be chosen without prior knowledge of the total iteration budget. We show that {\sf RGR-SPIDER} reaches an $\varepsilon$-critical point using $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$ iterations and $\mathcal{O}(N+\sqrt{N}\varepsilon^{-2})$ component-gradient evaluations, where $N$ denotes the number of component functions. For the online setting, {\sf RGR-SRM} and {\sf RGR-EMA} achieve iteration complexities of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\varepsilon^{-3})$ and $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\varepsilon^{-4})$, respectively. Experiments on principal component analysis, low-rank matrix completion, and orthogonal convolutional neural networks demonstrate faster empirical convergence than methods that construct recursive gradient estimators directly in Riemannian tangent spaces.

title: The physical and chemical structure of TMC-1. The spatial distribution and excitation conditions of carbon, oxygen, and sulfur bearing species: Depletion of CO and CS
abstract: We present a detailed study of the physical and chemical structure of TMC-1 from the observed spatial distribution of HC3N, NNH+, CN, and their isotopologues, the O-bearing species C18O, C17O, CH3OH, CH3CHO, and H2CO, and the S-bearing species CS, HCS+, H2CS, and H2CCS. The well known filamentary structure of TMC-1 can be interpreted as a single cloud with a velocity gradient perpendicular to the filament, or less likely as due to the alignment of three independent clouds in the line sight with velocities of 5.3-5.7, 5.7-5.9, and 5.9-6.3 km/s. The main contribution to the emission of all studied C-bearing species is found at 5.83 kms/s. We conclude that the three velocity components are dynamically connected and that C-bearing molecules show a different behavior of their abundances compared to O-bearing species, which have emission peaks at 5.7 and 6.25 km/s, and appear at different spatial locations than cyanopolyynes and CnH and CnN radicals. The detection of 13C18O, with exactly the same line profile than that of C18O and C17O, excludes the possibility that the decrease of their emission at 5.83 km/s, could be due to self absorption or absorption by a foreground cloud component. Hence, as indicated by the spatial distribution of C18O and C17O, CO is significantly depleted at the velocities and positions where the emission of the carbon chains and radicals is found. This suggests that the emission of O-bearing species is coming from the external layers of the carbon-rich filaments. A comparison between S-bearing species and other molecules indicates that CS, CCS, HCS+, and H2CS are significantly depleted in the zone of CO depletion. A clear increase of the deuteration of several molecular species is found in the zones where CO and CS are depleted.
authors: J. Cernicharo;B. Tercero;N. Marcelino;G. Esplugues;G. Molpeceres;M. Agúndez

title: The Role of Environment in Shaping the Assembly Timelines of Massive Quiescent Galaxies at Cosmic Noon
abstract: JWST observations of massive quiescent galaxies (MQGs) at $z\sim2$ have revealed diverse star formation histories (SFHs). In this letter, we investigate whether these variations are linked to the environment in which MQGs reside, as quantified by the host dark matter halo mass. We identify 12 MQGs from a representative sample of galaxies at $1.6<z<3.5$ obtained by the Blue Jay survey, a JWST Cycle 1 program, and infer their SFHs via modelling of the deep NIRSpec medium-resolution spectra along with multi-band photometry. By correlating the formation and quenching epochs of individual MQGs with their respective host halo masses from the 3D-HST survey, we find that after accounting for the redshift range of the sample ($1.8<z<2.5$), MQGs in more massive haloes formed at significantly earlier cosmic epochs. Meanwhile, although these galaxies also quenched earlier overall, the scatter in quenching epochs across similar halo masses indicates that the quenching process likely involves other contributing factors and is not solely determined by halo mass.
authors: Tianmu Gao;J. Trevor Mendel;Letizia Bugiani;Minjung Park;Sirio Belli;Joel Leja;Claudia del P. Lagos;Amir H. Khoram;Rebecca L. Davies;Razieh Emami;Gabriel Maheson;Anita Zanella;Benjamin P. Collins

title: Sleeping or Dead? Probing the Quenching Mechanism of JWST Dormant Galaxies at z > 3 with ALMA
abstract: JWST has revealed a population of "dormant'' galaxies at z>3 with strong Balmer breaks and weak emission lines, whose star formation appears to have declined only recently. Whether these galaxies are undergoing a lasting transition toward quiescence or merely experiencing a temporary suppression of star formation remains unclear. We investigate their molecular gas content using archival ALMA observations of [CII]158um and CO rotational transitions. Starting from all publicly available JWST/NIRSpec prism observations and using joint spectrophotometric fitting, we construct a parent sample at z>3 and log(Mstar/Msun)>9.5 in the ALMA-accessible COSMOS, UDS, and GOODS-South fields. Our final sample comprises 7 dormant galaxies and 15 quiescent galaxies with ALMA constraints on their molecular gas content (mostly 3 sigma upper limits). We find that dormant galaxies exhibit systematically lower star formation rates averaged over the past 10Myr (SFR10Myr) than over the past 100Myr (SFR100Myr), supporting a recent rapid decline in their star formation. For the ~70% of the sample with sufficiently constraining ALMA observations, their molecular gas fractions lie at least ~0.3-2dex below those expected for main-sequence galaxies. Moreover, the molecular gas fractions of dormant galaxies show no systematic difference from those of quiescent galaxies in our sample. This indicates that dormant galaxies have already reached a gas-poor state shortly after quenching and favors a scenario in which the rapid shutdown of star formation is associated with depletion or removal of the molecular gas reservoir, rather than primarily with suppressed star formation efficiency while retaining a substantial molecular gas reservoir. Our results suggest that, if no substantial gas replenishment occurs in the future, dormant galaxies are more consistent with becoming "dead'' than with being temporarily "sleeping''.

title: Convergence Rates of Gaussian Process Thompson Sampling for Efficient Global Optimization
abstract: Efficient global optimization aims to identify a global optimum of an expensive black-box function within a limited evaluation budget $N$. We investigate the convergence rates of Gaussian process Thompson sampling (GP-TS) under noiseless observations, assuming a fixed objective function in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). For Matérn kernels with smoothness parameter $ν$ in dimension $d$, we establish a worst-case expected simple-regret upper bound of $O(N^{-ν/d}\sqrt{\log N})$ for both discrete GP-TS on sufficiently fine grids and its continuous counterpart. For the continuous implementation, we develop a nested-grid argument to control posterior sample paths over the entire domain. We further establish matching lower bounds of $Ω(N^{-5/2}\sqrt{\log N})$ for both implementations under a fixed one-dimensional Matérn-$5/2$ kernel, demonstrating that the logarithmic penalty is intrinsic to standard GP-TS in this setting. Motivated by this limitation, we propose Gaussian Process Capped Thompson Sampling (GP-CTS), which caps posterior sample paths using a valid RKHS norm upper bound while preserving optimism. This modification successfully eliminates the logarithmic penalty and achieves the minimax-optimal rate $Θ(N^{-ν/d})$ for both discrete and continuous implementations.

title: Beyond DFT electronic band structures via dual-space orbital learning
abstract: Accurate electronic band structures are essential for predicting material properties, but high-fidelity calculations are computationally demanding. We introduce O-kRystal, a dual-space orbital-learning framework that uses a lower-cost Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) calculation as both an energy baseline and a source of structured orbital information. Combining PBE band energies with real- and reciprocal-space orbital matrices, O-kRystal predicts higher-level corrections for individual electronic states as a function of crystal momentum and spin. For states within 5 eV of the band-edge midpoint, it predicts Heyd-Scuseria-Ernzerhof (HSE06) band energies with a mean absolute error of $0.171 \pm 0.009$ eV across nearly 6,000 three-dimensional materials spanning insulating, metallic, magnetic, and nonmagnetic systems. On a separate benchmark of six strongly correlated materials, it reduces the corresponding PBE band-energy MAE by 68.7% and resolves orbital-dependent changes in the relative placement of transition-metal d and ligand p states. Despite training only at high-symmetry points, it maintains comparable accuracy at unseen points along band paths and reconstructs HSE06 densities of states from dense Brillouin-zone predictions. Finally, training O-kRystal on $G_0W_0$ quasiparticle energies for two-dimensional materials demonstrates its applicability across levels of theory and the potential of orbital learning for higher-fidelity, momentum-resolved electronic-structure prediction beyond density functional theory.
authors: Minhyuk Kang;Beom Seok Kang;Nikolai Argatoff;Miguel Nouman;Danish Khan;William A. Goddard;Anima Anandkumar
comment: 46 pages, 10 figures (including 4 supplementary figures); Supplementary Information included

title: On the Mechanism of Multi-Cluster System Separation Under Extreme Events
abstract: Historical blackout events demonstrate that, under complex multi-event contingencies, interconnected power systems can split into multiple areas exhibiting distinct dynamic behavior while remaining physically connected. This work provides a rationale for this phenomenon. Typical N-1 contingency analysis leads to a response dominated by a single unstable mode, supporting the two-cluster conjecture used by transient stability assessment tools such as the SIME method. However, extreme events, often involving cascading N-k contingencies, can excite multiple unstable modes. We establish a proof of concept based on linear modal expansion to show how such concurrent excitation leads to multiple coherent areas. The resulting behavior is illustrated through simulations on the standard WSCC 9-bus, IEEE 14-bus, and IEEE 39-bus systems, demonstrating the limitations of conventional two-cluster representations under extreme events.

title: On the Regularization of Primal-Dual Dynamics in Time-Dependent Nonconvex Optimization
abstract: We study continuous-time primal-dual dynamics for tracking solutions of time-dependent constrained optimization problems. First, for uniformly strongly convex-strongly concave saddle functions, we establish explicit finite-time tracking and additive-disturbance bounds. For convex problems, we then introduce a directional primal regularization, combined with dual Tikhonov regularization, and quantify the resulting optimization bias and constraint violation. For smooth nonconvex problems, we couple a proximal local convexification with a two-time-scale primal-dual flow and obtain a local tracking result under constraint qualification, second-order sufficiency, and temporal regularity. Numerical traffic-signal experiments at a single intersection evaluate the proposed method under vehicle-throughput and pedestrian-aware objectives, comparing it with standard signal-control schemes.

title: Maximum likelihood, neural networks and posterior mean for inferring fractional Brownian motion parameters
abstract: Fractional Brownian motion (fBM) is a model of anomalous diffusion parameterised by a Hurst exponent $H \in (0,1)$ and a generalised diffusion coefficient $D_H > 0$. We jointly estimate $H$ and $D_H$ using maximum likelihood (MLE) from density measurements with Poisson counting noise and single-particle trajectory with Gaussian localisation error. We show that one density measurement in time cannot infer both $H$ and $D_H$ and that several time points are needed, which matters most for inference precision. For trajectories, we show that a neural network trained with a squared error loss approximates the posterior mean of $H$, which can be computed exactly at negligible cost. Paired with the profile-likelihood estimate of $D_H$, the posterior mean has the lowest root mean squared error in both $H$ and $D_H$, except near $H=0$ and $H=1$ where MLE estimates $H$ better. In vesicle trajectories from two cell types, $H$ and $D_H$ form a continuum rather than distinct modes of motion. The posterior probability that each window within a track is subdiffusive or superdiffusive shows that $26\%$ of MRC5 fibroblast and $21\%$ of HeLa vesicle trajectories contain both subdiffusive and superdiffusive windows, against $2\%$ and $7\%$ expected from estimation uncertainty alone. Intracellular cargoes therefore switch between subdiffusion and superdiffusion over time rather than forming populations with fixed $H$.
authors: Daniel S. Han;Vaishnavi Ananthanarayanan;Matthew J. Simpson

title: PDRs4All XXIII. JWST-MIRI template spectra of PAHs in the Orion Bar obtained with blind signal separation
abstract: The aromatic infrared bands (AIBs) are observed in a wide variety of astrophysical sources, and now in unprecedented detail by the James Webb space telescope (JWST). These bands are generally attributed to the emission from polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAHs). Our aim is to extract mid-infrared AIB template spectra from JWST observations of the Orion Bar photo-dissociation region that can be used to derive PAH properties from observations of other objects. We used the JWST MIRI-MRS observations from the PDRs4All program. We first isolated the AIBs from the data using a multi-component fitting approach. We then applied a non-negative matrix factorization to the isolated AIB spectra and extracted two templates, named AIBirrad and AIBshield following previous work. The spatial distribution and spectral characteristics of these two spectra suggest that they originate from two chemical distinct populations. We interpret AIBirrad as emission originating from a PAH population strongly exposed to ultra-violet (UV) radiation and mainly composed of large, compact ionized PAHs. Conversely, AIBshield is interpreted as originating from a more shielded population of PAHs, which is less exposed to the UV by being more embedded in the cloud. This population consists of small, asymmetric and mainly neutral PAHs with bonded aliphatic side groups. These templates can serve to analyze PAH emission in a wide variety of objects observed with MIRI-MRS.
authors: P. Amiot;O. Berné;J. Roux-Morin;I. Schroetter;C. Boersma;A. Fuente;J. R. Goicoechea;E. Habart;A. Maragkoudakis;T. Onaka;E. Peeters;M. Robberto;A. G. G. M Tielens;D. Van De Putte;S. Vicente

title: Black Hole Binary Mergers in Galactic Nuclei: Combined Effects of Secular Dynamics and Stellar Flybys
abstract: Galactic nuclei, with the central supermassive black holes (SMBHs) and surrounding dense star clusters, serve as natural laboratories for studying gravitational dynamics in extreme gravitational environments. In this work, we model the long term evolution of black hole binaries (BHBs) in these environments by incorporating the tidal influence of the central SMBH, the potential of the nuclear star cluster, SMBH induced relativistic precession, and stochastic perturbations from stellar flybys. Our numerical simulations show that the long term evolution of BHBs is predominantly governed by the SMBH-driven ZLK mechanism. However, once stellar flybys are included, they can modify both the binary angular momentum and energy. The cumulative effect of repeated flyby encounters substantially reshapes the long term dynamical evolution, eventually leading systems toward either merger or disruption. Based on a population synthesis study, we find that this combined secular and non-secular channel produces a merger rate of approximately $\mathcal{R}\simeq16\mathrm{Gpc^{-3}yr^{-1}}$, which is significantly higher than the rates predicted by dynamical channels that neglect stellar flybys. Furthermore, we predict that a non-negligible fraction of merging systems would retain detectable eccentricities at low frequencies around 5 Hz, thus providing a distinctive observational signature for next generation ground based GW detectors. Our results demonstrate that the stochastic perturbations from the surrounding environment are essential for modeling BHB evolution in galactic nuclei, and that this channel may contribute a major fraction of observed mergers.
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, accepted for publication in ApJ

title: Neural Wasserstein Splines: Representation-Invariant Second-Order Priors for Trajectory Inference
abstract: Population dynamics are often observed only as unpaired snapshots, which leave the evolution between measurements underdetermined. Second-order regularization can constrain it, but a penalty on the accelerations of sampled particles is a prior on joint particle paths, and different particle representations of the same marginal curve can have different acceleration costs. We therefore introduce Neural Wasserstein Splines (NWSP), a sample-based method that learns a continuous population curve under a Wasserstein smoothness prior. A neural network maps latent variables to the control points of a cubic spline in time, so samples at any time come from the spline basis without numerical integration. We project the generator's velocity onto gradients of a finite dictionary of scalar potentials and differentiate this measure-dependent projection in time, obtaining a finite-dimensional surrogate for the intrinsic Wasserstein acceleration, trained jointly with distributional fit losses. For a fixed dictionary and ridge parameter, we prove that the population penalty depends only on the marginal curve and bound its sensitivity to moment-estimation errors. Learned potentials (NWSP-N) sharpen acceleration estimates. On various synthetic and single-cell benchmarks, NWSP is highly competitive with transport and flow-based methods, ranking in the top two in 11 of 16 settings. The penalty improves on an unregularized spline in 13 of 16 settings and, while competitive with a particle-acceleration penalty, adds provable representation invariance.

title: specwizard: A Public Python Framework for Creating Synthetic Absorption Spectra from Hydrodynamical Simulations
abstract: We present specwizard, a publicly available modular Python package for generating synthetic absorption spectra from hydrodynamical simulations. The code combines atomic data from the National Institute of Standards and Technology database with ionisation fractions computed using the cloudy spectral synthesis code for multiple ionising backgrounds, enabling consistent modelling of bound--bound and bound--free absorption for resonant transitions of all ions. specwizard employs a column-density--conserving projection scheme, includes natural line broadening for the Lyman series, and offers optional treatments of instrumental resolution and noise for direct comparison with high-resolution quasar spectra. As example applications of the code, we shoot sightlines through the eagle cosmological simulation to generate a z = 3.2 synthetic quasar spectrum containing H i Lyman-series transitions, including damping wings and Lyman-limit absorption. Additionally, we compute metal-absorption lines probing the circumgalactic medium of simulated galaxies, and investigate the correlated absorption of H i and Si iii. We demonstrate that specwizard applied to outputs from eagle accurately reproduces key observational diagnostics of the Lyman-alpha forest, including the redshift evolution of the mean transmission, the transmission PDF and the transmission power spectrum. We take advantage of the fact that the eagle simulation also reproduces the measured evolution of the temperature-density relation to infer the evolution of the amplitude of the ionizing background, finding excellent agreement with recent theoretical models and measurements.

title: On the Optimisation Landscape of Overparameterised Weighted MMD
abstract: We study the optimisation landscape of the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) over weighted atomic measures. For the one-dimensional Gaussian kernel, we show that, for any compactly supported target distribution, sufficiently many particles ensure that every local minimum has arbitrarily small MMD. Moreover, any stationary point whose MMD remains bounded away from zero is unstable under an unweighted gradient flow over the particle locations. These results hold both when the weights are constrained to the simplex, and when they are unconstrained but optimised at each step. When the target is itself finitely supported, we further strengthen this result: beyond an explicit particle threshold, there are no spurious local minima, and every spurious stationary point is unstable. To our knowledge, these are the first finite-particle overparameterisation guarantees of their kind for weighted MMD optimisation.

title: Text-Informed Training Data Filtering for Enhanced Virtual Flow Meter Performance
abstract: In sectors such as energy, aquaculture and chemical processing, the effectiveness of both mechanistic and data-driven models is frequently limited by poor-quality training data, which obscures underlying physical laws and degrades predictive accuracy. Such quality issues commonly manifest as anomalies in the dataset, ranging from sensor faults to process upsets and incorrect operator inputs. While traditional rule-based filtering can remove a subset of the anomalies, it is unable to leverage contextual information stored as unstructured text, such as engineer comments and operational logs that explain under what conditions the data was collected. We propose a text-informed data filtering method that leverages large language models (LLMs) to integrate unstructured operational data with tabular sensor data. The method consists of two steps: (1) contextual anomaly detection by reasoning over both data modalities, and (2) generation of a binary mask that is applied to filter the training dataset for model development. To investigate the potential benefit, a steady-state soft-sensor regression model, namely a virtual flow meter that estimates well flow rates, is used as the downstream evaluation target. Experiments on a synthetic oil and gas dataset show improved model performance compared to traditional rule-based filtering. Ablation studies show that textual operator comments can provide filtering-relevant signals beyond sensor data alone, with the multimodal approach reducing downstream MAPE from 7.1% to 5.4% relative to sensor-only filtering. This work demonstrates that integrating unstructured operational knowledge with sensor data through LLMs can improve data quality for industrial machine learning applications, offering a scalable alternative to manual data curation.

title: Actuation-Aware Pinching-Antenna Placement Under Blockage and User Mobility
abstract: Existing placement studies for pinching-antenna systems (PASS) usually assume that antenna movement is instantaneous and free. In practice, actuators move at finite speeds and must pause radiation while repositioning. This makes performance depend on consecutive antenna positions, turning placement into an edge-weighted longest-path problem on a temporal trellis. We also show that an obstacle blocks a wider range of antenna positions as it approaches the user, causing sudden performance drops that make multi-step lookahead essential, and that once obstacle height is included every blockage event shadows at least a fixed minimum length of waveguide. We give an exact offline solution with complexity O(TMS) and bound the per-slot loss of a W-step receding-horizon policy by O(1/W). Measurements show that the required lookahead window is set by shadow width rather than by waveguide length. Across 20 random seeds, the exact policy delivers 17.7% higher max-min throughput than per-slot optimization under blockage, and matches it when no blockers are present.

title: ANOVA approximation for high-dimensional control systems
abstract: We study the data-driven approximation of control-affine systems, where the drift and each control vector field exhibit a low-dimensional structure. While the ANOVA (ANalysis Of VAriance) decomposition is tailored to low-dimensional structures, a straightforward implementation does not exploit control affinity, rendering the approximation computationally expensive. We propose a coupled least squares approach for given state-control samples, whose ansatz is affine linear in the control by construction and can be realized by a preprocessing of the ANOVA index sets. Based on a Marcinkiewicz--Zygmund inequality for the resulting ansatz space, we prove a probabilistic $L_2$-error bound with explicitly given constants. Separate error control on drift and input vector fields renders the approach flexible to, e.\,g., parameter changes. Finally, we numerically illustrate the identification of the coupling structure via global sensitivity indices on discretizations of a nonlinear advection-diffusion equation, the shallow water equations and the viscous Burgers equation.

title: Does Policy Mirror Descent Converge in Policy with Non-Decomposable Mirror Maps? A Counterexample
abstract: Policy mirror descent (PMD) refers to a class of policy optimization methods associated with different mirror maps. For a broad class of decomposable Legendre mirror maps encompassing many standard choices, Li and Wei [2026] show that the PMD policy sequence converges to an optimal policy from any admissible initialization under any positive constant step size, even when the optimal policy is not unique. In this note, we provide a counterexample with assistance from OpenAI's GPT-5.6 model, showing that PMD with a non-decomposable Legendre mirror map need not converge in policy.

title: Andreev-reflection spectroscopy of SrPt3P single crystals
abstract: The interplay between inversion symmetry breaking and superconducting pairing mechanisms is a long-standing puzzle of solid-state physics. Ternary platinum phosphide SrPt$_3$P is an excellent case study in this regard, since it shares the distorted anti-perovskite crystal structure of non-centrosymmetric superconductor CePt$_3$Si but preserves the inversion symmetry center, enabling a direct comparison between the two compounds. Despite intense scrutiny, the superconducting pairing strength, gap symmetry, and magnitude of SrPt$_3$P remain an open question. Here, we study the gap structure of high-quality SrPt$_3$P single crystals with $T_c = 8.6$ K by using point-contact Andreev-reflection spectroscopy. The spectra systematically showed symmetric conductance maxima and a zero-bias minimum, as is typical of fully gapped superconductors, and dips at finite voltage $V_\mathrm{dip}$ due to the local transition of the contact region to the resistive state. In contacts with high resistance, where the dips fall sufficiently far from the gap features, the conductance curves can be well fitted with a single isotropic $s$-wave gap. The temperature dependence $Δ(T)$ of the gap amplitude extracted from the fit is in good agreement with the one predicted by the BCS theory, with a zero-temperature mean value $Δ(0)=1.88\pm0.08$ meV, and a mean gap ratio $2Δ/k_\mathrm{B}T_c = 5.2\pm0.2$.
authors: Valeriy A. Stepanov;Nikolai D. Zhigadlo;Erik Piatti;Dario Daghero

title: A practical route to amorphous solid-state electrolyte structures by hybrid reverse Monte Carlo with foundation potentials
abstract: Amorphous alkali oxychlorides are fast ion conductors, but their atomic structure remains unresolved. Total scattering sums all partial pair correlations into one curve that has no unique inversion, so the structure must be modeled. Melt-quench molecular dynamics builds a model from the interatomic potential alone, and reverse Monte Carlo (RMC) builds one from the measurement alone. The two have rarely been compared with all else held fixed. We benchmark both routes and two hybrid schemes on amorphous \ce{Li_{0.9}NbO_{0.9}Cl_{4.1}} against one neutron pair distribution function with one foundation potential. The hybrid schemes put the energy either in the acceptance rule (inline) or in short relaxations between blocks of refinement (alternating). Each refinement starts from a melt-quench glass or from a random packing of isolated units. The glass has the lowest energy and places the first-shell peaks correctly, but carries almost none of the oscillation beyond 6~Å (goodness of fit $R^{2} = 0.29$). Pure RMC fits the measurement to within its counting noise ($R^{2} = 0.99$), but at more than $1.3$~eV/atom above the glass, and niobium loses about half of its first-shell chlorine. Started from the glass, both hybrid schemes reach $R^{2} = 0.92$ within $0.1$~eV/atom of its energy and keep its coordination chemistry. Structures from the two inputs fit almost equally well and differ in energy by a tenth of the RMC penalty, yet they differ in whether their polyhedra are connected. The input is therefore part of the method. We recommend quenching a glass with a foundation potential and refining it against the measurement with a hybrid scheme. The resulting structure carries both the local chemistry and the medium-range order, and it is the starting point for modeling ion transport in these conductors.
authors: Xintian Wang;Xinyu Zhang;Denys Butenko;Bolong Hong;Jinlong Zhu;Peichen Zhong

title: Nonadiabatic polaron dynamics from machine-learned hopping trajectories
abstract: The formation and motion of small polarons are ubiquitous in energy materials and influence photoinduced processes. Polaron transport is governed by thermally activated lattice dynamics and rare hopping events, requiring spatial and temporal scales only attainable with machine-learning molecular dynamics, which enables extensive sampling of atomic trajectories and polaron configurations over nanoseconds. Moreover, the Born-Oppenheimer approximation underlying standard ab initio molecular dynamics cannot describe the nonadiabatic coupling between electronic states mediated by nuclear motion, which controls energy exchange and excited-state relaxation. Here, we develop a simulation framework that combines machine-learning-assisted polaron dynamics with nonadiabatic molecular dynamics to bridge these complementary aspects of polaron physics, and determine how different polaron-hopping mechanisms affect excited-state dynamics. The enlarged trajectory space allows us to provide the first direct dynamical confirmation of the adiabatic or nonadiabatic classification of polaron hopping regimes originally proposed on the basis of static Marcus-theory arguments, and to connect individual hopping events directly to nonadiabatic electronic transitions. In bulk TiO$_2$, nonadiabatic hoppings occur preferentially when the energy of the polaron-induced gap state approaches the conduction-band manifold, promoting both electronic de-excitation and, via a Landau-Zener mechanism, excitation from the ground state. In MgO, the predominantly adiabatic character of hole-polaron hopping suppresses these effects, leading to longer charge-carrier lifetimes and an absence of thermally activated excitations. At the rutile TiO$_2$(110) surface, hopping events are rarer than in bulk because the excess electron is strongly stabilized in the subsurface region, leading to correspondingly longer de-excitation times.

title: Error-controlled switching between discrete and continuum dislocations in a unified defect framework
abstract: Simulating defects of every dimension together is expensive, and the savings of adaptive methods are rarely tested at equal accuracy. We present a variational framework in which fields, dislocation lines and defect densities share one free energy, one dissipation law and exact ledgers of mass and Burgers vector, so that a region can change its representation without gaining or losing defects. On this basis, an allocator switches the dislocations themselves between discrete particles, where they are sparse, and a continuous density, where they are dense. The switch is made block by block from local counts, conserves the Burgers vector exactly and is controlled by a single threshold. For $5\times10^5$ dislocations, the allocator reproduces the discrete model to within 1% in the sparse region at 14-37 times lower cost, depending on the machine; the advantage grows to 81 times at $10^6$ dislocations, and a threshold calibrated on one ensemble meets its error target on an independent one. For an idealized array of dislocation walls in copper, the allocator is 37.5 times cheaper than particle dislocation dynamics and, at almost the same cost, six times more accurate than continuum dislocation dynamics between the walls. In a three-dimensional copper model coupling grain-boundary cavitation with damage, ligaments left at nominal coalescence delay creep rupture by 25-48% (post hoc sweep). By contrast, grids refined at interfaces gain less than twofold once the active region exceeds about 30% of the domain, so representation switching, rather than grid refinement, is the effective form of adaptivity for defect-rich microstructures.

title: GPU-Accelerated Preprocessing for Large-Scale Linear Programming
abstract: GPU-accelerated first-order methods are increasingly effective for solving large-scale linear programs (LPs), yet LP preprocessing remains predominantly CPU-based and can become costly. A key challenge is that dependencies among presolve reductions and frequent modifications to sparse LP data make efficient GPU parallelization difficult. To address this challenge, we develop GPU-Preprocessor, a GPU-native LP preprocessing framework that integrates folding and presolve. To efficiently implement folding on GPUs, we adapt a randomized partition refinement algorithm to LP folding, using sparse matrix-vector products and parallel sorting to construct stable row and column partitions. For presolve, we introduce a new piecewise-linear reformulation rule that exploits underlying convex piecewise-linear structure to obtain sparser LP representations. We also develop a framework that combines phase scheduling with a Scan-Plan-Apply design to coordinate presolve rules and reduce sparse-matrix reconstruction overhead through batched updates. Numerical experiments on three LP benchmark sets show that GPU-Preprocessor achieves greater average problem-size reductions than PSLP and Gurobi Presolve, with SGM10 preprocessing-time speedups of up to $43.9\times$ and $677.7\times$, respectively. Here, SGM10 denotes the shifted geometric mean with a 10-second shift. On the largest tested quadratic assignment problem LP relaxation, these speedups reach $126.3\times$ and $2{,}207.9\times$. When integrated with the GPU-accelerated LP solver HPR-LP, GPU-Preprocessor achieves SGM10 speedups of $2.5\times$ to $5.0\times$ in combined preprocessing and solving time over HPR-LP without preprocessing. The code is available at https://github.com/PolyU-IOR/GPU-Preprocessor.

title: A heterogeneous set of unusual quasars selected from astrometry and broad-band photometry
abstract: The aim of this study is to explore methods for how to identify new quasars with different properties with regard to reddening, redshift, the presence of broad absorption lines from outflows, or other rare properties affecting the broad-band colours. We use Gaia-based astrometric pre-selection to study only sources that have zero parallax and zero proper motion within errors. We subsequently match these sources with information from wide-area photometric surveys and build colour-colour diagrams. Based on these diagrams we select targets for follow-up spectroscopy. In the subsequent analysis we also apply observations from SPHEREx to firmly establish redshifts. We secure spectroscopic observations for 24 sources. Of these, three are found to be stars and the remaining 21 are classified as quasars spanning a redshift range from z=0.139 to z=3.732. The majority of the sources located away from the normal quasar locus in colour-colour diagrams are found to be broad-absorption-line quasars. A single source, the lowest redshift source at z=0.139, is reminiscent of the so-called Little Red Dots found at high redshifts with JWST. Using the simple procedure followed here it is possible to locate previously undiscovered quasars with interesting properties, in particular Broad Absorption Line quasars and quasars with unusual extinction.

title: Strong gravitational lensing with Euclid
abstract: Euclid data is going to lead to the discovery of approximately 10^5 new strong gravitational lenses, thereby increasing the number of known lenses by a factor of 30. Such an impressive jump has the potential to revolutionise the field of strong lensing, by covering an ever-increasing range in the parameter space occupied by the lenses and lensed sources, and by uncovering rare and precious strong lens systems. The first quick data release of Euclid has already revealed hundreds of lenses, giving us a taste of what the final Euclid strong lens sample might look like. These lenses include a variety of objects acting as deflectors, from isolated galaxies to clusters, from early-type galaxies to edge-on disks. As many as four double-source plane lenses, in which one foreground object lenses two galaxies at two different redshifts, have already been discovered. As more data are acquired, it might become possible to detect the strong lensing signature of dwarf galaxy satellites, and to find lenses with an unusually large number of images. In this paper, we try to anticipate the kind of discoveries that these data will bring along.
