title: A Conservative Darcy-Brinkman-Stokes Formulation for PHREEQC-Coupled Reactive Transport with Cell-Based Surface Complexation
abstract: We present a mass-conservative Darcy-Brinkman-Stokes (DBS) formulation for reactive transport with cell-based surface complexation in image-based porous media, coupled to PHREEQC and implemented in GeoChemFoam, an OpenFOAM-based toolbox. Dissolved species are transported in the physical mobile-water fraction, adsorbed species are stored as conservative cell-scale surface inventories, and each reactive cell is coupled to PHREEQC. Reactive surface area is prescribed independently as a cell field, so that internal area left unresolved by segmentation of microporous phases can be represented while DBS flow and transport are retained in the resolved pore space. The implementation is verified with a test suite that isolates the coupling of transport and chemistry from the construction of reactive surface area. Aqueous and adsorbed mass balance is evaluated against a one-dimensional analytical retardation benchmark and closed-system batch calculations. The smooth-interface surface-area algorithms are tested on idealised two- and three-dimensional geometries. In a two-scale lithium micromodel, DBS reproduces fully resolved aqueous and sorbed inventories within 0.6% across Pe=0.1-10. The applications comprise Pb2+ retardation by hydrous ferric oxide coatings in a two-dimensional fracture network, competitive Mn2+/Mg2+ exchange in a three-dimensional Kelvin-cell sorbent, and Sr2+/Ca2+ exchange in Estaillades limestone. In the fracture-network and limestone cases, the formulation yields spatially resolved aqueous and adsorbed inventories even where reactive surface area is only partly resolved at the image scale. The framework therefore supports conservative surface-complexation modelling in both resolved and unresolved pore structures, with relevance to contaminant retention, selective ion capture, and radionuclide transport.

title: What Information Buys in Active Inference
abstract: Information-theoretic exploration is of primary interest in methodological studies of reinforcement learning (RL) and computational cognitive neuroscience, while the established RL theory builds regret guarantees on confidence sets. This situation leaves open the conditions under which the information-driven exploration found in nature is more advantageous than the exploration of the established RL theory. We put the state-of-the-art methods of these two paradigms, Active Inference (AIF) and Bayes-UCBVI, on an equal footing: both act through the same state abstraction of a tabular MDP with $S$ states, and their greedy forms differ only in the exploration term. We find that AIF's information gain decays too fast to serve as a confidence width, locking greedy agents that explore by it out of the optimal action. Calibrating the information gain by a square root yields calibrated AIF, which attains regret of order $\sqrt T$ for an exact abstraction, but no better guarantee than Bayes-UCBVI for a fixed reward. When an adversary chooses rewards from the agent's data, Bayes-UCBVI's value-specific widths lock out, whereas calibrated AIF pays a factor $\sqrt S$, which no goal-memoryless agent avoids on some MDP whose start states the adversary also chooses. Calibrated information gain thus acts as a reward-agnostic $\ell_1$ confidence set, preferable to value-specific widths when rewards are chosen from the agent's data, not when they are fixed.

title: Long Term Pediatric Vaccine Tender Scheduling with Quantity Discounts
abstract: Pediatric vaccine procurement for low- and lower-middle-income countries (LICs and LMICs) requires long-term coordination across heterogeneous vaccine markets, competing stakeholder objectives, and uncertain demand, yet tenders are currently scheduled as a series of independent renewals. We extend the Hypothetically Coordinated Vaccine Market (HCVM) framework to schedule multi-year tenders with flexible lengths and all-unit quantity discounts, and compare three objectives: a balanced coordinatingentity model (UG), a social-benefit model that minimizes missed doses (SB), and a producer profit-maximizing model (MP). Using UNICEF ten-year demand forecasts and 30 demand replications across six discount scenarios, we find that the procurement objective, not demand variability, drives cost-to-tender and schedule complexity. Quantity discounts favor large producers, concentrating the market and increasing supply chain vulnerability. Discount effectiveness depends on market maturity rather than valency: pentavalent and hexavalent vaccines are already near their price floor, and among monovalent vaccines only rotavirus responds to discounts, whereas HPV and PCV remain too expensive to compete. Removing pentavalent and hexavalent vaccines from the procurement pool sharply increases missed doses. These results give planners practical guidance on objective selection, discount design, and protecting access to combination vaccines.

title: Graph Coarsening Enables Escaping Local Optima in Compute-Constrained Nonconvex MAX-CUT
abstract: Because its binary optimization landscape contains exponentially many local optima, MAX-CUT is highly sensitive to initialization. We study Particle Polynomial Relaxation (PPR), a moment-based nonconvex continuous reformulation possessing an advantageous optimization landscape. We warm-start PPR with Combinatorial Multigrid (CMG), a spectral graph-coarsening method that produces structure-aware initial solutions in near-linear time without training data. On \texttt{t2g20} ($n=400$), benchmark instance with known exact optimum, the combined CMG+PPR pipeline reaches $97.5\%$ of optimum on average and $98.4\%$ on the best run. An extended variant with discrete local-search refinement reaches the published optimum on all sixty Biq Mac instances evaluated by a recent neural branch-and-bound method. Using a sparse CSR representation, the same approach scales to G-set instances with up to $20{,}000$ vertices reducing memory requirements by up to $3333\times$ while maintaining a consistent improvement over the CMG warm start. Gains are largest on sparse weighted graphs; on dense graphs we complement the pipeline with spectral sparsification.
authors: M. Harper Langston;Pierre-David Letourneau;Dalton Jones;Harris Teague;Peter Scott;Mingu Lee;Richard Lethin;Chris Lott;Roland Memisevic;Fatih Porikli

title: Loss Curvature as a Sampling-Free Proxy for Memorization in Diffusion Models
abstract: Understanding the mechanism behind why diffusion models memorize their training data remains an open question in generative modeling. In this paper, we examine this question from two perspectives: (a) the model-level perspective concerning the onset of memorization in a model during training, and (b) the sample-level perspective concerning the proclivity of an individual sample to be memorized by a given model. We show that the so-called input loss curvature, or the Frobenius norm of the Hessian of the diffusion model's training loss, is an effective metric for quantifying both perspectives on memorization. In particular, we empirically demonstrate that input curvatures averaged across training and validation samples can identify when a model is likely to start regurgitating its training data when tracked over training time. However, this metric is not sufficient for measuring an individual sample's likelihood of being memorized. To address this perspective, we introduce a counterfactual definition of memorization in diffusion models, extending the analogous notion from supervised learning proposed by [Feldman, 2019]. We prove that this counterfactual memorization is controlled by the input curvature of the leave-one-out model, thus establishing a direct theoretical link between a sample's local loss landscape and its generation likelihood. We validate our derived bounds through several empirical experiments and show that input-dependent curvature provides a proxy for memorization.
authors: Shashank Sule;Xinyue Yu;Boonam Shin;Yuxuan Liu;Abolfazl Hashemi;Hayden Schaeffer

title: Lag: A Mean-Field Optimal Policy for Online Assignment with Reusable Resources
abstract: We study online task assignment with reusable resources. This problem arises in peer reviewer assignment, skill-based call routing, rideshare matching, emergency dispatch, and crowdsourcing: Tasks arrive according to a geometric process and must be immediately assigned to servers that become temporarily busy, yielding rewards that depend on the task-server pair. The goal is to maximize long-run average reward. We cast the problem as a contextual restless multi-armed bandit (CRMAB). We derive an occupancy-measure LP (OCC-LP) that upper-bounds the reward of any work-conserving policy. From its dual we obtain Lag, a closed-form index policy. We introduce a scaling regime in which the number of copies of each server and the number of arrivals per step grow together. This regime yields the first deterministic fluid limit for a contextual bandit. In it, Lag is asymptotically optimal. Finally, we evaluate our algorithms on peer review datasets and call center routing. The Lagrangian index achieves 83-99% of the LP upper bound across all load levels. Moreover, the Lagrangian index policy significantly outperforms the natural greedy assignment scheme, improving reward by up to 12.3% on journal data and 36% on structured synthetic instances.

title: The connection between massive galaxies and their dark matter haloes from $z=0.25$ to $z \sim 4$ from the combined COSMOS, XMM-LSS and ECDF-S fields
abstract: Understanding how galaxies populate and grow within dark matter haloes is essential for linking the observed evolution of galaxies to the hierarchical growth of structure. We present a galaxy clustering analysis using optical and near-infrared data from the UltraVISTA and VIDEO surveys covering $9.3$ deg$^2$ across the COSMOS, XMM-LSS and ECDF-S fields, $\sim 5\times$ larger than previous comparable studies, providing sufficient volume to determine the halo occupation of the most massive galaxies to $z\sim 4$. We measure the angular two-point correlation function for stellar-mass-selected galaxies over $0.25<z<4$ and by combining the three fields, we reduce the cosmic variance by a factor of $\sim2$ compared to the individual fields. The stellar-to-halo mass ratio peaks at a halo mass of $M_{h}\approx10^{12} {\rm M}_{\odot}$ and is a maximum at $z\sim 1$. For the most massive galaxies, the peak halo mass ($M_{h}^{\rm peak}$) increases from $z=1\rightarrow 0$, while the peak stellar mass in such haloes remains approximately constant, indicating that at $z<1$ massive galaxy formation becomes less efficient. We also find a steady increase in the satellite fraction since $z\sim 1$, from which we infer that massive halos continue to grow hierarchically while their central galaxies experience suppressed stellar-mass growth. We suggest this is due to the central massive galaxies having their growth controlled by feedback from active galactic nuclei feedback, likely from low-power stochastic radio emission.

title: Optimization for One, Feasibility for Most: Decoupling Optimization from Feasibility in Chance-Constrained Programs
abstract: Chance-constrained stochastic programs (CCSPs) require solutions that satisfy uncertain constraints with high probability. Standard approaches either embed scenarios directly into optimization by considering sample average approximation (SAA)-based reformulations, growing prohibitively expensive and often failing to find feasible solutions; or employ conservative reformulations that guarantee feasibility but sacrifice objective quality by design. We propose ACCESS (Adaptive Chance-Constrained Exploration via Structured Sampling), a structured sampling framework that decouples optimization from feasibility evaluation. First, high-quality candidate solutions are generated by solving many inexpensive single-scenario subproblems, avoiding sampling directly in the constrained high-dimensional solution space. Second, feasibility is assessed separately via large-scale batched simulation over a massive number of scenarios, which is naturally amenable to GPU parallelism. That reduces the search from a high-dimensional solution space to a two-dimensional parameter space controlling conservatism and scenario diversity; while concentrating on candidates near the feasibility boundary, where high-quality feasible solutions lie. We also introduce a variant, ACCESS($δ$), which provides certified feasibility guarantees with probability $1-δ$. Experiments across three benchmark classes and five scenario distributions show that ACCESS matches or exceeds the best objective found by any method in nearly every setting, while ACCESS($δ$) is empirically feasible on every instance. The conservative reformulations remain several percent worse in objective, and SAA is frequently infeasible while taking an order of magnitude longer on the harder benchmarks.

title: A Performative Control Approach to Day-to-Day Traffic Signal Retiming
abstract: Conventional fixed-time traffic signal optimization and recent day-to-day signal retiming generally model route adaptation under prescribed route-choice behavior and origin-destination (OD) demand, while neglecting the fact that travelers' behavior can be performative to the signal control policy. A signal timing policy learned from historical traffic observations must therefore account for how its own deployment changes the distribution on which it will be evaluated in the future. We formulate this problem as performative signal control under observed traveler responses and characterize performative stability of the coupled policy-demand system. We propose incremental day-to-day retiming using the local policy gradient at the current operating point, estimated offline through simulation-based zeroth-order optimization without an explicit day-to-day demand-response model. This gradual approach provides a feasible path for policy and demand to co-evolve toward stability. Experiments on a downtown Denver network show that our approach improves congestion, throughput, and stability, generalizes across different demand levels, and remains effective when the offline simulator contains mismatched travel demand and routing behaviors.

title: Discrete Diffusion Models are Minimax Optimal Under Sparsity
abstract: Discrete diffusion models have emerged as a leading alternative to autoregressive models for generating text and other categorical data, yet their theoretical foundations remain less developed than those of their continuous counterparts. For continuous diffusion models, a prominent line of theory suggests that these models can adapt to low-dimensional structure in the data, thereby improving statistical efficiency and generalization. In this work, we investigate the discrete analogue of this phenomenon by studying the statistical rates of discrete diffusion models under sparsity assumptions. By analyzing a nonparametric estimator derived from a regularized score-entropy objective, we establish minimax-optimal rates in the sparse regime. The proposed regularization can be viewed as an adaptation of label smoothing techniques introduced for classification, and does not require the knowledge of the sparsity parameter. This shows that discrete diffusion models can adapt intrinsically to sparsity.

title: Topological superconductivity in layered d-wave altermagnetic metals
abstract: We investigate multilayer d-wave altermagnetic metals with odd-parity helical p-wave pairing. In the minimal bilayer system, interlayer tunneling reconstructs the spin-split Fermi surfaces and generates two layer-hybridized sectors with distinct effective chemical potentials. Without Rashba spin-orbit coupling (RSOC), the emergent mirror symmetry and subsystem chiral symmetry stabilize phases with different numbers of helical Majorana edge-mode pairs and additional counterpropagating pairs, jointly characterized by the mirror Chern number and the winding numbers defined along high-symmetry lines. The combination of RSOC and the altermagnetic exchange field gaps out the helical Majorana pairs while, in a certain parameter regime, leaving another pair of counterpropagating Majorana edge modes gapless, giving rise to second-order topological phases with isolated or twofold Majorana corner modes, as well as a hybrid-order phase in which gapless Majorana edge modes coexist with Majorana corner modes. We identify a layer symmetry that elucidates the physical origin of these phases. For an arbitrary N-layer system, such a symmetry naturally arises from the interlayer-coupling matrix, allowing N-fold Majorana corner modes to emerge when all layer-hybridized sectors enter the nontrivial second-order regime. Our results establish the interplay among the layer degree of freedom, odd-parity pairing, and Fermi-surface configurations as a controllable route to engineering topological superconductivity in layered altermagnetic systems.

title: Electron-Mediated Phonon Polaritons in Quantum Cavities
abstract: Phonon-photon coupling in quantum materials is commonly treated as an effective direct interaction, neglecting the crucial role played by electrons. Here we develop a gauge-invariant theory of cavity phonon polaritons that captures electronic screening, dissipation, and hybridization. We show that screening can suppress polariton formation in metals, severely constraining cavity control of phonon-mediated superconductivity. By contrast, interband electronic resonances in time-reversal-symmetric gapped systems can strongly enhance phonon-photon coupling, enabling robust polariton formation down to the monolayer limit despite electronic absorption. We illustrate these effects in NbSe2, hBN, and gapped graphene. Finally, we show that gauge invariance enforces photon decoupling from a critical soft phonon, establishing a general no-go mechanism for photon condensation.

title: The convective-transition gap in 47 Tucanae with JWST
abstract: We report the detection of the convective-transition gap along the lower main sequence (MS) of the Galactic globular cluster (GC) 47 Tucanae using deep James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations. We analyse the stellar luminosity function (LF) in the vicinity of the gap location using two independent colour-magnitude diagrams (CMDs). In both cases, the LF is characterised by a narrow gap followed by a discontinuous increase in the stellar number counts, and presents an overall morphology qualitatively consistent with that reported in previous studies. By modelling the observed LFs with an empirical likelihood model, we estimate the statistical significance of the observed feature. Additional JWST passbands exhibit similar signatures, providing further evidence for the presence of a discontinuity.

title: The mass functions of multiple stellar populations in 47 Tucanae
abstract: We used a combination of James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and Hubble Space Telescope (HST) observations to investigate the mass functions (MFs) of the different stellar populations in the globular cluster (GC) 47 Tucanae (NGC 104) over a wide stellar-mass interval. We identified the multiple populations along the lower main sequence using only JWST photometry and, in particular, colour combinations sensitive to variations in oxygen abundance. We derived the MFs of the first- and second-population (1P and 2P) stars separately and found that in the low-mass regime, the present-day MF of the 1P population is significantly steeper than that of the 2P population, which appears nearly flat. We also present the results of a dynamical model showing that this behaviour requires a different initial mass function (IMF) for the 2P and the 1P populations in the 0.1-0.4 solar masses mass range, thus providing a new fundamental constraint for the study of the star formation of multiple populations in GCs.

title: JWST observations of 47 Tucanae: I. The low-mass main sequence down to the hydrogen-burning limit
abstract: We present the first results of a series of studies based on JWST observations of the globular cluster 47 Tucanae (47 Tuc, or NGC 104) obtained with NIRCam. By combining new data with earlier JWST observations, we derive high-precision proper motions (PMs) over a multi-year baseline (of ~3 years) and construct a clean sample of cluster members extending to very faint magnitudes (F444W~24.25 mag, corresponding to ~0.077 solar masses, slightly above the estimated hydrogen-burning limit of 47 Tuc, ~0.074 solar masses) along the main sequence (MS). We investigated the presence of the low-mass MS kink previously identified in 47 Tuc using the new F090W and F444W photometry. No significant signature of the feature is found using these filters, consistent with its proposed physical interpretation as a consequence of the transition in carbon chemistry toward a methane-dominated equilibrium in very low-mass stars. A comparison with theoretical isochrones indicates that the stellar population near the bottom of the MS is likely dominated by oxygen-poor stars, in agreement with previous findings. Using artificial-star tests, we quantify the completeness of our sample and show that the requirement of PM-based membership significantly limits the detection of the faintest objects, indicating that current JWST observations of 47 Tuc are not sufficiently deep to reliably trace the cluster's brown dwarf cooling sequence. The mass function (MF) of 47 Tuc shows a structured behaviour, with a break at ~0.15 solar masses not associated with the onset of convection, and a mild but systematic radial variation consistent with mass segregation. Our analysis indicates that the MF shape in this mass regime is more complex than a simple power-law description. This feature in the MF may point to a presently unrecognised mechanism affecting the formation or dynamical evolution of low-mass stars in globular clusters.

title: Substructure-enhanced Collisional Relaxation in Stellar Systems
abstract: Two-body collisional relaxation in stellar systems is conventionally estimated using the classical Chandrasekhar theory, in which a subject star is assumed to be embedded in a homogeneous medium of field stars and their velocity distribution taken to be isotropic and Gaussian. Real stellar systems, however, can exhibit pronounced spatial and kinematic substructures. We investigate how such substructures -- particularly the non-classical spatial inhomogeneity -- modify the two-body diffusion coefficient. We retain hyperbolic two-body encounters but generalize the encounter calculation by integrating explicitly over the spatial distribution $n(\mathbf{r})$, while evaluating the velocity contribution from the full distribution $f_v(\mathbf{v})$. This yields a separable tensor expression for the diffusion coefficient. We find that spatial substructure produces the dominant enhancement. The enhancement of the diffusion coefficient increases systematically as the effective fractal dimension $D_{\rm frac}$ decreases, $\log ζ_r(D_\text{frac}) \sim \left(1-D_\text{frac}/3\right)^q$ with $q \approx 4.28$. For the observationally motivated case with $D_{\rm frac}\approx 1.5$, the enhancement is moderate, whereas substantially lower fractal dimensions produce much larger enhancements. In contrast, the anisotropic, power-law-tailed, and fractal-like velocity distributions modify the diffusion coefficient only by factors of order unity. Our representative substructured model yields enhancement ratios $ζ_r\simeq3.45$ and $ζ_v\simeq1.33$ when the measured particle-number trends are extrapolated to $N=10^{11}$, corresponding to an overall enhancement of $ζ\simeq4.6$. Therefore, within the two-body encounter framework and the commonly used separable distribution functions, the enhanced collisional relaxation still has little impact on the mean-field nature of typical galactic systems.

title: GroArnold: A Framework for Constructing Action-based Models for Triaxial Galaxies and Dark Matter Halos
abstract: Action-based distribution functions $f(\mathbf{J})$ provide a powerful description of stellar systems. Consequently, the construction of physically accurate and dynamically stable $f(\mathbf{J})$ for galactic components has emerged as a key challenge in the field. In this study, we present GroArnold, a computational framework designed to construct analytical $f(\mathbf{J})$ expressions for axisymmetric and triaxial galaxies and dark matter halos. The framework integrates modules for $N$-body initial condition generation, $N$-body simulation, angle--action variable estimation, and distribution-function fitting into a unified workflow. It supports a wide range of density profiles and kinematic properties, and is uniquely designed to generate stable $N$-body models for user-specified galactic systems, with the aim of obtaining an $f(\mathbf{J})$ that approximates a dynamically stable and physically consistent state. To this end, we extend the triaxial Stäckel Fudge method of the TACT code, implemented in our Nbody-TACT module, to enable action estimation directly from $N$-body gravitational potentials. GroArnold provides a robust and flexible tool for deriving numerically empirical, explicitly analytical distribution functions for user-specified galaxies or halos, thereby facilitating a wide range of practical $f(\mathbf{J})$-based modeling applications. In addition, it serves as a powerful tool for investigating the dynamics of realistic triaxial galaxies and halos beyond the scope of traditional spherical or axisymmetric models. We assessed the accuracy of the output $f(\mathbf{J})$ by comparing its predicted spatial and velocity distributions with those of the input $N$-body snapshot, and confirmed that it provides a reasonably accurate representation of the input. The code is modular, publicly available, and designed to support future extensions and adaptations.

title: A Nonlinear General Implicit Runge-Kutta Integrator for Multifluid Charged Dust and Gas
abstract: Charged dust in magnetized gas is subject to aerodynamic drag and the Lorentz force, both of which can be difficult to model numerically in a fluid simulation where their characteristic timescales are shorter than the timestep set by the Courant condition. We present a two-stage general implicit Runge-Kutta (GIRK) source integrator for multifluid charged dust coupled to an ideal magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) gas, implemented in the open source GPU-accelerated quokka code. Drag and Lorentz forces are advanced together in one implicit source update, avoiding errors in the terminal drift that can arise when the two forces are advanced in separate substeps. The timestep is compared with a drag-Lorentz timescale to select between resolved and stiff branches. The resolved branch uses Gauss-Legendre coefficients, while the stiff branch uses a coefficient set designed to recover the terminal drift set by the drag-Lorentz balance. We also allow the dust stopping time and charge-to-mass ratio to depend on the evolving state, evaluating them separately at the two implicit stage states and solving the resulting nonlinear stage equations by Picard iteration. The source update conserves total gas-dust momentum, and its computational cost scales linearly with the number of dust species. Tests reproduce the expected drag damping and terminal drift, confirm the predicted gyromotion amplitude and phase errors, demonstrate accurate treatment of state-dependent source coefficients, and recover the expected wave, shock, and instability dynamics in dusty MHD flows.

title: Wave Cold Dark Matter Can Reproduce the Radial Acceleration Relation in X-ray Elliptical Galaxies
abstract: Wave cold dark matter (wave CDM) is a well-motivated variant within the collisionless CDM paradigm, in which the de~Broglie wavelengths of ultralight bosons become relevant on galactic scales. While many of the previous tests of wave CDM have focused on small-scale tensions involving solitonic cores and certain soliton--halo relations in galaxies, the radial acceleration relation (RAR) provides a complementary test: for a given baryonic mass distribution, it probes whether the DM halo can reproduce the observed total gravitational field. In this work we test wave CDM against the RAR using eight X-ray elliptical galaxies from the compilation of Lelli et al. We perform a suite of 3D Schrödinger--Poisson simulations and evolve the wave-CDM halos to virialized quasi-stationary states. For each galaxy and each adopted boson mass, we select the realization whose final snapshot most closely matches the empirical RAR. We find that the selected wave-CDM realizations for these elliptical galaxies can reproduce the RAR without including baryonic feedback or dark-matter self-interactions. At the boson mass $m_a=10^{-23}$eV, the combined fit to the eight galaxies gives $a_0=1.19\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, consistent with the canonical value inferred from disk galaxies. When the boson mass is varied over $3\times 10^{-24}$ eV $\le m_a \le 2\times 10^{-23}$ eV, the best-fit value of $a_0$ changes by only $\sim 11\%$, and this variation shows no systematic trend with $m_a$. This insensitivity to boson mass arises because, over the radial range relevant for the RAR, the virialized halos are supported mainly by their velocity field, whereas the boson-mass-dependent quantum-pressure term is dynamically subdominant. These results show that wave CDM can reproduce the RAR in elliptical galaxies, and provide a new galactic-scale test of the model beyond the previous focus on solitonic cores.

title: The Dance of the Little Red Dots: Spectroscopy of Two Blue Companions at z = 3.9 and 5.5 Reveals Young, Metal-Poor Starbursts Merging with Their LRDs within a Few Hundred Myr
abstract: The Little Red Dots (LRDs) are compact, red sources, abundant at $4 \lesssim z \lesssim 9$ and likely powered by massive black holes. Photometric studies have found blue companions around them, but none has yet been confirmed spectroscopically. This Letter presents the only two LRD-companion pairs with spectroscopy of both members in the literature: "Waltz" at $z = 3.9$ and "Tango" at $z = 5.5$, with projected separations of $3.6$ and $2.5$ kpc. Both companions lie at the redshift of their LRD, within $132 \, \rm km \, s^{-1}$ and $57 \, \rm km \, s^{-1}$, and are physically identical, but $524$ Myr apart: starbursts $\lesssim 50$ Myr old, metal-poor ($0.2 \, \rm Z_\odot$), dust-free, dynamically cold, and as bright as the LRDs themselves in the rest-frame UV. The LRD in Waltz hosts a $\approx 3 \times 10^{6} \, \rm M_\odot$ black hole accreting at half the Eddington rate, a factor of a few above the birth mass of a direct collapse black hole, and is embedded in gas as metal-poor as its companion. Orbital modeling shows that Tango is bound in $81\%$ of the allowed orbits and that Waltz is bound if its host halo exceeds $5 \times 10^{10} \, \rm M_\odot$. Both blue companions then merge with their respective LRD within a few hundred Myr. We conclude that we are observing what heavy seeding requires: a young black hole beside the metal-poor starburst that the synchronized-pair scenario predicts, in the last steps of a cosmic dance that ends in a merger, and in a galaxy seeded by its black hole.

title: EMRIs in Kerr Spacetime: The Role of Inclination Diffusion
abstract: Extreme mass ratio inspirals (EMRIs) are expected to be a major source of gravitational waves (GWs) for the future {\it Laser Interferometer Space Antenna} ({\it LISA}). An EMRI occurs when a compact object, driven by the emission of gravitational radiation, slowly inspirals into a massive black hole (MBH). The classical formation channel involves repeated two-body interactions within dense nuclear star clusters. However, both EMRI event rates and the expected distribution of their orbital parameters remain highly uncertain. A major source of this uncertainty is the poorly constrained ratio between gradually inspiraling EMRIs and direct plunges, which do not produce detectable GWs. While most studies of astrophysical EMRI production focus on the Schwarzschild limit, previous work examining the Kerr metric found that the spin of the central MBH can significantly affect the EMRI-to-plunge ratio. This enhancement depends sensitively on orbital inclination, yet earlier studies held inclination fixed. In this work, we develop the mathematical framework describing inclination evolution driven by two-body encounters evolving along Kerr geodesics. By implementing 3D diffusion into Monte Carlo simulations, we show that initially prograde orbits may evolve into retrograde states, thereby converting potential EMRIs into plunges or vice versa. We estimate the EMRI-to-plunge ratio and find that substantial MBH spin enhances the EMRI rate by a factor of $\sim 2.5$. Additionally, even for a non-spinning MBH, modeling the orbits as relativistic geodesics rather than Newtonian trajectories increases the number of EMRIs by a similar factor of $\sim 2.5$. The distribution of Kerr EMRI inclinations has a substantial prograde bias that may aid in identifying the subset of loss cone EMRIs within large future EMRI samples.

title: How JWST is Revolutionizing Our View of Early Galaxy Formation
abstract: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has been revolutionizing our understanding of early galaxy formation over its first four years of science operations. With un- precedented sensitivity, spatial resolution, and wavelength coverage from the near- to mid-infrared, JWST has enabled astronomers to identify hundreds of star-forming galaxies at redshifts z>~8 (within ~650 million years of the Big Bang) through strong spectral breaks and characterize these galaxies through sensitive spectroscopy. These capabilities have provided new insights into the stellar populations, neutral gas, nebular continuum emission, chemical enrichment, dust content, and ionization conditions of galaxies during cosmic dawn, revealing more numerous and brighter systems than anticipated from pre-JWST models. We discuss the implications of these discoveries for reionization, the buildup of stellar mass and metals, and the evolution of galaxy populations and luminosity functions. JWST is also revealing a new physical picture of early galaxies, characterized by compact, clumpy star formation, high gas fractions, and intense radiation fields. Despite much progress, many open questions remain, including the efficiency, intermittency, and stellar initial mass function (IMF) of early star formation, conditions in the interstellar medium (ISM), masses, and structure of the earliest galaxies, and the topology of reionization. Resolving these open questions will require lensing magnification, sensitive spectroscopy to > 5 micron, including with the Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA), exploration to higher redshifts, and larger, more complete samples, helping to clarify how the first galaxies formed and evolved.

title: TNGC-SIDM I: Evolution of massive cluster mergers under the self-interacting dark matter paradigm
abstract: Merging galaxy clusters provide an ideal laboratory for testing the self-interacting nature of dark matter. In this paper, we present a pilot study of magnetohydrodynamical cosmological zoom-in simulations of two cluster mergers selected from TNG-Cluster, with $M_{\rm 200c} \sim 9\times10^{14}~M_\odot$ and $M_{\rm 200c}\sim 2\times10^{14}~M_\odot$. The simulations are performed with both standard collisionless cold dark matter (CDM) and self-interacting dark matter (SIDM), assuming an isotropic, velocity-independent cross-section of $σ_{\rm T}/m_χ= 1~\rm cm^2~g^{-1}$, with an additional $0.5~\rm cm^2~g^{-1}$ run for the low-mass system, and the mass resolution and galaxy formation model are unchanged from TNG-Cluster. We show how dark matter self-interactions produce an isothermal core in the dark matter halo, generate unique substructures in the intracluster light, and introduce variation in the multi-wavelength observables of the intracluster plasma. Using these simulations, we test the validity of observational probes for dark matter self-interactions in cluster mergers. We find that the shock-to-shock separation shows similar evolution in the self-interaction models tested here, providing a reference for distinguishing the $\sim100-200~\rm kpc$-scale difference in halo separation induced by self-interactions. Moreover, the dark matter halo centroid of the main cluster in the massive cluster merger is offset from the brightest cluster galaxy by as much as $\sim20~\rm kpc$, larger than the offset in the sub-cluster. This offset persists beyond 4 Gyr after the first pericenter passage. Our results indicate that sample selection plays a key role in testing the possible self-interacting nature of dark matter using cluster mergers, and that double radio relic cluster mergers and massive clusters with evidence of an ancient major merger offer a promising testbed for this purpose.

title: Joint Neural Posterior Estimation and Model Selection for Chemical Reaction Networks
abstract: Simulation-based Bayesian inference for Chemical Reaction Networks (CRNs) must simultaneously solve two computationally demanding problems: discriminating between overlapping reaction pathways and estimating reaction rate constants. Classical approaches, such as Sequential Monte Carlo ABC, rely on handcrafted summary statistics and scale poorly across large parameter spaces. To overcome this, we introduce a neural inference architecture. Our pipeline utilizes shared 1D-CNNs and a permutation-invariant Set Attention mechanism to learn low-dimensional summary statistics from variable-length, multi-experiment time-series data. These statistics simultaneously condition a model selection network to compute posterior model probabilities and model-specific conditional Invertible Neural Networks (cINNs) that estimate parameter posterior distributions. We demonstrate the practical utility of our approach on a real protodeboronation example, illustrating how it handles structural ambiguity and extracts kinetic parameters from competing catalyst deactivation pathways.

title: Optimizing Team Behavior via Extremum-seeking Control in Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning
abstract: In cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), agents must learn to coordinate their actions to achieve shared objectives. A key indicator of effective coordination is behavioral diversity, i.e., the agents' potential to enact distinct yet complementary control policies given the same set of observations. Although behavioral diversity can enable role specialization and richer joint behaviors, its appropriate level is highly context- and task-dependent and often costly to tune. We propose Adaptive Diversity Control (ADiCo), a two-timescale framework that adapts behavioral diversity online during training. On a fast timescale, Diversity Control (DiCo) regulates system diversity toward a target value. On a slower timescale, an Extremum Seeking Controller (ESC) adjusts this target using only mean episodic returns, without requiring an explicit model or analytical gradient of the diversity-performance landscape. We evaluate ADiCo on six configurations across two cooperative MARL tasks, where it maintains task-appropriate diversity levels: low diversity when homogeneous policies are beneficial and higher diversity when heterogeneous policies are required. Through this adaptation, ADiCo matches or exceeds the mean performance of DiCo (best grid-searched diversity target) and Unconstrained DiCo (diversity allowed to emerge without target regulation). These results demonstrate that incorporating classical feedback control into MARL training enables effective coordination by providing a systematic alternative to task-specific manual selection of the diversity target.

title: Designing for Prediction: Planning Formulas for Expected Out-of-Sample $R^2$ and $r$
abstract: Design calculations let researchers gauge, before data is collected, whether a planned study is likely to detect an effect. In this paper, we develop such calculations for predictive models using ordinary least squares and ridge regression under leave-one-out cross-validation. To do so, we derive closed-form expressions relating the expected out-of-sample $R^2$ and the expected correlation between observed and predicted outcomes to four design-stage quantities: sample size, number of predictors, an assumed population $R^2$ ($ρ^2_{in}$) and a design efficiency factor $D^*$ (which summarizes how leverage is distributed across observations). Unlike the classical shrinkage formulas, which depend only on sample size and dimension, these are sensitive to how covariates are arranged -- to imbalance and skew. A simulation study assesses the accuracy of the formulas against realized values under a variety of data generating mechanisms. We apply the methods to a published study predicting personality from smartphone behavior and show that the design formulas would have indicated, before any analyses were run, that least squares could not be expected to beat the sample mean while ridge could. An R package, predpower, implements the calculations.

title: Compositional Sensitivity Analysis for Multiobjective System Co-Design
abstract: Sensitivity analysis of coupled systems typically propagates derivatives of single-valued maps, whereas multiobjective optimization generally treats sensitivity at the system level rather than through interconnected subsystems. We develop a mathematical framework for compositional sensitivity analysis in multiobjective system design, building on monotone co-design. Subsystems are represented as design problems (DPs), interconnected through series, parallel, union, intersection, and feedback composition. We introduce tangential DPs (TDPs) to describe first-order variations around an operating point, show that they preserve the structure of DPs, and characterize their queries through graphical derivatives. To account for multiple internal realizations of a system-level operating point, tangential co-design problems compose families of local TDPs by taking a union over these realizations while retaining the original interconnection structure. We show that these compositions yield families of TDPs and establish conditions under which sensitivity analysis commutes with individual composition operations. Beyond infinitesimal sensitivity, we show that bounded tangential models of convex DPs provide tighter outer approximations of feasible finite changes, which can be propagated through co-design problems without union compositions. We conclude with several convex and nonconvex numerical examples that showcase the framework's accuracy and computational benefits.
authors: Alan Bonomi;Antonio Terpin;Yubo Cai;Yujun Huang;Meshal Alharbi;Gioele Zardini

title: A Rate Transfer Method: Convergence Rates in Stochastic Gradient Descent via Stochastic Calculus
abstract: We develop a rate-transfer method that converts finite-time Lyapunov estimates for an associated stochastic differential equation (SDE) into finite-time convergence bounds for stochastic gradient algorithms. Under generic moment and smoothness conditions, the convergence analysis of the stochastic gradient method reduces to a calculus argument verifying a Lyapunov generator inequality for the SDE. The method recovers established rates for classical stochastic gradient methods and provides a way to establish convergence rates for new optimization algorithms through calculus arguments applied to their associated SDEs.

title: From Fourier Amplitudes to Persistence Images for Impact-Echo Defect Detection
abstract: Impact-echo testing is a nondestructive testing method used to detect internal defects in concrete structures. However, boundary reflections, structured interference, and measurement noise can produce complex Fourier amplitude spectra, making defect classification difficult. We constructed a two-dimensional frequency--amplitude persistence image (FA-PI) from the Fourier amplitude spectrum. Using a fixed parameterization of exact multi-parameter persistent homology, each retained Fourier component is represented with frequency-bin location as one coordinate and amplitude as the other, and Gaussian kernels are then applied in this two-dimensional space. This construction has a direct analytical connection to the corresponding one-dimensional Gaussian-smoothed Fourier amplitude spectrum. FA-PI was evaluated on an experimental backfill-void dataset and a public bridge-deck impact-echo dataset, and compared with raw and Gaussian-smoothed Fourier amplitude spectra using a linear classifier with a Softmax output and identical signal-level data splits. The evaluation included original signals and signals corrupted by Gaussian noise, sinusoidal interference, or mixed noise, with matching noise types and signal-to-noise ratios during training, validation, and testing. Performance was assessed using accuracy and macro-averaged precision, recall, and F1-score. Across the two datasets, FA-PI consistently outperformed the raw and Gaussian-smoothed Fourier baselines in the noisy-condition summaries. These findings indicate that representing Fourier spectral components in a two-dimensional frequency--amplitude space can improve impact-echo defect classification beyond frequency-axis smoothing alone.

title: Superexchange coupling between a dilute Gd3+ probe and orphan spins in a valence-bond glass
abstract: The valence-bond-glass state of the 4d^1 double perovskite Ba2YMoO6 combines Mo^5+ singlets with residual paramagnetic "orphan" spins whose coupling is hard to reach with bulk probes. We probe them by electron paramagnetic resonance of a dilute Gd^3+ ion on the Y^3+ site via broadband coplanar-waveguide transmission at 5 K. The isostructural nonmagnetic niobate Ba2YNbO6, doped with the same Gd^3+ probe, is a fixed-lattice control. The Gd^3+ linewidth nearly doubles in the magnetic host. Dipolar coupling to the sparse orphans is nearly an order of magnitude too weak; the excess is instead reproduced by a transferred f-d superexchange of J ~ 0.2 K, so the width is a static measure of orphan-spin coupling. The half-field (Delta m_S = +/-2) satellite collapses in the magnetic host, a dynamical dephasing channel, while the unchanged g-factor marks a zero-mean random internal field. Together the two channels probe the coupling and dynamics of valence-bond-glass orphan spins.
authors: Patrick Colgan;Artur Solodovnyk;Jeremy P. Carlo;Scott Dietrich

title: Dynamic Attack Surfaces: A Queue of Branching Processes
abstract: Modern attack surfaces are inherently dynamic. Vulnerabilities emerge over time and they remain exposed to exploit until defenders discover and patch them. Artificial intelligence (AI) amplifies these dynamics by accelerating both offensive and defensive processes, making modern cybersecurity increasingly a competition among interacting time scales and resources. We capture this competition using a queue of branching processes that couples vulnerability discovery and resource-constrained patching with the evolving attacker population targeting each vulnerability. Our primary risk metric is the cumulative number of exploits a vulnerability experiences before it is patched. We derive the expected cumulative number of exploits under birth-death-immigration (BDI) and rise-decay (RD) models of attacker activity. Under a BDI model of attacker activity, we identify a phase transition: the expected cumulative number of exploits is finite only when attacker growth remains below both the vulnerability discovery rate and the effective patching rate. Across both attacker models, increasing the exploit rate does not necessarily increase the expected number of exploits because faster attacker departure can sufficiently limit the active attacker population. Finally, we show that equal proportional AI amplification of offensive and defensive capabilities need not preserve security: accelerating both sides can shift the defensive bottleneck and move the system into an unbounded-risk regime.
authors: Ismail Cosandal;Abdullah Y. Etcibasi;C. Emre Koksal;Sennur Ulukus

title: Rethinking electrified transportation: The case for dynamic wireless charging
abstract: Long-term infrastructure investment often requires choosing between an established technology and a capital-intensive alternative that gains value as demand matures. For electric vehicle (EV) charging, this trade-off is between incumbent stationary charging technology and emerging dynamic wireless charging (DWC). DWC could fundamentally alter transportation electrification by enabling high-throughput charging in motion and reducing reliance on large onboard batteries; however, its high upfront cost makes the timing and location of deployment critical. Overcommitting to stationary charging stations (SCS) risks technological lock-in and forgoing the benefits of DWC, whereas premature DWC deployment can strand capital in underutilized corridors. Through a joint investment assessment framework coupling DWC, SCS, and supporting grid infrastructure across nearly 49,000 miles of the US Interstate freight network, we find that higher utilization and longer project lifetimes rapidly shift investment toward DWC, whose share rises sharply from 48% at a project lifetime of 30 years to 100% at 32 years. Contiguous DWC segments can share grid connections, enabling them to provide over six times the rated charging capacity of SCS while requiring 46% less investment in new distribution-grid infrastructure. We also find that a combined DWC and SCS portfolio reaches a maximum lifetime value of USD 60 billion, 63% above the case with only SCS. We further identify specific traffic demand, construction, and grid access conditions that shape where each technology becomes advantageous, yielding actionable thresholds for SCS and DWC deployment that directly inform long-term EV charging infrastructure investment and policy.

title: Orientation Estimation of Cryo-EM Images for Molecules with Arbitrary Symmetry by Semidefinite Programming
abstract: This paper extends the non-unique games framework introduced in Bandeira et al. (2020) to address symmetric structures. Precisely, we consider the problem \[ \begin{aligned} \underset{g_1,\ldots,g_n\in \mathcal{G}}{\operatorname{min}}\,\, \frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{i,j=1}^n \sum_{s\in S} f_{ij}(g_i s g_j^{-1}), \end{aligned} \] where $\mathcal{G}$ is a compact group, $S\subset \mathcal{G}$ is a finite subgroup of symmetry elements, and $f_{ij}:\mathcal{G}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is a loss function. A notable example is common lines based orientation estimation of cryo-EM images for molecules with point group symmetry $S$, where $\mathcal{G}$ is the rotation group $\operatorname{SO}(3)$. With a semidefinite programming relaxation, we turn the problem into a convex program that is solved with the alternating direction method of multipliers. Unlike existing approaches which are tailored to specific symmetry groups, ours provides a unified computational framework for addressing all point group symmetries. We demonstrate the applicability of the proposed algorithm on the cryo-EM orientation estimation problem on both simulated and experimental datasets. In particular, our algorithm is effective in generating high-quality ab initio models from only a few class averages computed from experimental images.

title: Model-Based Online Decision Making via Generative Trajectory Planning
abstract: Online decision-making faces a tension between efficient inference and long-horizon reasoning. Value-based methods rely on short-horizon bootstrapping that limits the propagation of long-term information, while trajectory optimization methods plan explicitly but must solve a high-dimensional optimization problem at every decision step. We propose Generative Trajectory Planning (GTP), a model-based framework that addresses this tension by learning a generative model as a proposal distribution over action sequences. Instead of optimizing sequences from scratch, GTP samples candidate sequences from a diffusion prior and refines them using learned dynamics, reward, and value models, enabling efficient trajectory-level reasoning. Across continuous control and long-horizon manipulation tasks, GTP matches or exceeds state-of-the-art model-free, diffusion-policy, and model-based baselines, and remains stable in regimes where strong baselines degrade. Our results suggest that generative models are best understood not as policies, but as structured proposal distributions for planning, offering a new perspective on how to integrate generative modeling with model-based decision-making.

title: Optimal Decay Matrix Control Barrier Functions: Soundness and Completeness for Matrix Safety Constraints
abstract: Many safety requirements, such as keeping a manipulator away from kinematic singularities, a network connected, or a system observable, amount to keeping a state-dependent matrix positive definite. Matrix control barrier functions (MCBFs) enforce such requirements with a semidefinite program that minimally modifies a nominal control input. The MCBF constraint bounds how fast the safety margin, the smallest eigenvalue of the matrix, may decay. Yet a fixed decay rule is conservative, rejecting safe controls that drive the state quickly toward, but never across, the boundary of the safe set. Scalar optimal decay (SOD) addresses this issue by scaling the decay term by a scalar weight that is optimized together with the control. For scalar barrier functions, SOD then rejects a control at the boundary only if the control would decrease the margin. For MCBFs, however, SOD can reject controls that leave the margin unchanged, and near the safety boundary SOD accepts such controls only at a high cost. We introduce matrix optimal decay (MOD), which replaces the scalar weight with a matrix multiplier while keeping the semidefinite program convex. MOD is provably sound and complete, certifying at the boundary exactly the controls that do not decrease the margin. If some control can strictly increase the margin at every boundary point, the MOD-MCBF filtered controller is continuous and renders the safe set forward invariant. We also add an optional recovery condition that drives the system toward the safe set after a violation without affecting soundness or completeness. On a planar two-link arm avoiding singularities, MOD-MCBF certifies safe motions that both a fixed decay rule and SOD reject, and tracks an end-effector target more closely than SOD.
authors: Samuel G. Gessow;Albert Wu;Aaron D. Ames;Brett T. Lopez

title: Composition-controlled optical fingerprints and anisotropy of self-trapped excitons in double perovskites
abstract: Double perovskites (DPs) offer a compositionally versatile platform for photocatalysis and optoelectronics, but their soft lattices favor strong exciton-phonon coupling and self-trapped excitons (STEs), which produce broad, red-shifted photoluminescence (PL). Here, we combine optical spectroscopy and ab initio calculations to study lead-free, Sb-doped Cs2BInCl6 nanocrystals with B-site alloying from Na to K. Alloying tunes the PL energy from about 2.48 to 2.70 eV, while absorption features near 3.8 eV remain nearly unchanged. Calculations reveal that Sb doping enables bright radiative recombination channels and delocalizes the excitonic wavefunction. We identify STEs responsible for the large PL red shift, associated with an upward shift of dopant-hybridized in-gap states. Na-to-K substitution selectively changes the STE lattice distortion, explaining why PL varies strongly with composition while absorption does not. Theory further predicts pronounced PL polarization anisotropy that reflects the STE wavefunction's spatial structure and depends on B-site composition. Time-resolved anisotropy measurements closely agree with these predictions, providing experimental fingerprints of the excitonic wavefunction and its evolution with alloying. Together, these results disentangle the roles of doping and alloying in lead-free DPs and establish polarization-resolved spectroscopy as a probe of STE wavefunctions.
authors: Simone Grillo;Offir Zachs Maishlos;Liya Koren;Rotem Strassberg;Rachel Lifer;Edi Maizenberg;Umberto De Giovannini;Angel Rubio;Yehonadav Bekenstein;Ofer Neufeld

title: Virtual-Alloy Physics-Aware Semantic System for extrapolative prediction of perovskite solar cells
abstract: Existing machine-learning models for perovskite solar cells struggle to predict devices made from new materials. Most treat device layers as arbitrary categorical labels and represent perovskite absorbers either through featureless composition vectors or through rigid crystal graphs that require a pre-solved unit cell. As a result, they cannot generalize to unrecorded alloys or unfamiliar cell architectures. We present the Virtual-Alloy Physics-Aware Semantic System (V-PaSS), an architecture built around the physical continuity of perovskite solid solutions. V-PaSS represents arbitrary mixed-cation, mixed-halide absorbers by interpolating relaxed crystal graphs of 23 pure $ABX_3$ endpoint compounds via Vegard's law with learned bandgap bowing. For the device stack, it couples layer sequence and cell polarity (n-i-p or p-i-n) with interfacial band offsets and encodes chemical descriptions with a scientific language model. Evaluated under an institution-grouped protocol where test devices come exclusively from unseen laboratories, an untuned default configuration of V-PaSS achieves the lowest error among fourteen tested models (2.861% MAE, a 5.2% relative reduction over a gradient-boosted baseline at 3.017%, and outperforming the best tuned benchmark at 2.912%). V-PaSS pulls furthest ahead where test devices differ most from training: reducing error by 15.7-19.0% on unseen absorber alloys, by 16.1% on mixed absorbers from new laboratories, and widening its lead over the baseline by 3.6$\times$ on devices with unobserved transport layers. Combined with tree ensembles, V-PaSS sets a new state of the art across all five benchmark splits.
comment: 22 pages, 4 figures, 16 tables; Supporting Information included

title: The Connection Between the Growth of Massive Black Holes and Their Dynamical Histories
abstract: Massive black holes (MBHs) grow through both gas accretion and mergers and it remains unclear how variations to MBH growth and dynamical histories contribute to the spread in empirical scaling relations between MBHs and their host galaxies. We examine the ex- and in-situ growth of MBHs within large-scale cosmological simulations and compare the evolution of an outlier population of under-grown MBHs to the general population. We use the Romulus25 uniform volume cosmological simulation and the RomulusC cluster zoom-in simulation to examine the growth and merger histories of MBHs. We identify central MBHs that are undergrown relative to other MBHs in similar mass galaxies and investigate their accretion, merger, and orbital histories within the simulations. The contribution of ex-situ growth increases with MBH mass, with mergers becoming increasingly important in the most massive galaxies. We find no difference between cluster and field environments in terms of the importance of ex-situ growth, which is generally very low. Under-grown MBHs have experienced fewer mergers and have had complex dynamical histories, spending significant time 'drifting' within the galaxy or 'competing' with another MBH. Other under-grown MBHs have experienced a 'late entrance' into a galaxy which until then had no central MBH. Our results demonstrate that MBH assembly is dominated by in-situ growth, which in turn is impacted by the dynamical histories of MBHs within assembling galaxies. Prolonged off-centre evolution can suppress accretion and contribute to the formation of under-grown central MBHs at $z=0$.
authors: Lee A. Whitaker;Michael Tremmel;Angelo Ricarte;Priyamvada Natarajan

title: BridgeTwist: Twisting Schrödinger Bridges for Training-Free Conditional Sampling
abstract: Generative models are often required to serve many downstream conditional tasks. In the training-free setting, a pretrained unconditional model is reused as a prior and combined with a task-specific likelihood to sample from the corresponding posterior. While such training-free samplers have been developed for diffusion and flow models, their counterpart for Schrödinger bridge (SB) models remains unexplored, despite the growing appeal of SBs as flexible stochastic transport models between general source and target distributions. We propose BridgeTwist, a training-free conditional sampler for pretrained SB generative models, formulated as a tempered twisted sequential Monte Carlo scheme. Its twist is a closed-form plug-in surrogate, obtained by combining the velocity and score fields exposed by SB pretraining into an endpoint predictor and evaluating the likelihood there. Since this surrogate is less reliable near the source, we temper the twist with a time-varying exponent, downweighting its influence at early steps. We further introduce a bridge-shaped inference-time diffusion schedule that concentrates the proposal noise in the interior of the path. Telescoping importance weights then cancel all intermediate twist factors, yielding an asymptotically exact sampler for the posterior. Empirically, BridgeTwist outperforms training-free baselines on class-conditional and text-prompted image generation, and is competitive with specialized inverse problem solvers on inpainting, deblurring, and super-resolution.

title: Cosmic Evolution Survey: LOFAR 144 MHz imaging of the COSMOS field
abstract: We present the first deep, targeted LOFAR 144 MHz source catalogue of the COSMOS field, together with the first 144 MHz source counts in this field. The data comprise 48 h of observations. Over the 2.6 sq. deg. region adopted for the catalogue analysis, the final Dutch-array image reaches a median rms sensitivity of ~100 uJy/beam at an angular resolution of 15" x 6". The resulting catalogue contains 1984 radio sources; a peak S/N >= 5 selection is adopted for the resolved/unresolved classification and source-count analysis. We characterised the catalogue using Monte Carlo source-injection and recovery simulations, including dedicated simulations of extended sources, to quantify completeness, flux-density redistribution, and morphology-dependent source-recovery effects. The catalogue reaches 90% completeness at 1.48 mJy. The resulting Euclidean-normalised differential source counts are measured down to ~0.4 mJy and show good agreement with LoTSS DR3 144 MHz source counts and with the VLA-COSMOS 3 GHz counts scaled to 144 MHz, with ~5% of catalogue sources having multiple 3 GHz counterparts within a beam-matched search region. Comparison with the VLA-COSMOS 3 GHz catalogue shows good astrometric agreement, with median offsets of Delta_RA = 0.35" (+0.03"/-0.05") and Delta_Dec = -0.83" (+0.02"/-0.03"), approximately 6% of the corresponding synthesised-beam dimensions, and no significant radial dependence across the field. The resulting catalogue provides a low-frequency view of COSMOS and a reference dataset for future deeper LOFAR observations and multiwavelength studies of this extensively characterised extragalactic field.

title: Anchoring the Chromospheric Activity$-$Rotation Relation: A Study of the Pleiades and Group X
abstract: We present a study of the rotation and the chromospheric H$α$ activity of low-mass stars in the $\approx$120 Myr-old Pleiades and the $\approx$400 Myr-old Group X open clusters. We combine published and new rotation periods ($P_\mathrm{rot}$) from TESS and ZTF, and use LAMOST, SDSS, and MDM spectra to measure H$α$ equivalent widths (EWs). While overall the Group X distributions of $P_\mathrm{rot}$ and EWs are as expected, detailed comparisons to the Pleiades and to the 700-Myr-old benchmark Praesepe produce some surprises. For F through mid K stars, the Group X color$-$period sequence lies between those of the Pleiades and of Praesepe, as expected. But the $P_\mathrm{rot}$ for its late K and early M dwarfs and the Praesepe slow-rotator sequence overlap, indicating that the 700 Myr-old stars have not spun down significantly despite being nearly twice as old as their Group X counterparts. In the Rossby number$-L_\mathrm{Hα}/L_\mathrm{bol}$ plane, rapid rotators in Group X are saturated, as is seen in older clusters, whereas the rapid rotators in the Pleiades show a weak but measurable dependence of $L_\mathrm{Hα}/L_\mathrm{bol}$ on rotation. This implies that the chromospheric activity$-$rotation relation attains its mature form between 120 and 400 Myr. Dividing the sample by color reveals that K, M0, and M1 dwarfs are no longer saturated by $\approx$120 Myr, M2 and M3 dwarfs become unsaturated between $\approx$400 and $\approx$700 Myr, and later M dwarfs remain largely saturated through field ages even as their saturated $L_\mathrm{Hα}/L_\mathrm{bol}$ levels decline, indicating that chromospheric evolution is not determined by rotation period alone.
authors: A. Núñez;M. A. Agüeros;J. L. Curtis;C. A. Ospinal Achicanoy
comment: Accepted for publication in the AAS Journals

title: The ePESSTO+ census of ZTF nuclear transients. I. What flares in galactic nuclei?
abstract: Transients in galactic nuclei arise from distinct processes, only some of which trace the supermassive black hole (SMBH). These include tidal disruption events (TDEs), changing-look active galactic nuclei, Bowen fluorescence flares (BFFs) and ambiguous nuclear transients, alongside supernovae that appear nuclear but are unrelated to the SMBH. Reliable classification requires spectroscopy, which will not scale to the alert volumes of the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST). We aim to characterise the population of nuclear transients, to identify early observables capable of distinguishing SMBH-related flares, and TDEs in particular, from the dominant supernova background, and to assess the biases this selection introduces. We implemented a real-time filter on the Lasair broker, selecting transients from the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) alert stream by nuclear coincidence with the host galaxy, with no photometric cuts, to retain SMBH-related flares in both quiescent and active hosts. The filter ran over 16 months, with candidates reported for classification through ePESSTO+ and other facilities. The filter returned 476 candidates, of which 202 were spectroscopically classified, yielding predominantly supernovae, 10 confirmed TDEs (5%) and one BFF. The mean g-r colour and the rise time separate TDEs from the supernova background. Our filter recovers 10 of the 25 TDEs classified in the same period and declination range; most misses are technical or observational rather than physical. Simple real-time filtering combined with basic photometric criteria can already isolate TDEs efficiently from nuclear transient alert streams, and high completeness is achievable. In the LSST era, where samples will be predominantly photometric, selection bias will become as important as contamination, and retaining flares in active hosts is necessary if unusual events are not to be excluded.

title: Dynamic Programming for A Linear-Gaussian Dual Control Problem
abstract: We consider an infinite-horizon discounted dynamic programming (DP) problem for a countable-innovation belief-state model. The model is a surrogate for a linear-Gaussian dual control problem involving an unknown parameter vector and Gaussian observation noise. The surrogate preserves the first two moments of the Gaussian innovation and the resulting posterior second-moment structure. We allow unbounded belief and control spaces and nonnegative stage costs with quadratic growth in the posterior mean and covariance. Using a posterior-moment weight, we show that the Bellman operator is a contraction in a weighted sup-norm space. We characterize the optimal cost as the unique solution of the Bellman equation in this space, establish the existence of optimal stationary policies. We further prove weighted sup-norm convergence of value iteration, policy iteration, and optimistic policy iteration under vanishing approximation errors. The convergence results under vanishing approximation errors rely on general weighted sup-norm contraction properties and are applicable beyond the particular dual control problem considered here.

title: Minimax rates for pointwise CATE estimation: the role of design smoothness
abstract: We study the role of design smoothness in the minimax estimation of conditional average treatment effects at a fixed covariate point. For design densities bounded above and away from zero, without further regularity, we derive upper and lower risk bounds with an arbitrarily small gap in the convergence-rate exponent. Under uniform design, we obtain matching upper and lower bounds at interior points in the regime of low nuisance smoothness. These results show that rough covariate designs can lead to slower rates than uniform designs, even under the same smoothness assumptions on the treatment effect and nuisance functions, highlighting the role of the covariate distribution in pointwise causal estimation.

title: Two Routes to Interoceptive Prioritisation: Dissociating Likelihood Precision and Preference Reweighting in Active Inference
abstract: An embodied agent must prioritise among competing bodily needs. In active inference, it can respond to an urgent need by increasing the precision of information about that need or by increasing its preference for outcomes that relieve it. We compare these two interventions, separately and together, in a foraging gridworld with three lethal needs, and ask how each changes survival, perception and the body model the agent learns. Precision sharpens interoceptive posteriors and improves survival. Preference reweighting keeps bodily states further from their lethal boundaries and changes the states from which the agent learns, so its learned model covers fewer need levels, with lower quality across all levels but slightly higher quality on the levels it visits. An experiment on 72 further layouts does not establish the predicted preference benefit on difficult layouts, but both interventions improve average survival there and their interaction is positive. Survival alone therefore gives an incomplete account of how a model prioritises needs and learns about its body.
authors: St John Grimbly;Nicolas Kuske;Evert A. Boonstra;Charel van Hoof;Rowan Hodson;Benjamin Rosman;Ryan Smith;Mark Solms;Jonathan P. Shock
comment: Accepted at IWAI 2026, forthcoming in the Springer proceedings. 17 pages: the 13-page camera-ready paper, reproduced without alteration apart from one typographical fix, followed by 4 pages of supplementary material.
